Therefore, having removed the common line **f-g**, **a-g** will remain equal to **f-b**, because by the preceding <note>original: "p̄ pcedentē" refers to the previous step in the proof</note> again **a-c** is equal to **f-e**, and angle **b-f-e** is equal to angle **g-a-e** by the second part of Proposition 29—namely, the exterior angle is equal to the interior angle. Thus, by Proposition 4, triangle **a-c-g** will be equal to triangle **f-e-b**. Therefore, if the irregular quadrilateral figure **g-c-f-e** is added to both, the surface <note>The word "superficies" here refers to the area of the figure</note> **a-c-f-e** will be equal to the surface **g-c-b-e**, which is what was to be proved.

Now, let the line **c-g** cut the line **a-b** at point **f**, as appears in the second figure. By a similar argument as before, the two triangles **a-c-f** and **f-c-b** will be equal, wherefore by adding triangle **f-c-e** to both, the proposition is clear.

In a third way, let line **c-g** cut line **a-b** between the two points **f** and **b**, as appears in the third figure; and let it cut line **f-e** such as at point **k**. Because by a similar argument as before line **a-f** is equal to line **g-b**, and by making line **g-f** common, **a-g** will be equal to **f-b**, and triangle **a-g-e** equal to triangle **f-c-b**. Therefore, by adding triangle **c-k-e** to both and subtracting triangle **f-k-g** from both, the surface **a-c-f-e** will be equal to the surface **g-c-b-e**, which is what was to be proved.

## Proposition .36.

**It is necessary that all parallelograms established on equal bases and within the same parallel lines are equal.**
¶ A parallelogram <term>Parallellogramū: a four-sided figure where opposite sides are parallel</term> is defined as a surface of equidistant sides. Let there be two surfaces of equidistant sides, **a.b.c.d.** and **e.f.g.b.**, established between two equidistant lines, which are **a.f.** and **c.b.**, and upon equal bases, which are **c.d.** and **g.b.** I say that they are equal. For if I draw two lines **c.e.** and **d.f.**, the surface **c.d.e.f.** will be of equidistant sides by Proposition 33, because **e.f.** is equal and equidistant to **c.d.**, for each of them is equal to **g.b.** Since, therefore, by the premise, each of the two surfaces **a.b.c.d.** and **e.f.g.b.** is equal to the surface **c.d.e.f.**, they shall be equal to each other, which is what was to be proved.

## Proposition .37.

**All triangles that are established upon the same base and between two parallel lines are equal to one another.**
¶ Let there be two triangles, **a.b.c.** and **d.b.c.**, established upon the base **b.c.** between two lines **a.e.** and **b.f.** which are equidistant <note>parallel</note>. I say they are equal. For I shall draw **c.g.** parallel to **a.b.** and **c.h.** parallel to **d.b.** by Proposition 31. There will then be two surfaces **a.b.c.g.** and **d.b.c.h.**, which are equal by Proposition 35. And because the said triangles are half of them, by the corollary of Proposition 34, they will be equal to each other by the common science <note>original: "cōez sciam," referring to a Common Notion or Axiom in Euclid</note> which states that those things whose wholes are equal are also themselves equal in their halves; thus the proposition is clear.

## Proposition .38.

**If two triangles fall upon equal bases and between two parallel lines, it is necessary that they be equal.**
¶ Let there be two triangles, **a.b.c.** and **d.e.f.**, established upon equal bases **b.c.** and **e.f.** and between equidistant lines **a.g.** and **b.h.** I say they are equal. For I shall draw **c.k.** parallel to **a.b.** and **f.l.** parallel to **e.d.** There will then be two surfaces **a.b.c.k.** and **d.e.f.l.**, equal by Proposition 36. And since the said triangles are half of them by the corollary of Proposition 34, they will be equal by the aforementioned common science.

This is the converse of Proposition 37. From point **a**, I shall draw a line parallel to line **b-c**. If this line passes through point **d**, the proposition is evident. But if it passes above or below: let it first pass above, and let it be **a.e.**, and I shall extend **b.d.** until it cuts...

### ¶ Proposition 42

**To construct a parallelogram <note>literally "a surface of equidistant sides"</note> whose angle is equal to a given angle, and whose area is equal to a given triangle.**
¶ Let the given angle be **a** and the given triangle be **b-c-d**. I wish to describe a parallelogram equal to triangle **b-c-d**, in which each of the two angles positioned opposite each other is equal to angle **a**. I divide the base **c-d** in half at point **e**, and I draw line **b-e**. From point **b**, I draw **b-f** parallel to **c-d**. By Proposition 38, triangle **b-c-e** is equal to triangle **b-e-d**, and therefore triangle **b-e-d** is half of the total triangle **b-c-d**. Then, at point **e** on line **d-c**, I construct angle **d-e-g** equal to angle **a**, and I complete the parallelogram **g-e-d-f**. Because this figure is double the triangle **b-e-d** by the preceding proposition, it will also be equal to triangle **b-c-d** by this common notion <note>original: "cōam scienciam," referring to Euclid's Axioms</note>: those things whose halves are equal are also equal to each other. For triangle **b-e-d** is half of both; therefore, we have described the parallelogram **g-e-d-f** equal to triangle **b-c-d**, in which each of the two opposite angles **g-e-d** and **d-f-g** is equal to angle **a**, which was proposed.

### ¶ Proposition 43

**In every parallelogram, the complements <note>term: "supplementa," the areas remaining in a parallelogram when smaller parallelograms are constructed along the diagonal</note> of those parallelograms which are about the diagonal must be equal to one another.**
¶ Let there be a parallelogram **a-b-c-d** in which I draw the diagonal **b-c**. I draw **e-f** parallel to both sides **a-b** and **c-d**, intersecting the diagonal at point **k**. From there, I draw **k-g** parallel to both sides **a-c** and **b-d**, extending it until it intersects both sides **a-b** and **c-d**; let the whole line be **g-k-h**. The whole parallelogram **a-b-c-d** is thus divided into four parallelograms, two of which—namely **e-c-k-h** and **g-k-b-f**—are said to stand about the diagonal **c-b** because the diagonal passes through their centers. Therefore they are "about the diagonal." The remaining two—namely **a-e-g-k** and **k-h-f-d**—are called the complements. It is said that these two complements are equal. For the two triangles **a-b-c** and **c-d-b** are equal by the conclusion of Proposition 34. Similarly, the two triangles **g-k-b** and **f-k-b** are equal by the same conclusion. Likewise, the two triangles **c-e-k** and **k-h-c** are equal by that same conclusion. Therefore, if the two triangles **b-g-k** and **k-e-c** are subtracted from the whole triangle **a-b-c**, and the two remaining triangles **b-f-k** and **k-c-h** are subtracted from the other whole triangle **c-d-b**, the remainders will be equal by common notion. These remainders are the two aforementioned complements; which is what was proposed.

### ¶ Proposition 44

**Given a straight line, to construct upon it a parallelogram whose angle is equal to a given angle, and whose area is equal to a given triangle.**
¶ To construct a parallelogram upon a given line means to make that line one side of the figure. Let the given line be **a-b**, the given angle **c**, and the given triangle **d-e-f**. I wish to construct upon line **a-b** a parallelogram so that **a-b** is one of its sides, each of its opposite angles is equal to angle **c**, and the total area is equal to triangle **d-e-f**. This differs from Proposition 42 because here one side of the figure to be described is given (line **a-b**), whereas there no side was specified. Therefore, when I wish to do this, I join line **a-g**...

**I**f the product of one side of a triangle multiplied by itself <note>A literal translation of the Latin phrase for squaring a line.</note> is equal to the two squares which are described from the two remaining sides, then the angle which that side opposes is a right angle.

¶ A parallelogram is a surface of parallel sides.
¶ A rectangular parallelogram is one having all right angles. It is produced from one of its two containing sides, from one of its angles into the other; and therefore it is said to be contained under them. <note>In modern terms, the area of a rectangle is the product of its length and width.</note>

**O**f every parallelogrammic space, those parallelograms which the diameter cuts through the middle are said to stand around the same diameter. Of those parallelograms which stand around the same diameter, any one of them together with the two complements <note>original: "supplementis" — refers to the areas in a divided parallelogram that do not sit on the diagonal</note> is called a **gnomon**. <term>Gnomon</term><note>An L-shaped figure representing the area remaining when a smaller similar parallelogram is removed from a larger one.</note>
¶ Which parallelograms are said to stand around the diameter, and which are the complements, was explained above in the demonstration of <term>Proposition 43</term> of the first book. ¶ For let there be a parallelogram **a. b. c. d.** whose diameter is **a. d.** Let two lines **e. f.** and **g. h.** be drawn parallel to the opposite sides of the said parallelogram, intersecting each other upon the diameter **a. d.** at point **k**. The parallelogram itself will be divided into four parallelograms, and each of the two parallelograms which are **a. g. e. k.** and **k. f. h. d.**, which the diameter cuts through the middle, is said to stand around the diameter. The remaining two, which the diameter does not cut, are called complements. These two complements together with either of the said parallelograms standing around the diameter compose a certain figure which is called a **gnomon**. It lacks one remaining parallelogram standing around the diameter to complete the parallelogram; if that were added upon the diameter of the total composite, it would stand there, and it would be similar to the whole. Hence, although a parallelogram grows when a gnomon is added, it is not altered in shape; just as **Aristotle** said in the <term>Categories</term>. <note>original: "predicamentis" — Aristotle's work *The Categories*, where he uses the gnomon to illustrate things that change in quantity but not in quality/form.</note>

### Proposition .j.

<note>A geometric diagram for Proposition 1. A large rectangle AFGB is divided into three smaller vertical rectangles by lines DH and EK. The bottom vertices are labeled 'a', 'd', 'e', 'b' and the top vertices are 'f', 'h', 'k', 'g'. To the far left, a standalone vertical line 'c' is depicted, representing the constant multiplier.</note>

**I**f there be two lines, one of which is divided into any number of parts, the rectangle produced by the multiplication of one by the other will be equal to the rectangular parallelograms produced by the multiplication of the undivided line into each part of the divided line individually. <note>This is the geometric expression of the distributive law: a(b+c+d) = ab + ac + ad.</note>
¶ To lead a line into another line is to erect two lines perpendicularly from the ends of one, equal to the other, and to complete a rectangular surface of parallel sides which, by definition, is said to be contained under those two lines. ¶ There are two lines **a. b.** and **c.**, one of which, namely **a. b.**, is divided into any number of parts, which are **a. d.**, **d. e.**, and **e. b.** I say that the rectangle which is made from the multiplication of **c.** into the whole of **a. b.** is equal to those rectangular parallelograms joined together which are made from **c.** into **a. d.**, and from **c.** into **d. e.**, and from **c.** into **e. b.** ¶ Upon points **a.** and **b.**, I shall erect lines **a. f.** and **b. g.** perpendicular to the line **a. b.**, each of which shall be equal to line **c.**, and I will complete the rectangular surface **a. f. b. g.** by drawing line **f. g.**, which by definition is produced from **c.** into **a. b.** and is said to be contained under them. I shall also draw from points **d.** and **e.** the lines **d. h.** and **e. k.** parallel to the sides **a. f.** and **b. g.** Each of them will be equal to **c.** by <term>Proposition 34</term> of the first book, and each of them is equal to **a. f.** Therefore, by definition, the rectangle **a. d. f. h.** is produced from **c.** into **a. d.** and is said to be contained under them; and the rectangle **d. h. e. k.** from **c.** into **d. e.**; and the rectangle **e. k. b. g.** from **c.** into **e. b.** And since these rectangles joined together are equal to the total rectangle **a. f. b. g.**, it is clear that the proposition is true.

<summary>This page concludes Book I of Euclid's Elements and begins Book II, introducing the definitions of rectangular parallelograms and gnomons. It provides the proof for Proposition 1 of Book II, which geometrically demonstrates the distributive law of multiplication.</summary>

### ->Proposition 2<-

**I**f a line is divided into <term>parts</term><note>original: *partes* — the segments into which a line is cut</note>, the area <note>original: *illud quod* — literally "that which," referring to the resulting geometric figure</note> which is formed by the product of the whole line multiplied by itself is equal to the areas formed by the product of the same whole line multiplied by all its parts.
¶ Let line **a. b.** be divided at **a. c.**, **c. d.**, and **d. b.** I say that the area formed by the product of the whole line **a. b.** by itself—which is the square **a. c. b. f.**—is equal to the areas formed by the whole line multiplied by each of the said parts, as will be clearly shown by drawing lines **c. g.** and **d. h.** parallel to **a. c.** and **b. f.** <note>This is a geometric proof of the distributive law: if a line *x* is divided into segments *a, b, c*, then *x(a+b+c) = xa + xb + xc*. Since *x* is the whole line, this is expressed as *x² = xa + xb + xc*.</note>
¶ Alternatively, let line **k.** be taken equal to **a. b.** By the preceding proposition <note>Proposition 1 of Book II</note>, the area formed by the product of **k.** and the whole line **a. b.** is equal to the areas formed by the product of **k.** and all the parts of **a. b.** And because the product of **k.** and **a. b.** is the same as **a. b.** multiplied by itself, and the product of **k.** and all the parts of **a. b.** is the same as **a. b.** multiplied by all its own parts (because **k.** and **a. b.** are equal), it is clear that the proposition is true.

<note>A geometric diagram for Proposition 2. It shows a rectangle divided into three vertical rectangles labeled e, g, h, f across the top and a, c, d, b across the bottom. To the left is a separate vertical line segment labeled k.</note>

### ->Proposition 3<-

**I**f a line is divided into two parts, the area formed by the product of the whole line and either one of the parts is equal to the square of that same part and the area formed by the product of the two parts.
¶ Let line **a. b.** be divided at **a. c.** and **b. c.** I say that the area formed by the whole line **a. b.** multiplied by its part **a. c.** is equal to the square of the same part **a. c.** and the area formed by the product of the same part **a. c.** and the other part **b. c.** Let the square of line **a. c.** be formed as **a. c. d. f.** and let the surface **a. b. d. e.** be completed; the proposition will then be clear.
¶ Alternatively, let **g.** be taken equal to **a. c.** Because the product of **b. a.** and **a. c.** is the same as **a. c.** and **a. b.** inversely, and the product of **a. c.** and **b. c.** and itself is the same as **g.** multiplied by the same segments. But the product of **g.** and the whole **a. b.** is equal to the product of **g.** and **a. c.** and **c. b.** by the first proposition of this book. Thus the proposition is clear: namely, that the product of **a. c.** and **a. b.** is equal to the product of **a. c.** by itself and by **c. b.**, which is what we wished to demonstrate.

<note>A geometric diagram for Proposition 3. It shows a rectangle divided into two parts by a vertical line. The base is a horizontal line labeled a, c, b, and the top vertices/intersection points are labeled d, f, e.</note>

### ->Proposition 4<-

**I**f a line is divided into two parts, the area formed by the product of the whole line multiplied by itself <note>the square of the whole line</note> is equal to the squares of each of the two parts and twice the product of one part multiplied by the other. <insert>From this it is manifest that in every square, the two surfaces which the diameter <note>diagonal</note> cuts through the middle are both square.</insert>
¶ Let line **a. b.** be divided at **a. c.** and **b.** I say that the square of the whole **a. b.** is equal to the two squares of the two lines **a. c.** and **b. c.** and double the area formed by the product of one of them multiplied by the other. I shall describe the square of one of the parts: let **c. d. b. e.** be the square of line **c. b.**, to which I add a <term>gnomon</term> <note>An L-shaped geometric figure</note> following the direct path of the other line, namely **a. c.** I shall do it in this manner: in the described square I will draw the diagonal **b. d.**, and from point **a.** I will draw a perpendicular line to line **a. b.**, which shall be **a. k.** I will extend **a. k.** and the diagonal **b. d.** until they meet at point **f.** From point **f.** I will produce **f. b.** parallel to line **a. b.**, which is **f. h.**, and I will extend **b. e.** until it meets at point **g.**, and I will extend **c. d.** to **b.** and **e. d.** to **k.** And because the two sides **d. e.** and **b.** <note>referring to segment e.b.</note> of triangle **d. e. b.** are equal, then by the 5th proposition of the first book <note>The "Bridge of Asses," which states the base angles of an isosceles triangle are equal</note>, the two angles **e. d. b.** and **e. b. d.** are equal. And because angle **e.** is a right angle, then by the 32nd proposition of the first book <note>which states the sum of angles in a triangle is 180 degrees</note>, each of them is half of a right angle. For the same reason, each of the two angles **c. d. b.** and **c. b. d.** will be half of a right angle. Therefore, by the second part of the 29th proposition of the first book, each of the four angles **b. f. d.**, **b. d. f.**, **k. f. d.**, and **k. d. f.** is half of a right angle. Therefore, by the 6th proposition of the first book, **f. g.** and **g. b.** are equal. Likewise, **f. a.** and **a. b.**, and by the same reasoning **f. h.** and **h. b.**, and also **f. k.** and **k. d.** Wherefore each of the two surfaces **a. b. g. f.** and **k. d. h. f.** is square. And because the total square **a. b. f. g.** is the square of line **a. b.**, it consists of two squares which sit around the diagonal (which are the squares of the two lines **a. c.** and **c. b.**) and of two complements <note>original: *supplementis* — the rectangles in the corners not on the diagonal</note>, each of which is produced from **a. c.** multiplied by **b. c.** Thus our proposition is clear.
¶ Alternatively, let line **a. b.** be divided as before into **a. c.** and **c. b.**

<note>A complex geometric diagram for Proposition 4. It depicts a large square divided into four rectangular sections by internal perpendicular lines and a diagonal. Points are labeled f, h, g at the top edge; k, d, e on the horizontal midline; and a, c, b on the bottom edge. A diagonal line runs from the top-left vertex (f) to the bottom-right vertex (b).</note>

<header>BOOK II</header>

And by Proposition 2 of this book <note>original: *p.2.huius*</note>, it follows that the area formed by the whole line **a.b.** multiplied by itself is equal to the area formed by the same line multiplied by segments **a.c.** and **c.b.** But by the whole line multiplied by **a.c.**, there is produced exactly as much as from **a.c.** multiplied by itself and from **a.c.** multiplied by **b.c.**, according to Proposition 3 of this book. Likewise, from the whole line **a.b.** multiplied by **b.c.**, there is produced exactly as much as from **c.b.** multiplied by itself and from **c.b.** multiplied by **a.c.**, by the same proposition. Therefore, the area formed from the whole **a.b.** multiplied by itself is equal to the area formed by **a.c.** multiplied by itself and by **c.b.**, and by **c.b.** multiplied by itself and by **a.c.**, which is what was proposed. However, by this path the conclusion is not as clear as it is by the preceding path; wherefore the first method is more in harmony with the author's intent.

### ->Proposition 5<-

<note>A geometric diagram showing a large rectangle subdivided by vertical lines and a horizontal line. A diagonal line runs from the top left of the inner rectangle (e) to the bottom right (b). Points are labeled a, c, d, b on the bottom edge; k, l, h, m across the middle; and e, g, f across the top. This represents the "Gnomon" proof for Proposition 5.</note>

**I**f a straight line be cut into two equal and two unequal parts, the <term>rectangle</term><note>original: *rectangulum* — a four-sided figure with right angles</note> contained by the unequal segments of the whole, together with the square described on the segment between the two points of section, is equal to the square described on half of the whole line.
¶ Let line **a.b.** be divided equally at point **c.** and unequally at point **d.** I say that the square of **c.b.** is equal to the rectangle formed by **a.d.** multiplied by **d.b.** and the square of **c.d.** ¶ I shall describe the square of **c.b.**, which is **c.b.f.e.**, in which I shall draw the diameter **e.b.** and draw **d.g.** parallel to **b.f.**, which intersects the diameter **e.b.** at point **h.** And from point **h.** I shall draw a line parallel to line **a.b.**, which is **h.k.**, intersecting line **b.f.** at point **m.** and line **c.e.** at point **l.** And I shall draw **a.k.** parallel to **c.e.** By the corollary of the preceding [proposition], both of the two surfaces **l.g.** and **d.m.** will be squares. And by Proposition 43 of the First Book, the two <term>complements</term><note>original: *supplementa* — the areas remaining in a parallelogram when squares are drawn along the diameter</note> **c.h.** and **h.f.** are equal. Therefore, by adding the square **d.m.** to each, the parallelogram **c.m.** will be equal to the parallelogram **d.f.** And because **a.l.** is equal to **c.m.** by Proposition 36 of the First Book, the rectangle **a.b.** <note>The text here refers to the area created by the unequal segments</note> will be equal to the <term>gnomon</term><note>original: *gnomonem* — an L-shaped figure remaining after a smaller square is removed from a larger one</note> which surrounds the square **l.g.** Therefore, by adding the square **l.g.** to each, the rectangle **a.b.** with the square **l.g.** will be equal to the square **e.f.**, which is what was proposed.

### ->Proposition 6<-

<note>A geometric diagram showing a line a-b extended to point d. A large rectangle is constructed above it, divided into sections by vertical and horizontal lines, with a diagonal running from point e to point d. Points are labeled a, c, b, d along the bottom; k, l, h, m across the middle; and e, g, f along the top.</note>

**I**f a straight line be bisected, and another straight line be added to it in a straight line, the rectangle contained by the whole line made up of the original and the added part, multiplied by the added part, together with the square on the half, is equal to the square described on the line made up of the half and the added part.
¶ Let line **a.b.** be divided equally at point **c.**, and let line **b.d.** be added to it. I say that the square of **c.d.**, which is **c.d.e.f.**, is equal to the rectangle formed by the whole **a.d.** multiplied by **b.d.** and the square of **c.b.** I shall draw the diameter **d.e.** in the aforesaid square and draw line **b.g.** parallel to **d.f.**, which intersects the diameter **d.e.** at point **h.** From this point **h.** I shall draw a line parallel to line **a.b.**, which is **b.k.** <note>Likely h.k. in the diagram</note>, intersecting **d.f.** at point **m.** and **c.e.** at point **l.** And I shall draw **a.k.** parallel to **c.l.** By Proposition 36 of the First Book, **a.l.** will be equal to **c.b.** <note>referring to the area</note>. But **c.b.** will be equal to **h.f.** by Proposition 43 of the First Book. Wherefore **a.l.** is equal to **h.f.** Therefore, by adding **c.m.** to both sides, **a.m.** will be equal to the whole gnomon surrounding **l.g.** Wherefore, by adding **l.g.** to both sides, **a.m.** with **l.g.** will be equal to the whole square **c.f.** And because both of the two surfaces **l.g.** and **b.m.** are squares, the proposition is clear by the corollary of Proposition 4 of this book.

**I**f a line be divided into two parts, the square of the whole line multiplied by itself, together with the square of one of the parts, is equal to twice the rectangle contained by the whole line and that same part, together with the square of the other part.
¶ Let line **a.b.** be divided into two parts at point **c.** I say that the square of the whole **a.b.** with the square of **b.c.** is equal to twice the rectangle formed by **a.b.** and **b.c.**, together with the square of **a.c.** Let the square of the whole be described as **a.b.d.e.** and let the diameter **b.d.** be drawn and...

<note>Translation of technical vocabulary:
**Proposition** (*propositio*): A formal statement or theorem to be proved.
**Line** (*linea*): A geometric length.
**Square** (*quadratum*): A four-sided figure with equal sides and right angles.
**Rectangle** (*rectangulum*): A four-sided figure with right angles.
**Gnomon** (*gnomon*): The L-shaped area that remains when a smaller similar parallelogram is removed from a larger one.
**Diameter** (*diametrum*): A diagonal line through a figure.
**Parallel** (*equidistanter*): Lines that are always the same distance apart.
**Corollary** (*correlarium*): A direct consequence or additional truth following from a proved proposition.</note>

### ->Proposition 8<-

<note><image-desc>A geometric diagram illustrating Proposition 8. It consists of a large square labeled 'adef' partitioned into smaller rectangles and squares by horizontal and vertical lines. A diagonal line runs from point 'd' at the bottom right to point 'e' at the top left. Points are labeled: e, g, h, f along the top; r, k, q, p across an upper middle horizontal; o, n, l, m across a lower middle horizontal; and a, c, b, d along the bottom edge.</image-desc> This diagram represents a method of "completing the square" visually, showing how different rectangular areas fill a larger square.</note>

**I**f a line be divided into two parts: and a line equal in length to one of the parts be added to it: the square produced by the multiplication of the whole composed line by itself will be equal to four times the area produced by the first line multiplied by the added part, together with the square of the other segment.
¶ Let **a.b.** be divided at point **c.** in any way it may happen: to which is added **b.d.** equal to **c.b.** I say that the square of the whole **a.d.** (which is **a.d.e.f.**) is equal to four times the area formed from **a.b.** and **b.d.**, together with the square of **a.c.** This will be clear by drawing the diameter **d.e.** and the lines **c.g.** and **b.h.** parallel to line **d.f.**, cutting the diameter at points **k.** and **l.** Through these points let **p.q.k.r.** and **m.n.l.o.** be drawn parallel to **a.d.** For, by the corollary of the 4th proposition of this book, each of the areas **r.g.**, **n.q.**, and **b.m.** will be squares. And because **c.b.** was placed equal to **b.d.**, both of the areas **c.l.** and **l.p.** will be squares. And there will be 4 equal squares dividing the square **c.p.** And because the entire <term>gnomon</term><note>The L-shaped area remaining after a smaller square is removed from a larger one.</note> surrounding square **r.g.** is four times the area of **a.b.** multiplied by **b.d.** (since it is four times the area **a.l.**), the proposition is clear.

### ->Proposition 9<-

<note><image-desc>A geometric diagram illustrating Proposition 9. It features a triangle with a horizontal base 'ab'. A perpendicular height 'ec' rises from the midpoint 'c' to the apex 'e'. From a point 'd' on the base between 'c' and 'b', a vertical line 'df' rises to meet the hypotenuse 'eb' at point 'f'. A horizontal line 'gf' connects 'f' back to the vertical 'ec'. Labels: apex e; middle point g on height; point f on hypotenuse; base points a, c, d, b.</image-desc> This diagram uses a right-angled isosceles triangle to demonstrate the relationship between the squares of line segments.</note>

**I**f a line is divided into two equal and two unequal parts: the squares formed by the multiplication of the unequal segments by themselves, taken together, are double the squares formed from half the line and the segment between the points of division, taken together.
¶ Let line **a.b.** be divided into equal parts at **c.** and into unequal parts at **d.** I say that the square of **a.d.** and the square of **d.b.** joined together are double the square of **a.c.** and the square of **c.d.** joined together. ¶ Upon line **a.b.**, I erect line **c.e.** perpendicular and equal to each of those lines **a.c.** and **c.b.**, and I extend **e.a.** and **e.b.** By the 32nd proposition of the first book <note>The theorem stating the sum of angles in a triangle is two right angles.</note>, each of the angles **a.** and **b.**, and each of the partial angles at **e.**, will be half of a right angle; therefore the whole angle at **e.** is a right angle. And I extend **d.f.** parallel to **c.e.** and perpendicular to line **a.b.** Both angles at **d.** will be right angles, and angle **d.f.b.** will be half of a right angle by the 32nd proposition of the first book (or by the second part of the 29th proposition of the first book). Therefore, by the 6th proposition of the first book, **d.f.** and **d.b.** are equal. From point **f.** I lead **f.g.** parallel to **a.b.** By the second part of the 29th proposition of the first book, both angles at **g.** will be right angles, and angle **e.f.g.** will be half of a right angle; wherefore by the 6th proposition of the same book, sides **e.g.** and **g.f.** are equal. And because, by the penultimate proposition of the same book <note>original: *penult. eiusdem* — referring to Proposition I.47, the Pythagorean Theorem.</note>, the square of **e.f.** is equal to the square of **e.g.** and the square of **g.f.**, it will be double the square of **g.f.**, and therefore double the square of **c.d.** ¶ Likewise, because by the same [proposition], the square of **e.a.** is equal to the square of **a.c.** and the square of **c.e.**, it will be double the square of **a.c.** And because the square of **a.f.** is equal to the square of **e.f.** and **a.e.**, by the same it will be double the square of **a.c.** and the square of **c.d.** But the square of **a.f.** is again equal, by the same [proposition], to the square of **a.d.** and the square of **d.f.** Therefore, the square of **a.d.** and the square of **d.f.** are double the square of **a.c.** and the square of **c.d.** And because the square of **d.f.** is equal to the square of **d.b.**, they will be the squares of the two lines.

### ->Proposition 10<-

<note>A geometric diagram for Proposition 10 illustrates the theorem's logic. It shows a horizontal base line with points **a**, **c**, **b**, and **d**. A vertical line rises from the midpoint **c** to point **e**. Lines connect **a** to **e** and **e** to **b**. A horizontal line extends from the top point **e** to point **f**, positioned directly above the endpoint **d**. A diagonal line extends from **b** through **e** and another from **d** through **f**, meeting at a high point **g**. A final long diagonal connects **a** to **g**.</note>

**I**f a line be divided into two equal parts and another line be added to it in a straight line: the square which is described by the whole line with the added part, and the square which is described by the added part alone—both squares taken together—must be double the square described by the half of the original line and the square which is produced by the line composed of the half and the added part, both squares taken together.
¶ Let the line **a.b.** be divided into equal parts at **c.**, and let the line **b.d.** be added to it. I say that the two squares of the two lines **a.d.** and **b.d.**, taken together, are double the two squares of the two lines **a.c.** and **c.d.**, taken together. ¶ I erect **c.e.** <term>perpendicular</term> <note>at a right angle</note> to the line **a.b.** and equal to both lines **a.c.** and **c.b.**, and I complete the triangle **a.e.b.** by drawing lines **a.e.** and **e.b.** As in the previous proposition, each of the angles **a.** and **b.**, and each of those at **e.**, will be half of a right angle <note>original: *medietas recti*; i.e., 45 degrees</note> by the 32nd proposition of the first book; thus the whole angle at **e.** is a right angle. From point **e.**, I draw **e.f.** equal and parallel <note>original: *equidistantem*</note> to **c.d.**, and I extend **f.d.** and **e.b.** until they meet at point **g.**, and I draw the line **a.g.** By the last part of the 29th proposition of the first book, the angle **c.e.f.** is a right angle; but since the angle **c.e.b.** is half a right angle, the angle **b.e.f.** is likewise half a right angle. And because, by the 33rd proposition of the same book, **f.d.** is parallel to **c.e.**, the angle **f.** will be a right angle by the 34th proposition. Therefore, by the 32nd proposition, the angle **e.g.f.** will be half a right angle. Likewise, by the same proposition, the angle **d.b.g.** is half a right angle, because the angle **b.d.g.** is a right angle. Therefore, by the 6th proposition of the same book, the two sides **e.f.** and **f.g.** are equal. Also, the two sides **d.b.** and **d.g.** are equal. Therefore, by the <term>penultimate proposition</term> <note>referring to the Pythagorean Theorem, Proposition 47 of Book I</note> of the same book, the square of **e.g.** is double the square of **e.f.**, and thus double the square of **c.d.** ¶ Likewise, by the same proposition, the square of **a.e.** is double the square of **a.c.** And because the square of **a.g.** is, by the same proposition, equal to the squares of **a.e.** and **e.g.**, it is also equal to the squares of **a.d.** and **d.g.** But since the square of **d.g.** is equal to the square of **b.d.**, the two squares of the two lines **a.d.** and **b.d.** taken together will be double the two squares of the two lines **a.c.** and **c.d.** taken together, which is what was proposed. Furthermore, this and all the preceding propositions hold true for numbers just as they do for lines.

### Proposition 12.

<note>A geometric diagram for Proposition 12 shows an obtuse triangle with vertices **a**, **b**, and **c**. The angle at **a** is wide (obtuse). The base line **b-a** is extended outward to a point **d**, and a vertical perpendicular line drops from the top vertex **c** to meet this extension at **d**, forming a larger right-angled triangle **c-d-b** that contains the original triangle.</note>

**I**n those triangles which have an obtuse angle: the [square of] the side which <term>subtends</term> <note>lies opposite to</note> the obtuse angle is greater than the [squares of] both remaining sides containing the obtuse angle by twice the rectangle contained under one of them and that line which is joined to it in a straight line from the obtuse angle to the perpendicular falling outside.

¶ Let there be a triangle **a.b.c.** having an obtuse angle at **a.** From point **c.**, let a perpendicular line be drawn to the line **b.a.**, which must necessarily fall outside the triangle **a.b.c.**—otherwise the obtuse angle would be a right angle or less than a right angle, according to the 16th proposition of the first book. Let **c.d.** therefore be the perpendicular upon the line **a.b.** extended to **d.** I say that the square of the side **b.c.**, which is opposite the obtuse angle, is greater than the two squares of the two lines **a.b.** and **a.c.** (which surround that obtuse angle) by twice that which is formed from **b.a.** by **a.d.** For the "power" <note>original: "potentia" — in classical geometry, the 'power' of a line refers to the area of the square built upon it.</note> of a line is in respect to its square; hence any line is said to be as "powerful" as the product of it being multiplied by itself. For by the 4th [proposition] of this book, the square of **b.d.** will be equal to the two squares of the two lines **b.a.** and **a.d.** and double that which is formed from **b.a.** by **a.d.** And because the square of **b.c.** (by the next-to-last proposition of the first book <note>This refers to the Pythagorean Theorem, Prop. I.47.</note>) is equal to the square of **b.d.** and the square of **d.c.**, it will itself be equal to the squares of the three lines **b.a.**, **a.d.**, and **d.c.** and double that which is formed from **b.a.** by **a.d.** But by that same [proposition], the square of **a.c.** is equal to the squares of **a.d.** and **d.c.** Therefore, the square of **b.c.** is equal to the squares of the two lines **b.a.** and **a.c.** and double that which is formed from **b.a.** by **a.d.** Wherefore **b.c.** is more powerful than the two lines **b.a.** and **a.c.** by twice that which is formed from **b.a.** by **a.d.** For we have already said that any line is called as powerful as the product of itself multiplied by itself, which is what was proposed.

-> To describe a square equal to a given triangle. <-

<note>Geometric diagrams for Proposition 14. 
Top: A semicircle construction. A horizontal diameter is labeled with points **b** (left), **g** (center), **c** (between center and right), and **f** (right). **T**o describe a square equal to a given triangle.
¶ Let there be a given triangle **a**, to which we wish to describe an equal square. I shall designate a surface of parallel sides and right angles <note>A rectangle</note> equal to the given triangle, following what the 42nd [proposition] of the first [book] teaches; let that surface be **b.c.d.e.** If its sides are equal, we have what we seek, for it will be a square by definition. If, however, the sides are unequal, then I shall join the shorter of the sides to the longer in a straight line; let the line **e.f.** be equal to the shorter of the two sides, which is **c.e.**, joined to the longer, which is **b.c.**, in a straight line. I shall divide the whole **b.f.** into two equal parts at point **g.**, and with **g.** as the center above line **b.f.**, according to the quantity of line **g.b.**, I shall describe a semicircle **b.h.f.**, and I shall extend the side **e.c.** until it intersects the circumference at point **h.** I say that the square of line **e.h.** is equal to the given triangle. I shall draw the line **g.h.**, and since line **b.f.** is divided into equal parts at **g.** and into unequal parts at **c.**, it will be, by the 5th [proposition] of this [book], that the product of **b.c.** and **c.f.** with the square of **c.g.** is equal to the square of **g.f.**, and therefore to the square of **g.h.**; which, by the second to last [proposition] of the first [book], is equal to the two squares of the two lines **g.c.** and **c.h.** Therefore, having removed the square of **c.g.** from both, that which is formed from **b.c.** by **c.f.**—which is equal to the surface **b.c.e.d.** because **c.f.** is equal to **c.e.**—will be equal to the square of line **c.h.** Wherefore the square of line **c.h.** is equal to triangle **a.**, which is what was proposed.
¶ And note that by this is found the <term>tetragonal side</term> <note>The "tetragonal side" refers to the side of a square whose area is equal to a given non-square figure; in modern terms, the square root of the area.</note> of any <term>oblong</term> <note>original: "altera parte longioris" — literally "longer in one part," referring to a rectangle that is not a square.</note> and simply of every figure contained by straight lines, whatever it may be. For we resolve every such figure into triangles, and we shall find the tetragonal side of each of those triangles according to the teaching of this [proposition]. And we shall find, by the second to last of the first, one single line which is able to represent all the tetragonal sides found. For example, I wish now to find the tetragonal side of the irregular rectilinear figure **a.b.c.d.e.f.**; I resolve it into 3 triangles, which are...

Those circles whose diameters are equal are themselves equal. ¶ Those are larger whose diameters are larger, and smaller whose diameters are smaller. ¶ A line is said to touch a circle when, although it touches the circle, it does not cut the circle even when extended in either direction. ¶ Circles are said to touch one another which, while touching each other, do not cut one another. ¶ Straight lines in a circle are said to be equally distant from the center when the perpendiculars drawn from the center to them are equal. ¶ That line is said to be at a greater distance from the center upon which a longer perpendicular falls. ¶ A straight line containing a portion of a circle is called a chord <note>original: "corda"</note>. ¶ A portion of the circumference is called an arc <note>original: "arcus"</note>. ¶ An angle of a portion is that which is contained by a chord and an arc. ¶ An angle is said to stand upon an arc which is contained by two straight lines starting from any point on the arc and ending at the extremities of the chord. ¶ A sector of a circle <note>original: "sector circuli"</note> is a figure contained under two lines drawn from the center and the arc which is enclosed by them. ¶ The angle which is enclosed by those lines is said to stand at the center. ¶ Similar segments of circles are those in which the angles standing upon them are equal to one another. ¶ Arcs are also similar which subtend equal angles in the manner previously described.

### Proposition .1.

To find the center of a proposed circle. From which it is manifest that of two straight lines terminated at the circumference in the same circle, neither bisects the other perpendicularly unless that line passes through the center.

¶ Let the proposed circle be **a.b.c.**, of which we wish to find the center. I draw within the circle itself a line **a.c.** in any way it may happen, which I divide into two equal parts at point **d.** From this point, I draw a perpendicular to the line **a.c.**, which I extend to the circumference on both sides; let this be **e.d.b.** This line I again divide into two equal parts at point **f.**, which I say is the center of the circle. For if it is not, it will be either elsewhere on the line **e.b.** or outside it. It cannot be on the line **e.b.** [other than at **f.**]: for if it were on it, as at point **g.**, the line **e.f.** would be greater than line **e.g.**, namely the part [being equal] to the whole, which is impossible. But if it were outside the line **e.b.**, as at point **h.**, let lines **h.a.**, **h.d.**, and **h.c.** be drawn; and because the sides **h.d.** and **d.a.** of triangle **h.d.a.** are equal to sides **h.d.** and **d.c.** of triangle **h.d.c.**, and the base **h.a.** is equal to the base **h.c.** <note>Because they would both be radii from the assumed center **h**</note>, then by the 8th [proposition] of the first [book], angle **a.d.h.** will be equal to angle **c.d.h.**; therefore both are right angles. And because angle **a.d.b.** was also a right angle [by construction], then **a.d.h.** would be equal to **a.d.b.** by the 3rd petition <note>Postulate</note> of the first [book], namely the part [being equal] to the whole, which is impossible. Therefore, the center of the given circle is not anywhere other than at point **f.**, which was to be proposed.

## Proposition 2

If two points are marked on the circumference of a circle, the straight line drawn from one to the other must necessarily cut the circle <note>original: "circulum secare necesse est"; meaning the line must pass through the interior of the circle, not stay on the edge or go outside</note>.

¶ Let there be, as on the circumference of circle $a.b.$ whose center is $c$, two marked points $a$ and $b$. I say that the straight line joining one with the other will cut the circle. Otherwise, it would fall outside the circle. Let $a.e.b.$ be a straight line [outside the circle] if such a thing were possible. I shall draw the lines $c.a.$ and $c.b.$ By the fifth [proposition] of the first [book], the angles $c.a.b.$ and $c.b.a.$ will be equal. I shall also draw line $c.e.$, which cuts the circumference at point $d$. By the sixteenth [proposition] of the first [book], the angle $a.e.c.$ is greater than the angle $c.b.e.$, and therefore greater than angle $c.a.e.$ Consequently, by the eighteenth [proposition] of the same [book], the side $a.c.$ is greater than side $c.e.$ And because $c.d.$ is equal to $c.a.$ <note>as they are both radii</note>, $c.d.$ would be greater than $c.e.$—the part being greater than the whole, which is impossible. Therefore, because the line joining the two points $a$ and $b$ does not pass outside the circle, it must cut it, which is what was proposed.

## Proposition 3

If a line placed within a circle, but not passing through the center, is bisected by another line coming from the center, the latter stands upon it orthogonally <note>original: "orthogonaliter"; at a right angle</note>; and if it stands upon it orthogonally, it must necessarily divide it into equal parts.

¶ Let there be a line $a.b.$ placed within circle $a.b.$ whose center is $c$. Let line $c.d.$ coming from the center divide it into equal parts. I say that it divides it orthogonally; and conversely, if it divides it orthogonally, it divides it into equal parts. I shall draw lines $c.a.$ and $c.b.$ First, let us suppose that it divides it into equal parts. Therefore, the two sides $c.d.$ and $d.a.$ of triangle $c.d.a.$ are equal to the two sides $c.d.$ and $d.b.$ of triangle $c.d.b.$, and the base $c.a.$ is equal to the base $c.b.$ Therefore, by the eighth [proposition] of the first [book], the angle $d$ of one is equal to the angle $d$ of the other, so each is a right angle. Thus, $c.d.$ is perpendicular to $a.b.$, which is what was proposed.

¶ Next, let us suppose that $c.d.$ is perpendicular to $a.b.$ I shall show that it divides $a.b.$ into equal parts. Because of this position, each of the angles at $d$ will be a right angle, so one is equal to the other. And since, by the fifth [proposition] of the first [book], angle $c.a.d.$ is equal to angle $c.b.d.$, and side $c.a.$ is equal to side $c.b.$, then by the twenty-sixth [proposition] of the same first [book], line $a.d.$ will be equal to line $d.b.$, which is what was proposed.

## Proposition 4

If two lines within a circle intersect each other and do not pass through the center, they must necessarily not be bisected by each other <note>original: "non per equalia eas secari"; they cannot both cut each other exactly in half</note>.

¶ Let there be in circle $a.b.c.d.$ (whose center is $e$) two lines $a.c.$ and $b.d.$ intersecting at point $f$. Let both, or at least one of them, not pass through the center. I say that they do not divide each other into equal parts, such that each is bisected by the other. ¶ If this were possible, let us suppose it is so. First, if neither passes through the center, let a line $e.f.$ be drawn from center $e$. Then, by the first part of the previous [proposition], each of the four angles $a.f.e.$, $c.f.e.$, $b.f.e.$, and $d.f.e.$ would be a right angle, which is impossible, as a right angle would then be smaller than a right angle.

¶ Now let one of them pass through the center and the other not. Let $b.d.$ pass through the center. I still say they do not divide each other into equal parts. If they did, then by the first part of the previous [proposition], since $b.d.$ (drawn from the center) bisects $a.c.$, it must bisect it orthogonally. Therefore, $a.c.$ would also divide $b.d.$ orthogonally. And since $a.c.$ bisects $b.d.$ as the opponent suggests, it would have to pass through the center by the corollary of the first [proposition] of this [book]. Thus, both would pass through the center, which contradicts the hypothesis.

## Proposition 5

Intersecting circles have different centers.
<note>original: "Circulorum se inuicem secantium centra diuersa esse."</note>
¶ Let there be two circles, $a.c.b$ and $a.d.b$, intersecting each other at two points, $a$ and $b$. I say that they have different centers. ¶ For if they were to have the same center, that point would, by definition, be within the area common to both circles; let that point be $e$. If the lines $e.a$, $e.f$, and $e.c$ are drawn, then by definition the two lines $e.a$ and $e.f$ would be equal <note>as they are radii of the first circle</note>. ¶ Likewise, by definition, the two lines $e.a$ and $e.c$ would be equal <note>as they are radii of the second circle</note>. Therefore, $e.f$ would be equal to $e.c$, since both are equal to $e.a$. This would mean a part is equal to the whole, which is impossible.

## Proposition 6

It is necessary that circles which touch one another do not have the same center.
<note>original: "Circulorum se se contingentium nō idem centrum esse necesse est."</note>
¶ Let there be two circles, $a.b$ and $a.c$, touching each other at point $a$. I say that their centers are different. For if they had the same center, it would, by definition, lie within the smaller circle (when the smaller is placed inside the larger); let that point be $d$. If the lines $d.a$ and $d.b$ are drawn, then by definition each of the two lines $d.b$ and $d.a$ would be equal <note>original: "equalis a.d."</note> to the radius of the larger circle, which is impossible <note>because $b$ lies on the inner circumference and $a$ on the outer</note>. ¶ Regarding circles that touch externally—where one is outside the other—it is manifest by the definition of a center that they do not share the same center.

## Proposition 7

If a point is marked on the diameter of a circle other than at the center, and several lines are drawn from it to the circumference: the line that passes through the center will be the longest of all. The line that completes the diameter will be the shortest of all. Of the others, those closer to the center will be longer than those further away. ¶ It follows that the further a line is from the center, the shorter it must be. ¶ It is also necessary that two lines on either side of the shortest line, at equal distances from it, be equal to each other.
¶ Let there be a diameter $a.f$ of a circle $a.b.c$ whose center is $b$, and let point $k$ be marked on it other than the center. From $k$, let several lines be drawn to the circumference: $k.a, k.h$ <note>the OCR reads k.b, likely a transcription error for the line to point h</note>, $k.c, k.d, k.e, k.f,$ and $k.g$. Let $a.k$ pass through the center $b$, and let $k.f$ be the completion of the diameter. Let the lines $k.e$ and $k.g$ be at equal distances from $a.k.f$—that is to say, let the angle $e.k.f$ be equal to the angle $f.k.g$. I say that $k.a$ is the longest of all, and $k.f$ is the shortest. The others are longer the closer they are to the center: thus, $k.h$ is longer than $k.c$, and $k.c$ is longer than $k.d$, and $k.d$ is longer than $k.e$. Furthermore, $k.e$ and $k.g$ are equal. Now, in the triangle $b.k.h$, the two sides $b.h$ and $b.k$ are together greater than the side $k.h$ by the 20th [proposition] of the first [book] <note>which states that any two sides of a triangle must be longer than the third side</note>. Since those two sides together are equal to the line $a.k$ <note>because $b.h$ and $b.a$ are both radii</note>, $a.k$ must be greater than $k.h$. By the same reasoning, it is greater than all the others, and this is the first point. ¶ Likewise, because in the triangle $e.b.k$, the two sides $b.k$ and $k.e$ are greater than the side $b.e$ by the same rule, and $b.e$ is equal to line $b.f$ <note>as radii</note>, they will be greater than the line $b.f$. Therefore, if the common line $b.k$ is removed, the remaining $k.e$ will be greater than $k.f$. By the same reasoning, any of the others will be greater than $k.f$, and this is the second point. ¶ Again, because the two sides $b.h$ and $b.k$ of the triangle $b.h.k$ are equal to the two sides $c.b$ and $b.k$...

By the same reasoning, $k.c$ will be greater than $k.d$, and $k.d$ will be greater than $k.e$. And this is the third part of the proof.

Therefore, the two lines $k.g$ and $k.e$ must be equal, which is what we proposed to show. This is the fourth part.

### Proposition 8.

<note>A large geometric diagram for Proposition 8 is positioned on the left side of the page. It depicts a circle with its center labeled 'n'. A point 'a' is located outside the circle at the top. A straight line 'a-k-n-b' passes from point 'a', through point 'k' on the near circumference, through the center 'n', to point 'b' on the far circumference. Several other lines radiate from 'a' to various points on the circumference: to the left (points 'f' and 'g') and to the right (points 'c', 'd', and 'e'). Radii are drawn from the center 'n' to several of these points on the circumference. Additional labels 'h', 'l', 'o', and 'm' denote points used in the proof, specifically for demonstrating the properties of lines equidistant from the diameter.</note>

**I**f a point is marked outside a circle and many lines are drawn from it to the circumference, intersecting the circle: that which passes through the center will be the longest of all. ¶ Moreover, of the others, those closer to the center are longer than those farther away. ¶ As for the external line segments <note>original: "linee vero partiales... extrinsecus," referring to the parts of the lines outside the circle's boundary</note> reaching the circumference: that which lies in a straight line with the diameter is the shortest of all, and those closer to it are shorter than those farther away. ¶ Finally, the two lines that are equally close on either side to the shortest line are equal to one another.
¶ Let point $a$ be assigned outside circle $b.c.d$ whose center is $n$. Let many lines be drawn to the circumference, cutting the circle, which are $a.k.n.b$, $a.h.c$, $a.g.d$, and $a.f.e$. I say that line $a.b$, passing through the center, will be the longest of all. Also, that $a.c$ is greater than $a.d$, and $a.d$ is greater than $a.e$. Further, I say that $a.k$ is the shortest of all the external segments; and that $a.h$ is less than $a.g$, and $a.g$ is less than $a.f$. Finally, I say that if line $a.l$ is drawn such that it and $a.h$ are at an equal distance from the shortest line $a.k$—that is, the angle $k.a.h$ is equal to the angle $l.a.k$—then they will be equal to each other.
¶ I will draw from center $n$ the lines $n.c, n.d, n.e, n.f, n.g,$ and $n.b$ <note>these are the radii</note>. By Proposition 20 of the First Book, the two sides $a.n$ and $n.c$ of triangle $a.n.c$ are greater than $a.c$. And since these are equal to line $a.b$ <note>because $n.c$ and $n.b$ are both radii</note>, $a.b$ will be greater than $a.c$. By the same reasoning, it will be greater than all the other lines, which is the first part. And because sides $a.n$ and $n.c$ of triangle $a.n.c$ are equal to the two sides $a.n$ and $n.d$ of triangle $a.n.d$, and angle $a.n.c$ is greater than angle $a.n.d$, it will be by Proposition 24 of the First Book that base $a.c$ is greater than base $a.d$. By the same reasoning, $a.d$ will be greater than $a.e$, which is the second part. ¶ Again, because in triangle $a.n.b$, the two sides $a.b$ and $n.b$ are greater than $a.n$ by Proposition 20 of the First Book, and $b.n$ is equal to $n.k$, it will be by common notion <note>original: "communem scientiam," referring to the mathematical axioms used by Euclid</note> that $a.b$ is greater than $a.k$. By the same reasoning, any of the external segments will be greater than $a.k$, which is the third part. ¶ Also, because by Proposition 21 of the First Book, the two lines $a.b$ and $b.n$ <note>referring to the internal geometry</note> are less than the two lines $a.g$ and $g.n$, and $b.n$ is equal to $g.n$, it follows by common notion that $a.g$ is greater than $a.b$ <note>Note: There appears to be a slight label discrepancy in the 1482 text's letters here, but the logical proof follows Euclid's intended structure</note>. By the same reasoning, $a.f$ will be greater than $a.g$, which is the fourth part. ¶ If $a.l$ were not equal to $a.h$, though they are at equal distances from $a.k$, one would be larger; let it be $a.l$. I will then set $a.m$ equal to $a.h$ and extend the line $n.o.m$. Since the two sides $m.a$ and $a.n$ of triangle $m.a.n$ are equal to the two sides $h.a$ and $a.n$ of triangle $h.a.n$, and angle $m.a.n$ is equal to angle $h.a.n$, it will be by Proposition 4 of the First Book that base $m.n$ is equal to base $n.b$ <note>a radius</note>. And since $m.o$ <note>the total line from the center to $m$</note> is equal to $n.b$, then $n.o$ would be equal to $n.m$—meaning the part would be equal to the whole, which is impossible. And this is the fifth part.

### Proposition 9.

**I**f more than two lines drawn from a point marked within a circle to the circumference are equal to one another, it is necessary that the point is the center of the circle.
¶ Let there be a point *a* marked within circle *b.c.d*, from which three lines—*a.b*, *a.c*, and *a.d*—are drawn to the circumference. I posit these lines to be equal. I say that point *a* is the center of the circle. For I shall draw two lines, *c.b* and *d.c* <note>these are chords, or straight lines connecting two points on a curve</note>, and divide each of them into two equal parts: *c.b* at point *e* and *d.c* at point *f*. I then draw lines *e.a* and *f.a* and extend them to the circumference on both sides. By Proposition 8 of the First Book, each of the angles at *e* will be equal to the other. Therefore, by Proposition 13 <note>which deals with lines meeting at a point on a straight line</note>, each will be a right angle. Similarly, by the same reasoning, each of the angles at *f* is a right angle. Therefore, by the corollary of the first proposition of this book <note>Book III</note>, because line *a.e* divides *c.b* into equal parts and at right angles <term>orthogonally|at a 90-degree angle</term>, it must pass through the center. Likewise, *a.f* must pass through the center because it divides *d.c* into equal parts and at right angles. Since both lines pass through the center and intersect at point *a*, it follows that *a* is the center, which is what was proposed.

<note>A circular diagram illustrating Proposition 9. Inside a circle, a point 'a' is shown with three lines radiating to the circumference at points 'b', 'c', and 'd'. Two chords, 'bc' and 'cd', are drawn and bisected at points 'e' and 'f' respectively. Lines from the center 'a' pass through these bisection points to the circumference.</note>

### Proposition 10.

**I**f one circle intersects another circle, it is necessary that it intersects in only two places.
¶ If it were possible, let two circles intersect in more than two places, such as at three points: *a*, *b*, and *c*. I shall draw lines *a.b* and *a.c* and divide them into equal parts at points *d* and *e*. From point *e*, I draw line *e.f* perpendicular to line *a.c*, and from point *d*, I draw line *d.f* perpendicular to line *a.b*. These two lines, *e.f* and *d.f*, will intersect at point *f*. By the corollary of the first proposition of this book, point *f* would be the center of both circles. However, this is impossible according to Proposition 5 of this book <note>Proposition 3.5 states that circles which cut one another cannot have the same center</note>.

<note>A diagram for Proposition 10 showing two intersecting circles. The overlapping area is shaped like a lens. Chords 'ab' and 'ac' are drawn within the circles, and their perpendicular bisectors are shown intersecting at point 'f', which would imply a shared center.</note>

### Proposition 11.

**I**f one circle touches <term>contingat|touches or is tangent to</term> another circle, and a line passes through their centers, it is necessary that the line meets at the point of contact.
¶ For if the line passing through the centers of two circles—*m.c.e* and *d.e*—touching each other internally or externally does not go to the point of contact, let it cut the circumference of both. Let *a* be the center of circle *e.d* and *b* be the center of circle *e.c*, and let a straight line *a.b.c.d* be drawn cutting the circumference of both. Let lines be drawn from point *e* (the point of contact) to the centers, which are *e.a* and *e.b*. In the case of internal contact, by Proposition 20 of the First Book <note>the triangle inequality, which states any two sides of a triangle are together greater than the third</note>, the two lines *e.b* and *b.a* together are longer than *e.a*. Therefore, they are longer than *a.d*, for *a.e* and *a.d* are equal radii of the same circle. And since *b.c* is equal to *e.b* <note>as both are radii of the smaller circle</note>, it would mean that the segment *c.a* is longer than the whole line *a.d*, which is impossible. ¶ In the case of external contact, the two lines *a.e* and *e.b* will be longer than the line *a.b*. This would mean that the radii *a.d* and *c.b* together would be greater than the entire line *a.b*, which is false.

<note>A diagram for Proposition 11 depicting two circles where one is inside the other, touching at point 'e'. Centers 'a' and 'b' are marked on a line passing through the point of tangency.</note>

### Proposition 12.

**I**f one circle touches another circle, whether internally or externally, it is necessary that they touch in only one place.
¶ For if it were possible for a circle to touch another circle in two places, let circle *a.b.e* touch circle *a.b.c.d* internally at two points *a* and *b*, or externally at two points *c* and *d*. If we draw a straight line from *a* to *b*, and it falls outside the inner circle *a.b.e*, this would contradict the second proposition of this book <note>which states that a line connecting two points on a circle falls within that circle</note>. If the line falls inside, and we divide it into equal parts and draw a perpendicular from that point to the circumference on both sides, it would pass through the center of both circles. This would lead to a contradiction of the previous proposition. ¶ In the case of a circle touching externally at points *c* and *d*, if we draw a straight line from point *c* to point *d*, it must necessarily result in a contradiction of the same second proposition. Therefore, both cases are impossible.

<note>A series of diagrams for Proposition 12. The top one shows two circles touching internally at two points 'a' and 'b' (intended to be proven impossible). Below it, another diagram shows two circles touching internally with centers and chords. The bottom diagrams show circles touching externally at one or two points (c, d) to illustrate the impossibility of multiple contact points.</note>

BOOK III

### Proposition 13.

<note>A circular diagram for Proposition 13. Within the circle, two vertical chords are drawn. The left chord has endpoints 'a' at the top and 'b' at the bottom, with its midpoint marked 'f'. The right chord has endpoints 'd' at the top and 'c' at the bottom, with its midpoint marked 'g'. The center of the circle is point 'e'. Lines connect 'e' to the midpoints 'f' and 'g', and to the four endpoints 'a', 'b', 'c', and 'd', forming four internal triangles.</note>

**E**qual straight lines in a circle are at an equal distance from the center; and if they are at an equal distance from the center, it is necessary that they are equal to one another.
¶ Let there be a circle *a.b.c.d*, the center of which is *e*. Let two lines, *a.b* and *c.d*, be equal. I say that they are at an equal distance from the center, and vice versa. For let lines *e.f* and *e.g* be drawn from the center *e* perpendicular to *a.d* and *b.c* <note>The text labels here vary slightly from the diagram; these refer to the chords being measured</note>. By the second part of the third proposition of this book, *a.d* will be divided into equal parts at *f*, and *b.c* at *g*. Therefore, since two sides *e.d* and *d.a* of triangle *e.d.a* are equal to the two sides *e.c* and *c.b* of triangle *e.c.b*, and the base *e.a* is equal to the base *e.b*, then by Proposition 8 of the First Book, angle *d* is equal to angle *c*. And because two sides *e.d* and *d.f* of triangle *e.d.f* are equal to the two sides *e.c* and *c.g* of triangle *e.c.g*—for *d.f* is equal to *c.g* because the whole line *a.d* was posited as equal to *b.c*—and angle *d* is equal to angle *c*, then by Proposition 4 of the First Book, the base <note>here meaning the distance from the center</note> *e.f* is equal to the base *e.g*. And because these are the perpendiculars coming to the lines from the center, it is clear by the definition (specifically the 4th definition of this book) that they are at an equal distance from the center.
¶ **Alternatively, the same may be proved thus:** The square of *e.d*, by the second-to-last proposition of the first book <note>The Pythagorean Theorem, Proposition I.47</note>, is equal to the squares of the two lines *e.f* and *f.d*. Likewise, the square of *e.c* is equal to the squares of the two lines *e.g* and *c.g*. And because the square of *d.e* is equal to the square of *e.c*, and the square of *d.f* is equal to the square of *g.c*, the square of *e.f* will be equal to the square of *e.g*. Therefore, line *e.f* is equal to line *e.g*, and so the same result is clear.
Now, let *e.f* be equal to *e.g*, which is to say they are at an equal distance from the center. I say then that line *a.d* is equal to *b.c*. Since the squares of the two lines *e.d* and *e.c* are equal, if the equal squares of the two lines *e.f* and *e.g* are subtracted, there remain (by the same second-to-last proposition of the first book) the squares of the two lines *f.d* and *g.c*. By common knowledge <note>original: "commune̅ scientiam," referring to Euclid's Common Notions</note>, these must be equal. Therefore, line *f.d* is equal to *g.c*. Thus, the double of *f.d* (which is *a.d*) is equal to the double of *g.c* (which is *b.c*). And this is the second part of what was proposed.

### Proposition 14.

<note>A circular diagram for Proposition 14. A circle contains a horizontal diameter 'ad' with point 'a' on the left and 'd' on the right, passing through center 'e'. Above the diameter are two horizontal chords: the topmost 'hk' and another 'fs' below it. Below the diameter, two chords 'ab' and 'ac' extend from point 'a' to the lower circumference. Radial lines connect the center 'e' to points 'h', 'f', 'k', 's', 'c', and 'b'.</note>

**I**f several straight lines are placed within a circle, the diameter is the longest of them all; and those closer to the diameter <note>meaning closer to the center</note> are necessarily longer than those further away.
¶ Let there be a circle *a.b.c* with center *e*. Let several lines fall within it, which are *a.b*, *a.c*, *a.d*, *f.g*, and *b.k*. Let *a.e.d* be the diameter. I say that the diameter is the longest, and the others are larger the closer they are to it. For let lines be drawn from the center *e* to the endpoints of all the lines, which are *e.b*, *e.c*, *e.f*, *e.g*, and *e.k*. By Proposition 20 of the First Book <note>The triangle inequality: any two sides of a triangle are greater than the third</note>, the two sides *e.f* and *e.g* of triangle *e.f.g* are longer than *f.g*. And because these radii are together equal to the diameter *a.d*, then *a.d* is greater than *f.g*. By the same reasoning, the diameter is greater than *a.c*, because *a.e* and *e.c* are greater than *a.c* and equal to *a.d*. Therefore, *a.d* is greater than *a.c*. So also it is greater than *b.k* and greater even than *a.b*.
Furthermore, that *f.g* is greater than *b.k*, and *a.c* is greater than *a.b*, is clear. For by Proposition 24 of the First Book, since the two sides *f.e* and *e.g* of triangle *f.e.g* are equal to the two sides *b.e* and *e.k* of triangle *b.e.k*, and the angle *f.e.g* is greater than angle *b.e.k*, the base *f.g* will be greater than the base *b.k*. Similarly, because *a.e* and *e.c* are equal to *a.e* and *e.b*, and angle *a.e.c* is greater than angle *a.e.b*, the base *a.c* will be greater than the base *a.b*. And so it is proposed.

### Proposition 15.

**I**f a straight line is drawn at right angles <term>orthogonally|at a 90-degree angle</term> from either endpoint of the diameter of any circle, it is necessary that it falls outside the circle. ¶And between that line and the circle, no other straight line can fall...

<meta>This page continues Euclid's Book III, moving from the properties of chords to the properties of tangents and the specific nature of the 'angle of contingency'—the angle formed between a curved circumference and a straight tangent line.</meta>

...is impossible. ¶ Moreover, it is necessary that the angle contained by that circumference <note>original: "7 circumferentia"; the '7' is a common medieval shorthand for 'et' (and)</note> is the narrowest of all acute angles. ¶ Truly, it is necessary that the internal angle contained by the diameter and the circumference is the widest of all acute angles. ¶ From this it is also manifest that every straight line drawn <term>perpendicularly</term><note>original: "orthogonaliter"; drawn at a 90-degree angle</note> from the endpoint of any diameter of a circle touches that circle.

¶ Let it be that from the endpoint **a** of the diameter **a.c** of the circle **a.b.c**, whose center is **d**, a line is drawn perpendicularly: I say that it falls outside the circle, and that between that line and the circumference no other straight line can be intercepted; and that the angle which it and the circumference contain is smaller than any <term>rectilinear angle</term><note>An angle formed by two straight lines, as opposed to an angle formed between a curve and a line.</note> (namely, one contained by two straight lines). And I say that the angle contained by the diameter and the circumference is greater than every acute rectilinear angle. ¶ For if the line drawn from **a** perpendicularly over the line **a.c** can fall within the circle: let that line be **a.b**, and let the line **a.d.b** be drawn. Therefore, by the 5th proposition of the First Book, the angle **d.a.b** will be equal to the angle **d.b.a**. And because the angle **d.b.a** is a right angle by <term>hypothesis</term><note>original: "ypotheſim"; a starting assumption for the sake of proof.</note>, the triangle **a.b.d** would have two right angles, which is impossible by the 32nd proposition of the First Book. ¶ Therefore, it falls outside; let it be **a.e**. If any straight line can be intercepted between it and the circumference, let it be **a.f**, to which the perpendicular **d.g** is drawn. And because the angle **d.g.a** is a right angle, by the 18th proposition of the First Book, the line **a.d** will be longer than the line **d.g**, which is impossible <note>Since d.g would then be shorter than the radius d.a, placing point g inside the circle</note>. Wherefore, no straight line shall be intercepted between it and the circumference. ¶ Because of which, it is clear that the angle contained by **e.a** and the circumference, which is called the <term>angle of contingency</term><note>original: "angulus contingentie"; also known as a 'horn angle,' this is the infinitesimal gap between a tangent line and the curve of the circle.</note>, is smaller than every angle contained by two straight lines. For if any rectilinear angle were equal to the angle of contingency, or smaller than it, since every such angle can be divided into equal parts according to the teaching of the 9th proposition of the First Book, a straight line could be intercepted between line **a.e** and the circumference, which we have demonstrated cannot be. By this, it is clear that the angle contained by the diameter and the circumference is greater than all acute rectilinear angles, because it does not differ from a right angle except by the angle of contingency, which we have shown to be smaller than any rectilinear angle. ¶ The <term>corollary</term><note>A natural consequence or secondary proof following from the main proposition.</note> is clear through the first part. For since the line **a.e** raised on either side does not cut the circle and touches it at point **a**, it is a <term>tangent</term><note>original: "contingens"</note> by definition. ¶ From this it should be noted that the following argument is not valid: "this passes from the smaller to the larger and through all intermediate steps, therefore it passes through an equal." Nor is it valid to say: "one happens to find a greater than this and a smaller than the same, therefore one happens to find an equal." This is shown thus: Let there be a circle **a.b** upon center **c**, whose diameter is **a.c.b**, and let line **a.d** be drawn perpendicularly from its endpoint **a**; it will be tangent to the circle by the corollary of this proposition. Again, let a circle **b.e.d** be described upon point **a** according to the quantity of the diameter **a.b**, and imagine the line **a.b** moving upon point **a** through the circumference of the arc **b.c.d**, so that point **b** counts all the points of arc **b.c.d** until it reaches the line **a.d** and covers it. And because the angle **b.a.d** is a right angle, it follows that there is no acute angle that line **a.b** does not make equal with the diameter **a.c.b** of the smaller circle, because it passed to a right angle by numbering the positions of all acute angles. It is manifest that some of these are smaller than the <term>angle of the semicircle</term><note>The angle formed between the diameter and the curved arc.</note> contained by the semi-circumference **a.b** and the diameter **a.c.b**, and it is manifest that the right angle is greater than the same. I say that in the transition from the smaller acute angles to the greater right angle, no intermediate angle was equal to it. For if there were any, let it be that which line **a.b** made when point **b** was at point **c** of the arc **b.e.d**; because therefore the angle...
