**e.a.b.** is equal to the aforementioned angle of the semicircle: but the angle of the semicircle is the greatest of all acute angles through the last part of this [proposition]: therefore angle **e.a.b.** will be the greatest of all acute angles. Therefore, let angle **e.a.d.** be divided into equal parts, as proposed in the 9th proposition of the First Book, by drawing line **a.f.**. By common conception, angle **f.a.b.** will then be greater than angle **e.a.b.**; whereby there would be something greater than the "greatest," which is impossible. ¶ Or thus: since angle **e.a.b.** is equal to the angle of the semicircle, as is posited; and the angle of the semicircle together with the <term>angle of contingency</term><note>The "angle of contingency" (also called a horn-like angle) is the infinitesimal space between a curved circumference and a straight tangent line.</note> is equal to one right angle; and similarly, since angle **e.a.b.** with angle **e.a.d.** is equal to one right angle: then angle **e.a.d.** will be equal to the angle of contingency. And because the angle of contingency is the narrowest of all acute angles by the 5th part of this [proposition], angle **e.a.d.** (being equal to it) will likewise be the narrowest of all acute angles. But angle **e.a.f.** is narrower than it by common conception: therefore there would be something narrower than the "narrowest," which is impossible. ¶ Therefore, a <term>rectilinear angle</term><note>An angle formed by two straight lines.</note> cannot be equal to the angle of a semicircle, because it passes from the smaller to the greater and not through the equal. Likewise, because it is possible to find a smaller and a greater [angle], an objection is evident against both aforementioned arguments. Wherefore, one must respond to that through interruption.

<note>A geometric diagram shows two circles of unequal size touching at point **g**. A vertical line **e-f** passes through the point of contact. Various points (**c**, **h**, **e**, **k**, **b**, **f**, **g**) are labeled to demonstrate that the infinitesimal angle between two curved surfaces is itself divisible by a straight line.</note>

It could be proved that the angle of contingency is divisible by a straight line, as is evident through the figure placed here at the side. It is certain that the angle caused by the contact of two circles or spheres is an angle of contingency; and such an angle is divided by line **e.g.**, because here we have triangle **b.g.k.**, whose base **b.k.** is divided into equal parts at point **e**, and a line is drawn toward the contact point **g**, argued through the 4th proposition of the First Book and then the 26th of this book; and thus the proposition is clear.

### Proposition 16.

<note>A geometric diagram showing a circle with center **c** and an external point **d**. A larger concentric arc is drawn through **d**. A tangent line **d-b** is constructed from the point **d** to the circle by using a perpendicular line **a-e** and intersecting radii. This demonstrates Euclid's method for "dropping" a tangent onto a circle from a distance.</note>

To draw a tangent line from a given point to a given circle.
¶ Let the given circle be **a.b.**, whose center is **c**, and let the given point be **d**. I wish, therefore, to draw a line touching circle **a.b.** from point **d**. I draw line **d.c.** cutting the circumference of circle **a.b.** at point **a**, upon which I describe circle **d.e.** according to the length of line **d.c.**, concentric with circle **a.b.**. And from point **a**, I draw line **a.e.** perpendicular to line **d.c.**, which cuts the circumference of circle **d.e.** at point **e**. I then draw line **e.c.** cutting the circumference of circle **a.b.** at point **b**. Finally, I draw line **d.b.**, which will be tangent to circle **a.b.** For the two sides **a.c.** and **e.c.** of triangle **a.c.e.** are equal to the two sides **b.c.** and **c.d.** of triangle **b.c.d.**, and angle **c** is common to both; therefore, by the 4th proposition of the First Book, angle **c.a.e.** is equal to angle **d.b.c.**. Since angle **e.a.c.** is a right angle, angle **d.b.c.** must also be a right angle. Therefore, by the <term>corollary</term><note>A logical consequence that follows naturally from a previously proven statement.</note> of the preceding proposition, line **d.b.** will be tangent to circle **a.b.**, which is what was proposed.

### Proposition 17.

<note>A geometric diagram showing a circle with center **d** and a tangent line **a-b** touching at point **c**. A radius **d-c** is drawn to the point of tangency, and another line **d-f** is drawn to the tangent line at point **f**. This setup is used for a "proof by contradiction" to show that no line other than the radius can be perpendicular to the tangent at that point.</note>

If a straight line touches a circle, and a straight line is drawn from the point of contact to the center, it is necessary that it be perpendicular to the tangent line.
¶ Let line **a.b.** be tangent to circle **c.e.**, whose center is **d**, at point **c**. Let this point be joined to the center by line **c.d.**. I say that this line is perpendicular to the tangent line. For if it is not perpendicular to it, let **d.f.** be the perpendicular to the same, which cuts the circumference of the circle at point **e**. Each of the angles at **d.f.** would then be a right angle; therefore, by the 18th proposition of the First Book, line **c.d.** is greater than line **d.f.** <note>In a right triangle, the hypotenuse (c.d.) must be longer than the leg (d.f.), but here d.f. extends outside the circle while c.d. is just the radius, creating a contradiction.</note>, which is impossible. It is therefore established that **d.c.** is perpendicular to **a.b.**, which is what was proposed.

### Proposition .18.

<note>A geometric diagram showing a circle with a tangent line 'a-b' touching at point 'c'. A line 'e-c' passes through the center 'd' and is perpendicular to the tangent.</note>

**I**f a straight line touches a circle, and from the point of contact a certain line is drawn perpendicularly into the circle, it is necessary that the center be on that same line.
¶ Let there be, as before, a line **a.b.** touching circle **c.e.** at point **c.**, and from the point of contact let a line **c.e.** be drawn within the circle perpendicular to line **a.b.** I say that the center of the circle is on line **c.e.** This is the <term>converse</term><note>A converse proposition is one where the "if" and "then" parts of a previous theorem are swapped; here, it reverses the logic of the previous proposition regarding tangents and radii.</note> of the previous one. For if the center were not on line **c.e.**, let it be elsewhere wherever it may be, and let it be **d.** Let line **d.c.** be produced; then **d.c.** would be perpendicular to line **a.b.** by the preceding proposition. This is impossible, since **e.c.** was already posited as being perpendicular to it; therefore the proposition is clear.

### Proposition .19.

<note>Three geometric diagrams showing different cases for the relationship between an angle at the center of a circle and an angle at the circumference subtended by the same arc. 
1. Case where the center is within the angle at the circumference.
2. Case where one side of the angle at the circumference passes through the center.
3. Case where the center is outside the angle at the circumference.</note>

**I**f within a circle an angle stands at the center, while another angle standing on the circumference has the same base, the lower angle will be double the upper one.
¶ Let it be that in circle **a.b.c.**, whose center is **d.**, an angle **a.d.c.** is formed at the center and an angle **a.b.c.** on the circumference, and let both angles have the same base, which is arc **a.c.** I say that angle **a.d.c.** is double angle **a.b.c.** ¶ This is proven as follows: Either the two lines **a.b.** and **b.c.** enclose the two lines **a.d.** and **d.c.**, or one of them forms a single straight line with one of the others, or else one of the first lines cuts the other of the latter lines.
¶ First, let it be that they enclose them, as appears in the first figure. Let line **b.d.e.** be produced; by the 32nd proposition of the First Book, the external angle **a.d.e.** will be equal to the two internal angles, which are angles **b.a.d.** and **a.b.d.** And because these are equal <note>They are equal because they form an isosceles triangle with two radii of the circle.</note> by the 5th proposition of the same book, angle **a.d.e.** will be double angle **a.b.d.** Similarly, angle **e.d.c.** will also be double angle **d.b.c.**; therefore the whole angle **a.d.c.** is double the whole angle **a.b.c.**, which is what was proposed. ¶ If one of the two lines **a.b.** and **b.c.** forms a single line with one of the two lines **a.d.** and **d.c.**, as appears in the second figure, the proposition is clear by the same principles as before and in a similar manner. ¶ If one of the first two lines cuts the other of the latter two, as appears in the 3rd figure, where line **a.b.** cuts line **d.c.**, let line **b.d.e.** be produced. By the same principles we assumed before and in a similar manner, angle **e.d.a.** will be double angle **d.b.a.**, and the whole angle **e.d.c.** will be double the whole angle **d.b.c.**; wherefore angle **a.d.c.** <note>original: "d.b.c." — The Latin text here contains a likely scribal error, as the logic requires the subtraction of the smaller central angle from the larger to prove the theorem for angle a.d.c.</note> is double angle **a.b.c.**, which is what was proposed.

### Proposition .20.

<note>A geometric diagram showing a circle with a chord 'a-b'. Three angles (c, d, e) are drawn from the same chord to the circumference, and another angle (f) is drawn to the center, illustrating that angles in the same segment are equal.</note>

**I**f in one segment of a circle various angles stand upon an arc, it is necessary that any of those angles be equal to one another.
¶ Let it be that in segment **a.d.b.** of circle **a.d.b.**, whose center is **f.**, various angles stand upon arc **a.d.b.**, which are **c.**, **d.**, and **e.** I say they are equal. For let chord **a.b.** be drawn, and from its extremities let lines **a.f.** and **b.f.** be drawn to the center. By the preceding proposition, angle **f.** standing at the center will be double each one of them; therefore they are equal, which is what was proposed.

angle C-A-D and angle A-B-D <note>original: "angulo.c.a.d. z angulus.a.b.d."</note> to angle A-C-D. Wherefore the whole angle A-B-D will be equal to the two angles which are A-C-D and C-A-D. ### Proposition .22.

<note>A sequence of four geometric diagrams arranged vertically on the left.
1. A circle with an inscribed quadrilateral labeled a-b-c-d and intersecting diagonals.
2. A circular segment on base a-b with two points c and d on the arc, where d is "higher" than c.
3. A circular segment on base a-b where a line from a to d intersects the line segment c-b.
4. A circular segment on base a-b with an internal point e and various connecting lines to points a, b, c, d.</note>

**I**t is impossible for two <term>similar segments</term><note>Similar segments of circles are those that contain equal angles. Essentially, they have the same "curvature" relative to their base line.</note> of circles that are unequal to be constructed upon the same assigned straight line on the same side.
¶ Let the assigned straight line be **a.b.**, upon which let a segment of a circle **a.c.b.** be made. I say that upon the same line and on the same side, another segment cannot be made that is similar to this one, whether it be larger or smaller. For if this were possible, let there be a segment **a.d.b.** larger than the other, which is nevertheless similar to it. Therefore, let there be an angle **a.c.b.** in the smaller segment, and an angle **a.d.b.** in the larger. It will then be as if lines **a.d.** and **d.b.** include lines **a.c.** and **c.b.**, as is seen in the first figure. Or, let one of the first lines be the same as one of the latter, as in the second figure. Or, let one cut the other, as in the third figure. Now, if it were the first case, then by the 21st [proposition] of the First [Book], angle **c** would be greater than angle **d**; therefore they are not similar segments by the definition. If it were the second case, angle **c** would still be greater than angle **d** by the 16th [proposition] of the same [Book]; thus, neither would they be similar segments. But if it were the third case, so that line **a.d.** cuts line **c.b.** and also cuts the circumference of the smaller segment at point **e.**, and line **e.b.** is drawn, then by the same 16th [proposition] of the First [Book], the angle **a.e.b.** standing in the segment **a.c.b.** would be greater than angle **d.** But **e.** is equal to **c.** by the 20th [proposition] of this book; wherefore **c.** is greater than **d.**, and thus they are in no way similar. ¶ In a similar way, you will also prove that upon line **a.b.** there shall not be a segment similar to segment **a.c.b.** that is smaller than it, by placing **c** in the location of **d** and **d** in the location of **c** in the aforementioned figures. For by the premises—namely by the 21st and 15th [propositions] of the First [Book] and in the manner previously shown—angle **d** in all the figures would be greater than angle **c**, wherefore the segments would not be similar. ¶ And note that although it is proposed that unequal segments cannot be made on the same side of a single line, it is also true that they cannot be made on opposite sides; this may be proven by placing the smaller segment, which is on one side, beneath the larger one on the other side. For by <term>common notion</term><note>Fundamental mathematical axioms Euclid considers self-evident, such as "the whole is greater than the part."</note>, it is necessary for the smaller to be exceeded by the larger; therefore they are not similar by this 22nd proposition.

### Proposition .23.

<note>Two side-by-side diagrams of semi-circular segments. Left: arc 'e' on base 'a-b'. Right: arc 'f' on base 'c-d'.</note>

**I**f similar segments of circles are placed upon equal lines, it is necessary that those segments be equal to one another.
¶ Let there be two equal lines **a.b.** and **c.d.** upon which are two segments of circles, **a.e.b.** and **c.f.d.**, which are similar. I say that they are equal. For if they are not equal, then one of them, when placed upon the other, will exceed the other. But line **a.b.** does not exceed line **c.d.**, nor is it exceeded by it, since they are equal. Wherefore the contrary of the premise occurs, which is impossible; for **a.b.** and **c.d.** would be the same line.

<header>III</header>

From which [arc] I wish to complete the circle, I will draw in it two lines, however they may happen to fall, which shall be **a.c.** and **b.d.** These I will divide into equal parts: **a.c.** at point **e.** and **b.d.** at point **f.** Then I will draw **e.g.** perpendicular to **a.c.** and **f.b.** perpendicular to **b.d.** <note>original: "perpendicularem"</note>, which intersect each other at point **k.** By the corollary of the first [proposition] of this book <note>Prop. III.1 states that the center of a circle lies on the perpendicular bisector of any chord.</note>, the center of the circle will be on both lines **e.g.** and **f.b.** Therefore, the center is point **k.** 

However, if **e.g.** does not intersect **f.b.** but they form a single line—which occurs if the two lines **a.c.** and **b.d.** are parallel—then that line will meet the circumference of the given arc at both ends. Thus, that line being divided in the middle at point **k.** will be the center of the circle by the same corollary. Lines **e.g.** and **f.b.** will not be parallel because, since the center of the circle lies on both by the said corollary, the same circle would have two centers. Thus, it can be demonstrated for every arc or every segment generally how the circle may be completed from it. 

¶ Because the author seems to vary this conclusion according to the different types of arcs, enumerating the types of all segments, we shall demonstrate separately by type how a circle is completed from every given segment. 

Let the first given segment **a.b.** be a semicircle. By the definition of a semicircle, the line **a.b.** will be the diameter. Therefore, being divided in the middle at point **c.**, **c.** will be the center of the circle. 

¶ Again, let the segment **a.c.b.** be greater than a semicircle <note>A "segment greater than a semicircle" looks like a circle with a small slice removed; the arc is longer than half the circumference.</note>, the chord of which is **a.b.**, which I divide into equal parts at point **d.** From this point I lead **d.c.** perpendicular to it, which will pass through the center by the corollary of the first [proposition] of this book. I also draw the line **a.c.** And because line **a.b.** is smaller than the diameter (since segment **a.c.b.** is greater than a semicircle), **a.d.** will be smaller than the semi-diameter <note>The "semi-diameter" is the radius.</note>. But **d.c.** is greater than the semi-diameter. Therefore, **d.c.** is greater than **a.d.** Thus, by the 19th [proposition] of the First Book, angle **c.a.d.** is greater than angle **a.c.d.** 

Let there be made then, by the 23rd [proposition] of the First Book, angle **c.a.e.** equal to angle **a.c.d.**, by drawing line **a.e.** which intersects line **c.d.** at point **e.** By the 6th [proposition] of the First Book, line **a.e.** will be equal to line **e.c.** Then let line **e.b.** be drawn, and by the 4th [proposition] of the First Book, line **e.b.** will be equal to line **a.e.** Since the three lines **e.a.**, **e.b.**, and **e.c.** are equal, then by the 9th [proposition] of this book, **e.** is the center of the circle.

¶ Again, let the segment **a.c.b.** be smaller than a semicircle, the chord of which is **a.b.**, which I divide into equal parts at point **d.** From which I draw the line **c.d.e.** perpendicular to line **a.b.**, which intersects the circumference at point **c.** It is manifest that this passes through the center by the corollary of the first [proposition] of this book. I draw again the line **a.c.**; angle **a.c.d.** will be greater than angle **c.a.d.** (If it were equal, the segment **a.c.b.** would be a semicircle; and if it were smaller, it would be greater than a semicircle). But it is posited that it is smaller. I draw therefore line **a.e.**, which with line **a.c.** makes an angle equal to angle **c.**, and it intersects line **c.f.** at point **e.** It is manifest that point **e.** falls outside the given segment. I draw line **e.b.**, and because the total angle **a.** is equal to angle **c.**, by the 6th [proposition] of the First Book, line **e.a.** will be equal to line **e.c.** And because by the 4th [proposition] of the First Book, line **e.b.** is equal to line **e.a.**, then by the 9th [proposition] of this book, point **e.** will be the center of the circle. Wherefore the proposition is clear according to all types of circular segments.

<note>A vertical column of five geometric diagrams illustrates segments of circles and angles. The first shows a circular segment with a chord a-b and two smaller internal chords with perpendicular bisectors meeting at center k. The second shows a semicircle with its center c on diameter a-b. The third depicts a large segment (greater than a semicircle) with the center e located inside the arc. The fourth shows a small segment (less than a semicircle) where the center e is located outside the segment's boundary. The fifth shows two equal circles with equal central angles at b and d, subtending equal arcs.</note>

<header>BOOK III</header>

<note>Five geometrical diagrams are arranged vertically in the left margin. 
1. A circle with center **b**, an inscribed triangle with vertices **f**, **e**, and **g**. Lines connect the center **b** to vertices **f**, **e**, and **g**.
2. A circle with center **d**, an inscribed triangle with vertices **b**, **a**, and **c**. Lines connect the center **d** to vertices **b**, **a**, and **c**.
3. A circle similar to the first, with center **b** and triangle **feg**. A point **k** is located outside the circle below the arc **eg**, with lines connecting **k** to **e** and **g**.
4. A circle with center **d** and points **a**, **b**, and **c** on the circumference, with lines connecting **d** to **a**, **b**, and **c**.
5. A circle with center **b** and points **e**, **f**, and **g** on the circumference, with lines connecting **b** to **e**, **f**, and **g**.</note>

By the definition of equal circles, the radii <note>original: "semidiametri"</note> are equal. And because the two angles **d.** and **b.** are equal, then by the 4th [proposition] of the First Book <note>Prop. I.4 is the Side-Angle-Side theorem for triangle congruence.</note>, the line **a.c.** will be equal to line **e.g.** Furthermore, by the 19th [proposition] of this book <note>referring to the relationship between angles at the center and circumference</note>, angle **b.** will be equal to angle **f.** since angle **d.** is equal to angle **b.** Therefore, by the definition of similar segments, the two segments **a.b.c.** and **e.f.g.** are similar. And because they stand upon equal lines **a.c.** and **e.g.**, they themselves will be equal by the 23rd [proposition] of this book. Wherefore, the arcs **a.b.c.** and **e.f.g.** are equal. 

But if the angles **b.** and **f.**, which are at the circumference, are set as equal, then by the definition, the segments will be similar, and the angles **d.** and **b.** [at the centers] will be equal by the 19th of this book. And because the circles are equal by hypothesis, then by the 4th of the First Book, the two lines **a.c.** and **e.g.** will be equal. Wherefore, as before, the segments are equal by the 23rd of this book, since they are similar and stand upon equal lines. Therefore, the arcs are also equal, which is what was proposed.

---

### Proposition 26.

**If** in equal circles equal arcs are taken, it is necessary that the angles formed within them—whether they are constructed at the centers or at the circumferences—be equal.

Let there be, as before, two circles **a.b.c.** (whose center is **d.**) and **e.f.g.** (whose center is **b.** <note>The letter **b** is used here as both a center and a vertex in the diagrams; in early geometry texts, labeling could sometimes overlap between different figures.</note>). Let the two arcs **a.b.c.** and **e.f.g.** be equal. Upon these arcs, let there be two angles at the center, which are **d.** and **b.**, by drawing lines **a.d.**, **c.d.**, **e.b.**, and **g.b.** Likewise, upon the same arcs, let there be two other angles at the circumference, which are **b.** and **f.**, by drawing lines **a.b.**, **c.b.**, **e.f.**, and **g.f.** 

I say that the two angles **d.** and **b.** are equal to each other, and likewise the two angles **b.** and **f.** are equal to each other. This is the converse of the previous [proposition]. For if the angles **d.** and **b.** are not equal to each other, let **b.** be the greater, from which the angle **k.b.g.** is cut off, which is equal to angle **d.** Then, by the previous proposition, the arc **k.e.f.g.** would be equal to arc **a.b.c.** But the two arcs **a.b.c.** and **e.f.g.** were established as equal. It would then follow that a part is equal to the whole, which is impossible. Therefore, the total angles **d.** and **b.** are equal. In a similar way, you will prove that the angles **b.** and **f.** are equal. Or, if you prefer, once it is proven that angles **d.** and **b.** are equal, it follows that **b.** and **f.** are equal by the 19th [proposition] of this book, and vice versa.

---

### Proposition 27.

**If** in equal circles equal lines <note>Here, "lines" refers specifically to chords.</note> cut off arcs, then the arcs will also be equal. However, if the lines are unequal, the arcs will also be unequal; it is necessary that the greater arc be cut off by the greater line, and the smaller arc by the smaller line.

Let there be two equal circles **a.b.c.** (whose center is **d.**) and **e.f.g.** (whose center is **b.**). Let chord **a.c.** be equal to chord **e.g.** I say that the two arcs **a.b.c.** and **e.f.g.**, which the said chords cut from the said circles, are equal. But if chord **e.g.** is set as greater than chord **a.c.**, I say that arc **e.f.g.** is greater than arc **a.b.c.** 

The first part is proved thus: let lines be drawn from the centers to the ends of the chords, which are **d.a.**, **d.c.**, **b.e.**, and **b.g.** Because the circles are established as equal, these radii will be equal. And because line **a.c.** is established as equal to line **e.g.**, then by the 8th [proposition] of the First Book <note>Prop I.8 is the Side-Side-Side congruence theorem.</note>, angle **d.** will be equal to the total angle **b.** Wherefore, by the 25th of this book, arc **a.b.c.** will be equal to arc **e.f.g.**, and thus the first part is clear. 

The second part is thus: let **e.g.** be greater than **a.c.** Then, by the 25th of the First Book <note>Prop I.25 relates the relative lengths of sides to the sizes of opposite angles in triangles.</note>, angle **b.** will be greater than angle **d.** Therefore, let angle **f.b.g.** be made equal to angle **d.** Then, by the 25th of this book, arc **f.g.** will be equal to arc **a.b.c.** Wherefore, arc **e.f.g.** is greater than arc **a.b.c.**, which is the second thing proposed.

### Proposition 28.

**In equal circles**, equal arcs must have equal chords.
Let there be two equal circles **a.b.c.** (whose center is **d.**) and **e.f.g.** (whose center is **b.**) and let arc **a.b.c.** be equal to arc **e.f.g.** I say that chord **a.c.** is equal to chord **e.g.**; and this is the converse of the first part of the preceding [proposition]. Let lines **d.a.**, **d.c.**, **b.e.**, and **b.g.** be drawn. By the 26th [proposition] of this book <note>Prop. III.26 states that in equal circles, angles standing on equal arcs are equal.</note>, angles **d.** and **b.** will be equal. Wherefore, by the 4th [proposition] of the first [book] <note>The Side-Angle-Side theorem for triangle congruence.</note>, **a.c.** will be equal to **e.g.**, which is what was proposed. Furthermore, whatever properties <note>original: "passiones"</note> are proven regarding different equal circles, understand that they are even more certainly true regarding the same circle.

### Proposition 29.

**To divide** a given arc into two equal parts.
Let the given arc be **a.b.c.**, let chord **a.c.** be subtended beneath it, and let that chord be divided into two equal parts at point **d.** From this point, let a perpendicular line be drawn to the chord, which shall be **d.b.**, cutting the circumference of the given arc at point **b.** I say that this point divides the given arc into two equal parts. For let lines **b.a.** and **b.c.** be drawn; these will be equal by the 4th [proposition] of the first [book]. Wherefore, by the first part of the 27th [proposition] of this book <note>Prop. III.27 states that equal chords subtend equal arcs.</note>, arc **a.b.** will be equal to arc **b.c.**, which is what was proposed.

### Proposition 30.

**If a rectilinear angle** is constructed in a semicircle upon an arc, it is a right angle. If, however, it is in a segment <note>original: "portione"</note> smaller than a semicircle, it is greater than a right angle. But if it is in a segment greater than a semicircle, it is smaller than a right angle. Likewise, the angle of every segment greater than a semicircle will of necessity be greater than a right angle; and that of a smaller segment, less than a right angle.
Let it be as in circle **a.b.c.**, whose center is **d.** and diameter is **a.d.c.**, forming semicircle **a.b.c.** In the circumference of this semicircle, let angle **a.b.c.** be made by drawing lines **a.b.** and **b.c.** I say that this angle is a right angle. Let line **b.d.** be extended from the angle to the center. By the 5th [proposition] of the first [book] <note>The Base Angles Theorem for isosceles triangles.</note>, angle **a.b.d.** will be equal to angle **a.**, and angle **d.b.c.** equal to angle **c.** And because angle **c.d.b.** is equal to the two angles **d.b.a.** and **a.** by the 32nd [proposition] of the first [book] <note>The exterior angle of a triangle equals the sum of the two opposite interior angles.</note>, it will be double the angle **d.b.a.** By the same reasoning, angle **a.d.b.** will be double the angle **d.b.c.** Therefore, the two angles **c.d.b.** and **a.d.b.** are double the total angle **a.b.c.** But those [first two] angles are equal to two right angles by the 13th [proposition] of the first [book] <note>Angles on a straight line sum to 180 degrees.</note>. Therefore, the total angle **a.b.c.** will be half of two right angles; wherefore it is a right angle, which is the first thing proposed.
The same may be shown otherwise: let **b.c.** be extended to **e.** By the 32nd [proposition] of the first [book], angle **a.b.c.** <note>Wait, the text says a.b.c here, likely referring to the exterior angle e.b.a or a similar construction.</note> will be equal to the two angles **a.** and **c.** And because angle **a.** is equal to angle **a.b.d.** and angle **c.** to angle **c.b.d.**, the angle **a.b.c.** [the whole] will be equal to [the sum of its parts]. Therefore, each of them is a right angle by definition.
Secondly, it is clear thus: let there be in circle **a.b.c.** (whose center is **d.**) a segment **a.b.c.** whose chord **a.c.** is greater than a semicircle <note>The text says "maior semicirculo," implying the segment cut off by the chord is larger than a semicircle.</note>, and let angle **a.b.c.** be made upon its circumference by drawing lines **b.a.** and **b.c.** I say that this angle is less than a right angle. For let the diameter **a.d.e.** and line **e.b.** be drawn. By the first part of this proposition, the total angle **b.** [angle **a.b.e.**] is a right angle. Wherefore, angle **a.b.c.** will be less than a right angle by common knowledge <note>The axiom that "the whole is greater than the part."</note>, since it is a part of it. Thus the second part is clear.
Thirdly, thus: Let there be again in circle **a.b.c.**...

**c.** Let its center be **d.**, and the segment be **a.b.c.** whose chord is **a.c.**, which is less than a semicircle; and let an angle **a.b.c.** be formed upon its circumference by drawing lines **b.a.** and **b.c.** I say that this angle is greater than a right angle. Wherefore, by the 13th [proposition] of the First Book, the angle **f.a.c.** is similarly a right angle. Because, therefore, the first is a right angle and the second is a part of a right angle, both are evidently clear. Thus, this five-part <note>original: "pēthamēbris" — meaning "five-membered" or having five parts.</note> conclusion is fully clarified. ¶ From these last two parts, note also a counter-argument <note>original: "instantiam"</note> against those two arguments to which we brought a counter-argument in Proposition 15 of this book. For a transition is made from the angle of a segment less than a semicircle—which is less than a right angle by the last part of this [proposition]—to the angle of a segment greater than a semicircle—which is greater than a right angle by the penultimate part of this. Yet it does not pass through an equal [right angle]. For since every segment of a circle is either a semicircle, or greater than a semicircle, or less than a semicircle: while both the angle of a semicircle (by the first part of Proposition 15) and the angle of a lesser segment (by the last part of this) are less than a right angle, and the angle of a greater segment is greater than a right angle; nevertheless, there will not be any angle of a segment, nor simply any angle contained by a circumference and a straight line, that is either a right angle or equal to a right angle. To make this more clearly evident, let there be in circle **a.b.c.** (whose center is **d.**) a line **a.b.** which has no fixed end at **b.**, cutting from it a segment less than a semicircle; by the last part of this [proposition] it will be less than a right angle. Let the diameter of this circle be **a.d.c.**, and imagine the line **a.b.** moving toward the direction of **c.** upon the point **a.**. As long as it remains on this side of **c.** or at **b.**, overlapping the diameter **a.d.c.**, it will make with the arc an angle less than a right angle. However, at every point beyond **c.**, such as at **e.**, it will make an angle greater than a right angle by the penultimate part of this. It therefore passes from the lesser to the greater, but not through the equal. And just as among rectilinear angles it is possible to find one greater than the angle of a semicircle and one smaller, yet not one equal (as was shown in Proposition 15 of this book); so in the angles of segments it is possible to find one greater than a right angle and one smaller, yet not one equal, as is clear from this demonstration.

-># Proposition 32.<-

Upon a given line, to describe a segment of a circle containing <note>The term "containing" here refers to the angle formed at the circumference by lines drawn from the ends of the segment's chord.</note> an angle equal to a given angle: whether that angle be a right angle, or greater than, or less than a right angle.
¶ Let **a.b.** be the given line and **c** the given angle; I wish to describe upon line **a.b.** a segment of a circle that receives on its circumference a rectilinear angle equal to angle **c**. If, therefore, angle **c** should be a right angle, having divided **a.b.** through the middle, I shall describe a semicircle upon it; and the task will be done, by the first part of Proposition 30 of this book. ¶ If, however, it be obtuse, I shall draw the line **d.a.** making with line **b.a.** an angle equal to angle **c**; and from point **a** I shall draw line **a.e.** perpendicular to line **a.d.**; and at point **b** I shall make an angle (by Proposition 23 of the First Book) equal to angle **e.a.b.**, in which the obtuse angle exceeds a right angle. Having drawn line **b.f.** to the perpendicular **a.e.**, the lines **f.a.** and **f.b.** will be equal by Proposition 6 of the First Book. Thus, having made point **f** the center of the circle, I shall describe a circle **a.b.b.** <note>The OCR likely reflects a repeated letter for a point on the arc.</note> according to the length of line **f.a.**; and by the corollary of Proposition 15 of this book, line **a.d.** will be tangent to the circle. Wherefore, by the preceding proposition, the angle formed in segment **a.b.b.** is equal to angle **d.a.b.**, and thus also to angle **c**, which is what was proposed. ¶ If, however, angle **c** be acute, I shall produce line **a.g.** making with line **a.b.** an angle equal to angle **c**; and from point **a** I shall draw **a.e.** perpendicular to line **a.g.**; and at point **b** I shall make an angle equal to angle **e.a.b.**, in which a right angle exceeds the acute. Having drawn line **b.f.** to the perpendicular **a.e.**, lines **f.a.** and **f.b.** will be equal by Proposition 6 of the First Book. Thus, having made point **f** the center of the circle, I shall describe a circle **a.k.b.** according to the length of line **f.a.**; and by the corollary of Proposition 15 of this book, line **a.g.** will be tangent to the circle. Wherefore, by the preceding proposition, the angle formed in segment **a.k.b.** is equal to angle **g.a.b.**, and thus also to angle **c**, which is what was proposed.

-># Proposition 33.<-

From a given circle, to cut off a segment containing an angle equal to a given angle.
¶ Let **a.b.** be the given circle, and **c** the given angle. I wish, therefore, to cut off from circle **a.b.** one segment containing an angle equal to angle **c**. I produce line **d.a.e.** tangent to the given circle at point **a**, from which I draw into the circle line **a.b.** making with line **a.e.** an angle equal to angle **c**. And by Proposition 31 <note>original: ".31. huius"</note> of this book, segment **a.b.** lying on the side of line **a.d.** will receive an angle equal to angle **c**, which is what was proposed.

## Proposition 34

If two straight lines intersect one another within a circle, the <term>rectangle</term> <note>In Euclidean geometry, a "rectangle" described by two lines refers to the area formed by the product of their lengths.</note> contained by the two parts of one of them is equal to the rectangle contained by the two parts of the other line.

Let there be two lines **a.c.** and **b.d.** intersecting each other in circle **a.b.c.d.** at point **e**. I say that the rectangle formed by **a.e.** and **e.c.** is equal to that formed by **b.e.** and **e.d.** For either both lines **a.c.** and **b.d.** pass through the center of the circle, or only one does, or neither. If both pass through the center, then **e** will be the center of the circle, and all four lines will be equal <note>as they are all radii</note>; therefore, the proposition is clear. 

But if only one of them passes through the center, let that be **b.d.**, and let the center of the circle be **f**. Then **b.d.** will cut **a.c.** either into equal or unequal parts. First, let it cut it into equal parts. Then, by the first part of Proposition 3 of this book, it cuts it <term>orthogonally</term> <note>original: "orthogonaliter," meaning at right angles</note>. Let line **f.c.** be drawn. By Proposition 5 of the Second Book, the rectangle formed by **b.e.** and **e.d.** together with the square of **e.f.** is equal to the square of line **f.d.**, and therefore also to the square of line **f.c.** <note>since f.d. and f.c. are both radii</note>. Therefore, by the <term>penultimate proposition of the First Book</term> <note>This refers to Proposition 47 of Book I, commonly known as the Pythagorean Theorem.</note>, this is equal to the squares of the two lines **f.e.** and **e.c.** By subtracting the square of **e.f.** from both sides, the rectangle of **b.e.** and **e.d.** will be equal to the square of line **e.c.**; and because **a.e.** is equal to **e.c.** <note>by the bisection</note>, the proposition is clear.

If **b.d.**, passing through the center, cuts **a.c.** into unequal parts, let the perpendicular **f.g.** be drawn from center **f** to **a.c.** By the second part of the third proposition of this book, **a.g.** will be equal to **g.c.** Let line **f.c.** be drawn. By Proposition 5 of the Second Book, the rectangle formed by **b.e.** and **e.d.** with the square of **e.f.**—and therefore, by the penultimate of the first, with the squares of the two lines **f.g.** and **g.e.** (because angle **f.g.e.** is a right angle)—is equal to the square of line **d.f.**, and thus also to line **f.c.** Because of this, by the penultimate of the first, it is also equal to the squares of the two lines **f.g.** and **g.c.** By subtracting the square of line **f.g.** from both sides, the rectangle formed by **b.e.** and **e.d.** with the square of line **g.e.** will be equal to the square of line **g.c.** But by Proposition 5 of the Second Book, the rectangle formed by **a.e.** and **e.c.** with the square of line **g.e.** is equal to that same square of **g.c.** Therefore, by subtracting the square of line **g.e.** from both sides, the rectangle of **b.e.** and **e.d.** will be equal to the rectangle of **a.e.** and **e.c.**, which is what was proposed.

If neither of them passes through the center, whether one bisects the other or not, let a diameter **g.f.e.h.** <note>original: "g.f.e.b." appears to be a typo for the diameter labeled g.f.e.h. in the diagram</note> be produced through the circle passing through their point of intersection. If one bisects the other, as **b.d.** by **a.c.**, then **g.h.** also bisects **a.c.** Therefore, they are orthogonal by the third proposition of this book. Thus, by the second case of this conclusion, the rectangle of **g.e.** and **e.h.** is equal to that of **a.c.** and **e.c.**, and by the third case, the rectangle of **g.e.** and **e.h.** is equal to that of **b.e.** and **e.d.** Therefore, the rectangle of **a.e.** and **e.c.** is equal to that of **b.e.** and **e.d.**, which is what was proposed. 

And if neither bisects the other, by the third case of this conclusion, the rectangle of **g.e.** and **e.h.** will be equal to each of those formed by **a.e.** by **e.c.** and **b.e.** by **e.d.**; wherefore one of them will be equal to the other: which is what was proposed.

## Proposition 35

If two lines are drawn to a circle from an external point, one of which, **a.b.**, is a tangent, and the other, **a.c.d.**, is a secant, I say that the <term>rectangle</term> <note>The area formed by multiplying the lengths of two segments.</note> formed by **a.c.** and **d.a.** is equal to the <term>square</term> of line **a.b.** Either line **a.d.c.** passes through the center or it does not. First, let it pass through the center, which is **e**, and let line **e.b.** be drawn, which by the 17th proposition of this book <note>Modern Proposition 18: a tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact.</note> will be perpendicular to line **a.b.** Because line **d.c.** is divided into equal parts at point **e** and the line **d.a.** is added to it, then by the sixth proposition of the second book <note>original: "sextam secundi"</note>, the rectangle formed by **c.a.** and **a.d.** plus the square of line **e.d.** is equal to the square of line **e.a.** And therefore, by the <term>penultimate proposition of the first book</term> <note>original: "penultimam primi". This refers to Proposition 47, the Pythagorean Theorem.</note>, it is equal to the squares of the two lines **e.b.** and **b.a.** because angle **b** is a right angle. Subtracting the square of **e.b.** from both sides <note>Since **e.d.** and **e.b.** are both radii, their squares are equal.</note>, the rectangle formed by **c.a.** and **a.d.** will be equal to the square of line **a.b.**, which is what was proposed. 

¶ If the line **a.d.c.** does not pass through the center, let **a.f.e.g.** be taken passing through the center, and let lines **e.d.** and **e.b.** be drawn, and let **e.h.** be perpendicular to **a.d.c.** By the 3rd proposition of this book, **d.h.** will be equal to **h.c.** Because line **d.c.** is divided into equal parts at point **h** and the line **a.d.** is added to it, then by the 6th proposition of the second book, the rectangle formed by **c.a.** and **a.d.** plus the square of **d.h.** is equal to the square of line **a.h.** Therefore, adding the square of **h.e.** to both sides, the rectangle of **c.a.** and **a.d.** plus the squares of the two lines **d.h.** and **h.e.**—which by the penultimate of the first book is the square of **e.d.** (because angle **h** is a right angle) and therefore the square of **e.f.** (because **e.d.** and **e.f.** are equal radii)—is equal to the squares of the two lines **a.h.** and **h.e.**, and thus by the penultimate of the first book, equal to the square of line **a.e.** But because by the 6th proposition of the second book, the rectangle of **g.a.** and **a.f.** plus the square of **f.e.** is equal to the square of line **a.e.**, and since both the rectangle of **c.a.** and **a.d.** and the rectangle of **g.a.** and **a.f.** (each with the square of line **f.e.**) are equal to the square of line **a.e.**, they must be equal to each other. Subtracting the square of line **e.f.** from both sides, the rectangle of **c.a.** and **a.d.** will be equal to the rectangle of **g.a.** and **a.f.** But the rectangle of **g.a.** and **a.f.** is equal to the square of line **a.b.** by the previous case of this proposition; therefore, the rectangle of **c.a.** and **a.d.** is equal to the square of line **a.b.**, which is what was proposed. 

¶ And from this, note that if from a point marked outside the circle any number of secant lines are drawn to the circle, the rectangles contained by the whole lines and their external parts are equal to one another, since they are all equal to the square of the tangent line. 

¶ Note also that if from any point marked outside a circle two tangent lines are drawn to the circle itself, they will be equal to one another. For the square of each of them will be equal to the rectangle formed by a secant line drawn from that same point into the circle and its external part. However, this is more evidently shown by the penultimate proposition of the first book. 

¶ Let **a.** be a point marked outside circle **b.c.d.**, whose center is **e**, and from it let two lines **a.b.** and **a.d.** be drawn tangent to the circle at points **b** and **d**. I say that these lines are equal. I will draw lines **e.a.**, **e.b.**, and **e.d.** By the 17th proposition of this book, both angles **b** and **d** are right angles. Therefore, by the penultimate of the first book, the square of **a.e.** will be equal to the two squares of lines **a.b.** and **b.e.** Likewise, it is also equal to the two squares of **a.d.** and **d.e.** Therefore, the squares of lines **a.b.** and **b.e.** are equal to the squares of **a.d.** and **d.e.** Since the squares of **b.e.** and **e.d.** are equal <note>As radii of the same circle.</note>, the squares of **a.b.** and **a.d.** will be equal. Therefore, **a.b.** is equal to **a.d.**, which is what was proposed. 

¶ Alternatively, let line **b.d.** be drawn. By the 5th proposition of the first book <note>The base angles of an isosceles triangle are equal.</note>, angle **e.b.d.** will be equal to angle **e.d.b.** because line **e.b.** is equal to line **e.d.** Since both angles **b** and **d** are right angles, by <term>common notion</term> <note>original: "comunem scientiam". Referring to Euclid's Axioms, specifically "If equals are subtracted from equals, the remainders are equal."</note> the remaining angle **a.b.d.** is equal to the remaining angle **a.d.b.** Then, by the 6th proposition of the first book, line **a.b.** is equal to line **a.d.**

<summary>This page proves the Tangent-Secant Theorem (the square of a tangent equals the product of the whole secant and its external segment) and demonstrates that two tangents drawn from the same external point are equal in length.</summary>

### Proposition 36.

If a point is marked outside a circle, and from it two lines are drawn to the circumference, one of which cuts the circle and the other is applied to the circumference <note>original: "applicata"; referring to a line that meets the circle's edge</note>, and if the <term>rectangle</term> <note>The product of the lengths of two segments.</note> formed by the whole secant line and its external part is equal to the <term>square</term> <note>original: "quadrato"; the product of a line multiplied by itself.</note> of the applied line: then the applied line must necessarily be tangent to the circle.
¶ Let **a** be a point marked outside the circle **b.c.d.**, whose center is **e**. From this point, let the line **a.b.d.** be drawn cutting the circle, and let line **a.c.** be applied to the circumference. Let the product of **d.a.** and **a.b.** be equal to the square of **a.c.** I say that the line **a.c.** is a tangent, and this is the converse of the previous proposition. For if it is not a tangent, let line **a.f.** be a tangent. Then, by the preceding proposition, the product of **d.a.** and **a.b.** would be equal to the square of line **a.f.** Thus, the square of line **a.f.** would be equal to the square of line **a.c.**, and therefore **a.c.** would be equal to **a.f.**, which is impossible by the 8th proposition of this book <note>The 8th proposition discusses the varying lengths of lines drawn from a point to a circumference.</note>. Therefore, **a.c.** must be a tangent, which is what was proposed.
¶ This can also be proved demonstratively: let the previous arrangement and hypothesis remain. If the line **a.b.d.** passes through the center, let line **c.e.** be drawn. By the 6th proposition of the second book, the product of **d.a.** and **a.b.** plus the square of **e.b.**—and thus plus the square of **c.e.** <note>Because **e.b.** and **c.e.** are both radii.</note>—is equal to the square of **a.e.** But the product of **d.a.** and **a.b.** was stated to be equal to the square of **a.c.** Therefore, the square of **a.c.** plus the square of **c.e.** is equal to the square of **a.e.** Consequently, by the last proposition of the first book <note>The Pythagorean Theorem.</note>, the angle **c** is a right angle. Therefore, by the 15th conclusion of this book, the line **a.c.** is tangent to the circle, which is what was proposed.
¶ However, if **a.b.d.** does not pass through the center, let a line be drawn from point **d** passing through the center. Because the product of this whole line and its external part is equal to the product of **d.a.** and **a.b.** by the preceding proposition, it will also be equal to the square of line **a.c.** Thus, as before, **a.c.** will be tangent to the circle.

->The third book ends. The fourth book begins.<-

A figure is said to be **inscribed** within another figure when each of the angles of the inscribed figure touches the sides of the figure in which it is inscribed from the inside.
¶ A figure is said to be **circumscribed** about another figure whenever all the sides of the circumscribing figure touch all the angles of the figure it surrounds.

### Proposition 1.

Within a given circle, to fit a straight line equal to a given straight line, provided that the given line is not greater than the diameter.
¶ Let the given line be **a.b.** and the given circle be **c.d.e.**, whose diameter is **c.d.**, which is not smaller than line **a.b.** I wish to fit a line equal to **a.b.** within the given circle. If the given line is equal to the diameter, the proposition is already satisfied. But if it is smaller, let a segment **d.f.** equal to it be taken from the diameter. Around point **d**, with a radius equal to the length of line **d.f.**, let a circle **f.e.g.** be described, cutting the given circle at points **g** and **e**. Let a line be drawn from point **d** to either of these, such as **d.e.** or **d.g.** Either of these will be equal to line **a.b.**, because both are equal to line **d.f.** by the definition of a circle. Thus, we have achieved what was proposed.

### Proposition 2.

**To inscribe a triangle equiangular to a given triangle within a given circle.**

Within a given triangle **a.b.c.** and a given circle **d.e.f.** <note>The OCR reads "d.c.f.", but the context of the proof requires the third point to be 'e'.</note>, I wish to place a triangle equiangular to triangle **a.b.c.** within this circle. While it is not necessary for it to be equilateral <note>Having sides of equal length.</note>, it is possible to do so. I draw the line **g.d.h.** tangent to the circle at point **d**. At this point, I construct angle **b.d.f.** (by drawing line **d.f.**) equal to angle **c**, and angle **g.d.e.** (by drawing line **d.e.**) equal to angle **b**. Then I draw the line **e.f.** By the 31st proposition of the third book <note>This theorem states that the angle between a tangent and a chord is equal to the angle in the alternate segment of the circle.</note>, angle **e** will be equal to angle **c**, because both are equal to angle **b.d.f.**—one by construction, and the other by the 31st of the third book. By the same reasoning, angle **f** will be equal to angle **b**. Therefore, by the 32nd of the first book <note>The sum of angles in a triangle is equal to two right angles; thus, if two angles are equal to two others, the third must also be equal.</note>, the third angle **d** will be equal to the third angle **a**. Thus, we have achieved what was proposed.

### Proposition 3.

**To circumscribe a triangle equiangular to a given triangle about a given circle.**

As before, let there be a given triangle **a.b.c.** and a given circle **d.e.f.** with its center at **g**. About this circle, I wish to describe a triangle equiangular to triangle **a.b.c.**; for it is not necessary that it be equilateral, though it is possible. I will extend the base **b.c.** in both directions so that two external angles are formed. From the center **g**, I will draw line **g.d.** to the circumference, and I will construct angle **d.g.e.** (by drawing line **g.e.**) equal to the external angle at **b**, and angle **d.g.f.** (by drawing line **g.f.**) equal to the external angle at **c**. From the points **d, e,** and **f**, I will draw lines perpendicularly in both directions, which, according to the corollary of the 15th proposition of the third book, will be tangent to the circle. I will extend these tangents until they meet at points **h, k,** and **l**. It is necessary that they meet; for since both angles at **d** and both angles at **e** are right angles, if line **d.e.** is understood to be drawn, the two internal angles on the side of **h** will be less than two right angles. Therefore, by the penultimate petition <note>original: "penultimā petitionē"; This refers to Euclid’s Fifth Postulate, the Parallel Postulate, which states that lines will meet if the interior angles are less than two right angles.</note>, the lines **l.d.h.** and **k.e.h.** will meet when extended in that direction. By the same reasoning, the two lines **h.d.l.** and **k.f.l.** will meet, since both angles at **f** are also right angles. Because in the quadrilateral **h.d.g.e.** the two angles at **d** and **e** are right angles, the two angles at **g** and **h** together must be equal to two right angles—since the four angles of any quadrilateral are equal to four right angles, as was shown above in the 32nd of the first book <note>Euclid's proof for the sum of interior angles of polygons.</note>. And because the interior and exterior angles at **b** are likewise equal to two right angles by the 13th of the first book, and since the exterior angle at **b** was made equal to angle **d.g.e.**, the interior angle at **b** will be equal to angle **h**. By similar reasoning, the interior angle at **c** will be equal to angle **l**. And because the two interior angles **h** and **l** are less than two right angles by the 32nd of the first book, the two lines **h.e.** and **l.f.** when extended will meet at point **k**. Thus, the triangle **h.k.l.** is formed. Since angle **h** is equal to the interior angle **b**, and angle **l** to the interior angle **c**, then by the 32nd of the first book, angle **k** must be equal to angle **a**. Thus, we have achieved what was proposed.

<note>Three geometric diagrams are located in the left margin illustrating the propositions:
1. Top diagram (Proposition 4): A triangle with vertices **b** (top left), **c** (top right), and **a** (bottom). Inside the triangle is an inscribed circle with center **d**. Radii are drawn from **d** to the points where the circle touches each side: **e** on side **ab**, **f** on side **bc**, and **g** on side **ac**. Dotted auxiliary lines connect the center **d** to the vertices **a** and **b**.
2. Middle diagram (Proposition 5 - Acute): A circle drawn around an acute-angled triangle with vertices **a** (top), **b** (bottom left), and **c** (bottom right). The center of the circle is marked **f**. Perpendicular lines—acting as side bisectors—are drawn from the center **f** to the midpoints **d** (on side **ab**) and **e** (on side **ac**). Lines (radii) connect the center **f** to all three vertices.

Bottom diagram (Proposition 5 - Right-angled): A circle drawn around a <term>right-angled triangle<note>A triangle containing one 90-degree angle.</note></term> with the right angle at vertex **a** (top). The vertices **b** and **c** form the hypotenuse (the longest side). The center of the circle, **f**, is located exactly at the midpoint of the hypotenuse **bc**. ### To describe a circle within a given triangle.

Let the assigned triangle be **a.b.c.** I wish to describe a circle within it; this is, in a sense, the converse of the second proposition. I divide two of its angles, **a** and **b**, into equal parts <note>This process is known as angle bisecting.</note> by drawing line **a.d.** and line **b.d.**, which meet at point **d**. From this point, I shall draw perpendicular lines to the three sides of the triangle: line **d.e.** to side **a.b.**, line **d.f.** to side **b.c.**, and line **d.g.** to side **a.c.** 

Because in the two triangles **e.a.d.** and **g.a.d.**, the angle **a** of one is equal to the angle **a** of the other, and both angles **e** and **g** are right angles, and side **a.d.** is common to both, it follows from the 26th proposition of the first book <note>The "Angle-Angle-Side" theorem for triangle congruence.</note> that line **d.e.** is equal to line **d.g.** By the same reasoning, since in the two triangles **e.b.d.** and **f.b.d.**, angle **b** of one is equal to angle **b** of the other, both angles **e** and **f** are right angles, and side **d.b.** is common, it follows by that same proposition that line **e.d.** is equal to line **d.f.** 

Therefore, the three lines **d.e.**, **d.f.**, and **d.g.** are all equal. Thus, if the center is placed at **d** and a circle is drawn according to the length of one of these lines, it will pass through the endpoints of the other two, according to the 9th proposition of the third book. And because, by the corollary of the 15th proposition of the third book, each of the lines **a.b.**, **b.c.**, and **c.a.** will be tangent to the circle, it is clear that the goal has been perfectly achieved.

---

### Proposition 5.

**To describe a circle about a given triangle, whether it be a <term>right-angled<note>original: "orthogonium"</note></term>, <term>obtuse-angled<note>original: "ambligonium"</note></term>, or <term>acute-angled<note>original: "oxigonium"</note></term> triangle.**

Let the assigned triangle be **a.b.c.** I wish to describe a circle about it; this is effectively the converse of the third proposition. I divide two of its sides, **a.b.** and **a.c.**, into equal halves: side **a.b.** at point **d**, and side **a.c.** at point **e**. From these points, I extend perpendicular lines to the lines **a.b.** and **a.c.**, and I draw them until they meet at point **f**. Let these lines be **d.f.** and **e.f.** They will indeed meet because, since both angles at **d** and **e** are right angles, if line **d.e.** were drawn, the two interior angles on the side where they are extended would be less than two right angles; therefore, they must meet according to the <term>penultimate postulate<note>This refers to Euclid's famous Parallel Postulate.</note></term>. 

From point **f**, which is the point of intersection and which I claim to be the center of the required circle, I draw lines to each of the angles: **f.a.**, **f.b.**, and **f.c.** Because in triangle **a.d.f.**, the two sides **a.d.** and **d.f.** are equal to the two sides **b.d.** and **d.f.** of triangle **b.d.f.**, and the angle **d** of one is equal to angle **d** of the other (since both are right angles), it follows from the 4th proposition of the first book <note>The "Side-Angle-Side" theorem.</note> that **f.a.** is equal to **f.b.** By the same reasoning, **f.a.** will be equal to **f.c.** when comparing the sides and angles of the two triangles **a.e.f.** and **c.e.f.** Therefore, by the 9th proposition of the third book, point **f** will be the center of the required circle. 

This is a universal demonstration for all types of triangles. However, because the author <note>Referring to Euclid.</note> seems to wish to vary the method by distinguishing between the right-angled, obtuse-angled, and acute-angled cases, each must be demonstrated individually. 

Let the proposed triangle be right-angled, and let angle **a** be the right angle. I divide side **b.c.**, which faces this right angle <note>The hypotenuse.</note>, into equal halves at point **f**. From this point **f**, which I claim is the center of the circle, I draw line **f.d.** to the midpoint of one of the two remaining sides, which is **d**. Because line **f.d.** divides two sides (**a.b.** and **b.c.**) of triangle **a.b.c.** equally, it will be parallel to the third side, namely line **a.c.**; for this was demonstrated above in the 39th proposition of the first book. 

And because angle **a** was set as a right angle, it follows from the second and third parts of the 29th proposition of the first book that both angles at point **d** are right angles. If line **f.a.** is then drawn, by the 4th proposition of the first book, line **a.f.** will be equal to line **b.f.** when comparing the sides and angles of triangles **a.d.f.** and **b.d.f.** against each other. Since line **b.f.** is equal to line **c.f.**, all three lines **b.f.**, **a.f.**, and **c.f.** will be equal to one another. Therefore, by the 9th proposition of the third book, **f** will be the center of the required circle. 

Next, let triangle **a.b.c.** be obtuse-angled, and let the [obtuse] angle be **a**...

<margin>
<note>Three geometric diagrams illustrate the circle constructions described in the text:
1. Top: A circle drawn around an <term>obtuse triangle<note>A triangle with one angle greater than 90 degrees.</note></term> **abc**. The center **f** lies outside the triangle. Midpoints **d** and **e** are marked on the sides, and a point **h** is shown on the base **bc**.
2. Middle: A circle drawn around an <term>acute triangle<note>A triangle where all angles are less than 90 degrees.</note></term> **abc**. The center **f** is located inside the triangle, where the perpendicular bisectors from midpoints **d** and **e** meet.
3. Bottom: A circle containing an <term>inscribed square<note>A square drawn so its four corners touch the edge of the circle.</note></term> **abcd**. Two diameters, **ac** and **bd**, intersect at the center **e** at right angles, defining the square's corners.</note>
</margin>

...is obtuse; side **b.c.**, which faces this obtuse angle, I divide into equal parts at point **h** <note>The original Latin reads "b," likely an OCR error for "h" as indicated in the diagram description.</note> from which, to the midpoints of the two remaining sides—which are **d** and **e**—I draw lines **h.d.** and **h.e.** Line **d.h.** will be parallel to **a.c.**, and **e.h.** parallel to **a.b.**, because of what was demonstrated above in the 39th [proposition] of the first [book] <note>original: 39.pꝛimi</note>: namely, that a line cutting two sides of any triangle into equal parts is parallel to the third side. Therefore, by the second part of the 29th [proposition] of the first [book], each of the two angles **h.d.b.** and **c.e.h.** will be equal to angle **a**, and thus each is obtuse. Therefore, having drawn perpendicular lines **d.f.** to line **a.b.** and **e.f.** to line **a.c.** until they meet at point **f**, I say that this point is the center of the circle. It is clear that they meet for the reason stated previously; each of them will cut line **b.c.**, which faces the obtuse angle, and they will meet outside the triangle **a.b.c.** Therefore, from point **f**, which is the point of their meeting, I draw lines **f.a.**, **f.b.**, and **f.c.** By the 4th [proposition] of the first [book] applied twice—first by comparing the sides and angles of the two triangles **a.d.f.** and **b.d.f.**, and then the other two, **a.e.f.** and **c.e.f.**—these lines will be equal. Therefore, by the 9th [proposition] of the third [book], **f** is the center of the sought circle.

Next, let the triangle **a.b.c.** be <term>acute-angled<note>original: oxigonius</note></term>. All its sides having been divided into equal parts—namely, side **a.b.** at point **d**, side **a.c.** at point **e**, and **b.c.** at point **h**—I draw lines **d.e.**, **d.h.**, and **e.h.** Line **d.h.** will be parallel to **a.c.** and **e.h.** to **a.b.** because of what was demonstrated in the 39th [proposition] of the first [book]. Therefore, by the second part of the 39th [proposition] of the first [book] <note>The text repeats 39, though likely referring to 29 again</note>, each of the angles **h.d.b.** and **c.e.h.** will be equal to angle **a**, and thus acute. Therefore, having drawn perpendiculars **d.f.** to line **a.b.** and **e.f.** to line **a.c.**, it is clear that they meet inside the triangle **a.b.c.** Let the point of meeting be **f**, which I say is the center of the circle. For I draw lines **f.a.**, **f.b.**, and **f.c.**, which by the 4th [proposition] of the first [book]—applied twice as before—will be equal. Therefore, by the 9th [proposition] of the third [book], **f** shall be the center of the sought circle.

¶ From the preceding, it is evident that if the triangle is <term>right-angled<note>original: orthogonius</note></term>, the center of the circumscribing circle will fall on the middle of the side that is opposite the right angle <note>The hypotenuse.</note>. If it is <term>obtuse-angled<note>original: ambligonius</note></term>, the center will fall outside the triangle. If, however, it is <term>acute-angled<note>original: oxigonius</note></term>, it will fall inside the triangle.

### Proposition 6.

### To describe a square within a given circle.

Let the given circle be **a.b.c.d.**, whose center is **e**. I wish to describe a square within it. I shall draw within it two diameters, **a.c.** and **b.d.**, intersecting each other at right angles <note>original: orthogonaliter</note> at the center **e**. I join their endpoints by drawing lines **a.b.**, **b.c.**, **c.d.**, and **d.a.**, which I say contain the sought square. For these lines will be equal to one another by the 4th [proposition] of the first [book] applied three times, because the four lines **e.a.**, **e.b.**, **e.c.**, and **e.d.** are equal [as radii], and the four angles at **e** are right angles. Each of the four angles **a**, **b**, **c**, and **d** is a right angle by the first part of the 30th [proposition] of the third [book], because each of them is [subtended] in a semicircle. Therefore, **a.b.c.d.** will be a square by definition, which is what was proposed.

# BOOK [IV]

<margin>
<note>A geometric diagram illustrates the conclusion of Proposition 7, showing a circle enclosed within a large square. Two perpendicular diameters intersect at the center point **c**, and lines drawn through the endpoints of these diameters form the outer square **fghk**. The square is divided into four smaller quadrants by the diameters.</note>
</margin>

...[ortho]gonally through the center **c**, and from the endpoints I draw lines in both directions at right angles <note>original: "orthogonaliter"</note> until each of them meets with the two side lines; and let the points of their intersection be **f, g, h, k** <note>The OCR reads "b" instead of "h", but the geometric logic and diagrams indicate "h" is the correct point.</note>. By the 15th conclusion of the third [book], each of the angles at the four points **a, b, c, d** will be a right angle. Since in the <term>quadrilateral<note>A four-sided polygon.</note></term> **a.f.b.c.** three angles (**a, b,** and **c**) are right angles, the fourth angle, **f**, must also be a right angle; for every quadrilateral has four angles equal to four right angles, as was demonstrated above in the 32nd [proposition] of the first [book]. By the same reasoning, each of the angles **g, h,** and **k** will be a right angle. Therefore, by the second part of the 28th [proposition] of the first [book], the two lines **f.g.** and **k.h.**, as well as the two lines **f.k.** and **g.h.**, are <term>parallel<note>original: "equidistantes"</note></term>. Thus, by the 34th [proposition] of the first [book], **f.k.** is equal to **g.h.**, and **f.g.** is equal to **k.h.** Furthermore, because by that same proposition **f.k.** is equal to **b.d.** and **f.g.** is equal to **a.c.**, and since **b.d.** is equal to **a.c.**, it follows that all four lines **f.k., g.h., f.g.** and **k.h.** are equal. Since the four angles **f, g, k,** and **h** are right angles, as proved before, therefore **f.g.k.h.** is a square by definition; which is what was to be proposed.

### Proposition .8.

<margin>
<note>A geometric diagram for Proposition 8 shows a square **abcd** with a circle drawn inside it. Lines connect the midpoints of the opposite sides (**f** to **h** and **g** to **e**), meeting at the center point **k**, which serves as the center for the inscribed circle.</note>
</margin>

**To describe** a circle within a given square.
¶ Let the given square be **a.b.c.d.** I wish to describe a circle within it; this is essentially the converse of [Proposition] 6. I divide each of its sides into two equal parts: **a.b.** at point **f**, **b.c.** at point **g**, **c.d.** at point **h**, and **d.a.** at point **e**. I then draw lines **e.g.** and **f.h.** intersecting each other at point **k**, which I claim to be the center of the circle. Indeed, **f.b.** will be parallel and equal to [the corresponding segment of] **a.b.** <note>The text likely means a segment like **e.k.**</note> by the 33rd [proposition] of the first [book], because **a.f.** and **d.b.** are equal and parallel. Similarly, by the same reasoning, **d.c.** and **a.b.** [are related]. Because all halves of the four sides of the square are equal to one another, then by the 34th [proposition] of the first [book], the four lines **k.e., k.f., k.g.,** and **k.h.** are equal. Therefore, by the 9th [proposition] of the third [book], **k** is the center of the sought-circle.

### Proposition .9.

<margin>
<note>A geometric diagram for Proposition 9 shows a square **abcd** inside a circle. The diagonals **ac** and **bd** intersect at the center point **e**, which is the center of the circle that passes through all four corners of the square.</note>
</margin>

**To describe** a circle about a given square.
¶ Let the square be **a.b.c.d.** I wish to describe a circle around it; this is essentially the converse of [Proposition] 7. I draw two diameters <note>In this context, diameters of the square, or diagonals.</note> **a.c.** and **b.d.** within it, intersecting at point **e**, which I claim is the center of the circle. Since lines **a.d.** and **a.b.** are equal, the angles **a.d.b.** and **a.b.d.** will be equal by the 5th [proposition] of the first [book]. And because the total angle **a** is a right angle, each of those angles will be half of a right angle by the 32nd [proposition] of the first [book]. ¶ In a similar way, it will be proved that any of the partial angles contained by the aforementioned diameters and the sides of the proposed square is half of a right angle. Therefore, because angle **e.a.d.** is equal to angle **e.d.a.**, the line **e.a.** will be equal to line **e.d.** by the 9th [proposition] of the first [book]. By the same reasoning, **e.a.** will be equal to **e.b.**, and **e.c.** equal to **e.d.** Consequently, because the four lines **e.a., e.b., e.c.,** and **e.d.** are equal, **e** will be the center of the sought-circle by the 9th [proposition] of the third [book]; which is what was to be proposed.

### Proposition .10.

**To construct** an <term>isosceles triangle<note>original: "duum equaliū laterum triangulum" — a triangle with two equal sides.</note></term> in which each of the two angles at the base is double the remaining angle.
¶ The intention is to describe a triangle with two equal sides and a third unequal side, where each of the angles upon the side which is the remainder <note>the base</note> is double the third angle. To do this, let any line be taken, which shall be **a.b.**, and let it be divided at point **c** according to what the 11th [proposition] of the second [book] teaches, so that the <term>rectangle<note>original: "illō quod fit ex..." — literally "that which is made from," referring to the area.</note></term> formed by **a.b.** and **b.c.** is equal to the square of **a.c.**

# BOOK IV

<margin>
<note>A geometric diagram illustrates the construction. A circle is shown with center point **a**. Points **e**, **d**, and **b** are marked on its circumference. Once point **a** is established as the center, let a circle **b.d.e** be described according to its magnitude. Within this circle, by the first [proposition] of this [book], let line **b.d** be fitted equal to line **a.c**, and let the two lines **d.a** and **d.c** be drawn. I say that triangle **a.b.d** is of the kind proposed <note>That is, an isosceles triangle where the base angles are double the vertex angle.</note>. Let a circle **d.c.a** be circumscribed around triangle **d.c.a** by the 5th [proposition] of this [book]. Because line **d.b** is equal to line **a.c**, the rectangle formed by <term>segments<note>Parts of a line.</note></term> **a.b** and **b.c** will be equal to the square of line **b.d**. Therefore, by the last [proposition] of the third [book], line **b.d** is <term>tangent<note>A line that touches the circumference of a circle at exactly one point without cutting through it.</note></term> to circle **d.c.a**. And by the 31st [proposition] of the same book, angle **c.d.b** is equal to angle **c.a.d**. If angle **c.d.a** is then taken as a common angle, the whole angle **b.d.a** will be equal to the two angles **c.a.d** and **c.d.a**. But by the 32nd [proposition] of the first [book], angle **b.c.d** is equal to these same angles because it is external to them. Therefore, angle **b.d.a** is equal to angle **b.c.d**. And since angle **a.d.b** is equal to angle **a.b.d** by the 5th [proposition] of the first [book] (because sides **a.d** and **a.b** are equal), angle **b.c.d** will be equal to angle **c.b.d**. Therefore, by the 6th [proposition] of the first [book], line **c.d** is equal to line **b.d**, and thus also equal to line **c.a**. Consequently, by the 5th [proposition] of the first [book], angle **c.a.d** is equal to angle **c.d.a**. Because each of the angles **c.d.b** and **c.d.a** is equal to angle **c.a.d**, the whole angle **a.d.b** is double the angle **d.a.b**. And therefore angle **a.b.d**, being equal to it, is also double the angle **b.a.d**, which is what was proposed. 

¶ Perhaps an opponent might say that circle **d.c.a**, circumscribed around the partial triangle, cuts circle **b.d.e** at some point on the <term>arc<note>A section of the curve of a circle.</note></term> **b.d**, such that it would simultaneously cut line **b.d**. In that case, the line would not be applied to the circle as the demonstration supposes, but would be a <term>secant<note>A line that intersects a circle at two points.</note></term> cutting through it. Let it be as the opponent proposes, if it were possible.

</margin>

And from point **b**, let a tangent **b.f** be drawn to that smaller circle, and let lines **f.a** and **f.d** be drawn. By the penultimate [proposition] of the third [book], the product of **a.b** and **b.c** will be equal to the square of **b.f**. Therefore, **b.f** is equal to **b.d**. Thus, by the 5th [proposition] of the first [book], angle **b.f.d** is equal to angle **b.d.f**. And because by the 31st [proposition] of the third [book] angle **b.f.a** is equal to angle **a.d.f**, it would follow that angle **b.d.f** is greater than angle **a.d.f**, which is impossible, since the latter is only a part of the former. 

¶ We can repel this in another way and show that the smaller circle will in no way cut line **b.d**. For perhaps he might say it cuts it without cutting arc **d.b** of the larger circle. Then the rectangle formed by **a.b** and **b.c** would be equal to the product of **d.b** and **b.h** <note>The OCR reads "b.b", but the logic of secants implies point **h**.</note>.
