### Proposition 11

<margin>
<note>A geometric diagram shows a regular pentagon inscribed within a circle. The vertices are labeled **a**, **d**, **b**, **c**, and **e**. Internal lines connect these vertices to form a five-pointed star (pentagram). To the left of the circle is an auxiliary triangle labeled with the number 2, representing the triangle constructed in the previous proposition.</note>
</margin>

To describe an equilateral and equiangular pentagon <note>A regular five-sided polygon where all sides and all internal angles are equal.</note> within a given circle.

¶ Let the given circle be **a.b.c**. I wish to describe an equilateral and equiangular pentagon within it. I designate a triangle such as the previous [proposition] proposed, which is [labeled] **2**. I describe another equiangular triangle within the given circle as the second [proposition] of this [book] teaches, which is triangle **a.b.c**. Let both angles **a.b.c** and **a.c.b** be double the angle **c.a.b**. I divide each of these [base angles] into equal parts by drawing lines **b.e** and **c.d**. By [Proposition] 25 of the third [book], the five arcs into which the five points **a, d, b, c, e** divide the circle will be mutually equal to each other, because the five angles that fall upon said arcs are mutually equal. Therefore, by connecting those five points with straight lines, which are **a.d, d.b, b.c, c.e,** and **e.a**, the pentagon **a.d.b.c.e** will be inscribed <note>Drawn inside a shape so that its vertices touch the boundary of the outer shape.</note> in the given circle as proposed. For it is equilateral by [Proposition] 28 of the third [book], since the five sides are <term>chords<note>Straight line segments whose endpoints both lie on a circular arc.</note></term> of five equal arcs; and it is also equiangular by [Proposition] 26 of the same [book], because the five arcs **d.a.e, a.e.c, e.c.b, c.b.d,** and **b.d.a**, upon which the angles of the pentagon itself fall, are mutually equal. Thus, the proposition is established.

### Proposition 12

<margin>
<note>A geometric diagram shows a regular pentagon circumscribed about a circle. The center of the circle is labeled **f**. The points where the pentagon touches the circle (tangency points) are **a**, **d**, **b**, **c**, and **e**. The vertices of the outer pentagon are **g**, **h**, **k**, **l**, and **m**. Radial lines connect the center **f** to each of the tangency points and each of the outer vertices.</note>
<note>Below the pentagon diagram is a smaller, fainter circle with several internal intersecting lines and construction points, likely representing a preliminary sketch or a different geometric proof.</note>
</margin>

To describe an equilateral and equiangular pentagon around <note>Circumscribing, or drawing a shape outside another so that they touch but do not intersect.</note> a given circle.

¶ Let the given circle be **a.b.c**, whose center is **f**. I wish to describe an equilateral and equiangular pentagon around it. Upon the circumference of this circle, as if I had inscribed a pentagon according to the teaching of the previous [proposition], I will mark five angular points, which are **a, d, b, c, e**. To these I will draw lines from the center: **f.a, f.d, f.b, f.c,** and **f.e**. From these same points, I will draw perpendicular lines to these [radial] lines in both directions until they meet at points **g, h, k, l,** and **m**. These lines will be <term>tangents<note>Lines that touch the circle at only one point.</note></term> to the circle by the corollary to [Proposition] 15 of the third [book]. To these points of intersection, I will draw lines from the center: **f.g, f.h, f.k, f.l,** and **f.m**. And because it was shown in the penultimate [proposition] <note>Proposition 36 of Book III in the standard numbering.</note> of the third [book] that if two tangent lines are drawn to a circle from any point marked outside it, those lines will be equal, line **g.a** will be equal to line **g.d**, and **h.d** to **h.b**, and **b.k** to **b.c**, and so on for the others. Furthermore, since the five arcs into which the five points **a, d, b, c, e** divide the circle are mutually equal, by [Proposition] 26 of the third [book], the five angles **a.f.d, d.f.b, b.f.c, c.f.e,** and **e.f.a** standing upon these arcs at the center **f** will be mutually equal to each other. Now, the two sides **a.g** and **f.a** of triangle **f.g.a** are equal to the two sides **d.g** and **f.d** of triangle **f.g.d**, and the side **g.f** is common [to both]. Therefore, by [Proposition] 8 of the first [book], their two angles, which are **a.f.g** and **d.f.g**, are mutually equal. For the same reason, the two angles **d.f.h** and **b.f.h** in triangles **d.f.h** and **b.f.h** [are equal]. Likewise, the two angles **b.f.k** and **c.f.k** are mutually equal. Similarly, each of the three remaining angles, which are **b.f.c, c.f.e,** and **e.f.a**, and each of the three [vertices] which are **k, l, m**, are divided into equal parts: the first by line **f.k**, the second by line **f.l**, and the third by line **f.m**. And because these three angles **b.f.c, c.f.e,** and **e.f.a** are mutually equal to each other and to the other two, which are **a.f.d** and **d.f.b**, their halves—which are the ten angles made at the center **f**—[will also be equal].

Because, therefore, the two angles **a** and **f** of triangle **g.a.f** are equal to the two angles **a** and **f** of triangle **m.a.f**, and side **a.f** is common, then by Proposition 26 of the first book, angle **g** of the one is equal to angle **m** of the other, and side **g.a** is equal to side **a.m**. But it is also equiangular; for since the two angles at **g** are equal to each other, and the two at **m** are likewise equal to each other, and partial angle **g** is equal to partial angle **m** (for both were proved before), then by the same common notion, total **g** will be equal to total **m**. And by the same reasoning, you will prove equality in the remaining angles; therefore it is equiangular. And thus what was proposed is established.

### Proposition 13

<margin>
<note>A geometric diagram shows a regular pentagon with vertices **a, b, c, d, e**. A circle is inscribed within the pentagon, with its center at **f**. Lines are drawn from the center **f** to each vertex (**a, b, c, d, e**) and perpendicular lines from the center **f** to points on the sides of the pentagon, labeled **g, h, k, l, m**. Below the main figure are two intersecting circles used for auxiliary geometric construction.</note>
</margin>

To describe <note>meaning to inscribe</note> a circle within a given equilateral and equiangular pentagon.
¶ Let the given equilateral and equiangular pentagon be **a.b.c.d.e** (for regarding others <note>irregular pentagons</note> it is not necessarily possible to do this). I wish to inscribe a circle within it. This is almost the converse of Proposition 11. I divide two of its adjacent angles, which are **a** and **e**, into equal parts by drawing lines **a.f** and **e.f**, until they meet at point **f** within the pentagon itself, which I say is the center of the circle. For they will meet because half of total angle **a**, and similarly total angle **e**, is less than a right angle.
¶ For if they do not meet inside the pentagon, they must meet either outside the pentagon, or on a side of the pentagon, or in its angle which is opposite to both of the diverse angles. Suppose first they meet outside at point **f**, and let line **b.f** be drawn. And because the two sides **e.a** and **a.f** of triangle **e.a.f** are equal to the two sides **b.a** and **a.f** of triangle **b.a.f**, and angle **a** of the one [is equal to] angle **a** of the other, then by Proposition 4 of the first book, base **e.f** will be equal to base **f.b**. And since partial angle **a** is equal to partial angle **e** (because total **a** is equal to total **e**), then by Proposition 6 of the first book, **f.a** will be equal to **f.e**. Therefore **f.a** is equal to **f.b**. Thus by Proposition 5 of the first book, the two angles, total **b** and partial **a**, are equal. Therefore, partial **a** is equal to or greater than total **a**, which is impossible. Therefore, let them meet at point **f** upon side **b.c**. By arguing through the premises and in the aforementioned manner, partial angle **a** would be equal to total angle **a**, which is impossible. But if perhaps they meet in angle **c**, it will be by the same reasoning and in the same way that **c.b** is equal to **c.a**, and therefore as before, partial angle **a** would be equal to total angle **a**. Since this cannot be, let the point of meeting, which is **f**, be inside the pentagon, from which I draw five perpendiculars to its five sides, which are **f.g, f.h, f.k, f.l, f.m** <note>The printed text uses **b** where modern conventions or standard proofs usually place **h** in this sequence</note>. And to two of its neighboring angles on either side of the equally divided angles, which are **b** and **d**, I draw lines **f.b** and **f.d**. And because the two angles **a** and **m** of triangle **a.f.m** are equal to the two angles **a** and **g** of triangle **a.f.g**, and side **a.f** is common, then by Proposition 26 of the first book, **f.m** is equal to **f.g**. By the same you will also prove **f.l** equal to **f.m** by taking the two triangles **e.f.m** and **e.f.l**. Because, again, the two sides **a.f** and **a.b** of triangle **a.f.b** are equal to the two sides **a.f** and **a.e** of triangle **a.f.e**, and the angle **a** of the one is equal to the angle **a** of the other, then by Proposition 4 of the first book, partial angle **b** will be equal to partial angle **e**. And because total **b** is equal to total **e**, and total **e** is divided into equal parts, total **b** will also be divided into equal parts. ¶ In the same way, you will prove total **d** is divided into equal parts on account of the equality of partial **d** and partial **a**, by taking triangles **e.a.f** and **e.d.f**. Because therefore

### Proposition 14.

<margin>
<note>A geometric diagram depicts a regular pentagon with vertices **a, b, c, d, e** and center point **f**. Lines connect the center **f** to each vertex. A circumscribed circle is drawn so that its circumference passes through all five vertices of the pentagon.</note>
</margin>

**T**o circumscribe a circle about a given pentagon that is equilateral and equiangular.
Let the given equilateral and equiangular pentagon be **a.b.c.d.e.**, as before. This construction is only necessary for regular polygons <note>Euclid specifies equilateral and equiangular because irregular pentagons may not have a single point equidistant from all vertices.</note>. I wish to circumscribe a circle about it; this is essentially the converse of Proposition 12. I divide its two adjacent angles, **a** and **e**, into equal parts by drawing lines **a.f.** and **e.f.** until they meet inside the pentagon at point **f**. They will indeed meet inside the pentagon, as was proven in the previous proposition. From this point of intersection, I draw lines to the remaining angles: **f.b.**, **f.c.**, and **f.d.** Since the two sides **a.f.** and **a.b.** of triangle **a.f.b.** are equal to the two sides **a.f.** and **a.e.** of triangle **a.f.e.**, and angle **a** of the one is equal to angle **a** of the other, then by Proposition 4 of the first book, **f.b.** will be equal to **f.e.**, and the partial angle at **b** will be equal to the partial angle at **e**. And because the whole angle at **b** is equal to the whole angle at **a**, and the whole angle at **e** was divided into equal parts, the whole angle at **b** will similarly be divided into equal parts. In this same way, you will prove that each of the angles at **c** and **d** is divided into equal parts, and that the five lines **f.a.**, **f.b.**, **f.c.**, **f.d.**, and **f.e.** are equal. Therefore, by Proposition 9 of the third book, **f** will be the center of the circle; and thus the proposition is clear.

### Proposition 15.

<margin>
<note>A geometric diagram illustrates the construction of an inscribed hexagon. A circle with center **e** has a vertical diameter **a-e-c**. A second circle of the same radius is drawn with its center at the bottom point **c**, passing through the center **e** and intersecting the main circle at points **b** and **d**. Diameters are drawn through these intersections (**b-e-g** and **d-e-f**). Connecting the points **a, f, g, c, d, b** forms a regular hexagon.</note>
</margin>

**T**o inscribe an equilateral and equiangular hexagon within a proposed circle. From this it is also manifest that the side of a hexagon is equal to the half-diameter <term>semidiameter|The radius of the circle.</term> of the circle in which it is inscribed.
Let the proposed circle be **a.b.c.d.**, with center **e**. I wish to inscribe within it an equilateral and equiangular hexagon. I draw the diameter **a.e.c.** and, using the length of the radius **e.c.**, I set the center at point **c** and describe a circle **e.b.d.**, cutting the first circle at two points, **b** and **d**. From these points, I draw two diameters through the first circle, which are **b.e.g.** and **d.e.f.** I then join the ends of these three diameters with six lines: **a.f.**, **f.b.**, **b.c.**, **c.d.**, **d.g.**, and **g.a.**, which I say form the sought-after hexagon. For as the first proposition of the first book demonstrates, each of the triangles **b.e.c.** and **c.e.d.** is equilateral. Therefore, they are also equiangular by Proposition 5 of the same book. Thus, by Proposition 32 of the first book, the two angles **b.e.c.** and **c.e.d.**, along with another equal to them, make up two right angles, because each of them is a third of two right angles <note>In modern terms, each angle is 60 degrees, and three of them make 180 degrees.</note>. But by Proposition 13 of the same book, these together with angle **d.e.g.** are equal to two right angles. Therefore, angle **d.e.g.** is equal to each of the others. Wherefore, by Proposition 15 of the same book, the six angles at **e** are equal to one another. Consequently, by Proposition 25 of the third book, the arcs upon which they fall are equal. Therefore, their chords—which are the sides of the hexagon—are also equal by Proposition 28 of the third book. It is therefore equilateral; but it is also equiangular by Proposition 26 of the third book, because the six arcs into which the vertices of the hexagon divide the circle, when taken two by two, are equal to each other—as arc **a.f.b.** is equal to arc **f.b.c.** Thus, angle **f**, which stands upon the first segment <note>original: "prooemio"</note>, is equal to angle **b**, which stands upon the second. The same holds for the others. Therefore, the proposition is established.
From this, the corollary is clear: that the radius and the side of a hexagon are...

By doing this for all of them, it will be clear that they are equiangular by this common principle of knowledge: those things whose halves are equal must also be equal as wholes.

### Proposition 16.

<margin>
<note>A geometric diagram shows a circle with various points marked on its circumference. Point **a** is at the far left, **c** is at the right, and **b** is toward the bottom. Point **d** is marked exactly halfway along the arc between **b** and **c**. Radii extend from the center to each of these points.</note>
</margin>

**T**o design an equilateral and equiangular <term>quindecagon</term><note>original: "quindecagonum"; a polygon with fifteen sides.</note> within a given circle.
Furthermore, to describe an equilateral and equiangular quindecagon about any assigned circle, and to describe a circle within a given quindecagon.
Let **a.b.c.** be the given circle. I wish to inscribe an equilateral and equiangular quindecagon within it; then also to circumscribe one, and to describe a circle within such a proposed quindecagon. The author does not, however, propose to describe a circle *around* such a quindecagon, because he gives enough understanding of this through the other things he proposes.

In the given circle, according to the teaching of the second proposition of this book <note>Reference to Proposition 2: Inscribing an equilateral triangle.</note>, I draw the side of an equilateral triangle, let it be **a.c.**, and according to the teaching of the eleventh <note>The text says "scđi" (second), but likely refers to Proposition 11: Inscribing a regular pentagon.</note>, the side of an equilateral and equiangular pentagon, let it be **a.b.**
Because the arc **a.c.** is a third part of the entire circumference, and the arc **a.b.** is a fifth part of it, the remainder between them—which is arc **b.c.**—will be two-fifteenths of the whole circumference. For in every whole, a third exceeds a fifth by two-thirds of that same fifth, or by two-fifths of that same third, which is to say, by two-fifteenths of the whole. This is evident in the numbers 5 and 3, which are the fifth and third parts of the number 15. Its third (5) exceeds its fifth (3) by two units, which are two-thirds of the three (the fifth part), or two-fifths of the five (the third part), or two-fifteenths of 15 (the whole).
Therefore, by dividing the arc **b.c.** into equal parts at point **d**, it is clear that each of the two arcs **c.d.** and **d.b.** is one-fifteenth of the entire circumference. Thus, by drawing the chords **c.d.** and **d.b.** and fitting equal chords continuously within the given circle according to the first proposition of this book, the proposed figure will be completed.

to circumscribe [a 15-sided polygon around a circle] and to inscribe a circle within a quindecagon <note>original: "quindecagono"; a fifteen-sided polygon</note> and also to circumscribe it, which you will easily accomplish if propositions 12, 13, 7, and 14 of this book are fully understood. ¶ And note that for whatever equilateral figure we know how to inscribe in a circle, we also know how to inscribe and circumscribe a figure of double the number of sides in a circle, and the circle within it. For this was demonstrated above in Proposition 15 of this book: that every equilateral figure inscribed in a circle is also equiangular. And because we know how to inscribe this in a circle, the other three operations follow through propositions 12, 13, and 14 of this book. ¶ Therefore, because we know how to inscribe an equilateral triangle, we shall know through this how to inscribe a hexagon <note>original: "exagonū"; a 6-sided polygon</note>, and through the hexagon a dodecagon <note>original: "duodecagonū"; a 12-sided polygon</note>, and through the dodecagon a figure of 24 sides, and so on to infinity by doubling. Understand the same regarding the quindecagon; for through it, figures of 30 and 60 sides will be known, and all those whose number of sides is continually doubled. ¶ However, the knowledge of other figures which this [book] does not teach, or which cannot be obtained through these, is difficult and of little use, such as heptagons <note>7-sided</note>, nonagons <note>9-sided</note>, and hendecagons <note>11-sided</note>. <note>A geometric diagram showing a circle with several construction lines. Points labeled f, g, o, e, c, m, h, b, a, l, d illustrate the geometric process of trisecting an angle. Lines connect the center c to various points on the circumference and across the interior.</note>

**Given** an angle, to divide it into three equal parts. Let the given angle be **c**. I wish to divide it into three equal angles, which I do in this way. <meta>This page transitions from the conclusion of Book IV, which dealt with the inscription and circumscription of polygons in circles, to the beginning of Book V. <header>BOOK V</header>

->Definition 1<-

<note>An ornamental woodcut initial 'P' is decorated with floral and leaf-like motifs.</note>
A **P**art is a quantity of a [larger] quantity, the lesser of the greater, when the lesser measures the greater. <note>original: "numeret"; in Euclidean geometry, one magnitude "measures" another if it divides into it exactly without a remainder. We might call this a "factor" or "divisor" today.</note>
¶ A part is sometimes taken in the strict sense: and this is that which, taken a certain number of times, constitutes its whole precisely, without deficiency or excess. It is said to "measure" its whole by that number according to which it is taken for the constitution of that whole. This type of part, which we call "multiplicative," is defined here. ¶ Sometimes it is taken in the general sense: and this is any lesser quantity which, no matter how many times it is taken, constitutes either less or more than its whole. This we call "aggregative," <note>An "aggregative" part is any portion of a whole, like 3 being a part of 4, whereas a "multiplicative" part must divide the whole evenly, like 2 being a part of 4.</note> because together with another different quantity it constitutes its whole, but by itself, no matter how many times it is taken, it does not produce it.

->Definition 2<-

<note>An ornamental woodcut initial 'M' is decorated with floral and leaf-like motifs.</note>
A **M**ultiple is the greater of the lesser when the lesser measures it.
¶ "Part" is said in relation to the "whole," and their mutual relation consists in these two extremes. Therefore, having defined the lesser extreme, he here defines the greater. He calls it "multiple" because the lesser constitutes it when taken a certain number of times. Therefore, part and multiple are relative terms. For every part is a submultiple, as is clear from its definition.

->Definition 3<-

<note>An ornamental woodcut initial 'P' is decorated with floral and leaf-like motifs.</note>
A **R**atio <note>original: "Proportio"; while the Latin says "proportion," in modern mathematical English, Euclid’s "proportio" in this context refers to a "ratio" between two things. "Proportion" is reserved for the equality of two ratios.</note> is a certain relation in respect of size between two quantities of the same kind.
¶ A ratio is the relation of two things of the same kind to one another in that one of them is greater or lesser than the other, or equal to it. For ratio is found not only in quantities, but in weights, powers, and sounds. Indeed, Plato in the *Timaeus* <note>A famous dialogue by the Greek philosopher Plato concerning the nature of the physical world and the cosmos.</note> wishes there to be ratio in weights and powers where he shows the number of the elements. That there is ratio in sounds is clear from music. For as Boethius <note>An influential 6th-century scholar; his works on the "quadrivium" (arithmetic, music, geometry, and astronomy) were the standard textbooks of the Middle Ages.</note> says in his fourth book, if any string is divided into two unequal parts, there will be the same ratio between the parts and their sounds, in an inverse manner. But in whatever things ratio is found, they participate in the nature and property of quantity. For it is not found in any two things except in that one of them is greater or lesser than the other, or equal to it. ¶ Now, the property of quantity is to be called equal or unequal according to it, as Aristotle <note>The Greek philosopher; this refers to his work "The Categories" (*Predicamenta*).</note> wishes in his *Categories*. From this it is clear that ratio is found primarily in quantity, and through quantity in all other things. Nor is there a ratio in any things to which there is not a similar ratio in some quantities. For this reason Euclid rightly said that ratio exists simply in quantity when he defined it through the relation of two quantities of the same kind to one another. ¶ The meaning of this definition is: that a ratio is the relation of two quantities to one another which is observed in that one of them is greater than, lesser than, or equal to the other. From this it is clear that they must be of the same kind: such as two numbers, or two lines, or two surfaces, or two bodies, or two places, or two times. For it cannot...

<header>BOOK V</header>

...cannot say a line is greater or smaller than a surface, or a body <note>original: "corpore"; referring to a three-dimensional solid.</note>, nor time than a place. Rather, a line is compared to a line, and a surface to a surface. For only things of the same kind <note>original: "univoca"; items belonging to the same category of measurement.</note> are comparable. However, when it says a "certain relationship," do not understand this as "noted" or "known," but as "determined." So the sense is: A proportion <note>The Latin "proportio" here refers to the relationship between two magnitudes, which modern mathematics calls a "ratio."</note> is a determined relationship of two quantities; so determined, I say, that it is this and no other. It is not necessary that every relationship of two quantities be known by us, or even known by nature.
¶ For there is a proportion of discrete things, such as numbers, and another of continuous things. In numbers, the smaller is a "part" or "parts" of the larger, as is demonstrated in the seventh book; therefore, in all of them, there is a certain and known relationship.
¶ But in continuous things, proportion is more broad: it exists where the smaller quantity is a part or parts of the larger; and in all such cases, through the mediation of numbers, the proportion is known, and it is called **rational**. All such quantities are also called **communicating** <note>original: "communicantes"; in modern terms, these are "commensurable" magnitudes that can be measured by a common unit.</note> because one and the same measure necessarily measures them. Hence all numbers are communicating, for unity measures all of them. There is also a case where the smaller is not a part or parts of the larger, and in such cases the proportion is not known, neither to us nor to nature. This is called an **irrational** proportion, and these quantities are **incommunicating** <note>original: "incommunicantes"; in modern terms, "incommensurable." A famous example is the relationship between the side and the diagonal of a square.</note>. From this it follows: whatever proportion is found in numbers is found in every kind of continuous thing—as in lines, surfaces, bodies, and times—but not conversely. For there are infinite proportions found in continuous things which the nature of numbers does not support. But whatever proportion is found in one kind of continuous thing is found in all others. For in whatever way any line relates to any other, so any surface relates to some other, and any body to some other; and similarly with time. But it is not so with any number to any other. Thus, proportion is broader in continuous things than in discrete things. From which it is manifest that geometric proportion is of greater abstraction than arithmetic proportion; for every proportion with which arithmetic deals is rational, but geometry considers rational and irrational proportions equally.

**P**roportionality is the similarity of proportions.
¶ As if we say that as is the proportion of *a* to *b*, so also is the proportion of *c* to *d*. The proportion that is between *a* and *b* is similar to that which is between *c* and *d*. This similarity which results from these proportions is called proportionality.

**Q**uantities which are said to have a **continuous proportionality** are those whose equal multiples are either equal, or add to or subtract from themselves equally without interruption.
¶ Having assumed a division of proportionality into "continuous" and "discontinuous," he defines the dividing members. And first, the continuous—or to speak more truly, having assumed a division of proportionals into "continuously proportional" and "not continuously proportional"—he defines not "continuous proportionality," but "continuously proportional" and "incontinually proportional." However, the definition of continuous proportionality and discontinuous proportionality is clear enough through the definition of continuous and discontinuous proportionals.
¶ Continuous proportionality occurs when, in any number of quantities of the same kind, the first precedes the second in the same proportion as any other precedes its nearest follower—as when we say, as *a* is to *b*, so is *b* to *c*, and *c* is to *d*. Each of them will be both antecedent and consequent, except the first, which is only an antecedent, and the last, which is only a consequent. <meta>This page continues the introductory concepts of Book V, specifically defining how proportions (ratios) are compared. It concludes the discussion on why only like-quantities can be compared and introduces the distinction between "continuous" proportionality (a:b = b:c) and "discontinuous" or "discrete" proportionality (a:b = c:d). It also begins explaining Euclid's famous "equimultiple" definition of equal ratios.</meta>

<header>BOOK V</header>

...of proportions <note>original: "proportionum"; continuing from the previous page's discussion on why measurements must be of the same kind.</note>, because no proportion exists between quantities of different kinds; and this will be established, at a minimum, in three terms. ¶ However, in discontinuous <note>original: "incontinua"; though the OCR text here appears to say "continua," the context of four terms and the ability to compare different kinds of pairs clearly describes discrete or discontinuous proportionality.</note> proportionality, there are four quantities, whether all are of the same kind or the first two are of one kind and the last two are of another. In this proportion, as the first precedes the second, so the third precedes the fourth: as when we say, as *a* is to *b*, so *c* is to *d*. Any of these will be either an antecedent <note>The first term in a ratio.</note> or a consequent <note>The second term in a ratio.</note>; and it is not necessary that all four be of the same kind, as was required in continuous proportionality. This is because the consequent of the first proportion does not continue into the antecedent of the second; rather, it is possible for them to be of the same kind, and it is possible for them to be different. For just as it happens that a line is found to be double or triple to another line, so a surface is to a surface, a body to a body, a time to a time, and a number to a number. 
¶ Having seen what continuous and discontinuous proportionality are, let us explain the aforementioned definition of continuous proportionals. It says that quantities are in continuous proportion when their multiples are either equal to each other, or they equally add to or subtract from one another without interruption. For example: Let there be three quantities of the same kind, *a*, *b*, and *c*, for which equimultiples *d*, *e*, and *f* are taken. Thus, just as *d* is a multiple of *a*, so *e* is a multiple of *b*, and *f* of *c*; and all will be of the same kind. For multiples and submultiples <note>original: "submultiplicia"; an aliquot part or a quantity that fits into another a whole number of times.</note> are of the same kind. Let it be that *d*, *e*, and *f* are either equal to one another, or they behave similarly in adding or subtracting, so that just as *d* adds to *e* or subtracts from it, so *e* adds to *f* or subtracts from it. When these multiples behave in this way, the three quantities *a*, *b*, and *c* will be in continuous proportion. 
¶ However, you should not understand these multiples to behave "similarly in adding or subtracting" in terms of the specific quantity of the difference—that is, exceeding by equal differences—otherwise the definition would be false. For if you take any quantities of the same kind exceeding by equal differences, and take their equimultiples, those multiples will also exceed each other by equal differences. Thus they behave "similarly" in adding and subtracting regarding the quantity of the excess. Yet, the original quantities are not in continuous proportion; rather, the smaller ratio is always followed by a larger ratio. This happens because their multiples do not exceed each other similarly in terms of **proportion**, but only in terms of the amount of excess. In such cases, there is a larger proportion among the smaller multiples. For example: take three numbers exceeding each other by equal differences, specifically in an arithmetic progression <note>original: "arismetice"</note>, such as 2, 3, and 4. All equimultiples of these three exceed each other equally: their doubles by two, their triples by three, and so on. Yet 2, 3, and 4 are not in continuous proportion. In fact, the first ratio is larger than the second: the proportion of 3 to 2 is **sesquialteral** <term>sesquialtera: a ratio of 1.5 to 1, or 3:2</term>, while the proportion of 4 to 3 is **sesquitertial** <term>sesquitertia: a ratio of 1.33 to 1, or 4:3</term>. Because there is no similarity of proportions between them, there is no proportionality, neither continuous nor discontinuous. It is clear, therefore, that this "similarity" of addition or subtraction is not to be understood regarding the quantity of the excess, but regarding the proportion. Thus, the sense of the previous definition is: continuous proportionals are those whose multiples are all in continuous proportion. But he [Euclid] did not wish to propose the definition in this form because then he would be defining the same thing by the same thing <note>This is a critique of circular definitions; Euclid avoids using the word "proportion" to define "proportion."</note>. However, this is clearly interchangeable with his definition. 
The three quantities *a*, *b*, and *c* must be of the same kind so that their multiples may be equal to each other or behave similarly in addition and subtraction. For if *a* and *b* were of different kinds, then *d* and *e* (the multiples of *a* and *b*) would also be of those same different kinds. Because multiples and submultiples are of the same kind as their originals, *d* would not be equal to *e*, nor greater, nor smaller. For quantities of different kinds are not comparable to one another.

The top diagram shows three horizontal lines of decreasing length, labeled 'a', 'b', and 'c' with the numbers 4, 2, and 1 written above them respectively. These represent a continuous proportion where each magnitude is double the next (4:2 = 2:1). Below them is a small segment labeled 'd' with the number 1, acting as a unit. The second diagram illustrates a more complex relationship with lines: a long line 'a' (12) is shown alongside segments 'e' (6) and 'f' (3), and a separate pair 'b' (2) and 'c' (1), illustrating how different sets of magnitudes can share the same ratios (12:6 = 2:1).</note>

# BOOK V

<note>A diagram in the left margin shows eight horizontal line segments of varying lengths. They are labeled with letters and numerical values to illustrate the concept of proportionality through multiples: f (12), e (8), c (6), a (4), d (3), b (2), h (9), g (6).</note>

Quantities which are said to be in **one and the same proportion**—the first to the second and the third to the fourth—are those for which, if any equal multiples <term>equimultiples; multiples of the same degree, such as doubling or tripling both terms</term> are taken of the first and third, and any equal multiples are taken of the second and fourth, the multiples of the first and third are either both greater than, both less than, or both equal to the multiples of the second and fourth, respectively, when compared in that same order.

¶ Having previously set down the definition of **continuously proportional** quantities, he here sets down the definition of **discontinuously proportional** <note>Also known as "discrete" proportion (a:b = c:d).</note> quantities. This occurs when, for any four quantities, if equal multiples are taken of the first and third, and likewise equal multiples of the second and fourth, and the multiple of the first relates to the multiple of the second by way of addition <note>original: "additione"; meaning the first multiple is greater than the second</note>, or subtraction <note>original: "diminutione"; meaning it is less than the second</note>, or equality, in the same way that the multiple of the third relates to the multiple of the fourth; then the proportion of the first to the second will be the same as the third to the fourth. 
*For example:* Let there be four quantities: **a, b, c, d**. Take equal multiples of the first (**a**) and third (**c**), such as the doubles, which are **e** and **f**. Likewise, for the second (**b**) and fourth (**d**), take other equal multiples, such as the triples, which are **g** and **h**. Let these four multiples be compared to one another according to the order of the first four quantities: specifically, **e** compared to **g**, and **f** to **h** (rather than **e** to **f** or **g** to **h**). If they match in addition, subtraction, or equality—meaning that if **e** is greater than **g**, then **f** is also greater than **h**; or if **e** is less than **g**, then **f** is also less than **h**; or if **e** is equal to **g**, then **f** is equal to **h**—then the proportion of **a** to **b** is the same as **c** to **d**. 
This "similarity" in adding or subtracting should be understood here as in the definition of continuous proportions: not regarding the *amount* of the excess <note>the specific numerical difference</note>, but regarding the proportion itself. As for the phrase "taken in the same order," it should be understood as explained: the multiples are not compared according to the order of the quantities from which they were derived (e.g., the multiple of the first compared to the multiple of the third), but according to the original order of the four quantities: specifically, the multiple of the first to the multiple of the second, and the multiple of the third to the multiple of the fourth.
Therefore, the sense of this definition is: Four quantities are **discontinuously proportional** when the proportion of the first to the second is the same as the third to the fourth, provided that when equal multiples are taken of the first and third, and equal multiples of the second and fourth, the proportion of the first multiple to the second will be as the third multiple is to the fourth. However, he did not define it in this exact form for the reason previously stated, although in reality they are the same.
It is not necessary for the four quantities (**a, b, c, d**) to be of the same kind, because the second (**b**) does not continue into a proportion with the third (**c**); rather, the first two can be of one kind and the following two of another. This is evident because it is necessary to relate the multiple of the first to the multiple of the second, and the multiple of the third to the multiple of the fourth—not the multiple of the first to the third, nor the second to the fourth—since the first and third (or second and fourth) are not always of the same kind. It was necessary to take equal multiples of the first and third, and likewise equal multiples of the second and fourth (rather than equal multiples of the first and second), because unless the terms of the first proportion are linked with the terms of the second through the taking of multiples, there would be no way to explain why the proportion of **a** to **b** is the same as **c** to **d**.

# BOOK V

<note>Five groups of horizontal line segments are arranged in pairs in the right margin to illustrate the numerical proportions and comparisons discussed in the text.

> When equimultiples are taken of the first and the third quantities, and likewise equimultiples are taken of the second and the fourth, if the multiple of the **first exceeds** the multiple of the **second**, but the multiple of the **third does not exceed** the multiple of the **fourth**, then the first is said to have a **greater ratio** to the second than the third has to the fourth.

¶ Having defined proportional quantities, the author now defines **non-proportional** <term>improportional; quantities that do not share the same ratio</term> quantities. Non-proportionality exists when the similarity of proportions is lacking, which happens in two ways: either because the ratio of the first to the second is greater than the third to the fourth, or because it is less. Therefore, there are two species of this condition. The first is when the ratio of the first to the second is greater than the third to the fourth, which is called **greater non-proportionality**. ¶ The second is when the ratio of the first to the second is less than the third to the fourth, called **lesser non-proportionality**. He defines here those among which there is a greater ratio of the first to the second than the third to the fourth; however, he does not provide a separate definition for the lesser ratio, as it is evident from the other.

Therefore, when there are four quantities, and equimultiples <term>multiples of the same degree, such as both being tripled</term> are taken of the first and the third, and equimultiples of the second and the fourth, and the multiples of the first and second do not relate to each other in the same way as the multiples of the third and fourth do in terms of excess, deficit, or equality, then those four quantities are non-proportional. 

If it should happen that the multiple of the first is equal to the multiple of the second, but the multiple of the third is less than the multiple of the fourth; **or** that the multiple of the first is greater than the multiple of the second, while the multiple of the third is equal or less; **or** if the multiple of the first is greater than the multiple of the second, and similarly the multiple of the third is greater than the multiple of the fourth, but the first pair exceeds by a larger proportion (not necessarily a larger absolute quantity); **or** if the multiple of the first is less than the multiple of the second, and similarly the third is less than the fourth, but the first pair is less diminished in its proportion—in any of these four ways, the ratio of the first to the second is greater than the third to the fourth. 

Examples of all these can be clearly taken from numbers. That "excess" of the first multiple over the second (while the third does not exceed the fourth), of which the author speaks in the definition, has a broad meaning that encompasses these four modes. Thus, the sense of this definition is: when multiples are taken as proposed, if the ratio of the first multiple to the second is greater than the ratio of the third multiple to the fourth, then the ratio of the first quantity to the second is greater than the third to the fourth. He did not define it under this general form for the common reason mentioned before <note>Euclid often preferred specific, testable conditions over abstract generalities</note>. Or we can say that the "excess" of the first multiple over the second—while the third does not—is taken literally as the words sound; although this technically only describes the second of the four modes mentioned, it is in fact sufficient to establish a greater ratio in any of the cases. Euclid chose this particular phrasing because it is the clearest of all the modes and sufficient for a formal definition.

...for there is a greater ratio of the first of four quantities to the second than of the third to the fourth, whenever it happens that some equimultiples <note>equimultiples: multiples of different quantities multiplied by the same number (e.g., 2 times A and 2 times C)</note> can be found for the first and the third. When these are compared to any equimultiples of the second and the fourth, the multiple of the first is found to exceed the multiple of the second, but the multiple of the third does not exceed the multiple of the fourth. Nor can this be found to happen unless there is a greater ratio of the first to the second than of the third to the fourth, as we shall demonstrate below after the tenth proposition of this book.

However, these <term>non-proportional; quantities that do not share the same ratio</term> quantities can be of different kinds, just as <term>non-continuously; discrete quantities that are not part of a single sequence</term> proportional quantities are, if there is a non-continuous non-proportionality between them: as if it were said that the ratio of **a** to **b** is greater than **c** to **d**. If, however, there is a continuous non-proportionality, they will all necessarily be of the same kind, just as they are in continuous proportionality, as if it were said that the ratio of **a** to **b** is greater than that of **b** to **c**.

### Definition 9

> **A proportion is established among at least three terms.**

¶ After the author has defined ratio, proportion, and proportional or non-proportional quantities, he now shows what is the minimum number of terms among which a proportion can exist. He does not set a maximum number because it is not possible to reach one; for any ratio can be continued through infinite terms, whether it is a <term>rational; a ratio that can be expressed as a ratio of whole numbers</term> proportion or an <term>irrational; a ratio that cannot be expressed as simple whole numbers, like the square root of two</term> one. 

For a proportion, at least two similar ratios are required, because a proportion is a similarity of ratios. Every ratio has an <term>antecedent; the first term in a ratio</term> and a <term>consequent; the second term in a ratio</term>. Therefore, every proportion has at least two antecedents and two consequents. This is impossible to achieve in fewer than three terms, in which the middle term becomes both an antecedent and a consequent; and therefore the proportion will be continuous. Thus, a continuous proportion will be established among at least three terms. A non-continuous <note>also called discrete</note> proportion, however, will not be found in fewer than four terms, because in such a case every term is either only an antecedent or only a consequent. Understand the same regarding the minimum number of terms for non-proportionality: if it is continuous, it will be among at least three terms; if non-continuous, among at least four.

### Definition 10

> **If there are three continuously proportional quantities, the ratio of the first to the third is called the duplicate ratio of the first to the second.**

¶ He defines the ratio that exists between the extreme terms of a continuous proportion consisting of three terms. He says that if the ratio of the first to the second is as the second is to the third, then the ratio of the first to the third will be as the <term>duplicate; a ratio composed by multiplying a ratio by itself</term> ratio of the first to the second—that is, composed of two such ratios. Or, which is the same thing: the ratio of the first to the third will be as the ratio of the first to the second multiplied by itself. 

For example, in numbers: Let there be three continuously proportional numbers, and let them be continuously double, such as 2, 4, and 8. The ratio of the first to the third (2 to 8) will be like the ratio of the first to the second (2 to 4) multiplied by itself. Now, the ratio of the first to the second is double; but double multiplied by itself produces quadruple <note>2/4 x 4/8 results in 2/8, which is a 1:4 ratio</note>. Hence, the ratio of the extremes is quadruple—namely, a double of a double. Or, according to the previous explanation, the ratio of the extremes is as the duplicate ratio of the first to the second, because quadruple consists of two doubles.

### Definition 11

> **When there are four continuously proportional quantities, the ratio of the first to the fourth is called the triplicate ratio of the first to the second.**

¶ He defines the ratio that exists between the extreme terms <note>extreme terms: the first and last values in a sequence or proportion</note> of a continuous proportionality <term>continuous proportionality: a sequence where the second term of one ratio becomes the first term of the next, such as A:B = B:C = C:D</term> consisting of four terms. He says that if there are four quantities in continuous proportion, the ratio of the first to the fourth will be like the ratio of the first to the second **triplicated** <note>triplicated: in modern terms, this is the ratio cubed (x³)</note>; that is, composed of three such ratios. This is because three such ratios are found within it. Or, what is the same thing: the ratio of the first to the fourth will be like the first to the second triplicated—that is, multiplied by itself and then multiplied by the resulting product. **For example**, in numbers: Suppose there are four numbers in continuous proportion, and let them be in a triple ratio, such as 1, 3, 9, and 27. The ratio of the first to the fourth <note>Here, the ratio of 27 to 1</note> will be like the ratio of the first to the second <note>3 to 1</note> multiplied by itself and then multiplied by that product. The ratio of the first to the second is triple; triple multiplied by itself produces a ninefold ratio, and triple multiplied by that ninefold ratio produces a twenty-sevenfold ratio. Therefore, the ratio of the extremes will be twenty-sevenfold, which is the "triple of the triple" <note>original: "triplum tripli," meaning the cube of the base ratio</note>. Or, according to the previous explanation, the ratio of the extremes is like the ratio of the first to the second triplicated, because a twenty-sevenfold ratio consists of three triple ratios.

He did not, however, define the ratio of the extremes of a continuous proportionality consisting of more than four terms, because the dimensions found in natural things do not exceed three <note>This reflects the Aristotelian and Euclidean view that space is three-dimensional (length, width, depth), so ratios beyond "triplicate" (3D) lacked a physical geometric counterpart</note>. ¶ Furthermore, the **denomination** <term>denomination: the numerical value or name of a ratio (e.g., the denomination of 6:2 is 3)</term> of a ratio of two quantities between which no middle term is placed has the nature of a **line**. But the denomination of those between which one middle term is placed in continuous proportionality has the nature of a **surface**, because it results from the multiplication of the denomination of the first two by itself. For everything produced from the multiplication of a line by a line has the nature of a surface: if multiplied by itself, it is a square; if by another, it is an "other-side-longer" <note>original: "altera parte longioris," a rectangle where one side is longer than the other</note>.

But the denomination of the ratio of those quantities between which two middle terms are placed in continuous proportion has the nature of a **solid**, because it arises from the multiplication of the denomination of the first two first by itself—by which multiplication a surface is produced—and then by that product, from which multiplication a solid or body arises. For everything produced from the multiplication of a line by a surface grows into a solid.

¶ It is, therefore, as if he were saying: the ratio of two quantities is a **simple interval**, having the nature of a single dimension like a line. Proportionality of three terms is a **double interval**, having the nature of a double dimension like a surface. Proportionality of four terms is a **triple interval**, having the nature of a triple dimension like a solid. And because dimensions do not proceed further, he did not define the ratio contained between the extremes of a proportionality consisting of five or more terms. Or, perhaps he did not define the ratio in these cases because their ratio can be understood from the previous definitions. For if in three terms the ratio of the extremes consists of the ratio of the first terms **doubled** <note>squared</note>, and in four terms it consists of the same **tripled** <note>cubed</note>, then in five terms it consists of the same **quadrupled**, and in six of the same **quintupled**. 

Thus, just as in three terms in continuous proportion the ratio of the extremes contains the ratio of the first terms twice—and in four terms thrice—so in five terms it will contain it four times, and in six terms five times, and so on. In this way, the ratio of the extremes in terms of continuous proportion always contains the ratio of the first terms as many times as there are total terms minus one. Similarly, if the ratio of the extremes in a continuous proportionality consisting of three terms is that which is produced by the ratio of the first terms multiplied by itself once—and in four terms multiplied by itself twice—in five terms it is that produced by the ratio of the first terms multiplied by itself thrice, and in six terms four times. This continues so that the number of terms is always two more than the number of multiplications, or so that the number of multiplications is equal to the number of middle terms.

<summary>This page defines triplicate ratios within a four-term continuous proportion and explains how these mathematical relationships correspond to the three physical dimensions: lines (1D), surfaces (2D), and solids (3D).</summary>

<note>Two mathematical diagrams using semi-circular arcs to illustrate proportions.

...with the extremes placed between. And note that even in a continuous proportionality <term>continuous proportionality: a sequence where the second term of one ratio is the first term of the next, e.g., A:B = B:C</term>, the ratio of the extremes is produced from all the intermediate ratios. ¶ From what has been said, it appears that the ratio of the extremes of a continuous proportionality consisting of three terms is named from a **square** <note>original: "a quadrato"</note>; while one consisting of four terms is named from a **cube** <note>original: "a cubo"</note>. The "side" of these squares and cubes is the value of the ratio of the first term to the second. **For example**, in numbers: Let there be four numbers in continuous proportion which are continuously tripled: 3, 9, 27, 81. The ratio of the first to the second is named from a "three" (it is a triple ratio); the ratio of the first to the third is named from a "nine," which is the square of three, for it is a nine-fold ratio. But the ratio of the first to the fourth is named from "27," which is the cube of the first ratio's value—namely, three—for it is a twenty-seven-fold ratio. ¶ And the ratio of the extremes of a non-continuous proportionality <note>original: "improportionalitatis continuae," referring to a sequence of ratios that are not the same</note> consisting of three terms is named from a "surface" that is not a square, whose sides are the values of the individual ratios. In four terms, it is named from a "solid" that is not a cube, whose three sides are the values of the three ratios. This is also clear in numbers. Let there be four numbers that are not in a single continuous proportion: 2, 4, 12, 48. In these, the ratio of the first to the second is double; the second to the third is triple; and thus the first to the third is six-fold. The third to the fourth is quadruple; and thus the first to the fourth is twenty-four-fold. Therefore, six, which is the value of the ratio of the first to the third, is a "surface" whose sides are two and three (the values of the first two ratios). Twenty-four, which is the value of the ratio of the first to the fourth, is a "solid" whose sides are 2, 3, and 4, which are the values of the three ratios existing between those four terms.

## Definition 12

<note>A geometric diagram showing a horizontal line with four marked points of varying distances. Labels 'c' and 'd' are placed over the first segment (labeled 6 and 3 respectively). Labels 'b' and 'a' are placed over the second segment (labeled 2 and 4 respectively).</note>

Quantities that are in one proportion—the antecedent to the consequent and the antecedent to the consequent—will also be said **inversely** <note>original: "econtrario"</note> as the consequent is to the antecedent, so the consequent is to the antecedent. ¶ Likewise, **alternately** <note>original: "permutatim"</note>, as the antecedent is to the antecedent, so also the consequent is to the consequent.
¶ He defines the species of proportionality, which are six: namely, **converse**, **disjunct**, **conjunct**, **everted**, and **equal**. ¶ These species are like certain modes of reasoning. He first defines converse proportionality and permuted proportionality, in which the antecedents <term>antecedent: the first term of a ratio (the 'A' in A:B)</term> and consequents <term>consequent: the second term of a ratio (the 'B' in A:B)</term> remain the same in substance—which is not the case in disjunct, conjunct, or everted proportions—and in which nothing is taken from outside, as happens in the "equal" type. He calls the "antecedent" the first extreme of the proportion, and the "consequent" the second. ¶ Through this definition, he means that if there is a proportion of *a* to *b* as *c* is to *d*, and from this I conclude: therefore *b* is to *a* as *d* is to *c*—namely, by making consequents out of the antecedents and antecedents out of the consequents—this mode of reasoning is called **inverse** or **converse** proportionality. But if I argue thus: *a* is to *b* as *c* is to *d*, therefore *a* is to *c* as *b* is to *d*—namely, so that both antecedents of the original ratios become a new ratio, and both consequents become the other—he means that this mode of reasoning is called **permuted** proportionality. In this mode of reasoning, the antecedent of the second ratio becomes a consequent, and the consequent of the first ratio becomes an antecedent.

### Proposition 13.

<note>A geometric diagram consisting of two horizontal line segments. The top segment begins at point "a" and ends at a point marked "4". A middle point is labeled "b", and the number "8" is written above the segment between "a" and "b". The bottom segment begins at "c", ends at "3", has a middle point "d", and the number "6" is written above the segment between "c" and "d". This illustrates "composition": if 8:4 is equal to 6:3, then (8+4):4 is equal to (6+3):3.</note>

**C**omposed <term>composed: also called "joined"; Latin "coniuncta"</term> proportionality is said to occur whenever the antecedent with the consequent is to the consequent, as the [other] antecedent with the [other] consequent is to the [other] consequent.
¶ He defines the composed, disjoined, and everted proportions, in which nothing extra is taken from the outside, yet the terms do not remain as they were. The substance of the meaning is this: he intends that if it were the case that *a* is to *b* as *c* is to *d*, and I conclude from this that the whole *a-b* is to *b* as the whole *c-d* is to *d*, then this mode of arguing is called composed proportionality.

### Proposition 14.

<note>A geometric diagram identical in structure to the one above: two horizontal segments. The top segment is labeled a-b (with "8" above) and ends at "4". The bottom segment is labeled c-d (with "6" above) and ends at "3". This illustrates "disjunction": if (8+4):4 is equal to (6+3):3, then 8:4 is equal to 6:3.</note>

**D**isjoined <term>disjoined: also called "separated"; Latin "disiuncta"</term> proportionality is said to be the equal comparison of the excesses of the antecedents over the consequents.
¶ He intends that if there were a proportion of the whole *a-b* to *b* as the whole *c-d* is to *d*, and from this I conclude that *a* is to *b* as *c* is to *d*, then this mode of arguing is called disjoined proportionality.

### Proposition 15.

<note>A geometric diagram identical in structure to the previous two: two horizontal segments. The top segment is labeled a-b (with "8" above) and ends at "4". The bottom segment is labeled c-d (with "6" above) and ends at "3". This illustrates "eversion": if (8+4):4 is equal to (6+3):3, then (8+4):8 is equal to (6+3):6.</note>

**E**verted <term>everted: also called "converted"; Latin "eversa"</term> proportionality is said to be the similarity of proportions of any antecedents to their own excesses over their own consequents.
¶ He intends that if *a-b* were to *b* as *c-d* is to *d*, and from this I conclude that *a-b* is to *a* as *c-d* is to *c*, then this mode of arguing is called everted proportionality.

### Proposition 16.

<note>A complex geometric diagram showing two sets of related proportions. The top set consists of three points labeled "a", "b", and "c" with numerical values "8", "4", and "2" respectively. The bottom set consists of three points labeled "d", "e", and "f" with numerical values "12", "6", and "3" respectively. This illustrates "proportionality by equality": because 8:4 = 12:6 and 4:2 = 6:3, it follows that the ratio of the first to the last in each set is the same, i.e., 8:2 = 12:3.</note>

**E**qual <term>equal: often called "proportionality by equality" or "ordinate"; Latin "equa"</term> proportionality is said to occur when many quantities are proposed, and others equal in number are applied in one proportion; by removing an equal number of middle terms, the similarity of the proportions is found between the two extremes.
¶ He defines equal proportionality, which requires taking something from the outside to prove the proposition. He intends that if any number of quantities are taken, such as *a, b, c*, and likewise as many others—whether they are of the same kind as the first or another—such as *d, e, f*; and the second set are in the proportion of the first, either in the same order (as if it were said *a* to *b* as *d* to *e*, and *b* to *c* as *e* to *f*) or in a reversed order (as if it were said *a* to *b* as *e* to *f*, and *b* to *c* as *d* to *e*); and if from this it is concluded that *a* is to *c* as *d* is to *f*, then this mode of arguing is called equal proportionality. Regarding these six modes of arguing, which are called the species of proportionality, the author proves four of them in the text <note>original: "in litera", referring to the formal proofs</note> later in this fifth book. Indeed, he proves permuted proportionality in Proposition 16 of this book; disjoined in 17; composed in 18; and he demonstrates equal proportionality in 22 and 23. But in 22, he does so when the quantities of the two ranks are proportional in the same order, whereas in 23, they are proportional in a reversed order. However, they do not demonstrate "converse" or "everted" proportionality, because converse is clear from the definition of quantities in a non-continuous proportion. Everted proportionality is clear from Proposition 19, as we shall say regarding that same 19th proposition. How everted proportionality is manifest from the definition of quantities in a non-continuous proportion, let us now demonstrate. ¶ Let there be, therefore, a proportion of *a* to *b* as *c* to *d*; I wish to demonstrate that *b* will be to *a*...

the same as another, how shall he know that two equal quantities 
have the same proportion to a third? Therefore, the intellect undoubtedly 
requires—before it can grasp that proposition which seemed so easily conceivable—a 
cognition of this matter which is held through its definition. Afterward, it requires a

proposition is concluded; if not, then the opposite. second, but the multiple of the third does not exceed the multiple of the fourth. It is from this that the

proportional and which are non-proportional. Proportional quantities are

<meta>This page continues the technical commentary on Book V of Euclid’s Elements. # BOOK V

He also defined quantities that are non-proportional <note>original: "inproportionales"</note>, in which one ratio is greater than another. And if every ratio were known or rational <term>rational: a ratio that can be expressed as a relationship between whole numbers</term>, then it would be easy for the mind to recognize which ratios were the same and which were different. ¶ For those that have the same denomination <term>denomination: the numerical value or name of a ratio, such as "triple" or "one-and-a-half"</term> would be the same, and those with different denominations would be different. This ease of identification is evident in arithmetic, because the ratio of all numbers is known and rational. Wherefore Jordanus <note>Jordanus de Nemore, a 13th-century mathematician</note>, in the second book of his *Arithmetic*, defining which ratios are the same and which are different, says that those are the same which receive the same denomination. ¶ A greater ratio is that which receives a greater denomination, and a smaller ratio is that which receives a smaller one. 

But there are infinite irrational ratios <note>original: "proportiones irrationales"</note> whose denomination is not knowable. Therefore, since Euclid considers proportional things generally in this book—not restricting himself to rational or irrational ones, since he considers ratio as found in continuous magnitudes <note>continuous magnitudes: geometric objects like lines or areas, as opposed to discrete numbers</note> which include both—he could not define the identity of ratios through the identity of denominations as the arithmetician does. This is because, as has been said, the denominations of many ratios are simply unknown. However, a definition must be made from things that are known; hence, the "malice" <note>malice: here meaning the "stubborn" or "difficult" nature</note> of irrational ratios compelled Euclid to set down such definitions. 

Because he could not, as is clear from the premise, define proportionality (or the identity of ratios) by the identity of their relationships or their denominations—due to the irrationality of the relationships and the incommensurability of the terms—he was forced to retreat to the multiples of the terms. He sought the proposed definition by considering the multiples of the terms in regard to their excess, equality, or deficiency when taken in equal numbers <note>equimultiples</note>, through which they are reduced to the nature of the irrationality. For nothing in any kind of inequality is more identical to the terms than their multiples, nor is anything more identical to the relationships of the terms than the relationships of their multiples.

¶ And because a ratio is a certain relationship of two quantities of the same kind, considered in terms of whether they are equal or whether one is greater, therefore the identity of ratios existing between the first of four quantities to the second, and the third to the fourth, is a similar equality of the first to the second and the third to the fourth; or a similar "greater-ness," or a similar "lesser-ness." Moreover, this similar equality, greater-ness, or lesser-ness exists among any four quantities when it exists among all their equal multiples. 

¶ Regarding what he says in the **fifth definition**: "quantities which are said to have continuous proportionality," and so on—it is as if he were saying: I call all those quantities "continuously proportional" (which means they are similarly equal, similarly greater, or similarly smaller in a continuous sequence) when all their equal multiples are also similarly equal, greater, or smaller to one another. This means the multiples themselves are also continuously proportional. If this relationship fails in any multiple, I say they are not continuously proportional. 

¶ Regarding what he says in the **sixth definition**: "quantities which are said to be according to one ratio, the first to the second and the third to the fourth," and so on—it is as if he were saying: I call all four quantities "discontinuously proportional" (meaning the first is to the second as the third is to the fourth) when the first to the second and the third to the fourth behave similarly in being equal, adding, or diminishing. This occurs when all equal multiples of the first and third relate to all equal multiples of the second and fourth in the same way—either in being equal, exceeding, or being less. This means the multiples of the first have the same ratio to the multiples of the second as the multiples of the third have to the multiples of the fourth. If this relationship fails in any instance among the multiples, I say there is no proportion.

It details the logic behind Definitions 5 and 6 of Book V regarding continuous and discontinuous proportions.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the technical commentary on Book V of Euclid’s Elements, focusing on the definition of proportionality for both rational and irrational magnitudes. # BOOK V

...of the first to the second as of the third to the fourth. But what he says in the fifth definition <note>original: "5. diffinitione"</note> is as if he were to say: I call it a "greater ratio" <note>This refers to Definition 7 in many modern editions, which defines when one ratio is greater than another using equimultiples.</note> of four quantities—of the first to the second compared to the third to the fourth—when the first exceeds the second by more than the third exceeds the fourth. This occurs when some multiple of the first is greater than some multiple of the second, while some multiple of the third—taken according to the same multiplier <note>original: "numerationẽ"</note> as the multiple of the first—does not exceed a multiple of the fourth—taken according to the same multiplier as the multiple of the second. This constitutes a greater ratio of the multiple of the first to the multiple of the second than of the multiple of the third to the multiple of the fourth.

¶ However, some have attempted to demonstrate <term>demonstrate: in a geometric context, to provide a logical proof based on established axioms</term> these definitions. Among them, Ametus, son of Joseph <note>Ahmed ibn Yusuf, a 9th-century mathematician whose work on proportions was highly influential in medieval Europe</note>, tried to demonstrate them in his letter <note>original: "epiſtola"</note> which he composed *On Ratio and Proportionality*. He accepted three things by way of postulates as if they were principles, which he says are self-evident and require no proof.

¶ The first of these is that if there are four quantities where the ratio of the first to the second is as the third to the fourth, then inversely <note>original: "ecõuerſo"</note>, the ratio of the second to the first will be as the fourth to the third. This is the mode of reasoning which Euclid earlier called "inverse proportionality" <term>inverse proportionality: the rule that if A:B = C:D, then B:A = D:C</term>. And he [Ametus] erred because he said this proposition was self-evident, even though its starting premise <note>original: "antecedens"</note> and its result <note>original: "cõſequẽs"</note> are unknown. For it is unknown what it means for the ratio of a first quantity to a second to be the same as a third to a fourth; therefore, while this remains unknown, it is impossible to understand what follows from it. Similarly, because the result is unknown, it is impossible to understand what leads to it.

¶ His second principle was: that if there are four quantities where the ratio of the first to the second is as the third to the fourth, if the first is greater than the second, the third will be greater than the fourth; and if smaller, smaller; and if equal, equal.

¶ The third was that if there are four quantities where the ratio of the first to the second is as the third to the fourth: the ratio of the first to any multiple of the second will be as the third to the same multiple of the multiples of the fourth. The same error occurred in these two principles as occurred in the first. For in all of them, he took unknown things as if they were known; therefore, he did not demonstrate them. He also erred in his second demonstration, and in the third and fifth. In each of these, he reasons from the 8th or 10th proposition of this book, which are themselves proved from the definition of continuous proportionality. 

For he reasons thus: if the ratio of *a-b* to *c* is greater than *g* to *d*, let there be a part *v-b* of *a-b* such that its ratio to *e* is as *g* to *d*. By this, it appears he assumes that of two unequal quantities *a-b* and *v-b* related to the same quantity *e*, the greater one possesses a greater ratio and the smaller one a smaller ratio; or that a quantity which has a smaller ratio to *e* than *a-b* does, will be smaller than *a-b*. The first of these is demonstrated in the 8th proposition of this book, and the second in the 10th. For when you wish to take a quantity that relates to *e* in the ratio of *g* to *d*, I can give you one greater, smaller, or equal to *a-b* indifferently as I wish. Because he does not demonstrate this, he falls into circular reasoning <note>original: "circulus"</note>, and his principles are more obscure than his conclusions. Therefore, the principles must be assumed with Euclid as known, and they should not be proven from conclusions, but the conclusions must be demonstrated from the principles.

### ->Proposition 1<-

<note>A geometric diagram shows two horizontal line segments. The upper segment is divided into three parts by vertical ticks, labeled 'a', 'b', and 'c' at the vertices, with the numbers 2, 3, and 4 written above the segments respectively. The lower segment is similarly divided and labeled 'd', 'e', and 'f', also with the numbers 2, 3, and 4 above the segments. This illustrates equimultiples of different quantities.</note>

**I**f there are any number of quantities which are equimultiples <term>equimultiples: products of different numbers multiplied by the same value (e.g., 2*3 and 2*4)</term> of as many others, or each equal to each, it is necessary that just as one of them is to its corresponding quantity, so also the whole aggregate of these is to all those taken together.

¶ Let there be any number of quantities, which are *a*, *b*, and *c*, and as many others, which are *d*, *e*, and *f*, each being equimultiples of its corresponding quantity, or each equal to each, specifically thus...

# BOOK V

...which as **a** is a multiple of **d**, so **b** is a multiple of **e**, and **c** a multiple of **f**. For instance, if **a** is equal to **d**, then likewise **b** should be equal to **e** and **c** equal to **f**. I say that as **a** relates to **d**, so the aggregate <term>aggregate: the sum or total resulting from adding several quantities together</term> of all those which are **a**, **b**, and **c** relates to the aggregate of all those which are **d**, **e**, and **f**. ¶ If each individual is equal to each individual, the proposition is clear through this common notion <term>common notion: a fundamental mathematical axiom that Euclid considers self-evident</term>: if equals be added to equals, the wholes will also be equal. But if all are equally multiple of their counterparts, by dividing them according to the quantity of their submultiples, the aggregate of the first part of **a**, and the first of **b**, and the first of **c** will be equal to the aggregate of **d**, **e**, and **f**, by the aforesaid common notion aided by this: things that are equal to the same thing are equal to each other. ¶ Similarly, also, the aggregate of the second parts of the quantities **a**, **b**, and **c** will be equal to the aggregate of **d**, **e**, and **f**, and so for the rest. And because this can be done as many times as **d** is contained in **a**, it will be that an equal aggregate of **d**, **e**, and **f** is contained in the aggregate of **a**, **b**, and **c** as many times as **d** is contained in **a**. Because, therefore, as many times as **d** measures **a**, so many times the aggregate of **d**, **e**, and **f** measures the aggregate of **a**, **b**, and **c**, it is clear that as **a** is a multiple of **d**, so the aggregate of **a**, **b**, and **c** is of the aggregate of **d**, **e**, and **f**, which is what was proposed.
