## Proposition .2.

If there be six quantities, of which the first is the same multiple of the second as the third is of the fourth, and the fifth is also the same multiple of the second as the sixth is of the fourth: then the whole of the first and fifth to the second, and the whole of the third and sixth to the fourth, will be found to be equally multiple.

¶ Let there be six quantities: **a** first, **b** second, **c** third, **d** fourth, **e** fifth, **f** sixth. And let **a** and **c** be equally multiple to **b** and **d**, and likewise **e** and **f** be equally multiple to the same. I say that as the whole aggregate of **a** and **e** is a multiple of the quantity **b**, so the whole aggregate of **c** and **f** is a multiple of the quantity **d**. For because the number according to which **b** is contained in **a** is equal to the number according to which **d** is contained in **c**; and similarly the number according to which **b** is contained in **e** is equal to the number according to which **d** is contained in **f**; it will follow by the common notion which is: if equals be added to equals, etc., the number according to which **b** is contained in the aggregate of **a** and **e** is equal to the number according to which **d** is contained in the aggregate of **c** and **f**. Wherefore, as the aggregate of **a** and **e** is a multiple of **b**, so the aggregate of **c** and **f** is a multiple of **d**, which is what was proposed.

<note>A geometric diagram illustrating Proposition 2. It shows horizontal line segments. A long segment labeled "ae" is 8 units long (marked 8). Below it, "a" is 4 units and "b" is 2 units. Another long segment "cf" is 12 units long (marked 12). Below it, "c" is 6 units and "d" is 3 units.</note>

## Proposition .3.

If a first be the same multiple of a second as a third is of a fourth; and if equal multiples be taken of the first and the third, then the [resulting] multiple of the first to the second and the multiple of the third to the fourth will also be equimultiples.

¶ Let there be six quantities: **a** first, **b** second, **c** third, **d** fourth, **e** fifth, **f** sixth. And let **a** to **b** and **c** to **d**, and likewise **e** to **a** and **f** to **c**, be equally multiple. I say that as **e** is a multiple of **b**, so **f** is of **d**. For let **e** be divided according to the quantity of **a**, its multiple, and **f** according to the quantity of **c**. Because of the equality of the parts of **e** to **a** and the parts of **f** to **c**, any of the parts of **e** will be the same multiple of **b** as any of the parts of **f** is of **d**. Because, therefore, as the first part of **e** is a multiple of **b**, so the first part of **f** is a multiple of **d**. And likewise as the second part of **e** is a multiple of **b**, so the second of **f** is of **d**. Therefore, by the previous [proposition], the aggregate of the two first parts of **e** will be the same multiple of **b** as the aggregate of the two first parts of **f** is of **d**. And because again the third part of **e**, if there be any third part, is the same multiple of **b** as the third of **f** is of **d**, it will follow by the same [proposition] that the whole aggregate of the first three parts of **e** <note>original: "c", likely a typo for 'e' in original</note> is the same multiple of **b** as the whole aggregate of the first three parts of **f** is of **d**. ¶ And so if there be more parts of **e** and **f**, by always combining the following part with the aggregate of the previous ones, concluding [the proof]...

## Proposition .4.

If there be a proportion of a first to a second as of a third to a fourth; and if to the first and third equimultiples <term>equimultiples: quantities multiplied by the same number, such as 2x and 2y</term> be assigned, and likewise to the second and fourth equal multiples be assigned, the resulting multiples will be proportional in the same order.

¶ Let the proportion of *a* (the first) to *b* (the second) be as *c* (the third) to *d* (the fourth). Let *e* be taken as a multiple of *a* and *f* as a multiple of *c*, such that they are equimultiples. Likewise, let *g* be a multiple of *b* and *h* as a multiple of *d*, such that they are equimultiples. I say that the proportion of *e* to *g* is as *f* to *h*. I shall take *k* as a multiple of *e* and *l* as a multiple of *f*, such that they are equimultiples. Likewise, *m* as a multiple of *g* and *n* as a multiple of *h*, such that they are equimultiples. And because *e* and *f* are equimultiples of *a* and *c*, and likewise *k* and *l* are equimultiples of *e* and *f*, they will be, by the preceding proposition, *k* and *l* equimultiples of *a* and *c*. By the same reasoning, *m* and *n* will be equimultiples of *b* and *d*. Wherefore, by the converse of the definition of discrete proportionality <note>original: "diffinitionis incontinue pꝛopoꝛtionalitatis"</note>, *k* to *m* and *l* to *n* will behave similarly in exceeding, falling short, or being equal <term>exceeding, falling short, or being equal: the standard Greek method (Eudoxan) for proving two ratios are equal by comparing all possible multiples</term>. Since therefore *k* and *l* are equimultiples of *e* and *f*, and likewise *m* and *n* are equimultiples of *g* and *h*, it will be, by the definition of discrete proportionality, that the proportion of *e* to *g* is as *f* to *h*, which is what was proposed.

## Proposition .5.

<note>A geometric diagram in the left margin consisting of several arcs. The largest arc at the top is labeled 32. Below it are two arcs labeled 24 and 24, with smaller arcs labeled 8 and 8. Further down are arcs labeled 6, 2, and 8. Letters a, b, c, d, e, f, g, and s are placed relative to these arcs to denote points or segments.</note>

If there be two quantities of which one is a part of another, and there be subtracted from each of them the same part, the remainder will be to the remainder as the whole was to the whole: namely, equally multiple.

¶ Or thus: if a part is an aliquot <term>aliquot: a part that measures the whole exactly, like 2 is an aliquot part of 6</term>, the remainder of the one will be the same part of the remainder of the other as the whole is of the whole. Let the quantity *ab* be the same part of the quantity *cd* as *eb* is of *ab*. Let *ab* be subtracted from the quantity *cd*, and let the remainder be *fc*; and let *fd* be equal to *ab*. Likewise, also let *eb* be subtracted from the quantity *ab*, and let the remainder be *ea*. I say that whatever part the quantity *ab* is of the quantity *cd*, the same part is the quantity *ae* of the quantity *cf*. For since *fd* is equal to *ab*, *fd* will be the same multiple of *eb* as *cd* is a multiple of *ab*. I shall therefore set *dg* to be the same multiple of *ae* as *fd* is a multiple of *eb*. From the first proposition of this book, the quantity *fg* will be the same multiple of *ab* as *fd* is a multiple of *eb*. And because *cd* was such a multiple of *ab* as *fd* was a multiple of *eb*, both of the two quantities *cd* and *fg* are equimultiples of the quantity *ab*. Wherefore, by common science <note>original: "communem ſcientiam" — referring to self-evident mathematical axioms</note>, *cd* and *fg* are equal to each other. Therefore, with the quantity *fd* subtracted from both of them, *cf* will be equal to *dg*. And because *dg* was the same multiple of *ae* as *fd* was of *eb*, and therefore as *ab* was of *eb*, wherefore also as *cd* was of *ab*, *cf* will be the same multiple of *ae* as the whole *cd* is of the whole *ab*, which is what was proposed.

## Proposition .6.

If there be two quantities that are equimultiples of two others, and two smaller quantities be subtracted from the two larger ones, each from its own multiple: the two remainders will either be equimultiples of those same parts, or equal to them.

¶ Let quantities *ab* be to *c* and *de* to *f* equimultiples <term>equimultiples: quantities that are the same multiple of their respective bases, such as 10 being 5x2 and 12 being 6x2</term>; and let *c* be subtracted from *ab* and *f* from *de*. Let there be remainders: from *ab* indeed *ag*, and from *de* [let there be] *db*. Then *gb* will be equal to *c* and *db* equal to *f*. I say that the two remainders *ag* and *db* will be equal to the two quantities *c* and *f*, or they will be equimultiples of them. First, therefore, let *ag* be equal to *c*. I say that *db* is equal to *f*. For I shall take the quantity *ek* equal to *f*; and by the previously mentioned hypotheses, as many times as *f* is in *bk*, so many times is *c* in *ab*. Wherefore, just as *ab* is a multiple of *c*, so *bk* is a multiple of *f*. But thus also was *de* a multiple of that same *f*. Therefore, by common knowledge <note>original: "commem scientiam," referring to the common notions or axioms used as the foundation of geometric proof</note>, *bk* will be equal to *de*. Therefore, subtracting their common quantity *be*, *db* will be equal to *ek*, and wherefore equal to *f*, which is what was proposed. ¶ If, however, *ag* be a multiple of *c*, I shall set *ek* to be the same multiple of *f*. And it will be as before: as many times as *f* is in *bk*, so many times is *c* in *ab*. But it was also that many times in *de*. Therefore, as before, *de* is equal to *bk*, and *db* to *ek*. Wherefore, just as *ag* is a multiple of *c*, so *db* is a multiple of *f*, which is what was proposed. Alternatively, since the quantity *ab* contains the quantity *c* according to the same number as the quantity *de* contains the quantity *f*, and if one unit is subtracted from it, there remains a unit or a number according to which *ag* contains *c* and *db* contains *f*; it is clear that the quantities *ag* and *db* are equal to, or equimultiples of, the quantities *c* and *f*.

## Proposition .7.

¶ If two equal quantities are compared to any other third quantity, their ratio <note>original: "proportio"</note> to it will be the same; and likewise the ratio of that third quantity to them will be one and the same.

<margin>
<note>A geometric diagram on the right side next to Proposition 7. It features a horizontal line at the top labeled with points d, 12, e, and another 12. Below this, there are two segments of equal length, one labeled a and the other labeled b, both with the number 6 below them. Below those is a shorter segment labeled c with the number 3 below it. At the bottom is a segment labeled f with the number 6 below it. This visualization helps demonstrate that if a=b, then the ratio a:c is the same as b:c.</note>
</margin>

¶ Let there be two equal quantities *a* and *b*, which are compared to any third quantity *c*. I say that the ratio of *a* to *c* is the same as *b* to *c*; and likewise the ratio of *c* to *a* is the same as *c* to *b*. The first is proved thus: since *c* is the consequent <term>consequent: the second term in a ratio (the 'B' in A:B)</term> to *a* (the first) and to *b* (the third), it will stand in the position of the second and fourth terms. I shall therefore take *d* as a multiple of *a* (the first) and *e* as a multiple of *b* (the third) as equimultiples. And I shall take *f* as any of the multiples of *c*, which is the second and fourth term. And because *a* and *b*, of which *d* and *e* are equimultiples, are posited as equal: if *d* be divided according to the quantity *a*, and *e* according to the quantity *b*, their parts in both cases will be equal in number and quantity. Equal in number by hypothesis, on account of the equality of the multiplication in both cases; and equal in quantity by this common knowledge, repeated as often as necessary: things which are equal to the same thing are equal to each other. Because, therefore, the first of the parts of *d* is equal to the first of the parts of *e*, and the second to the second, and the rest to the rest; and there are as many parts in *d* as there are in *e*, it follows by the first [proposition] of this book that *d* is equal to *e*. Wherefore, by common knowledge: if two equal quantities are compared to another third, either both quantities *d* and *e* are similarly greater than *f*, or similarly less, or equal to it. Therefore, by the definition of discrete proportionality <note>original: "incontinue proportionalitatis," referring to Definition 5 of Book V, which establishes the criteria for four magnitudes to be in the same ratio</note>, the ratio which *a* (the first) has to *c* (the second) is the same as *b* (the third) has to *c* (the fourth), which is what was proposed. ¶ The second part you shall prove in the same way with the order reversed: so that *c* is placed as the first and third, while *a* is the second and *b* the fourth. Since the quantity *f*, which is the equimultiple of the first and third, is either similarly greater than quantities *d* and *e* (which are equimultiples of the second and fourth), or similarly less, or equal to them; it will be, by the same definition, the ratio of *c* (the first) to *a* (the second) as *c* (the third) is to *b* (the fourth), which is the second thing proposed.

## Proposition 8

If two unequal quantities are compared in ratio to one and the same quantity, the larger quantity will have a larger ratio to it, while the smaller quantity will have a smaller ratio. Conversely, the ratio of that same quantity to the smaller quantity will be larger, and its ratio to the larger quantity will be smaller.

¶ Let there be two unequal quantities *a* and *bc*, and let *bc* be the larger. Let them both be compared in ratio to the same quantity, which is *d*. I say that the ratio of *bc* to *d* is greater than the ratio of *a* to *d*, and conversely, that the ratio of *d* to *a* is greater than the ratio of *d* to *bc*. 

The first part is proved thus: I will set *eb* equal to *a* and I will multiply *ec* so many times that the resulting quantity is larger than *d*; let this be *fg*. I will take *kf* to be the same multiple of *be*, and similarly *b* to be the same multiple of *a*, as *fg* is a multiple of *ec*. By the first proposition of this book, *b* will be the same multiple of *a* as *kg* is a multiple of *bc*. Also, *b* will be equal to *kf* because their submultiples, which are *a* and *be*, were set equal. 

I will also ensure that *b* is not smaller than *d*, but either equal or larger. For I will multiply each of the three quantities *ec*, *be*, and *a* equally, so that the multiple *fg* of *ec* becomes larger than *d*, and the multiple *b* of *a* does not become smaller than the same [*d*]. Next, I will multiply *d* so many times that the resulting quantity is larger than *b*; let it be *m*, the first quantity among the multiples of *d* that is larger than *b*. Beneath this, I will take the largest multiple of *d* [that is less than or equal to *b*]; if *m* is the first in the order of multiples of *d*, let the one before it be *l*. It will follow that *l* is not larger than *b*, and *m* will consist of *d* and *l*, because every multiple consists of the next preceding multiple plus the simple [base] quantity—for example, a triple consists of a double plus the simple quantity—except for the first multiple, which consists of twice the simple quantity. 

¶ Since, therefore, *b* is equal to *kf*, *kf* will not be smaller than *l*. Thus, *kf* and *d* together will not produce less than *l* and *d*; consequently, they will not produce less than *m*. And because *fg* is larger than *d*, *kg* will be larger than *m*. 

¶ I understand, therefore, the quantity *bc* as the first, *d* as the second, *a* as the third, and *d* as the fourth. And because equal multiples have been taken for the first and the third (namely *kg* and *b*), and similarly for the second and the fourth equal multiples (indeed, the same value for both, which is *m*), and the multiple of the first (*kg*) exceeds the multiple of the second (*m*), but the multiple of the third (*b*) does not exceed the multiple of the fourth (*m*), it follows by the definition of greater disproportion <term>greater disproportion: Definition 7 of Book V, which explains how to determine if one ratio is larger than another by comparing their equimultiples</term> that the ratio of the first, *bc*, to the second, *d*, is greater than the ratio of the third, *a*, to the fourth, *d*. This is the first part. 

¶ The second part you will prove by the same definition with the order reversed: let *d* be the first and third, *a* the second, and *bc* the fourth. For the multiple of the first (*m*) exceeds the multiple of the second (*b*), but the multiple of the third (*m*) does not exceed the multiple of the fourth (*kg*). Therefore, the ratio of *d* to *a* is greater than the ratio of *d* to *bc*. This is the second part. 

¶ From this method of demonstration, the sufficiency of the definition of greater disproportion <note>original: "maioris improportionalitatis"</note>, which the author placed at the beginning of this fifth book, is clear. For there is never a greater ratio of the first of four quantities to the second than of the third to the fourth without some equimultiples being found for the first and third which, when compared to some equimultiples of the second and fourth, show the multiple of the first to be greater than the multiple of the second, while the multiple of the third is not greater than the multiple of the fourth. We shall find these multiples as we demonstrate below, after Proposition 12 of this book.

## Proposition 9

If the ratio of certain quantities to a single quantity is the same, those quantities are equal to each other. If, however, the ratio of a single quantity to several others is the same, those quantities must necessarily be equal.

¶ Let there be two quantities, *a* and *b*, having the same ratio to a third quantity *c*. I say that they are equal. And if, conversely, there is the same ratio of *c* to both of them, I still say they are equal. This is the converse of Proposition 7. The first part is evident: for if they were not equal, but one of them was larger—for instance, *a*—then by the first part of the preceding proposition, the ratio of *a* to *c* would be greater than the ratio of *b* to *c*, which contradicts our hypothesis. The second part is also clear: because if *a* is greater than *b*, then by the second part of the preceding proposition, the ratio of *c* to *b* would be greater than its ratio to *a*, which also contradicts the hypothesis.

## Proposition 10

If the ratio of one quantity to another is greater than the ratio of a different quantity to that same second quantity, then the first quantity is the greater of the two. If, however, the ratio of a single quantity to another is greater than its ratio to a third, it is necessary that the second quantity be the smaller.

¶ In the case where the ratio of *a* to *c* is greater than the ratio of *b* to *c*, I say that *a* is greater than *b*. And if the ratio of *c* to *b* is greater than the ratio of *c* to *a*, I still say that *a* is smaller than *b* <note>original: "minorem b"</note>. This is the converse of Proposition 8. The first part is clear through the first part of Proposition 7 and the first part of Proposition 8. For by the first part of the seventh, *a* will not be equal to *b*; nor will it be smaller, by the first part of the eighth. The second part is evident from the second parts of those same propositions.

<margin>

## Proposition 11

If the ratios of quantities are equal to some one ratio, those ratios must also be equal to one another.

¶ This proposition, which Euclid numbered among the <term>common notions</term> <note>original: "communes animi conceptiones" — these are self-evident axioms like 'things equal to the same thing are equal to each other'</note> at the beginning of the first book, is demonstrated here as it applies specifically to ratios. Let each of two ratios, which are *a* to *b* and *c* to *d*, be equal to the ratio of *e* to *f*. I say the ratios of *a* to *b* and *c* to *d* are equal to each other. For I will take *g* as a multiple of *a*, *h* as a multiple of *c*, and *k* as a multiple of *e*, all being <term>equimultiples</term> <note>multiplied by the same factor</note>. Likewise, let *l* be a multiple of *b*, *m* a multiple of *d*, and *n* a multiple of *f*, also being equimultiples. Because by the hypothesis the ratio of *e* to *f* is the same as *a* to *b*, and similarly the same as *c* to *d*, it will follow—by applying the definition of <term>discrete proportionality</term> <note>original: "incontinue proportionalitatis" — referring to a proportion between four distinct terms (A:B = C:D)</note> twice—that if *k* is greater than *n*, then *g* is greater than *l* and *h* is greater than *m*. And if *k* is less than *n*, then *g* is less than *l* and *h* is less than *m*. And if *k* is equal to *n*, then *g* is equal to *l* and *h* is equal to *m*. Therefore, since *g* to *l* and *h* to *m* behave in the same way regarding addition, subtraction, and equality through the mediation of *k* and *n*, it follows by the definition of discrete proportionality that *a* is to *b* as *c* is to *d*, which is what was proposed.

## Proposition 12

If the ratio of the first to the second is as the third to the fourth, but the ratio of the third to the fourth is greater than that of the fifth to the sixth, then the ratio of the first to the second will be greater than the ratio of the fifth to the sixth.

¶ Just as in the preceding proposition, what is demonstrated here regarding proportions is also conceivable regarding quantities: namely, that if two quantities are to each other...

...equal, whichever of them was the greater, that same one will be greater than the other. ¶ In proportions, however, this is demonstrated: suppose the ratio of **a** to **b** is as **c** is to **d**, but **c** to **d** is a greater ratio than **e** to **f**. Then **a** to **b** will also be greater than **e** to **f**. Let us take **g** as a multiple of **a**, **h** as a multiple of **c**, and **k** as a multiple of **e**, all being <term>equimultiples</term><note>Equimultiples are numbers or magnitudes multiplied by the same factor; for example, if you double a, c, and e, the results are equimultiples.</note>. Likewise, let **l** be a multiple of **b**, **m** of **d**, and **n** of **f**, also being equimultiples. And because, by the hypothesis, the ratio of **c** to **d** is the same as **a** to **b**, and it is greater than **e** to **f**, it will follow by the conversion of the definition of <term>discrete proportionality</term><note>original: "incontinue proportionalitatis"; this refers to Euclid's Definition 5 of Book V, which defines when four magnitudes are in the same ratio even if they are not part of a continuous chain.</note> that if **h** exceeds **m**, then **g** also exceeds **l**. And by the conversion of the definition of a greater ratio, it is not necessary for **k** to exceed **n**. Therefore, since by the mediation of **h** and **m**, if **g** exceeds **l** it is not necessary for **k** to exceed **n**, it will be by the definition of a greater ratio that the ratio of **a** to **b** is greater than **e** to **f**, which is what was proposed. ¶ In a similar way, you will also prove that if **a** is to **b** as **c** is to **d**, and **c** to **d** is a lesser ratio than **e** to **f**, then **a** to **b** will be lesser than **e** to **f**. For since **c** to **d** is less than **e** to **f**, then **e** to **f** is greater than **c** to **d**. Therefore, by the conversion of the definition of a greater ratio: if **k** exceeds **n**, it is not necessary that **h** exceeds **m**. But if **h** does not exceed **m**, then **g** does not exceed **l**. Therefore, if **k** exceeds **n**, it is not necessary that **g** exceeds **n**. By the definition of a greater ratio, the ratio of **e** to **f** will be greater than **a** to **b**; therefore, conversely, **a** to **b** will be lesser than **e** to **f**, which is what was proposed.

<margin>
<note>A geometric diagram with four horizontal lines used to visualize the relationships between the magnitudes.
Row 1: Labels 'h' (24), 'k' (18), and '36'.

¶ From the method of demonstration of the eighth [proposition] of this book and this one, it will become manifest that if the ratio of the first of four quantities to the second is greater than the ratio of the third to the fourth, it will be possible to find some equimultiples of the first and the third which, when compared to any equimultiples of the second and the fourth, the multiple of the first will be found to exceed the multiple of the second, but the multiple of the third will not exceed the multiple of the fourth. This is shown thus: Let the ratio of **a** to **b** be greater than **c** to **d**. I shall set it so that the ratio of **a-f** to **b** is as **c** to **d**. Then by this [proposition] 12 and by [proposition] 10, **a-f** is less than **a-b**; let it be less by the quantity **f-b**, which I shall multiply so many times that it produces a quantity greater than **b**, which let be **g-b**, on this condition: that **c** multiplied just as many times produces a quantity not less than **c**, which let be **k**. Then I shall set **l-g** to be the same multiple of **a-f** as **g-b** is of **f-b**, or **k** of **c**. Then by the first [proposition] of this book, **l-b** will be the same multiple of **a-b** as **k** is of **c**. Next, I shall set **m** to be the first multiple of **d** that is greater than **k**, and I shall set **n** to be the same multiple of **b** as **m** is of **d**. It will follow from the preceding hypotheses and the conversion of the definition of proportionality that the quantity **n** is the first of the multiples of **b** that will be greater than **l-g**, nor will **l-g** be less than **a-f**. I shall therefore take below **n** the greatest of the multiples of **b**, or equal to it if perhaps **n** is the first of its multiples, which let be **o**. It will be established that **n** is composed of **o** and **b**. Because therefore **l-g** is not less than **o**, and **g-b** is greater than **f-b**, then **l-b** is greater than **n**. Wherefore, since **k** is less than **m**, the proposition is clear.

¶ We can also demonstrate the converse of this, namely that if it happens that some equimultiples of the first and third can be found such that the multiple of the first exceeds some multiple of the second, and the multiple of the third does not exceed the multiple of the fourth, the ratio of the first to the second will be greater than that of the third to the fourth. This is proved thus: Let there be four quantities: **a** the first, **b** the second, **c** the third, and **e** the fourth. Let **f** be a multiple of **a** and **g** a multiple of **c**, being equimultiples. Similarly, let **h** be a multiple of **b** and **k** a multiple of **e**, also being equimultiples. And let **f** exceed **h**, but let **g** not exceed **k**. I say that the ratio of **a** to **b** is greater than **c** to **e**. For if it were equal, then by the conversion of the definition of proportionality, **g** would exceed **k**, which is contrary to the hypothesis. If, however, the ratio were less, such as **c** to **e** is to **a** to **b**, then by the 10th [proposition] of this book, **c-l** would be less than **c**, and let it be less by the quantity **l-d**. I shall therefore set **m-n** to be the same multiple of **c-l**, and **n-p** the same multiple of **l-d**, as **f** is a multiple of **a**.

...and it will be, by the first proposition of this book, that **m.p.** is the same multiple of **c.d.** as **f** is a multiple of **a**. Therefore, each of the two quantities **m.p.** and **g** is an <term>equimultiple</term><note>Magnitudes multiplied by the same factor; for example, if you double two different numbers, the results are equimultiples of the originals.</note> of the quantity **c.d.**; therefore they are equal. For this inference was demonstrated in the 7th proposition of this book; and because **g** is not greater than **k**, **m.p.** will not be greater than the same. But by the conversion of the definition of <term>discrete proportionality</term><note>original: "incontinue proportionalitatis"; This refers to Euclid's definition of magnitudes that are in the same ratio but are distinct from one another, rather than forming a continuous chain.</note> **m.n.** is greater than **k** because **f** is greater than **b**. Therefore **m.n.** is greater than **m.p.**, which is impossible. Thus the proposition remains proven.

### Proposition 13.

If there are any number of quantities proportional to as many others, the ratio of one to one will be the same as the ratio of all those taken together to all the others taken together.

<margin>
<note>A geometric diagram illustrates Proposition 13 with four rows of horizontal lines representing proportions. 
Row 1: Line segments labeled with numerical values 5, 24 (with 'h' above), 20 (with 'k' above), and 16.
Row 2: Line segments labeled with 'a' (12), 'c' (10), and 'e' (8).
Row 3: Line segments labeled with 'b' (6), 'd' (5), and 'f' (4).
Row 4: Line segments labeled with 'l' (16), 'm' (15), and 'n' (12).
These segments represent the relationship where the ratio of individual parts ($a:b = c:d = e:f$) is the same as the ratio of their sums ($(a+c+e):(b+d+f)$).</note>
</margin>

¶ Whereas he first proposed concerning multiples, here he proposes concerning all proportions; hence this is more general than the former, because every multiplicity is a proportion, but not vice versa. Let, therefore, the ratio of **a** to **b**, **c** to **d**, and **e** to **f** be one ratio. I say that the ratio which **a** has to **b** is the same as the sum of **a, c, e** has to the sum of **b, d, f**. Let us take **g** as a multiple of **a**, **h** of **c**, and **k** of **e**, all being equimultiples. Likewise, let **l** be a multiple of **b**, **m** of **d**, and **n** of **f**, also being equimultiples. It will be, by the first proposition of this book, that the sum of **g, h, k** is the same multiple of the sum of **a, c, e** as **g** is a multiple of **a**. Similarly, by the same proposition, the sum of **l, m, n** will be the same multiple of the sum of **b, d, f** as **l** is a multiple of **b**. And by the conversion of the definition of discrete proportionality, taken twice: if **g** is greater than **l**, then **h** is greater than **m**, and **k** is greater than **n**; and if it is less, it is less; and if equal, it is equal. Therefore, by common knowledge, if **g** is greater than **l**, the sum of **g, h, k** is greater than the sum of **l, m, n**; if it is less, it is less; and if equal, it is equal. Therefore, by the definition of discrete proportionality, the ratio of **a** to **b** is as the sum of **a, c, e** is to the sum of **b, d, f**, which is what was proposed.

### Proposition 14.

If there are four proportional quantities, and the first is greater than the third, it is necessary that the second be greater than the fourth. If the first is less than the third, the second will be less than the fourth. If equal, they will be equal.

<margin>
<note>A geometric diagram for Proposition 14 shows two pairs of horizontal lines. 
The top pair consists of segments labeled '6' (marked 'c') and '8' (marked 'a'). 
The bottom pair consists of segments labeled '3' (marked 'd') and '4' (marked 'b').
This visually demonstrates that if $a:b$ is the same as $c:d$, and $a$ is larger than $c$, then $b$ must be larger than $d$.</note>
</margin>

¶ Let the ratio of **a** to **b** be as **c** is to **d**. I say that if **a** is greater than **c**, then **b** will be greater than **d**; and if less, then less; and if equal, then equal. For if **a** is greater than **c**, then by the first part of the 8th proposition of this book, the ratio of **a** to **d** will be greater than **c** to **d**. Therefore, the ratio of **a** to **d** will be greater than the ratio of **a** to **b**. Thus, by the second part of the 10th proposition of this book, **b** will be greater than **d**, which was the proposition. Likewise, if **a** is less than **c**, then by the first part of the 8th proposition, the ratio of **a** to **d** will be less than **c** to **d**. Therefore, the ratio of **a** to **b** will be greater than **a** to **d**; by the second part of the 10th proposition, **b** will be less than **d**. If, however, **a** is equal to **c**, then by the first part of the 7th proposition, **a** has the same ratio to **d** as **c** has to **d**. Therefore, **a** is to **d** as it is to **b**; thus, by the second part of the 9th proposition, **b** will be equal to **d**. Thus the proposition is clear.

### Proposition 15.

If equimultiples are assigned to any quantities, the ratio of the multiples and the submultiples will be one and the same.

<margin>
<note>A diagram showing proportional multiples for Proposition 15. 
The top line is divided into three segments of length '8' (total length 24, labeled 'c'). 
The bottom line is divided into three segments of length '4' (the first segment is labeled 'b', the total length 12 is labeled 'a'). 
This illustrates that the ratio of the wholes ($24:12$) is the same as the ratio of their corresponding parts ($8:4$).</note>
</margin>

¶ Let **c** be a multiple of **a**, and **d** be a multiple of **b**, and let them be equimultiples. I say that the ratio of **a** to **b** is the same as the ratio of **c** to **d**. Let **c** be divided according to the quantity of **a**, and **d** according to the quantity of **b**. There are as many parts in **c** as there are in **d**. And because any part of **c** is to any part of **d** as **a** is to **b**, it will be, by the 13th proposition of this book, that **c** is to **d** as **a** is to **b**, which is what was proposed.

### Proposition 16.

> If four magnitudes are proportional, they will also be proportional alternately. <note>original: "pmutatim" (permutatim). This refers to the mathematical rule of "alternando," where if a:b = c:d, then a:c = b:d.</note>

¶ Let there be a proportion of **a** to **b** as **c** is to **d**. I say that it will also be that **a** is to **c** as **b** is to **d**. This is the method of reasoning called <term>permuted proportionality</term><note>The practice of exchanging the inner terms (the "means") of a proportion.</note>, the demonstration of which is shown thus: Take **e** as an <term>equimultiple</term><note>Magnitudes multiplied by the same factor.</note> of **a**, and **f** as an equimultiple of **b**; likewise, take **g** as an equimultiple of **c**, and **h** as an equimultiple of **d**. By the preceding proposition, **e** will be to **f** as **g** is to **h**. Therefore, by Proposition 14, if **e** is greater than **g**, then **f** is also greater than **h**; if it is less, it is less; and if equal, it is equal. Therefore, by the definition of <term>discrete proportionality</term><note>original: "incontinue proportionalitatis." This refers to the standard definition of four magnitudes in proportion (Euclid’s Book V, Definition 5).</note>, **a** will be to **c** as **b** is to **d**, which is what was proposed. It is necessary, however, that in permuted proportionality, all four magnitudes are of the same kind. <note>This is a crucial restriction: you can only compare "a" to "c" if they are both the same type of magnitude, such as two lines or two areas. You cannot have a ratio between a line and a square.</note>

### Proposition 17.

> If magnitudes are proportional when combined, they are also proportional when separated. <note>original: "disiunctim" (disjunctim). This is the rule of "separando": if (a+b):b = (c+d):d, then a:b = c:d.</note>

<margin>
<note>A geometric diagram illustrating ratios. The top line shows points g, h, k, p with segments valued 16, 8, and 12. The second line shows points a, c, b with segments valued 8 and 4. The third line shows points d, f, e with segments valued 6 and 3. The fourth line shows points l, m, n, q with segments valued 12, 6, and 9.</note>
</margin>

¶ Having demonstrated the method of reasoning called permuted proportionality, he now demonstrates that which is called <term>disjunct proportionality</term><note>Also known as "separation of ratios."</note>. Let there be, therefore, a proportion of the whole **a.b.** to the part **b.c.** as the whole **d.e.** is to the part **e.f.** I say that the remainder **a.c.** will be to **c.b.** as the remainder **d.f.** is to **f.e.** Let us take **g.h.** as an equimultiple of **a.c.** and **h.k.** as an equimultiple of **c.b.** Likewise, take **l.m.** as an equimultiple of **d.f.** and **m.n.** as an equimultiple of **f.e.** By the first proposition of this book, the whole **g.k.** is the same multiple of **a.b.** as **g.h.** is of **a.c.**, and the whole **l.n.** is the same multiple of **d.e.** as **l.m.** is of **d.f.** Therefore, by the preceding hypotheses, **g.k.** is the same multiple of **a.b.** as **l.n.** is of **d.e.** Furthermore, let us take **k.p.** and **n.q.** as equimultiples of **c.b.** and **f.e.** respectively. By the second proposition, **h.p.** and **m.q.** will be equimultiples of **c.b.** and **f.e.** Therefore, by the conversion of the definition of discrete proportionality, if **g.k.** is greater than **h.p.**, then **l.n.** is greater than **m.q.**; if less, it is less; and if equal, it is equal. By removing the common segments **h.k.** and **m.n.**, it follows by <term>common knowledge</term><note>A reference to "Common Notions" or axioms—basic logical truths that if equals are subtracted from equals, the remainders are equal.</note> that if **g.h.** is greater than **k.p.**, then **l.m.** is greater than **n.q.**; if less, it is less; and if equal, it is equal. Therefore, by the definition of discrete proportionality, the ratio of **a.c.** to **c.b.** is as **d.f.** is to **f.e.**, which is what was proposed.

### Proposition 18.

> If magnitudes are proportional when separated, they will also be proportional when combined. <note>original: "coniunctim" (conjunctim). This is "componendo": if a:b = c:d, then (a+b):b = (c+d):d.</note>

<margin>
<note>A geometric diagram identical to the previous one, showing four lines with points g-h-k-p (16, 8, 12), a-c-b (8, 4), d-f-e (6, 3), and l-m-n-q (12, 6, 9).</note>
</margin>

¶ He demonstrates the method of reasoning called <term>combined proportionality</term>, which is the converse of the previous one. To demonstrate this, let us resume the arrangement of the preceding proposition, and let all its hypotheses remain, except that it is now assumed that the ratio of **a.c.** to **c.b.** is as **d.f.** is to **f.e.** I say that the ratio of the combined whole **a.b.** to **b.c.** will be as the whole **d.e.** is to **e.f.** It follows from this hypothesis and the other hypotheses of the preceding proposition regarding equimultiples that, by the conversion of the definition of discrete proportionality: if **g.h.** is greater than **k.p.**, then **l.m.** is greater than **n.q.**; if less, it is less; and if equal, it is equal. Therefore, when the common segments **h.k.** and **m.n.** are added, it follows by common knowledge that if **g.k.** is greater than **h.p.**, then **l.n.** is greater than **m.q.**; if less, it is less; and if equal, it is equal. Therefore, by the definition of discrete proportionality, the ratio of **a.b.** to **b.c.** will be as **d.e.** is to **e.f.**, which is what was proposed. This can also be proved indirectly thus: Since the ratio of **a.c.** to **c.b.** is as **d.f.** to **f.e.**, if it were not that **a.b.** is to **b.c.** as **d.e.** is to **e.f.**, then **d.e.** would have that ratio to some other magnitude, which would be either greater or less than **e.f.**; for if it were equal to it, the proposition would already be established.

These proofs allow mathematicians to manipulate equations by switching terms or adding/subtracting parts of a ratio while maintaining equality.</summary>

So let it first be greater, and let it be **e. g.**; and by the previous proposition, **a. c.** will be to **c. b.** as **d. g.** is to **g.** [e] . . . . 
whereby **d. g.** to **g. e.** is as **d. f.** to **f. e.** It follows, therefore, that since **d. g.** (the first) is less than **d. f.** (the third), then **g. e.** (the second) will be less than **e. f.** (the fourth); but it was assumed that it was greater. ### Proposition 19.

<margin>
<note>A geometric diagram showing two lines with labeled segments. The top line is divided into segments by points **a**, **e**, and **b**. Segment **a-e** is labeled with the number 12, and segment **e-b** is labeled with 4. The bottom line is divided by points **c**, **f**, and **d**. Segment **c-f** is labeled with 6, and segment **f-d** is labeled with 2.</note>
</margin>

> If from two wholes two portions are cut off, and the whole is to the whole as the part cut off is to the part cut off, then the remainder will be to the remainder as the whole is to the whole.

¶ Just as the fifth proposition deals with multiples, this one proposes a rule universally for all proportions; hence, it is as much more general as a proportion is more general than a simple multiple. Therefore, let there be two quantities **a. b.** and **c. d.**, from which two portions are cut off, namely **b. e.** and **d. f.** Let the proportion of the whole **a. b.** to the whole **c. d.** be as the cut-off portion **b. e.** is to the cut-off portion **d. f.** I say that the ratio of the remainder **a. e.** to the remainder **c. f.** will be the same as that of the whole **a. b.** to the whole **c. d.** For since **a. b.** is to **c. d.** as **b. e.** is to **d. f.**, then <term>alternately</term><note>original: "permutatim." If a:b = c:d, then a:c = b:d.</note> **a. b.** is to **b. e.** as **c. d.** is to **d. f.**; and <term>by separation</term><note>original: "disiunctim." If (a+b):b = (c+d):d, then a:b = c:d.</note> **a. e.** is to **e. b.** as **c. f.** is to **f. d.**; and again alternately **a. e.** is to **c. f.** as **e. b.** is to **f. d.** And because it was already established that **a. b.** was to **c. d.** in this same ratio, the proposition is clear. ¶ From this 19th proposition and from permuted proportionality, we can demonstrate the method of reasoning called <term>inverted proportionality</term><note>original: "proportionalitas eversa." A method where if a:b = c:d, then a:(a-b) = c:(c-d).</note>. For example, if **a. b.** is to **b. e.** as **c. d.** is to **d. f.**, I say that **b. a.** will be to **a. e.** as **c. d.** is to **c. f.** For since **a. b.** is to **b. e.** as **c. d.** is to **d. f.**, it will be alternately **a. b.** to **c. d.** as **b. e.** to **d. f.** Wherefore, by this 19th proposition, **b. a.** is to **d. c.** as **a. e.** is to **c. f.**; therefore, alternately, **b. a.** is to **a. e.** as **c. d.** is to **c. f.**, which is what was proposed. ¶ Since we also demonstrated the rule of <term>inverse proportionality</term><note>original: "proportionalitas... ex diffinitione incontinue proportionalitatis." If a:b = c:d, then b:a = d:c.</note> from the definition of discrete proportionality when explaining the principles of this fifth book, it can also be demonstrated here indirectly from permuted proportionality and the 9th proposition of this book. For if the proportion of **a.** is to **b.** as **c.** is to **d.**, I say that **b.** will be to **a.** as **d.** is to **c.** If it were not so, let **d.** be to **c.** as **b.** is to some other quantity **a. e.** Since **a.** is to **b.** as **c.** is to **d.**, it will be alternately **a.** to **c.** as **b.** to **d.** And because again **b.** is to **a. e.** as **d.** is to **c.**, it will also be alternately **b.** to **d.** as **a. e.** is to **c.** Wherefore **a.** to **c.** will be as **a. e.** is to **c.** If, therefore, **e.** were not equal to **c.** <note>The text likely means if **a.** were not equal to **a. e.**</note>, an impossibility would occur, contrary to the second part of the 9th proposition. If they are equal, then **b.** will be to **a.** as **d.** is to **c.**, which is what was proposed.

### Proposition 20.

> If there are any number of magnitudes, and others equal to them in number, which taken two by two in the same ratio, it is necessary in a proportionality of equality that if the first of the first set is greater than the last, the first of the second set is also greater than the last. If it is less, it is less; and if equal, it is equal.

¶ Euclid, being about to demonstrate the method of reasoning called <term>equal proportionality</term><note>original: "eq̄ ppoꝛtionalitas" (aequa proportionalitas). Also known as 'ex aequali.' If a:b = d:e and b:c = e:f, then a:c = d:f.</note> (whether the quantities of two orders are proportioned directly or inversely), sets forth two preceding principles necessary to prove the proposition: by the first, he demonstrates equal proportionality when the quantities of two orders are proportioned directly; by the second, however, when they are proportioned inversely. He proposes these two antecedents regarding quantities of two orders equal in number, whatever that number may be. For even if more quantities are taken on both sides according to any number, they hold true. It is not...

<margin>
<note>A geometric diagram for Proposition 20. A top horizontal line is labeled **a** at the left, **b** in the middle, and **c** at the right. The total value is marked as 12, with the segment **a-b** being 6 and **b-c** being 6. To the right, another line has a total value of 16, divided by point **d** into two segments of 8. Below these are two smaller isolated segments: segment **e** labeled 3, and segment **f** labeled 4.</note>
<insert>that is, let it be first: **d.** 2, **a.** 4, **b.** 4, **e.** 4; but truly **b.** 6... <note>original: "i e ſit pꝛ. d. 2 . az b . 4 . e 4 . er uerū . b . 6 . m"</note></insert>
</margin>

However, it is not necessary that we demonstrate these except only for three [quantities], for this is entirely sufficient for the proposition. And for any number more than that, it will be clear by equal proportionality <term>ex aequali|A term used when the first and last of one set of magnitudes are compared to the first and last of another set.</term> when the demonstration itself has been performed.

¶ Let there be, therefore, three quantities **a, b, e** <note>The OCR reads a, b, c, but the mathematical logic of the proof requires a, b, e to correspond with the secondary set.</note> and let there be three others which are **c, d, f**. Let the proportion of **a** to **b** be as **c** is to **d**, and let **b** be to **e** as **d** is to **f**. I say that if **a** is greater than **e**, then **c** will be greater than **f**; and if it is less, it will be less; and if it is equal, it will be equal. For if **a** is greater, then by the first part of the 8th proposition, the proportion of **a** to **b** will be greater than the proportion of **e** to **b**. Wherefore, by the 12th proposition, the proportion of **c** to **d** will be greater than **e** to **b**. And because by converted proportionality **e** to **b** is as **f** is to **d**, then **c** to **d** will be greater than **f** to **d**. Thus, by the first part of the 10th proposition, **c** is greater than **f**, which is what was proposed. 

¶ And if **a** were less than **e**, it will be proved by the same means and in the same way that **c** is less than **f**. For the proportion of **a** to **b** will be less than **e** to **b** by the first part of the 8th proposition; and therefore by the 12th and by converted proportionality, **c** to **d** will be less than **f** to **d**. Thus, by the first part of the 10th proposition, **c** will be less than **f**, which is what was proposed. If, however, **a** is equal to **e**, then by the first part of the 7th proposition, the proportion of **a** to **b** will be as **e** to **b**; and therefore by the second part of the 11th and by converted proportionality, **c** to **d** will be as **f** to **d**. Wherefore, by the first part of the 9th proposition, **c** is equal to **f**, which is what was proposed. 

¶ Certain people, however, have demonstrated this conclusion through alternate proportionality <note>original: "permutatim"</note> in this way: the proportion of **a** to **b** is as **c** to **d**, therefore alternately **a** is to **c** as **b** is to **d**. And because again **b** is to **e** as **d** is to **f**, then alternately **b** is to **d** as **e** is to **f**. But **b** was to **d** as **a** was to **c**; therefore by the 11th proposition, **a** will be to **c** as **e** is to **f**. Thus, by the 14th proposition, if **a** (the first) is greater than **e** (the third), then **c** (the second) will be greater than **f** (the fourth); and if less, less; and if equal, equal; which is what was proposed. 

These people, however, erred in their demonstration; for if it were the intention of Euclid <term>Euclidis|The Latin genitive for Euclid, the ancient Greek mathematician and author of the Elements.</term> to demonstrate it thus, it would not have been necessary for him to premise this conclusion as an antecedent to equal proportionality. For if one were to again perform a permutation of the proportionality arrived at—which is **a** to **c** being as **e** to **f**—it follows that **a** is to **e** as **c** is to **f**, and this is "equal proportionality" itself. Furthermore, their conclusion does not follow unless all the quantities of both orders were of one kind <note>The commentator notes that the "alternate" proof only works for homogeneous magnitudes (e.g., all lines), whereas Book V applies to magnitudes of different kinds, such as lines compared to times.</note>. For if **a, b, e** are lines and **c, d, f** are surfaces—or bodies, or times—one will not then be able to alternate the proportions. They sin, therefore, by demonstrating a universal statement in a particular way.

### Proposition 21.

<margin>
<note>A geometric diagram for Proposition 21. A top line is labeled **a** at the start, **b** in the middle, and **f** at the end, with a total value of 16 divided into segments of 8. Below it, a line **c** has a total of 12, divided by point **d** into segments of 6. Two smaller segments are below: segment **e** labeled 4, and segment **i** (likely intended as **f** in the text) labeled 3.</note>
</margin>

> If there be any number of quantities, and others equal to them in number, which, when taken two and two among the former and two and two among the latter, are compared cross-wise according to their proportion; it is also necessary that if in the proportion of equality the first of the first set be greater than the last, then the first of the second set will also be greater than the last; if less, then less; and if equal, then equal.

¶ Following the antecedent, let there be three quantities **a, b, e**, and let there be another three which are **f, c, d**. Let the proportion of **a** to **b** be as **c** is to **d**, and the proportion of **b** to **e** as **f** is to **c**. I say that if **a** is greater than **e**, then **f** will be greater than **d**; and if less, less; and if equal, equal. This, moreover, is proved by the same means and in the same way as the preceding one. For if **a** be greater than **e**, the proportion of **a** to **b** will be greater than **e** to **b**. Wherefore the proportion of **c** to **d** is greater than **e** to **b**, and therefore greater than **c** to **f** <note>Because b:e = f:c, the ratio e:b is the same as c:f.</note>. Therefore, **f** is greater than **d** by the second part of the 10th proposition, which is what was proposed. If **a** be less than **e**, then finally **c** to **d** will be less than **c** to **f**, wherefore by the same part of the same proposition, **f** will be less than **d**. If, however, **a** is equal to **e**, it follows that the proportion of **c** to **d** is as **c** is to **f**; therefore, by the second part of the 9th proposition, **f** will be equal to **d**, which is what was proposed.

### Proposition 22.

<margin>
<note>A geometric diagram illustrates proportional line segments. At the top, a horizontal line is divided into two parts labeled **g** (16) and **h** (24). Below it, pairs of bracketed line segments are arranged vertically: **k** (8) and **l** (12); **m** (4) and **n** (6); **a** (8) and **c** (12); **b** (4) and **d** (6); **e** (2) and **f** (3); **i** (1) and **q** (1 ½). This visual aid helps the reader track the scaling of multiples across two different sets of quantities.</note>
</margin>

If there are any number of quantities and others equal to them in number, each of which two are proportional to two of the first in equal proportionality <term>ex aequali|A method of comparing the first and last terms of two sets of magnitudes when the intermediate ratios are known to be equal.</term>, they will be proportional.

¶ Having demonstrated the antecedents to equal proportionality, here he demonstrates the principle itself: first, when the quantities of the two orders are directly proportional. It is not necessary to demonstrate this except when there are only three quantities in each of the two orders. For it clearly follows from this when there are four quantities or more in each order. Therefore, it was not necessary to demonstrate the prior case except only when there are three quantities in each order. ¶ Let there be, therefore, three quantities **a, b, e** and let three others be taken which are **c, d, f**. Let the proportion of **a** to **b** be as **c** is to **d**, and let **b** be to **e** as **d** is to **f**. I say that the proportion of **a** to **e** will be as **c** is to **f**. For I shall take **g** as a multiple of **a** and **h** as a multiple of **c** in equal degrees <note>original: "eque multiplicia"</note>. Likewise, let **k** be an equal multiple of **b**, and **l** an equal multiple of **d**; and again let **m** be an equal multiple of **e**, and **n** be an equal multiple of **f**. By the fourth proposition, **g** will be to **k** as **b** is to **l**, and **k** will be to **m** as **l** is to **n**. Wherefore, by the twentieth proposition, if **g** is greater than **m**, **b** <note>The text likely intended the multiple **h** here for comparison with **n**</note> will be greater than **n**; and if it is less, it will be less; and if it is equal, it will be equal. Therefore, by the definition of discontinuous proportionality, the proportion of **a** to **e** is as **c** to **f**, which is what was proposed. ¶ This can also be demonstrated by the 15th proposition of this book, by taking **g, k, m** as equal multiples of **a, b, e** and **l, n** as equal multiples of **c, d, f**. For by the 15th proposition, **g** will be to **k** as **b** is to **l**, and **k** to **m** as **l** to **n**, with the rest proceeding as before. ¶ If there should be more than three quantities in each order—for instance, four—by adding **p** and **q** such that **e** is to **p** as **f** is to **q**, then again **a** will be to **p** as **c** is to **q**. This is because it has been demonstrated that **a** is to **e** as **c** is to **f**. Therefore, by removing **b** and **d**, there will be three quantities **a, e, p** and another three **c, f, q** as proposed; wherefore **a** is to **p** as **c** is to **q**. Thus it is demonstrated for four quantities by using the proof for three and removing one middle term. In the same way, you will demonstrate for five quantities by using the proof for four and removing two middle terms; and for six by using five and removing three; and so on for the rest.

### Proposition 23.

<margin>
<note>A geometric diagram showing proportional line segments for indirect or "perturbed" proportion. A top horizontal line is divided into segments **g** (16) and **k** (24). Below it, pairs of horizontal line segments are labeled: **l** (8) and **h** (12); **m** (4) and **n** (6); **a** (8) and **f** (12); **b** (4) and **c** (6); **e** (2) and **d** (3); **i** (1) and **q** (1 ½). The arrangement differs from the previous diagram to show how cross-wise ratios still result in a proportional relationship between the first and last terms.</note>
</margin>

If there are any number of quantities and others equal to them in number, each of which two are proportional to two of the prior ones in perturbed <note>original: "indirecte" or "perversum"</note> proportion, they will be in equal proportionality.

¶ He demonstrates equal proportionality in quantities of two orders that are proportional indirectly or cross-wise. Nor is it necessary to demonstrate this except when there are only three quantities in each of the two orders; for through this, it clearly follows for whatever number are placed in each order, just as was demonstrated in the preceding proposition concerning direct proportionality. Let there be, therefore, three quantities **a, b, e**, and let three others be taken which are **f, c, d**. Let the proportion of **a** to **b** be as **c** is to **d**, and **b** to **e** as **f** is to **c**. I say that the proportion of **a** to **e** will be as **f** is to **d**. For I shall take **g** as a multiple of **a**, and **h** <note>The text reads **b** here, likely a transcription error for the second set's corresponding multiple</note> of **c**, and **k** of **f** as equal multiples. Likewise, let **l** be a multiple of **b**, and **m** of **e**, and **n** of **d** as equal multiples. Then by the fourth proposition, **g** will be to **l** as **b** is to **n**; and by the 15th, **l** is to **m** as **k** is to **b**. Wherefore, by the 21st proposition, if **g** exceeds **m**, then **k** exceeds **n**; and if it is less, it is less; and if it is equal, it is equal. Therefore, by the definition of discontinuous proportionality, the proportion of **a** to **e** is as **f** is to **d**, which is what was proposed. ¶ This can also be demonstrated by the 15th proposition of this book, by taking **g, l, m** as equal multiples of **a, b, e** and **k, b, n** as equal multiples of **f, c, d**. For by the 15th, **g** is to **l** as **b** is to **n**, and **l** is to **m** as **k** is to **b**, with the rest proceeding as before. However, these and the preceding propositions are more conveniently demonstrated according to the first method. ¶ If there are more than three quantities in each order—for instance, four—by adding **p** and **q** such that **a** is to **b** as...

### Proposition 24.

<margin>
<note>A geometric diagram for Proposition 24. A horizontal line is divided into segments by the points a, g, b, d, e, and h. Numerical values are written above the segments: 9 (between a and g), 6 (between g and b), 8 (between b and d), 6 (between d and e), and 4 (between e and h). Below this main line are two shorter line segments: one labeled 'c' with the number 3, and another labeled 'f' with the number 2.</note>
</margin>

If the proportion of the first to the second be as that of the third to the fourth, and the proportion of the fifth to the second be as that of the sixth to the fourth: then the proportion of the first and fifth taken together to the second will be as that of the sixth and third taken together to the fourth.

¶ What the second proposition proposed concerning multiples, this one proposes universally concerning all proportions. Hence, this is as much more common as proportion itself is to multiplicity; just as the 13th proposition is to the first. Let, therefore, the proportion of **a-b** to **c** be as **d-e** to **f**, and again **b-g** to **c** as **e-h** to **f**. I say that the proportion of **a-g** to **c** is as **d-h** to **f**. For by converse proportionality, **c** to **b-g** will be as **f** to **e-h**. Wherefore by Proposition 22, it will be in equal proportionality <term>ex aequali|A method of comparing the first and last terms of two sets of magnitudes when the intermediate ratios are known to be equal.</term> **a-b** to **b-g** as **e-d** to **e-h**. Therefore, conjunctively by Proposition 18, **a-g** to **g-b** is as **d-h** to **h-e**. Thus by Proposition 22, it will be in equal proportionality **a-g** to **c** as **d-h** to **f**, which is what was proposed.

### Proposition 25.

<margin>
<note>A geometric diagram for Proposition 25. The top line segment is marked with points a, g, and b, with the numbers 8 and 4. Above the segment g-b is a mark for 'e'. Below this is a line segment marked with c, h, and d, with the numbers 4 and 2. To the right is a separate segment labeled 'f' with the number 2.</note>
</margin>

If four quantities be proportional, and the first of them be the greatest and the last the least, it is necessarily proven that the first and the last taken together are greater than the other two [taken together].

¶ What is proposed here has no place unless all four quantities are of the same kind. Let there be, therefore, four quantities of the same kind in the proportion of **a-b** to **c-d** as **e** to **f**. And let **a-b** be the greatest. It is not necessary to assume that **f** is the least, because it follows from the fact that **a-b** was set as the greatest. Therefore, the author did not place this in the conclusion as an assumption, but rather as a conclusion of the preceding assumption. I say that when it is so, the sum of **a-b** and **f** will be greater than that of **c-d** and **e**. For since **a-b** is greater than **e**, I shall cut off from **b-a** [the segment] **g-b** equal to **e**. ¶ Similarly, because **c-d** is greater than **f**, I shall cut off from **c-d** [the segment] **h-d** equal to **f**. And because of the hypothesis, **a-b** will be to **c-d** as **g-b** is to **h-d**. Wherefore by Proposition 19, the remainder **a-g** is to the remainder **c-h** as the whole **a-b** is to the whole **c-d**. Since therefore **a-g** is to **c-h** as **a-b** is to **c-d**, but **a-b** is greater than **c-d**, then **a-g** must be greater than **c-h**. Therefore, by adding the two quantities **g-b** and **h-d** to both, by common knowledge <note>original: "per communem scientiam" — refers to common notions or axioms in Euclidean logic</note> the sum of **a-b** and **h-d** will be greater than the sum of **c-d** and **g-b**. And because **d-h** was set equal to **f**, and **g-b** equal to **e**, the sum of **a-b** and **f** will be greater than the sum of **c-d** and **e**, which is what was proposed.

### Proposition 26.

If the proportion of the first of four quantities to the second be greater than that of the third to the fourth, then conversely and on the contrary the proportion of the second to the first will be less than that of the fourth to the third.

Let the proportion of **a** to **b** be greater than that of **c** to **d**. I say that conversely to the prior way, the proportion of **b** to **a** will be less than that of **d** to **c**. For if it were the same proportion of **b** to **a** as it is of **d** to **c**, it would be...

<meta>This page continues the logical proofs of Book V of Euclid’s Elements, specifically focusing on the properties of unequal ratios. It concludes the proof of Proposition 26 (regarding inverse proportions) and proceeds to demonstrate Propositions 27 and 28, which deal with alternating and compounded proportions in the context of inequalities.</meta>

conversely, <note>original: "econuerso"</note> a to b as c to d, but it is not; rather it is greater. If, however, the proportion of b to a is greater than d to c, let e to a be as d to c. By the 12th proposition, c to a will be less than b to a; therefore, by the first part of the 10th proposition, e is less than b. Consequently, by the second part of the 8th proposition, the proportion of a to e will be greater than a to b. Since by inverse proportionality a to e is as c to d, it follows from the 12th proposition that the proportion of c to d is greater than a to b—but it was stated to be less. Therefore, the proposition remains as stated. ¶ We can also, if desired, prove the proposition directly: for it is manifest from the first part of the 10th proposition that the quantity which has the same proportion to b as c has to d is less than a, because the proportion of a to b is assumed to be greater than c to d. Let that quantity be e. Since, therefore, the proportion of e to b is as c to d, conversely b to e will be as d to c. It is established from the second part of the 8th proposition that the proportion of b to a is less than the proportion of b to e. Thus, by the 12th proposition, the proportion of b to a is less than d to c, which is what we wished to show.

### Proposition 27.

<margin>
<note>A geometric diagram labeled with points and numbers used to illustrate the proof of Proposition 27. A line segment labeled 'a' is assigned the value 8, and a segment 'c' is 4. Below these, a segment 'b' is 4, and 'd' is 3. A separate segment 'e' is labeled with the number 6.</note>
</margin>

If of four quantities the proportion of the first to the second is greater than that of the third to the fourth, then by permutation <note>Permutation, or *alternando*, involves comparing the first quantity to the third, and the second to the fourth.</note> the proportion of the first to the third will be greater than that of the second to the fourth.
¶ Let here also the proportion of a to b be greater than c to d. I say that by permutation the proportion of a to c will be greater than b to d. For it will not be equal, because then by permutation a to b would be as c to d; nor will it be less. For if this is assumed: let e to c be as b to d. By the 12th proposition, the proportion of e to c will be greater than a to c, wherefore by the first part of the 10th proposition, e is greater than a. Thus, by the first part of the 8th proposition, the proportion of e to b is greater than a to b. And because it was assumed that e to c is as b to d, by permutation e to b will be as c to d. Therefore, by the 12th proposition, the proportion of c to d will be greater than a to b—but the opposite was assumed. Therefore, the proposition is true. ¶ The same is also shown directly, as in the previous case: for if e to b is taken as c to d, e will be less than a by the first part of the 10th proposition. Wherefore, by the first part of the 8th proposition, a to c will be greater than e to c. But by permuted proportionality, e to c is as b to d; therefore, by the 12th proposition, a to c is greater than b to d, which is the proposition.

<note>A second geometric diagram for Proposition 27 using different values. Line segment 'a' is 12, and 'c' is 4. Below them, 'b' is 3, and 'd' is 2. An auxiliary segment 'e' is assigned the value 9.</note>
</margin>

### Proposition 28.

<margin>
<note>A geometric diagram for Proposition 28 showing the composition of ratios. A horizontal line connects points 'a' and 'b'. A diagonal line descends from a point above 'a' toward 'b'. The number 12 is written under the horizontal line, and 4 is at the end. Labels '2' and 'o' appear near the diagonal. Below are segments 'c' with the value 6 and 'd' with the value 3.</note>
</margin>

If there are four quantities whose first has a greater proportion to the second than the third has to the fourth, then by addition <note>Also known as *composition* (coniunctim), this rule states that if a:b > c:d, then (a+b):b > (c+d):d.</note> the proportion of the first and second [combined] to the second will also be greater than the proportion of the third and fourth [combined] to the fourth.
¶ Let the proportion of a to b be greater than c to d. I say that the proportion of the whole a,b to b will be greater than the whole c,d to d. For it will be neither equal nor less. For if equal, then by division <note>original: "disiunctim"</note> a to b would be as c to d. But if it is less: let e,b to b be as c,d to d. By the 12th proposition, the proportion of e,b to b will be greater than a,b to b. Thus, by the first part of the 10th proposition, e,b is greater than a,b, and by common conception <note>A self-evident logical axiom.</note> e is greater than a. Wherefore, by the first part of the 8th proposition, the proportion of e to b is greater than a to b. But e to b is as c to d by divided proportionality, because e,b to b was as c,d to d. Therefore, by the 12th proposition, c to d is greater than a to b, which is contrary to the hypothesis. <note>original: "ypothe"</note> ¶ The same is also shown directly: since it is proposed that the proportion of a to b is greater than c to d, let the proportion of e to b be as c to d; then by the first part of the tenth, e is less than a.

proportion, quantity, by permutation, by addition (jointly), lesser, greater, by division (disjointly), hypothesis.</note>

If there be four quantities of which the first and second added together <note>original: "prime & secunde"</note> to the second has a greater proportion than the third and fourth added together to the fourth, then by separation <note>original: "disiunctim"; the ratio of the difference between the first and second to the second</note> the proportion of the first to the second will also be greater than the third to the fourth.
¶ Let the proportion of *a. b.* to *b.* be greater than *c. d.* to *d.* I say that by separation, the proportion of *a.* to *b.* will be greater than *c.* to *d.* Otherwise, it would be equal or less. If it were equal, then by compounded proportionality *a. b.* to *b.* would be as *c. d.* to *d.* If, however, it were less, then *c. d.* to *d.* would be greater than *a. b.* to *b.* Thus, by the preceding proposition, *c. d.* to *d.* would be greater than *a. b.* to *b.*, which is inconsistent <note>original: "inconueniens"; a logical contradiction</note>, because it was stated to be less. Therefore, what is said is true. We shall also establish this demonstratively in this way: let us set the proportion of *e. b.* to *b.* to be as the proportion of *c. d.* to *d.* By the first part of Proposition 10, *e. b.* will be less than *a. b.*, wherefore by common knowledge *e.* is less than *a.* Therefore, by the first part of Proposition 8, the proportion of *e.* to *b.* is less than *a.* to *b.* But the proportion of *e.* to *b.* is as *c.* to *d.* by separated proportionality <note>original: "disiuncta proportionalitate"</note>; thus, by Proposition 12, the proportion of *a.* to *b.* is greater than *c.* to *d.*, which is what was proposed.

### Proposition 2.

<margin>
<note>A geometric diagram showing a triangle with vertices labeled 'a' at the top, 'b' at the bottom left, and 'c' at the bottom right. A horizontal line segment labeled 'd' on the left side (ab) and 'e' on the right side (ac) is drawn parallel to the base bc. This is a classic illustration of the Thales's Theorem or the Side-Splitter Theorem.</note>
</margin>

**I**f a straight line cutting two sides of a triangle is parallel <note>original: "equidistans"</note> to the remaining side: it cuts those two sides proportionally. Conversely, if it cuts them proportionally, it is necessary that it is parallel to the remaining side. 

Let there be a triangle **a.b.c.** whose two sides **a.b.** and **a.c.** a line **d.e.** cuts parallel to the third side, which is **b.c.** I say that the ratio of **a.d.** to **d.b.** will be as **a.e.** to **e.c.** And conversely, if the ratio of **a.d.** to **d.b.** is as **a.e.** to **e.c.**, the line **d.e.** will be parallel to the line **b.c.** 

For I shall draw two lines **e.b.** and **d.c.**, and by the 37th [proposition] of the first [book], triangle **e.d.b.** will be equal to triangle **d.e.c.** because they are both upon the line **d.e.** and between parallel lines. Therefore, by the second part of the 7th [proposition] of the fifth [book], the ratio of triangle **a.d.e.** to each of them will be one and the same. But by the preceding [proposition], the ratio of it [triangle **a.d.e.**] to triangle **e.d.b.** is as the line **a.d.** to the line **d.b.**; and to triangle **d.e.c.**, as the line **a.e.** to the line **e.c.** For each of them is of equal height; therefore the ratio of **a.d.** to **d.b.** will be as **a.e.** to **e.c.**, which is the first part. 

And if this [the ratio] is so, by the preceding [proposition], there will be one ratio of [triangle] **a.d.e.** to each of them; therefore by the second part of the 9th [proposition] of the fifth [book], they are equal to one another. And because they are upon the same base, namely the line **d.e.**, and on the same side, it follows by the 39th [proposition] of the first [book] that the line **d.e.** is parallel to the line **b.c.**, which is the second part.

### Proposition 3.

<margin>
<note>A geometric diagram showing a large triangle with vertices 'e' (top right), 'b' (top left), and 'c' (bottom left). Inside this, another triangle 'a-b-c' is formed. A line 'a-d' bisects the angle at 'a' and meets the base 'bc' at 'd'. A line 'b-e' is drawn parallel to 'a-d', meeting the extension of side 'ca' at point 'e'. This illustrates the Angle Bisector Theorem.</note>
</margin>

**I**f a straight line drawn from any angle of a triangle to the base bisects that angle equally: the two parts of the base will be proportional to the remaining sides of the same triangle. Conversely, if the two parts of the base which the line drawn from the angle distinguishes are proportional to the remaining sides of the triangle, it is necessarily proved that the line divides the angle equally.

Let there be a triangle **a.b.c.** whose angle **a** is divided equally by line **a.d.** I say that the ratio of **b.d.** to **d.c.** is as **b.a.** to **a.c.** And conversely: for I shall draw **b.e.** parallel to **a.d.** and I shall extend **c.a.** until it meets with **b.e.** at point **e.** By the first part of the 29th [proposition] of the first [book], angle **e.b.a.** will be equal to angle **b.a.d.**, and by the second part of the same [proposition], angle **e** is equal to angle **d.a.c.** Therefore angle **e** is equal to angle **e.b.a.**; so, by the 6th [proposition] of the first [book], [side] **e.a.** is equal to **a.b.** And thus by the first part of the 7th [proposition] of the fifth [book], the ratio of **e.a.** to **a.c.** is as **b.a.** to **a.c.** But by the preceding [proposition], **e.a.** to **a.c.** is as **b.d.** to **d.c.** Therefore **b.a.** to **a.c.** is as **b.d.** to **d.c.**, which is the first part. 

The second part, which is the converse of the first part, shall be proved in the opposite way. For keeping the same arrangement, if the ratio of **b.a.** to **a.c.** is as **b.d.** to **d.c.**, then by the preceding [proposition] **e.a.** to **a.c.** is as **b.d.** to **d.c.**, and the ratio of **e.a.** to **a.c.** will be the same as **b.a.** to **a.c.** Therefore, by the first part of the 9th [proposition] of the fifth [book], **e.a.** and **a.b.** are equal. Thus by the 5th [proposition] of the first [book], the two angles **e** and **e.b.a.** are equal. Therefore by the first and second parts of the 29th [proposition] of the first [book], angle **b.a.d.** is equal to angle **d.a.c.**, which is the second part.

### Proposition 4.

**O**f any two triangles whose angles of the one are equal to the angles of the other: the sides looking toward <note>original: "respicientia," meaning the sides opposite to the equal angles</note> the equal angles are proportional.
¶ Let there be two <term>equiangular</term><note>Having equal angles.</note> triangles **a.b.c.** and **d.e.f.** Let angle **a** be equal to angle **d**, angle **b** to angle **e**, and angle **c** to angle **f**. I say that the <term>proportion</term> <note>In modern terms, the ratio.</note> of **d.e.** to **a.b.** and **d.f.** to **a.c.** is as **e.f.** to **b.c.** For I shall place both triangles upon one line which is **e.c.**, so that the two angles of the one which will be upon this line are equal to the two of the other which will be upon the same. Not indeed middle to middle or extreme to extreme, but the middle of one to the extreme of the other. And I shall place two of their middle angles to meet at the same point. Let **a.f.c.** be that same triangle which was **a.b.c.** And because angle **a.f.c.** is equal to angle **c**, and angle **d.f.e.** to angle **c** by the hypothesis <note>original: "ypothesiz"</note>: it will be, by the first part of the 28th [proposition] of the first [book] <note>Book I, Prop 28 deals with parallel lines and corresponding angles.</note>, that line **a.f.** is parallel <note>original: "equidistans"</note> to **d.e.**, and **d.f.** is parallel to **a.c.** Therefore, I will complete the parallelogram <note>original: "superficiem equidistantium laterum"</note> which shall be **g.f.** By the 34th [proposition] of the first [book], **g.a.** will be equal to **d.f.**, and **g.d.** equal to **a.f.** Because, therefore, by the second [proposition] of this [book], **g.a.** is to **a.c.** as **e.f.** is to **f.c.**, and by the same, **e.f.** is to **f.c.** as **e.d.** is to **d.g.**, it will be by the 7th [proposition] of the fifth [book] that **d.f.** is to **a.c.**, and by the same, **e.d.** to **a.b.** <note>original: "c.d. ad f.a."</note> is as **e.f.** to **b.c.** <note>original: "f.c."</note>, which is what was proposed.

</margin>

### Proposition 5.

**O**f any two triangles of which all the sides looking toward each other have one single proportion: the angles contained by the proportional sides are proven to be equal to one another.
¶ This is the converse of the previous [proposition]; nor did he make from it and the preceding one a single conclusion, as he did in the second and third of this book: because it is demonstrated neither by the same configuration nor by the same means as the preceding. Let there be, therefore, two triangles **a.b.c.** and **d.e.f.**, and let the proportion of **a.b.** to **d.e.** and **a.c.** to **d.f.** be as **b.c.** to **e.f.** I say that angle **a** is equal to angle **d**, and angle **b** to angle **e**, and angle **c** to angle **f**. I shall construct upon line **e.f.**, on the opposite side of triangle **d.e.f.**, angle **f.e.g.** equal to angle **b**, and angle **e.f.g.** equal to angle **c**. By the 32nd [proposition] of the first [book], angle **g** will be equal to angle **a**. Therefore, by the preceding [proposition 4], the proportion of **a.b.** to **e.g.** and **a.c.** to **f.g.** is as **b.c.** to **e.f.** Since **a.b.** is to **d.e.** as it is to **e.g.**, and **a.c.** is to **d.f.** as it is to **f.g.**; therefore, by the second part of the 9th [proposition] of the fifth [book], **d.e.** is equal to **e.g.**, and by the same, **d.f.** is equal to **f.g.** Wherefore, by the 8th [proposition] of the first [book], the two triangles **d.e.f.** and **g.e.f.** are equiangular: wherefore, triangle **g.e.f.** is also equiangular to triangle **a.b.c.** The proposition is established.
