### Proposition 6.

**A**ny two triangles of which one angle of the one is equal to one angle of the other, and the sides containing those two equal angles are proportional to each other, are mutually equiangular.
¶ Let the previous arrangement remain. And let only angle **b** be equal to angle **e** <note>original: "d.e.f."</note>, and the proportion of **a.b.** to **d.e.** be as **b.c.** to **e.f.** I say that the two triangles **a.b.c.** and **d.e.f.** are still equiangular. For since, by the 4th [proposition] of this book, on account of the hypotheses of the previous conclu... <meta>catchword: /</meta>

...[of the ratio] **a.b.** to **c.g.** as **b.c.** to **e.f.**, it will be that **a.b.** is to **d.e.** as **a.b.** is to **e.g.**; wherefore by the second part of the ninth [proposition] of the fifth [book] <note>original: "none quinti"; Euclid's Elements, Book V, Prop 9 states that if two magnitudes have the same ratio to a third, they are equal to each other.</note>, **d.e.** is equal to **e.g.** Since, therefore, the two sides **d.e.** and **e.f.** of triangle **d.e.f.** are equal to the two sides **e.g.** and **e.f.** of triangle **g.e.f.**, and angle **e** of one is equal to angle **e** of the other (since each is equal to angle **b**), they will be <term>equiangular</term><note>Having all corresponding angles equal.</note> by the fourth [proposition] of the first [book]. And since triangle **e.g.f.** is also equiangular to **a.b.c.**, the proposition is clear.

### Proposition 7.

<note>A geometric diagram showing two triangles side-by-side. The left triangle has vertices labeled a (top), b (bottom-left), and c (bottom-right). A point g is marked on the side ab, and a line segment gc is drawn to create a smaller internal triangle. The right triangle is labeled with vertices d (top), e (bottom-left), and f (bottom-right).</note>

**I**f there are two triangles in which one angle of the one is equal to one angle of the other, and the sides of two of the remaining angles are proportional; and if, of the final remaining angles, either both or neither are less than a right angle <note>90 degrees</note>: it is necessary that those two triangles be equiangular to each other in all their angles.
¶ Let there be two triangles **a.b.c.** and **d.e.f.**, and let angle **a** be equal to angle **d**, and the proportion of **a.c.** to **d.f.** be as **c.b.** is to **f.e.**, and let both of the two angles **b** and **e**, or neither, be less than a right angle: I say that they are equiangular. For if angle **c** of one is equal to angle **f** of the other, the proposition is clear by the previous [theorem]. But if **c** should be greater, let angle **a.c.g.** be made equal to it; then by the 32nd [proposition] of the first [book] <note>The sum of angles in a triangle is equal to two right angles.</note>, triangle **a.g.c.** will be equiangular to triangle **d.e.f.** Wherefore, by the fourth [proposition] of this [book], the proportion of **a.c.** to **d.f.** is as **g.c.** is to **e.f.** But it was also thus for **b.c.** to **e.f.** <note>original: "c.f." is likely an OCR error for "e.f." or "f.e."</note>; therefore, by the 9th [proposition] of the fifth [book], **g.c.** and **b.c.** are equal. Therefore, by the fifth [proposition] of the first [book], angle **b** is equal to angle **b.g.c.** If, therefore, neither of the two angles **b** and **e** were less than a right angle, it would follow that two angles of one triangle are not less than two right angles, which cannot be by the 32nd [proposition] of the first [book]. But if both were less than a right angle, angle **a.g.c.** would be greater than a right angle by the 13th [proposition] of the first [book] <note>Angles on a straight line sum to two right angles; if one is acute, its neighbor is obtuse.</note>; wherefore angle **e**, being equal to it, would also be greater than a right angle, which is against the <term>hypothesis</term><note>The initial assumption or given conditions of the proof.</note>. Therefore, the opposite being destroyed, the proposition remains. It is necessary, however, that both of the remaining angles, or neither, be less than a right angle. For it is possible in the same triangle, as in triangle **a.b.c.**, for line **g.c.** to be equal to **b.c.**, and thus there will be one proportion of **a.c.** to each of them by the 7th [proposition] of the fifth [book]. Yet triangles **a.g.c.** and **a.b.c.** will not be equiangular, although one angle of one is equal to one angle of the other—indeed, the same angle, as angle **a**—and the proportion of line **a.c.** as it is a side of the large [triangle] to **a.c.** as it is a side of the small [triangle] is as **b.c.**, a side of the large, to **g.c.**, a side of the small. For both are equal; and this is because angle **g** of the smaller is greater than a right angle, and angle **b** of the larger is less. For in every triangle of two equal sides, each of the angles at the base is less than a right angle.

### Proposition 8.

**I**f a <term>perpendicular</term><note>A line at a right angle (90°) to another.</note> line is drawn from the right angle of a <term>right-angled</term><note>original: "orthogonij"</note> triangle to the base: the two partial triangles formed will be similar to the whole triangle and to each other. From this it is also manifest that in every right-angled triangle, if a perpendicular is drawn from its right angle to the base, the perpendicular itself will be a <term>mean proportional</term><note>original: "proportionalis"; a value that mediates the ratio between two others (a:b as b:c).</note> between the two sections of the base. Likewise, each side is [a mean proportional] between the whole base and the portion of the base adjacent to it.
¶ Let triangle **a.b.c.** be right-angled and its angle **a** be a right angle, from which **a.d.** is drawn...

This illustrates how the altitude of a right triangle creates two smaller triangles, a-b-d and a-d-c, which are both similar to the original and to each other.</note>

perpendicular to the base. I say that each of the two partial triangles, which are **a.b.d.** and **a.d.c.**, is similar to the whole triangle **a.b.c.** and one of them is similar to the other. For each of them is <term>equiangular</term><note>original: "equiangulus"; meaning all corresponding angles are equal.</note> to the whole by the 32nd [proposition] of the first [book] <note>This rule states that the interior angles of a triangle sum to two right angles.</note>, because each is <term>orthogonal</term><note>original: "orthogonius"; right-angled.</note> and shares one angle with the whole; wherefore they are also equiangular to each other. Thus, angle **b.** is equal to angle **d.a.c.**, and angle **b.a.d.** is equal to angle **c.**, and the two angles which are at **d.** are equal to each other and equal to the whole angle **a.** Wherefore, by the 4th [proposition] of this [book], the sides <term>subtending</term><note>original: "respicientia"; literally "looking at" or opposite to.</note> their equal angles are proportional; therefore, by definition, they are similar, which is what was proposed. Both corollaries clearly appear from these facts.

### Proposition 9.

<margin>
<note>A geometric diagram displays a semicircle drawn on the diameter a-d. A vertical line segment b-e is drawn from a point b on the diameter up to the circumference. Lines connect e to a and e to d, forming a right-angled triangle within the semicircle. Below are two reference lines labeled b and c.</note>
</margin>

**T**o find a <term>mean proportional</term><note>original: "tertiam inter eas sub proportionalitate continua"; literally "a third placed between them in continuous proportion." This is the geometric mean, where line A is to B as B is to C.</note> between two proposed lines.
¶ Let the two proposed lines be **a.b.** and **c.**, between which I wish to place one line in continuous proportion. I shall join one to the other, and let the whole line composed of them be **a.d.**, so that **b.d.** is equal to **c.** Upon the whole line, I describe a semicircle **a.e.d.**, and I extend **e.b.** perpendicular to the line **a.d.** up to the circumference. I say that line **b.e.** is the one we seek. For I extend the lines **e.a.** and **e.d.**, and by the 31st [proposition] of the third [book] <note>original: "30. tertij"; most editions of Euclid list the theorem that an angle inscribed in a semicircle is a right angle as Proposition 31.</note>, the whole angle **e.** will be a right angle. Therefore, by the first part of the corollary of the preceding [proposition], the proportion of **a.b.** is to **b.e.** as **b.e.** is to **b.d.**, which is what was proposed.

### Proposition 10.

<margin>
<note>A geometric diagram shows an angle with two radiating lines. One line contains points a, b, and g; the other contains a, d, and f. Two parallel lines, d-b and f-g, connect the rays. This construction is used to find a third or fourth proportional using the properties of parallel lines intersecting an angle.</note>
</margin>

**T**o find a <term>third proportional</term><note>original: "tertiam eis in continua proportionalitate subiungere"; given lines A and B, find X such that A:B = B:X.</note> to two given lines.
¶ Let the two proposed lines be **a.b.** and **c.**, to which I wish to add a third in continuous proportion. I join line **c.** at an angle, as it happens, with line **a.b.**; let **a.d.** be equal to it. I extend line **a.b.** to **e.** until **b.e.** is equal to **a.d.** Having drawn line **b.d.**, from point **e.** I draw a line parallel to it, and I extend line **a.d.** until they meet at point **f.** I say, therefore, that line **d.f.** is the one we seek. For by the 2nd [proposition] of this [book], the proportion of **a.b.** to **b.e.** is as **a.d.** to **d.f.** But **a.b.** to **b.e.** is as **a.b.** to **a.d.** by the second part of the 7th [proposition] of the fifth [book]; wherefore **a.b.** is to **a.d.** as **a.d.** is to **d.f.**, which is what was proposed.

And if, three lines being proposed, we wish to find a <term>fourth proportional</term><note>Given A, B, and C, find X such that A:B = C:X.</note> to which the third has the same ratio as the first to the second: let one line be made from the first and second, and let the third be joined to the whole composite line at an angle. From the common endpoint of the first and second, let a line be drawn to the extremity of the third; and from the other endpoint of the second, let a line parallel to this line be drawn until it meets the third, which has been extended in a continuous straight line. By the 2nd [proposition] of this [book], the line which this parallel cuts off will be the one sought; just as if in this figure the first were **a.b.**, the second **b.e.**, and the third **a.d.**, the fourth would be **d.f.**

### Proposition 11.

**T**o cut off any required part from a given line.
¶ Let **a.b.** be the assigned line; from it, I wish to cut off a certain part, for instance, a third. I join to it at an angle, as it happens, a line of indefinite quantity, which shall be **a.c.**, from which I cut off three equal portions.

### Proposition 12.

<margin>
<note>A triangle is shown with vertices a (left), b (bottom right), and c (top right). Several interior lines are drawn: vertical segments from points d and e on the base line a-b, and lines connecting these to points f and g on the side a-c. A point k is marked at an interior intersection point, demonstrating the proportional division of two lines.</note>
</margin>

**T**wo lines being proposed, one undivided and the other divided into parts: to divide the undivided one in the same manner as the divided one.
¶ Let there be two lines which I shall join at an angle as it happens, **a.b** and **a.c**. And let **a.b** be divided into three or any number of portions marked on it by points **d** and **e**. I wish to divide the line **a.c** according to those same portions. When, therefore, I have joined them at an angle, I shall draw the line **b.c** and the parallel lines **e.i**, **d.f**, and **e.g**. I say that these parallel lines divide the line **a.c** into parts proportional to the parts of **a.b**. For I shall draw **f.h** parallel to **a.b**, which intersects **e.g** at point **k**. By the second [proposition] of this [book], the ratio of **g.f** to **f.a** will be as **e.d** to **d.a**, and **c.g** to **g.f** as **h.k** to **k.f**; and wherefore as **b.e** to **e.d**, by the 34th [proposition] of the first [book] and the second part of the 7th of the fifth [book], which is what was proposed. It is necessary, however, to repeat the second [proposition] of this [book] as many times as there are parts of the line **a.b**, minus one; and indeed the 34th of the first and the 7th of the fifth, minus two.

### Proposition 13.

<margin>
<note>A diagram showing three rectangles. A large rectangle is formed by points a, d, h, b, c, g, e, f. It is divided into four smaller rectangles by a vertical line d-h and a horizontal line b-f. The central intersection point is labeled c. This visualizes the concept of reciprocal proportion in equal areas.</note>
</margin>

**I**f two <term>parallelograms</term><note>original: "superficies equidistantium laterum"; literally "surfaces of equidistant sides."</note> which have one angle of the one equal to one angle of the other are equal in area, then the sides containing those two equal angles will be <term>reciprocally proportional</term><note>original: "mutekelia"; a medieval Latin term derived from an Arabic corruption of the Greek term for reciprocal proportion.</note>. If, however, the sides containing the two equal angles are reciprocally proportional, it is necessary that the two surfaces be equal.
¶ Let there be two parallelograms, **a.b.c.d** and **c.e.f.g**, being equal. Let angle **c** of one be equal to angle **c** of the other. I say that the ratio of **b.c** to **c.g** is as **e.c** to **c.d**. And if the ratio of **b.c** to **c.g** were as **e.c** to **c.d**, and the aforementioned angles were still equal, I say that those two parallelograms are equal. For I shall join them at an angle, namely angle **c** of one with angle **c** of the other, so that their two sides, which are **b.c** and **c.g**, become one single line. Similarly, the two remaining sides **d.c** and **c.e** will be one line. Otherwise, it would follow from the present hypothesis—which is that angle **c** of one is equal to angle **c** of the other—and by the 15th of the first [book] <note>This proposition states that vertical angles are equal.</note>, that a part would be equal to the whole. I shall therefore complete the parallelogram by extending lines **a.d** and **f.g** until they meet at **h**. By the first part of the 7th of the fifth [book], the ratio of each surface **a.c** and **c.f** to the surface **c.b** will be the same ratio. And because, by the first [proposition] of this [book], the ratio of surface **a.c** to surface **c.b** is as the line **b.c** to the line **c.g**, and the surface **c.f** to the same surface **c.b** is as **e.c** to **c.d**, the first part of the proposed conclusion is manifest. The second part is proved thus: for by the first [proposition] of this [book], the ratio of **b.c** to **c.g** is as **a.c** to **c.b**, and **e.c** to **c.d** is as **c.f** to the same **c.b**. And because it was posited that the ratio of **b.c** to **c.g** is as **e.c** to **c.d**, there will be one ratio for each of the two surfaces **a.c** and **e.g** to the surface **c.b**. Therefore, by the first part of the 9th of the fifth [book], **a.c** is equal to **c.f**, and thus the second part is clear.

If, however, the sides containing the two equal angles are reciprocally proportional, the two triangles will be equal...

...are proven to be so.
¶ Let there be two equal triangles, **a.b.c** and **c.d.e**; and let angle **c** of the one be equal to angle **c** of the other. I say that the proportion of **a.c** to **c.e** is as **d.c** to **c.b**. And if the proportion of **a.c** to **c.e** is as **d.c** to **c.b**, and the aforementioned angles are still equal, I say those two triangles are equal. Otherwise, it would follow that a part is equal to the whole, according to the 15th [proposition] of the first [book] <note>original: "15. primi"; Proposition I.15 deals with vertically opposite angles being equal.</note>. And since, by the first [proposition] of this [book], the ratio of the first of them to it is as **a.c** to **c.e**, and the ratio of the second of them to the same is as **d.c** to **c.b**, the first part of the proposed conclusion is manifest. ¶ The second part is proved conversely: because **a.c** to **c.e** is as the first triangle to triangle **b.c.e**, and **d.c** to **c.b** is as the second to the same, by the first [proposition] of this [book]; and because it was posited that **a.c** to **c.e** is as **d.c** to **c.b**, there will be one proportion of both of the said triangles to triangle **b.c.e**. Wherefore, by the first part of the 9th [proposition] of the fifth [book], they are themselves equal. Thus the second part is clear.

### Proposition 15.

<margin>
<note>A geometric diagram shows four horizontal line segments at the top labeled a (length 16), b (8), c (4), and d (2). Below them are two rectangles. The first rectangle is tall and labeled d on its vertical side and a on its horizontal side. The second rectangle is shorter and wider, labeled b on its vertical side and c on its horizontal side. This illustrates that if a:b = c:d, then the area of rectangle ad equals the area of rectangle bc.</note>
</margin>

**I**f there are four proportional lines, the rectangle <term>contained</term><note>In Euclidean geometry, a rectangle is "contained" by its two adjacent sides; this refers to the area calculated by multiplying the lengths of the two lines.</note> by the first and the last will be equal to that which is contained by the two remaining. If indeed the rectangle contained by the first and last is equal to the rectangle contained by the two remaining, it follows that the four lines are proportional.
¶ Let there be four proportional lines **a**, **b**, **c**, and **d**. And let the proportion of **a** to **b** be as **c** to **d**. I say that the surface <note>The word "superficies" refers to the area or the geometric plane figure.</note> contained by **a** and **d** is equal to the surface contained by **b** and **c**. And if the surface contained by **a** and **d** is equal to the surface contained by **b** and **c**, I say that the proportion of **a** to **b** is as **c** to **d**. For let there be the surface contained by **a** and **d** and the surface contained by **b** and **c**. If therefore the proportion of **a** to **b** is as **c** to **d**, the sides of those surfaces will be <term>reciprocal</term><note>original: "mutekeſia," a Latinization of the Greek "mutuekesia." It describes sides that are inversely proportional, a requirement for equal areas.</note>. But also the angles contained by them are equal, because each consists of right angles. Wherefore, by the second [part] of the 14th [proposition] of this [book], they are equal, which is the first part. ¶ The second part is clear through the first part of the same. For if they are equal, since all their angles are right angles, their sides will be reciprocal; wherefore the proportion of **a** to **b** is as **c** to **d**, which is the second part.

---

### Proposition 16.

<margin>
<note>A geometric diagram shows three horizontal line segments at the top labeled a (length 8), b (4), and c (2). Below them is a single rectangle labeled b on its vertical side and c on its horizontal side. This diagram supports the proof that if a:b = b:c, then the rectangle formed by the extremes (a and c) equals the square of the mean (b).</note>
</margin>

**I**f there are three proportional lines, the rectangle contained by the first and the third will be equal to the square described from the second. If indeed the rectangle contained by the first and third is equal to the square produced from the second, those three lines will be proportional.
¶ Let the proportion of line **a** to line **b** be as line **b** to line **c**. I say that the surface contained by **a** and **c** is equal to the square of **b**. And if the surface contained by **a** and **c** is equal to the square of **b**, I say that the proportion of **a** to **b** is as **b** to **c**. This however is evident through the preceding [proposition] by positing another line which is equal to **b**, so that **b** stands in the ratio of the second and the third.

### Proposition 17.

<margin>
<note>Two geometric diagrams are presented side-by-side. The left diagram shows a large triangle with vertex **a**. From vertex **a**, lines are drawn to points **f**, **g**, and **b** on the base line. The base line is labeled with points **e**, **f**, **g**, **s**, **b**, **g**, and **c** from left to right. The right diagram shows a smaller triangle with vertex **d** and base points **f** and **g**, with a line continuing to point **b** on the left.</note>
</margin>

**I**f there are two similar triangles, the proportion <note>meaning the ratio of their areas</note> of one to the other is as the duplicate proportion <note>original: "proportio... duplicata"; in modern terms, the square of the ratio. If the sides are in ratio a:b, the areas are in ratio a²:b².</note> of any of its sides to its corresponding side of the other. ¶ It is also manifest from this that for any three lines in continued proportion <note>three lines where the ratio of the first to the second equals the ratio of the second to the third</note>, as the first is to the third, so will be the surface area established upon the first to the surface area established upon the second, provided it is similar in its drafting and creation.
¶ Let there be two similar triangles, **a.b.c.** and **d.e.f.** By definition, they will be equiangular <note>having equal angles</note> and their sides will be proportional. Let, therefore, angle **a.** be equal to angle **d.**, angle **b.** to angle **e.**, and angle **c.** to angle **f.** The proportion of **a.b.** to **d.e.** and **a.c.** to **d.f.** will be as **b.c.** to **e.f.** I say that the proportion of triangle **a.b.c.** to triangle **d.e.f.** is as the duplicate proportion of **b.c.** to **e.f.** For let there be joined, according to the teaching of the 10th [proposition] of this [book], a third line in continued proportionality to the two lines **b.c.** and **e.f.**, which shall be **c.g.**, extended or cut off from **b.f.** if **c.g.** is greater or smaller than it; and let line **g.a.** be drawn. By the second part of the 14th [proposition] of this [book], triangle **a.g.c.** will be equal to triangle **d.e.f.**, because the proportion of **a.c.** to **d.f.** is as **e.f.** to **c.g.** and angle **c.** is equal to angle **f.** Wherefore, by the second part of the 7th [proposition] of the fifth [book], there will be one proportion of triangle **a.b.c.** to both of them. But by the first [proposition] of this [book], the proportion of triangle **a.b.c.** to triangle **a.g.c.** is as **b.c.** to **g.c.** Truly, the proportion of **b.c.** to **c.g.** is as the duplicate proportion of **b.c.** to **e.f.** by the 10th definition of the fifth [book]; and the proportion of triangle **a.b.c.** to triangle **d.e.f.** is as the duplicate proportion of **b.c.** to **d.f.**, which is what was proposed.
If, however, **c.g.** were equal to **b.c.**, then by the second part of the 14th [proposition] of this [book], triangle **a.b.c.** would be equal to triangle **d.e.f.**; for an equal proportion is composed of an equal duplicate or triplicate, or however many times it is taken. We could demonstrate this same property in the same way and through the same means regarding similar surfaces of equidistant sides <note>parallelograms</note> by using only the 13th [proposition] of the present [book] in place of the 14th. He <note>Euclid</note> does not demonstrate it here, however, because it is demonstrated universally for all similar surfaces in the following [proposition]. Wherefore, that which is concluded universally regarding all similar surfaces is not yet evident except for triangles; but once the following is demonstrated, it will be evident for all. He placed this [proposition] here and not in the following one because it is a corollary of this one, not the next; for its truth is made manifest by the method of this demonstration, not by the method of that one.

**A**ll two similar multi-angled surfaces <note>polygons</note> are divisible into similar triangles and are equal in number. And the proportion of one of them to the other is as the duplicate proportion of any of its sides to its corresponding side of the other.

Therefore, since they are equal in number, the first [part] is clear. ¶ The second [part] is as follows: let **b.d.** be extended, which intersects **a.c.** at point

¶ Otherwise, it can be demonstrated thus: since the triangles into which the pentagons are divided are similar to one another, by the preceding proposition, the proportion of **a.b.c.** to **f.g.b.** will be as the duplicate proportion of **b.c.** to **g.b.**; and **a.c.d.** to **f.b.k.** as the duplicate proportion of **c.d.** to **b.k.**; and **a.e.d.** to **f.l.k.** as the duplicate proportion of **d.e.** to **k.l.** Since all these duplicate proportions are equal (because the sides were set as similar and equal), then by the 13th proposition of the fifth book, the whole pentagon will be to the whole pentagon as the duplicate proportion of one side to its relative side in the other.

### Proposition 19.

-> To describe upon a given line a surface similar to a given surface. <-

**L**et the given line be **a.b.**, upon which I wish to construct a surface similar to the given surface, which is a pentagon **c.d.e.f.g.** I divide this pentagon into triangles by drawing lines **d.f.** and **d.g.** At point **a.**, I construct an angle equal to angle **c.** by drawing line **a.h.** At point **b.**, I construct another angle, **a.b.h.**, equal to angle **c.d.g.**, extending line **b.h.** until it meets **a.h.** at point **h.** By the 32nd proposition of the first book, angle **a.h.b.** will be equal to angle **c.g.d.**, and therefore, by the 4th proposition of this book, the sides of the two triangles **g.c.d.** and **h.a.b.** are proportional. 

I also make angle **h.b.k.**, by drawing line **b.k.**, equal to angle **g.d.f.**; and angle **k.b.l.**, by drawing line **b.l.**, equal to angle **f.e.d.**; and angle **b.h.k.**, by drawing line **h.k.**, equal to angle **d.g.f.**; and angle **b.k.l.**, by drawing line **k.l.**, equal to angle **d.f.e.** The result will be a complete pentagon constructed upon line **a.b.** This is indeed equiangular to the given pentagon because of the equality of the angles of the triangles into which both are divided, and its sides are proportional because of the proportionality of the sides of those triangles, which clearly appears from the 4th proposition of this book. Wherefore, by the definition of similar surfaces, the pentagon constructed upon line **a.b.** is similar to the given pentagon, which is what was proposed.

For each of them is equiangular to pentagon **g.b.k.** by the converse of the definition of similar surfaces; wherefore they are equiangular to each other. Likewise, also by the converse of the same definition...

**I**f there be any number of proportional lines, and similar surfaces are described upon each pair of them, those surfaces will also be proportional. But if similar surfaces constructed upon each pair are proportional, it is necessary that those lines also be proportional.
¶ Let there be four proportional lines **a, b, c,** and **d**, and let the proportion of **a** to **b** be as **c** to **d**. I say that if similar surfaces are constructed upon **a** and **b** (for instance, two similar pentagons) and other similar surfaces are constructed upon **c** and **d** (for instance, two similar triangles), the proportion of the pentagons will be as the proportion of the triangles. Because, therefore, by the corollary of the 17th <note>modern editions often cite Prop. 19 or 20 here</note> of this book, the proportion of the pentagons is as **a** to **e**, and the proportion of the triangles is as **c** to **f**, the proportion of the pentagons will be as the triangles; and this is the first part. ¶ The second part is clear thus: Let there be two similar pentagons and two similar triangles, and let the proportion of the pentagons be as the proportion of the triangles. And let there be made upon **g**, as the 19th proposition of this book teaches, a surface similar to that which is constructed upon line **c**. But the proportion was also the same for triangle **c** to triangle **d**. Therefore, by the second part of the 9th proposition of the fifth book, triangle **d** is equal to triangle **g**. And because they are similar, line **g** will be equal to line **d** by the first part of the 17th of this book, since triangles are upon lines **c, d,** and **g**; or by the second part of the 18th, when they are any other many-angled figures <note>original: "multiangule"; referring to polygons with more than three sides</note>. For equality is not produced from any duplicate or triplicate proportion, or however many times taken, except from equality. Therefore, **c** will be to **d** as **a** is to **b**, which is what was proposed.

## ¶ Proposition 23.

<margin>
<note>A geometric diagram consists of a large rectangle labeled with points a, b, c, and d. A diagonal line runs from a to c. Inside the rectangle, smaller geometric figures and line segments are labeled with the letters e, f, g, h, and k.</note>
</margin>

**I**f within its own space a partial parallelogram, distinct from the whole, is similar to the entire parallelogram and shares a common angle with it, then it is situated around the same diagonal.
¶ Let there be a parallelogram **b.d.**, and within it a distinct parallelogram **f.g.**, which is similar to it and shares the common angle **c.** I say that the parallelogram **f.g.** is situated around the diagonal of parallelogram **b.d.**, and this is the converse <note>term: 'converse' refers to a theorem that reverses the hypothesis and conclusion of a previous one</note> of the preceding proposition. For let I produce the line **a.e.c.**; if this is the diagonal of parallelogram **b.d.**, the proposition is established. But if not, let **a.b.c.** <note>The text likely contains a minor typo here, common in early printings; it describes the construction of a hypothetical diagonal to prove the true one by contradiction.</note> be its diagonal, and let **b.k.** be drawn parallel to **f.c.** By the previous proposition, the parallelogram **f.k.** would be similar to the parallelogram **b.d.** Therefore, by the conversion of the definition of similar surfaces, the proportion of **b.c.** to **k.c.** is as **d.c.** to **f.c.** But by that same definition, the proportion of **b.c.** to **g.c.** is as **d.c.** to **f.c.** because the parallelogram **f.g.** was assumed to be similar to parallelogram **b.d.** Therefore, by the 11th proposition of the fifth book, the proportion of **b.c.** to **g.c.** is as **b.c.** to **k.c.**, for both are as **d.c.** to **f.c.** Wherefore, by the second part of the ninth proposition of the fifth book, **g.c.** is equal to **k.c.**—namely, the part is equal to the whole, which is impossible. Therefore, **a.e.c.** must be the diagonal of parallelogram **b.d.**, which is what was proposed.

## ¶ Proposition 24.

<margin>
<note>A geometric diagram shows two adjacent rectangles sharing a common vertex b. One rectangle is labeled with points a, b, c, d, and e. Below the rectangles are three horizontal line segments of varying lengths labeled f, g, and h.</note>
</margin>

**F**or any two surfaces with equidistant sides <note>term: 'surfaces with equidistant sides' is the literal translation for parallelograms</note> in which one angle of the one is equal to one angle of the other, the ratio of the one to the other is produced from the two ratios of their sides which contain the two equal angles.
¶ Let there be two parallelograms **a.c.** and **e.d.**, and let angle **b** of the one be equal to angle **b** of the other. I say that the ratio of one to the other is produced <note>original: "producitur"; in modern geometry, we say the ratio is 'compounded' from the other two ratios</note> from the ratio of **a.b.** to **b.d.** and the ratio of **c.b.** to **b.e.** For I shall arrange these two surfaces exactly as I arranged them in the 13th proposition of this book, with the parallelogram **c.d.** joined to both. And I shall set it so that the ratio of line **f** to line **g** is as **a.b.** to **b.d.**, and the ratio of **g** to **h** is as **c.b.** to **b.e.** Let this be done equally, as was said above in the 10th proposition of this book. Then, by the first proposition of this book and the 11th of the fifth book, **a.c.** is to **c.d.** as **f** is to **g**, and **c.d.** is to **d.e.** as **g** is to **h.** Wherefore, by the 22nd proposition of the fifth book, by equal proportionality, **a.c.** will be to **d.e.** as **f** is to **h.** And because the ratio of **f** to **h** is produced from the ratios of **f** to **g** and **g** to **h**, as stated at the end of the exposition of the 11th definition of the fifth book, it follows that the ratio of **a.c.** to **d.e.** is produced from the same; wherefore the proposition is established.

## ¶ Proposition 25.

<margin>
<note>Two polygons, a pentagon labeled A and a hexagon labeled B, both subdivided into triangles. The triangles in pentagon A are labeled c, a, and d. The triangles in hexagon B are labeled e, b, f, and g. Below these are further geometric constructions involving rectangles and triangles.</note>
</margin>

**T**o describe a surface similar to a given one and equal to another given one.
¶ Let there be two given rectilinear surfaces: **A**, a pentagon, and **B**, a hexagon. I wish to create one surface similar to **A** and equal [in area] to **B**. I resolve each of the proposed surfaces into triangles: **A** into triangles **c, a, d**, and **B** into triangles **e, b, f, g.** Upon the base of surface **A**, which is **b.k.**, I construct—according to the teaching of the 44th proposition of the first book—a rectangular parallelogram equal to triangle **c**, which shall be **b.l.**; then **l.m.** equal to triangle **a**, and **m.n.** equal to triangle **d**, so that the whole parallelogram **b.n.** constructed upon base **b.k.** is equal to pentagon **A**. In the same way, upon the line **k.n.**, which is the side of this surface, I construct another rectangular surface equal to hexagon **B**; for I make **k.o.** equal to triangle **e**, **o.p.** equal to triangle **b**, **p.q.** equal to triangle **f**, and **q.r.** equal to triangle **g**, so that the whole rectangular surface **n.r.** is equal to the hexagon.

<meta>This page concludes the proof of Proposition 25 in Book VI of Euclid’s Elements, which demonstrates how to construct a figure that is both equal in area to one given figure and similar in shape to another. VI

And I place, by the 9th proposition of this book, a line **f.t.** as a mean proportional <note>A mean proportional is a middle value in a geometric ratio; for two lengths $a$ and $b$, the mean proportional $x$ satisfies $a:x = x:b$.</note> between line **b.k.** and line **k.r.**; and upon it, according to the teaching of the 19th proposition of this book, I construct a surface **v.** similar to surface **a.** I say that this is the one we seek, and it is equal to surface **b.** For since the three lines **b.k.**, **f.t.**, and **k.r.** are in continuous proportion, and upon the first and second are constructed similar surfaces—namely **a.** and **v.**—then by the corollary of the 17th proposition of this book <note>original: "correl. 17. huius"; in modern editions, this refers to the corollary of Book VI, Proposition 20, regarding the ratio of similar figures.</note>, **a.** is to **v.** as **b.k.** is to **k.r.** Wherefore, by the first proposition of this book, [this is] as **b.n.** is to **n.r.**, and therefore, by the first part of the 7th proposition of the fifth book, as **a.** is to **n.r.**; and because of this, by the second part of the same, as **a.** is to **b.** Thus, by the second part of the 9th proposition of the fifth book, **v.** is equal to **b.**, which was proposed. ¶ Which we can also easily prove from permuted proportionality: because since **a.** is to **v.** as **b.n.** is to **n.r.**, it will be, by permutation, **a.** to **b.n.** as **v.** to **n.r.** And because **a.** is equal to **b.n.**, then **v.** will be equal to **n.r.** Wherefore **v.** is also equal to **b.** by this common notion <note>original: "commune scientiam"; referring to the "Common Notions" or axioms that ground Euclid's logic.</note>: things which are equal to the same thing are equal to each other. It is not necessary, however, that the parallelograms <term>parallelograms: literally "surfaces of equidistant sides"</term> **b.l.**, **l.m.**, and **m.n.** equal to triangles **c.**, **a.**, **d.**, or the surfaces **k.o.**, **o.p.**, **p.q.**, and **q.r.** equal to triangles **e.**, **b.**, **f.**, **g.**, be rectangular; but only that the external angle of surface **l.m.** be equal to the internal angle of surface **l.b.**, and the external of **m.n.** to the internal of **m.l.** Similarly also, the external angle of surface **k.o.** must be equal to the internal of surface **b.n.**, and the external of **o.p.** to the internal of **k.o.**, and so on for the others. For when this is the case, each of the lines **k.n.** and its opposite **b.m.**, as well as **b.r.** and its opposite **n.q.**, [becomes] a single line by the last part of the 29th proposition of the first book and by the 14th of the same, as many times as it is necessary to repeat them equally; because all the surfaces **b.l.**, **l.m.**, and **m.n.**, as well as **k.o.**, **o.p.**, **p.q.**, and **q.r.**, are parallelograms and the external angle of each subsequent one is equal to the internal of the preceding one. Wherefore the two surfaces **b.n.** and **n.r.** will be parallelograms and between parallel lines, and of equal altitude. Therefore, argue the rest as before.

## ¶ Proposition 26.

<margin>
<note>Two diagrams demonstrating Proposition 26. They show how parallelograms applied to a line segment relate to the parallelogram formed on exactly half of that segment. The lines and diagonals help prove that the figure on the half-mark has a larger area than other similarly constructed figures on the same line.</note>
</margin>

**A** parallelogram described on the half of a given line is greater than any parallelogram applied to the same line which is deficient by a parallelogram similar to and situated around the same diagonal as the one placed upon the half.
¶ Let the given line be **a.b.**, upon half of which, **c.b.**, let the parallelogram **c.d.** be constructed, whose diagonal is **b.e.**; and let there be applied to line **a.b.** a parallelogram **a.f.**, one side of which cuts **e.c.** at point **g.**, so that for the completion of the whole line **a.b.** there is lacking the surface **f.b.**, which is similar to surface **c.d.** and situated around its diagonal; I say then that parallelogram **c.d.** is greater than parallelogram **a.f.** For by the first proposition of this book, **a.g.** is equal to **g.b.**, and by the 43rd proposition of the first book, **c.f.** is equal to **f.d.**; therefore, by this common notion—if you add equals to equals, etc. <note>original: "si equalibus equalia addas. &c."; a reference to Common Notion 2: 'If equals be added to equals, the wholes are equal.'</note>—the gnomon <term>gnomon: the L-shaped figure remaining after a smaller similar parallelogram is removed from the corner of a larger one.</term> consisting of the three parallelograms **c.f.**, **f.b.**, and **f.d.** will be equal to parallelogram **a.f.** Wherefore parallelogram **c.d.** is greater than parallelogram **a.f.** by the parallelogram **e.f.**, which was to be shown. The same would also be true if the surface **a.f.** were made taller than surface **c.d.**, as you can see in the second figure, in which also, by the first proposition of this book, **a.g.** is equal to **g.b.**; thus, having subtracted from both the two supplements of surface **f.b.**, parallelogram **c.d.** will exceed parallelogram **a.f.** by the parallelogram **f.e.**

## ¶ Proposition 27.

**W**ith a triangular surface <term>original: "trilatera superficie"; a three-sided figure.</term> proposed, to describe on any assigned line a parallelogram equal to it, which is deficient by a parallelogram similar to another proposed surface, provided that this parallelogram is not greater than the one placed upon the half of the given line.

BOOK VI

<note>Geometric diagrams. On the left, two small triangles are labeled **c** and **d**. Below them is a complex square construction labeled with points **k**, **l**, **f** along the top; **n**, **p**, **o** across the middle; and **b**, **e**, **m**, **a** along the bottom. A diagonal line (the diameter) connects **k** and **b**. To the right, a separate vertical line segment is labeled **h**.</note>

¶ Let the line **a.b.** be assigned, and the proposed triangle **c**, and the proposed parallelogram **d**. I wish to describe upon the line **a.b.** a parallelogram equal to triangle **c**, such that there is lacking <note>This is the concept of "application with a deficiency" (elliptical application), where the constructed area is smaller than the area formed by the whole line.</note> from the completion of line **a.b.** a parallelogram similar to **d**. It is so conditioned that triangle **c** must not be greater than the parallelogram similar to **d** when placed upon half of line **a.b.**; otherwise, the task would be impossible according to the previous proposition. I therefore divide line **a.b.** into equal parts at point **e**, and according to the teaching of the 19th proposition <note>original: "19. huius"; in many editions of Euclid, this corresponds to Book VI, Proposition 18, regarding the construction of a similar figure.</note> of this book, I construct upon its half **e.b.** a parallelogram **e.f.** similar to **d**, and I shall complete the parallelogram **b.g.** upon the whole line **a.b.** Since, therefore, **c** is not greater than parallelogram **e.f.**, but is equal to it or smaller as was established: If it were equal to it, then parallelogram **e.g.** would be what was intended, as shown by the 36th proposition of the first book <note>regarding parallelograms on equal bases</note>, supported by the first part of the 9th proposition and the definition of similar figures and the 20th of this book. But if it is smaller, let it be smaller by some surface area to which a figure **b** is made equal and similar to **d**, according to the 25th proposition of this book. Then **b** will be similar to **e.f.** by the 20th proposition of this book; wherefore, by the converse of the definition of equiangularity <term>equiangular: having all corresponding angles equal</term> and proportional sides: I will therefore draw the diameter **b.k.** in parallelogram **e.f.** and I will cut off the sides **k.f.** and **e.k.** of the surface **e.f.** to the measure of the sides of surface **b.** having drawn the lines **l.m.** and **n.o.** parallel to the sides of surface **e.f.**, intersecting each other at point **p**, so that surface **k.p.** is equal and similar to surface **b.** By the 23rd proposition of this book, point **p** will be on the diameter **k.b.** Having thus extended **o.n.** as far as **a.g.**, I say that the parallelogram **a.p.** is that which was proposed. For it lacks, for the completion of line **a.b.**, the parallelogram **p.b.** which, by the 22nd and 20th propositions of this book, is similar to parallelogram **d**. But even parallelogram **a.p.** is equal to triangle **c**. For by the first proposition of this book, **a.n.** is equal to **n.b.**; therefore by the 43rd proposition of the first book <note>which states that the complements of parallelograms around a diagonal are equal</note> and this common knowledge: if you add equals to equals, etc., the parallelogram **a.p.** is equal to the gnomon <term>gnomon: the L-shaped figure remaining after a smaller similar parallelogram is removed from a corner of a larger one</term> **n.b.l.** And because this gnomon is equal to triangle **c**, because parallelogram **e.f.** was established to be greater than triangle **c** by the parallelogram **b** (which is equal to parallelogram **k.p.**), the proposition is clear.

### Proposition .28.

<note>A decorative drop-cap letter 'S' featuring a landscape scene. To its left are geometric diagrams: two triangles labeled **c** and **d**, and a rectangular construction below them labeled with points **k**, **m**, **h** along the top; **a**, **e**, **b** along a middle line; and **g**, **f**, **l** along the bottom. A diagonal line connects **g** and **b**. A small letter **n** is placed between the middle and bottom horizontal lines.</note>

To construct a parallelogram equal to a given three-sided surface <note>original: "superficiei trilatere"; a triangle</note> upon a given line, which exceeds <note>This is "application with an excess" (hyperbolic application).</note> the completion of the given line by a surface of parallel sides similar to a given surface of parallel sides.

¶ Let there be, as before, a given line **a.b.**, a given triangle **c**, and a given parallelogram **d**. I wish to construct upon the line **a.b.** a parallelogram equal to triangle **c**, which exceeds the whole line **a.b.** by a parallelogram similar to **d**. I divide line **a.b.** into equal parts at point **e**, and upon its half **e.b.** I make **e.f.** similar to **d**, according to what the 19th proposition of this book teaches. And according to the teaching of the 25th proposition of this book, I make **k.l.**, whose diameter is **g.b.**, similar to **d** and equal to the two surfaces **e.f.** and **c**. By the 20th proposition of this book, **k.l.** will be similar to **e.f.** Therefore, having placed surface **k.l.** upon surface **e.f.** so that they both share the angle **g**, then by the 23rd proposition of this book, surface **e.f.** will lie around the diameter of surface **k.l.**; wherefore point **b** is on the diameter **g.b.** I will therefore complete the parallelogram **a.b.**, which I say is such as was proposed. This is established by extending line **f.b.** to **m** and line **e.b.** to **n**. For by the first part of this book, **a.k.** is equal to **k.b.**, and therefore by the 43rd of the first book, it is also equal to **n.f.** Therefore, by adding **e.b.** to both, by common knowledge, **a.b.** will be equal to the gnomon **e.b.f.** But this gnomon is equal to triangle **c**, because parallelogram **k.l.** was established as equal to the two surfaces **c** and **e.f.** Therefore, parallelogram **a.b.** is equal to **c**, and it adds to the completion of line **a.b.** the parallelogram **m.n.**, which by the 22nd and 20th of this book is similar to parallelogram **d**. Wherefore it is established that what was sought is perfected.

VI

...we wish. We are also able to apply <note>The term "apply" (Latin: *adiungere*) refers to the Greek method of *parabole*, where a figure of a certain area is drawn along a specific line segment.</note> to a given line a parallelogram equal not only to a given triangular surface, but also to any given <term>rectilinear figure</term> <note>A shape bounded by straight lines.</note> whatsoever, such that there is lacking <note>Known as "elliptical application."</note> from the completion of the given line a surface similar to a given parallelogram: just as the previous proposition teaches, provided the condition is observed so as not to labor toward the impossible. Or, as the present conclusion proposes, such that it exceeds the given line <note>Known as "hyperbolic application."</note> by a parallelogram similar to a given surface. For the proposed surface, to which an equal parallelogram must be applied to a given line (whether it exceeds or falls short of the completion of the line by a parallelogram similar to a given one), we shall resolve into triangles. And through their mediation, we shall describe a parallelogram equal to the total proposed surface. How this is done, if you wish to know, look to the 25th proposition of this book. Then, upon double its base and of equal height, we shall construct a triangle which, if you diligently inspect the 44th proposition of the first book, you will find to be equal to the previously designated parallelogram, and therefore to the proposed surface. If you then apply to this triangle an equal parallelogram to the given line—which either adds to or subtracts from the completion of the line a parallelogram similar to the given one, as this and the previous proposition teach—you should not doubt that you have accomplished what was proposed.

### Proposition 29.

<note>Three geometric diagrams are located in the right margin. The top diagram depicts a triangle positioned on top of a rectangle. The middle diagram shows a large rectangle subdivided into smaller rectangular sections, with points labeled with letters **a**, **c**, **e** across the top; **d**, **f** in the center; and **b** at the base. The bottom diagram shows two triangles, **abc** and **dce**, joined at a single vertex, **c**.</note>

**T**o cut any proposed line according to a ratio having a mean and two extremes. <note>original: "secundum proportionem habentem medium duoque extrema"; this is the classic definition of the Golden Ratio. In modern editions, this is often Proposition 30.</note>
¶ Let the proposed line be **a.b.**, which I wish to divide according to a ratio having a mean and two extremes. From this line I describe a square **b.c.**, and to its side **a.c.** I apply—according to what the previous proposition teaches—a parallelogram **e.d.** equal to the square **b.c.**, which adds to the completion of the line **a.c.** a parallelogram **a.d.** that is similar to **b.c.** Let the side of the parallelogram be **c.d.**, which is parallel to **a.c.** and **d.e.**, and let it cut the line **a.b.** at point **f.** I say that line **a.b.** is divided at point **f** as was proposed. For **a.d.** is a square because it is similar to **b.c.**; therefore **a.f.** is equal to **f.d.** But **f.e.** is also equal to **a.b.** because it is equal to **a.c.** through the 34th proposition of the first book. And because **c.d.** <note>meaning the rectangle **c.d.** or segment</note> is equal to **b.c.**, once **c.f.** is taken away from both, **a.d.** will be equal to **e.b.**, and the angle **f** of one is equal to the angle **f** of the other. Therefore, by the 13th proposition of this book <note>original: "per .13. huius"; refers to the proportionality of sides in equal parallelograms.</note>, the sides are mutually proportional; thus **e.f.** is to **f.d.** as **a.f.** is to **f.b.** And since **e.f.** is equal to **a.b.**, and **f.d.** is equal to **a.f.**, then **a.b.** will be to **a.f.** as **a.f.** is to **f.b.** Therefore, by definition, it is divided as proposed. The same can also be demonstrated from the 11th proposition of the second book; for let **a.b.** be divided at point **f** according to what the 11th proposition of the second book teaches. Let **e.b.** be the rectangle contained under the whole line **a.b.** and its part **f.b.**, so that **f.e.** is equal to **a.b.**, and **a.d.** is the square of **a.f.** It is therefore, by the aforementioned 11th proposition of the second book, that **e.b.** is equal to **a.d.**, which remains to be argued as before through the 13th proposition of this book. Or likewise, since **a.b.** is divided at point **f** according to the 11th of the second book, that which is produced from the first line **a.b.** and the third **f.b.** is equal to the square of the second **a.f.** Therefore, by the second part of the 16th proposition of this book, the ratio of the first line **a.b.** to the second **a.f.** is as the second **a.f.** to the third **f.b.** Thus, by definition, **a.b.** is divided as proposed.

# BOOK VI

<margin>
<note>Two triangles, DCE and ABC, sharing the vertex C. Triangle DCE is on the left with D at the top, E at the bottom left, and C at the bottom right. Triangle ABC is on the right with A at the top, B at the bottom right, and C at the bottom left. This diagram illustrates the collinearity of the bases BC and CE.</note>

...and let the proportion of side AC to DE be the same as the proportion of AB to DC. I say that their two bases, BC and CE, form a single straight line. For angle A is equal to angle D, because each of them is equal to angle ACD by the first part of Proposition 29 of Book I <note>original: "per primam partem .29. primi"</note>. Therefore, by the present hypothesis and Proposition 6 of this book, these triangles are <term>equiangular</term> <note>Having all their corresponding angles equal.</note>. Angle B is equal to angle DCE, and angle ACB is equal to angle C <note>Specifically, angle DEC</note>. Therefore, by Proposition 32 of Book I, the three angles at point C are equal to two right angles, for they are equal to the three angles of either of the two triangles. Thus, by Proposition 14 of Book I, BCE is a single straight line, which is what was proposed.

### Proposition 31

<margin>
<note>A right-angled triangle ABC with the right angle at vertex A. A perpendicular line AD is dropped from vertex A to the hypotenuse BC.</note>
<note>A similar right-angled triangle ABC with additional markings and labels (D, F) on the sides, used for the demonstration of the Pythagorean theorem generalized to similar figures.</note>
</margin>

In every right-angled triangle, the figure <note>original: "superficies"</note> described on the side that subtends the right angle <note>The hypotenuse.</note> is equal to the figures described on the two sides containing the right angle, taken together, when those figures are similar to one another in form and construction.

While the second-to-last proposition of the first book <note>Modern Proposition I.47, the Pythagorean theorem.</note> proposes this for square surfaces, the second-to-last proposition of this sixth book proposes it for all similar surfaces. Thus, this rule is as much more universal as a <term>rectilinear figure</term> <note>A shape made of straight lines.</note> is more general than a square. 

Therefore, let there be a right-angled triangle ABC whose angle A is a right angle. I say that the figure constructed upon side BC is equal to the two figures constructed upon AB and AC, when all three figures are similar in shape and orientation. I shall draw a perpendicular line AD to the line BC. By the second part of the corollary to Proposition 8 of this book, the proportion of BC to CA is as CA to DC, and the proportion of CB to BA is as BA to DB. 

If, therefore, on each of the three lines BC, CA, and AB, a figure is made similar to the others in shape and orientation, it will be (by the corollary to Proposition 17 of this book) that the proportion of the first figure (on BC) to the second figure (on CA) is as the first line BC is to the third line DC. Likewise, the proportion of the same first figure (on BC) to the second figure (on AB) is as the first line BC is to the third line DB by the same corollary. Therefore, by converting the proportionality, the figure AC is to the figure CB as CD is to CB; and the figure AB is to the figure BC as BD is to the surface BC. 

Let figure AC be the first, CB the second and fourth, CD the third, AB the fifth, and BD the sixth. It is argued by Proposition 24 of Book V that the proportion of the figure constructed on BC to the two figures constructed on CA and AB together is the same as the proportion of line BC to the sum of lines CD and DB. Since line BC is equal to the two lines CD and DB taken together, the figure constructed on BC will be equal to the two figures constructed on CA and AB taken together, which is what was proposed.

We are also able to easily demonstrate the converse of this by the method of the final demonstration of the first book <note>Modern Proposition I.48.</note>. For let there be a triangle ABC, and let the figure constructed on BC be equal to the two similar figures constructed on the two lines AB and AC. I say that angle A is a right angle. For let I construct angle CAD as a right angle, and line AD equal to AB. I close the figure by drawing line DC. By this Proposition 31, the figure constructed on CD is equal to the two similar figures constructed on the two lines CA and AD. Consequently, it is also equal to those constructed on BC, for the figure on BC was given as equal to those on AB and AC. Therefore, line BC is equal to CD. Thus, by Proposition 8 of Book I, angle A is a right angle, which is what was proposed.

### Proposition 32

<margin>
<note>A circular diagram with points A, B, C, K on the circumference and center D. Lines radiate from the center to the circumference (DA, DB, DC, DK). Additional lines connect points on the circumference (AB, AC), illustrating central and inscribed angles subtending the same arcs.</note>
</margin>

If in equal circles angles stand upon the center or upon the circumference, the proportion of the angles will be the same as the proportion of the arcs subtending those angles.

Let there be equal circles ABC with center D, and EFG with center H. Upon their centers let there be two angles BDC and FHG, and upon their circumferences two others, BAC and FEG. I say that the proportion of the angles, both those at the centers...

<meta>This page concludes the final proposition of Book VI, which demonstrates the proportional relationship between angles at the center or circumference of a circle and the arcs that subtend them. It then transitions into the foundational definitions for Book VII, marking Euclid's shift from geometry to arithmetic (number theory).</meta>

<margin>
<note>A circular geometric diagram demonstrating the relationship between arcs and angles. It features two partially overlapping circles or sectors. Several points are labeled including e, l, m, a, k, b, c, d, h, f, and g. Lines radiate from centers (labeled a and d/b) to the circumference, forming triangles and sectors to illustrate proportionalities between arcs and subtended angles.</note>
</margin>

...because the proportion of those angles which are upon the circumferences is as the arc BC is to the arc FG. For I will continue from those two arcs other equal arcs, either according to the same number or according to different ones. Let arc KB be equal to arc BC, and let each of the two arcs LM and FL be equal to arc FG. I will then draw the lines KD, KA, MB, LB, MC, and LC. By the 26th proposition of the third book <note>original: "per .26. tertij"</note>, the angles which are at D will be equal to one another. Likewise, those which are at B are equal to one another. The same also applies to those at A and those at E. Therefore, just as arc KC is a multiple of arc BC, so is angle KDC a multiple of angle BDC, and angle KAC a multiple of angle BAC. Similarly, as arc MG is a multiple of arc FG, so is angle MBG a multiple of angle FBG, and angle MEG a multiple of angle FEG. But if arc KC is equal to arc MG, then angle KDC is equal to angle MBG, and angle KAC is equal to angle MEG; and if the arc is greater, the angles are greater; and if the arc is smaller, the angles are smaller, by the 26th proposition of the third book. Therefore, by the definition of <term>proportionality</term> <note>Euclid refers here to the theory of proportions established in Book V, which allows for the comparison of different types of magnitudes.</note>, the proportion of arc BC to arc FG is as the angle BDC is to the angle FBG, and as the angle BAC is to the angle FEG, which is what was proposed. Understand the same to be true in the same circle.

# HERE ENDS THE SIXTH BOOK.
# HERE BEGINS THE SEVENTH BOOK.

**Unity** <note>original: "Unitas"</note> is that by which each thing is said to be one.
¶ **Number** is a multitude composed of unities.
¶ The **natural series of numbers** is that in which their calculation occurs according to the addition of unity.
¶ The **difference of numbers** is called the number by which the greater exceeds the lesser.
¶ A **prime number** is called that which is measured only by unity.
¶ A **composite number** is called that which another number measures.
¶ Numbers **prime to each other** are those which are counted by no number except unity alone.
¶ Numbers **composite to each other** or **communicating** are called those which a number other than unity measures, and none of them is prime to the other.
¶ A number is said to be **multiplied** by another when it is added to itself as many times as there is unity in the multiplier.
¶ The **product** is that which grows from their multiplication.
¶ A number is said to **measure** another when, being multiplied by some number, it produces it.
¶ A **part** is a number of a number, the lesser of the greater, when the lesser measures the greater. And that which is measured is called the **multiple** of the measurer.
¶ The **denominator** is the number according to which a part is taken in its whole.
¶ **Similar parts** are those named by the same number.
¶ The first, simple part of a number is **unity**.
¶ When two numbers have a common part, the lesser is said to be so many parts of the greater as that same part is in the lesser, and as many parts [of the whole] as it is in the greater.
¶ The **proportion** of a number to a number is called that of the lesser to the greater in that it is a part or parts of the greater.
¶ And of the greater to the lesser according to how it contains it and its part or parts.
¶ When there are any number of **continually proportional** numbers, the proportion of the first to the third is said to be as the first <term>squared</term> <note>original: "duplicata," referring to the duplicate ratio.</note>, and to the fourth, <term>cubed</term> <note>original: "triplicata," referring to the triplicate ratio.</note>.
¶ When the same or different proportions have been continued, the proportion of the first to the last is said to be **composed** of all of them.

¶ The **denomination** <note>original: "Denominatio"; in this context, it refers to the name or numerical value of a ratio</note> of a ratio is called the part (or parts) of the smaller number in relation to the larger that are contained within the larger. Of the larger to the smaller, it is called the whole, or the whole and a part (or parts), according to how much the larger exceeds the smaller. ¶ **Similar** or identical ratios are said to be those that receive the same denomination. ¶ A **greater** ratio is that which receives a greater denomination. ¶ A **lesser** ratio is that which receives a smaller one. ¶ Numbers whose ratio is the same are called **proportional**. ¶ **Terms** or **roots** <note>original: "Termini siue radices"</note> are said to be those numbers in a ratio which are the smallest possible, such that no smaller numbers can be found in that same proportion. ¶ There are four **Postulates** <note>original: "Petitiones"</note>: ¶ That for any number, as many equals or multiples as desired can be taken. ¶ That for any number, it is possible to take another as much larger as one wishes. ¶ That the series of numbers can proceed toward infinity. ¶ That no number can be diminished toward infinity <note>Because the unit (1) is the absolute limit of number; unlike geometric lines, numbers cannot be divided forever</note>. ¶ There are ten **Common Notions**: ¶ Every part is smaller than its whole. ¶ Whatever numbers are equal multiples of the same number (or of equal numbers) will also be equal to each other. ¶ Those of which the same number is an equal multiple, or those whose equal multiples are equal, are themselves equal. ¶ Every part of a number is the **unit** <note>original: "vnitas"; the number 1</note> named by that number <note>For example, 1 is the "fifth" part of 5</note>. ¶ Every part is smaller if it has a larger denomination, and larger if it has a smaller one <note>e.g., 1/10 is smaller than 1/2</note>. ¶ Any whole number is composed of units, just as the unit is a part of it. ¶ Any number multiplied by the unit produces itself. Also, the unit multiplied by any number produces that same number. ¶ Any number that <term>measures</term> <note>original: "numerat"; to "measure" means to divide a number exactly without a remainder</note> two numbers also measures the sum composed of them. ¶ Any number that measures another measures every number measured by that one. ¶ Any number that measures a whole and a part taken away also measures the remainder.

**I**f, when the smaller of two numbers is subtracted from the larger until a remainder less than itself is left, and then that remainder is subtracted from the smaller until a new remainder is left, and this process of continual subtraction continues, and no remainder is found that measures the one before it until the unit (1) is reached: then those two numbers are necessarily **prime to one another** <note>original: "contra se primos"; today called "relatively prime" or "coprime"</note>.

¶ Let there be two numbers, **a.b.** and **c.d.** Let the smaller, **c.d.**, be subtracted from the larger, **a.b.**, as many times as possible, and let the remainder be **e.b.**, which will be smaller than **c.d.** (otherwise it could be subtracted again). Let **e.b.** be subtracted from **c.d.** as many times as possible, and let the remainder be **f.d.** Then let **f.d.** be subtracted from **e.b.** as many times as possible, and if the remainder **g.b.** is the unit (1), I say then that the two numbers **a.b.** and **c.d.** are prime to one another. For if they are composite <note>meaning they share a common divisor</note>, some number other than the unit will measure them both by definition; let this common measure be **h**. Because **h** measures **c.d.**, it will also measure **a.e.** by the second-to-last common notion. And because the same **h** measures **a.b.**, it will also measure the remainder **e.b.** by the last common notion. Therefore, it will also measure **c.f.** by the second-to-last, and consequently **f.d.** by the last. Thus, it will measure **g.e.** by the second-to-last, and finally **g.b.** by the last. But because **g.b.** is the unit, it would follow that the number **h** is a part of the unit or equal to it, which is impossible. Therefore, **a.b.** and **c.d.** will be prime to one another, which is what was proposed. ¶ If the two numbers **a.b.** and **c.d.** are prime to one another, there will be no stopping point in this mutual subtraction until the unit is reached. This is the converse of what the author proposes. But if in this mutual...

For if, by such mutual subtraction being done, it reaches unity, they are prime to each other. But if there is a stop before reaching unity, they are composite.

### ¶ Proposition 2

<note>A geometric diagram representing numerical lengths. It consists of three horizontal line segments. The first segment is the longest, with labels 'a' at the left, 'b' at the right, and 'e' at an intermediate point. The second segment is shorter, with labels 'c' at the left, 'd' at the right, and 'f' at an intermediate point. The third segment is the shortest and is labeled 'g'.</note>

Given two numbers composite to each other, to find the **greatest common number** measuring them. From which it is manifest that every number measuring two numbers also measures the greatest number measuring both.
¶ Let the two composite numbers be *a.b.* and *c.d.*, with *c.d.* being the smaller. Because some number measures them commonly by definition, I wish to find the greatest number commonly measuring them. Following the manner and similarity of the previous [proposition]: I subtract the smaller from the larger as many times as possible, namely *c.d.* from *a.b.*, and let the remainder be *e.b.* Likewise, I subtract *e.b.* from *c.d.* as many times as possible, and let the remainder be *f.d.* And because this reduction cannot be done infinitely by the final postulate, nor can it reach unity in this case according to the preceding proposition (because then the given numbers would be prime to each other, which is contrary to the hypothesis), let it be that when I have subtracted *f.d.* from *e.b.* as many times as possible, nothing remains as a remainder. I say then that *f.d.* is the greatest number measuring *a.b.* and *c.d.* That it indeed measures them is clear by the penultimate and antepenultimate common notions, repeated alternately as many times as necessary, just as in the demonstration of the converse of the preceding proposition. For *f.d.* measures *e.b.*, because when it is subtracted from it as many times as possible, nothing remains. Therefore it measures *c.f.* by the penultimate common notion; therefore *c.d.* by the antepenultimate; wherefore *a.e.* by the penultimate; and therefore *a.b.* by the antepenultimate. That no number greater than *f.d.* measures *a.b.* and *c.d.* is thus clear: For if it were possible, let the number *g* be greater than *f.d.* measuring both of the two numbers *a.b.* and *c.d.* Because, therefore, *g* measures *c.d.*, it will measure *a.e.* by the penultimate common notion. And because it measures *a.b.*, it will measure *e.b.* by the final common notion. Therefore, by the penultimate, it measures *c.f.*, and because it also measures *c.d.*, it will measure *f.d.* by the final common notion—a greater number measuring a smaller, which is impossible. From this second process, the conclusion is clear.

Given three numbers composite to each other, to find the greatest of the numbers commonly measuring them.

If *d* measures *c*, then *a, b, c* will be composite to each other by definition. ¶ In a similar way, it will also be known for any number of proposed quantities greater than three whether they are all mutually composite. ### Proposition 4

Of any two unequal numbers, the smaller is either a part or parts of the larger.

<note>A diagram with two horizontal line segments. The upper segment is longer and labeled 'a'; the lower segment is shorter and labeled 'b'. This illustrates the comparative relationship between a smaller and larger magnitude.</note>

¶ Let there be two numbers, *a* and *b*, with *b* being the smaller. I say that *b* is either a part or parts of *a*. For either *b* measures *a*, or it does not. If it measures it, it is a **part** of it by definition. <note>In Euclid's terminology, a "part" (pars) is a unit fraction, like 1/3, 1/4, etc., where the smaller number fits into the larger exactly a certain number of times.</note> If it does not measure it, then they are either prime to each other or they are not. If they are not prime to each other, they will have, by definition, a common part; however many times that part is in *b*, so many **parts** of *a* will *b* be said to be by definition. <note>"Parts" (partes) refers to a non-unit fraction, like 2/3 or 3/4. It means the smaller number is a multiple of a common measure of the larger.</note> If, however, they are prime to each other, because unity <note>The number 1</note> is a part of every number denominated by that number, the same is clear through units.

If there be four numbers of which the first is the same part of the second as the third is of the fourth, the first and third taken together will be the same part of the second and fourth taken together as the first is of the second.

Let there be, therefore, four numbers: *a*, *b*, *c*, and *d*. Let *b* be the same part of *a* as *d* is of *c*. For having divided *a* and *c* according to the quantity of *b* and *d*, argue just as in the first [proposition] of the Fifth [Book]. For it will be that there are as many parts of *a* as there are of *c* by position; and as the aggregate of the first part of *a* and the first of *c* is equal to the aggregate of *b* and *d*, so also is the aggregate of the second part of *a* and the second of *c*. ### Proposition 6

> **If there are four numbers of which the first is the same parts of the second as the third is of the fourth, then the first and third taken together will be the same parts of the second and fourth taken together that the first was of the second.**

¶ What the previous proposition proposed concerning a "part" <note>original: "de parte" — Euclid uses "part" to refer to a unit fraction, such as 1/3.</note>, this one proposes concerning "parts" <note>original: "de partibus" — Euclid uses "parts" to refer to a proper fraction, such as 2/3.</note>. Let there be, as before, four numbers *a, b, c, d*. Let *b* be the same "parts" of *a* as *d* is of *c*. I say that *b* and *d* taken together will be the same parts of *a* and *c* taken together as *b* is of *a*. I say "parts" because a plurality is defined by two numbers, of which one is called the <term>numerator</term> <note>The number that counts the parts.</note> and the other the <term>denominator</term> <note>The number that names the size or type of the parts.</note>. For example, when we say "three fifths," three "numerates" and five "denominates." 

Since, therefore, *b* represents parts of *a*, let those parts be numerated by *b* and denominated by *k*. Similarly, by the setup, *d* will be parts of *c* numerated by *b* and denominated by *k*. Let one of the parts of *b* be *e*, and let one of the parts of *d* be *f*. By the hypothesis, *e* will be a part of *b* denominated by *b* and a part of *a* denominated by *k*. Likewise, *f* will be a part of *d* according to *b* and a part of *c* according to *k*. Therefore, let *g* be the composite of *e* and *f*. By the previous proposition, *g* will be a part of *b* and *d* taken together according to *b*, and similarly, by the same logic, it will be a part of *a* and *c* taken together according to *k*. Wherefore, by the 16th definition, *b* and *d* taken together will be the parts of *a* and *c* taken together numerated by *b* and denominated by *k*, because their common part is *g*—being the smaller part according to *b* and the larger according to *k*. And since this was the relationship of *b* to *a*, the proposition stands.

<note>A geometric diagram consisting of several horizontal line segments of varying lengths. On the top left is segment 'a' with segment 'c' to its right. Below them are segments 'b' and 'd'. At the bottom, a continuous line is divided into segments labeled 'h', 'f', 'e', and 'k'. These segments represent the numerical quantities and parts described in the proof of Proposition 6.</note>

¶ You can also extend what is proposed regarding four numbers to any number of quantities by using this and the previous proposition. If any number of smaller quantities are compared to as many larger ones, and each is the same part or parts of its respective larger quantity as the first is of the second, then all the smaller ones taken together will be the same part or parts of all the larger ones taken together as the first was of the second. This is easily proved by repeating this and the previous proposition as often as necessary. 

If we believed it were Euclid’s intention to assume anything from previously demonstrated proofs for these demonstrations—specifically from Proposition 13 of Book V <note>Book V deals with magnitudes in general (geometry), while Book VII focuses specifically on whole numbers (arithmetic).</note>—we could have easily demonstrated this sixth proposition. Now, however, because we see the opposite—otherwise he would have superfluously proposed many things concerning numbers that were already demonstrated in the fifth book concerning quantities in general—we have found it necessary to use specific demonstrations here, taking nothing from previous books and contenting ourselves only with the principles of this seventh book. For this reason, we have appropriately placed the petitions <note>Postulates.</note> and common notions <note>Axioms.</note> specific to this seventh book at its beginning.

### Proposition 7

> **If there are two numbers, of which one is a part of the other, and a part [of the same proportion] is subtracted from both, the remainder will be the same part of the remainder as the whole was of the whole.**

¶ What Euclid proposed here concerning numbers, he proposed earlier in the fifth proposition of the fifth book regarding quantities in general. Therefore, let the whole *a* be a certain part of the whole *b*. Let *c* be subtracted from *a*, and *d* be subtracted from *b*. I say that the remainder *e* (from *a*) will be the same part of the remainder *f* (from *b*) as the whole *a* was of the whole *b*. This is, as it were, the converse of the fifth proposition. For, by petition, let *e* be the same part of *g* as *c* is of *d*. By the 5th proposition, the whole *a* (composed of *e* and *c*) will be the same part of the sum of *g* and *d* as *c* is of *d*. Since *a* is also that same part of *b*, then by the second common notion, the sum of *g* and *d* is equal to *b*. Subtracting *d* from both numbers, *g* will be equal to *f*. Therefore, it will be...

### Proposition 8

<margin>
<note>A complex diagram of line segments and numbers. The top line is labeled 'b' with the number 18 above and parts 6 and 12 indicated. Below it is another segment labeled 'f' with 12 above and subdivisions of 4 and 8. Further down are segments 'c' and 'g', 'c' again, and at the bottom segments labeled 'k' and 'h' with the number 4.</note>
