> **If from two numbers, one of which is "parts" of the other, those same "parts" are subtracted: the remainder will be the same "parts" of the remainder as the whole was of the whole.**

¶ This is, as it were, the converse of the sixth proposition: so that if the whole *a* is so many and such "parts" <note>Euclid distinguishes between a "part" (a unit fraction like 1/3) and "parts" (a composite fraction like 2/3).</note> of the whole *b*, and the "parts" *c* subtracted from *a* are the same "parts" of *d* subtracted from *b*, then the remainder *e* of *a* will be the same "parts" of the remainder *f* of *b* as the whole *a* was of *b*. 

For let *g* be one of the parts of *a* and *b* <note>The text likely means one of the unit parts that compose the fraction.</note>, and one of the parts of *c*. By the <term>hypothesis</term> <note>The starting assumptions of the proof.</note>, *g* will be the same part of the whole *a* as it is of *b*, and the same of *c* and *d*. Therefore, let *h* be subtracted from *g*, and let *k* remain. By the preceding proposition, the whole *e* will be the same part as *g* is of *a*, and the whole *f* by the same reasoning will be the same part as *g* is of *b*. Since, therefore, *e* and *f* have a common part which is *k*, it will be (by the 16th definition) that *e* is "parts" of *f*, as many as the part *k* is of *e* and as many as *k* is of *f*. And because these were the same "parts" as *a* was of *b*, the proposition is established.

### Proposition 9

<margin>
<note>Four line segments labeled 'b', 'd' (longer) and 'a', 'c' (shorter). Segments 'b' and 'd' are divided by vertical tick marks.</note>
</margin>

> **If there are four numbers, of which the first is the same "part" of the second as the third is of the fourth: then, alternately, the first will be the same "part" or "parts" of the third as the second is of the fourth.**

¶ Let *a* be the first, being the same part of the second *b* as the third *c* is of the fourth *d*. Let *a* and *b* be smaller than *c* and *d*; for otherwise, the proposition would be the reverse. I say that whatever part or parts *a* is of *c*, the same part or parts *b* is of *d*. Let *b* be divided according to the quantity of *a*, and *d* according to the quantity of *c*. By the present hypothesis, there will be as many parts in *b* as there are in *d*. And because each of the parts of *b* is equal to *a*, and each part of *d* is equal to *c*, and since *a* is a part or parts of *c* by the present hypothesis and by Proposition 4: then each part of *b* will be the same part or parts of its corresponding part in *d* (as the first is to the first, the second to the second, and so on). Therefore, by Proposition 5 or 6 (repeated as many times as necessary under the division), the whole *b* will be the same part or parts of *d* as *a* is of *c*, which is what was proposed.

### Proposition 10

<margin>
<note>Four line segments labeled 'b', 'd', 'a', 'c' similar to the previous diagram. Below are numbers 5, 6, and 7 aligned with tick marks on the segments.</note>
</margin>

> **If there are four numbers, of which the first is the same "parts" of the second as the third is of the fourth: then, alternately, the first will be the same part or parts of the third as the second is of the fourth.**

¶ Let there be four numbers as before, of which *a* and *b* are similarly the smaller, and let *a* be the same "parts" of *b* as *c* is of *d*. I say that whatever part or parts *a* is of *c*, the same part or parts *b* is of *d*. For let the smaller numbers *a* and *c* be divided into those parts. By the present hypothesis, there will be as many parts in *a* as in *c*. And because each of the parts of *a* is the same "part" of *b* as each of the parts of *c* is of *d*—which we have from our hypothesis—it will follow <term>alternately</term> <note>original: "permutatim" — changing the order of the terms in a proportion.</note> by the preceding proposition: that whatever part or parts *b* is of *d*, the same will be each of the parts of *a* of its corresponding part in *c*. Therefore, by Proposition 5 or 6 (repeated as many times as necessary), the whole *b* will be the same part or parts of *d* as *a* is of *c*, which is what was proposed.

### Proposition 11

> **If there are four proportional numbers of which the first is greater than the second and the third is greater than the fourth: then the second will be the same part or parts of the first as the fourth is of the third. If the second is the same part or parts of the first as the fourth is of the third, then the four numbers will be proportional.**

¶ Let the proportion of *a* to *b* be as *c* is to *d*, and let *a* and *c* be the greater numbers. I say that whatever part or...

<header>XVII</header>

...is a part. *b* is of the whole *a*, just as *d* is of the whole *c*, and vice versa: for by the conversion of the definition of similar proportions, as many times as *b* is in *a*, so many times will *d* be in *c*. And if any part or parts of *b* remain <note>original: "superfluunt" — literally "overflow" or "remain as a surplus."</note> in *a*, the same part or parts of *d* remain in *c*. If, therefore, *b* is contained in *a* without a remainder <note>original: "sine superfluitate"</note>, because it is contained as many times without a remainder as *d* is in *c*, it will be by the definition of similar parts: as much a part as *b* is of the whole *a*, so is *d* of the whole *c*. But if *b* is contained as many times as you like in *a* with a remainder of a part, because *d* is contained just as many times in *c* with a remainder of a similar part, with *a* being divided according to *b* so that *e* remains, and *c* according to *d* so that *f* remains, then the whole part *e* will be of *b* as much as *f* is of *d*. And because *b* is contained in all of *a* up to *e* as many times as *d* is in all of *c* up to *f*, it will be by <term>common science</term> <note>original: "commuunem scientiam" — referring to a "common notion" or mathematical axiom recognized as self-evident.</note> that *c* is in *a* as many times as *f* is in *c*. Since, therefore, *a* and *b* have *e* as a common part, and similarly *c* and *d* have *f*: let it be that *e* is in *b* as many times as *f* is in *d*, and likewise *e* is in *a* as many times as *f* is in *c*. It will then be, by the 16th definition, that *b* is as many and such "parts" <note>In Euclidean arithmetic, a "part" (pars) is a unit fraction like 1/3, while "parts" (partes) refers to a composite fraction like 2/3.</note> of *a* as *d* is of *c*. If, however, *b* is contained any number of times in *a* with a remainder of parts, because *d* is contained just as many times in *c* with a remainder of just as many and similar parts: with *a* divided according to *b* so that *e* remains, and similarly *c* according to *d* so that *f* remains, then *e* will be as many and such parts of *b* as *f* is of *d*. Taking one from them, the argument proceeds as before; and thus the first part is clear. 

¶ The second part is as follows. Let *b* be as many and such a part or parts of *a* as *d* is of *c*. I say that the proportion of *a* to *b* will be as *c* to *d*. For if it is a single part, the proposition is established. If, however, they are multiple "parts," once they are divided according to those parts, it will be clear that *b* is in *a* as many times as *d* is in *c*, and that *b* leaves as a remainder the same part or parts in *a* as *d* leaves in *c*. Therefore, by the definition, the proportion of *a* to *b* is as *c* to *d*, and thus the whole is clear.

### Proposition 12

<margin>
<note>A diagram representing numerical ratios. At the top, a line labeled 'a' represents the number 12, divided into three parts of 4, with a segment 'b' of 4 below and a remainder 'e' of 2. Next to it, a line 'c' represents 15, divided into parts of 6, 6, and 3, with segment 'd' of 6 and 'f' of 3.</note>
</margin>

> **If from two numbers two numbers are subtracted according to their proportions: the proportion of the remainder to the remainder will be as the proportion of the whole to the whole.**

<margin>
<note>A line segment diagram for Proposition 12. The top line shows segments 'b' and 'f' which together form 'a'. The bottom line shows segments 'd' and 'e' which together form 'c'.</note>
</margin>

¶ What Euclid proposed in the 19th proposition of the Fifth Book concerning quantities in general, he proposes here concerning numbers. For example, if the proportion of the whole *a* to the whole *b* is as *c* (subtracted from *a*) is to *d* (subtracted from *b*), then the proportion of the residue *e* (of *a*) to the residue *f* (of *b*) will be as *a* is to *b*. For if *a* is less than *b*, it will be by the present hypothesis and by the conversion of the definition that *c* is the same part or parts of *d* as *a* is of *b*. By Proposition 7 or 8, therefore, *e* will be the same part or parts of *f* as *a* is of *b*. By the definition, therefore, there will be one proportion, which is what was proposed. But if *a* is greater than *b*, it will be by the first part of the premise that *b* is the same part or parts of *a* as *d* is of *c*. Therefore, by Proposition 7 or 8, *f* will be the same part or parts of *e*. Thus, by the second part of the premise, *e* is to *f* as *a* is to *b*, and the proposition stands. Furthermore, Propositions 7 and 8 yield to this one; for this one alone contains what both of those contain. 

¶ Some wish to prove the second part of this through the 19th proposition of the Fifth Book; but if Euclid had intended this—since he proposes here specifically what he proposed there universally—he would have demonstrated that in the Fifth Book in vain only to propose it again here in the Seventh. Furthermore, they do not demonstrate it simply through the 19th of the Fifth. Indeed, they cannot even apply the method of that demonstration to the demonstration of this one, since that is demonstrated for quantities in general through <term>alternating proportionality</term> <note>original: "proportionalitatem permutatam" — the rule that if a/b = c/d, then a/c = b/d.</note>, which is demonstrated below specifically for numbers. I believe, and it seems reasonably proven, that Euclid assumed the role of an arithmetical demonstrator for the sake of the Tenth Book <note>The Tenth Book deals with irrational magnitudes, which required a rigorous understanding of rational numerical ratios first.</note>, which cannot be traversed without some prior knowledge of numbers; for this reason, he repeats many of those things which he demonstrated in the Fifth regarding quantities in general, demonstrating them here specifically for numbers, since they are better known to the intellect through other principles—namely those proper to numbers—than...

<header>BOOK VII</header>

He intends to demonstrate those same principles through which he proceeded in the fifth book: for the principles of the fifth book are difficult because of the troublesome nature <note>original: "maliciam" — literally "malice" or "wickedness," but used here to describe the mathematical complexity or "perversity" of quantities that do not share a common measure.</note> of incommensurable quantities; however, the principles of numbers apply themselves more spontaneously to the intellect and are easier than the former. For those [of the fifth book] require a more prepared mind.

### Proposition 13

<margin>
<note>A diagram illustrating proportional numbers with three pairs of horizontal line segments: 'a' over 'b', 'c' over 'd', and 'e' over 'f'. This visual representation helps the reader see the three distinct ratios being compared.</note>
</margin>
If there are any number of proportional numbers, as one <term>antecedent</term> <note>The first term in a ratio (the "if" part).</note> is to its own <term>consequent</term> <note>The second term in a ratio (the "then" part).</note>, so will all the antecedents taken together be to all the consequents taken together.

¶ That which Euclid proposed in the 13th proposition of the fifth book concerning quantities in general, he proposes here concerning numbers: as if *a, b, c, d,* and *e, f* are proportional, I say that the ratio of *a* to *b* is the same as the ratio of *a, c, e* taken together to *b, d, f* taken together. For if *a, c, e* are smaller than *b, d, f*, it will be (by the conversion of the definition) that *a* is the same part or parts of *b* as the whole or wholes *c, d* and *e, f* are by the 5th or 6th proposition <note>Refers to previous proofs in this book regarding parts and multiples.</note>, repeated as many times as necessary: *a* will be the same part or parts of *b* as the sum of *a, c, e* is of the sum of *b, d, f*: wherefore, by the definition, the proportion is the same. If, however, *a, c, e* are greater than *b, d, f*, it will be by the first part of the 11th proposition that *b* is the same part or parts of *a* as *d* is of *c* and *f* is of *e*: therefore by the 5th or 6th, repeated as many times as necessary, *b* will be the same part or parts of *a* as the sum of *b, d, f* is of the sum of *a, c, e*. Thus, by the second part of the 11th proposition, the ratio of *a* to *b* is as the sum of *a, c, e* is to the sum of *b, d, f*: which is what was proposed.

### Proposition 14

<margin>
<note>Two sets of diagrams for proportionality. Each set shows horizontal segments 'a' over 'b' and 'c' over 'd'. The lower set has longer lines than the upper set, representing different magnitudes maintaining the same relative proportions.</note>
</margin>
If four numbers are proportional, they will also be proportional alternately <note>original: "permutatim" — a mathematical operation where the inner terms of a proportion are swapped (if a:b = c:d, then a:c = b:d).</note>.

¶ The method of arguing which is called "permuted proportionality," which Euclid demonstrated through the 16th proposition of the fifth book regarding quantities in general, he proposes here to be demonstrated in numbers: as if the ratio of *a* to *b* is as *c* to *d*, it will be, alternately, *a* to *c* as *b* is to *d*. For *a* will be either greater or smaller than *b*; and similarly *c* will be greater or smaller [than *d*]. Let it first be that *a* is smaller than both [b and c]: therefore, by the present hypothesis and the conversion of the definition, *a* is the same part or parts of *b* as *c* is of *d*. By the 9th or 10th proposition, it will be alternately that *a* is the same part or parts of *c* as *b* is of *d*, wherefore by the definition the proportion is one and the same. Now let *a* be greater than both: and by the first part of the 11th proposition, as *b* is a part or parts of *a*, so let *d* be of *c*. Wherefore by the 9th or 10th proposition, *b* will be the same part or parts of *d* as *a* is of *c*. Therefore by the second part of the 11th, *a* will be to *c* as *b* is to *d*. Let it be thirdly that *a* is greater than *b* and smaller than *c*: it will be by the first part of the 11th that *b* is the same part or parts of *a* as *d* is of *c*. Wherefore by the 9th or 10th, as *a* is a part or parts of *c*, so will *b* be of *d*. By the definition, therefore, the proportion is one. Finally, let *a* be greater than *b* and also greater than *c*: it will be that as *c* is a part or parts of *d*, so is *a* of *b*. By the 9th or 10th, *d* will be the same part or parts of *b* as *c* is of *a*. Wherefore by the second part of the 11th, *b* is to *d* as *a* is to *c*. And so the proposition stands; however, the 9th or 10th propositions are central to this, because this proposition alone is what both of those together propose.

### Proposition 15

<margin>
<note>A diagram showing horizontal segments 'a' over 'b' and 'c' over 'd', serving as a simplified visual for the "equality" proportionality.</note>
</margin>
If there are any number of numbers, and others equal to them in number, and all pairs from the first set are in the same ratio as all pairs from the second set, they will be proportional by the ratio of equality <note>original: "in proportione equalitatis" — also known as the "ex aequali" property (if a:b = d:e and b:c = e:f, then a:c = d:f).</note>.

¶ The method of arguing which is called "equal proportionality," which Euclid demonstrated through the 22nd proposition of the fifth book concerning quantities in general, he proposes here to be demonstrated in numbers.

<meta>This page continues the arithmetical proofs of Book VII, specifically focusing on the properties of proportions (ratios) between whole numbers. <header>VII</header>

<margin>
<note>A diagram in the right margin showing three pairs of horizontal line segments. The first pair consists of 'a' and 'c', the second 'b' and 'd', and the third 'e' and 'f'. Each pair is horizontally aligned.</note>
</margin>
...of direct proportionality. As for <term>equal proportionality</term> <note>Latin: *equa proportionalitas*. This refers to the 'ex aequali' rule: if a:b = d:e and b:c = e:f, then a:c = d:f.</note>, which he demonstrated in the 23rd proposition of the fifth book, he does not propose to demonstrate it here for numbers in a state of <term>indirect proportionality</term>; however, we will demonstrate that below in the 19th proposition of this book. Nor is it necessary that we pre-demonstrate in numbers what was demonstrated in the 11th proposition of the fifth book concerning quantities in general—namely, that if any number of proportions in numbers are equal to or the same as one, they are equal to or the same as each other. For this is manifest through the definition: as if *a* to *c* and *c* to *f* were as *b* to *d*, then both *a* and *c*, as well as *c* and *f*, will be the same part or parts (of whatever size or number) as *b* and *d*. Or, *a* and *c* and *c* and *f* will contain [their counterparts] as many times as *b* and *d*; and the whole part or parts by which *c* exceeds *a* and *f* exceeds *e* will be the same as those by which *d* exceeds *b*. Therefore, because *a* and *c* are the same part or parts as *c* and *f*, or as many times as *a* contains *c*, so does *c* contain *f*, and the part or parts by which *c* exceeds *a* is the same as *f* in *e*, it will be (by definition) that *a* is to *c* as *e* is to *f*. Let there be, therefore, as proposed, numbers *a, b, e* and another set of the same number *c, d, f*. Let *a* be to *b* as *c* is to *d*, and *b* to *e* as *d* is to *f*. I say that in <term>equal proportionality</term>, *a* will be to *e* as *c* is to *f*. For by the preceding [proposition], *a* will be to *c* as *b* is to *d*; but *b* is to *d* as *e* is to *f*; therefore *a* is to *c* as *e* is to *f*. Consequently, by the same rule, *a* is to *e* as *c* is to *f*. The same will hold if more numbers are taken, and thus the proposition stands.

Since Euclid did not propose that the other four species of proportionality—which are <term>converse</term>, <term>disjunct</term>, <term>conjunct</term>, and <term>evert</term>—be demonstrated in numbers, we think it fitting to demonstrate those which the author passed over as being easily provable. First, therefore, we shall demonstrate the **Converse**: as if *a* is to *b* as *c* is to *d*, I say that conversely *b* will be to *a* as *d* is to *c*. For if *a* is smaller than *b*, then *c* will also be smaller than *d*, and *a* is the same part or parts of *b* as *c* is of *d*; wherefore, by the second part of the 11th proposition, *b* will be to *a* as *d* is to *c*. But if *a* is greater than *b*, then *c* will also be greater than *d*, and by the first part of the 11th proposition, *b* is the same part or parts of *a* as *d* is of *c*. Therefore, by definition, *b* is to *a* as *d* is to *c*.

<margin>
<note>A diagram showing two pairs of horizontal segments. The upper segments 'a' and 'c' are significantly longer than the lower segments 'b' and 'd'.</note>
</margin>
¶ To show **Disjunct** proportionality: as if *a-b* <note>The notation 'a-b' or 'ab' here refers to a total quantity composed of two parts, a and b.</note> is to *b* as *c-d* is to *d*, then *a* will be to *b* as *c* is to *d*. For by <term>permutation</term> <note>Switching the inner terms of the proportion.</note> *a-b* will be to *c-d* as *b* is to *d*, and by the 12th proposition, as *a* is to *c*. Since therefore *a* is to *c* as *b* is to *d*, it will be by permutation that *a* is to *b* as *c* is to *d*.

¶ To provide the demonstration for **Conjunct** proportionality: as if *a* is to *b* as *c* is to *d*, then *a-b* will be to *b* as *c-d* is to *d*. For by permutation *a* is to *c* as *b* is to *d*; wherefore by the 13th proposition, *a-b* is to *c-d* as *b* is to *d*. Therefore, by permutation, *a-b* will be to *b* as *c-d* is to *d*.

<margin>
<note>Two long horizontal line segments. The top one is labeled with 'a' and 'b' at its endpoints, and the bottom one is labeled 'c' and 'd'.</note>
</margin>
¶ It remains to establish **Evert** proportionality in numbers: as if *a-b* is to *a* as *c-d* is to *c*, then *a-b* will be to *b* as *c-d* is to *d*. For by permutation *a-b* will be to *c-d* as *b* is to *d*, and by the 12th proposition, as *a* is to *c*. Therefore, by permutation, *a-b* will be to *a* as *c-d* is to *c*. Thus the whole is clear. From these it is also easy to demonstrate in numbers what Euclid proposes in the penultimate proposition of the fifth book regarding quantities in general, namely:

<margin>
<note>A diagram showing two sets of proportional line segments. On the left, two smaller segments 'a' and 'e' are placed above a single segment 'b'. On the right, two smaller segments 'c' and 'f' are placed above a single segment 'd'.</note>
</margin>
¶ If the proportion of a first to a second is as a third to a fourth, and a fifth to the second is as a sixth to the fourth: the proportion of the first and fifth taken together to the second will be as the third and sixth taken together to the fourth.

As if *a* is to *b* as *c* is to *d*, and likewise *e* is to *b* as *f* is to *d*, then *a* and *e* taken together will be to *b* as *c* and *f* taken together are to *d*. For by <term>converse proportionality</term>, *b* will be to *e* as *d* is to *f*; wherefore by <term>equal proportionality</term>, *a* is to *e* as *c* is to *f*. Therefore, <term>conjunctly</term>, *a* and *e* are to *e* as *c* and *f* are to *f*. Thus, by equal proportionality, *a* and *e* are to *b* as *c* and *f* are to *d*, which is what was proposed. And in the same way you will prove the reverse: if *b* is to *a* as *d* is to *c*, and likewise *b* is to *e* as *d* is to *f*, then *b* will be to *a* and *e* as *d* is to *c* and *f*. For by converse proportionality *a* is to *b* as *c* is to *d*; wherefore by equal proportionality *a* is to *e* as *c* is to *f*, and conjunctly *a* and *e* are to *e* as *c* and *f*...

<header>BOOK VII</header>

...to *f*. Therefore, conversely, *c* to *a* and *c* [is] as *f* to *d* and *f*. Therefore, by <term>equal proportionality</term> <note>Latin: *equam proportionalitatem*. This is the "ex aequali" rule, which allows for comparing the first and last terms in a series of ratios.</note>, *b* to *a* and *c* will be as *d* to *c* and *f*, which was the proposition. From this it is also manifest that if the proportion of any number of [numbers] to the first is as the same number of others to the second, then the proportion of the sum of all the <term>antecedents</term> <note>The "antecedent" is the first term in a ratio (the "a" in a:b).</note> to the first will be as the sum of all the antecedents to the second. Likewise conversely, if the proportion of the first to any number of numbers is as the second to the same number of others, then the proportion of the first to the sum of all [the numbers] following it will be as the second to the sum of all those following it.

### Proposition 16

<margin>
<note>A line segment diagram. At the top left, a segment is labeled '1' (as a unit) above and 'a' below. To its right, another segment is labeled with 'b' over 'c' above it. These represent the numbers used in the proof of alternating ratios.</note>
</margin>

If a <term>unit</term> <note>Latin: *vnitas*. In Greek mathematics, the unit (1) was not considered a "number" but the source or principle of numbers, which were defined as a multitude of units starting from 2.</note> measures any number as often as any third [number] measures a fourth, then by permutation, as often as the unit measures the third, so often the second will measure the fourth.
As if the unit were to *a* as *b* is to *c*, then by permutation the unit will be to *b* as *a* is to *c*. This demonstrated permutation is not superfluous; for it cannot be concluded from the previous rule [for general proportions]. For that was demonstrated for four proportional *numbers*, but the unit is not a number by definition. Let the proposition be shown in this manner: divide *a* into units and *c* according to the quantity of *b*. By the present hypothesis, there will be as many parts of *a* as of *c*. And because each of the parts of *a* is a unit, and each of the parts of *c* is equal to *b*, then as often as the unit is in *b*, so often is each of the parts of *a* in its corresponding part of *c*. Therefore, by the method of demonstration 5, it follows that *a* is in *c* as many times as the unit is in *b*, which was the proposition.

### Proposition 17

<margin>
<note>A diagram with four horizontal line segments. Segment 'a' has the number '3' above it. Segment 'b' has the number '4' above it. Below them, segment 'c' has the number '12' to its left. Below that, segment 'd' is equal to 'c' and also has '12' to its left. This illustrates that 3 times 4 equals 4 times 3.</note>
</margin>

If each of two numbers is multiplied by the other, the products produced from them will be equal.
As if from *a* times *b* comes *c*, and from *b* times *a* comes *d*, then *c* and *d* will be equal. Since *b* multiplied by *a* produces *c*, then by the converse of the definition, *b* is in *c* as often as the unit is in *a*. Therefore, by the preceding [proposition], *a* is in *c* as often as the unit is in *b*. And because *a* is also in *d* as many times—since *d* is made from *b* times *a*—it follows that *a* is in *c* as many times as it is in *d*. Therefore, by common conception, *c* and *d* are the same. We can also propose this conclusion in another way: if each of two numbers is led into the other, the same number will be produced in both cases. As if from *a* times *b* comes *c*, the same will also come from *b* times *a*. For because *c* is made from *a* times *b*, then as before, by the converse of the definition, *b* is in *c* as often as the unit is in *a*. And permutatively by the preceding [proposition], *a* is in *c* as often as the unit is in *b*. Because therefore *a* accumulates itself in *c* as many times as there are units in *b*, it follows by definition that *c* is produced from *b* times *a*.

### Proposition 18

<margin>
<note>A diagram showing five horizontal line segments. Segment 'd' has '20' above it, 'e' has '30' above it. Below them, 'c' has '4' above it, 'b' has '6' above it, and 'a' has '5' below it between 'c' and 'b'. At the bottom is a single unit segment labeled '1'. This demonstrates that 5x4 : 5x6 is the same as 4 : 6.</note>
</margin>

If one number is multiplied by two [others], the ratio of the two products will be the same as the ratio of the two numbers being multiplied.
Let *a* multiply each of the two numbers *b* and *c*, and let *d* and *e* be produced. I say that the proportion of *d* to *e* will be as *b* is to *c*. For it follows by the converse of the definition of multiplication that *b* is in *d* and *c* is in *e* as often as the unit is in *a*. Wherefore, by the definition, the proportion of *d* to *b* is as *e* to *c*; for they contain them equally, specifically as many times as *a* [contains] the unit. Therefore, permutatively, *d* is to *e* as *b* is to *c*, which was the proposition.

### Proposition 19

If two numbers multiply one [number], the ratio of the two products will be as the ratio of the two multipliers.
From the converse of the preceding [proposition], this same property is concluded as in the previous one; as if each of the two numbers *b* and *c* multiplies *a*, and...

One can also extend what is proposed by this and the previous proposition from two numbers to any number of them: since if one number multiplies any number of others, the ratio of the products and the numbers multiplied will be the same. Similarly, if any number of numbers multiply a single number, the ratio of the products and those multiplying will be the same, which you will easily prove by repeating this and the previous proposition as often as necessary. Here, however, as we promised above, we wish to demonstrate <term>equal proportionality</term> <note>Latin: *equam proportionalitatem*. This is the "ex aequali" rule, which allows mathematicians to skip middle terms in a series of ratios to compare the first and last terms directly.</note> in any number of numbers of two orders of <term>indirect proportionality</term> <note>Latin: *indirecte proportionalitatis*. Often called "perturbed" or "cross" proportion, this occurs when the ratios in two sets of numbers are matched in reverse order (e.g., a:b = d:f and b:e = c:d).</note> which Euclid demonstrated through Proposition 23 of the Fifth Book regarding magnitudes in general; we say, therefore, that:

If any number of numbers are indirectly proportional to as many others, the extremes will also be proportional in the same ratio.

As if *a* were to *b* as *d* is to *f*, and *b* to *e* as *c* is to *d*, then *a* will be to *e* as *c* is to *f*. Likewise, let *f* be multiplied by *d*, and let the result be *k*; then by this 19th proposition, *g* will be to *k* as *c* is to *f*. And since from *f* multiplied by *d* comes *k*, the same will result conversely by Proposition 10 <note>Latin: *e converso*. You will prove the same if there were more than three numbers in each order, just as it is proved in Proposition 23 of the Fifth Book regarding magnitudes when they are more than three in number.

### Proposition 20

If four numbers are proportional, that which is produced from the multiplication of the first by the last will be equal to that which is produced from the multiplication of the second by the third. If, however, that which is produced from the first by the last is equal to that which is produced from the second by the third, those four numbers are proportional.

What Euclid proposed through Proposition 15 of the Sixth Book regarding four proportional lines, he proposes here regarding four proportional numbers. For example: let the proportion of *a* to *b* be as *c* to *d*, and let *e* be the product of *a* and *d*, and *f* the product of *b* and *c*. I say that *e* and *f* are equal. Conversely: let *a* be multiplied by *b* and let the result be *g*. Then by Proposition 18, *g* will be to *h* as *b* is to *d*. And since by Proposition 17, from *b* multiplied by *a* comes *g*, and from the same *b* multiplied by *c* comes *f*, then by Proposition 18, *g* will be to *f* as *a* is to *c*. But by Proposition 14, *a* is to *c* as *b* is to *d*; therefore *g* will be to *f* as *g* is to *e*. Therefore *f* and *e* are equal, which is the first part. Nor is it necessary to demonstrate beforehand that if there is one ratio of one number to two others, those two are equal; or if they are equal, that the ratio of one to them is the same. For if there is one ratio of *g* to *e* and to *f*, then either *g* will be the same <term>part or parts</term> <note>In Greek and Medieval mathematics, a "part" (Latin: *pars*) refers to a unit fraction like 1/3, while "parts" (*partes*) refers to a non-unit proper fraction like 2/3.</note> of *e* as it is of *f*, and then it is clear by <term>common notion</term> <note>Latin: *conceptionem*. These are the fundamental axioms or "Common Notions" that Euclid establishes at the very beginning of the Elements.</note> that *e* and *f* are equal; or *g* will contain *e* as many times as it contains *f*, and there will remain in it the same part or parts of *e* as there will remain of *f* in the same, and then also by common notion it is clear that they are equal. If they are equal, it is clear by common notion that either *g* will be the same part or parts of *e* as of *f*, and then by the definition, the proportion of *g* to each of them will be one; or it will contain each equally with a remainder of similar and as many parts in number, and then also by the definition, its proportion to each will be one.

</margin>

The second part is shown thus: let *e*, the product of *a* and *d*, be equal to *f*, the product of *b* and *c*. I say that the proportion of *a* to *b* is as *c* is to *d*, and this is the converse of the first part. For let it be as before...

# Proposition 21

<margin>

**Numbers that are the least in any given ratio measure any other numbers in that same ratio an equal number of times—the smaller measuring the smaller and the larger measuring the larger.** <note>In modern terms, if a/b is in lowest terms and equals c/d, then a divides c the same number of times that b divides d.</note>

¶ Let *a* and *b* be the least numbers in their ratio. And let *c* be to *d* as *a* is to *b*. I say that *a* measures *c* and *b* [measures] *d* equally. For since *a* is to *b* as *c* is to *d*, by permutation *a* will be to *c* as *b* is to *d*. Therefore, *a* will be the same part or parts of *c* as *b* is of *d*. If, therefore, it is a single part, the proposition is established. But if it is parts <note>Euclid distinguishes between a "part" (a unit fraction like 1/3) and "parts" (a non-unit fraction like 2/3).</note>, let *e* be one of the parts of *a*, and *f* one of the parts of *b*. And because the whole part *c* is to *e* (by hypothesis) as *f* is to *d*, then by definition the ratio of *e* to *c* will be as *f* to *d*. Therefore, by permutation, *e* is to *f* as *c* is to *d*, and therefore also as *a* is to *b*. Thus, *a* and *b* are not the least in their ratio, which is contrary to what was stated. ->Likewise also.<-

<note>A diagram with three columns of stacked horizontal line segments. Top row: d, e, f. Middle row: a, b, c. Bottom row: g, h, k.</note>
</margin>

¶ Any number of numbers, whether in the same ratio or in different ones, if they are the least, they measure all others in that same ratio—each measuring its corresponding number—an equal number of times.

¶ As if *a*, *b*, and *c* are the least in the same ratio or in different ones; and let *d*, *e*, and *f* be in that same or those same ratios, so that *d* is to *e* as *a* is to *b*, and *e* is to *f* as *b* is to *c*. I say that *a* measures *d*, *b* [measures] *e*, and *c* [measures] *f* equally. For because *a* is to *b* as *d* is to *e*, by permutation *a* is to *d* as *b* is to *e*. And because *b* is to *c* as *e* is to *f*, then by permutation *b* is to *e* also as *c* is to *f*. Therefore, *b* is to *e* and *c* is to *f* just as *a* is to *d*. Since *a*, *b*, and *c* are smaller than *d*, *e*, and *f*, then *b* to *e* and *c* to *f* will be the same part or parts as *a* is to *d*. If, therefore, it is a part, the proposition is established. But if it is parts, let *g* be one of the parts of *a*, *h* one of the parts of *b*, and *k* one of the parts of *c*. Then by the present hypothesis, the whole part *b* is to *e* and *c* is to *f* as *g* is to *d*. Therefore, by definition, *b* is to *e* and *k* is to *f* as *g* is to *d*. By permutation, therefore, *g* will be to *b* as *d* is to *e*, and *b* will be to *k* as *e* is to *f*. Therefore, *g* is to *b* as *a* is to *b*, and *b* is to *k* as *b* is to *c*. Since *g*, *b*, and *k* are smaller than *a*, *b*, and *c* and in the same ratio, the contrary of the position follows.

# Proposition 23.

<note>Three pairs of line segments representing numerical ratios. Top pair: a and b. Middle pair: c and d. Bottom: a single segment e representing a potential common measure.</note>

**A**ny numbers that are prime to each other are the least in their proportion.
¶ This is the converse of the previous [proposition]. For if two numbers *a* and *b* are prime to each other, they will be the least in their proportion. If, however, there were others that were the least in that same proportion—if possible, let them be *c* and *d*—it then follows by [Proposition] 21 that *c* measures *a* and *d* measures *b* equally. Let this measure be according to *e*. By [Proposition] 17, conversely, *e* measures *a* and *b*: *a* according to *c* and *b* according to *d*. Therefore, *a* and *b* are not prime to each other, which contradicts the hypothesis.

# Proposition 24.

<margin>
<note>Two pairs of line segments. Top: a and b. Bottom: c and d. This diagram supports the logic that if a number measures one of two coprime numbers, it cannot share a factor with the other.</note>

**I**f two numbers are prime to each other, if any number measures one of them, it is necessarily proved to be prime to the other.
¶ Let *a* and *b* be prime to each other, and let *c* measure *a*. I say that *c* is prime to *b*. Otherwise, some number *d* would measure both of them. Because *d* measures *c*, and *c* measures *a*, then *d* would also measure *a*. Therefore, *a* and *b* would not be prime to each other, because *d* measures both of them.

### Proposition 26.

If there are two numbers prime to each other, the number produced from one of them [multiplied] by itself is prime to the other.
¶ Let *a* and *b* be prime to each other, and from *a* times itself let *c* be produced <note>In this context, *c* is the square of *a*.</note>. I say that *c* is prime to *b*. For let *d* be equal to *a*; then *d* will be prime to *b*. And from *a* times *d*, *c* is produced. Therefore, by the preceding proposition, it is clear that *c* is prime to *b*, which is what we proposed.

### Proposition 27.

If, when two numbers are compared to two other numbers, each of the first pair is prime to each of the second pair, the product of the first two will be prime to the product of the second two.
¶ Let *a* and *b* be the first numbers, and *c* and *d* the latter numbers. Let both *a* and *b* be prime to both *c* and *d*. Let *e* be the product of *a* times *b*, and *f* the product of *c* times *d*. I say that *e* is prime to *f*. This is evidently concluded by applying Proposition 25 three times: for since *e* is produced from *a* and *b*, each of which is prime to *c* and *d*, then by that proposition *e* will be prime to *c*, and likewise prime to *d*. Because *f* is produced from *c* and *d*, and each of them is prime to *e*, then by that same proposition *f* will be prime to *e*, which is what was proposed.

<note>A line diagram for Proposition 28 showing multiple segments labeled f, e, d, c, b, and a, illustrating multiplicative relationships between numbers.</note>

### Proposition 28.

If there are two numbers prime to each other and each is multiplied by itself, the resulting products will be prime to each other. Likewise, if each product is multiplied by its original starting number <note>Latin: "principium" — referring here to the base number that was squared; the resulting product would be a cube.</note>, the resulting products will also be prime to each other.
¶ Let *a* and *b* be prime to each other; let each be multiplied by itself, and let *c* result from *a*, and *d* result from *b*. Likewise, let *a* be multiplied by *c* to produce *e*, and *b* by *d* to produce *f*. I say that *c* and *d* are prime to each other, and likewise *e* and *f* are prime to each other. For by Proposition 26, *c* is prime to *b*. Therefore, by the same logic, *d* will be prime to *a* and to *c*; thus it is established that the first pair, *c* and *d*, are prime to each other. ¶ The remainder follows thus: since each of the two numbers *a* and *c* is prime to both *b* and *d*, then by Proposition 27, *c* will be prime to *f*. Not only will *c* be prime to *f*, but also by Proposition 25 to *b* and to *d*; likewise by the same proposition *f* will be prime to *a* and *c*. Thus, if each product were multiplied by its starting number infinitely many times, all the resulting products would be prime to each other; and not only that, but any number derived [by multiplication] from *a* would be prime to any number derived from *b*.

<note>A line diagram for Proposition 29 showing a long segment labeled a and b representing a sum, with segments a, b, and d shown below it.</note>

Conversely, if the sum of two numbers is prime to each of them, the two numbers will also be prime to each other.
¶ Let *a* and *b* be prime to each other: I say that the sum composed of them, *a+b*, will be prime to each of them, and vice versa. Specifically, if a number divides a whole and one part, it must divide the remaining part.</note>. In that case, they would not be prime to each other, but this was the starting assumption; thus the first part is clear. are prime to each other <note>original: "cōtra ſe pꝛimi" — coprime; having no common divisor other than 1.</note>; for if we suppose that *d* measures both of the two numbers *a* and *b*, it follows by a common notion <note>original: "cōem ſciam" — *communem scientiam*, referring to the self-evident axioms Euclid uses to build his proofs.</note> that it also measures *a* and *b* composed together <note>meaning the sum of a + b.</note>; therefore, *a + b* would not be prime to either of the two numbers *a* and *b*. But it was posited that it was prime to both. Thus, an impossibility occurs. In the same way, if the sum of two numbers is prime to one of them, it will also be prime to the other, and therefore the sum and the parts are prime to each other; for let the number composed of *a* and *b* be prime to *a*. I say that it will also be prime to *b*. Otherwise, let *d* measure them, which by common conception will measure *a* since it measures the whole and the part taken away; but this was inconsistent, for the sum of *a* and *b* was prime to *a*.

### Proposition 30.

<note>A line diagram with four horizontal segments of decreasing length, labeled a, b, c, d from top to bottom.</note>

Every composite number is measured by some prime number.
¶ Let *a* be any composite number <note>A number that has divisors other than 1 and itself.</note>: I say that some prime number measures <note>In Euclidean geometry, to "measure" a number means to divide it exactly without a remainder.</note> it. Since it is composite, it will be measured by some number *b*. If *b* is prime, what is said is true. But if it is composite, let *c* be the number that measures it; which also, by a common notion, will measure *a*. If *c* itself is prime, what is said is confirmed. But if it is composite, it must necessarily be measured by another, let it be *d*, which also by a common notion will measure *a*. Reason about this as before: because whenever a composite number occurs, it is necessary to take a smaller one that measures the composite one encountered, it follows that at last one must arrive at some prime number; otherwise an impossibility would occur, and contrary to the postulate, numbers would decrease into infinity <note>Euclid assumes a "principle of finite descent"—you cannot keep finding smaller and smaller whole number divisors forever.</note>.

### Proposition 31.

<note>A line diagram with a single horizontal segment labeled a.</note>

Every number is either prime or is measured by a prime.
¶ Let *a* be any number: I say that it is either prime or measured by a prime. Because if it is not prime, it will be composite; and every such number is measured by some prime by the preceding proposition. Therefore, *a* is either prime or is measured by a prime; which is what was proposed.

### Proposition 32.

<note>A line diagram with a long segment a and a shorter segment c below it.</note>

Every prime number is prime to every number that it does not measure.
¶ Let *a* be a prime number not measuring *b*: I say that *a* and *b* are prime to each other. For if *c* measures both of them, it would not be true that *a* is prime <note>Because a prime number can only be measured by 1 and itself; if *c* measures *a*, then *c* must be 1.</note>.

### Proposition 33.

<note>A line diagram showing two segments a and b joined end-to-end. Below them is segment c. Below c are two segments d and e placed side-by-side.</note>

If a number produced from two numbers is measured by any prime number, it is necessary that the same prime measures one of those two.
¶ Let *c* be the product of *a* multiplied by *b*, and let *d* be a prime number which is posited to measure *c*. I say that *d* measures *a* or *b*. For let it measure *c* according to *e*. If therefore it does not measure *a*, it will be prime to it by the preceding proposition; and therefore they will be the least in their proportion by Proposition 23. And by Proposition 20, *a* is to *d* as *e* is to *b*. It follows then that *d* measures *b* by Proposition 21, which is what was proposed. Whence it is manifest that if any number measures a product of two, or if it is commensurable <note>Sharing a common measure or factor.</note> to it, it will also be commensurable to one of them.

¶ Let *a* and *b* be the proposed numbers in whose proportion we wish to find the least. If therefore they are prime to each other, they are the ones we seek by Proposition 23. But if they are composite, let the greatest common measure be taken as the second proposition teaches, which shall be *c*; and let it measure them according to...

¶ As let *a, b, c* be [the numbers] according to whose ratios we wish to find the least [numbers], whether they be in the same ratio or in different ones: if no number measures them all, they are those which we seek by [Proposition] 23, for this was demonstrated there. Thus *d* was not the greatest number measuring them; wherefore an impossibility follows: for *d* was the greatest [number] measuring *a, b, c*.

->Proposition 35.<-

<margin>
<note>A line diagram with segments. Top pair: a, b. Middle pair: c, d. Middle-low pair: e, f. Bottom pair: g, h.</note>

Any two numbers, by multiplying the least numbers of their ratio—the greater by the lesser and the lesser by the greater—produce the least number measured by them <note>This proposition describes how to find the Least Common Multiple (LCM) of two numbers by using the smallest numbers that represent their ratio.</note>. From which it is manifest that the least [number] which two numbers measure, measures any [other] number measured by them.
¶ Let there be two numbers *a* and *b*, and the least in their ratio be *c* and *d*. And it will be by the first part of [Proposition] 20, that from *a* into *d* and *b* into *c* the same number is produced, which let be *e*, which I say is the least [number] measured by *a* and *b*. For otherwise, let it be *f*, which *a* and *b* measure according to *g* and *h*. And it will be by the second part of [Proposition] 20, *b* to *g* just as *a* to *b* and just as *c* to *d*. And by [Proposition] 18, *c* will be to *b* as *e* is to *f*. Since therefore by [Proposition] 21 *c* measures *b*, *e* will measure *f*, the greater [measuring] the lesser; because this is therefore impossible, it stands that what was said is true.

->Proposition 36.<-

<margin>
<note>A line diagram with two columns of segments. Left column: a, b, c, d. Right column: e, f, g, h.</note>
</margin>
Given any number of numbers, to find the least number measured by them. It is also manifest from this that the least of the numbers which any number [of given numbers] measure, measures any [other] number measured by them.
¶ Let the proposed numbers be *a, b, c, d*. I wish to find the least of the numbers measured by them. I find therefore first the least [number] measured by *a* and *b*; for if *a* measures *b*, there will be no other than *b*. But if it does not measure it, nor vice versa: if they are prime to each other <note>original: "ꝓtra ſe pꝛmi" — coprime; having no common factor other than 1.</note>, that which comes from one into the other will be the least by [Proposition] 23 and the premise. But if they are communicating <note>original: "cōicantes" — commensurable; having a common factor.</note>: let the least in their ratio be taken as [Proposition] 34 teaches, and let the greater multiplied into the lesser of them produce *e*, which will be the least measured by them by the premise. In a similar way also let the least measured by *e* and *c* be found, which let be *f*. And *f* will be the least measured by *a, b, c*. But also let the least which *f* and *d* measure be *g*. And *g* will be the least which the proposed numbers measure: for that they all measure it is clear by conception. But if it is not the least, let *h* be posited; because *a* and *b* measure it, it will also follow by the premise that *e* measures it. By the same logic it will also follow that *f* measures it, and also *g*. Thus a greater [number] measures a lesser, which is impossible. These and the premise are proposed in another place under three conclusions, of which the first is equivalent to the premise: the second is composed of both corollaries: the third proposes concerning three [numbers] what this does concerning any number of numbers. It is therefore the first.
¶ Given two numbers, to find the least number measured by them.

# BOOK VII

<margin>
<note>A line diagram used for mathematical proof. It shows two horizontal segments at the top labeled 'a' and 'b'. Below segment 'a' is segment 'c', and below 'b' is segment 'd'. At the bottom are segments 'e' and 'f'.</note>

¶ The given numbers are *a* and *b*. If the smaller measures <note>original: "numerat" — divides exactly without a remainder.</note> the larger, the larger is the number we seek <note>The Least Common Multiple (LCM). If 3 divides 6, 6 is their LCM.</note>. Otherwise, the larger of them would measure the smaller. If, however, neither measures the other, and they are relatively prime <note>original: "contra se primi" — numbers that share no common factor other than 1.</note> to each other, then the product of *a* multiplied by *b*, which let be *c*, will be the least of all numbers that *a* and *b* measure. For if they measured any smaller number, let it be *d*, which they measure according to *e* and *f*, it will be (by the second part of Proposition 20) that *a* is to *b* as *f* is to *e*. And because *a* and *b* are the least in their ratio (by Proposition 23), *a* will measure *f* (by Proposition 21). And because (by Proposition 18) *c* is to *d* as *a* is to *f*—for from *b* into *a* and *f* are produced *c* and *d*—it follows that *c* measures *d*. But *d* was posited as smaller than *c*, which is impossible. If, however, *a* and *b* are commensurable <note>original: "coicantes" — sharing a common factor.</note>, the proposition is handled as in Proposition 35, and the second of the three conclusions is established from both corollaries.

¶ If several numbers measure one number, it is necessary that the least number they measure also measures that same number.

<margin>
<note>A geometric line diagram. A single long segment 'd' is at the top. Below it is a line divided into segments 'a', 'e', 'b', and 'f'. A shorter segment 'c' is at the bottom.</note>

¶ As if *d* be any number that *a* and *b* measure, and the least measured by the same is *c*, it will be that *c* measures *d*. For since *d* is greater than *c*, if *c* does not measure it, it will nonetheless measure some part of it. Let the greatest amount that *c* measures be *e*, and the remainder be *f*. Thus *f* will be less than *c*. Since therefore *a* and *b* measure *c*, they will measure *e* by common knowledge <note>original: "comem scientiaz" — a mathematical axiom or "common notion".</note>. But they also measure *d*; therefore, by another common axiom, they will measure *f*. Consequently, an inconsistency <note>original: "inconueniens" — a logical contradiction.</note> follows: that *c* was not the least number that *a* and *b* measure. ¶ The same is proven in the same way for any number measured by any number of others; namely, that the least number measured by those others measures that same number. This is the last of the three conclusions.

<margin>
<note>A diagram showing two vertical stacks of three horizontal segments each. The left stack contains segments 'a', 'b', and 'c'. The right stack contains segments 'd', 'e', and 'f'.</note>

¶ Given three numbers: to find the least of the numbers measured by them.
¶ Let the three proposed numbers be *a, b, c*. Let the least that *a* and *b* measure be *d*, which is found as the first of the three conclusions teaches. If, therefore, *c* measures *d*, know that *d* is the one we seek. For if *a, b, c* measure a smaller number, let it be *e*, which (by the previous conclusion) *d* will measure, which is impossible. If, however, *d* does not measure *c*, let *e* be taken as the least measured by them. That *e* is measured by *a, b, c* is clear, because *c* measures it, and *d* similarly. Therefore, *a* and *b*, which measure *d*, also measure *e*. Wherefore *e* will be measured by *a, b, c*, and *e* will be the least that *a, b, c* measure. If, however, there were another, *f*, which (by the previous conclusion) *d* would measure, then *c* also measures *f* because *a, b, c* measure it. Wherefore *c* and *d* would measure it. Wherefore (by the previous [proposition]) *e* would measure it, and *e* is greater than it; but a greater cannot measure a smaller, which cannot be. You will find the same in the same way for any number of proposed numbers.

->Proposition 37<-

<note>A line diagram with a long horizontal segment 'a' at the top. Below 'a' are segments 'c' and 'b'. A vertical line segment 'I', representing unity (1), is placed below 'c'.</note>
</margin>

**If** any number measures another number, there will be in the number measured a part named after the measuring number.
¶ The meaning of this is that every number measured by three has a third part, and every number measured by five has a fifth part, and so on for the rest. As if *b* measures *a*, there will be in *a* a part named from *b*. For let it measure it as many times as unity <note>original: "vnitas" — the number 1, the basic unit of arithmetic.</note> is in *c*. It will be (by Proposition 16) that *c* also measures *a* as many times as unity is in *b*. Therefore, the whole part is *c*, of which unity is the *b*-th part. And because unity is a part of every number named from itself by common knowledge, *c* will be a part of *a* named from *b*, which is what was proposed.

->Proposition 38<-

<margin>
<note>A line diagram identical to the one for Proposition 37, with segments 'a', 'b', 'c' and the unit marker 'I'.</note>
</margin>

**If** any number has any part whatever, the number called according to that part will measure it.
¶ This is the converse of the previous [proposition], the intention of which is: that every number having a third is measured by three, and having a fifth by five, and so on for the rest. As if *b* is a part of *a* named from *c*, it follows that *c* measures *a*, because *b* is a part of *a* named from *c*.

# BOOK VII

...but also unity is a part of *c* denominated <note>original: "denominata" — named or categorized as a specific fraction (e.g., "a third").</note> by it through conception <note>A logical understanding or definition.</note>; it follows that as often as unity measures *c*, so often *b* measures *a*. Therefore, by Proposition 16, as often as unity measures *b*, so often *c* measures *a*, which establishes the proposition. ¶ **Alternatively, the same proof:** since *b* is a part of *a*, if the whole is unity *c*, it will follow by this common notion <note>original: "communem scientiam" — a fundamental axiom or self-evident truth.</note> that unity is a part of every number denominated by it. Thus, *c* denominates *b* in *a*; and because *b* is in *a* as often as unity is in *c*, the proposition evidently follows by Proposition 16.

->### Proposition 39<-

<margin>
<note>A mathematical line diagram shows horizontal segments organized into three columns. At the top are segments labeled 'e' and 'l'. **To find the least number having parts of the proposed denominations.** From which it is manifest that the least number measured by any given numbers is the least number having parts denominated by them.
¶ Let *a, b, c, d* be the denominators of the proposed parts, and let *e* be the least number measured by them, taken according to Proposition 36. I say that *e* is the number we seek. For let *f, g, h, k* be the parts by which they measure it; it will follow by Proposition 16 and this common notion: unity is a part of every number named by it, and vice versa. Thus *f, g, h, k* measure *e* according to *a, b, c, d*; wherefore they are the parts of it named by those denominators. Therefore, *e* possesses the parts of the proposed denominations. ¶ It is also the least, for if there were another, such as *l*, let the parts of *l* named by them be *m, n, p, q*. Then by Proposition 16 and the aforementioned common notion, *a, b, c, d* would conversely be the parts of *l* named by *m, n, p, q*. Therefore *e* would not be the least number that *a, b, c, d* measure, which is an inconsistency <note>original: "inconueniens" — a logical contradiction or reductio ad absurdum.</note>. ¶ Having found the minimum: if there is a need to find the second, or whichever you please: for the second, take double the minimum; for the third, triple; and in this manner for the others. For since every multiple of *e* is measured by *a, b, c, d* through this common notion: every number measuring another necessarily measures every number measured by that one (by Proposition 32), so every multiple of *e* must have parts denominated by *a, b, c, d*. If, therefore, the double of *e* were not the second number having the proposed parts, there would be another which, just as it follows to be greater than *e*, so it follows to be less than the double; and because *a, b, c, d* measure it by Proposition 38, it follows by the conclusion of Proposition 36 that *e* would measure it, which is impossible. For since it measures itself, it would measure (by this common notion: every number measuring a whole and a part subtracted from it also measures the remainder) the difference between that number and itself. Since that difference is smaller than *e*, a larger number would measure a smaller one, which cannot be. It follows that the double of *e* is the second number having the proposed denominations. ¶ Similarly, you will argue that the triple of *e* is the third, having proved the double is the second. Otherwise, because it would be less than the triple and greater than the double, it would follow that *e* measures something between its double and triple, which as before is seen to be impossible. Having proved the triple is the third, you will prove the quadruple is the fourth by this same likeness, and so on for the rest.

->**¶ To find the least number having parts of proposed denominations**<-
->**taken continuously.**<-

¶ To find the least number having a third, which third has a fourth, which fourth also has a fifth, or a seventh, or however it happens that they are denominated by the same or different [numbers]. ¶ It is necessary to multiply the denominator of the first part by the denominator of the second, and the product of those by the denominator of the third, and that product into the denominator of the fourth, and so on for the others until the last—either from the first to the last or from the last to the first. The resulting number will be what is sought, such as 60 or 84 in the proposed case. ¶ That this is so by demonstration, take it thus: Let *a, b, c, d* be the numbers denominating the proposed parts. We wish to find the least number that has a part denominated by *a*, such that that part has a part denominated by *b*, and that one another denominated by *c*, and this one yet another named by *d*...

Therefore, let *d* be multiplied by *c*, and let it produce *e*. Then let *e* be multiplied by *b*, and let it produce *f*. Finally, let *f* be multiplied into *a*, and let *g* be produced, which I say is the number we seek. For since *g* is produced from *a* and *f*, then according to Proposition 17, *f* will be a part of *g* denominated by *a* <note>In this context, being "denominated by *a*" means that *f* is the 1/*a* part of *g*. For example, if *a* is 3, *f* is one-third of *g*.</note>. And because *f* is produced by the same rule from *b* and *e*, then *e* will be a part of *f* denominated by *b*. Furthermore, for this same reason, *d* will be a part of *e* denominated by *c*. And since unity <note>The number 1, which Euclid considers the indivisible building block of all numbers.</note> is a part of *d* denominated by *d* itself, it is clear that *g* has the parts as proposed. If, therefore, *g* were not the least such number, let there be a smaller one, *h*. Let *k* be its part denominated by *a*, and *l* its part denominated by *b*, and *m* its part denominated by *c*, and *n* also its part denominated by *d*. It follows by Proposition 18 that *g* is to *f* as *h* is to *k*; and *f* is to *e* as *k* is to *l*; and *e* is to *d* as *l* is to *m*. But also *d* is to unity as *m* is to *n*. Therefore, by Proposition 15 <note>Regarding equal proportions in a series.</note>, in a proportion of equality, *g* will be to unity as *h* is to *n*. Alternately, then, *g* will be to *h* as unity is to *n*. Thus, since *h* is less than *g*, it follows that *n* must be less than unity. This leads to an impossibility, for a part of a number cannot be less than unity <note>In ancient Greek mathematics, 1 is the smallest possible unit; there are no "fractions of 1" in the sense of modern decimals within this discrete number system.</note>. Therefore, *g* is the least number having the parts as proposed. Having found this, if one desires to have the second-least or any subsequent numbers, they must be taken from the multiples of this least number, as was said before. # ¶ Given any number of parts: to find the least number containing them.

<margin>
<note>A diagram below the first one in the right margin. It shows two long horizontal line segments at the top labeled 'h' and 'g'. Below these are two columns of three shorter segments each: segments 'a', 'b', and 'c' on the left, and segments 'd', 'e', and 'f' on the right.</note>
</margin>

¶ **A**s if the proposed parts were *a, b, c*, and let those naming them <note>The "denominators."</note> be *d, e, f*. Let the least number which *d, e, f* measure <note>The Least Common Multiple (LCM).</note> be taken, which is *g*. I say this is the number we seek, for the proposed parts will be in it by Proposition 37. If this were not the least number containing them, let it be *b* <note>The letter 'b' here is used as a generic variable for a hypothetical smaller number.</note>, which *d, e, f* will measure by Proposition 38. Therefore, *g* would not be the least number measured by them, which is a contradiction, because it was stated to be so. 

However, I understand that the parts *a, b, c* are set down indefinitely and not as specific quantities; otherwise, it would not be necessary for the least number measured by *d, e, f* to be the least number containing the proposed parts. For it happens that many parts may be found which a number measured by their denominators does not contain. For example: three numbers which are 120, 90, and 72 are parts of the same number; the first is a third, the second a fourth, and the third a fifth <note>120 is 1/3 of 360, 90 is 1/4 of 360, and 72 is 1/5 of 360.</note>. Yet the least number measured by the denominators (which is 60) <note>The LCM of 3, 4, and 5 is 60.</note> does not contain these parts <note>Because 60 is smaller than 120, 90, and 72.</note>. 

Therefore, one must insist, if the parts are set down as certain quantities, on the first logical consequence of this demonstration: for it does not follow as argued by Proposition 37 that "if three measures this number, then this number is its third part." Rather, it follows that it "has a third part." Therefore, the proposition is the same in either case, but the first way seems more suitable to what is intended. One should note that since every part has a quantity in that which it is placed, it is possible to set down any number of parts according to quantity, and ask what is the least number that contains them and under what denominations. 
¶ It is established that the least number containing them is the least number measured by them <note>The LCM of the quantities.</note>; those which measure it are those which name the parts in that number. Conversely, one may set down any number of denominations and ask in what least number these denominations are found and according to what quantities. 
¶ It is also established that the least such number is the least number measured by those denominations; those which measure it are those which determine the quantities. In both cases, the "least" is sought because there are infinite numbers which contain these parts, or in which these denominations are found. One might also set down any number of parts and the same number of denominations, or vice versa—but not just any part with any denomination; rather, specific ones with specific ones. For if I set down the parts three, four, and five, and their denominations as 6, 7, and 8, and I ask what number contains these parts under those denominations, I would be a vain seeker of the impossible <note>Because 3 is not 1/6 of any integer that also has 4 as 1/7 and 5 as 1/8.</note>. Therefore, it is appropriate to set down specific parts with specific denominations, and not just by chance, to find what number contains the proposed parts under the proposed denominations. This is not about finding "which" least number, for there is only one; whether one part and one denomination are proposed, or many of each.

<b>

There is also only one whose third is an eighth, and whose sixth is a fourth: no more. Therefore, when proposing parts and their denominations within a whole, one should not ask which *smallest* number contains these parts under those denominations, but rather which *single* number contains them. However, when proposing parts only, it is appropriate to ask which smallest number contains them and by which numbers they are denominated in it. Likewise, when proposing only denominations, it is appropriate to ask which parts are designated by them and in what smallest number they are found. It seems more convenient to inquire after parts through denominations than denominations through parts; for the diversity of proportions accompanies the diversity of denominations, not of parts. **The seventh book ends; the eighth book begins.**

**Sides** <note>term: *latera* — the factors of a number, visualized as the sides of a geometric shape</note> of numbers are said to be those by whose multiplication numbers are produced. ¶ A **surface** <note>term: *superficies* — a "plane number," or the product of two factors, like an area</note> is called a number which is contained by two sides. ¶ A **solid**, however, is that which is contained under three [sides], having been produced from their continuous multiplication. ¶ A **square** is a surface number consisting of equal sides. ¶ A **cube** is a solid consisting of equal sides. ¶ **Similar** surface or solid numbers are said to be those whose sides are proportional.

## ¶ Proposition 1.

If any number of continuously proportional numbers have their two extremes prime to one another <note>Numbers that share no common divisor except for 1.</note>, it is necessary that they all be the least in their proportion.
¶ Let *a*, *b*, and *c* be continuously proportional, and let the two extremes, which are *a* and *c*, be prime to each other. I say that in the same proportion, an equal number of smaller ones will not be found. But if it should happen, let them be *d*, *e*, and *f*. By Proposition 15 of Book VII, *a* will be to *c* as *d* is to *f*. And because *a* and *c* are the least in their proportion by Proposition 23 of the same book, it follows by Proposition 21 that *a* measures *d* and *c* measures *f*; that is, larger numbers measure smaller ones, which is impossible.

## ¶ Proposition 2.

To find any number of continuously proportional numbers in a given proportion that are the least. From which it will be manifest: that if there are three numbers of continuous proportionality that are the least, the two extremes will be squares; and if there are four, the extremes will be cubes.
¶ Let *a* and *b* be the least in the given proportion. Let *a* be multiplied by itself to produce *c*, and by *b* to produce *d*. Also, let *b* be multiplied by itself, and let *e* result. Then *c*, *d*, and *e* will be continuously proportional in the proportion of *a* to *b* by Propositions 18 and 19 of Book VII. And because *c* and *e* are prime to each other by Proposition 28 of the same book, *c*, *d*, and *e* will be the least in the given proportion by the preceding proposition. Again, let *a* be multiplied into all of those, and let *f*, *g*, and *h* result; and let *b* be multiplied into *e*, and let *k* result. Then *f*, *g*, *h*, and *k* will also be continuously proportional in the proportion of *a* to *b* by Propositions 18 and 19 of Book VII. They will also be the least by Proposition 28 of the same book and the preceding proposition. In this way and by this method, find 5 or 6 or any number.

If any number of continuously proportional numbers are the least in their proportion, it is necessarily proved that their two extremes are prime to one another.
¶ This third proposition is the converse of the first. For let *a*, *b*, *c*, and *d* be continuously proportional...

## ¶ Proposition 4

To find continued proportionals in the smallest numbers according to the similarity of assigned proportions.

¶ Let the assigned proportions in their smallest terms be found as taught in Book VII, Proposition 34. Let the first be between **.a.** and **.b.**, the second between **.c.** and **.d.**, the third between **.e.** and **.f.**, and let there be more if there were more. I wish to continue these proportions in four smallest numbers. I take, therefore, **.g.** as the smallest number which **.b.** and **.c.** both measure <note>term: *numerat* — "measures" or divides evenly into. Here, .g. is the Least Common Multiple (LCM) of .b. and .c.</note>. As many times as **.b.** measures **.g.**, let **.a.** measure **.h.** Likewise, as many times as **.c.** measures **.g.**, let **.d.** measure **.k.** If **.e.** measures **.k.**, let **.f.** measure **.l.** just as many times. Then **.h.g.k.l.** will be those we seek. For it is established by Book VII, Proposition 18, that **.h.** is to **.g.** as **.a.** is to **.b.**, and **.g.** is to **.k.** as **.c.** is to **.d.**, and **.k.** is to **.l.** as **.e.** is to **.f.** 

¶ They are also the smallest; for if others were the smallest, such as **.m.n.p.q.**, it would be necessary by Book VII, Proposition 21 (applied twice) that both **.b.** and **.c.** measure **.p.**, wherefore **.g.** would measure the same. By the corollary of Book VII, Proposition 35, this is impossible <note>Because .g. was defined as the least common multiple.</note>. Therefore, **.h.g.k.l.** are the smallest. 

But if **.e.** does not measure **.k.**, let **.m.** be the smallest number measured by them, namely **.e.** and **.k.** As many times as **.m.** measures **.k.**, let **.n.** measure **.h.** and **.p.** measure **.g.** By Book VII, Proposition 18, **.n.p.m.** will be in the proportion of **.h.g.k.** Therefore, **.n.** is to **.p.** as **.a.** is to **.b.**, and **.p.** is to **.m.** as **.c.** is to **.d.** But as many times as **.e.** measures **.m.**, let **.f.** measure **.q.**, and by the same rule **.m.** will be to **.q.** as **.e.** is to **.f.** 

¶ It is manifest, therefore, that the assigned proportions have been continued in the four numbers **.n.p.m.q.** If these are not the smallest, let there be others if possible, **.r.s.t.x.** Since by Book VII, Proposition 21 (applied twice) both numbers **.b.** and **.c.** measure **.s.**, it follows by the corollary of Book VII, Proposition 35 that **.g.** measures the same; wherefore also **.k.** will measure **.t.** And because by Book VII, Proposition 21, **.e.** measures that same **.t.**, **.m.** would not be the smallest number that **.k.** and **.e.** measure. By this reasoning, you will be able to continue a fourth proportion and as many others as you like without any hindrance.

## ¶ Proposition 5

The proportion of any two composite numbers to one another is produced from the proportions of their sides.

¶ What Proposition 24 of Book VI <note>original: "24. sexti"</note> proposes concerning the surfaces of parallelograms, this proposes here concerning composite numbers <note>term: *numeris compositis* — numbers that have factors (sides), i.e., non-prime numbers</note>. Let there be two composite numbers **.a.** and **.b.** Let the sides of **.a.** be **.c.** and **.d.**, and let the sides of **.b.** be **.e.** and **.f.** I say, therefore, that the proportion of **.a.** to **.b.** consists of the proportion of **.c.** to **.e.** and that of **.d.** to **.f.** For let **.g.** be produced from **.d.** multiplied by **.e.** Since **.a.** is from **.d.** times **.c.**, and **.b.** is from **.f.** times **.e.**, by the conversion of the definition of sides it will be (by Book VII, Proposition 18) that **.a.** is to **.g.** as **.c.** is to **.e.**, and (by Proposition 19 of the same book) **.g.** is to **.b.** as **.d.** is to **.f.** Therefore, by definition, the proportion of **.a.** to **.b.** is composed <note>term: *composita* — a "compounded ratio," which in modern terms is the product of two ratios</note> of the proportion of **.c.** to **.e.** and that of **.d.** to **.f.**; which is what was proposed. 

Nor is it necessary that we continue the proportions of the sides—namely that of **.c.** to **.e.** and that of **.d.** to **.f.**—into the smallest numbers found according to the doctrine of the preceding proposition, as some teach; for this is more than is necessary for the proposal. For they argue, having posited that those smallest numbers are **.h.k.l.** such that **.h.** is to **.k.** as **.c.** is to **.e.** and **.k.** is to **.l.** as **.d.** is to **.f.**, that the proportion of **.h.** to **.l.** is composed of the proportions of the proposed sides. And having taken **.g.** to be made from **.d.** and **.c.**, they argue **.a.** to **.g.**...

## Proposition 6

If, among any number of continued proportionals <note>A series of numbers where the ratio between each consecutive pair is the same, such as 2, 4, 8, 16.</note>, the first does not measure the second, then none of them will measure the last.

¶ Let **a, b, c, d,** and **e** be continued proportionals. I say that if **a** does not measure <note>original: "numeret" — in Euclidean arithmetic, to "measure" or "number" a value means to divide into it exactly without a remainder.</note> **b**, then none of them will measure **e**. ¶ It is evident that if the first did measure the second, then all would measure **e**; simply put, every preceding term would measure every following term. If, however, it does not measure it, it is clear that **d** will not measure **e**, nor will any of them measure the term immediately following it, because they are placed as continued proportionals. But it is also established that no other term, such as **c**, measures **e** in the following way: let there be taken, according to the teaching of the second proposition of this book, as many smallest continued proportionals in the same proportion as there are terms starting from **c** and all those following it, which are **f, g,** and **h**. By the 3rd proposition of this book, **f** and **h** will be prime to each other <note>meaning they share no common divisor other than 1.</note>. By equal proportion, **c** is to **e** as **f** is to **h**. Since **f** does not measure **h**, then **c** cannot measure **e**. In the same way, none of the others will measure it; therefore, what was proposed is clear.

## Proposition 7

If, among numbers in continued proportion, the first measures the last, then that same first term will also measure the second.

¶ Let there be continued proportionals as before. I say that if **a** measures **e**, then it will also measure **b**. Otherwise, by the previous proposition, it would not measure **e**, which is contrary to the premise and impossible. Not only will it measure **b**, but also all the other terms, and each of them will measure every term following it.

## Proposition 8

<note>Three parallel vertical stacks of horizontal line segments used to visualize the relationship between different sets of proportional numbers. The first stack is labeled **a, c, d, b**. The second stack is labeled **g, h, k, l**. The third stack is labeled **e, m, n, f**.</note>

If any number of terms fall in continued proportion between two numbers, then the same number of terms must necessarily fall between any other two numbers related in the same ratio.

¶ Let **a** and **b** be two numbers between which fall **c** and **d** in continued proportion, having the same ratio as **e** to **f**. I say that just as many terms fall between **e** and **f** in the same proportion as fall between **a** and **b**. For let **g, h, k,** and **l** be as many smallest numbers as there are in the sequence of **a** and **b** and those falling between them. As the second proposition of this book teaches, let these be continued proportionals in the same ratio. By the 3rd proposition, **g** and **l** will be prime to each other, and by equal proportion, **g** is to **l** as **a** is to **b**, and therefore as **e** is to **f**. And because these are the smallest numbers in their ratio (by Book VII, Proposition 23), it follows (by Book VII, Proposition 21) that **g** measures **e** and **l** measures **f** the same number of times. Let it therefore measure **h** into **m** and **k** into **n** the same number of times. With **m** and **n** placed between **e** and **f**, it is established (by Book VII, Proposition 18) that **e, m, n,** and **f** are continued proportionals, just as **g, h, k,** and **l** are, and therefore just as **a, c, d,** and **b** are. Thus, what was stated is clear. 

From this, it is established that no <term>superparticular ratio</term> <note>original: "superticularem" — a ratio where the larger number contains the smaller number plus exactly one part of it, such as 3:2 (1 + 1/2) or 9:8 (1 + 1/8).</note> can be divided into equal parts. If this were possible, it would require a middle number to fall between two numbers that differ only by a single unit, which is impossible. Therefore, the **tone** in music—which consists of the <term>sesquioctave</term> proportion (the 9:8 ratio)—cannot be divided into two equal **semitones**; it is necessarily divided into a minor semitone and a major semitone.
