## Proposition 10.

If between two numbers and unity there should fall any
number of continued proportionals, it is necessary that
between those two numbers there be as many terms
in continued proportionality.
¶ Let there be two numbers **a** and **b**, and let **c** and **d** be continued proportionals between **a** and unity, and let **e** and **f** be continued proportionals between **b** and unity. I say that there are as many continued proportionals between **a** and **b**. This is the converse of the prior [proposition], except that in the previous one it was assumed that **a** and **b** were prime <note>Prime to one another, meaning they share no common divisor other than 1.</note>, which is not required here; for this reason, this proposition is more general than the previous one. Because, therefore, as many times as unity is in **d**, so many times is **d** in **c**, and **c** in **a**, it is established that **c** is produced from **d** squared <note>original: "ex d. in se fit c." — literally "from d into itself comes c."</note>, and **a** is produced from **d** multiplied by **c**. Similarly, **e** and **b** are produced from **f** squared and from **f** multiplied by **e**. Let **d** be multiplied by **f**, and let the product be **g**. Then let the same **d** be multiplied by **g** and **e**, and let the products be **h** and **k**. It is established from the 18th [proposition] of the seventh [book] that **c** is to **g** as **d** is to **f**; and from the 19th [proposition], **g** is to **e** as **d** is to **f**. Therefore, **c, g,** and **e** are continued proportionals in the ratio of **d** to **f**. Furthermore, by the 18th [proposition] again, **a** is to **h** as **c** is to **g**, and **h** is to **k** as **g** is to **e**. And by the 19th [proposition], **k** is to **b** as **d** is to **f**. Therefore, **a, h, k,** and **b** are continued proportionals; thus, what was proposed is established.

</margin>

## Proposition 11.

If both numbers are squares, the ratio of one to the other
will be as the duplicate ratio of its side to the side of the other.
If, however, both are cubes: the ratio of one to the other
will be as the triplicate ratio of its side to the side of the other.
¶ Let there be two squares **a** and **b**, and two cubes **c** and **d**. Let the sides <note>term: "latus" (plural "latera") — In Euclidean geometry, the "side" of a square or cube is equivalent to what we now call the square root or cube root.</note> of the squares and cubes be **e** (for **a** and **c**) and **f** (for **b** and **d**). I say that the ratio <note>original: "proportio"</note> of **a** to **b** will be as the duplicate ratio <note>term: "proportio duplicata" — This is the ratio of the squares of the terms. If the ratio of the sides is x:y, the duplicate ratio is x²:y².</note> of **e** to **f**, and that of **c** to **d** will be as the triplicate ratio <note>term: "proportio triplicata" — The ratio of the cubes of the terms, or (x:y)³.</note> of the same. ¶ For it is clear that **a** is produced from **e** multiplied by itself, and **c** is produced from the same **e** multiplied by **a**. Similarly, **b** is produced from **f** multiplied by itself, and **d** from the same **f** multiplied by **b**. Therefore, let **e** be multiplied by **f**, and let the product be **g**; then let **e** be multiplied by **g** and **b**, and let the products be **h** and **k**. By the 18th [proposition] of the seventh [book], **a** is to **g** as **e** is to **f**, and by the 19th, **g** is to **b** as **e** is to **f**. Therefore, by definition, **a** is to **b** as the duplicate ratio of **e** to **f**, which is the first [part]. The second [part] is established in the same way. For by the 18th, **c** is to **h** as **a** is to **g**, and **h** is to **k** as **g** is to **b**. By the 19th, **k** is to **d** as **e** is to **f**. Therefore, **c, h, k,** and **d** are also continued proportionals in the ratio of **e** to **f**. By the definition, therefore, **c** will be to **d** as the triplicate ratio of **e** to **f**, which is the second [part].

## Proposition 12.

If each of a series of continued proportional numbers is
multiplied by itself: those produced therefrom will also be in
continued proportionality. And if those products are again
multiplied by their original values: those produced therefrom
must also be in continued proportionality; and this remains
true for all subsequent terms produced in this manner.

<note>A diagram consisting of two vertical columns of horizontal line segments of varying lengths. The left column is labeled from top to bottom: g, n, p, h, q, r, k. The right column is labeled: o, l, a, e, b, m, c, f.</note>
</margin>

¶ Let **a, b,** and **c** be continued proportionals, and let each be multiplied by itself to produce **d** from **a**, **e** from **b**, and **f** from **c**. I say that **d, e,** and **f** are also continued proportionals. Furthermore, if **a** is multiplied by **d** to produce **g**, and **b** is multiplied by **e** to produce **h**, and **c** is multiplied by **f** to produce **k**, I say that **g, h,** and **k** will also be continued proportionals. For let **l** be produced from **a** multiplied by **b**, and let **m** be produced from **c** multiplied by the same [**b**]. By the 18th and 19th [propositions] of the Seventh Book, **d, l, e, m,** and **f** will be continued proportionals in the ratio of **a, b,** and **c**. Therefore, by equality of proportion <note>original: "per equam proportionalitatem" — a logical step where if a:b = d:e and b:c = e:f, then a:c = d:f.</note>, it is argued that **d** is to **e** as **e** is to **f**, which is the first [part to be proven]. 

The remainder is proven thus: let **a** be multiplied by **l** and **e** to produce **n** and **p**; also let **c** be multiplied by **e** and **m** to produce **q** and **r**. By the same [propositions], **g, n, p, h, q, r,** and **k** will also be continued proportionals in the ratio of the first [terms]. Therefore, by equality of proportion, conclude that **g** is to **h** as **h** is to **k**, which is the remainder. The same reasoning will hold as many times as the first numbers are multiplied into the products <note>This implies the rule extends to fourth powers, fifth powers, and so on.</note>.

## Proposition 13

<margin>
<note>A diagram with two groups of horizontal line segments. On the left, a stack of three segments labeled a, e, b. On the right, a stack of two segments labeled c, d.</note>
</margin>

If any square number measures <note>In Euclidean geometry, to "measure" (numerare) means to divide exactly without a remainder.</note> another square number, it is proved that its side also measures the side of that other number. If, however, its side measures the side of the other, the square measures the square.

¶ Let there be two square numbers, **a** and **b**, and their sides **c** and **d**. I say that if **a** measures **b**, then **c** will also measure **d**, and vice versa. It is established that from **c** [multiplied] by itself comes **a**, and from **d** [multiplied] by itself comes **b**. Let **e** be produced from **c** multiplied by **d**. By the 18th and 19th [propositions] of the Seventh Book, **a, e,** and **b** will be continued proportionals in the ratio of **c** to **d**. If, therefore, **a** measures **b**, the same **a** will measure **e** by the 7th [proposition] of this book <note>If the first of three continued proportionals measures the third, it also measures the second.</note>. Therefore, **c** measures **d**, which is the first [part]. The converse is thus evident: if **c** measures **d**, then **a** will measure **e**, because the ratio of **a** to **e** is as **c** to **d**. And if it measures **e**, it will also measure **b**, because they are continued proportionals.

## Proposition 14

<margin>
<note>A diagram with three groups of horizontal line segments. On the left, four segments labeled a, h, k, b. In the middle, three segments labeled e, g, f. On the right, two segments labeled l, i.</note>
</margin>

If a cube measures another cube, its side will also measure the side of the other. If, however, its side measures the side of the other, the cube will measure the cube.

¶ Let there be two cube numbers, **a** and **b**, and their sides **c** and **d**. I say that if **a** measures **b**, **c** will also measure **d**, and vice versa. For let **c** be multiplied by itself to produce **e**, and **d** by itself to produce **f**. It is established that from **c** multiplied by **e** comes **a**, and from **d** multiplied by **f** comes **b**. Let **g** be produced from **c** multiplied by **d**. By the 18th and 19th [propositions] of the Seventh Book, **e, g,** and **f** will be continued proportionals in the ratio of **c** to **d**. But let **h** and **k** be produced from **c** multiplied by **g** and **f**. By the same [propositions], **a, h, k,** and **b** will also be continued proportionals in the same ratio. Therefore, if **a** measures **b**, it will also measure **h** by the 7th [proposition] of this book. Consequently, **c** measures **d**, for **c** is to **d** as **a** is to **h**. Thus the first part is established. The converse is evident, just like the converse of the previous [proposition]. For if **c** measures **d**, then **a** will also measure **b**, and if it measures that, it must necessarily measure **h**.

## Proposition 15

<margin>
<note>A simple diagram with two groups of segments. On the left, two segments labeled a and b. On the right, two segments labeled c and d.</note>
</margin>

If a square number does not measure another square number, neither will its side measure the side of that other. If, however, its side does not measure the side of the other, that square is necessarily proved not to measure that other square.

¶ This 15th [proposition] proposes that the negations are converted, which are opposed to the affirmations that the 13th [proposition] of this book proposed to be converted. As, for example, if there are two square numbers **a** and **b**, whose sides are **c** and **d**: if **a** does not measure **b**, then **c** will also not measure **d**. Conversely, if **c** does not measure **d**, then **a** does not measure **b**. First, let it be that **a** does not measure **b**. If, then, **c** measures **d**, by the second part of the 13th [proposition] of this book, **a** would measure **b**, which is contrary to the position; thus the first [part] is clear. The second part is also clear: let it be that **c** does not measure **d**. If, then, **a** measures **b**...

VIII

...by the first part of Proposition 13, it is necessary that **c** measures **d**. It is therefore necessary that **b** measures it, even though it does not measure it—which is impossible. Moreover, just as it is necessary for the negative statements opposite to the affirmations proved in Proposition 13 to be convertible, so too must the negative statements opposite to those affirmations proved by the previous proposition be convertible. Hence, if a cube does not measure a cube, neither will its side measure the other's side. Conversely, if the side of one does not measure the side of the other, neither will the cube itself measure the other cube. This is demonstrated by the previous proposition through the "destruction of the consequent" <note>original: "a destructione prosequentis" — a logical method also known as Modus Tollens: if the effect is absent, the cause must also be absent.</note>, just as was proposed in Proposition 13. Therefore, the author [Euclid] did not explicitly state this as a proposition, but allowed it to be understood through what he did propose.

## Proposition 16.

<margin>
<note>A geometric diagram consists of two vertical stacks of horizontal line segments. The left stack contains three segments labeled **a, g, b** from top to bottom. The right stack contains four segments labeled **c, d, e, f** from top to bottom.</note>
</margin>
IF two plane numbers <term>plane numbers: numbers that can be represented as the product of two factors, visualized as the area of a rectangle</term> are similar, it is necessary that one middle number falls between them in continued proportion; and the ratio of one number to its similar counterpart is the duplicate ratio <note>original: "proportio duplicata" — the square of the ratio. For example, if the sides are in a 2:3 ratio, the plane numbers are in a 4:9 ratio.</note> of the ratio of one of its sides to the corresponding side of the other.
¶ Let **a** and **b** be two similar plane numbers. I say that one number falls between them in continued proportion. For let the sides of **a** be **c** and **d**, and let the sides of **b** be **e** and **f**. By the definition of similar numbers, **c** is to **e** as **d** is to **f**. It is established that **a** is produced from **c** times **d**, and **b** is produced from **e** times **f**. Now, let **g** be produced from **e** multiplied by **d**. By the 19th proposition of the Seventh Book, **a** is to **g** as **c** is to **e**; and by the 18th proposition of the same book, **g** is to **b** as **d** is to **f**. Therefore, **a** is to **g** as **g** is to **b**. Thus, **g** is the middle term between **a** and **b** in continued proportion, which is what was proposed. The conclusion is evident: since **a** is to **b** (by definition) as the duplicate ratio of **a** to **g**, which is the same ratio as **c** to **e**.

## Proposition 17.

<margin>
<note>A geometric diagram consists of two vertical stacks of horizontal line segments. The left stack contains three segments labeled **a, c, b**. The right stack contains four segments labeled **d, f, e, g**.</note>
</margin>
IF one middle number falls between two numbers in continued proportion, those two numbers are similar plane numbers.
¶ This is the converse of the previous proposition: if **c** is placed between **a** and **b** in continued proportion, then **a** and **b** will be similar plane numbers. For let **d** and **e** be the smallest numbers in the ratio by which **a, c,** and **b** are continued. By the 21st proposition of the Seventh Book, these will measure <note>original: "numerabunt" — in ancient mathematics, one number "measuring" another means it is a divisor or factor.</note> **a** and **c** equally; let this be according to factor **f**. By the same logic, they will measure **c** and **b** equally; let this be according to factor **g**. Therefore, by definition, **a** and **b** are plane numbers; and by definition, **d** and **f** are the sides of number **a**, while **e** and **g** are the sides of number **b**. How they are similar is shown as follows: since **d** multiplied by **g** produces **c**, and **e** multiplied by **f** produces the same **c**, then by the second part of the 20th proposition of the Seventh Book, **d** is to **e** as **f** is to **g**. Therefore, by definition, **a** and **b** are similar, which is what was proposed. This last point—that **a** and **b** are similar—can also be obtained through the 19th and 18th of the Seventh Book and from these hypotheses: that **a, c,** and **b** are continued proportionals in the ratio of **d** to **e** (the smallest numbers measuring **a** and **c** according to factor **f**, and **c** and **b** according to factor **g**).

## Proposition 18.

IF two solid numbers <term>solid numbers: numbers represented as the product of three factors, visualized as the volume of a solid body</term> are similar, it is necessary that two middle numbers fall between them in continued proportion; and the ratio of one solid to its similar counterpart is the triplicate ratio <note>original: "proportio triplicata" — the cube of the ratio. If the sides are in a 2:3 ratio, the solid volumes are in a 8:27 ratio.</note> of the ratio of any of its sides to the corresponding side of the other.
¶ Let **a** and **b** be similar solid numbers. I say that two numbers fall between them in continued proportion. For let the sides of number **a** be **c, d,** and **e**, and let the sides of **b** be **f, g,** and **h**. By the definition of similar numbers, **c** is to **f** and **d** is to **g** as **e** is to **h**. Thus, let **k** be produced from **c** multiplied by **d**, and let **l** be produced from **f** multiplied by **g**. By definition, **k** and **l** are similar plane numbers...

Therefore, by Proposition 16 of this book, one number will fall as a mean between them according to the proportion of **c** to **f**, which shall be **m**. It is evident that from **e** multiplied by **k**, **a** is produced; and from **g** multiplied by **l**, **b** is produced. If, therefore, from **e** multiplied by **m** and **l**, **n** and **p** are produced, then by Proposition 18 of the Seventh Book, **a** is to **n** as **k** is to **m**, and **n** is to **p** as **m** is to **l**. Therefore, **a**, **n**, and **p** are in continued proportion in the ratio of **c** to **f**. And because by Proposition 19 of the same book, **p** is to **b** as **c** is to **f**, it follows that the four numbers **a**, **n**, **p**, and **b** are in continued proportion according to the ratio of **c** to **f**. Thus, between **a** and **b**, two mean numbers **n** and **p** are placed in continued proportionality between their sides; which is what was proposed. The corollary <note>original: "Consec'.", abbreviation for *consectarium*</note> is evident, since the proportion of **a** to **b** is, by definition, the triplicate ratio of **a** to **n**, which is the same as that of **c** to **l**.

## Proposition 19

<margin>
<note>A diagram with letters and numbers representing line segments.
Top row of segments: **a** (12), **c** (18), **d** (18), **b** (27)
Second row: **e** (4), **f** (6), **g** (9)
Third row (below **e**): **h** (2), **k** (2), **n** (2)
Fourth row (below **f**): **l** (3), **m** (3), **p** (3)
The diagram visualizes the factors of similar solid numbers.</note>
</margin>
If two mean numbers lie between two numbers in continued proportionality, those two numbers are solid and similar.
¶ This is the converse of the preceding proposition. If between **a** and **b** there are two mean numbers **c** and **d** in continued proportion, then **a** and **b** will be <term>solid numbers: numbers resulting from the product of three factors, visualized as a 3D volume</term> and similar. For let the three smallest numbers in the same proportion be taken, which are **e**, **f**, and **g**; by Proposition 17, **e** and **g** will be <term>plane numbers: numbers resulting from the product of two factors</term> and similar. Therefore, let **h** and **k** be the sides of **e**, and **l** and **m** be the sides of **g**. By the corollary of Proposition 16 of this book, **e** is to **f** as **h** is to **l**, or as **k** is to **m**. It is manifest from the third [book] that **e** and **g** are prime to one another, and therefore by Proposition 23 of the Seventh Book, they are the smallest in their proportion. And because by equal proportionality, **a** is to **d** and **c** is to **b** as **e** is to **g**, it follows by Proposition 21 of the Seventh Book that they measure **a** and **d** equally, which we shall call **n**; and likewise **c** and **b** equally, which we shall call **p**. Therefore, because **e** is produced from **h** times **k**, and **a** is produced from **e** times **n**, it follows by definition that **a** is a solid number and its sides are **h**, **k**, and **n**. Similarly, because **g** is produced from **l** times **m**, and **b** is produced from **g** times **p**, it follows also that **b** is a solid and its sides are **l**, **m**, and **p**. That they are similar will be established thus: since from **g** times **n**, **d** is produced, and from the same [**g**] times **p**, **b** is produced, then by Proposition 18 of the Seventh Book, **n** is to **p** as **d** is to **b**. And since **h** was to **l** and **k** was to **m** in that ratio, it is manifest by definition that **a** and **b** are similar; which is what was proposed.

## Proposition 20.

<margin>
<note>Three horizontal line segments labeled **a**, **b**, and **c** representing a continued proportion.</note>
</margin>
If of three numbers in continued proportion the first is a square, the third must also be a square.
¶ Let there be three numbers in continued proportion, **a**, **b**, and **c**, and let **a** be a square. I say that **c** is also a square. For by Proposition 17, **a** and **c** are similar plane numbers. Therefore, since **a** is a square by hypothesis, **c** will also be a square <note>A square is simply a similar plane number whose sides are equal; if one of two similar plane numbers is square, its ratio of sides is 1:1, meaning the other must also have a 1:1 side ratio.</note>.

## Proposition 21

<margin>
<note>Four horizontal line segments labeled **a**, **b**, **c**, and **d** representing a sequence in continued proportion.</note>
</margin>
If of four numbers in continued proportion the first is a cube, it is necessary that the fourth be a cube.
¶ Let there be four numbers in continued proportion, **a**, **b**, **c**, and **d**, and let **a** be a cube. I say that **d** is also a cube. For it is established by Proposition 19 that **a** and **d** are similar solids. And since **a** is a cube by hypothesis, **d** will also be a cube.

## Proposition 22.

<margin>
<note>Four horizontal line segments arranged in two pairs: **a** above **b** on the left, and **c** above **d** on the right.</note>
</margin>
If the ratio of two numbers is as the ratio of a square to a square, and one of them is a square, the other must also be a square.
¶ Let there be two numbers **a** and **b** in the proportion of two squares, which are **c** and **d**. Let either **a** or **b** be a square. I say the remaining one is a square. For since **c** and **d** are squares, it follows that they are similar plane numbers. Therefore, by Proposition 16, one mean number falls between them in continued proportion. Wherefore, by Proposition 8 [of this book] and between **a** and **b** by Proposition 20, the proposition is established.

## Proposition 23.

<header>IX</header>
<page-num>IX</page-num>

<margin>
<note>A diagram consisting of two vertical stacks of horizontal line segments. On the left, segments are labeled **a** and **b**. On the right, segments are labeled **c** and **d**. These represent the numerical values being compared in the proof.</note>
</margin>
If two numbers have a ratio to one another that is as a cube to a cube, and one of them is a cube, then the other must also be a cube.
¶ Let there be two numbers, **a** and **b**, in the ratio of two cubes, which are **c** and **d**; and let **a** (or **b**) be a cube. I say that the remaining number is also a cube. For it is necessary that **c** and **d** are similar solid numbers <note>original: "solidi similes"; in Euclidean arithmetic, numbers are "similar solids" if their sides are proportional</note>, since all cubes are similar and solid. Therefore, by Proposition 18 <note>of Book VIII</note>, two mean numbers in continued proportion fall between them; just as many, therefore, by Proposition 8, will fall between **a** and **b**. Thus, by Proposition 21, it is manifest what was stated.

## Proposition 24

<margin>
<note>A diagram consisting of two vertical stacks of horizontal line segments. The left stack contains segments **a**, **c**, and **b**. The right stack contains **d**, **e**, and **f**. These segments represent the terms of the continued proportions used in the proof.</note>
</margin>
The ratio of similar plane <note>original: "superficialium"; numbers that are the product of two sides</note> numbers to one another is as the ratio of a square to a square.
¶ Let **a** and **b** be similar plane numbers. I say that the ratio of one to the other is as the ratio of a square to a square. For by Proposition 16, there will be one mean proportional number between them, which shall be **c**. Taking, therefore, the three least numbers in their proportion, which are **d**, **e**, and **f**, they will be squares by the corollary of Proposition 2. And because by equal proportionality <note>original: "equam proportionalitatem"; the "ex aequali" rule</note>, **a** is to **b** as **d** is to **f**, it stands that what was proposed is true.

## Proposition 25

<margin>
<note>A diagram consisting of two vertical stacks of horizontal line segments. The left stack contains segments **a**, **c**, **d**, and **b**. The right stack contains **e**, **f**, **g**, and **h**. These represent the four terms in a continued proportion (two means between two extremes).</note>
</margin>
The ratio of any two similar solid numbers to one another is as the ratio of some cube to another cube.
¶ Let **a** and **b** be similar solid numbers. I say that the ratio of one of them to the other is as the ratio of some cube to some other cube. Indeed, by Proposition 18, there are two mean numbers between them according to continued proportion, which shall be **c** and **d**. Let there be four numbers in their proportion, **e**, **f**, **g**, and **h**, of which **e** and **h** will be cubes by the second corollary. Since, therefore, by equal proportionality, **a** is to **b** as **e** is to **h**, the proposition is clear.

An **even number** is that which can be divided into two equal parts. ¶ An **odd number** is that which cannot be divided into two equal parts, or which exceeds an even number by one unit. ¶ **Even-times even** <note>original: "Pariter par"</note> is a number which all even numbers measuring it do so by even times. ¶ **Even-times odd** <note>original: "Pariter impar"</note> is a number which all even numbers measuring it do so by odd times. ¶ **Even-times even and odd** <note>original: "Pariter par 7 impariter"</note> is a number which even numbers measure, some by even times and some by odd times. ¶ **Odd-times odd** is a number which all odd numbers measuring it do so by odd times. ¶ A **perfect number** is so called when it is equal to the sum of all its parts <note>its proper divisors</note>. ¶ A number is called **abundant** when it is less than the sum of all its parts. ¶ A number is called **deficient** <note>original: "Diminutus"</note> when it is greater than the sum of its parts.

## Proposition 1

<margin>
<note>A diagram of two pairs of horizontal line segments. The left pair consists of **a** and **d**, and the right pair consists of **b** and **c**. A faint baseline connects the lower segments, indicating a proportional relationship between these two sets of numbers.</note>
</margin>
If there are two similar plane numbers, the number produced from the multiplication of one by the other must necessarily be a square number.
¶ Let **a** and **b** be similar plane numbers, from the multiplication of which **c** is produced. I say that **c** is a square. For let **d** be produced from **a** multiplied by itself. Then, by Proposition 18 of the Seventh Book, **d** will be to **c** as **a** is to **b**. And because one mean falls between **a** and **b** according to continued proportionality by Proposition 17 of the Eighth Book, it follows by Proposition 8 of the same book that one mean also falls between **d** and **c**. Therefore, since **d** is a square, by Proposition 20 of the same book, **c** is also a square, which is what was proposed.

<header>BOOK IX</header>

## Proposition 2

<margin>
<note>Four horizontal line segments representing numbers are arranged in two columns and two rows. In the top row, the left segment is labeled **b** and the right is **a**. In the bottom row, the left is **c** and the right is **d**. These represent the proportional relationships between factors and their products.</note>
</margin>

If the product of two numbers is a square <note>original: "tetragonus"</note>, then those two numbers are similar plane numbers <note>original: "superficiales similes"; numbers are "similar plane" if their sides are proportional, like 2×3 and 4×6</note>. From this, the following is evident: that if a square is multiplied by a square, the product will be a square. If, however, the product of a square and some other number is a square, then that other number must also be a square. Likewise, if a square is multiplied by a number that is not a square, the product will not be a square. Finally, if a square is multiplied by a number that is not a square, it is necessary that the resulting product is not a square.
¶ This is the converse of the previous proposition: as if from **a** multiplied by **b** comes **c**, and **c** is a square, then **a** and **b** will be similar plane numbers. For let **d** be the product of **a** multiplied by itself; then by Proposition 18 of Book VII, the ratio of **d** to **c** is as the ratio of **a** to **b**. By Proposition 16 or 8 <note>of Book VIII</note>, since **d** and **c** are similar plane numbers (because they are both squares), there is one mean proportional number between them by Proposition 8. Therefore, there is also one mean proportional between **a** and **b**. Thus, by Proposition 17 of that same book, **a** and **b** are similar plane numbers, which is what was proposed. The first part of the conclusion is clear through the premise, for all squares are similar plane numbers. The second part is clear from this proposition, as only a square is similar to another square. The third part is clear from the first part of this conclusion by denying the consequent <note>a logical form where if the effect is missing, the cause must be too</note>. The fourth part follows from the second part by the same logical denial.

## Proposition 3

<margin>
<note>A vertical stack of line segments and notations: a long segment labeled **b**, a medium segment labeled **a**, a short segment marked with a line above it and the numeral **1** (representing unity) below it, a shorter segment labeled **c**, and the shortest labeled **d**.</note>
</margin>

If a cube number is multiplied by itself, the product will be a cube.
¶ Let **a** be a cube, which, when multiplied by itself, produces **b**. I say that **b** is a cube. For let **c** be the "cubic side" <note>original: "latus cubicum"; what we now call the cube root</note> of **a**. Let **d** be produced from **c** multiplied by itself. It is thus clear that **a** is produced from **c** multiplied by **d**. Therefore, unity <note>the number 1</note>, **c**, **d**, and **a** are in continued proportion, which is manifest from Proposition 18 of Book VII and the present hypotheses. Because the ratio of **a** to **b** is as the ratio of unity to **a** (since unity is in **a** as many times as **a** is in **b**), there will be two mean numbers in continued proportion between **a** and **b** by Proposition 8 of Book VIII. Since, by hypothesis, **a** is a cube, it follows by Proposition 21 of the same book that **b** is also a cube, which was to be demonstrated.

## Proposition 4

<margin>
<note>Four horizontal line segments arranged in two columns and two rows: **a** and **b** in the top row, and **d** and **c** in the bottom row.</note>
</margin>

If a cube is multiplied by another cube, the product will be a cube.
¶ Let **a** and **b** be cubes, and let **c** be produced from **a** multiplied by **b**. I say that **c** is a cube. For let **d** be produced from **a** multiplied by itself; by the preceding proposition, **d** is a cube. And since by Proposition 18 of Book VII the ratio of **a** to **b** is as the ratio of **d** to **c**, it is established by Proposition 23 of Book VIII that **c** is a cube, which is what was proposed.

## Proposition 5

<margin>
<note>Four horizontal line segments arranged in two columns and two rows: **b** and **a** in the top row, and **c** and **d** in the bottom row.</note>
</margin>

If a cube number is multiplied by another number, and the product is a cube, then the number it was multiplied by must necessarily be a cube. From this it is also manifest: that the product of a cube and a non-cube will be a non-cube. Furthermore, if a cube is multiplied by a number and the product is not a cube, it is necessary that the number it was multiplied by is not a cube.
¶ For let the product of the cube **a** and the number **b** be the cube **c**. I say that **b** is a cube. For let **d** be produced from **a** multiplied by itself, which by the proposition before the last <note>Proposition 3</note> will be a cube. Since, therefore, by Proposition 18 of Book VII, the ratio of **a** to **b** is as **d** to **c**, and **a** is a cube, as are **d** and **c**, it follows by Proposition 23 of Book VIII that **b** is a cube, which is the proposal. The first part of the conclusion is clear from this fifth proposition by denying the result; the second part follows similarly from the preceding proposition by the same logic.

## Proposition 6

<margin>
<note>The diagram shows three horizontal lines representing numerical values. Line **c** is the longest, followed by **b**, with **a** being the shortest, illustrating the factors and products discussed in the proof.</note>
</margin>

If a number multiplied by itself produces a cube <note>original: "cubus"; a number formed by multiplying a factor by itself three times, like 2 × 2 × 2 = 8</note>, then that initial number is necessarily proved to be a cube.
¶ Let it be that from **a** multiplied by itself comes **b**, and let **b** be a cube. I say, therefore, that **a** is also a cube. For let **c** be produced from **a** multiplied by **b**. By definition, **c** will be a cube <note>because a square **b** multiplied by its root **a** creates a cube</note>. Since it is established from Proposition 18 of Book VII that the ratio of **a** to **b** is the same as the ratio of **b** to **c**, and since **b** and **c** are both cubes, it follows from Proposition 23 of Book VIII that **a** must be a cube; which is what was to be proposed.

## Proposition 7

<margin>
<note>Two pairs of horizontal lines are shown. The top pair is labeled **a** and **b**, representing the numbers being multiplied. The bottom pair is labeled **d** and **e**, representing the component factors of the composite number.</note>
</margin>

If a composite number <note>original: "numerus compositus"; a number that can be divided by numbers other than 1 and itself</note> is multiplied by any other number, the resulting product will be a solid number <note>original: "solidus"; a number representing a three-dimensional volume, having three factors</note>.
¶ Let **a** be a composite number, which is multiplied by **b** to produce **c**. I say that **c** is a solid number. Since **a** is composite, it is measured by some number, let it be **d**. Let **d** measure **a** according to the units in **e** <note>meaning d × e = a</note>. Therefore, because **e** multiplied by **d** makes **a**, and **a** multiplied by **b** makes **c**, then by the definition of solid numbers, **c** is a solid whose sides are **e**, **d**, and **b**. This is what was to be proposed.

## Proposition 8

<margin>
<note>A complex diagram featuring a stack of thirteen horizontal lines of varying lengths, labeled from **n** at the top down to **a** and the numeral **1** (unity) at the bottom. Vertical dotted lines connect the endpoints of the segments to visualize the geometric progression and proportional relationships between the numbers.</note>
</margin>

If there are numbers in a continuous proportion starting from unity <note>original: "vnitas"; the number 1</note>: the third number from unity will be a square <note>original: "quadratus"</note>, and every second number thereafter (skipping one). The fourth from unity will be a cube, and every third number thereafter (skipping two). Furthermore, the seventh from unity is a square-cube <note>original: "quadratus cubicus"; a number that is both a square and a cube, such as 64 ($8^2$ and $4^3$)</note>, and every sixth number thereafter (skipping five) is also a square-cube.
¶ Let the numbers in continuous proportion be unity, **a, b, c, d, e, f, g, h, k, l, m, n**. I say that **b** is a square, and skipping **c**, **d** is a square, and so on, skipping one each time. Thus, simply put, all numbers in odd-numbered positions are squares, such as the third, fifth, and seventh. I also say that **c** is a cube, and skipping two, **f** is a cube, and so on. Simply put, every number is a cube if its position from unity is one more than three or any multiple of three—such as the fourth, seventh, tenth, and sixteenth positions; for in these positions, all those that skip two numbers are found. Furthermore, I say that **f**, being the seventh from unity, is a square-cube, and similarly **n**, with five numbers skipped in between, and so on. In simple terms, I say that any number whose position from unity is one more than six or any multiple of six—such as the seventh, thirteenth, nineteenth, and twenty-fifth—is a square-cube. It is a square because its position is odd, and it is a cube because its position is one more than a multiple of three (since all multiples of six are necessarily multiples of three). What has been proposed is established as follows: By hypothesis, unity is to **a** as **a** is to **b**; therefore **b** is a square by definition. Because **b, c, d** are in continuous proportion and **b** is a square, it is clear from Proposition 17 or 20 of Book VIII that **d** is also a square. By the same reasoning, **f** is a square, and because **d, e, f** are in continuous proportion and **d** is a square, the same applies to the others skipping one; thus the first part is proven. The second part follows because **b** is to **c** as **a** is to **b**; by definition, since **a** multiplied by its square **b** produces **c**, then **c** is a cube. And since **c, d, e, f** are in continuous proportion, as are **f, g, h, k**, and **c** is a cube, it is necessary by Proposition 19 or 21 of Book VIII that **f** and **k** are also cubes, and so on, skipping two. Finally, regarding **f** (the seventh), **n** (the thirteenth), and others skipping five: in all these positions, which are one more than a multiple of six, the calculations for squares and cubes coincide. By the first part, they are squares (skipping one), and by the second part, they are cubes (skipping two). Therefore, they are square-cubes. Thus, the whole of what was stated is established.

## Proposition 9.

If any number of numbers are arranged in a continuous proportion starting from unity, and the number following unity is a square <note>original: "quadratus"; a number produced by multiplying a value by itself, like 2 × 2 = 4</note>, then all the others will also be squares. If, however, the number following unity is a cube <note>original: "cubus"; a number produced by multiplying a value by itself twice, like 2 × 2 × 2 = 8</note>, all the others will also be cubes.
¶ Let there be numbers in continuous proportion starting from unity as before. Let **a** be a square; I say that all the following numbers are squares. Or, let the same **a** be a cube; then I also say all the others are cubes. It is established that **b** is a square through the preceding proposition <note>Proposition 8, which states that if 1, a, b are in proportion, and a is square, then b is square</note>. Because the ratio of **a** to **b** is the same as **b** to **c**, it follows from Proposition 27 of Book VIII that **c** is a square. You can also argue the same from Propositions 17 or 20 of the same book. Regarding the subsequent numbers, you shall prove them in the same way; thus the first part is evident.
The second part is shown as follows: since **b** is produced from **a** multiplied by itself, if **a** is a cube, then by Proposition 3, **b** will also be a cube. It is established that **c** is a cube by the preceding proposition. Thus, by Proposition 23 of Book VIII, you will prove that **d** and all following numbers are cubes; for the ratio of **g** to **b** is as **c** to **d**. You can also argue this from Propositions 19 or 21 of the same book, for **a, b, c, d**, and also **b, c, d, e**, and each set of four taken in succession, are in continuous proportion.

## Proposition 10.

If any number of numbers are arranged in continuous proportion starting from unity, and the number following unity is not a square, then none of the other numbers will be squares, except for unity, the third number, and those found thereafter by always skipping one. <note>In the sequence 1, a, a², a³, a⁴, if 'a' is not a square, then only a² (the 3rd term) and a⁴ (the 5th term) are squares.</note> If, however, the second number from unity is not a cube, none of the others will be cubes, except for unity, the fourth number, and those formed thereafter by always skipping two.
¶ This proposition infers the opposite of the previous one. I say "part of the opposite" because it allows that all odd-positioned terms <note>the 3rd, 5th, etc.</note> are squares, and all those whose place is the fourth or any multiple of three plus one <note>the 4th, 7th, 10th, etc.</note> are cubes. Let there be numbers in continuous proportion from unity as before. Let **a** be neither a square nor a cube. I say that none of the numbers are squares or cubes except those which Proposition 8 proposes. For if any other were assumed to be a square, it would follow from Proposition 22 of Book VIII that **a** is a square. If it were a cube, it would follow from Proposition 23 of the same book that **a** is a cube. Since both of these contradict the hypothesis <note>original: "ypothesi"; the initial assumption that 'a' is not a square or cube</note>, the proposition is established.

## Proposition 11.

<margin>
<note>Two groups of vertical stacks of horizontal lines are shown for comparison. The left stack consists of five lines labeled from top to bottom: f, g, h, e, and 1. The right stack consists of five lines labeled from top to bottom: d, c, b, a, and 1. These represent the factors and products being tested for divisibility by a prime number.</note>
</margin>

If any number of numbers are arranged in continuous proportion starting from unity, and some prime number <note>original: "numerus primus"; a number divisible only by 1 and itself</note> divides the last number, it is necessary that it also divides the number following unity.
¶ Let there be numbers in continuous proportion from unity up to **d**. Let **e** be a prime number which is assumed to divide **d**. I say that the same number will divide **a**. For if it does not, it will be prime relative to it, by Proposition 32 of Book VII. And because **b** is produced from **a** multiplied by itself, it follows from Proposition 26 of the same book that **e** is also prime to **b**, and likewise to **c** and **d**. It follows that it is prime to **d** by Proposition 25 of the same book, because **c** is produced from **a** times **b**, and **d** from **a** times **c**. Therefore, it does not divide **d** since it is prime to it; which contradicts the hypothesis.
The same is shown another way: since **e** is prime, if it does not divide **a**, it will be prime to it by Proposition 32 of Book VII. Thus, by Proposition 32 of the same book, they will be the least in their proportion. Since **e** by hypothesis divides **d**, let it be according to **f**. It is established that **d** is produced from **a** times **c**. Therefore, by the second part of Proposition 20 of Book VII, **a** is to **e** as **f** is to **c**. Thus, by Proposition 21 of the same book, **e** will divide **c**; let it be according to **g**. And because **c** is produced from **a** times **b**, it follows by the same means that **e** divides **b**; let it be according to **h**. Since, again, **b** is produced from **a** multiplied by itself, it is necessary by the same logic that **e** divides **a**. But it was assumed not to divide it, which results in an impossibility.

## Proposition 12.

<term>proportionalitas</term> <note>Proportionality; the equality of ratios.</note>
<term>quadratus</term> <note>Square; a number multiplied by itself.</note>
<term>cubus</term> <note>Cube; a number multiplied by itself twice.</note>
<term>numerus primus</term> <note>Prime number; a number only divisible by 1 and itself.</note>
<term>tetragonus</term> <note>Tetragon; another term for a square number.</note>
<term>ypothesi</term> <note>Hypothesis; the starting assumption of a proof.</note>

<summary>This page explains how square and cube properties propagate through a geometric sequence starting from 1, and proves that if a prime number divides the final term of such a sequence, it must also divide the sequence's base.</summary>
<keywords>geometric progression, unity, square numbers, cube numbers, prime numbers, divisibility, Euclid's Elements, Book IX</keywords>

<page-num>IX</page-num>

<margin>
<note>A vertical diagram consists of seven horizontal line segments of decreasing length from top to bottom, labeled from top to bottom: f, e, d, c, b, a, and a short segment labeled 1. These represent a sequence of numbers in continuous proportion, such as 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64.</note>
</margin>

In a series of numbers in continuous proportion starting from unity <note>original: "ab unitate"; starting from the number 1</note>, a smaller number divides <note>original: "numerat"; literally "measures," meaning it divides into the larger number without a remainder</note> a larger one according to some number placed within that same proportion.
¶ Let there be numbers in continuous proportion from unity up to **f**. I say that each of these divides **f** according to one of the others: for it is clear that **e** divides **f** according to **a**; for as **e** is to **f**, so is unity to **a**. Furthermore, **d** divides the same **f** according to **b**; for by equal proportion <note>original: "per equam proportionalitatem"; a rule of ratios where intermediate terms are skipped</note>, **d** is to **f** as unity is to **b**. Concerning **c**, it is also clear in the same way that it divides it according to itself <note>if c is the middle term, c × c would equal f in certain sequences</note>. Conversely, **a** also divides it according to **e**, because just as unity is to **a**, so is **e** to **f**. Likewise, **b** divides according to **d**, for as unity is to **d**, so is **b** to **f**. It is therefore true that the last is divided by those beneath it according to a value greater than unity; that it divides it is proved by equal proportion and the definition.

## Proposition 13

<margin>
<note>A diagram shows two parallel columns of line segments. The left column contains five segments labeled d, c, b, a, and 1. The right column contains five segments labeled g, h, k, e, f. This illustrates the relationship between terms in a sequence and potential external divisors.</note>
</margin>

If, in any number of numbers in continuous proportion starting from unity, the number following unity is a prime number, then no number shall divide the greatest of them except for those numbers arranged within that same proportion.
¶ Let there be, as before, numbers in continuous proportion from unity up to **d**, and let **a** be a prime number <note>a number divisible only by 1 and itself</note>. I say that no number will divide the last, nor simply any of them, unless it is one of those that precedes the last or the one being divided. For let it be, if possible, that **e** is a different number from them that divides **d**. If **e** is prime, then by Proposition 11 <note>of this same book</note>, it will divide **a**; therefore **a** would not be prime, which contradicts the hypothesis. If, however, **e** is composite <note>original: "compositus"; a number that is not prime</note>, it is necessary by Proposition 30 of Book VII that some prime number divides it, which can be none other than **a**. For if it were another besides **a**, such as **f**, since it must divide **d**, it would be argued that the same also divides **a** by Proposition 11; thus **a** would again not be prime. Therefore, **a** is the prime number dividing **e**. Since **e** divides **d**, let it be according to **g**. By the second part of Proposition 20 of Book VII, **a** is to **e** as **g** is to **c**; for **d** is produced from **a** times **c**. Therefore, since **a** divides **e**, **g** will also divide **c**. Let it be according to **b**. It follows that **a** divides **g** just as it followed that it divided **c**. Otherwise, if **g** were prime while dividing **c**, it follows from Proposition 11 that it divides **a**. If it were composite, by the same rule it follows that the prime number dividing **g** divides **a**, which is inconsistent <note>original: "inconveniens"; a mathematical absurdity or contradiction</note>. Thus **a** divides it. It follows then by the second part of Proposition 20 of Book VII that it also divides **b**, because it is established that **c** is produced both from **a** times **b** and from **g** times **b**. Let it divide **b**, therefore, according to **k**.

## Proposition 14

<margin>
<note>A geometrical diagram shows three horizontal line segments. The top line is labeled 'a'. The middle line is divided into three segments labeled 'b', 'c', and 'd'. The bottom line is divided into two segments labeled 'e' and 'f'. These represent the relationships between a composite number and its prime factors.</note>
</margin>

**I**f a number is the least that the assigned prime numbers divide <note>original: "numerant"; meaning the smallest number that is a multiple of those primes</note>, no prime number other than those assigned will divide it.
¶ Let **a** be the least number divided by the prime numbers which are **b**, **c**, and **d**. I say that no other prime besides them will divide **a**. For if there were another prime number **e** <note>original: "quam bru. f."; likely a corruption in OCR for "different from them, let it divide a according to f"</note> which divides **a** according to **f**, then since each of the numbers **b**, **c**, and **d** divides **a** (the product of **e** and **f**) and each of them is prime, it follows from the 33rd proposition of the seventh book <note>The 33rd proposition of Book VII establishes that if a prime divides a product of two numbers, it must divide at least one of them.</note> that each of them must divide either **e** or **f**. But none of them divides **e**, since **e** is prime. Therefore, each of them must divide **f**. Since **f** is smaller than **a** (as it divides it according to **e**), then **a** would not be the least number divided by them, which is inconsistent.

## Proposition 15

<margin>
<note>A numerical diagram showing proportional relationships in rows.
a 81 | b 108 | c 144 | d 192 | e 256
k 27 | l 36 | m 48 | n 64
p 9 | q 12 | r 16
f 3 | g 4
h
This table illustrates a geometric progression where each number is in the ratio of 3 to 4. For example, 81 is to 108 as 3 is to 4.</note>
</margin>

**I**f any number of continuous proportional numbers <note>numbers in a geometric sequence, like 2, 4, 8, 16</note> are the least in their ratio: whoever divides any one of them will be commensurable <note>original: "commensurabilis"; meaning they share a common divisor</note> to one of the terms of that ratio.
¶ Let **a**, **b**, **c**, **d**, and **e** be in continuous proportion and the least in the ratio of **f** to **g**, which are themselves the least in their ratio. And let it be posited that some number divides **b**. I say that this divisor is commensurable to **f** or **g**. For let four least numbers in the same proportion be taken, which are **k**, **l**, **m**, and **n**. It is clear from the second proposition of the eighth book that **c** is produced from **f** multiplied by **m**; otherwise, it would happen that a number is smaller than the least, which cannot be. Therefore, by the corollary of the 33rd proposition of the seventh book, the divisor of **b** will be commensurable to **f** or **m**. If it is to **f**, the proposition is established. If it is to **m**, let three least numbers in the same proportion be taken, which are **p**, **q**, and **r**. It will be, from the second proposition of the eighth book, that **m** is produced from **f** multiplied by **r**, lest we be forced to grant something smaller than the least. Wherefore, by the aforesaid corollary, the divisor is commensurable to **f** or **r**. But if it were not to **f**, then the proposition would still stand; thus it is commensurable to **r**. Since **r**, from the second proposition of the eighth book, is produced from **g** multiplied by itself, it follows from the said corollary that the divisor of **b** is commensurable to **g**, which is what was proposed.

## Proposition 16

<margin>
<note>A geometrical diagram with multiple horizontal lines.
Top: line divided into segments 'a', 'b', 'c'.
Second: line divided into segments 'a', 'b', 'c', 'd'.
Third: line divided into segments 'a', 'b', 'c'.
Below: isolated segment 'e'.
Below that: two segments 'f' and 'g'.
Bottom: isolated segment 'h'.
These lines represent the parts of a sum in a geometric progression.</note>
</margin>

**I**f there be any number of continuous proportional numbers that are the least in their ratio, any one of them is necessarily proved to be prime <note>original: "primi"; meaning coprime or having no common factor other than 1</note> to the sum composed of the remaining numbers.
¶ Let **a**, **b**, **c**, and **d** be in continuous proportion and the least. I say the sum composed of **a**, **b**, and **c** is prime to **d**. For if it were not, some number **e** would divide both the sum of **a**, **b**, and **c** and the number **d**. By the previous proposition, **e** will share a factor with one of the terms of the ratio, which are **f** and **g**. There would then be some number dividing **e** and one of the two, **f** or **g**, let it be **b** <note>here 'b' is used as a generic divisor label in the proof</note>. Because **b** divides **e**, it will divide **d** and the sum of **a**, **b**, and **c**. And because it divides **f** or **g**, each of which divides both of the means—and simply all of them if there are more than two—it follows from the second proposition of the eighth book that it divides **b** and **c**. Therefore, it also divides **a**, because it divides the whole sum of **a**, **b**, and **c**. Thus, **a** and **d** are not prime to each other, which is inconsistent by the 3rd proposition of the eighth book. Similarly, it will be established that the sum of **a**, **b**, and **d** is prime to **c**. For if, as before, **e** divides both, it follows by the previous proposition that some number, let it be **b**, divides **e** and one of the two, **f** or **g**. Thus, **b** divides **c** and the whole sum of **a**, **b**, and **d**. But since **b**, with each of the "roots" <note>original: "radicū"; the basic terms of the ratio</note>, divides all the means, it therefore divides the sum of **a** and **d**. And since it must divide one of the two, **a** or **d**, since it divides one of the two, **f** or **g**, it will also divide the other. Therefore, **a** and **d** are not prime to each other, which is the same inconsistency as before. ¶ They also demonstrate the same thing differently for three continuous proportionals that are the least, without the aid of the previous proposition; for they prove from any two that the sum is prime to the remaining one. Let there be 3 continuous proportionals and least: **a**, **b**, and **c**, whose terms <note>base ratio</note> are **d** and **e**. I say then that the sum of **a** and **b** is prime...

...is prime to **c**, and the sum of **b** and **c** is prime to **a**, and likewise the sum of **a** and **c** is prime to **b**. For it is manifest from the second proposition of the eighth book that the product of **d** times itself produces **a**, and its product with **e** produces **b**, and the product of **e** times itself produces **c**. And from the 22nd proposition of the seventh book <note>original: "ex 22. ſeptimi"</note>, **d** and **e** are prime to each other. Therefore, from the first part of the 29th proposition of the same book, the whole sum of **d** and **e** <note>OCR "d. c." likely intended as the sum d+e</note> will be prime to each of them. Since, therefore, each of the two numbers **d** and the sum of **d** and **e** is prime to **c**, it will follow from the 25th proposition of the same book that their product—which is the sum of **a** and **b**—is prime to **e**. It follows then, by the 26th of the same book, that the sum of **a** and **b** is also prime to **c**; for **c** is produced from **e** times itself.

¶ By a similar demonstration, you shall prove that the sum of **b** and **c** is prime to **a**. Truly, that the sum of **a** and **c** is prime to **b** is held thus: since each of the two, **d** and **e**, is prime to the whole sum of **d** and **e**, it follows from the 25th of the seventh book that their product—which is **b**—is prime to the sum of **d** and **e**. Thus, by the 26th of the same book, the square of the sum of **d** and **e**—which is the sum of **a** and **c** plus twice **b** <note>This is a numerical expression of the algebraic identity (d+e)² = d² + e² + 2de</note>—will be prime to **b**. It follows therefore that the sum of **a** and **c** is prime to **b**. For it is necessary that when a sum of two numbers is prime to one of its components, it must be prime to the remaining part; this was demonstrated above in the 29th proposition of the seventh book. To strengthen this demonstration, it must be established that the sum of **a** and **b** is produced from **d** multiplied by the sum of **d** and **e**, assuming that **d** times itself is **a** and **d** times **e** is **b**. Likewise, that the sum of **a** and **c** and twice **b** is produced from the square of the sum of **d** and **e**, assuming as before that **e** times itself is **c**. For the sake of this, these following points are proposed to be demonstrated.

A bracket below identifies segments 'd' and 'e', which are the roots or components of the larger numbers.</note>

¶ **T**hat which results from the multiplication of one number into any number of others is equal to the product of that same number into the sum of those others. <note>This is the Distributive Law of Multiplication: a(b + c + d) = ab + ac + ad.</note>
¶ The same is proposed in the first proposition of the second book regarding lines. For let it be that from **a** multiplied into **b**, **c**, and **d**, there result **e**, **f**, and **g**. I say that from **a** multiplied into the sum of **b**, **c**, and **d**, there results the sum of **e**, **f**, and **g**. For it follows from the conversion of the definition of multiplication <note>In Euclid, multiplication is defined through repeated addition or proportional parts.</note> that the whole part **b** is to **e**, and the whole **c** to **f**, and the whole **d** to **g**, as the unit is to **a**. Therefore, by the fifth proposition of the seventh book, the whole sum of **b**, **c**, and **d** will be the same multiple of the sum of **e**, **f**, and **g** as the unit is of **a**. Therefore, by definition, from **a** multiplied into the sum of **b**, **c**, and **d** comes the sum of **e**, **f**, and **g**, which is what was proposed.

<margin>
<note>A geometric diagram shows a single vertical-style segment 'a' acting as a multiplier against three horizontal segments 'b', 'c', and 'd', producing the resulting products 'e', 'f', and 'g'.</note>
</margin>

¶ **T**hat which results from the multiplication of any number of numbers into one is equal to the product of their sum into that same one.
¶ This is the converse of what was just demonstrated: as if from **b**, **c**, and **d** multiplied into **a**, there are produced **e**, **f**, and **g**. The sum of these will also be produced by the sum of the numbers multiplied into the same one; which is easily concluded from the 17th proposition of the seventh book and the previous demonstration.

<margin>
<note>A geometric diagram similar to the one above, but arranged to show multiple numbers ('e', 'f', 'g') being compared to a single multiplier ('a') and its components.</note>
</margin>

¶ **T**hat which results from the multiplication of any number of numbers into any number of others is equal to the product of the sum of the former into the sum of the latter. <note>In modern terms: (a+b+c)(d+e+f) = a(d+e+f) + b(d+e+f) + c(d+e+f).</note>
¶ As if **a**, **b**, and **c** multiply **d**, **e**, and **f**, each multiplying each, and the products are joined. I say the aggregate of the products is equal to the product of the sum of **a**, **b**, and **c** into the sum of **d**, **e**, and **f**. For by the previous lemma, the product of the sum of **a**, **b**, and **c** into **d** is as much as each individual one multiplied into that **d**; and likewise for **e** and **f**. It follows that the sum of these into any of **d**, **e**, or **f** is, by the lemma before the previous one, as much as the sum multiplied into the sum. Thus the proposition stands.

<margin>
<note>A diagram showing two sets of segments, 'd, e, f' and 'a, b, c', illustrating the complex distribution of multiplication across two different sums.</note>
</margin>

¶ **I**f a number is divided into any number of parts, the square of the whole <note>original: "quod fit ex toto eo in ſe"</note> is equal to the product of the whole multiplied by all its parts.
¶ The same is proposed in the second proposition of the second book regarding lines. For if **a** is divided into **b**, **c**, and **d**, I say that the product of **a** into itself is as much as its product into all those parts **b**, **c**, and **d**. For if **e** is set equal to **a**, it is clear from the first of these incidental lemmas that the product of **e** into **a** is as much as its product into all parts of **a**. But by common conception, the product of **e** into **a** is the same as **a** into itself, and **e** into the parts of **a** is the same as **a** into those same parts. Therefore, it is manifest that what is said is true.

<margin>
<note>A diagram showing a long segment 'a' and a parallel segment of the same length divided into parts 'b', 'c', 'e', and 'd' to demonstrate the identity a² = a(b+c+d).</note>
</margin>

¶ **I**f a number is divided into two, the product of the whole into one of the parts is equal to the product of that same part into itself and into the other part.
¶ The same is proposed in the third proposition of the second book regarding lines. Let **a** be divided into **b** and **c**. I say that the product of **a** into **c** is equal to the product of **c** into itself and into **b**. For the product of **a** into **c** is the same as **c** into **a** by the 17th of the seventh book. Taking **d** as equal to **c**, then **a** times **c** will be equal to **d** times **a**. But by the first of these lemmas, **d** times **a** is equal to its product into **b** and **c**. Because **d** times **a** (into **b** and **c**) is equal to **c** times **a** (and into **b** and itself) because of the equality of **c** and **d**, the proposition is established.

<margin>
<note>A diagram showing segment 'a' composed of 'b' and 'c', with an auxiliary segment 'd' used to prove the distribution of the product.</note>
</margin>

¶ **W**hen a number is divided into two parts, the product of the whole multiplied by itself is equal to the sum of the squares of the two parts and twice the product of one part multiplied by the other. <note>This is the numerical equivalent of the algebraic identity (b + c)² = b² + c² + 2bc.</note>
¶ The same is proposed in the fourth proposition of the second book <note>original: "quarta ſcđi"</note> regarding lines: as if **a** is divided into **b** and **c**, I say as much is produced from **a** multiplied by itself as from **b** by itself and **c** by itself, and from **b** twice into **c**. For it is shown through the fourth of these <note>referring to the propositions of Book II</note> that the square of **a** is as much as the product of itself into **b** and into **c**. Moreover, the product of **a** into **b**, by the preceding proposition, is equal to the square of **b** and the product of **b** into **c**. But the product of **a** into **c**, by the same logic, is as much as the square of **c** and the product of **c** into **b**. And because the product of **c** into **b** is the same as the product of **b** into **c**, by the 17th proposition of the seventh book <note>original: "17. ſeptimi"</note>, it is clear that what is proposed is true.

<margin>
<note>A geometric diagram consisting of a horizontal line with points marked a, c, d, and b from left to right. There is a small vertical tick between c and d.</note>
</margin>

¶ **W**hen a number is divided into two equal parts and also into two unequal parts, the product of the larger unequal part multiplied by the smaller, together with the square of the segment between the points of division, is equal to the square of half the whole. <note>In modern terms: (x + y)(x - y) + y² = x².</note>
¶ The same is proposed regarding lines in the fifth proposition of the second book: as if **a b** is divided into two equal numbers which are **a c** and **c b**, and likewise into two unequal parts of which the larger is **a d** and the smaller **d b**. I say that the product of the whole **a d** into **d b**, together with the square of **c d**, is equal to the square of **c b**. For by the preceding, the square of **c b** is equal to the square of **c d** and the square of **d b**, and that which is produced from **b d** into **c d** twice. But the product of **b d** into itself and into **c d** is only as much as the product into **c b**, according to the first of these; and therefore as much as the product into **a c**. Thus, the product of **b d** into itself and into **c d** twice is as much as the product of the same **b d** into **a d**. By the same logic, therefore, the square of **c b** exceeds the product of **b d** into **a d** by the square of **c d**; thus the proposition is established.

<margin>
<note>A geometric diagram consisting of a horizontal line with points marked a, c, b, and d.</note>
</margin>

¶ **W**hen a number has been divided into two equal parts and another number is added to it: the product of the whole composite number multiplied by the added part, together with the square of the half, is equal to the square of the composite formed from the half and the added part. <note>This describes the identity (2a + b)b + a² = (a + b)².</note>
¶ The same is proposed in the sixth proposition of the second book regarding lines: Let **a b** be divided into two equal numbers which are **a c** and **c b**, and let the number **b d** be added to it. I say that the product of the whole **a d** into **d b**, together with the square of **b c**, is equal to the square of **c d**. For from the sixth of these, the square of **c d** is equal to the square of **d b** and the square of **b c**, and that which is produced from **d b** into **b c** twice. But by the first of these, the product of **b d** into itself and into **b c** twice is as much as the product of **b d** into **d a**. For **a c** and **c b** are equal. Thus, the square of **c d** exceeds the product of **b d** into **d a** by the square of **c b**, which is what was proposed.

<margin>
<note>A geometric diagram consisting of a horizontal line with points b, a, and d.</note>

¶ **W**hen a number is divided into two parts, the product of the whole multiplied by itself together with the square of one of the parts is equal to twice the product of the whole multiplied by that same part together with the square of the other part. <note>This represents the identity (a + b)² + a² = 2(a + b)a + b².</note>
¶ The same is proposed in the seventh proposition of the second book regarding lines. Let the number **a** be divided into **b** and **d**. I say the square of **a** with the square of **d** is as much as twice the product of **a** and **d** with the square of **b**. It is established from the sixth of these <note>referring to previous logical steps</note> that the square of **a** is as much as the square of **d** and the square of **b** and twice the product of **d** into **b**. Therefore, the square of **a** with the square of **d** is as much as twice the square of **d** and twice the product of **d** into **b** with the square of **b**. But twice the square of **d** and twice the product of **d** into **b** is as much as twice the product of **d** into **a**, by the first of these. Therefore, twice the product of **d** into **a** with the square of **b** is as much as the square of **a** with the square of **d**; wherefore the proposition is evident.

¶ **W**hen a number is divided into two equal and two unequal parts: the sum of the squares of the two unequal parts is double the sum of the square of the half and the square of the difference by which the greater portion exceeds the smaller. ¶ The same is proposed in the ninth proposition of the second book <note>original: "nona ſcđi"</note> regarding lines. For let **a.b.** be divided by two equals, which are **a.c.** and **c.b.**, and by two unequals, which are **a.d.** and **d.b.** I say that the squares of the two numbers **a.d.** and **d.b.** taken together are double the two squares of the two numbers **a.c.** and **c.d.** taken together. For by the sixth proposition of these <note>referring to the numerical versions of Book II's identities</note>, the square of **a.d.** is as much as the square of **a.c.** and the square of **c.d.** and twice that which is produced from **a.c.** into **c.d.** Since, however, **a.c.** is equal to **c.b.**, the square of **a.d.** will be as much as the square of **b.c.** and the square of **c.d.** By the 9th proposition of these, therefore, the square of **a.d.** with the square of **b.d.** are as much as the square of **b.c.** and the square of **c.d.** and twice that which is produced from **b.c.** into **c.d.** and the square of **b.d.** But twice that which is produced from **b.c.** into **c.d.** with the square of **b.d.** is equal to the square of **b.c.** and the square of **c.d.** by the 9th of these. Therefore, the squares of the two numbers **a.d.** and **d.b.** are as much as the squares of the two numbers **b.c.** and **c.d.** doubled; and because **b.c.** and **c.a.** are equal, the proposition is clear.

¶ **W**hen a number is divided into two equal parts and another is added to it: the square of the whole composite <note>the original number plus the added segment</note> with the square of the added part is double the square of the half with the square of the composite of the half and the added part. ¶ The same is proposed in the 10th proposition of the second book regarding lines. For let the number **a.b.** be divided into two equals, **a.c.** and **c.b.**, and let the number **b.d.** be added to it. I say the square of **a.d.** with the square of **b.d.** is double the square of **a.c.** with the square of **c.d.** Since the number **c.d.** is divided into two, and **a.c.** is equal to one of those parts [c.b.], when added, the square of **a.d.** will be—by the 10th of these—as much as what is produced from **c.d.** into **c.a.** four times with the square of **b.d.** Since **a.c.** is equal to **c.b.**, the square of **a.d.** will be as much as four times the product of **d.c.** and **c.b.** with the square of **b.d.** Thus the square of **a.d.** with the square of **d.b.** will be as much as four times the product of **d.c.** and **c.b.** with double the square of **b.d.** This, however, by the 19th <note>likely a cross-reference to the numerical equivalent of Book II identities</note> of these, is double the square of **c.d.** with the square of **c.b.** Since, therefore, the square of **c.b.** is equal to the square of **a.c.**, the proposition is established.

<note>A diagram showing a horizontal line with points marked a, c, e, d, and b, used to demonstrate the impossibility of the "Golden Ratio" in whole numbers.</note>

¶ **T**o divide any number so that the product of the whole and one of its portions is equal to the square of the other portion is impossible. ¶ While the 11th proposition of the second book proposes this to be done with lines, he demonstrates here that this is impossible in numbers. For let there be any number **a.b.** I say it is impossible for it to be divided as proposed: for to divide it thus would be according to a <term>proportion having a mean and two extremes</term> <note>This is the "Golden Ratio." In modern terms, it is an irrational number and cannot be expressed as a ratio of two integers.</note>, as is clear from the definition in the 20th proposition of the seventh book. If it could be done, let it be divided at **c**, such that **a.b.** is to **b.c.** as **b.c.** is to **c.a.** Therefore, **a.c.** will be smaller than **c.b.** Let a segment equal to it, **c.d.**, be subtracted from it. Because the proportion of the whole **a.b.** to the whole **b.c.** is the same as **b.c.** subtracted from **a.b.** is to **c.d.** subtracted from **b.c.**, the ratio of the remainder **a.c.** to the remainder **b.d.** will be the same. Wherefore **b.c.** is to **c.d.** as **c.d.** is to **d.b.** Thus **c.d.** will be greater than **d.b.** Subtracting **d.e.** from **c.d.** so that **d.e.** is equal to **d.b.**, the proportion of **b.c.** to **c.d.** will also be as **c.d.** to **d.e.**, and as the remainder **d.b.** is to the remainder **c.e.** Therefore **c.e.** can be subtracted from **e.d.**, and there will be no end to this subtraction <note>This process of infinite subtraction, or "anthyphairesis," was the Greek method of proving that a ratio is irrational and cannot be represented by whole numbers.</note>, which is impossible in finite numbers. Now let us return to the proposal.

### Proposition 17

**I**f there are two numbers <term>prime to each other</term> <note>original: "contra ſe pꝛimi"; numbers that share no common divisor other than 1.</note>, it is impossible for any third number to exist such that the first is to the second as the second is to the third.

For if it can be, let it be **c.** Since therefore **a.** is to **b.** as...

### ¶ Proposition 18.

<margin>
<note>A diagram showing four horizontal line segments labeled a, b, c, and d.</note>
</margin>

**I**f, of any number of continued proportionals <note>A sequence of numbers where the ratio between each consecutive pair is constant, such as 2, 4, 8, 16.</note>, the two extremes are prime to one another, it is impossible for the first to have the same ratio to the second as the last has to any other number.
¶ Let **a, b, c** be continued proportionals, and let **a** and **c** be prime to one another. I say that in the same proportion, another number cannot be added to them. For if it were possible, let it be **d**. Because therefore **a** is to **b** as **c** is to **d**, by permutation **a** is to **c** as **b** is to **d**. However, **a** and **c** are the smallest in their proportion by Proposition 23 of the seventh book; thus, by Proposition 21 of the same, **a** divides **b**. Therefore, it also divides **c**; for in a sequence of continued proportional numbers, if the first divides the second, it divides all of them, and simply any preceding number divides any following number. But since **a** also divides itself, **a** and **c** will not be prime to one another, which is inconsistent.

### ¶ Proposition 19.

<margin>
<note>A diagram showing three horizontal line segments labeled a, b, and d, with a longer line segment labeled c positioned below them.</note>
</margin>

**G**iven two numbers, to investigate whether there is a third number in continued proportion with them.
¶ Let **a** and **b** be two proposed numbers; I wish to inquire whether a third can be added to them under continued proportionality. Therefore, if they are prime to one another, it is impossible. If, however, they are not <note>Meaning they share a common factor</note>, let **b** be multiplied by itself to produce **c**. If **a** divides **c**, it will exist; if it does not divide it, it will not exist. For let it divide it according to **d**, which will be the one we seek by the second part of Proposition 20 of the seventh book. Let it be then that it does not divide it; it is nevertheless that **a** is to **b** as **b** is to **d**. Thus, because from **b** multiplied by itself **c** is produced, it follows by the first part of Proposition 20 of the seventh book that from **a** multiplied by **d** the same is produced. Therefore, **a** divides **c** according to **d**, but it was established that it did not, which leads to an impossibility.

### ¶ Proposition 20.

<margin>
<note>A diagram showing four horizontal line segments labeled a, b, c, and e, with a longer line segment labeled d positioned below them.</note>
</margin>

**G**iven three continued proportional numbers, to inquire whether there is any fourth number in continued proportion with them.
¶ Let **a, b, c** be continued proportionals. I wish to inquire whether another can be added to them under continued proportionality. Therefore, if **a** and **c** are prime to one another, it is impossible by Proposition 18. If, however, they share a factor, let **d** be produced from **b** multiplied by **c**. If **a** divides it, it will exist; if it does not divide it, it will not exist. For let it divide it according to **e**, which will be the one we seek, by the second part of Proposition 20 of the seventh book. Let it be then that it does not divide it. It is nevertheless that **a** is to **b** as **c** is to **e**. Thus, because from **b** multiplied by **c** comes **d**, it follows by the first part of Proposition 20 of the seventh book that from **a** multiplied by **e** the same is produced. Therefore, **a** divides **d** according to **e**, but it was established that it did not. You can investigate the same for any number of continued proportionals. For if the two extremes are prime to one another, the objective is reached by Proposition 18. If, however, they share a factor: with the second multiplied by the last, if the first divides the product, that number by which it divides it is the one we seek by the second part of Proposition 20 of the seventh book. If the first does not divide the product, there will be no such number; for whatever number is proposed, by the first part of the same, according to that which is proposed, the first will divide the product, which was established as not dividing.

**G**iven any number of prime numbers, it is necessary that there be some prime number different from them.

Let **d-f** be the smallest number that they divide <note>This is the "least common multiple" (LCM) of a, b, and c.</note>, to which, with a unit added, **d-g** is made, which...
