...is either prime or composite. If it is prime, the proposition is proven. If it is composite, it is measured <note>In Greek and Latin geometry, a number "measures" another if it divides it evenly, like a yardstick measuring a length.</note> by some prime number **b**, which cannot be any of the original primes proposed. For if it were one of them, since each of those measures **d.f.** <note>Latin: *numeret*, meaning "counts" or "divides."</note>, it would also measure that same number. But because it measures **d.g.**, it would also have to measure the difference **f.g.**, which is unity <note>The number 1.</note>; which is impossible. The same follows if **d.f.** is set as any number that **a, b, c** measure; thus the proposition is established.

### ¶ Proposition 22.

<margin>
<note>A diagram in the right margin consisting of three separate horizontal segments labeled a, b, and c at the top. Below them is a continuous horizontal line divided into three segments labeled d, e, and f. At the bottom is a single shorter segment labeled h. **I**f any number of even numbers are added together, the total will also be even.
¶ Let each of the numbers **a, b, c** be even; I say that the sum composed of them is even. For, by the converse of the definition <note>Euclid defines an even number as one that can be divided into two equal parts.</note>, each of them has a half. Let their halves be **d, e, f**. Since, therefore, as **a** is to **d**, so is **b** to **e**, and **c** to **f**, it follows from Proposition 13 of the seventh book that as **a** is to **d**, so is the whole sum **a, b, c** to the whole sum **d, e, f**. Thus, **d, e, f** is the half of **a, b, c**. Therefore, by the definition, **a, b, c** is even: which is what was proposed.

### ¶ Proposition 23.

<margin>
<note>A horizontal line divided into four segments labeled a, b, c, and d. Below it, a horizontal line divided into three segments labeled d, e, and f.</note>
</margin>

**I**f an even number of odd numbers are added together, the total will also be even.
¶ Let any number of odd numbers **a, b, c, d** be given <note>The author specifies an even count of numbers here, even though the letters only go to d.</note>; I say that the sum composed of them is even. For if unity <note>The number 1.</note> is taken away from each, it is certain that the remainders are even; and since those units that were taken away also compose an even number (since they are even in number), the proposition is established by the preceding one.

### ¶ Proposition 24.

<margin>
<note>A horizontal line divided into three segments labeled a, b, and c.</note>
</margin>

**I**f an odd number of odd numbers are added together, the total sum of them will be odd.
¶ Let any of the numbers **a, b, c** be odd; I say the whole sum composed of them is odd. For, by the preceding proposition, the sum of **a** and **b** will be even; and because **c**, when unity is taken away, is even, the whole sum **a, b, c** with unity taken away will be even by the proposition before the last. Therefore, by the definition, it is established that the total is odd.

### ¶ Proposition 25.

<margin>
<note>A horizontal segment labeled a. Below it, a line divided into segments b and c. Below that, a segment labeled d. Below that, a line divided into segments e and f.</note>
</margin>

**I**f an even number is subtracted from an even number, the remainder will be even.
¶ Let the whole **a** be even, from which is subtracted **b**, which is also even; and let the remainder be **c**. I say that **c** is even. For let **d** be the half of **a**, and let **e** be the half of **b**. When **e** is subtracted from **d**, let the remainder be **f**. By Proposition 13 of the seventh book, **c** is to **f** as **a** is to **d**. Therefore, **f** is the half of **c**, and thus **c** is even: which is what was proposed.

### ¶ Proposition 26.

<margin>
<note>A long horizontal line segment with endpoints a and b, and interior points c and d. A Roman numeral I is placed below the right end.</note>
</margin>

**I**f an odd number is subtracted from an odd number, the remainder will be even.
¶ Let the number **a. b.** be odd, from which **b. c.** (which is also odd) is subtracted. I say that the remainder, which is **a. c.**, is even. For let unity—which is **b. d.**—be subtracted from both numbers **a. b.** and **b. c.**. Each of the two remainders, which are **a. d.** and **d. c.**, will be even by the preceding logic; thus it is established that **a. c.** is even: which is what was proposed.

### ¶ Proposition 27.

<margin>
<note>A long horizontal line segment with endpoints a and b, and interior points c and d. A Roman numeral I is placed below the right end.</note>
</margin>

**I**f you subtract an even number from an odd number, the remainder is odd.
¶ Let **a. b.** be odd, from which **a. c.** (which is even) is subtracted. I say that the remainder **c. b.** is odd. For let **b. d.** be unity; then **a. d.** will be even. And because **a. c.** is even, then by Proposition 25, **c. d.** will be even. Since **d. b.** is unity, **c. b.** must be odd: which is what was proposed.

BOOK IX

### ¶ Proposition 28.

<margin>
<note>A horizontal line with points marked and labeled a, d, c, and b from left to right. Below the first segment (a to d) is a shorter separate line segment labeled I <note>The Roman numeral for 1, representing "unity."</note>.</note>
</margin>

**I**f an odd number is subtracted from an even number, the remainder is odd.
¶ Let **a.b.** be an even number from which the odd number **a.c.** is subtracted; I say that the remaining part **c.b.** is odd. For if one unit, **c.d.**, is subtracted from **a.c.**, then **a.d.** will be even. Therefore, by Proposition 25, **d.b.** will also be even. Because **d.c.** is a unit, it follows that **c.b.** is odd; which is what was proposed.

### ¶ Proposition 29.

**I**f an odd number is multiplied by an even number, the resulting product will be even.
¶ This is evident from Proposition 23.

### ¶ Proposition 30.

**I**f an odd number is multiplied by an odd number, the resulting product will be odd.
¶ This is also evident from Proposition 24.

### ¶ Proposition 31.

**I**f an odd number divides <note>Latin: *numeret*, literally "counts," meaning to divide without a remainder.</note> an even number, it will divide it an even number of times.
¶ For if it divided it an odd number of times, an even number would be produced from an odd multiplied by an odd; which is inconsistent with the previous premise.

### ¶ Proposition 32.

**I**f an odd number divides an odd number, it divides it an odd number of times.
¶ For if it divided it an even number of times, an odd number would be produced from an odd number multiplied by an even number, which is inconsistent according to Proposition 29.

### ¶ Proposition 33.

<margin>
<note>Two horizontal lines. The upper line is divided into three segments labeled f, b, and a. The lower line is divided into three segments labeled c, d, and e.</note>
</margin>

**I**f an odd number measures <note>Divides evenly.</note> an even number, it is necessary that it also measures half of that same number.
¶ Let **a** be an even number whose half is **b**, and let **c** be an odd number that divides **a**. I say that **c** will also divide **b**. For let **c** divide **a** according to the number **d**; by Proposition 31, **d** will be an even number. Therefore, let its half be **e**. When **c** is multiplied by **e**, let it produce **f**. Then, by Proposition 18 of the seventh book, as **a** is to **f**, so is **d** to **e**. And since **a** is to **b** as **d** is to **e**, it follows that **b** and **f** are equal. Since **c** divides **f**, it will also divide **b**, which is what was proposed.

### ¶ Proposition 34.

<margin>
<note>Three horizontal line segments. The top-most is labeled c. Below it, to the left, is a segment labeled b with a shorter segment labeled d beneath it. To the right of b is a separate segment labeled a.</note>
</margin>

**I**f an odd number is prime to <note>Sharing no common factors other than 1.</note> any other number, it will also be prime to the double of that number.
¶ Let **a** be an odd number prime to **b**, and let **c** be the double of **b**. I say that **a** is prime to **c**. For if some number **d** were to divide them, since **a** is odd, it follows that **d** is odd; for whoever divides an odd number is odd, according to the previous premise. Therefore **d** would divide **b**. Thus **a** and **b** would not be prime to one another, which is against the hypothesis.

### ¶ Proposition 35.

<margin>
<note>A diagram showing five horizontal lines stacked vertically, decreasing in length from top to bottom. The top line is labeled d and 16. The second c and 8. The third b and 4. The fourth a and 2. The shortest, bottom line is labeled I <note>Unity.</note>.</note>
</margin>

**N**umbers doubled starting from two are "even-times even" <note>Latin: *pariter pares*. These are numbers that are powers of 2 ($2^n$), which can be halved repeatedly until reaching the number 1 without ever encountering an odd divisor.</note> only.
¶ Let unity, **a, b, c, d** be continuously proportional <note>A geometric progression: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16...</note>. Let **a** be the number two; I say all these are "even-times even," and if increased infinitely according to this proportion, no others are even-times even. This is established by definition, since by Proposition 12, any preceding number divides any following number by some of those same numbers, all of which must be even; and no other number divides any of them by Proposition 13, because **a**, which is two, following unity, is prime. That no other number aside from these is even-times even is established thus: if such a number is posited, let it be divided into two halves, and its half into two, and let this be done until a number or unity prevents further division, which must happen by the final postulate. If a number prevents this, that number will be odd, and since it divides the posited "even-times even" number, the original was not "even-times even." If unity prevents it, the number will be nothing other than those in the continuous doubling from unity.

### ¶ Proposition 36.

**A** number whose half is odd is <term>evenly odd</term> <note>Latin: *pariter impar*. In ancient number theory, this refers to an even number that, when divided by two, yields an odd number (e.g., 6, 10, 14).</note>.
¶ Let **a.** be a number whose half, let it be **b.**, is odd; I say that **a.** is evenly odd. For let **c.** be the number two <note>Latin: *binarius*</note>; it is thus manifest that from **c.** multiplied by **b.** comes **a.** Now let **d.** be any even number dividing **a.**, which divides it according to the quotient **e.** By the second part of Proposition 20 of Book VII, it will be that **c.** is to **d.** as **e.** is to **b.** Therefore, **c.** divides **b.** <note>The text suggests a proportional relationship where the factors must correspond.</note> because **c.** <note>the number two</note> divides **d.** <note>an even number</note>; thus, **e.** must be an odd number. For **b.** was odd by definition; therefore **a.** is evenly odd.

### ¶ Proposition 37.

**E**very even number that is not a power of two <note>Latin: *non duplus a duobus*, literally "not a double from two," referring to numbers like 12 or 20 which are not 2, 4, 8, 16, etc.</note> and whose half is even, is both <term>evenly even and oddly even</term> <note>Latin: *pariter par & impariter*. These are numbers that can be divided by two multiple times but eventually yield an odd factor.</note>.
¶ Let the number be **a.**, which is not a power of two, and let its half, **b.**, be even. I say that it is both evenly even and oddly even. For let **c.** be the number two, which clearly divides **a.** according to the quotient **b.** Because **a.** is not a power of two, it is necessary that if its half **b.** is divided into two other halves, and that half of a half into two others, eventually a number will be encountered that prevents further division <note>the division "stops" at a prime factor</note>; this number, because it does not accept division, will be odd. Let this number where the division stops be **d.** It is necessary to stop at some number, because if the division reached all the way to unity <note>the number 1</note>, then **a.** would be one of the numbers that are powers of two, which it is not. Regarding **d.**, it is manifest that it divides **a.** by this common notion: every number dividing another also divides every number multiplied by it. Therefore, let it divide **a.** according to the quotient **c.**, and **c.** will be even. Otherwise, if **d.** were a larger odd number, it would follow from Proposition 30 that **a.** would be odd <note>The text here follows the logic of factors</note>. Therefore, since the even number **b.** divides **a.** according to **c.**, which is also even (for it is two), and yet the even number **c.** divides the same **a.** according to **d.**, which is odd, it stands by definition that the number **a.** is both evenly even and oddly even; which is what was proposed.

Vertical dashed lines show how segments of the larger numbers correspond to the total lengths of the smaller numbers.</note>
</margin>

### ¶ Proposition 38.

**I**f from the second and the last of a series of numbers in continued proportion <note>A geometric progression, e.g., 8, 12, 18, 27 where the ratio is 1.5</note> an amount equal to the first is subtracted, then it is necessarily proved that as the remainder of the second is to the first, so is the remainder of the last to the sum of all those preceding it.
¶ Let **a.b., c.d., e.f., g.h.** be in continued proportion. Let **c.k.** be subtracted from **c.d.** equal to **a.b.**, and let **g.l.** be subtracted from **g.h.** also equal to **a.b.** I say then that the ratio of the remainder **k.d.** to **a.b.** is as the remainder **l.h.** is to the sum of **e.f., c.d.,** and **a.b.** Let **g.m.** be taken from **g.h.** equal to **e.f.**, and **g.n.** equal to **c.d.** Then **l.n.** will be equal to **k.d.** It is manifest through Proposition 12 of Book VII that since **g.h.** is to **g.m.** as **g.m.** is to **g.n.**, then the remainder **h.m.** is to the remainder **m.n.** as **g.h.** is to **g.m.**, and therefore as **e.f.** is to **c.d.** Similarly, **m.n.** will be to **l.n.** as **c.d.** is to **a.b.** By permutation, therefore, **h.m.** will be to **e.f.** and **m.n.** to **c.d.** as **n.l.** is to **a.b.** Thus, by joining them according to Proposition 13 of Book VII, the total **l.h.** (composed of **h.m., m.n.,** and **n.l.**) will be to the sum of **e.f., c.d.,** and **a.b.** as **l.n.** is to **a.b.**, and therefore as **k.d.** is to **a.b.**; which is what was proposed.

### ¶ Proposition 39.

**W**hen numbers beginning from unity are doubled continuously until their sum becomes a prime number, the last of these doubled numbers multiplied by the sum of them all produces a <term>perfect number</term> <note>A perfect number is a positive integer that is equal to the sum of its proper divisors, such as 6 or 28.</note>.
¶ Let **a., b., c., d.** be continuously doubled starting from unity <note>i.e., 1, 2, 4, 8</note>. Let their sum (including unity) be **e.**, and let **e.** be a prime number. Let **d.** be multiplied by **e.** to produce **f.g.** I say that **f.g.** is a perfect number. Let **e., b.k., l.** be taken as continuously doubled from **e.**, so that there are as many numbers in the sequence **e., b.k., l.** as there were in the sequence from unity to **d.** By equal proportionality, **l.** is to **e.** as **d.** is to **a.** Therefore, by the first part of Proposition 20 of Book VII, the product of **a.** and **l.** is **f.g.** Because **f.g.** comes from **d.** multiplied by **e.**, and because **a.** is the number two, **f.g.** is double **l.** Thus we have the series **e., b.k., l.,** and **f.g.**

...continually proportional: therefore, let there be taken from **b.** a part equal to **e.**, which is **m.b.**, and the remainder **b.n.q.** will also be equal to **e.** Likewise, from **f.g.** let there be taken a part equal to the same, which is **f.n.**, and by the preceding proof, **n.g.** will be equal to the sum of **e.** and **b.** and **b.k.** and **l.** But since **f.n.** is equal to **e.**, it is equal to the sum of **a.**, **b.**, **c.**, **d.**, and the unit <note>In Euclidean mathematics, the "unit" or "unity" refers to the number 1, the building block of all integers.</note>. Likewise, the whole **f.g.** is equal to the sum of all these doubled—namely **a.**, **b.**, **c.**, **d.**, and the unit—along with **e.**, **b.**, **k.**, and **l.** From all of these, it is manifest that they measure **f.g.**; specifically, **c.** according to **b.**, and **b.** according to **k.**, which is proven by the first part of the 20th proposition of Book VII, aided by equal proportionality where necessary. For as **d.** is to **c.**, so is **b.** to **e.**; and as **d.** is to **b.**, so is **k.** to **e.** by equal proportionality. Therefore, from **c.** into **b.** and from **b.** into **k.**, it is necessary to arrive at **f.g.**, which **d.** into **e.** had previously produced. If, therefore, no other number besides these measures **f.g.**, then by the definition, it will be a **perfect number** <term>numerus perfectus: a number equal to the sum of its proper divisors</term>. ¶ That no other number measures it is shown thus: if it were possible, let there be some number **p.** which measures it according to **q.**; then by the 33rd proposition of Book VII, **e.** would measure one of them. Let it be supposed that it measures **p.**, and because by the second part of the 20th proposition of Book VII, **q.** is to **d.** as **e.** is to **p.**, it follows that **q.** measures **d.** Therefore, since **a.**, which follows the unit, is prime <note>Euclid is using 2 as the first prime number here.</note>, for it is the number two <note>Latin: *binarius*</note>, then **q.** must be (by the 13th proposition of this book) either **a.**, **b.**, or **c.** Whichever of these it may be, **p.** will be either **l.**, **k.**, or **b.** For if **q.** were **a.**, it is established that **p.** would be **l.**; if it were **b.**, **p.** would be **k.**; and if **c.**, **p.** would also be **b.** Therefore, **p.** is not different from those already established, as had been supposed. It remains, therefore, that **f.g.** is a perfect number, which was to be demonstrated.

<note>A large ornamental woodcut drop cap 'Q' featuring leafy scrolls and a circular center.</note>
**Q**uantities for which there is a single common quantity measuring them are called **commensurable** <term>communicantes</term>. However, those for which there is no single common quantity measuring them are called **incommensurable** <term>incommensurabiles</term>. Lines are said to be commensurable in power <note>This refers to the squares of the lines being commensurable, even if the lines themselves are not.</note> when a single common surface measures their square surfaces. Lines are called incommensurable in power when no single common surface measures their square surfaces. Since this is so, it is manifest that to any given line, many others are incommensurable: some in length only, and some in both length and power. Furthermore, let the given line with which we reason be called **rational** <term>rationalis</term>. Lines commensurable to it are called rational; those incommensurable to it are called **irrational** <term>irrationalis</term> or **surds** <term>surdae: from the Latin word for 'deaf' or 'mute', used here for numbers that cannot be expressed as a ratio</term>. Likewise, the square of the surface from which we reason by hypothesis is called rational. Surfaces commensurable to it are called rational. Those surfaces incommensurable to it are called irrational or surds. The sides that can produce those squares are called rational. ¶ Any quantity can be multiplied so that it exceeds any given quantity of the same kind.

### ¶ Proposition 1.

<margin>
<note>A geometrical diagram consisting of two horizontal arrangements of line segments. The upper set shows segments a, b, and c. The lower set shows a continuous line divided into segments d, e, and f, with shorter segments g, h and k, l, m placed below them for comparison. This illustrates the process of "exhaustion" or repeated subtraction.</note>
</margin>

<note>A large ornamental woodcut drop cap 'D' decorated with floral patterns and a small figure.</note>
**G**iven two unequal quantities, if from the greater is subtracted more than its half, and from the remainder more than its half is subtracted, and this is done successively in the same manner, it is necessary that at length a quantity remains which is less than the lesser of the two given quantities. ¶ Let there be two unequal quantities, **a.** and **b.c.**, where **b.c.** is the greater. I say that more than the half can be subtracted from **b.c.** or its remainder so many times that a quantity less than **a.** must necessarily remain. For let **a.** be multiplied as many times as it takes to exceed **b.c.**, and let its multiple be **d.e.f.**, which is greater than **b.c.** Now let there be subtracted from **b.c.** more than its half, which is **b.g.**; and from the remainder, which is **g.c.**, let more than its half be subtracted, which is **g.h.** Let this be done as many times as **b.c.** is divided into parts, as many times as **a.** is contained in **d.e.f.** I say then that the final remainder, which is here **h.c.**, is less than **a.** Multiply...

<meta>This page continues the demonstration of Proposition 1 of Book X, regarding the "method of exhaustion," and proceeds to the foundational propositions concerning commensurable and incommensurable magnitudes (the Euclidean algorithm applied to geometry).</meta>

...for however many times **b.c.** is multiplied, **a.** [is exceeded by] **d. e. f.**; and let its multiple be **k. l. m.** Since, therefore, each of the quantities **k., l.,** and **m.** is equal to **b.c.**, it follows that **z.k.** is less than **b.g.**, but **z.l.** is less than **g.b.** And because **m.** is equal to **b.c.**, it will be, by common notion <note>original: *conceptionem*; Euclid's "Common Notions" are the basic axioms or self-evident truths used as the foundation for his proofs</note>, that **k. l. m.** is less than **d. c. f.** Since **d. e. f.** is to **a.** as **k. l. m.** is to **b.c.**, and **d. e. f.** is greater than **k. l. m.**, it follows by the 14th proposition of the Fifth Book <note>Book V, Proposition 14 states that in four proportional magnitudes, if the first is greater than the third, the second will be greater than the fourth.</note> that **a.** is greater than **b.e.**, which is what was proposed. Thus, it follows that if from the greater magnitude **a.** more than half is taken, and from the remainder more than half is taken, and this is done as many times as necessary, the greater magnitude will eventually be divided into as many parts as the smaller is contained in any of its multiples, with the greater of the proposed quantities exceeding it by as much as one likes.

¶ One must observe, however, that the 15th proposition of the Third Book <note>Book III, Proposition 15 (in some editions numbered 16) discusses the "angle of contingency" or "horn angle" between a tangent and the circumference of a circle, which Euclid argues is smaller than any acute rectilinear angle.</note> seems to contradict this by proposing that the angle of contingency is smaller than any angle contained by two straight lines. For if any rectilinear angle is given, and from it more than half is taken, and again more than half of the remainder, it seems necessary that this could be done so many times that a rectilinear angle smaller than the angle of contingency would remain. The 15th proposition of the Third Book argues the opposite; but these angles are not of the same name <note>original: *univoce*; meaning they are not comparable in the same category or "univocal."</note>, for they are not of the same kind, being simple curves versus straight lines. In truth, the angle of contingency cannot be taken so many times that it exceeds any rectilinear angle. As is clear from the previous demonstration, for the present to follow from the antecedent, it is plain that any rectilinear angle is greater than an infinite number of angles of contingency.

### Proposition 2

<margin>
<note>A geometric line diagram shows various segments labeled 'a' through 'e'. Line 'a' represents the primary magnitude being analyzed, while segments 'b', 'd', and 'e' illustrate the "Euclidean Algorithm"—the process of repeated subtraction used to find a common measure or prove its absence.</note>
<note>Two rectangular figures of different proportions are shown, likely representing the magnitudes whose commensurability is being tested in the proof.</note>
</margin>

If there are two unequal quantities, and from the greater a part equal to the smaller is subtracted as many times as possible until a remainder less than the smaller is left; and then from the smaller a part equal to that remainder is subtracted until a remainder less than it is left; and again from the first remainder a part equal to the second remainder is subtracted until a remainder less than it is left; and if in this continuous process of subtraction no remainder is ever found that measures the one left before it: then those two quantities are necessarily incommensurable <note>original: *incommensurabiles*; magnitudes that have no common unit of measure, such as the side and the diagonal of a square.</note>.

¶ A similar rule was proposed for numbers in the first proposition of the Seventh Book. Let there be two unequal quantities **a.** and **b.**, with **a.** being the greater. If reciprocal subtraction is performed as far as possible, and no quantity is ever reached that—even if done infinitely—stops the subtraction or measures the one left before it, I say they are incommensurable. If, however, there were a common measure **c.** for them: let **b.** be subtracted from **a.** as many times as possible, and let the remainder be **d.** Then let this remainder **d.** be subtracted from **b.** as many times as possible, and let the remainder be **e.** Let this subtraction be performed as many times as necessary until from either of the two quantities **a.** or **b.** there remains a part less than **c.** (for this must be possible by the preceding proposition). If, in this case, **e.** is less than **c.**; since **c.** measures **b.** which was subtracted from **a.**, and also measures **a.**, it will also measure the remainder **d.** by common notion. Therefore, since it measures **d.** (which was subtracted from **b.**), and also measures **b.** itself, it will also measure the remainder **e.** But **e.** was smaller than the measure **c.**; therefore, a quantity would measure one smaller than itself, which is impossible.

### Proposition 3

Given two unequal commensurable <note>original: *communicantibus*; literally "sharing" or "communicating," referring to magnitudes that share a common measure.</note> quantities, to find the greatest common quantity that measures them both. From this it is manifest: that which measures two quantities also measures the greatest common measure that measures them both.
¶ If you are familiar with the second proposition of the Seventh Book, you cannot be ignorant of this demonstration, for the process is the same in both.

### Proposition 4

Given three commensurable quantities, to find the greatest common quantity that measures them both.
¶ This is evident from the third proposition of the Seventh Book, just as the previous was from the second of the Seventh.

The ratio of any two commensurable <term>commensurable: quantities that can be measured by the same shared unit</term> quantities is as the ratio of a number to a number.
¶ Let there be two commensurable quantities, **a.** and **b.**; I say that their ratio is as that of some number to another number. For let **c.** be the <term>greatest common measure: the largest unit that fits perfectly into both quantities without leaving a remainder</term> found as taught in the second proposition of this book. Let it measure **a.** according to the number **d.**, and **b.** according to the number **e.** <note>original: "c."; the OCR likely misread 'e' as 'c' here, as the logic requires a new number for the second quantity</note>. Therefore, **a.** is to **c.** as **d.** is to one, because just as **a.** is a multiple of **c.**, so is **d.** a multiple of unity. And **c.** is to **b.** as one is to **e.**, since just as **c.** is a sub-multiple of **b.**, so unity is a sub-multiple of **e.** Therefore, by equal proportionality <note>original: *equam proportionalitatem*; a logical step where if a:b and b:c, then a:c</note>, **a.** is to **b.** as **d.** is to **e.**, which is what was proposed.

### Proposition 6.

<margin>
<note>A geometric diagram showing several horizontal line segments. A longer segment is labeled 'f', with points marked 'g' and 'e' along its length. Below it is a segment labeled 'b'. To the right are two small segments labeled 'c' and 'd'.</note>

If there are two quantities whose ratio to each other is as a number to a number, those two quantities must be commensurable.
¶ This is the converse of the previous proposition: if **a.** is to **b.** as the number **c.** is to the number **d.**, the two quantities **a.** and **b.** will be commensurable. For let **e.** measure **a.** as many times as unity is in **d.**, and measure **f.** as many times as unity is in **c.** Since, therefore, **f.** is to **e.** as **c.** is to unity, and **e.** is to **b.** as unity is to **d.**, it will be by equal proportionality that **f.** is to **b.** as **c.** is to **d.**, and therefore also as **a.** is to **b.** Thus, by the first part of the 9th proposition of the Fifth Book, **f.** is equal to **a.** Since **e.** measures **f.**, by common notion <note>original: *conceptionem*; self-evident mathematical axioms</note> it will also measure **a.** Therefore **a.** and **b.** are commensurable, for **e.** also measured **b.**, which is what was proposed.

For any two square surfaces whose sides are commensurable in length, the ratio of one to the other is as a square number to a square number. If, however, the ratio of one square surface to another square surface is as the ratio of a square number to a square number, their sides will be commensurable in length. But if the ratio of the square surface to the square surface is not as a square number to a square number, their sides will be incommensurable <term>incommensurable: having no common unit of measurement, like the side and diagonal of a square</term> in length.

But if the ratio of **c.** to **d.** is not as a square number to a square number, **a.** and **b.** will be incommensurable in length, and vice versa. The first is clear thus: if **a.** and **b.** are commensurable in length, then by the 5th proposition they will be in the ratio of two numbers, which are **e.** and **f.**, whose squares are **g.** and **h.** Because **c.** is to **d.** as the square of **a.** is to the square of **b.** by the 18th proposition of the Sixth Book, it follows that **c.** is to **d.** as the duplicate ratio of **e.** to **f.** But also **g.** is to **h.** as the duplicate ratio <note>original: *duplicata*; in Euclidean geometry, the ratio of areas is the "duplicate" (square) of the ratio of the sides</note> of **e.** to **f.**; therefore **c.** is to **d.** as **g.** is to **h.**, which is the first part. The second is thus: let **c.** be to **d.** as the square number **g.** is to the square number **h.**; I say that **a.** and **b.** will be commensurable in length. For since **c.** is to **d.** as the duplicate of **a.** to **b.** by the 18th of the Sixth Book, and **g.** is to **h.** by the 11th of the Eighth Book as the duplicate of **e.** to **f.**, it follows that the simple ratio of **a.** to **b.** is as the simple ratio of **e.** to **f.** by the 6th proposition; therefore **a.** and **b.** are commensurable, which is the second part. The third part is clear from the first by the destruction of the consequent <note>a logical proof method (modus tollens)</note>. ...[if the ratio] is not as that of square numbers, it follows that the diagonal is incommensurable <term>incommensurable: quantities that have no common unit of measure, like the side and diagonal of a square</term> to the side in length. Otherwise, since four is a square number, all even-times-even numbers would be squares, as would infinitely many others that are not squares. Aristotle <note>original: "Ar."; referring to Aristotle’s *Prior Analytics*, where he famously mentions the proof of the diagonal's incommensurability</note> leads to this absurdity: if the diagonal is assumed to be commensurable to the side, then an odd number will be equal to an even number, which is shown thus: 

Let the diagonal be **a.b.** and let it be commensurable to the side **a.c.** By the fifth proposition [of this book], the ratio of **a.b.** to **a.c.** will be as some number to another. Let these numbers be **e.** and **f.**, which are the smallest in their proportion <note>meaning the fraction is in its simplest form</note>; because of this, one of them must be odd. Now let **k.** be double **h.**; by definition, **k.** will be even. Since the ratio of **a.b.** to **a.c.** is as **e.** to **f.**, then by the 8th proposition of Book VI and the 11th of Book VIII, the square of **a.b.** is to the square of **a.c.** as **g.** is to **h.** Now, **g.** is double **h.** because the square of the diagonal is double the square of the side—according to the second-to-last proposition of the first book <note>Prop. I.47, the Pythagorean Theorem</note>. And because **k.** is also double **h.**, it follows by the 9th proposition of Book V that the odd number **g.** is equal to the even number **k.**

On the other hand, if **e.** is even and **f.** is odd: the ratio of **f.** to half of **e.** (which we call **l.**) will be as **a.c.** is to half of **a.b.** (which we call **a.d.**). Therefore, the ratio of the square of **a.c.** to the square of **a.d.** is as the ratio of the number **h.** (which is odd by the 30th of Book IX) to the square of the number **l.** (which we call **m.**). Let **k.** be double **m.**; by definition, **k.** is even. But since the square of **a.c.** is double the square of **a.d.** by the second-to-last of the first book, **h.** will be double **m.** Since **k.** is also double **m.**, then by the 9th of Book V, the odd number **h.** is equal to the even number **k.**, which is what was to be proven.

### Proposition 8.

If there are two quantities commensurable with one [same] quantity, it is necessary that they are also commensurable with each other.
¶ Let each of the two quantities **a.** and **b.** be commensurable with quantity **c.** I say that **a.** and **b.** are commensurable. For by the 5th proposition, the ratio of **a.** to **c.** is as a number to a number; similarly, by the same proposition, the ratio of **c.** to **b.** is as a number to a number. Let the ratio of number **d.** to number **e.** be as **a.** to **c.**, and the ratio of number **f.** to number **g.** be as **c.** to **b.** Now, the ratios **d.** to **e.** and **f.** to **g.** are contained in three terms, which are **h.**, **k.**, and **l.**, as the 4th proposition of Book VIII teaches. By equal proportionality, the ratio of **a.** to **b.** will be as number **h.** to number **l.** Therefore, by the 6th proposition, **a.** and **b.** are commensurable, which is what was proposed.
¶ From this it also follows that if two quantities are commensurable with each other, whatever one of them is commensurable with, the other is as well; and whatever one is not commensurable with, neither is the other. For let two quantities **a.** and **b.** be commensurable, and let there be any quantity **c.** with which **a.** is commensurable. I say that **b.** will be commensurable with the same, which is evident from this eighth proposition, since both are commensurable with **a.** by hypothesis. Furthermore, if **a.** and **b.** are commensurable as before, and **c.** is any quantity with which **a.** is not commensurable, I say that **b.** will not be commensurable with the same. For if **c.** were commensurable with **b.**, since by hypothesis **a.** is also commensurable with **b.**, then by this eighth proposition **a.** and **c.** would be commensurable. But it was posited that they were not; therefore, what we said stands.

<note>A geometric diagram shows a square with vertices labeled b (top-left), c (top-right), and a (bottom-right). A diagonal line connects b and a. A point d is marked at the center of the square. Above the square is a horizontal line segment with three points labeled b, d, and c.</note>
...[If line a and] **b.** are incommensurable <term>incommensurable: quantities that have no common unit of measure</term>: I say that line **c.** will also be incommensurable to each of them, and vice versa: just as if **c.** were incommensurable to either one of them, it would also be incommensurable to the other, and they would be incommensurable to each other. 
First, let **a.** and **b.** be commensurable <term>commensurable: quantities that can be measured by the same shared unit</term>; let their common measure be **d.** Since **d.** measures both of them, by a principle similar to the third-to-last proposition, it will also measure the whole, line **c.** Therefore, by definition, **c.** will be commensurable to both **a.** and **b.** Conversely, if **c.** is commensurable to both, and **d.** is the common measure of all, it stands by definition that **a.** and **b.** are commensurable. But if **c.** is commensurable with only one of them, say **a.**, I say it will also be commensurable with **b.**, and that **a.** and **b.** will be commensurable with each other. For let **d.** be the common measure of **c.** and **a.** Since **d.** measures the whole [c] and the part taken away [a], by the general principle it will also measure the remainder, namely **b.** By definition, therefore, **c.** is commensurable with **b.**, and **a.** is also commensurable with **b.** If, however, **a.** and **b.** are incommensurable, **c.** will be incommensurable to both; for if it were commensurable with both or even one of them, then **a.** and **b.** would be commensurable with each other, which contradicts the hypothesis. Similarly, conversely, if **c.** is incommensurable to both or even to one of them, it will be incommensurable to the remaining part, and they will be incommensurable to each other. This is clear from what was demonstrated before by the denial of the consequence <note>original: "a destructione consequentis"; a logical method (Modus Tollens) where one proves a premise false by showing its conclusion is impossible</note>.

->Proposition 10<-

<note>Two sets of horizontal line segments. The upper set consists of two segments labeled 'a' and 'c'. The lower set consists of two segments labeled 'b' and 'd'.</note>
<note>A decorative drop cap 'O' depicts foliage patterns inside a square frame.</note> Of any four proportional quantities, if the first is commensurable to the second, the third will also be commensurable to the fourth. If, however, the first is incommensurable to the second, the third will also be incommensurable to the fourth.
Let there be four proportional quantities **a. b. c. d.** I say that if **a.** is commensurable with **b.**, then **c.** will also be commensurable with **d.** If **a.** is incommensurable to **b.**, then **c.** will also be incommensurable to **d.** And if **a.** is commensurable with **b.** in power <term>in power: quantities whose squares are commensurable, even if the lines themselves are not</term> only, then **c.** will also be commensurable with **d.** in power only. However, the author <note>Euclid</note> does not explicitly state this last point, though it is easily seen from the prior demonstration. For if **a.** is commensurable with **b.**, then by the 5th proposition [of this book], the ratio of **a.** to **b.** will be as a number to a number. Let this ratio be as the number **e.** to the number **f.** And since, by the hypothesis, the ratio of **a.** to **b.** is as **c.** to **d.**, then **c.** to **d.** will also be as the number **e.** to the number **f.** Thus, by the 6th proposition, **c.** is commensurable with **d.**, which is the first point. The second point is clear from the first by the denial of the consequence. For if **a.** is incommensurable to **b.**, it is necessary that **c.** be incommensurable to **d.**; for if **c.** were commensurable to it, then since **c.** is to **d.** as **a.** is to **b.** by hypothesis, then by the first part, **a.** would be commensurable with **b.**, but it was not. Thus all that the author proposes is established. Furthermore, regarding what we added—namely that if **a.** is commensurable with **b.** in power only, then **c.** is commensurable with **d.** in power only—it is demonstrated thus: if **a.** is not commensurable with **b.** in length <term>in length: quantities that can be measured by the same line segment</term>, then by the second part of this proof, **c.** will not be commensurable with **d.** in length. But since the square of **a.** is commensurable with the square of **b.** by hypothesis, then by the 5th proposition the ratio of the square of line **a.** to the square of line **b.** will be as a number to a number, which we call **e.** and **f.** And because the ratio of the square of **c.** to the square of **d.** is as the square of line **a.** to the square of line **b.**, it follows that the square of **c.** to the square of **d.** is also as the number **e.** to the number **f.** Therefore, by the 6th proposition, **c.** and **d.** are commensurable in power; and since they are not commensurable in length, the proposition is proven.

<meta>This page continues the demonstration of Book X of Euclid's Elements, following the previous discussion on the properties of commensurable and incommensurable magnitudes. Here, the text provides a practical construction for finding lines that are incommensurable to a given line, and then transitions into Proposition 12 regarding the proportions of squares between four lines.</meta>

<margin>
<note>A geometric diagram in the top right margin shows the construction of line segments. A vertical line **e.** meets a horizontal line containing segments **a.**, **f.**, and **D.** To the left are two separate reference segments: **b.** with the number 4 below it, and **c.** with the number 3 below it.</note>
</margin>
I therefore take two numbers that do not have the same proportion as any two square numbers <note>original: "numerorum quadratorum"</note>. Let these be **b.** and **c.** It is easy to find such numbers because any square number to any non-square number has a proportion that no two square numbers share, as confirmed by Proposition 22 of the Eighth Book. Having taken two such numbers, I find a line **d.** such that the square of line **a.** is to the square of line **d.** as the number **b.** is to the number **c.** I find this line in the following way: I divide line **a.** into as many equal parts as there are units in number **b.**, which I do easily with the help of Propositions 11 or 12 of the Sixth Book. From there, I erect line **e.** perpendicularly at the end of line **a.**, and let it contain the same measurement of one of the parts of **a.** as many times as there are units in **c.**

Because, therefore, according to the first proposition of the Sixth Book, the proportion of the square of line **a.** to the area <term>area: the text uses "superficies," referring to the rectangle formed by two lines</term> produced by **a.** and **e.** is as line **a.** is to line **e.**, and thus as number **b.** is to number **c.** If line **d.** is placed as a mean proportional <term>mean proportional: a value between two others such that the first is to the mean as the mean is to the last (a:d = d:e)</term> between **a.** and **e.**—as taught in Proposition 9 of the Sixth Book—then, according to the first part of Proposition 16 of that same book, the square of **d.** will be equal to the area produced by **a.** and **e.** Thus, the proportion of the square of line **a.** to the square of line **d.** will be as number **b.** is to number **c.** For this reason, **a.** and **d.** are commensurable in power <term>commensurable in power: lines whose squares can be measured by the same shared area</term> by definition and by the final part [of the previous theorem], yet they are incommensurable in length <term>incommensurable in length: lines that cannot be measured by a single shared unit of length</term>. Thus, the first line **d.**, which was sought, has been found.

I find the other line in this way: I place line **f.** as a mean proportional between **a.** and **d.**, as taught in Proposition 9 of the Sixth Book. By the corollary of Proposition 17 of the Sixth Book, the square of **a.** will be to the square of **f.** as **a.** is to **d.** Therefore, by the second part of Proposition 10, the square of **a.** is incommensurable to the square of **f.** Consequently, line **f.** is incommensurable to line **a.** in power, and therefore also in length. Thus, **f.** is the second line that was to be found. And so the proposal is complete.

->### **Proposition 12**<-

<margin>
<note>A geometric diagram in the middle right margin shows a semicircle with internal chords and a vertical radius. Below the semicircle, sets of horizontal line segments are labeled **a.**, **b.**, **e.** on the left, and **c.**, **d.**, and **f.** on the right.</note>
</margin>
Of any four proportional lines, if the square of the first is greater than the square of the second by the square of some line commensurable to the first in length, it is necessary that the square of the third is also greater than the square of the fourth by the square of some line commensurable to the third in length. But if the square of the first is greater than the square of the second by the square of a line incommensurable to it in length, then the square of the third will also be greater than the square of the fourth by the square of a line incommensurable to it in length.

Let there be four proportional lines **a.**, **b.**, **c.**, and **d.** Let **a.** be greater than **b.**, and **c.** be greater than **d.** Let also the square of **a.** be greater than the square of **b.** by the square of line **e.**, and the square of **c.** be greater than the square of **d.** by the square of line **f.** I say that if **a.** is commensurable to **e.** in length, then **c.** will also be commensurable to **f.** in length. And if **a.** is not commensurable to **e.** in length, neither will **c.** be commensurable to **f.** in length. Furthermore, if **a.** is commensurable to **e.** only in power, **c.** will also be commensurable to **f.** only in power. However, the author does not propose this last point, as it is easily seen from the previous demonstration. Since the proportion of **a.** to **b.** is as **c.** to **d.**, the proportion of the square of **a.** to the square of **b.** will be as the square of **c.** is to the square of **d.** And since the square of **a.** is equal to the squares of the two lines **b.** and **e.**, and similarly the square of **c.** is equal to the squares of the two lines **d.** and **f.**, the proportion of the squares of the two lines **b.** and **e.** [to the square of **e.**] will be as the squares of **d.** and **f.** are [to the square of **f.**]. Therefore, by division, the square of **b.** will be to the square of **e.** as the square of **d.** is to the square of **f.** Thus, **b.** is to **e.** as **d.** is to **f.** Likewise, by equal proportionality, **a.** will be to **e.** as **c.** is to **f.** Therefore, through the first part of [this book], the first part of this proposition is established; through the second part, the second is established; and through the third part added there, the third part added here is established.

# BOOK X

It is necessary that the square of the longer line be greater than the square of the shorter line by as much as the square of some line that is commensurable <note>original: "communicantis", meaning they share a common measure</note> in length with that longer line. If indeed the longer line is more powerful <note>original: "potentior", a term meaning the square of the line is greater</note> than the shorter line by the square of a line commensurable to it in length, then if a surface equal to a fourth part of the square of the shorter line is applied to the longer line—such that it is deficient <term>deficient: a technical term in the "application of areas," where a shape is constructed along a line but stops short of the end by a specific geometric figure</term> by a square surface—it is necessary that the same longer line be divided into two commensurable parts.

<margin>
<note>A geometric diagram illustrates Proposition 13. It shows a horizontal line segment with points marked **a**, **d**, **f**, and **b**. A rectangle is built upon parts of this line. Below the main construction, a separate line segment labeled **c** is provided as a reference.</note>
</margin>

¶ Let there be two lines, **a b** and **c**, where **a b** is the greater. Let a fourth part of the square of line **c** be applied to line **a b** in such a way that a square surface is missing to complete the length of **a b**. This is indeed possible by Proposition 27 of the Sixth Book, which is easily done in this manner: let **a b** be divided into two lines **a d** and **d b** such that between them falls half of line **c** as a mean proportional <note>original: "continue proportionalis"</note>. How this is done will be taught at the end of this demonstration. By Proposition 16 of the Sixth Book, the surface of **a d** multiplied by **d b** (which let be **d c**) will be equal to the square of half of line **c**. Therefore, by Proposition 4 of the Second Book, this will be under four times the square of line **c**. There is also missing a square surface to complete line **a b**, since **a d** is equal to **d g** and **d b** is equal to **g e**. I say, therefore, that if the surface **d c** divides line **a b** into two commensurable parts, line **a b** will be more powerful than line **c** by the square of some line commensurable with it in length, and vice versa. However, since line **a b** is greater than line **c**, **a d** will not be equal to **d b**. For if they were, the surface **d e** would be a square; and since it is equal to the square of half of line **c**, **a d** would be equal to half of **c**, and the whole of **a b** would be equal to the whole of **c**, which is the hypothesis. Therefore, **a d** is not equal to **d b**. Thus, from the greater of them, which is **d b**, let **d f** be cut off equal to **a d**. By Proposition 8 of the Second Book, the square of the whole **a b** will be equal to twice the product of **d b** and **d a** four times, plus the square of **f b**. Therefore, line **a b** will be more powerful than line **c** by the square of line **f b**, which must be commensurable with the whole **a b** if line **a d** is commensurable with line **d b**. For if this is so, **d b** will be commensurable with **d f**, which is its equal. Therefore, by Proposition 9, **b f** is commensurable with **f d**, and thus with the whole **a d**, and because of this with the whole **a f**, and therefore with the whole **a b**. Thus the first part is clear.

¶ The converse of this is also clear: let **a b** be more powerful than **c** by the square of line **f b**, which is commensurable with it in length. I say then that if a fourth part of the square of line **c** is added to line **a b** so that a square surface is missing, it will divide line **a b** into two commensurable parts. Let **f a** be divided into equal parts at **d**, and let the surface **d c** be made from **d b** and **d a**. A square surface will be missing to complete line **a b**, and by Proposition 8 of the Second Book, the square of **a b** is equal to four times the surface **d e**, plus the square of **f b**. Therefore, four times the surface **d e** is equal to the square of **c**. Thus, the surface **d e** is equal to a fourth part of the square of **c**. I say, therefore, that **d b** is commensurable with **a d**, since **f b** is commensurable with **a b**. If this is so, and **a d** is commensurable with **a b**, it will also be commensurable with **a f** by Proposition 9; therefore also with **a d**, and also with **d f**. Thus **d b** is commensurable with **a d**, which was the second point.

<margin>
<note>The diagram shows the construction for finding the mean proportional. A semicircle is drawn over the diameter **a b**. From point **g** on the diameter, a perpendicular line **g f** rises to meet the arc. A line **e f** runs parallel to the base. Reference segments **d** and **c** are shown below.</note>
</margin>

¶ Now, however, it must be demonstrated how line **a b**, when it has been set as greater than line **c**, can be so divided that between its parts falls the half of line **c** as a mean proportional. ¶ For when it is so divided, the surface made from one part into the other will be equal to the square of half of line **c**, and that surface will be equal to a fourth part of the square of line **c** applied to line **a b** such that a square surface is missing. This is done by dividing **a b** into equal parts at **d**. Let a semicircle **a f b** be drawn over it, and similarly **b e** perpendicular to **a b**, which is set equal to half of line **c**. Let **e f** be drawn parallel to **a b** until it cuts the circumference of the semicircle at point **f**. It must necessarily cut it, since line **a b** is greater than line **c**. Let **f g** be drawn perpendicular to **a b**, which, since by Proposition 34 of the First Book it is equal to line **e b**, will also be equal to half of line **c**. Therefore, let lines **f a** and **f b** be drawn. By the first part of Proposition 30 of the Third Book, the angle **a f b** will be a right angle; and therefore, by the first part of the corollary to Proposition 8 of the Sixth Book, line **f g** will be a mean proportional between **a g** and **g b**. Therefore, half of line **c**, which is equal to it, will also be a proportional between the same, which is what we proposed.

->Proposition 14<-

<meta>This page continues the logical proofs for Proposition 14 and introduces Propositions 15, 16, and 17 of Euclid’s Book X. It builds upon the "application of areas" technique established on the previous page, focusing on the relationship between rational lines and the rectangular areas they form.</meta>

If there are two unequal lines, and if a surface equal to the fourth part of the square of the shorter line is applied to the longer line so that it is deficient by a square figure, and this application divides the longer line into two parts that are incommensurable <note>original: "incommensurabiles", meaning they share no common unit of measurement</note>; then the square of the longer line is more powerful <note>original: "potentior", meaning the square of this line is greater than the square of the other</note> than the shorter by the square of a line incommensurable in length with the longer line. If, however, the longer line is more powerful than the shorter by the square of a line incommensurable in length with it, and if a surface equal to the fourth part of the square of the shorter is applied to the longer and is deficient by a square surface, it is necessary that the applied surface divide that longer line into two incommensurable portions.

<margin>
<note>A geometric diagram showing a horizontal line segment with points labeled **a**, **d**, **f**, **b** from left to right. Above point **d** is a point **g**, and above point **b** is a point **e**. A rectangle is formed above segment **db**. A diagonal line connects point **a** to point **g**.</note>
</margin>

¶ This 14th proposition follows from the previous premise and its converse, and its arrangement does not differ from the arrangement of that premise. Indeed, the method of reasoning is the same in both cases. For if **a.d.** is not commensurable <note>original: "non communicet"</note> with **d.b.**, then **d.f.** (which is equal to it) will not be commensurable with the same **d.b.**; thus, by the 9th proposition, **d.f.** will not be commensurable with **f.b.**, and therefore neither will **a.f.** For **a.f.** and **e.f.** are commensurable as a multiple and its part. Thus, neither will **a.b.** be commensurable with line **f.b.** If this is the case—namely, if **a.b.** is not commensurable with **f.b.**—it will not be commensurable with **a.f.**, and therefore neither with **a.d.** nor **d.f.**; thus, **a.b.** is not commensurable with **d.a.** This 14th proposition can also be demonstrated through the preceding one: the first part of this from the second part of that, and the second from the first, by a proof through contradiction <note>original: "a destructione", referring to *reductio ad absurdum*</note>. For if **a.d.** and **d.b.** are not commensurable, then **a.b.** and **f.b.** will also not be commensurable; for if **a.b.** and **b.f.** were commensurable, it would follow from the second part of the premise that **a.d.** would be commensurable with **d.b.**, but it was assumed that they are not. The same logic applies to the second part: if **b.a.** and **b.f.** are not commensurable, then **a.d.** and **d.b.** will not be commensurable. For if they were, it would follow from the first part of the premise that **a.b.** and **b.f.** are commensurable, but they are not; therefore, the proposition is clear.

### Proposition 15.

<margin>
<note>A geometric diagram showing a horizontal line segment with points **a**, **b**, **d**. Arcs and lines connect them to a vertex above. A separate shorter line segment labeled **c** is placed below the main construction.</note>
</margin>

Every rectangular surface contained by two lines that are rational <note>original: "rationales", meaning their lengths can be expressed as a ratio</note> in length is proved to be rational.
¶ Let there be two lines, **a.b.** and **b.c.**, containing the rectangle **a.c.**, which are rational in length. I say that the surface **a.c.** is rational. For if a square is described on one of them, such as **c.d.** on line **b.c.**, then by the first proposition of the Sixth Book, the area **c.d.** is to **a.c.** as the length **b.d.** is to **a.b.** Since **b.d.** is commensurable in length with **a.b.** by hypothesis (because it is equal to **b.c.**), it follows from the first part of the 10th Book that **c.d.** is commensurable with **a.c.** Since **c.d.** is rational by definition, **a.c.** will also be rational, which is what was to be proved.

### Proposition 16.

<margin>
<note>A geometric diagram of a rectangle with vertices **a** and **b** at the bottom left and right corners. A point **d** is marked on the top edge. Below the rectangle is a separate line segment labeled **c**.</note>
</margin>

If a rational rectangular surface is applied <term>applied: the "application of areas" (parabolē) is a method where a known area is shaped into a rectangle along a given line to find the length of the unknown side</term> to a line rational in length, its second side will be rational in length and commensurable in length to the first side.
This is essentially the converse of the previous proposition. If the surface **a.c.** applied to line **a.b.** (which is rational in length) is rational, I say that its second side, **b.c.**, will also be rational in length and commensurable with the first side. For let **a.d.** be the square of **a.b.**; it will be rational by definition, and for this reason, it will be commensurable with the rational surface **a.c.** Since, by the first proposition of the Sixth Book, **a.d.** is to **a.c.** as **d.b.** is to **b.c.**, and since **d.a.** is commensurable with **a.c.**, it follows from the first part of the 10th Book that **b.d.** is commensurable with **b.c.** Therefore, it is commensurable with **b.a.**, which is equal to it. But **b.a.** is rational, therefore **b.c.** is also rational by definition; thus the proposition stands.

### Proposition 17.

To find two lines that are rational in power <note>original: "potentia tantum", meaning their squares are commensurable, but the lines themselves are not</note> only and are commensurable, such that the square of the longer is more powerful than the square of the shorter by the square of a line commensurable to it in length.
¶ The goal is to find two lines that are rational and commensurable only in their squares, where the square of the longer exceeds the square of the shorter by the square of a line that is commensurable in length with that longer line.

<note>A geometric diagram showing a semicircle with vertex **c** on the arc and a base line **ab**. Below the semicircle, a line segment is divided into parts by points **d**, **f**, and **e**, with the number 4 above segment **df** and the number 5 above segment **fe**.</note>

I take therefore a certain rational line which is **a. b.**, upon which I describe a semicircle **a. c. b.**; and having taken some number such as **d. e.**, I divide it into two numbers **d. f.** and **f. e.** such that the ratio <note>original: "proportio"</note> of **d. e.** to **d. f.** is as a square number to a square number, but let the ratio of **d. e.** to **f. e.** not be as a square number to a square number. Such a number is any square divisible into a square and a non-square, such as 9, which is divided into 4 and 5, and all their equal multiples. And I find a line to whose square the square of line **a. b.** has the same ratio as the number **d. e.** has to the number **d. f.**; the method for finding such a line was stated in the demonstration of the 5th [proposition]. This found line, which is necessarily smaller than **a. b.**, I fit within the semicircle **a. c. b.** according to the first [proposition] of the fourth [book], and let it be **a. c.**; then I draw the line **c. b.** I say that the two lines **a. b.** and **c. b.** are those we seek. 

Therefore, by the first part of the 30th [proposition] of the third [book], angle **c.** is a right angle; and thus, by the penultimate [proposition] of the first [book] <note>This refers to the Pythagorean Theorem, Proposition 47 of Book I.</note>, the square of **a. b.** is equal to the squares of the two lines **a. c.** and **c. b.** And because the ratio of the square of line **a. b.** to the square of line **a. c.** is as **d. e.** to **d. f.** by hypothesis, it will follow by the conversion of ratios <note>original: "eversam proportionalitatem"</note> that the ratio of the square of line **a. b.** to the square of line **c. b.** is as **d. e.** to **f. e.** Therefore the square of **c. b.** is commensurable <note>original: "communicat"</note> with the square of **a. b.**; by the 6th [proposition] of this [book], the square of **c. b.** will therefore be rational <note>original: "rationale"</note> by definition, since it is commensurable with a rational surface. And since **c. b.** and **a. b.** are incommensurable [in length] <note>original: "incommensurabiles"</note> by the last part of the 7th [proposition], it is established that the two lines **a. b.** and **c. b.** are rational, yet commensurable only in square <note>original: "potentia tantum communicantes"</note>. But because line **a. b.** is more powerful <note>original: "potentior", meaning the square of line a.b. exceeds the square of line c.b. by the square of line a.c.</note> than line **c. b.** by the square of line **a. c.**, which by the second part of the 7th [proposition] is commensurable with it in length, it is established that the proposition has been achieved.

¶ If, however, one wishes to find several lines that are rational and commensurable only in square, of which one is more powerful in length than any of the others by the square of some line commensurable with itself in length: let there be, as before, a rational line **a. b.** in length, upon which a semicircle **a. c. b.** is described. Let a square number **d.** be taken which is divisible into many squares and non-squares, among which the non-squares do not have a ratio to one another as square numbers; such numbers offer themselves readily, such as 36, which is divisible into 25 and 11, also into 16 and 20, again into 9 and 27, and also into 4 and 32. Among these non-squares, which are 11, 20, 27, and 32, there is no ratio of one to the other as of one square number to another. 

Therefore, let the square number **d.** be divided into the square **e.** and the non-square **f.**; and let the ratio of the square of line **a. b.** to the square of line **a. c.** be as the number **d.** to the number **e.**, and let line **c. b.** be drawn; it stands as previously demonstrated that **a. b.** and **b. c.** are two such lines as we require. Similarly, let **d.** be divided into square **g.** and non-square **h.**, and let the square of line **a. b.** be to the square of line **a. k.** as **d.** is to **g.**, and let line **k. b.** be drawn; as before, there will be two lines **a. b.** and **b. k.** of the kind we require. In the same way, if **d.** is again divided into square **l.** and non-square **m.**, and the ratio of the square of line **a. b.** to the square of line **a. n.** is set as **d.** to **l.**, and **n. b.** is produced, there will be two lines **a. b.** and **b. n.** of the kind we require. If again **d.** is divided into square **p.** and non-square **q.**, and the ratio of the square of line **a. b.** to the square of line **a. r.** is as **d.** to **p.**, and line **r. b.** is extended, there will also be two lines **a. b.** and **b. r.** of the kind we require. 

Thus the lines **a. b.**, **b. c.**, **b. k.**, **b. n.**, and **b. r.** are rational only in square and commensurable in that respect, of which one—namely **a. b.**—is more powerful than any of the others by the square of a line commensurable with it in length. If, therefore, none of the four lines **b. c.**, **b. k.**, **b. n.**, and **b. r.** are commensurable with another in length, the proposition stands. This is proved as follows: it is clear from the premises that the square of line **b. c.** to the square of line **a. b.** is as the number **f.** to the number **d.**, and the square of line **a. b.** to the square of line **b. k.** is as the number **d.** to the number **h.**; therefore, by equal proportionality, the square of line **b. c.** to the square of line **b. k.** is as the number **f.** to the number **h.** But none of the four numbers **f.**, **h.**, **m.**, **q.** has a ratio to another as a square number to a square number by hypothesis; wherefore by the 3rd part...

To find two lines that are rational in power <term>rational in power: lines whose squares are commensurable, even if the lines themselves are not</term> only, of which the square of the longer is more powerful than the square of the shorter by the square of a line incommensurable with it in length.
¶ In this case, the same arrangement and the same hypotheses as in the previous proposition remain, with this only changed: that the ratio <note>original: "proportio"</note> of the number **d. e.** to neither of the two numbers **d. f.** and **f. e.** is as a square number to a square number. This will be easily done: by setting **d. e.** as any square number divided into two non-square numbers, such as if **d. e.** is 9, **d. f.** is 6, and **f. e.** is 3. Following the same argument as before, with this only excepted: that **a. b.** and **a. c.** are incommensurable in length by the last part of [proposition] 7. ¶ And it should be known that two lines such as these and those the previous proposition teaches how to find, when joined together, compose a binomial <term>binomial: a line made of two parts that are incommensurable with each other</term>; and when the smaller of them is cut away from the larger, the remaining part is called a residue <term>residue: often called a 'potome' in Greek; the difference between two incommensurable lines</term>. Note also that lines which are rational in power only can be one rational and the other irrational, just as the square sides <note>original: "latera tetragonica"</note> of two areas, one of which is 25 feet and the other 24, are rational in power only; for the side of the first area is 5, but the side of the second is not a whole number. And both can be irrational, as the square sides of two areas, one of which is 24 feet and the other 23, for the side of neither is a whole number; and they are incommensurable in length from the last part of the seventh. ¶ But if it is also desired to find more than two lines rational in power only, of which one is more powerful than any of the others by the square of a line not commensurable with it in length: let such a number be taken which can be divided multiple times in this way, so that the ratio of the whole to none of its parts, nor of any part to another, is as a square number to a square number. For example, 25 can be divided into 2 and 23; likewise into 5 and 20; and again into 7 and 18. And so the process is the same as it was in the previous [proposition].

->Proposition 19.<-

<margin>
<note>A rectangular diagram divided into two parts. The top horizontal edge is labeled with points **a**, **b**, and **d**. A vertical line drops from point **b**. The bottom horizontal edge has point **c** located directly beneath point **b**.</note>
</margin>

Every area <note>original: "superficies"</note> contained by two lines rational in power only is irrational, and it is called a medial area; its square side <note>original: "latus tetragonicum"</note>, that is, the line which is powerful in that area, is irrational and is called a medial line.
¶ Let there be two lines **a. b.** and **b. c.** containing the area **a. c.**, being rational in power only; how these are found is manifest from the previous and the one before the previous. I say that the area **a. c.** is irrational. For let **c. d.** be the square of **b. c.**; it will be rational by hypothesis because the line **b. c.** is rational in power. And since, from the first [proposition] of the sixth [book], **a. c.** is to **c. d.** as **a. b.** is to **b. d.**, and **a. b.** is not commensurable with **b. d.** (because by hypothesis it is not commensurable with its equal, which is **b. c.**), it follows by the second part of the 10th [proposition] that **a. c.** is not commensurable with **c. d.** Therefore, by definition, the area **a. c.** is irrational. For that reason, its square side is also irrational. This area is called medial because it is a mean proportional between two rational areas, namely between the squares of the two lines containing it; and the line powerful in it is called medial because it also is a mean proportional between two lines rational in power only, and these two lines are the sides of the said area. And this is what we intended.

...the line **b.c.** is rational in length, to which is applied an area **b.d.** equal to the square of line **a.** This shall be done in this way: let line **c.d.** be added to the two lines **b.c.** and **a.** in continued proportionality <note>original: "continua proportionalitate"; this refers to a geometric progression where the ratio of the first to the second equals the ratio of the second to the third</note>, as [Proposition] 10 of the sixth book teaches. Therefore, the ratio of **b.c.** to **e.f.** is as **f.g.** to **c.d.** Wherefore, by [Proposition] 10, since **b.c.** is commensurable in power with **e.f.**—given that the squares of both are rational by the hypothesis—**f.g.** will be commensurable in power with **c.d.** Since, therefore, the square of **f.g.** is rational by the hypothesis, the square of **c.d.** will also be rational by definition. But because the area **b.d.** is irrational (just like its equal **e.g.** by the premise), it follows that the square of line **c.d.** is not commensurable with area **b.d.** And because the ratio of the square of line **c.d.** to the area **b.d.** is (by the first proposition of the sixth book) as **c.d.** is to **c.b.**, it follows by the second part of [Proposition] 10 that **c.d.** is not commensurable with **b.c.** Wherefore, since **b.c.** is rational in length by the hypothesis, **c.d.** will be irrational in length and rational in power only. Thus, the proposed conclusion is clear.

->Proposition 21<-

<margin>
<note>A geometric diagram showing a semicircle with a horizontal base line containing points **b**, **c**, and **a**. A vertical line segment **cd** is drawn from point **c** to the arc of the semicircle. A horizontal line segment extends from **d** to a point **g**.</note>

Every line commensurable with a medial line is medial.
¶ Let line **a.** be medial, and let line **b.** be commensurable to it, whether in length or in power only. I say that line **b.** is also medial.
For let there be a line **c.d.** rational in length, to which is applied an area
<margin>

## Proposition 22.

<margin>
<note>Two geometric diagrams positioned in the right margin. The upper set features two stacked rectangles on the left labeled 'b' (top) and 'a' (bottom). To their right is a larger rectangle divided horizontally, with labels f, e, c along the left vertical axis and g, d along the right vertical axis. The lower set of diagrams follows the same vertical stack and subdivided rectangle structure.</note>
</margin>

**E**very difference by which one medial area exceeds another is proved to be irrational.
¶ Let each of the two areas **a. b.** and **a.** be medial: I say that area **b.**, which is their difference, is irrational. For let line **c.d.** be rational in length, to which area **d.e.** is applied equal to area **a.**, and area **d.f.** equal to the total area **a.b.** How this is done was taught in the previous [proposition]: because therefore **d.f.** is equal to **a.b.** and **d.e.** is equal to **a.**, by common notion **e.f.** will be equal to **b.** If therefore area **b.** is not irrational but rational, then **f.g.**, which is equal to it, will also be rational. But since line **e.g.** is rational in length like its equal **c.d.**, by [Proposition] 16, line **e.f.** will be rational in length and commensurable to line **e.g.** By [Proposition] 20, however, each of the two lines **c.e.** and **c.f.** is rational in power <term>rational in power: a line is rational in power if its square is commensurable with a standard rational area, even if the line itself is not commensurable in length</term> only and incommensurable in length to line **c.d.**; thus line **e.f.** is incommensurable to line **c.e.** in length. And because by the first [proposition] of the sixth [book], the square of line **e.f.** to the area <note>original: "superficiem"; Euclid uses this term to refer to the interior space or area of a figure</note> formed by **e.f.** and **c.e.** is as **e.f.** to **c.e.**, it follows by the second part of [Proposition] 10 that the square of line **e.f.** is incommensurable to the area made from **e.f.** and **c.e.** Wherefore the square itself will be incommensurable to double the area from **e.f.** and **c.e.** But the square of **c.e.**, since it is rational, is commensurable with the square of **e.f.**; therefore the whole composed of both will be, by [Proposition] 9, commensurable with the square of **e.f.** and therefore incommensurable with double the area from **e.f.** and **c.e.** And because by the fourth [proposition] of the second [book] the square of line **c.f.** is equal to the two squares of the two lines **c.e.** and **e.f.** and double the area from **c.e.** and **e.f.**, and double the area of **c.e.** and **e.f.** is incommensurable to the sum <note>original: "aggregato"</note> of the two squares of the two lines **c.e.** and **e.f.**, it follows by those things added in [Proposition] 9 that the square of **c.f.** is incommensurable to the sum of the two squares of the two lines **c.e.** and **e.f.** But since the sum of these squares is rational, it follows that the square of line **c.f.** is not rational: and therefore line **c.f.** is not rational in power: and for that reason area **d.f.** will not be medial, nor **a.b.** which is equal to it, which is inconsistent since it is contrary to what was posited. It remains therefore that area **b.** is irrational: which is what was proposed.

## Proposition 23.

**E**very area contained by two medial lines commensurable in power only is either rational or medial.
¶ Let two lines **a.b.** and **b.c.** be medial and commensurable in power only: I say that area **a.c.** contained by them is either rational or medial.
¶ For let **c.d.** be the square of line **b.c.** and **a.e.** the square of line **a.b.** From the hypothesis, these two squares will be commensurable, and by the first [proposition] of the sixth [book], area **a.c.** will be the medial proportional <note>A value that falls between two others in a geometric progression (a:b = b:c)</note> between these squares. Therefore, let line **f.g.** be taken which is rational in length, to which area **f.b.** is applied equal to the square **a.e.**, and **b.k.** equal to area **a.c.**, and **k.l.** equal to the square **d.c.** These three areas **f.b.**, **b.k.**, and **k.l.** will be in continued proportion just as their equals are.

I say then that the two lines **c** and **d** are those which we seek: for it is clear from [Proposition] 19 that the area <note>original: "superficies"; literally a surface, used here to mean the product of two lines</note> which the lines **a** and **b** contain is medial; and because, by the first part of [Proposition] 16 of the sixth [Book], the square of line **c** is equal to the said area, line **c** will therefore be medial by [Proposition] 19. Therefore, by [Proposition] 21, since **c** is a medial line, **d** will also be medial. And by the first part of [Proposition] 12, line **c** will be more powerful than line **d** by the square of a line commensurable with it in length. If, therefore, the two lines **c** and **d** contain a rational area, they are such as we seek. That they contain a rational area is held thus: since **a** is to **b** as **c** is to **d**, then by permutation **a** is to **c** as **b** is to **d**. But **a** was to **c** as **c** was to **b**; therefore **c** is to **b** as **b** is to **d**. Thus, by the first part of [Proposition] 16 of the sixth [Book], the area contained by the two lines **c** and **d** is equal to the square of **b**. Moreover, the square of **b** is rational by the hypothesis, since [line **b**] is rational in power; therefore the area contained by the two lines **c** and **d** is rational, which establishes the proposition.
