### Proposition 30.

<margin>
<note>An illustration shows a horizontal line segment divided by a point 'b', with endpoints 'a' and 'c', representing the addition of two line segments to form a new whole.</note>
</margin>

If two rational lines, commensurable <term>commensurable in power: lines whose squares can be measured by the same unit area, even if the lines themselves cannot be measured by the same unit length</term> in power only, are joined together in a straight line: the whole line composed of them will be irrational, and it shall be called a **binomial**. <note>original: "binomium"; literally "two names," referring to a line composed of two incommensurable parts.</note>

¶ Let there be two lines **a.b.** and **b.c.** joined continuously in a straight line, being rational and commensurable in power only, which you will find according to [Propositions] 17 and 18: I say that the whole line **a.c.** composed of them is irrational, and it is called a binomial. For, by the fourth [proposition] of the second [Book], the square of **a.c.** is equal to the squares of the two lines **a.b.** and **b.c.** and to twice the area <note>original: "superficiei"; literally a surface or area, here referring to the rectangle formed by the two lines</note> of one of them by the other. Now, the squares of both make a rational area by the hypothesis; but twice the area of one by the other makes a medial area according to [Proposition] 19. Therefore, the squares of both taken together make an area incommensurable with twice the area of one of them by the other. It will follow then, from [Proposition] 9, that the square of **a.c.** is incommensurable with the two squares of the two lines **a.b.** and **b.c.** taken together. Wherefore it is irrational by definition, since those two squares [together] make a rational area. And for that reason, its square root <term>square root: literally the "tetragonic side," or the side of a square equal to that area</term> which is **a.c.** is also irrational by definition; thus the proposition stands proven.

### Proposition 31.

<margin>
<note>An illustration shows a horizontal line segment with endpoints 'a' and 'c' and a midpoint 'b'. A semi-circle is drawn above the segment connecting points 'a' and 'c', a standard construction for finding geometric means.</note>
</margin>

If two medial lines, commensurable in power only and containing a rational area, are joined in a straight line: the whole line composed of them will be irrational and shall be called the **first bimedial**.

¶ Let there be two lines **a.b.** and **b.c.** joined continuously in a straight line as proposed, which you will find through [Propositions] 24 and 25: I say that the whole line **a.c.** is irrational, and it is called the first bimedial. For twice the area of **a.b.** by **b.c.** is rational by the hypothesis, and the two squares of the two lines **a.b.** and **b.c.** taken together make a medial area. Since each square is medial by the hypothesis and one of them is commensurable with the other: therefore, twice the area of one of them by the other is incommensurable with the two squares taken together. Therefore, the whole aggregate of twice the area and the two squares—which itself is the square of the whole **a.c.** by the fourth [proposition] of the second [Book]—is incommensurable with twice the area of one of them by the other, according to [Proposition] 9 of this [Book]. Since therefore twice the area is rational, the square of **a.c.** will be irrational. Therefore, the line **a.c.** is also irrational, which is what was proposed.

</margin>

¶ The same [proven] otherwise: let line **d.e.** be rational in length, to which is applied the medial area **d.f.** Since each square is medial by the hypothesis and one of them is commensurable with the other, therefore by [Proposition] 20 the line **d.g.** is rational in power only, not commensurable in length with line **d.e.** Again, to line **f.g.** (which is equal to **d.e.**) let the area **f.b.** be applied, equal to twice the area of **a.b.** by **b.c.** Then **f.b.** will be rational by the hypothesis: wherefore by [Proposition] 16, line **g.b.** will be rational in length. Thus the two lines **d.g.** and **g.b.** are rational in power and commensurable in that way only: therefore by [Proposition] 30, the whole line composed of them, which is **d.b.**, is a binomial and irrational. Wherefore by [Proposition] 16, by the destruction of the consequent <note>a logical term meaning "by contradiction" or "reversing the argument"</note>, the area **e.b.** is irrational. And because by the fourth [proposition] of the second [Book] its square root is the line **a.c.**, that line will be irrational by definition, which was the proposition to be demonstrated.

But since their squares are commensurable by hypothesis, the said area—and therefore twice that area—will be incommensurable to their two squares taken together. Therefore, the two areas **d.f.** and **f.b.** are incommensurable. Thus, by the first of the sixth and the second of the 10th of this Book, the line **d.g.** will be incommensurable to the line **g.b.** Since these are rational in power [only], by the 30th [proposition] the whole line **d.b.** will be a **binomial** and irrational. Therefore, by the 16th [proposition], by the destruction of the consequent <note>original: "a destructione consequentis"; a logical term meaning that if the result is impossible, the premise must be false</note>, the area **e.b.** is irrational. And because its square side <note>original: "latus tetragonicum"; the side of a square, or what we would call the square root</note>, by the fourth [proposition] of the second [Book], is the line **a.c.**, it follows by definition that the line **a.c.** is irrational: which was what was proposed to be shown.

### Proposition 33.

<margin>
<note>A geometric diagram identical to the one above: a line segment a-b-c positioned over a rectangle divided horizontally, with labels b, g, d on the left vertical edge and f, e on the right.</note>
</margin>

When two lines, incommensurable in power and containing a medial area, are joined such that both their squares taken together are rational: the whole line will be irrational and shall be called the **greater line**.

¶ Let two lines **a.b.** and **b.c.** be joined to one another in a continuous straight line as is proposed, which may be found through the 27th [proposition]: I say that **a.c.** composed of them is an irrational line, and it is called the **greater line**. For since both squares taken together are rational, while the area of one multiplied by the other (and therefore twice that area) is medial by hypothesis, the whole [area] from the two squares taken together will be incommensurable to twice the area of one multiplied by the other. Thus the whole sum composed of the two squares and twice the area between them is equal to the square of **a.c.** by the fourth [proposition] of the second [Book]. By the 9th [proposition] of this Book, it will be incommensurable to the two squares **a.b.** and **b.c.** taken together. By definition, therefore, the square of line **a.c.** is irrational, and line **a.c.** is irrational, which is what was proposed. 

¶ Likewise, as in the previous [propositions], let the area **d.f.** be joined to the line **d.e.** (which is rational in length), such that it is equal to the two squares of the two lines **a.b.** and **b.c.** taken together; it will be rational by hypothesis. Wherefore, by the 16th [proposition], its second side, which is **d.g.**, will also be rational in length and commensurable to the line **d.e.** Again, let the area **f.b.** be joined to the line **f.g.**, equal to twice the area of **a.b.** multiplied by **b.c.**, and it will be medial by hypothesis. Wherefore, by the 20th [proposition], the line **g.b.**, which is its second side, is rational in power only. By the 30th [proposition], therefore, the line **d.b.** is a **binomial** and irrational. Therefore, by the 16th [proposition], by the destruction of the consequent, the area **e.b.** is irrational, wherefore its square side (which by the fourth of the second is **a.c.**) is irrational by definition: which we wished to show.

### Proposition 34.

# BOOK X

<margin>
<note>A geometric diagram displays a horizontal line segment divided into parts labeled **a**, **b**, and **c**. Below this, a rectangle is constructed, divided horizontally by a line marked **f** and **g**. The vertical edges and interior points are labeled with letters **b**, **g**, **d**, **f**, and **e**, representing the geometric relationships between the lines and the areas (surfaces) they contain.</note>
</margin>

When two lines are joined together that are incommensurable in power <term>incommensurable in power: lines whose lengths are not related by a rational ratio, but whose squares might be; here, even their squares do not share a common rational measure</term> and contain a rational area, and both of their squares taken together are medial <term>medial: an irrational area or line derived from the side of a rational rectangle, specifically the square root of a non-square rational number</term>, the whole line will be irrational and shall be called **powerful in a rational and a medial**.

¶ Let there be, as in the preceding sections, two lines **a.b.** and **b.c.** joined in a continuous straight line as proposed; these are to be taken from the 28th [proposition]. I say that the whole line **a.c.** composed of them will be irrational, and it is called a line **powerful in a rational and a medial** <note>original: "potens in rōnale 7 mediale"; this refers to a line whose square is equal to the sum of a rational area and a medial area</note>. Since the area of **a.b.** multiplied by **b.c.** is rational by hypothesis, therefore twice that area and both squares taken together are medial; it follows through the 4th [proposition] of the Second [Book] <note>Euclid II.4 states that $(a+b)^2 = a^2 + b^2 + 2ab$</note> and the 9th of this [Book]—just as in the preceding—that the square of the whole **a.c.** is incommensurable to twice the area of **a.b.** multiplied by **b.c.** By the definition, therefore, the square itself is irrational and the line **a.c.** is irrational, which was to be proved. ¶ The same is proved otherwise: let there be, as in the preceding, a line **d.e.** rational in length, and an area **d.f.** joined to it equal to the two squares of the two lines **a.b.** and **b.c.** taken together, which will be medial by hypothesis. Therefore, by the 20th [proposition], the line **d.g.** will be rational in power only, not sharing its length with line **d.e.** And let the area **f.b.** be joined to the line **g.f.** equal to twice the area of **a.b.** multiplied by **b.c.**; this will be rational by hypothesis. Therefore, by the 16th [proposition], its side, which is **g.b.**, is rational in length; wherefore, by the 30th [proposition], the line **d.b.** is a **binomial** <term>binomial: a line composed of two incommensurable rational parts</term> and irrational. Thus the area **e.b.**, by the 16th [proposition] and the destruction of the present [conditions], is irrational. Since, therefore, the line **a.c.** is its tetragonic side <term>tetragonic side: the square root of an area</term>, by the 4th [proposition] of the Second [Book], it follows that **a.c.** is irrational by definition; thus the proposition stands.

### Proposition 35.

<margin>
<note>A geometric diagram illustrates Proposition 35. It shows a horizontal line segment **a**, **b**, **c**. Beneath it is a rectangle divided by a horizontal line **gf**. The left-hand vertical boundary is marked with points **b**, **g**, and **d** from top to bottom. The point **f** is situated on the internal dividing line, and **e** is at the bottom right corner of the structure.</note>

When two lines are joined together that are incommensurable in power and contain a medial area, and both of their squares taken together are medial and incommensurable to twice the area of one multiplied by the other, the whole line will be irrational and shall be called **powerful in two medials**.

¶ Let there also be two lines here, **a.b.** and **b.c.**, joined in a continuous straight line as proposed, which are to be taken from the 29th [proposition]. I say that the line **a.c.** composed of them is irrational and is itself called **powerful in two medials**. For let there be joined to the line **d.e.** (which is rational in length) an area **d.f.** equal to the two squares of the two lines **a.b.** and **b.c.** taken together. This area will be medial by hypothesis, wherefore by the 20th [proposition] the line **d.g.** will be rational in power only and incommensurable to the line **d.e.**, which is rational in length. Again, to the line **g.f.** (which is equal to **d.e.**) let there be joined the area **f.b.** equal to twice the area of one multiplied by the other; this will also be medial by hypothesis. Wherefore, by the 20th [proposition], the line **g.b.** will be rational in power only. But because by hypothesis both squares taken together are incommensurable to twice the area of one multiplied by the other, it follows that **d.f.** is incommensurable to **f.b.** Wherefore, by the 1st [proposition] of the Sixth [Book] and the second part of the 10th of this [Book], the line **d.g.** is incommensurable to **g.b.** By the 30th [proposition], therefore, the line **d.b.** is a **binomial** and irrational. Thus the area **e.b.** is irrational and its tetragonic side is **a.c.**, as in the preceding; wherefore the proposition stands. But if twice the area of **a.b.** and **b.c.** were not incommensurable to both squares taken together, the line **a.c.** would be medial. For then **d.f.** would be commensurable to **f.b.** and therefore the line **d.g.** to line **g.b.** Thus the whole line **d.b.** would be rational in power only and incommensurable in length to line **d.e.** By the 19th [proposition], therefore, the area **e.b.** would be medial and its tetragonic side, which is **a.c.**, would be a medial line. In order that the teaching of the following things might be made easier, we think that two things should be demonstrated beforehand in this place, the first of which is:

<note>A square geometric diagram is divided into four regions by a horizontal and a vertical line. A diagonal line runs from the top right to the bottom left. Points **a**, **c**, **d**, and **b** are labeled along the base of the diagram, illustrating the relationships between the segments of a divided line.</note>

¶ If any line is divided into two unequal parts, the squares of both sections taken together are greater than twice the surface <note>The "surface of one in the other" refers to the area of a rectangle formed by the two segments.</note> of one by the other by exactly the square of the line by which the larger part exceeds the smaller.

¶ Let the line **a.b.** be divided into two unequal parts at point **c.**, and let the larger portion be **c.b.**, from which a segment **c.d.** is taken equal to **a.c.** I say that the squares of the two lines **a.c.** and **c.b.** are greater than twice the surface of one by the other by the square of line **d.b.** For that which is produced from **a.c.** multiplied by **c.b.** twice, together with the squares of the two lines **a.c.** and **c.b.**, is equal to that which is produced from **a.c.** multiplied by **c.b.** four times together with the square of **d.b.**, because both of these sums are equal to the square of the whole line **a.b.** This is known first by the fourth proposition of the second book <note>original: "per quartam secundi"; Proposition II.4 states that the square on a whole line is equal to the squares on the parts plus twice the rectangle contained by the parts.</note>, and secondly by the eighth proposition of the same book <note>original: "per 8. eiusdem"; Proposition II.8 relates the square of the sum of two lines to the rectangle and the square of their difference.</note>. Therefore, when the equal amounts—namely, twice the product of **a.c.** and **c.b.**—are subtracted from both sides, the remainders will be equal. From the first side, the squares of the two lines **a.c.** and **c.b.** remain; from the second, twice the product of **a.c.** and **c.b.** plus the square of **d.b.** remain. Thus, the proposition is established. From this, it is manifest that if any line is divided into two unequal parts, the squares of both parts taken together are more than twice the surface of one of them multiplied by the other. And it is for this reason that we have set this premise before.

<margin>
<note>A horizontal line segment is shown with five distinct points marked from left to right: **a**, **c**, **d**, **e**, and **b**.</note>
</margin>

¶ If any line is divided into two unequal parts, and likewise into another two unequal parts, the squares of the more unequal parts taken together are greater than the squares of the less unequal parts taken together by exactly twice the square of the line that lies between the two points of division, and four times the area produced by that same line and the line that lies between the point of the less unequal division and the point that divides the whole line into two equal halves.

¶ Let the line **a.b.** be divided into two unequal parts at point **c.**, and likewise by another less unequal division at point **d.**; furthermore, let it be divided into equal halves at point **e.** I say that the squares of the two more unequal parts, which are **a.c.** and **c.b.**, are greater than the two squares of the less unequal lines, **a.d.** and **d.b.**, by twice the square of line **c.d.** and four times the area produced from **c.d.** multiplied by **d.e.** For, by the ninth proposition of the second book <note>original: "per 9. secundi"</note>, the squares of the two lines **a.c.** and **c.b.** taken together are double the squares of the two lines **b.e.** and **e.c.** taken together. But by that same ninth proposition, the squares of the two lines **a.d.** and **d.b.** taken together are double the squares of the two lines **b.e.** and **e.d.** taken together. Thus, the squares of the two lines **a.c.** and **c.b.** taken together exceed the squares of the two lines **a.d.** and **d.b.** taken together by the amount that twice the square of line **e.c.** exceeds twice the square of line **d.e.** This, however, by the fourth proposition of the second book, is twice the square of line **c.d.** and four times the area produced from **c.d.** multiplied by **d.e.** Wherefore, the proposition stands. From this, it is manifest that the more unequal the sections of a line are, the greater the sum of their squares will be; and it is for this reason we have set this premise before.

### Proposition 37.

<note>A horizontal line segment is marked with four points: **a**, **d**, **c**, and **b**. This represents the division of a bimedial line at different points to demonstrate the impossibility of a second division.</note>

A **first bimedial** [line] <term>first bimedial: A line composed of two medial lines that are commensurable in power only and contain a rational rectangle.</term> divided according to its term into two medial lines, cannot be divided the same way into two other medial lines.

¶ Let there also be here a line **a.b.**, a first bimedial divided into two medial lines commensurable in power only <term>commensurable in power: Lines whose squares have a ratio that can be expressed as a ratio of two whole numbers.</term> and containing a rational surface; [Proposition] 31 asserts it is composed of these, which are **a.c.** and **c.b.** I say that it is impossible for it to be divided into two other lines under that same definition. If it were possible, let it be divided at point **d.** Taking a rational line **e.f.**, let **e.g.** be applied to it equal to the two squares of the lines **a.c.** and **c.b.**, and let surface **f.b.** be equal to the square of **a.b.**, and surface **f.k.** be equal to the squares of the two lines **a.d.** and **d.b.** Then, by the fourth [proposition] of the second [book], **g.b.** will be equal to twice the surface of **a.c.** by **c.b.**, and by the same [proposition], **k.l.** will be equal to twice the surface of **a.d.** by **d.b.** By the hypothesis, both surfaces **e.g.** and **f.k.** will be medial, and both lines **g.b.** and **k.l.** will be rational. However, this is impossible: for by the first part, surface **k.g.** would be irrational by [Proposition] 22, but by the second part, the same would be rational by the definition and the ninth [proposition], which is an absurdity <note>original: "quod est inconveniens"</note>.

### Proposition 38.

Since the said squares are commensurable with each other, it follows by the hypothesis that both squares taken together are incommensurable with the surface of one by the other, and therefore also with twice that surface. ### Proposition 39

A major line <term>major line: An irrational line formed by adding two lines that are incommensurable in power, such that the sum of their squares is rational while the rectangle they form is medial.</term> can only be divided into the two lines from which it is composed at their unique point of division.
¶ Let this major line **a.b.** be divided at point **c.** into two lines that are incommensurable in power <term>incommensurable in power: Lines whose squares have no common measure, meaning the ratio of their squares is not a ratio of square numbers.</term> and which contain a medial surface, and let both of their squares taken together be rational; for from such lines it is composed, as Proposition 33 asserts. I say that it is impossible for it to be divided at another point into two other lines under this definition. If it were possible, let it be at point **d.**; let the same figure and the same hypotheses remain as before, and argue just as in Proposition 36 that surface **g.k.** is both rational and irrational, which is impossible.

### Proposition 40

A line whose square is equal to a rational and a medial area <note>original: "Linea potens in rōnale 7 mediale"</note> is not divided except into its own two lines at its unique point of division.
This Proposition 40 is proved while keeping the previous figure and positions, except that line **a.b.** is divided at point **c.** into those two lines from which Proposition 34 says it is composed; it will be proved just as Proposition 37. If it were otherwise than proposed, surface **k.g.** would be both rational and irrational, which cannot be.

### Proposition 41

A line whose square is equal to two medial areas <note>original: "Linea potens in duo medialia"</note> cannot be divided into any other two lines at their point of division other than those from which it is joined; rather, it is divisible only into its own two parts from which it is composed.
For this Proposition 41, with line **a.b.** divided at point **c.** into those parts from which Proposition 35 asserts it is composed, and with the other figures and positions remaining as above, the proof is as in Proposition 38; for if the opposite of the proposition is granted, the opposite of Proposition 36 follows, which is impossible.
¶ If the greater part of a binomial <note>original: "binomij"</note> is more powerful than the lesser part by the square of a line commensurable to the greater in length, and if the greater part is commensurable in length with the given rational line, it shall be called a **first binomial**. If, however, the lesser part is commensurable in length with the given rational line, it shall be called a **second binomial**. But if neither of its parts is commensurable in length with the given rational line, it shall be called a **third binomial**. Likewise, if the greater part is more powerful than the lesser by the square of a line incommensurable in length to the greater part, and if the greater part is commensurable in length with the given rational line, it shall be called a **fourth binomial**. If the lesser part is commensurable in length with the given rational line, it shall be named a **fifth binomial**. But if neither of its parts is commensurable in length with the given rational line, it shall be a **sixth binomial**.

These propositions provide geometric methods for creating specific types of irrational lines based on the relationship between square and non-square numbers.</meta>

[Let] **f.g.** be commensurable in length with the given rational line **a** <note>original: "cōmunicans linee .a. rōnali poſite i longitudine"</note>. Therefore, let a semicircle **f.g.h.** be drawn upon it. Let the ratio of the square of line **f.g.** to the square of line **f.b.** be as [the ratio of number] **c** to **d**. And let line **g.b.** be drawn. I say, therefore, that the two lines **f.g.** and **g.b.**, when joined directly, compose the **first binomial** <term>first binomial: A line composed of two rational parts where the greater part is commensurable in length with the fixed rational "unit" line, and its square exceeds the square of the lesser part by the square of a line commensurable with itself.</term>. 

For the line **f.g.**, which is longer, is greater in power than the shorter line **g.b.** by the square of line **f.b.**, according to Proposition 30 of the third book and the penultimate [proposition] of the first book. However, line **f.b.** is commensurable with line **f.g.** in length by the second part of Proposition 7 <note>Euclid is referencing the relationship between numbers and the squares of lines.</note>. Since the ratio of the squares of **f.g.** and **f.b.** is as the square numbers **c** and **d**, the line **g.b.** is proved to be **rational in power only** <term>rational in power only: A line whose length is incommensurable with a given unit line, but whose square is commensurable with the square of the unit line.</term>, not being commensurable with line **f.g.** in length. Therefore, it is also not commensurable with the given rational line **a**. 

Since the square of line **f.g.** is to the square of line **f.b.** as the number **c** is to number **d**, it follows by inverse proportionality that the square of line **f.g.** is to the square of line **g.b.** as number **c** is to number **e**. Since **c** is a square number and **e** is not a square number, it follows by the last part of Proposition 7 that line **g.b.** is incommensurable in length with line **f.g.**. It remains, therefore, that **g.b.** is rational in power only, and by the definition, the lines **f.g.** and **g.b.** compose a first binomial, which was what was to be found.

### To find the second binomial. Proposition 43.

<note>A geometric diagram shows a semicircle with inscribed lines forming a triangle f-h-g. Below the semicircle are two horizontal line segments labeled 'a' and 'b'. Below those is a longer horizontal line divided into segments labeled with the numbers 9, 16, 4, and 7. This illustrates the numerical ratios required for the construction.</note>

<note>A second geometric diagram features a semicircle with a triangle f-h-g inscribed. Below are horizontal line segments labeled 'a' and 'b'. Further down is a horizontal line with points marked d, c, and e, and numbers 3, 12, and 9 below the segments, showing how a non-square number can be divided into square and non-square parts.</note>

<note>A third diagram shows three horizontal line segments. The first is labeled 'a' with the number 4. The second is labeled 'b' with the number 3. **B** Let **a** be a given rational line, as before. Let **b** be a square number, and let **c** be a non-square number divisible into **d** (a non-square) and **e** (a square), such that the ratio of the whole **c** (which is non-square) to **d** (which is also non-square) is as a ratio of square numbers. Such numbers are 12, 7, and 48. For 12 is divisible into 9 (a square number) and 3 (a non-square); and the ratio of 12 to 3 is as 16 to 4, both of which are square numbers. In the same way, 48 is divisible into 36 and 12. 

You shall find such numbers thus: Let **a** be a square number and **b** be one less than it, the square of which is **c**. Let **d** be produced from **b** multiplied by **a**. From the first [proposition] of the "incidentals" of the ninth book, **b** will be the difference between **d** and **c**. Let the same **a** be multiplied by **c** to produce **e**. Then **e** will be a square, by the first part of the consequence of the second [proposition] of the ninth book, because each of the numbers **a** and **c** is a square by hypothesis. Again, let **f** be produced from **a** multiplied by **d**. Then **f** will be what we seek. For by the last part of the aforementioned consequence, the number **f** is not a square because the number **d** is not a square. 

If number **d** were a square, then **b** would also be a square (from the second part of the same consequence of the ninth book and from Proposition 22 of the eighth book). And because **a** is a square, by Proposition 16 of the same book, there would be a third proportional number between **a** and **b**, which is impossible since they differ only by a single unit. Therefore, **d** is not a square, and thus **f** is not a square. Indeed, **f** is equal to **d** and **e**, because since **b** is the difference between **d** and **c**, as is clear from the premises, it will be (by the first incidental of the ninth book) that what is produced from **a** times **d** is equal to those produced from **a** times **b** and times **c**. Since **a** times **b** makes **d** and times **c** makes **e**, it follows that **d** is the difference between **f** and **e**. And because by Proposition 18 of the seventh book, **f** is to **e** as **d** is to **c**, it will be (by permutation) that **f** is to **d** as **e** is to **c**. Since both numbers **e** and **c** are squares, it is manifest that the number **f** is as we desire. For it is a non-square divisible into **d** (non-square) and **e** (square), whose ratio to **d** is as a square to a square (namely, **e** to **c**). 

Let all other things be as before. I say that the lines **f.g.** and **g.b.** compose a **second binomial** <term>second binomial: A binomial where the lesser part is commensurable in length with the rational unit line, and the square of the greater part exceeds the square of the lesser by the square of a line commensurable with itself.</term>. For since the square of **a** is to the square of **f.g.** as **b** is to **c**, and again the square of **f.g.** is to the square of **g.b.** as **c** is to **e**, it will be (by equal proportionality) that the square of **a** is to the square of **g.b.** as **b** is to **e**. Since both numbers **b** and **e** are squares, by the second part [of the proposition], the line **g.b.** will be commensurable in length with the given rational line **a**. Regarding line **f.g.**, it is established that it is rational in power only, not being commensurable with the rational line **a** in length by the last part of Proposition 7. Since it is greater in power than line **g.b.** by [the square of] line **f.b.** (by Proposition 30 of the third book and the penultimate of the first), and line **f.b.** is commensurable with line **f.g.** in length by the second part of Proposition 7, because...

Their squares are in the proportion of the numbers **c** and **d**, whose proportion is as that of square numbers by hypothesis: the proposition is established. ¶ Alternatively, the same result is achieved [if] line **g.b.** is commensurable in length with the given rational line, which is easy to find. Then **f.g.** will be incommensurable with line **g.b.** in length according to the last part of Proposition 7 <note>Book X, Proposition 7 deals with the commensurability of lines and their squares.</note> and more powerful than it in the square of line **f.b.**, with which it is commensurable in length: first by converse and then by everted proportionality <note>original: "per conuersā deinde per euersam proportionalitatem"</note>, and by the second part of Proposition 7. ### To investigate the third binomial. Proposition 44.

The **third binomial** is also discovered thus: as before, let line **a** be rational in length. Let **b** be a prime number <note>A prime number cannot be a square number in this context.</note> and **c** be a square number divisible into a square **d** and a non-square **e**. Let all other things be as before. I say that the two lines **f.g.** and **g.b.** compose a third binomial. For neither of them is commensurable in length with the given rational line **a**, but both are incommensurable. Line **f.g.** is indeed incommensurable by the last part of Proposition 7; line **b.g.** is so by equal proportionality and the last part of Proposition 7. For by equal proportionality, the square of line **a** is to the square of line **g.b.** as the number **b** is to the number **e**, with the square of line **f.g.** and the number **c** acting as intermediates. However, the numbers **b** and **e** are not in the proportion of any square numbers, since **b** is a prime number. For if they were in the proportion of square numbers, it would be necessary by the 16th and 8th propositions of the eighth book for a third [number] to exist between them in continuous proportionality. Therefore, by the 17th proposition of the same book, the number **b** would be a plane number <note>original: "superficialis" - here meaning a number that can be formed by the product of two integers, which a prime cannot be in this geometric sense.</note>, which is impossible since it is prime by hypothesis. Thus, line **g.b.** is incommensurable with the given rational line **a** by the last part of Proposition 7. Therefore, line **f.g.** is more powerful than line **g.b.** by the square of line **f.b.** (from Proposition 30 of the third book and the penultimate of the first), which is commensurable with it in length by the second part of Proposition 7. By the definition of the third binomial, our intention is made clear.

### Proposition 48.

<note>Two geometrical diagrams are presented in the left margin. The top diagram is a large rectangle with vertices labeled 'a' (bottom-left), 'b' (bottom-right), and 'c' (top-right). If a surface is contained by a **first binomial** and a **rational line**, the side which is equal in power to it must necessarily be a **binomial**.
¶ Let surface **a.c.** be contained by the rational line **a.b.** and the **first binomial** which is **b.c.** I say that the **square root** <term>latus tetragonicum|Literally the 'tetragonic side'; the side of a square whose area is equal to the given surface. In modern terms, the square root of the area.</term> of surface **a.c.** is a binomial. For let point **d** be the common boundary of the two parts of the first binomial **b.c.**, whose greater part is **b.d.**; it will be **rational in length** <note>original: "rationalis in longitudine"</note> by definition and commensurable with the given rational line **a.b.**. Likewise, let the smaller part **d.c.** be divided equally at point **e**, and let line **d.b.** be divided at point **f** under the condition that a **mean proportional** <note>A value that creates a geometric progression between two other values.</note> falls between its parts **b.f.** and **f.d.**; how this is done was stated in Proposition 13 <note>Likely referring to the construction in Book VI, Proposition 13, applied here.</note>. Let lines **c.g.**, **d.h.**, and **f.k.** be drawn parallel to line **a.b.** And because, by the definition of a **first binomial**, line **d.b.** is more powerful than line **d.c.** by the square of a line commensurable with it in length, it follows from the second part of Proposition 13 that the two lines **b.f.** and **f.d.** are commensurable. By Proposition 9, therefore, each of them is commensurable with the whole line **b.d.**, wherefore by definition both are **rational in length**. Therefore, by Proposition 15, each of the two surfaces **a.f.** and **f.b.** is rational. Therefore, let a square **l.m.** be described whose side **l.r.** is equal to surface **a.f.**, around which is placed a **gnomon** <term>gnomon|An L-shaped area that, when added to a square, results in a larger square.</term> by extending the diagonal **l.m.n.** to such an extent that the square of the gnomon itself, **m.n.**, is equal to surface **f.b.**; and let its two complements be **p.m.** and **m.q.**, which must necessarily be equal to the two surfaces **d.g.** and **g.c.** Gather it thus: for since line **d.e.** is a mean proportional between lines **b.f.** and **f.d.**, surface **d.g.** will be, by the first proposition of the sixth book, a mean proportional between surfaces **a.f.** and **f.b.**, and therefore also between the squares **l.m.** and **m.n.**. And because the complement **p.m.** is also a mean proportional between the said squares by the first of the sixth, it follows that **p.m.** is equal to **d.g.**, and likewise **m.q.** to **g.c.**. Therefore, line **l.p.** is the square root of surface **a.c.**. I say this line is a **binomial**. For since both squares **l.m.** and **m.n.** are rational, the two lines **l.r.** and **r.p.** will be **rational in power** by definition. Moreover, by the first of the sixth, **a.f.** is to **d.g.** as **b.f.** is to **d.e.**; but **b.f.** is incommensurable with **d.e.**, because **b.f.** is rational simply (as proved), but **d.e.** is rational only in power. This is manifest from the previous hypotheses. Therefore, by the second part of Proposition 10, surface **a.f.** is incommensurable with surface **d.g.**; thus also square **l.m.** with complement **p.m.** Wherefore, by the first of the sixth and the second part of Proposition 10, line **l.r.** is incommensurable with line **r.p.** By Proposition 30, it is established that line **l.p.** is a **binomial**, which was to be shown.

### Proposition 51.

If a surface is contained by a **rational line** and a **fourth binomial**, the line which is powerful in that surface is a **major line**.
¶ All things remaining as in the preceding [propositions], it will be from the hypothesis and the definition of the **fourth binomial** and the 19th [proposition] that each of the two surfaces **d.g.** and **g.c.** [is medial]; therefore both **p.m.** and **m.q.** are medial. However, the two squares **l.m.** and **m.n.** taken together are rational, because surface **a.d.** is rational by the definition of the fourth binomial and the 15th [proposition]. And because **d.b.** is divided at point **f.** into two incommensurable [parts] by the second part of the 14th [proposition], surface **a.f.** will be incommensurable with surface **f.b.** Thus, square **l.m.** is incommensurable with square **m.n.** Therefore, the two lines **l.r.** and **r.p.** are incommensurable in square. Since they contain a medial surface **p.m.**, and both their squares taken together are rational, it is established by the 33rd [proposition] that line **l.p.** is a **major line** <term>linea maior|An irrational line formed by the addition of two lines incommensurable in square, such that the sum of their squares is rational but the rectangle contained by them is medial.</term>; which was to be shown.

### Proposition 52.

If a surface is contained by a **rational line** and a **fifth binomial**, whatever line is powerful in it is necessarily proved to be a line **powerful in a rational and a medial**.
¶ Nor in this [proposition] is there anything to be changed from the arrangement and positions of the previous ones. For while these remain, it will be from those things set down in the definition of the **fifth binomial** and the 15th [proposition] that each of the two surfaces **d.g.** and **g.c.** [is rational]; thus each of the two **p.m.** and **m.q.** is rational. The whole **a.d.**, and therefore both squares **l.m.** and **m.n.** taken together, is medial according to the 19th [proposition]. Since by the second part of the 14th [proposition] line **f.b.** is incommensurable with line **f.d.**, and thus surface **a.f.** with surface **f.b.**, and square **l.m.** with square **m.n.**, the line **l.r.** will be incommensurable in square with line **r.p.** And since they contain a rational surface **p.m.**, and both their squares taken together are medial, conclude from the 34th [proposition] that line **l.p.** is **powerful in a rational and a medial** <term>potens in rationale et mediale|A line whose square is equal to the sum of a rational and a medial area.</term>; which is what was promised.

### Proposition 53.

If an area is contained by a sixth binomial line <note>original: *binomio sexto*</note> and a rational line, the line which can produce that area <note>meaning the square root of that area</note> is proved to be a line that is the side of the sum of two medial areas <term>in duo medialia potens|A specific irrational line whose square is equal to the sum of two medial areas that are incommensurable with one another.</term>.

Theorem 53 still allows you to refrain from drawing new figures; for it is satisfied by the arrangements and positions already set forth in the preceding proofs. Given these conditions, it is necessary from the positions themselves and the definition <note>original: *dispositione .i. diffinitione*</note> of the last binomial and Proposition 19, that any of the surfaces **a.d.**, **d.g.**, and **g.c.**—and consequently both squares **l.m.** and **m.n.** taken together, as well as the rectangles **p.m.** and **m.q.**—are medial. And since **b.f.** and **f.d.** are incommensurable, and because **a.f.** and **f.b.** are likewise, it follows that **l.m.** and **m.n.** are incommensurable. Thus, the two lines **b.c.** and **r.p.** will be incommensurable in square <note>original: *in potentia*</note>. ### Proposition 54.

If a rectangle equal to the square of a binomial line is applied to a rational line, its other side will be a first binomial <term>binomium primum|The first of six types of binomial lines, where the square of the greater term exceeds the square of the lesser by the square of a line commensurable with the greater, and the greater term is commensurable in length with the fixed rational line.</term>.

The six following theorems are the converses of the six preceding ones in order. The intent of this one is as follows: Let line **a.b.** be a binomial divided at point **c.** into two lines **a.c.** and **c.b.** according to its definition. Wherefore, by Proposition 16, each of the two lines **f.l.** and **l.n.**, and the whole line **f.n.**, is rational in length and commensurable to the rational line **e.f.** set previously. ### Proposition 58.

**If a rectangular area** <note>original: "parte altera longior forma," literally a "form longer on one side," the standard term for a rectangle in this context.</note> **equal to the square of a line which is "powerful" over a rational and a medial area is applied to a rational line, its other side must be a fifth binomial.**

If, therefore, either of the two lines $c$ and $d$ is rational in length, its counterpart from lines $e$ and $f$ will not be rational in length. **Every line commensurable with either of the bimedials: is necessarily proved to be of the same species of bimedial.**

[Paragraph mark] What is said is true, whether a line communicates with either of the bimedials in length or even in square only. And let $a$ be a first or second bimedial: I say that $b$ is also a first or second bimedial, according to what $a$ was. Therefore, as from the positioning $a$ and $b$ are communicating whether in length or in square, so $c$ and $e$ and likewise $d$ and $f$ will be communicating. But because $c$ and $d$ are medials communicating in square only: it follows from Proposition 21 that $e$ and $f$ are also medials and from Proposition 10 communicating in square only, since they themselves by hypothesis are proportional to $c$ and $d$. And since by the first proposition of the sixth book $g$ is to $b$ as $c$ is to $d$, and $k$ is to $l$ as $e$ is to $f$, $g$ will be to $b$ as $k$ is to $l$, and permuted $g$ to $k$ as $b$ to $l$. Because therefore $b$ is communicating with $l$ because two of their sides, which are $d$ and $f$, communicate in length or in square according to how $a$ and $b$ communicate in either of them: it follows from Proposition 10 that $g$ and $k$ also communicate with each other. Therefore $k$ will be rational or medial just as $g$ was, by the definition of a rational surface or Proposition 21. For in this only does a first bimedial differ from a second bimedial: that the portions of a first bimedial into which it is divided according to its term contain a rational surface: but those of a second bimedial a medial surface. If therefore $a$ was a first bimedial, surface $g$ will be rational, wherefore $k$ also is rational, and therefore $b$ is a first bimedial by Proposition 31. But if $a$ was a second bimedial, surface $g$ will be medial, on account of this $k$ also is medial; and so by Proposition 32 it will be a second bimedial, wherefore the proposition is established. 

The same otherwise: to the rational line $cd$, with $a$ being either of the bimedials and $b$ communicating with it in length or square: let surface $ce$ be applied equal to the square of $a$, and $fg$ equal to the square of $b$. Therefore $eg$ is a third binomial by the premise, wherefore also the square-root of surface $fg$—that is $b$—is a second bimedial by Proposition 50. It is manifest, therefore, that what is proposed is true.

### Proposition 62.

**Every** line commensurable <note>original: "cōicans"; in Euclid, "communicating" lines are commensurable, meaning they share a common measure.</note> to a major line is herself a major line.
¶ And this also holds true whether the line is commensurable to the major line in either way <note>That is, commensurable either in length or only in square.</note>. For let $a$ be a major line, and $b$ be any line commensurable to it in any way; $b$ will also be a major line. For since $a$ is divided into those portions of which it consists by Proposition 33, which are $c$ and $d$, and line $b$ is divided into $e$ and $f$ according to their proportion; and let it be set that $g$ is the surface <term>superficies|In this context, a surface refers to a geometric area, often a rectangle formed by two lines.</term> contained under $c$ and $d$, and $k$ under $e$ and $f$; and let $m$ and $h$ be the squares of $c$ and $d$, and $n$ and $l$ be the squares of $e$ and $f$. Then $m$ is to $h$ as $n$ is to $l$ by the second part of Proposition 18 of Book VI; and together $(m+h)$ is to $h$ as $(n+l)$ is to $l$; and alternately $(m+h)$ is to $(n+l)$ as $h$ is to $l$. Because, therefore, $h$ is commensurable with $l$—since $d$ is commensurable with $f$ either in length or in square, just as $a$ is commensurable with $b$—it follows that both squares $m$ and $h$ taken together are commensurable with both squares $n$ and $l$ taken together. Since, therefore, the first two taken together are rational by Proposition 33, the last two [the squares of $e$ and $f$] will also be rational by definition. But because it is necessary for the surface $k$ to be medial <note>A "medial" area is one whose side is the mean proportional between two rational lines that are commensurable only in square.</note> just as $g$ is by Proposition 21, and for the lines $e$ and $f$ to be incommensurable in square just as $c$ and $d$ are by Proposition 10, it is concluded by Proposition 33 that line $b$ is the line called "major," which is what was proposed. 
¶ The same is proved another way: since $a$ is a major line to which $b$ is commensurable, whether in length or in square: having taken a rational line $c$, let the surface $d e$ be applied to it equal to the square of line $a$; then let $f g$ be equal to the square of line $b$. Since, therefore, the squares of the two lines $a$ and $b$ are commensurable by hypothesis, the surface $c e$ will be commensurable to the surface $f g$; therefore, by the first proposition of Book VI and the 10th of this book, line $d e$ is commensurable to line $e g$ in length. But since by Proposition 57, line $d e$ is a fourth binomial <term>binomium|A "binomial" line is the sum of two terms that are commensurable only in square. Euclid classifies these into six types based on their relationship to a rational line.</term>, by Proposition 60 the line $e g$ will also be a fourth binomial. Therefore, by Proposition 51, the line $b$, which is "powerful" in the surface $f g$, is a major line.

### Proposition 63.

**If** any line is commensurable to a line that is powerful in a rational and a medial area, she herself is proved to be powerful in a rational and a medial area.
¶ It is also true that in whatever way a line is commensurable to one powerful in a rational and a medial—whether in length or in square only—she herself is also powerful in a rational and a medial area. This is proved in a twofold way as before. Regarding the first way, it is necessary that just as the two lines $c$ and $d$ are incommensurable in square, so also are $e$ and $f$ by Proposition 10. And just as $g$ is a rational surface—for the portions of a line powerful in a rational and a medial area contain such [a surface]—so also by definition $k$ becomes rational. And just as the two squares $m$ and $h$ taken together are medial, so also by Proposition 21, the two squares $n$ and $l$ taken together will be medial. Therefore, from Proposition 34, $b$ is powerful in a rational and a medial area. As for the second way, it is necessary by Proposition 58 that line $d e$ be a fifth binomial; therefore, by Proposition 60, line $e g$ is a fifth binomial. Wherefore, by Proposition 52, the square root <note>original: "lat⁹ tetragonicū"; literally the "tetragonal side," meaning the side of a square equal to that area.</note> of the surface $f g$, which is $b$, will be a line powerful in a rational and a medial area; which is what was proposed.

### Proposition 64.

**Every** line commensurable to a line powerful in two medials is also itself powerful in two medials.
¶ This is also proved to be true using the same arrangement and positions in the two ways used previously, whether line $b$ is commensurable with line $a$ (which is powerful in two medials) in length or in square. For regarding the first way of reasoning: by Proposition 35, surface $g$ will be medial, and therefore also $k$ by Proposition 21 since it is commensurable to it; also the two squares $m$ and $h$ taken together will be medial by the same Proposition 35, and therefore the two $n$ and $l$ taken together by Proposition 21. And since the two squares $m$ and $h$ taken together are, by the aforementioned Proposition 35, incommensurable to twice the surface $g$, it is equalized by Proposition 10 and our positions so that the two $l$ and $n$ taken together are also incommensurable...

### Proposition 65.

**If** two surfaces, one of which is rational and the other medial, are joined together: the line **powerful** in the whole surface composed from them will be one of four irrational lines: namely, either a **binomial**, or a **first bimedial**, or a **major line**, or **powerful in a rational and a medial**.

¶ As if *a* were a rational surface and *b* a medial surface, the line powerful in the whole area *a+b* will be one of the four aforementioned lines. For let there be a rational line *c.d.* to which is joined *c.e.* equal to *a*, and *f.g.* equal to *b*. Then by Proposition 16, line *d.e.* will be rational in length, commensurable with the rational line *c.d.* already set down. And by Proposition 20, line *e.g.* will be rational only in power <note>original: "rōnalis in potentia tm̄"; meaning the line's square is rational, but the line itself is not commensurable in length with the reference line.</note>. And by Proposition 30, line *d.g.* is a binomial. Since one of the binomial parts, which is *d.e.*, is rational in length and commensurable with the rational line *c.d.*, it follows from the definition of the types of binomials that it must be a first, second, fourth, or fifth binomial; it will not be a third or sixth binomial by definition. Therefore, by Propositions 48, 49, 51, and 52, the line powerful in the whole area *c.g.* (which is equal to *a* and *b* together) will be either a **binomial**, or a **first bimedial**, or a **major line**, or **powerful in a rational and a medial**; which is what was proposed. It will not be a second bimedial or powerful in two medials: for if it were a second bimedial, line *d.g.* would be a third binomial by Proposition 56; if it were powerful in two medials, *d.g.* would be a sixth binomial by Proposition 59. But it was neither; thus our intent is clear.

### Proposition 66.

**When** two medial surfaces that are incommensurable are joined together, the line powerful in the whole surface will be one of two irrational lines: namely, either a **second bimedial** or **powerful in two medials**.

¶ As if *a* and *b* were two incommensurable medial surfaces. For if they were commensurable, the surface composed of them would be medial by Propositions 9 and 21; wherefore the line powerful in it would be medial by Proposition 19. I say that the line powerful in the composition of both will be either a second bimedial or powerful in two medials. Let there be a rational line *c.d.*, and let the surface *c.e.* (equal to *a*) be joined to it, and surface *f.g.* (equal to *b*). By Proposition 20, line *d.e.* and similarly line *e.g.* will be rational only in power. Since surfaces *c.e.* and *f.g.* are incommensurable (just as *a* and *b* are equal to them), therefore by the first part of Book VI and Proposition 10 of this book, the lines *d.e.* and *e.g.* will follow. By Proposition 30, line *d.g.* will be a binomial, of which both binomial parts *d.e.* and *e.g.* are incommensurable with the set rational line *c.d.*. It will therefore be, by the definition, a third or sixth binomial. Thus, the line powerful in the whole area *c.g.* (equal to the sum of *a* and *b*) will be, by Propositions 50 and 53, either a **second bimedial** or **powerful in two medials**; which is what was proposed.

**When** a binomial line is set down, and the other irrational lines following it, none of them will be contained under the term of another.

### Proposition 68.

**If** a line is cut from another line, and both are rational **powerfully** <note>original: "potentialiter"; meaning their squares are rational areas.</note> only and commensurable <term>commensurable (communicantes)|Lines that can be measured by the same shared unit or "common measure."</term>, the remaining line will be irrational and shall be called the **remainder** <note>original: "residuum"; in modern editions of Euclid, this is known as an "apotome."</note>.

¶ Let line *b.c.* be cut from line *a.b.*, and let both be rational only in power and commensurable, as shown how to find in Propositions 17 and 18; these are the lines that compose a binomial. I say that the remaining part, *a.c.*, is irrational, and it is called a "remainder." It is clear from the seventh proposition of the second book <note>original: "7. secundi"; referring to Book II, Proposition 7 of the Elements.</note> that the squares of the two lines *a.b.* and *b.c.* taken together—which compose a rational surface by the hypothesis and the definition of a rational surface and the ninth proposition of this book—are equal to twice the surface of *a.b.* and *b.c.* combined with the square of *a.c.* Since, by Proposition 19, the surface of *a.b.* and *b.c.* is medial, its double is also medial by Proposition 21, and therefore irrational by Proposition 19. It follows that both squares of the two lines *a.b.* and *b.c.* taken together are incommensurable to twice the surface of one multiplied by the other; wherefore, by Proposition 9, they are also incommensurable to the square of line *a.c.* By definition, therefore, the square of line *a.c.* is irrational, as it is incommensurable to a rational thing (namely, the two squares of the two lines *a.b.* and *b.c.* taken together). Thus, by definition, line *a.c.* is irrational, which is what was proposed. For example, in the figure, let surface *e.g.* be equal to the two squares of the two lines *a.b.* and *b.c.* taken together: it will be rational. Likewise, let surface *d.f.* be equal to twice the surface of one multiplied by the other: it will be medial by Proposition 19. By Proposition 7 of the second book, surface *f.g.* will be equal to the square of line *a.c.* Since surface *e.g.* is incommensurable to surface *d.f.*, it will also be incommensurable to *f.g.* by Proposition 9. Wherefore, *f.g.* is irrational, as is its square root <note>original: "tetragonicum latus"; literally the "four-sided side," the side of a square of a given area.</note> *a.c.*

Because both squares taken together are composed of twice the surface of one multiplied by the other and the square of line *a.c.*, it follows by Proposition 9 that the square of line *a.c.* is incommensurable...

### Proposition 70.

**If** a line be cut from another line, and both are medial lines commensurable in power only, and containing a medial area: the remaining line will be irrational and shall be called the **second medial remainder** <term>second medial remainder|In Euclid's classification, this is the 'second apotome of a medial,' formed by subtracting one medial line from another when their rectangle is also medial.</term>.

I say that the remaining line, which is *a.c.*, is irrational and is called the second medial remainder. For by the hypothesis and Proposition 21, both squares of the two lines *a.b.* and *b.c.* taken together are medial. Similarly, twice the area of the one in the other <note>the rectangle of the two lines</note> is also medial. Since, therefore, by Proposition 22, a medial area does not differ from another medial area except in irrationality, the square of line *a.c.*—which by Proposition 7 of the Second Book is the amount by which the two squares of *a.b.* and *b.c.* taken together exceed twice the area of the one in the other—will be irrational. Wherefore line *a.c.* is also irrational.

For if *c.g.* is equal to both squares of *a.b.* and *b.c.*, and similarly *d.f.* is equal to twice the area of the one in the other, then *f.g.* will be, by Proposition 7 of the Second Book, equal to the square of *a.c.* Since this is the difference between one medial area *c.g.* and another medial area *d.f.*, it is itself irrational by Proposition 22, and its square root *a.c.* is irrational.

**The same alternatively:** Let *d.e.* be a rational line to which is applied area *d.f.* equal to twice the area of the one in the other, and *e.g.* equal to both squares taken together. Then by Proposition 7 of the Second Book, *f.g.* will be equal to the square of *a.c.* Since *e.g.* is medial, by Proposition 20, line *d.g.* will be rational in power only. Similarly, since *d.f.* is medial, by the same proposition, line *d.b.* will be rational—likewise in power only. And since *a.b.* and *b.c.* are incommensurable in length, the square of each of them and the area of the one in the other <note>the rectangle</note>, and for this reason both squares taken together (since they are commensurable by hypothesis), are also incommensurable to twice the area of the one in the other. It follows that *g.e.* is incommensurable to *d.f.*, and therefore line *d.g.* to line *d.b.* Therefore, from Proposition 68, line *g.b.* is a remainder and irrational. Thus, by Proposition 16, by the destruction of the present, area *f.g.* is irrational and its square root *a.c.* is irrational.

### Proposition 71.

**If** a line be subtracted from a line, and both are incommensurable in power, and they contain a medial area, while both their squares taken together form a rational area: the remaining line will be irrational and shall be called the **minor** line <term>minor line|An irrational line formed by the difference of two lines that are incommensurable in power, where the sum of their squares is rational but their rectangle is medial.</term>.

If *a.b.* and *b.c.* are as proposed (which are found by Proposition 27 and compose a "major" line), the line *a.c.* will be irrational, and it is that which is called the minor line. Whoever holds the preceding propositions firmly and attends to the positions diligently will easily prove this in two ways, as with the preceding ones.

¶ If there be four quantities such that the difference of the first to the second is as the difference of the third to the fourth, then by permutation <note>original: "permutatim"; a logical rearrangement of terms in a proportion</note>, the difference of the first to the third will be as the difference of the second to the fourth. ¶ This is to be understood regarding quantities related in the same way; just as when the first is greater than the second, so also the third is greater than the fourth, and when it is less, the other is less. For example, let the difference of *a.* to *b.* be as *c.* to *d.* I say that the difference of *a.* to *c.* will be as *b.* to *d.* For by this common perception <note>original: "coem ai pceptionē"; referring to a mathematical axiom or common notion</note>, the difference of the extremes is composed of the differences of those same extremes to the middle. The difference of *a.* to *c.* is composed of that which is *a.* to *b.* and that which is *b.* to *c.* But the difference of *b.* to *d.* by the same perception is composed of that which is *b.* to *c.* and that which is *c.* to *d.* And because by hypothesis the difference of *a.* to *b.* is as *c.* to *d.*, and that which is *b.* to *c.* is common to both, it follows by common science that *a.* to *c.* is as *b.* to *d.*, which was proposed.

¶ For let **a.c.** be a second medial residual from which line **b.c.** was cut off from **a.b.** And by Proposition 70, the two lines **a.b.** and **b.c.** will be medial, commensurable only in square <term>commensurable in square|Lines whose squares have a ratio that can be expressed by a whole number, even if the lines themselves do not.</term>, containing a medial area. I say that this **a.c.** can be joined to no other line than **c.b.** under this definition. But if it is joined to line **c.d.**, let line **e.f.** be rational in length to which is joined surface **e.h.** equal to the squares of the two lines **a.b.** and **b.c.** taken together, and **e.k.** equal to the squares of the lines **a.d.** and **d.c.** taken together, from which is cut off **e.g.** equal to the square of line **a.c.** Then by the 7th proposition of the second book, surface **l.b.** will be equal to twice the surface of **a.b.** into **b.c.**, and let **l.k.** by the same be equal to twice the surface of **a.d.** into **d.c.** Therefore, because the squares of both parts of the first section are medial, and twice the surface is also medial and incommensurable with the two squares taken together—which the diligent geometer who has carefully observed the positions cannot fail to know—surface **e.h.** will be medial since it is equal to the two squares taken together, and surface **l.h.** medial since it is equal to twice the surface of one into the other. By Proposition 20, therefore, each of the two lines **f.h.** and **g.h.** is rational in square only. And because one is incommensurable to the other (because surface **e.h.** is incommensurable to surface **h.l.**, just as two squares are to twice the surface), by Proposition 68 line **f.g.** will be a residual <term>residual|In Latin "residuum," often translated as "apotome." A line formed by subtracting a smaller magnitude from a larger one.</term>, wherefore line **f.g.** which is the residual is composed of line **g.h.** so that both are under the term of those that were before the separation. Similarly also you will prove the same **f.g.** to be composed with line **g.k.** by the same condition through the middle surfaces **e.k.** and **k.l.**, of which the first is equal to the squares of the two lines **a.d.** and **d.c.** taken together, and the second to twice the surface of one into the other; which is impossible by Proposition 74, and this method of demonstration can be common to Proposition 75 and the other four following it.

### Proposition 78

**N**o "minor" line can be joined to another so that it fits under its limit, except for the one that was originally joined to it before the cutting. <note>The "minor line" is a specific irrational line defined in Proposition 76. This proposition proves that if you have a "minor" line, there is only one specific magnitude that could have been subtracted from a larger magnitude to create it.</note>
¶ Understand what a minor line is: if you have forgotten, consult Proposition 21. 2. <note>original: ".21. 2." refers to Book X, Proposition 21, or perhaps a sub-definition.</note> without objection you will conclude the proposition. If you proceed as in Proposition 74, you will be able to proceed as in Proposition 76 if you wish.

### Proposition 78

**A** line which, when joined with a rational line, makes the whole [area] medial, can only be composed with one such line so that they meet at their limit. <note>This second "Proposition 78" appears to be a specific case or a variation found in this edition's layout, focusing on lines that produce medial areas.</note>
¶ You have learned what this proposed line is from Proposition 72. Therefore, when you wish to demonstrate what is said by this Proposition 78, do not deviate from the process of Proposition 75; but just as in Proposition 76, if it pleases you, you may proceed with your intellect as your guide.

### Proposition 79

**A** line which, when joined with a medial line, makes the whole [area] medial, cannot be joined to any except one line so that they meet at the limit they held before separation. The "teacher" <note>original: "mgr̃a" for magistra or "rule"</note> of this line, which when joined with a medial composes a medial whole, is Proposition 73. Concerning this, you will be compelled to conclude what Proposition 79 states in the same way you concluded the second medial residual stated in Proposition 76.

¶ Given two lines, one rational and the other a residual: when a line is added to that residual according to its limit, if the whole formed from it is "more powerful" <term>more powerful|A term meaning that the square of the longer line exceeds the square of the shorter line by the square of a third line.</term> than the added line by the square of a line commensurable to the whole in length; and if that same whole is commensurable in length to the designated rational line, it shall be called the **first residual**. 
But if the added line is commensurable in length to the designated rational line, it shall be called the **second residual**. 
And if both [the whole and the added part] are incommensurable in length to the designated rational line, it shall be called the **third residual**. 
If the whole line is more powerful than the added part by the square of a line *incommensurable* to the whole, and that same whole is commensurable in length to the designated rational line, it shall be named the **fourth residual**. 
But if the added line is commensurable in length to the designated rational line, it shall be called the **fifth residual**. 
And if both are incommensurable in length to the designated rational line, it shall be called the **sixth residual**.

### Proposition 80

**T**o find the first residual. The discovery of all types of binomials in order easily releases us for the discovery of all types of residuals. For in any type of binomial, if the smaller portion is cut away from the larger, the remaining line will be a residual of the same type, as is clear from the definitions of both binomials and residuals. Nevertheless, persisting in the specific discoveries of residuals, we seek the first as follows. Let line **a.** be the designated rational line, and let **b. c.** be commensurable to it in length. Let **e.** be a square number divided into **f.** (which is not a square) and into **g.** (which is a square). Let the proportion of the square of line **b. c.** to the square of line **c. d.** be as **e.** is to **f.** By the final part, **c. d.** will be rational only in power <note>original: "rōnalis i potētia tm̄" — meaning its square is rational, but the line itself is incommensurable to the unit.</note>. Since therefore **c. b.** is more powerful than **c. d.** by the square of a line commensurable to itself in length (which is clear from the explanation of the first binomial and the definition of lines), it stands that line **b. d.** is the **first residual**.

### Proposition 81

**T**o reveal the second residual. To obtain the second residual, let **a.** be the designated rational line, and let **c. d.** be commensurable to it in length. Let the square of **c. d.** to the square of **b. c.** be as **f.** to **e.** Thus **b. d.** will be the **second residual** by definition. If you doubt this, you either are not observing the given hypotheses or you need a repetition of the second binomial.

### Proposition 82.
### To investigate the third residual.

<margin>
<note>A geometric diagram illustrating proportions with line segments and numbers. A horizontal line is marked with points 'e', 'd', and 'b'. Below it is a line segment labeled 'a'. Further down are numerical and literal labels: '3', 'e', and '6', positioned above segments labeled 'f', 'h', and 'g'. At the very bottom is the number '7'.</note>
</margin>

**T**he third residual <note>original: "residuum tertium"; in modern geometry, these are called apotomes</note> is obtained in this way: let a rational line *a* be given as before, and let a square number *e* be divided into a non-square number *f* and a square number *g*. Let the first number *b* be assumed such that the square of line *a* is to the square of line *bc* as *b* is to *e*. Let the square of line *bc* be to the square of line *cd* as *e* is to *f*. It will then follow from the definition—and if you have any doubt, consult the third binomial—that the line *db* is the third residual.

### Proposition 83.
### To find the fourth residual.

**H**ere, just as in the finding of the first residual, let the line *bc* be commensurable in length with the given rational line *a*. Let the square number *e* be divided into *f* and *g*, both of which are non-square numbers. Let the square of line *bc* be to the square of line *cd* as *e* is to *f*. You will then know from the definition that line *db* is the fourth residual, provided you have not forgotten what you learned in the finding of the fourth binomial.

### Proposition 84.
### To demonstrate the fifth residual.

**W**hen you wish to find the fifth residual, let the line *cd* be commensurable in length with the given rational line *a*, just as it was in the inquiry of the second [residual]. Let the square number *e* be divided into *f* and *g*, neither of which is a square, as in the previous proposition. Let the square of line *cd* be to the square of line *bc* as *f* is to *e*. From these points, one may conclude by definition—having sufficient knowledge of the fifth binomial—that line *db* is the fifth residual.

### Proposition 85.
### Finally, to find the sixth residual readily.

**T**he sixth residual is found thus: let there be, as before, a given rational line *a* and a square number *e* divided into non-squares *f* and *g*. Let *b* be a first number <note>likely referring to a prime or fundamental number in the ratio</note>, and let the square of line *a* be to the square of line *bc* as *b* is to *e*. Furthermore, let the square of *bc* be to the square of *cd* as *e* is to *f*. It will follow from the definition that line *db* is the sixth residual. If your mind does not fully assent to this, it is proper for you to practice in the finding of the sixth binomial.

### Proposition 86.
### If an area is contained by a rational line and a first residual, its square root must be a residual.

<margin>
<note>A vertical rectangular diagram divided into three horizontal sub-rectangles by two internal lines. The left vertices are labeled from top to bottom: g, b, k, a. The right vertices are labeled from top to bottom: f, e, c, b.</note>
</margin>

**L**et the area <note>original: "superficies"</note> *ac* be contained by the rational line *ab* and the first residual *bc*. I say that the square root <note>original: "latus tetragonicū"; literally the 'tetragonal side,' the side of a square equal in area to the rectangle</note> of the area *ac* is a residual. For let a line *cd* be joined to line *bc*, and let it be that line which, by its subtraction, made *bc* a first residual. It follows by definition that *bd* is rational in length and *cd* is rational only in power <note>meaning its square is rational, but the line itself is not</note>. Also, *bd* will be more powerful than *dc* <note>meaning the square of bd exceeds the square of dc</note> by the square of a line commensurable with it in length. Therefore, let *dc* be divided into equal parts at *e*, and let the whole line *bd* be divided according to the [previously established] condition at *f*, so that between *bf* and *fd*, the line *ed* is a mean proportional. From the second part of Proposition 13, *bf* is commensurable in length with *fd* by Proposition 9; therefore both of them are commensurable with the whole line *bd*. Wherefore, by definition, both are rational in length. Let the lines *fg*, *eh*, and *ck* be drawn parallel to *ab*. By Proposition 15, each of the two areas *af* and *gd* will be rational. Therefore, let the square *lm* be equal to the area *af*; it will be rational, and its side rational in power. Within that square, having drawn the diagonal line *lm*, describe a square *ln* equal to the area *gd*. This will also be rational, and its side rational in power.

...let two lines, *m-p* and *q-n*, be drawn parallel to the sides of the whole square. I say, therefore, that the square *p-r* is equal to the surface <note>The word "surface" here refers to the area of a rectangle or geometric figure.</note> *a-c*, and its side, which is *n-p*, is a residual <note>original: "residuum"; a line formed by subtracting one magnitude from another, often called an "apotome" in modern geometry.</note>. For since line *d-e* is, by hypothesis, the mean proportional <note>A value between two others such that the first is to the mean as the mean is to the third.</note> between *b-f* and *f-d*, it follows from the first proposition of Book VI that the surface *d-b* is the mean proportional between the two surfaces *a-f* and *g-d*. Consequently, it is also the mean between the two squares *l-m* and *n-l*. Thus, the whole gnomon <note>The L-shaped figure remaining after a smaller square is removed from a larger one.</note> circumscribed around square *m-n* is equal to *c-g*. Since *l-m* was equal to *a-f*, there remains *m-n* equal to *a-c*. To understand why *n-p*, the side of square *m-n*, is a residual, consider this: both *p-t* and *t-n* are rational in power <note>original: "rōnalis in potentia"; this means their squares are rational areas, though the lines themselves may be irrational.</note>, because each square *l-m* and *n-l* is rational. Each of these is incommensurable to the other by the first proposition of Book VI and Proposition 10 of this book, because the square *l-m* is incommensurable to the surface *l-r*, just as surface *a-f* is to surface *b-d*. It is clear these are incommensurable; for by the first of Book VI, one is to the other as line *b-f* (which is rational in length) is to line *d-e* (which is rational in power only) by Proposition 68. Therefore, line *p-n*, which has power over surface *a-c* <note>Meaning the side of a square whose area is equal to surface a-c.</note>, is a residual: and this is what we intended to show.

### Proposition 87.
**I**f a surface is contained by a rational line and a second residual, the line having power over it will be a first medial residual.
<note>In this context, "contained by" refers to the sides of a rectangle. This proposition identifies the type of irrational line that results from taking the square root of such a rectangle.</note>
¶ In this case, argue as in the previous proposition, using the definition of the second residual and the second part of Propositions 13, 9, 19, 15, and 69.

### Proposition 88.
**I**f a surface is contained by a rational line and a third residual, the line having power over it will be a second medial residual.
¶ Persist in the previous demonstration and you will easily conclude the proposal from the definition of the third residual and the second part of Propositions 13, 9, 19, and 70.

### Proposition 89.
**I**f a surface is contained by a rational line and a fourth residual, the line having power over it will be a minor line.
¶ Proceed in this one no differently than before. It will be easy to conclude the proposal if you do not overlook the previous steps, using the definition of the fourth residual and the second part of Propositions 14, 9, 19, 15, and 71; thus the proposal will be clear.

### Proposition 90.
**I**f a surface is contained by a rational line and a fifth residual, its square root <note>original: "latus eius tetragonicum"; literally "its four-angled side."</note> will be a line which, when added to a rational, makes a medial area.
¶ Rely on the previous reasoning and the definition of the fifth residual and the second part of Propositions 14, 9, 19, 15, and 72 to conclude this proposal.

### Proposition 91.
**I**f a surface is contained by a rational line and a sixth residual, the square root which has power over it will be proven to be a line which, when added to a medial, makes a medial area.
¶ Now finally, for what is stated here, strive to conclude in the same manner as above, using the definition of the sixth residual and the second part of Propositions 14, 9, 19, and 73.

**Technical Vocabulary Glossary:**
- **Residual (residuū):** A line formed by subtracting a smaller magnitude from a larger one (apotome).
- **Rational (rationale):** A magnitude that can be expressed as a ratio or whose square is a known area.
- **Surface (superficies):** The area of a geometric figure.
- **Side (latus):** The length of a line, often the square root of an area.
- **Medial (mediale):** A type of irrational line whose square is a rational area.
- **Proposition (propositio):** A mathematical statement to be proven.
- **Definition (diffinitione):** The formal explanation of a term's meaning.
- **Square root (tetragonicum):** Pertaining to the side of a square.
- **Minor (minor):** A specific category of irrational line defined earlier in Book X.
</note>
