### Proposition .92.
**If a surface equal to the square of a residual <note>original: "residuum"; in modern geometry, this is often called an "apotome," a line formed by subtracting a smaller rational line from a larger one where they are commensurable only in power.</note> is applied to a rational line: the other side must be a first residual.**

These six following propositions are, in order, the inverses of the six preceding ones. The intention of this proposition is that if there is a surface *a-c* applied to a rational line *a-b* <note>The "application" of an area is a Greek method of division; it means forming a rectangle with a given area on a given line.</note> equal to the square of a residual *d-e*, then its second side *b-c* is necessarily a first residual. Let there be added to line *d-e* (which is proposed to be a residual) the line by whose subtraction it was made a residual; let this added line be *e-f*. Then, from Proposition 68, both lines *d-f* and *f-e* are rational in power <note>original: "rōnalis in potentia"; meaning the squares of the lines are rational, though the lines themselves may be irrational in length.</note> and one of them is incommensurable to the other. Therefore, let the square of line *f-e* be described as *e-g*, and the square of *d-e* (which was stated to be a residual) as *e-b*, and let the supplements *d-k* and *f-l* be added. The square *g-b* will then be as the square of line *d-f*, and the square *e-b* will be as the surface *a-c*. Also, both squares *g-b* and *g-e* will be rational. 

Therefore, let the surface *a-m* be applied to the line *a-b* equal to the square *g-b*; because of this, it will be rational. Therefore, by Proposition 16, line *m-n* is rational in length. Furthermore, let surface *p-n* be equal to square *e-g*; because of this, it will also be rational, and by Proposition 16, line *m-n* is rational in length. Thus, the whole line *b-n* is rational by Proposition 9. Now, let *c-n* be divided into two equal parts at *m-q*, and let *q-r* be drawn parallel to *a-b*. From the first proposition of Book VI, *c-r* is equal to *r-n*. It is clear that since the whole surface *a-n* is equal to the two squares *g-b* and *e-g* taken together (which are the squares of the two lines *d-f* and *f-e*), and the surface *a-c* is equal to the square of line *d-e* (which is *e-b*), then by the seventh proposition of Book II, the remaining surface from *a-n* (which is *c-f*) is equal to twice the surface formed by *d-f* and *f-e*. Therefore, their halves, which are *r-n* and *d-g*, must also be equal. 

Since, therefore, by the first proposition of Book VI, the surface *d-g* is the mean proportional <note>A geometric middle: the area of the middle figure is equal to the square root of the product of the two outer figures.</note> between the two squares *g-b* and *g-e*, the surface *r-n* will also be the mean proportional between the two surfaces *a-m* and *p-n*. Therefore, by the first of Book VI, line *q-n* will also be the mean proportional between the two lines *b-m* and *m-n*. Since *q-n* is half of line *n-c*, and line *b-n* is divided by point *m* into two commensurable parts between which *q-n* falls as a mean proportional, it follows from the first part of Proposition 13 that the square of line *b-n* is greater than the square of line *n-c* by the square of a line commensurable to it in length. Because surface *d-g* is medial <note>original: "medialis"; a type of irrational area whose side is the mean proportional between two rational lines.</note> by Proposition 19, and by hypothesis surface *c-r* is equal to it, then *c-r* is medial and line *c-q* is rational in power. Thus, its double, which is line *n-c*, is rational only in power. Since *b-n* is rational in length, commensurable to the line *a-b* (which was set as rational), and its square is greater than *n-c* by the square of a line commensurable to it in length, it follows from the definition that line *b-c* is a first residual; which is what was to be proven.

### Proposition .93.
**If a surface equal to the square of a first medial residual is applied to a rational line: its other side will be a second residual.**

In this case, line *d-e* will be a first medial residual, and line *e-f* will be that line by whose subtraction *d-e* was made a first medial residual. I say that *b-c* will be a second residual. You cannot fail to know this if you persist in the demonstration of the previous proposition until you have grasped it with a firm habit, and if you watchfully attend to what kind of lines *d-f* and *f-e* ought to be; if you doubt this, Proposition 69 should be consulted.

### Proposition .94.
**If a surface equal to the square of a second medial residual <note>original: "residuum mediale secundum"</note> is applied to a rational line, its other side will necessarily be a third residual.**
¶ Here also, *d.e.* will be a second medial residual, and it follows that *c.b.* will be a third residual. To conclude this easily, persist in the first demonstration and gather what kind of lines *d.f.* and *f.e.* turn out to be from [Proposition] 70.

### Proposition .95.
**When a surface equal to the square of a minor line <note>original: "linea minor"; in Euclid's classification, this is an irrational line whose square is the difference between two areas that are incommensurable with one another.</note> is applied to a rational line, its second side will be a fourth residual.**
¶ If *d.e.* is a minor line, this [Proposition] 95 asserts that *b.c.* will be a fourth residual. One must take from [Proposition] 71 what kind of lines *d.f.* and *f.e.* must be when *d.e.* is a minor line. The proposition is to be built up in the manner previously shown, except that in this and the two following propositions, it is necessary for line *b.n.* to be divided at point *m* into two incommensurable <note>original: "incommensurabilia"</note> parts, whereas in the three preceding ones it was necessarily divided into two commensurable parts. For in the three preceding cases, there were two lines *d.f.* and *f.e.* which were commensurable in power only <note>original: "communicantes in potentia tantum"; this means their squares have a rational ratio, but the lines themselves do not.</note>, and therefore their squares were commensurable. Because of this, the surfaces *a.m.* and *p.n.* (being equal to those squares) were also commensurable. Consequently, the two lines *b.m.* and *m.n.* were also commensurable, and thus in the three preceding cases, the line *b.n.* was more powerful than line *n.c.* by the square of a line commensurable with it in length, according to the first part of [Proposition] 13. However, in this and the following two cases, the two lines *d.f.* and *f.e.* are incommensurable in power, as appears from [Propositions] 71, 72, and 73; therefore their squares, and consequently the surfaces *a.m.* and *p.n.*, are incommensurable. Because of this, the two lines *b.m.* and *m.n.* are incommensurable. Therefore, by the first part of [Proposition] 14, in this as well as in the two following cases, line *b.n.* must be more powerful than line *n.c.* by the square of a line incommensurable with it in length. Investigate the rest as before.

### Proposition .96.
**If a surface equal to the square of a line which, when added to a rational area, produces a medial area <note>original: "linee cum rationali constituentis mediale"</note>, is applied to a rational line, its second side will be a fifth residual.**
¶ Similarly, set line *d.e.* here as that which, joined with a rational, produces a whole medial area, and observe from [Proposition] 72 what kind of lines *d.f.* and *f.e.* must be. You will conclude without stumbling, if you have skillfully attended to the previous demonstration, that line *b.c.* is a fifth residual.

### Proposition .97.
**If a surface equal to the square of a line which, when added to a medial area, produces a medial area <note>original: "linee cum mediali componentis mediale"</note>, is applied to a rational line, its other side will be a sixth residual.**
¶ Now, finally, it is appropriate that line *d.e.* be that which, joined with a medial area, composes a whole medial area, to which is joined line *e.f.*—specifically, that line by whose subtraction line *d.e.* was formed. If you learn from [Proposition] 73 what kind of lines *d.f.* and *f.e.* must be, and hold the previous argument firmly in mind, you will be able to conclude without obstacle that line *b.c.* is a sixth residual. But if by chance you happen to hesitate in anything, whatever it may be, it must be compared from the square *g.b.* to its equal surface *a.n.*, and thus our proposition will be clear.

**Every line commensurable with a residual <note>original: "residuum"</note> is itself also the same residual in both character and order.**

->Proposition 100<-

**If any line is commensurable with a minor line, it will itself also be a minor line.**
It is easy to prove this in two ways, just like the previous proposition: whether some line is commensurable with a minor line <note>original: "linea minor," an irrational line defined in Proposition 76</note> in length or in square <note>original: "in potentia," referring to the areas formed by the lines</note>. Therefore, from proposition 72, b is a line which produces a medial area when added to a rational area. As for the second method: d, e will be a fifth residual from proposition 69, and therefore so will e, g from proposition 98; wherefore b is a line which produces a medial area when added to a rational area, through proposition 90.

->Proposition .103.<-

If a **medial area** <note>An area whose side is the mean proportional between two rational lines commensurable only in power</note> is subtracted from a **rational area**, the line producing the remaining area will be one of two irrational lines: either a **residual** or a **minor line**.
¶ For let the whole rational area consist of **a** and **b**, from which **b** is subtracted, which is medial: I say that the line producing <note>original: "potens," meaning the line which, when squared, equals the area</note> area **a** is either a **residual** or a **minor line**. For let the line **c, d** be rational, and let the area **c, e** be applied to it equal to **a**, and **f, g** equal to **b**, and the whole **c, g** equal to the whole **a, b**. The whole **c, g** will be rational. Therefore, by proposition 16, the line **d, g** is rational in length, and **f, g** will be medial. Therefore, by proposition 20, **e, g** is rational in power only <note>original: "in potentia tm̄," meaning its square is rational but the line itself is not commensurable with the length</note>. It follows from the definition that the line **d, e** is a **first** or **fourth residual**. Therefore, by propositions 86, 87, and 89, the line producing the area **c, e** (and thus the area **a**, which is equal to it) is a **residual** or a **minor line**: which is what was proposed.

->Proposition .104.<-

If a **rational area** is subtracted from a **medial area**, the line producing the remaining area will be one of two irrational lines: either a **first medial residual** or a **line which with a rational area produces a medial area**.
¶ This is proven just like the preceding. For let the whole area **a, b** be medial, and let **b** be rational. I say that the line producing area **a** is either a **first medial residual** or a **line which with a rational area produces a medial area**. For since **c, g** is equal to **a, b**, then by proposition 20, the line **d, g** is rational in power only. And since **f, g** is equal to **b**, then by proposition 16, the line **e, g** is rational in length. Therefore, by definition, the line **d, e** will be a **second** or **fifth residual**. Wherefore, by propositions 87 and 90, the **square side** <note>original: "latus tetragonicū," the line which forms a square equal to the area</note> of area **c, e** (and thus of area **a**) is a **first medial residual** or a **line which with a rational area produces a medial area**: which is our proposition.

->Proposition .105.<-

If a **medial area** is subtracted from another **medial area**, and the remaining area is incommensurable with the whole, the line producing that remaining area will be one of two irrationals: namely, either a **second medial residual** or a **line which with a medial area produces a medial area**.
¶ If you do not deviate from the demonstrations of the two preceding propositions, you will conclude the proposal without difficulty. For let the whole **a, b** and the part **b** be medial, and let the remainder **a** be incommensurable with the whole. Otherwise, **a** would be medial by proposition 21, and its square side would be medial by proposition 19. Then I say that the line producing area **a** is a **second medial residual** or a **line which with a medial area produces a medial area**. For since **c, g** is equal to **a, b**, then by proposition 20, the line **d, g** is rational in power only. Likewise, since **f, g** is equal to **b**, then **e, g** is also rational in power only. And since **a** is incommensurable with the whole **a, b**, then **f, g** is incommensurable with **c, g**. Therefore, by the first proposition of the sixth book and the 10th of this book, **e, g** will also be incommensurable with **d, g**. Therefore, by definition, the line **d, e** will be a **third** or **sixth residual**. Wherefore, by propositions 88 and 91, the square side of area **c, e** (and thus of area **a**) is a **second medial residual** or a **line which with a medial area produces a medial area**.

### BOOK X

The irrational lines following it differ in species and in definition from one another, and no single line can fall under two or even more species of these six irrational lines, which are the **residual** <note>original: "residuum," also known in modern geometry as an apotome; a line formed by subtracting a smaller rational line from a larger one</note> and its five companions. Furthermore, all species of the residual differ from all species of the **binomial** <note>original: "binomium," a line composed of the sum of two rational parts that are only commensurable in square</note>; nor is it possible for one line to be simultaneously a residual and a binomial of any species. The first part is established as follows: since areas equal to the squares of the residual and its five companions, when applied to a rational line, have their second sides necessarily different from one another according to proposition 92 and the five following it. These second sides are the first residual, the second, and so on up to the sixth. The second part is established in this way: if the same line could be simultaneously a residual and a binomial, let it be **a**, and let its square be applied to the rational line **b, c**, and let the resulting area be **b, d**. Then, by proposition 54, the line **c, d** would be a first binomial, and by proposition 92, it would be a first residual. Insofar as it is a first binomial, let it be divided into its binomial portions at point **e**, and let the greater portion be **c, e**, which by definition was rational in length. However, insofar as it is a first residual, let the line **d, g** be added to it, by whose subtraction it had been a first residual; then, by definition, **c, g** would also be rational in length. Since, therefore, each of the two lines **c, e** and **c, g** is rational in length, then by proposition 9, the line **e, g** will also be rational in length. But since line **d, e** is rational in square only (as it is, by hypothesis, the lesser portion of a first binomial), then by proposition 68, the line **d, g** would be a residual. Yet, because it was rational in square only when its subtraction formed the residual line **c, d**, an impossibility follows according to proposition 68. To make this more clearly apparent: let the area **b, d** be applied to the rational line **b, c** equal to the square of line **d, g**. Since line **d, g** is rational in square, then by proposition 16, the line **c, d** will be rational in length. But since line **d, g** is also a residual, then by proposition 92, line **c, d** would be a first residual, which cannot be, since the line called a residual is irrational by proposition 68.

->Proposition .107.<-

The line which is called a **residual**, or any of the irrational lines which follow it, cannot fall under the term of a **binomial**, nor under the term and order of any of the other irrational lines that follow the binomial. Furthermore, while it is possible for the series of irrational lines to be produced unto infinity, it is not possible for any of them to coincide in term and order with one that precedes it.

¶ Through this final proposition of the tenth book, he intends to show that the 13 irrational lines demonstrated in this tenth book—which are the **medial line**, the **binomial** and its five companions, and the **residual** and its five companions—are each individually different in species from one another. No single line can be simultaneously classified under two or more species of them, and the species of irrational lines can be produced to infinity, as none of them coincides with another in definition and order. However, remember that it was demonstrated above how these 13 lines—namely the medial, the binomial and its 5 companions, and the residual and its 5 companions—are irrational: for the medial from proposition 19; for the binomial and its five companions from proposition 30 and the five following it; and indeed for the residual and its five companions from proposition 68 and the five following it. That none of these 13 irrational lines can coincide in species with any of the others, gather as follows: For let areas equal to the squares of the aforementioned 13 irrational lines be applied to one and the same line, rational in length, according to the order in which they follow each other. Then, by proposition 20, the second side of the first of these 13 areas and the five following it will be rational in square only. But the second sides of the second group of these 13 areas and the five following it will be all the species of binomials in order, namely the first, second, and so on up to the sixth, as you remember was demonstrated from proposition 54 and the five following it. Then, the second sides of the eighth area and the five following it are the species of residuals in order, namely the first residual and the residual...

...the second and so on up to the sixth, which you have learned from proposition 92 and the five following it. Since, therefore, a line that is rational only in square <note>original: "rationalis in potentia tantum"; a line whose square is rational and commensurable with a given rational area, but which is not commensurable in length with the standard unit line</note> does not coincide with any species of **binomials** or with any of the **residuals**, because every binomial (by proposition 30) and every residual (by proposition 68) is an irrational line both in length and in square. And since no species of residuals coincides with any species of binomials (from the second part of the penultimate proposition of this tenth book), it follows that all the second sides of these 13 areas <note>In Euclidean geometry, "applying an area" to a line creates a rectangle; the "second side" refers to the width of that rectangle</note> are different from one another. Therefore, by the first proposition of the sixth book, the 13 areas themselves are different, since the height of all of them is the same; wherefore these 13 proposed irrational lines are also each different from the others.

¶ Furthermore, the species of these 13 irrational lines can be extended to infinity. For there are infinite species of **medial** lines <note>original: "linea medialis"; the side of a square equal to a rectangle contained by two rational lines commensurable only in square</note>, and likewise infinite species of binomials, and so on for each type. This is demonstrated in this manner: let line **a** be medial. Let a unit be taken and any number of prime numbers, such as 3, 5, and 7. Let there be as many lines **b, c, d** as there are prime numbers taken. Let the squares of these lines **b, c, d** be to the square of **a** as these prime numbers are to the unit. Then lines **b, c, d** will be medial according to proposition 21, because they are commensurable in square with the medial line **a**. However, all of them will be different in length from **a** and from each other by the last part of proposition 7; for the ratio of none of these numbers to the unit, nor of any one of them to another (by propositions 16 and 8, the corollary of the second proposition of the eighth book, and the present hypothesis) is as a square number to a square number. Therefore, **a** and all lines commensurable with it in length fall under the first species of medial lines; **b** and all lines commensurable with it in length under the second; **c** and all those commensurable with it under the third; and **d** and all those commensurable with it in length under the fourth. And because prime numbers are infinite (as you learned from proposition 21 of the ninth book), it is necessary that the species of medial lines be infinite.

What has been said of the medial line should also be understood for the binomial and its five companions, and the residual and its five companions. For just as every line commensurable with a medial line is medial (whether it is commensurable in length or in square, as proved in proposition 21), so also every line commensurable in length or in square with a binomial, or any of its five companions, or even a residual or any of its five companions, is of the same species as that line (as proved in proposition 60 and the four following it, and proposition 98 and the four following it). Therefore, the species of these 13 irrational lines are infinite, and none of them will coincide with a preceding one in order or definition.

It is also agreed that in another way the species of irrational lines are infinite: for every **square side** <note>original: "latus tetragonicum"; what we today call a square root</note> of an area designated by a non-square number is irrational by the last part of proposition 7 and by the definition. Since such numbers are infinite, the species of these irrational lines will also be infinite.

In a third way, the second part of this last conclusion of the tenth book happens to be explained thus: we may say that from every line that is rational only in square, infinite species of irrational lines are produced, none of which can coincide in definition or order with any of those that preceded it. For example: Let some rational area be taken, designated by a non-square number such as 5. Its square side will be irrational in length, because it is incommensurable with the square side of a rational area designated by a square number (from the last part of proposition 7). I say, therefore, that the side of this side, and the side of that second side, and again the side of this third side, and so on to infinity, are irrational lines both in length and in square; and none of them coincides in definition or species with any that preceded it in order. And the square side of the premise area (whatever non-square number it was designated by) is like the root and origin of all of them, and each of them is the origin of all those following it. And whatever lines proceed from any square side of any such area are different in length and square from all those generated from any other square side of such an area; and I say this when the areas themselves...

### BOOK X

...is not a proportion <note>original: "proportio"; the relationship between two quantities</note> like that of square numbers. This, however, as we can gather by firm demonstration, it is necessary to set forth as a premise to these things. And let it be thus:

¶ Whenever any two [numbers] are multiplied by each other, if a product is generated, as many square roots <term>latus tetragonica: the side of a square, which we now call a square root</term> of the two preceding numbers as you multiply together, you will produce the entire square root of the product itself.

<note>A geometrical diagram on the left margin illustrates proportional relationships between squares and their roots. At the top is a line 'k' labeled '1296'. Below it are lines 'a' (81) and 'b' (16), joined by a bracketed line 'e' (36). Below these are lines 'c' (9) and 'd' (4), joined by line 'h' (6). At the bottom are lines 'f' (3) and 'g' (2), joined by a line 'i'. Vertical strokes connect corresponding endpoints to show that 81 times 16 equals 1296, 9 times 4 equals 36, and 3 times 2 equals 6, while also showing the square root relationships between the levels.</note>

¶ For example, let **k** be the product of **a** multiplied by **b**. Let **c** and **d** be the square roots of **a** and **b**. Let **e** be produced from **c** multiplied by **d**. Again, let **f** and **g** be the square roots of **c** and **d**, and let **h** be produced from **f** multiplied by **g**. I say that **h** is the square root of **e**, and that **e** in turn is the square root of **k**. For since **c** and **h** are produced from **f** multiplied by itself and by **g**, then **c** is to **h** as **f** is to **g**. But **h** is also to **d** as **f** is to **g**, because **h** and **d** are produced from **g** multiplied by **f** and by itself. Therefore, **c, h, d** are in continuous proportion <note>original: "continue proportionales"; a sequence where the ratio of each term to the next is constant, such as 4, 6, 9</note>. Thus, **h** multiplied by itself is as much as **c** multiplied by **d**; wherefore **h** is the square root of **e**. By the same reasoning, since **a** is from **c** multiplied by itself, and **e** is from **c** multiplied by **d**, and **b** is from **d** multiplied by itself, then **a, c, h** will also be in continuous proportion in the ratio of **c** to **d**. Since therefore **k** is from **a** multiplied by **b**, it follows also that **k** is from **e** multiplied by itself; wherefore **e** is the square root of **k**. Thus what was said is established. It remains, therefore, to demonstrate what was proposed.

Let there be, then, a surface area **a**, called rational but derived from a non-square number, such as 5. Let line **a** be its square root, and let any number of lines be taken that are rational in length <term>rationales i longitudine: lines whose length can be expressed as a whole number or fraction of the standard unit</term>, which shall be **b, c, d, e**. Let these be defined by numbers where each preceding one is the square root of the next following: as if **b** were 2, **c** 4, **d** 16, and **e** indeed 256. To these lines, rational in length, let a surface area equal to **a** be applied; the second sides of each will then be rational in length by the 16th proposition; for example, the second side of **b** would be 2 and a half; the second side of **c** would be one and a fourth; the second side of **d** would be one fourth and one sixteenth. But indeed, the second side of surface area **e** will be one sixty-fourth and one two-hundred-and-fifty-sixth. Let **f** be the square root of **b**, and **g** be the square root of the second side of area **b**. It will follow from the preceding premise that **a** is produced from **f** multiplied by **g**. Again, let **h** be the square root of the second side of **c**, and let **k** also be the square root of **b**. It will follow from the aforementioned premise that **a** is produced from **b** multiplied by **b** <note>This likely refers to the area application</note>, and from **f** multiplied by **k** comes the square root of **a**, which let be **l**. Again, let **m** be the square root of the second side of surface area **d**. But since **n** is the square root of **m**, and **p** the square root of **n**, it will follow from the aforementioned premise that from **c** multiplied by **m** becomes **a**, and from **b** multiplied by **n** comes **l**, and from **f** multiplied by **p** the square root of **l**, which let be **q**. Furthermore, let **r** be the square root of the second side of area **e**. Let **s** also be the square root of **r**, and **f** and **t** [be related to] **l**. Also let **u** be the square root of **t**. It follows through the stated premise that from **d** multiplied by **r** comes **a**, and from **c** multiplied by **s** comes **l**, and from **b** multiplied by **t** comes **q**, and also from **f** multiplied by **u** comes the square root of **q**, which let be **x**. And so on to infinity.

I say, therefore, that these lines **a, l, q, x**, of which **a** is like the radical origin, are irrational. Line **a** indeed is irrational in length only <note>Its square is rational, but the line itself is not commensurable with the unit</note>; the others, however, are irrational both in length and in square <term>in longitudine et in potentia: neither the line nor its square is commensurable with the rational standard</term>. And I say that none of them coincides with another in definition or order. Because **a** and **l** are produced from **f** multiplied by **g** and **k**, **a** is to **l** as **g** is to **k**. And as is clear from the stated hypotheses, **g** and **k** are incommensurable <note>original: "incommensurabiles"; having no common measure</note> in length and in square. It follows also that **a** and **l** are incommensurables in length and in square. By the same reasoning, so are **a** and **q**, for **a** is to **q** as **g** is to **p**. And for the same reason, **a** and **x** are as **g** and **u**. By this path it is also necessary that **l** and **q** be simply incommensurable both in length and in square. For since **l** and **q** are produced from **f** multiplied by **k** and **p**, **l** is to **q** as **k** is to **p**; but **k** and **p** are neither commensurable in length nor in square. If they were, then **b** and **n** would be commensurable, but they are not. Indeed, it is necessary that **l** and **x** be incommensurable in both ways: for **l** is to **x** as **k** is to **u**, because **l** and **x** are produced from **f** multiplied by **k** and **u**. However, **k** and **u** are incommensurable in both ways. Otherwise, it would happen that **d** and **b** are commensurable, which is impossible. That **q** and **x** are also incommensurable in square and length is clear from the fact that **q** is to **x** as **p** is to **u**.

It is established, moreover, that **p** and **u** are incommensurable. For if they were not, then **n**, **r**, and **c** would be commensurable, and thus also **m**, **r**, and **r**, but they are not. ¶ It is manifest, therefore, that infinite irrational lines, incommensurable in length and in power <term>potentia: "in power" refers to the area of a square built upon a line</term>, and therefore differing in definition and species, are produced from a rational line **a** that is rational in power only. It remains now to show that whatever irrational lines are generated in this way from any rational line that is rational in power only: they are different from all those which are produced—in both length and power—from any other rational line in power only, provided that the square of the latter to the square of the former is not as a square number to a square number. This is also established as follows. Let **a** and **b** be rational in power only, being the square roots <term>tetragonica latera: "tetragonal sides," the side of a square or a square root</term> of two surfaces described by non-square numbers; and let it be that those numbers are not in the proportion of any square numbers. Let the lines which proceed by this path from **a** be **c**, **d**, and **e**, and let those proceeding from **b** be **f**, **g**, and **h**. I say that none of the lines **c**, **d**, **e** communicate in length or power with any of the lines **f**, **g**, **h**. For since **c** and **f** are the square roots of **a** and **b**, and **d** and **g** are the square roots of **c** and **f**, and **e** and **h** are the square roots of **d** and **g**, it is not possible for any of **c**, **d**, **e** to communicate with its counterpart from **f**, **g**, **h** either in length or in power. For if **e** should communicate with **h** in either way, it follows that **d** would communicate with **g**, and **c** with **f**, and therefore **a** with **b** even in length, which is against the hypothesis. ¶ Generally, however, it is true to say that any of the former is incommensurable in both ways to any of the latter. For given that **d** communicates with **h** even in power only, it follows that **c** also communicates with **g**, and **a** with **f**, which is not possible. One must observe, however, that when I say the "side of a side" <note>original: "latus lateris"; effectively the fourth root or a nested square root</note> I mean nothing else than the side of a surface designated by the previous side. Wherefore I call the square root of line **a** that line which can form a surface described by line **a**. Such a surface is that which is contained by line **a** and a rational line in length called "one" <note>Euclid uses a unit line to convert a linear measure into a rectangular area for calculation</note>. If, therefore, one wishes to find the square root of any line: let **a** be the line whose square root I wish to find; let **b** be the rational line in length called "unity," which is the smallest of all rational lines numbered by integers; and let **c** be the mean proportional between them. It is therefore, by the 16th [proposition] of the Sixth Book, that **c** is the square root of **a**. For the same is produced from **a** times **b** as from **c** times itself. But indeed, from **a** times **b** comes the surface described by **a**. For whatever is produced from any thing led into one is denominated by that which the "one" multiplies. And note that when **c** is the square root of line **a**, it happens indifferently that line **c** may be greater than line **a** or smaller, according to whether **b** was also greater or smaller. ¶ Here ends the Tenth Book; here begins the Eleventh Book.

### BOOK XI

...if it contains a right angle, it shall be said to be **perpendicular** to that surface in which those lines are drawn, namely *b.c.* and *b.d.*, and any others with which it is understood to contain a right angle.

¶ A surface is **erect** upon another surface whenever, from one and the same point of the line which is the common boundary of those surfaces, two co-terminal perpendiculars are raised which, containing a right angle, are situated in those same surfaces. ¶ For example, let us imagine surface *a.b.c.d.* to rise up, while surface *c.d.e.f.* lies flat; and let us understand line *c.d.* to be the common boundary of both. In it, therefore, let a point *g* be marked, from which two perpendicular lines are drawn to line *c.d.*, one namely in surface *c.d.e.f.* which is *g.k.*, and another in surface *a.b.c.d.* which is *g.b.* If, therefore, the angle which these two perpendicular lines contain (namely *g.b.* and *g.k.*) is a right angle, surface *a.b.c.d.* is said to be **orthogonally erect** <note>original: "orthogonāliter erecta"; meaning at a perfect 90-degree angle</note> upon surface *c.d.e.f.*

¶ **Parallel surfaces** are those which, when extended in either direction, do not meet, even if they are produced to infinity. ¶ This definition is clearly understood. However, you ought to know that all plane surfaces are either parallel to one another, or, if extended in every direction, they will eventually meet somewhere and intersect along a straight line. But it is not necessary for straight lines <note>lines that are not in the same plane</note> to be either parallel or to meet when extended in both directions. Indeed, those lines which are not in the same surface are neither parallel to each other nor will they ever meet, no matter how far they are extended. ¶ **Equal and similar solids** are those whose boundary surfaces are equal in number and size, and are of one creation <note>original: "unius creationis"; implying they are generated by the same geometric rule or proportion</note> and similar. Similar solids are those contained by similar surfaces equal in number. ¶ If you do not understand these two definitions regarding equal and similar solids, return to the definition of similar surfaces placed at the beginning of the sixth book. ¶ A **serrated body** <term>corpus seratile: a prism, literally a "sawable" or "sawn" body</term> is said to be that which is contained by five surfaces, of which three are parallelograms and two are triangles.

¶ A house having four parallel walls with a roof placed upon it with a single ridge <note>original: "fastigio"; the peak of the roof</note> equal and parallel to the top sides of two of the walls, bears an express likeness to a **serrated body**. ¶ A **sphere** is the passage of the arc of the circumference of a semicircle whenever, the diameter line being held fixed, the arc itself is rotated until it returns to its place.

¶ When a semicircle is described upon any line, if that line is held fixed and the semicircle is rotated through a full revolution, the body which is described is named a **sphere**, whose center is established to be the center of the rotated semicircle. ¶ A **lateral pyramid** <term>piramis laterata: a polygonal pyramid</term> is a solid figure contained by surfaces raised upward from one base while the other faces meet at a single opposite point. ¶ In every lateral pyramid, all the surfaces surrounding it are raised from its base to a single point, which is called the **cone** <note>original: "conus"; in this context, it refers to the apex or vertex of the pyramid</note> of the pyramid; and all these lateral surfaces are triangles, but the base is frequently not a triangle. ¶ A **round pyramid** <term>piramis rotunda: a cone</term> is a solid figure; it is the passage of a right-angled triangle when one of its two sides containing the right angle is held fixed, and the triangle itself is rotated until it returns to the place from which it began to move. If the fixed side is equal to the rotated side <note>the other leg of the right triangle</note>, the figure will be **right-angled**. If the fixed side is longer, it will be **acute-angled**. If shorter, it will be **obtuse-angled**. The **axis** of this figure is the fixed side, and its base is a circle. This figure is also called the pyramid of a round column.

...until it returns to the place from which it began to move: the solid figure therefore which is described by the movement of this triangle is called a **round pyramid** <note>original: *piramis rotunda*; in modern geometry, we call this a **cone**</note>. Of these, there are three types. For one is **right-angled**, another is **acute-angled**, and the third is **obtuse-angled**. And the first is indeed when the side *a.b.* is equal to the side *b.c.* For let it be that when the line *b.c.*, by the rotation of the triangle, reaches the position of line *b.d.*, so that point *c* falls upon point *d*, one line is formed; that is, so that it then joins with the position from which it began to move in a straight line. The line here will be as *b.c.d.* And because from the 32nd proposition of the first book <note>Prop. I.32 states the sum of angles in a triangle is two right angles</note> and the 5th of the same, the angle *c.a.b.* is half of a right angle, then the angle *c.a.d.* will be a right angle. Therefore, this pyramid is called **right-angled**. But if the side *a.b.* is longer than side *b.c.*, it will be **acute-angled**; for then, from the 32nd and 19th of the first book, angle *c.a.b.* is less than half of a right angle. Therefore, the whole angle *c.a.d.* is less than a right angle and is acute; wherefore it is an acute-angled pyramid. But if the side *a.b.* is shorter than side *b.c.*, the angle *c.a.d.* will be greater than half of a right angle from the 32nd and 19th of the first book, and the whole angle *c.a.d.* (which is double the angle *c.a.b.*) is greater than a right angle and is obtuse. Therefore, the pyramid is then appropriately called **obtuse-angled**. The **axis** of this pyramid is called the line *a.b.*, and its **base** is the circle which the line *c.b.* describes around the center *b*. This pyramid is also related to that **round column** <note>A cylinder</note> which would be described by the movement of a **parallelogram** <note>specifically a rectangle</note> originating from sides *a.b.* and *b.c.*, with side *a.b.* remaining fixed.

¶ A **round solid figure** <note>A cylinder</note> whose bases are two plane circles, equal in their extremities and thickness (that is, height), is the passage of a rectangular parallelogram where one side containing the right angle is held fixed, and the surface itself is rotated until it returns to its place; and this figure is called a **round column**. Thus, for round columns, spheres, and circles, the center is one and the same. Let there be a rectangular parallelogram *a.b.c.d.* and let the side *a.b.* be fixed; with it fixed, let the whole parallelogram be rotated until it falls or returns to its place. The solid figure described by the movement of this parallelogram is named a **round column**, whose bases are two circles: one center is point *b*, and the other is that which the line *d.a.* designates by its movement, and its center is point *a*. The **axis** of this column is called the line *a.b.*, which remains fixed during the movement of the parallelogram. If we imagine the parallelogram *a.b.c.d.* when it has reached by its rotation the position *a.b.e.f.*, joining the position from which it began to move according to the continuity of a plane surface—so that the whole is one parallelogram *d.c.e.f.*—and we draw in it the diameter *d.e.*, then the diameter *d.e.* will also be the diameter of the column. As for the statement that the center of the column, the sphere, and the circle is the same: this must be understood when one and the same diameter belongs to them. For example, we have said that *d.e.* is the diameter of this column. Therefore, it is necessary that a sphere and a circle whose diameter is the line *d.e.* have the same center as the center of the corresponding column. For let it be that line *d.e.* cuts line *a.b.* at point *g*. Then *g* will be the center of the column; for it divides the axis of the column into equal parts and the diameter of the column into equal parts, which is proven by the 25th proposition of the first book. For the angles which are *a.d.g.* are equal by the 15th of the first book, and the angles at *a* and *b* are right angles by hypothesis; also line *a.d.* is equal to line *b.e.*, and so *d.g.* is equal to *e.g.*, and *a.g.* is equal to *g.b.* And since angles *c* and *f* are right angles, if a circle is described upon point *g* according to the distance *d.g.* and upon the line *d.e.*, it will pass through points *c* and *f* by the converse of the first part of the 30th proposition of the third book. Thus point *g* is the center of the circle whose diameter is the diameter of the column, and therefore also of the sphere. Wherefore it is manifest that a circle can be circumscribed around any rectangular parallelogram, and a sphere around any round column. And so it is clear what this theorem intended.

¶ A **corporeal or solid angle** is that which is contained by more than two plane angles which are situated in one surface at a single angular point...

[The previous text concluded the definition of a solid angle] ...meet. ¶ Two plane angles cannot complete a solid angle, just as two straight lines cannot enclose a surface. It is also not appropriate for the plane angles containing a solid angle to be located in the same surface, but rather in different ones, just as it is not appropriate for two straight lines forming a plane angle to be joined to each other along the same straight line <note>original: *secundum situm rectitudinis*; meaning they cannot be collinear</note>. ¶ Similar round solid figures—whether they are columns <note>term: *columne* — in modern geometry, these are called **cylinders**</note> or their pyramids <note>term: *piramides* — in modern geometry, these are called **cones**</note>—are those whose axes are proportional to the diameters of their bases. ¶ For given two round pyramids or two round columns, if the ratio of one of their axes to the diameter of its base is the same as the ratio of the other’s axis to the diameter of its base, those two columns or pyramids are said to be similar to each other.

### Proposition 1.

<note>A geometric diagram in the left margin consisting of a horizontal line with a point 'c' at the center and 'a' at the right end. A line segment 'c-b' extends diagonally upwards and to the left from 'c'. Another line segment extends horizontally to the left from 'c' to a point 'd'. This illustrates the impossibility of a single straight line bending out of a plane.</note>

**It is impossible for part of a straight line to be in a plane and part in the space above it.**
¶ Let there be a straight line *a.b.* I say that it is not possible for part of it to be in a plane and part elevated upwards. For if it were possible, let the part *a.c.* be situated in the plane and the part *c.b.* be positioned in the space above <note>original: *in sublimi*</note>, and let *a.c.* be extended directly in the plane in which it is situated as far as *d*. It would then follow that for one and the same line *a.c.*, there would be two entirely different lines, *c.b.* and *c.d.*, extending from it in the same direction, which is impossible according to the 13th [proposition] of the first book.

### Proposition 2.

<note>A geometric diagram in the left margin showing two lines 'a-b' and 'c-d' intersecting at a central point 'e'. A transverse line connects a point 'g' on 'a-b' to a point 'f' on 'c-d', forming triangle 'e-f-g'. This demonstrates that intersecting lines define a single flat surface.</note>

**Any two lines which intersect one another lie in a single surface, and every triangle consists entirely in one surface.**
¶ Let there be two straight lines *a.b.* and *c.d.* intersecting each other at point *e*. I say they are in one surface, and I say every triangle is situated entirely in one surface. For let a point *f* be marked on line *c.d.* and a point *g* on line *a.b.*, and let line *f.g.* be drawn. Because it is impossible for part of the triangle *e.f.g.* to be in a plane and part in the space above it—since that would mean part of one or more of its boundary lines would similarly be in the plane and part in the space above—and since this is impossible for lines by the preceding proposition, it will also be impossible for the triangle. Thus, the entire triangle *e.f.g.* is in one surface. From this second part and the preceding proposition, the first part of this second proposition is established.

### Proposition 3.

<note>A geometric diagram in the left margin illustrating two intersecting planes represented as rectangles. The planes intersect at a vertical line segment labeled 'e' and 'f'. Points 'a', 'b', 'c', and 'd' mark the outer boundaries, and points labeled 'h' are placed on either side of the intersection. This illustrates that where two planes meet, they form a straight line.</note>

**The common section of any two surfaces intersecting each other is a straight line.**
¶ This is to be understood regarding plane surfaces, and then what is said will be true. Let there be, then, two plane surfaces *a.b.* and *c.d.* intersecting each other. I say that their common section will be a straight line. For let two points *e* and *f* be the boundaries of their common section, which are joined by the straight line *e.f.* If, therefore, the line *e.f.* is in both surfaces *a.b.* and *c.d.*, the proposition is established. But if it were in neither, or if it were not in one of them—even though both points *e* and *f* are in both surfaces *a.b.* and *c.d.*—then in that surface in which the line did not lie, another straight line *e.b.f.* could be drawn. There would then be two straight lines, *e.f.* and *e.b.f.*, sharing two common boundaries, which is impossible. For in this way, two straight lines would enclose a surface <note>original: *superficiem*; here used in the sense of a two-dimensional area</note>, which is against the final postulate <note>original: *petitionem*; refers to the common notion that two straight lines cannot enclose a space</note> of the first book.

<note>A geometric diagram in the left margin showing a vertical line 'a-b' meeting a horizontal plane at its base point 'b'. The plane features two intersecting lines 'c-d' and 'e-f' crossing at 'b'. Diagonal lines connect 'a' to 'c' and 'a' to 'f'. This shows how a line becomes truly perpendicular to a whole surface.</note>

**If a line be erected at right angles from the intersection of two lines which cut each other, it will be perpendicular to the surface containing those lines.**
¶ Let line *a.b.* be erected at right angles upon the intersection of two lines...

<note>A geometric diagram in the upper right margin. It shows a central vertical line segment a-b meeting a horizontal plane. From point a at the top, several lines descend to points c, h, f, e, g, and d on the plane. The lines on the plane (c-d and e-f) intersect at point b.</note>

...lines c.d. and e.f. intersecting each other at point b, regarding which it is clear from the preceding proposition <note>original: *pro antepermissam*; referring to Proposition 2</note> that they are situated in one surface <note>term: *superficies* — here used to mean a 2D plane</note>. I say that line a.b. is perpendicular to that same surface. For let c.b. and b.d. be equal, and likewise f.b. and b.e. be equal, and let lines c.d. and c.f. be drawn, which will be equal by the 4th proposition of the first book and parallel by the 27th of the same. Therefore, having marked some point on line e.d., which is g, let line g.b. be drawn. From the 26th of the first book, e.g. will be equal to f.b. Therefore, from point a, or from any point on line a.b., let lines a.c., a.f., a.g., and a.b. be dropped as perpendiculars <note>original: *propothematiiter*; likely a variant of apothem-style perpendicular lines</note>. By the 4th proposition of the first book, a.c. will be equal to a.d., and a.e. equal to a.f. Likewise, by the 8th of the same, angle a.c.d. will be equal to angle a.f.c. Therefore, by the 4th of the same, a.g. will be equal to a.b., and thus by the 8th of the same, angle a.b.g. will be equal to angle a.b.h. <note>Note: 'h' likely refers to a corresponding point in the symmetry of the proof</note>. Therefore, by definition, each is a right angle, and line a.b. is perpendicular to line g.b. In a similar manner, you will prove the same line to be perpendicular to all lines drawn from point b in the surface of the two lines c.d. and c.f. Therefore, by definition <note>original: *ex dione*, abbreviation for *ex definitione*</note>, it is established that line a.b. is perpendicular to the surface in which are situated the two lines c.d. and e.f. intersecting each other, which is what was proposed.

### Proposition 5.

<note>A geometric diagram in the right margin for Proposition 5. It features a point b from which several lines radiate: b-a (vertical), b-c, b-e, and b-d. Another line b-f is also shown within the configuration.</note>

**If a line is erected orthogonally upon the common endpoint of three lines meeting at that point, those three lines will be situated in the same surface.**
¶ Let line a.b. be erected orthogonally over the common endpoint of three lines b.c., b.d., and b.e., which meet at angles at point b, none of which is placed directly in line with another—which is the same as saying they intersect each other at point b. For if they were extended, they would intersect. I say that the three lines b.c., b.d., and b.e. are situated in one surface. Now, it is clear regarding any two of them that they are situated in one surface by the 2nd proposition of this book, or by the first part of the 2nd. If, therefore, line b.d. were not in the surface of the two lines b.c. and b.e., but those two were in the plane and this one [b.d.] in the space above: it would be as if this surface in which the two lines a.b. and b.d. are situated, if it were extended, would intersect that [surface] in which b.c. and b.e. are situated, according to what is known from the 4th. And by the 3rd proposition of this book, their common section will be a straight line; let it be b.f. Since, therefore, from the preceding proposition line a.b. is perpendicular to the surface of the two lines b.c. and b.e., it follows by definition that it is perpendicular to line b.f. Wherefore angle a.b.f. is a right angle. And since angle a.b.d. is also a right angle by the hypothesis, an impossibility follows: namely, that a part would be equal to its whole <note>Euclid uses this logical contradiction to show that b.d. and b.f. must be the same line, meaning b.d. must lie in the original plane</note>.

### Proposition 6.

<note>A geometric diagram in the lower right margin for Proposition 6. It shows a three-dimensional perspective of a plane with two vertical lines a-b and c-d rising from it. Points f and e are marked on the plane, with auxiliary lines connecting them to form triangles d-e-f and b-e-f.</note>

**If two lines are perpendicular to the same surface, they must necessarily be parallel to each other.**
¶ Let there be two lines a.b. and c.d. perpendicular to one surface. I say they are parallel <note>original: *equidistantes*</note>. For let line b.d. be drawn; by definition, the two angles a.b.d. and c.d.b. will be right angles. If, therefore, the two lines a.b. and c.d. are in one surface, they are parallel by the second part of the 28th proposition of the first book. That they are in one surface, gather as follows: from point b, upon line b.d. in the plane upon which a.b. and c.d. stand perpendicularly, draw line b.f. orthogonally. From line c.d. take d.e. equal to b.f., and draw lines e.b. and e.f. Therefore, the two sides e.d. and d.b. of triangle c.d.b. <note>likely referring to triangle e.d.b.</note> will be equal to the two sides f.b. and d.b. of triangle f.d.b., and angle e.d.b. equal to angle f.d.b., since each is a right angle. Thus, by the 4th of the first book, line b.e. is equal to line d.f. Likewise, since the two sides e.b. and b.f. of triangle e.b.f. are equal to the two sides f.d. and d.e. of triangle f.d.e., and the base e.f. is common, then by the 8th of the first book, angle e.b.f. will be equal to angle f.d.e. Since each is a right angle—because angle f.d.e. is a right angle by definition—then angle e.b.f. will also be a right angle. Thus, line f.b. is erected perpendicularly over the common endpoint of the three lines b.a., b.d., and b.e. meeting at angles at point b. Therefore, by the preceding proposition, they are in one surface. Since, therefore, from the first part of the 2nd line c.d...

### Proposition .7.

<note>A geometric diagram in the upper left margin. It shows two parallel vertical lines, a-b and c-d. Two points, e on a-b and f on c-d, are connected by a curved line segment, representing a line within a plane defined by the parallel verticals.</note>

If a straight line is drawn between two points marked on two parallel lines, it is necessarily proven that this line lies in the same surface in which those two lines are situated.

Let there be two parallel lines, a.b. and c.d., which it is established by definition that they are in one surface. On them, let two points e. and f. be marked, and let a straight line e.f. be drawn. I say, therefore, that the line e.f. is situated in the surface of lines a.b. and c.d. For if e.f. were in another surface, as if hanging in the air <note>original: *in sublimi* — suspended in space above the plane</note>, then that surface, if extended, would necessarily cut the surface in which the two lines a.b. and c.d. are situated. And by the 3rd proposition of this book, their common section would be a straight line terminated by those same points, which is impossible; for in this way, two straight lines would enclose a surface <note>A fundamental axiom of Euclidean geometry is that two straight lines cannot enclose a space or area</note>.

### Proposition .8.

If two straight lines are erected parallel to one another in the same plane, and one of them stands perpendicularly <note>original: *orthogonaliter* — at right angles</note>, it follows that the other will also be perpendicular to the same plane.

This is essentially the converse of the sixth proposition. For let there be two parallel lines, a.b. and c.d., and let one of them, such as c.d., be erected perpendicularly upon any surface. I say the other of them, which is a.b., is perpendicular to that same surface. Let the arrangement be made exactly as it was in the sixth proposition; then, as it was there, each of the two angles f.d.b. and f.b.e. will be a right angle. The first is such by the initial position, and the second by the 29th of the first book <note>original: *.s. primi* — referring to the 29th proposition of Book I regarding parallel lines and interior angles</note>. Therefore, by the 4th of this book, line f.b. is erected perpendicularly over the surface in which the two lines b.d. and b.e. are. And since by the previous proposition the two lines a.b. and c.d. are in the same surface with the two lines b.d. and b.e., it follows that line f.b. is perpendicularly erected over the surface in which line b.a. is. From the definition, therefore, angle f.b.a. will be a right angle; and because angle d.b.a. is also a right angle by the last part of the 29th of the first book, it follows by the fourth of this book that line a.b. is perpendicular to the surface in which the two lines b.d. and b.f. are situated. Thus the proposition is established.

### Proposition .9.

<note>A geometric diagram in the lower left margin. It features two horizontal parallel lines, a-b and c-d. Between them is a horizontal segment e-f. A vertical transversal h-k passes through e-f at point g.</note>

If two lines are parallel to the same line, even if not in the same surface, it is necessary that they are also parallel to each other.

Let each of the two lines a.b. and c.d. be parallel to line e.f., and let them not all be in one surface. I say that they are also parallel to each other. Concerning those which are all in one surface, this was proven by the 30th proposition of the first book. But regarding those which are not in one surface, as is the case here—where e.f. may be understood as being raised up in the air <note>original: *in sublimi* — in three-dimensional space</note>—it remains to be proven here. Therefore, let a point g. be marked on it [line e.f.], from which two perpendiculars are drawn to the two lines a.b. and c.d., which are g.h. and g.k. By the 4th of this book, line e.f. will be perpendicular to the surface, namely that in which the two lines g.h. <note>OCR lists *g.b.*, likely a slip for *g.h.*</note> and g.k. are situated. Therefore, by applying the previous proposition twice, each of those two lines a.b. and c.d. is perpendicular to the same surface—namely, to that in which the said two lines g.h. and g.k. are situated. By the sixth proposition of this book, they are therefore parallel to each other, which is the proposition.

### Proposition .10.

<note>A geometric diagram showing a three-dimensional arrangement of triangles. At the top is vertex 'a'. Below it is a plane containing a triangle with vertices 'c', 'd', and 'b'. Below that is a base line with points 'f' and 'e'. Lines connect 'a' to 'c' and 'b', 'c' to 'f', 'b' to 'e', and 'd' to 'f' and 'e'.</note>

If two lines meeting at an angle are parallel to two other lines that also meet at an angle, but they are not in the same surface <note>term: *superficies* — here meaning a flat plane</note>, it is proved that the two angles formed by them are equal to each other.

Let there be two lines, a.b. and a.c., meeting at an angle at point .a., which are parallel to two other lines, .d.e. and .d.f., which also meet at an angle at point .d. Let them not be in the same plane with the first pair. I say that angle .a. is equal to angle .d. For let line .d.e. be equal to line .a.b., to which it is set as parallel; and let .d.f. be equal to .a.c., to which it is also set as parallel. Let the lines .d.a., .e.b., and .f.c. be drawn. From the 33rd proposition of the First Book <note>Book I, Prop 33: Lines joining the ends of equal and parallel lines are themselves equal and parallel</note>, applied twice, both lines .b.e. and .f.c. will be equal and parallel to line .a.d. Therefore, by a common conception and the preceding rule, these same lines are equal and parallel to each other. Thus, by repeating the 33rd proposition of the First Book again, the two lines .b.c. and .e.f. are also equal and parallel. Therefore, by the 8th proposition of the First Book <note>Book I, Prop 8: The SSS (Side-Side-Side) congruence theorem for triangles</note>, the proposition is established.

### Proposition .11.

<note>A geometric projection diagram. Point 'a' is positioned at the top. A vertical line 'af' is dropped to a base plane defined by a horizontal line 'bd' and an intersecting line 'de'. Another line 'ad' descends to point 'd'. Point 'g' is marked on a line parallel to 'bd' passing through 'f'.</note>

From a point assigned in the air, to draw a perpendicular line to a given surface.

Let point .a. be high in the air, from which we wish to draw a perpendicular line to the underlying surface. Therefore, let a line .b.c. be drawn anywhere in that plane. From point .a., let a perpendicular line .a.d. be drawn to that line .b.c., according to the teaching of the 12th proposition of the First Book. Again, from point .d. in that plane to which the perpendicular is to be drawn, let line .d.e. be extended from point .a. so that it is perpendicular to line .b.c., as the 11th proposition of the First Book teaches. To this line .d.e., let another perpendicular line be drawn from point .a., which shall be .a.f. I say that this is the line we intended to find. For let line .f.g. be parallel to line b.c. Since both angles .b.d.a. and .b.d.f. are right angles, by the fourth proposition of this book, line b.d. will be perpendicular to the surface in which triangle .a.d.f. exists. Therefore, also by the 8th proposition of this book, line .g.f. will be perpendicular to that same surface. Thus, by definition, angle .g.f.a. will be a right angle. Since angle .d.f.a. is also a right angle, it follows from the fourth proposition of this book that line .a.f. is perpendicular to the surface in which the two lines .d.f. and .f.g. are located, which is what was proposed.

### Proposition .12.

Given a surface and a point assigned within it, to erect a line perpendicularly <note>original: *orthogonaliter* — at right angles</note> from that point to the given surface.

When you wish to draw a perpendicular from any point assigned in the given surface, drop a perpendicular from any point placed at will high in the air to that same surface, just as the preceding proposition taught. If this line falls upon the assigned point, it is the one you seek. If it does not, draw a line from the assigned point parallel to the dropped perpendicular; and by the 8th proposition of this book, you will prove that it is the one you seek.

### Proposition .13.

It is impossible for two lines to stand perpendicularly over a single point to one and the same surface.

For if it were possible for two lines to stand perpendicularly to one and the same surface over a single point, let the surface in which those perpendiculars are situated be understood to be extended until it cuts the surface to which the said lines stand perpendicularly. By the 3rd proposition of this book, their common section will be a straight line. And because, by definition, each of those two perpendiculars forms a right angle with the common section, it follows that a right angle would be a part of a right angle, which is impossible. However, just as it has been demonstrated that it is impossible from one and the same point outside a surface...

...we shall demonstrate in the same way that it is impossible for two lines from one and the same point marked outside a surface <note>term: *superficies* — In this context, Euclid refers to a flat, two-dimensional plane.</note> to be drawn to that same surface as perpendiculars. For if this were the case, those lines would themselves be parallel to each other according to the 6th proposition of this book, which is impossible based on the definition of parallel lines <note>parallel lines can never meet if they originate from the same point</note>. It is therefore established from this that if any flat surface cuts another flat surface orthogonally <note>term: *orthogonaliter* — meeting at a 90-degree right angle</note>, and a perpendicular is drawn from any point of the intersecting surface to the intersected surface: it must necessarily fall on their common section. Otherwise, from that same point of the intersecting surface, a perpendicular would be drawn to their common section as shown in the 12th proposition of the First Book; and from the point where it falls upon the common section, another perpendicular to that same common section would be drawn in the intersected surface as shown in the 11th proposition of the First Book. Then, from the definition of a surface standing orthogonally upon another surface, the angle which these two perpendicular lines contain would be a right angle. Therefore, by the 4th proposition of this book, the first of these two perpendiculars is also perpendicular to the intersected surface. Thus, two perpendicular lines would be drawn from a single point to the same surface, which is impossible; therefore, our proposition remains proven.

### Proposition .14.

If one line stands orthogonally upon two assigned surfaces,
those two surfaces, even if they are extended infinitely in any
direction, shall never meet.

¶ For, given that one line stands orthogonally to two surfaces, if it were possible for those surfaces to meet at their common section—which, by the 3rd proposition of this book, would be a straight line—and if a point were marked in any way from which two lines were drawn in those two surfaces to the line that stands perpendicularly to them: a triangle would then be formed by these two lines and the perpendicular. In this triangle, each of the two angles that meet the perpendicular would be a right angle, as is clear from the definition of a line standing perpendicularly to a surface. However, this is impossible by the 32nd proposition of the First Book <note>Book I, Prop 32 states that the sum of the interior angles of a triangle is equal to two right angles; a triangle cannot have two right angles because the third angle would have to be zero.</note>.

¶ The converse is also true: namely, if a straight line falls upon two parallel <note>term: *equidistantes* — "equidistant," the term used by Euclid for parallel lines or planes</note> surfaces and is perpendicular to one of them, it will also be perpendicular to the other. ¶ For, given two parallel surfaces, let a straight line be understood to penetrate both, standing perpendicularly to one of them; I say that the same line stands perpendicularly to the other surface. For let there be a surface cutting the given parallel surfaces along the line penetrating them. The common section of this intersecting surface and the first of the cut surfaces (namely, the one the penetrating line is said to stand on perpendicularly) will contain a right angle with the penetrating line itself, by the definition of a line perpendicular to a surface. Therefore, if the other common section of the intersecting surface and the second of the two cut surfaces did not contain a right angle with that same penetrating line, it would follow from the final postulate of the First Book <note>The "Parallel Postulate": if a line falls on two lines such that the interior angles are less than two right angles, the lines will eventually meet.</note> that those two common sections, if extended in one direction, must necessarily meet. Consequently, the surfaces which were stated to be parallel would also necessarily meet. And because this is impossible, that angle must be a right angle. The same logic applies to any other surface cutting these same parallel surfaces along the same line. Therefore, by the 4th proposition of this book and by this 14th proposition, it is clear that what we have said is true.

### Proposition .15.

If there are two lines meeting at an angle that are parallel 
to two other lines meeting at an angle, but not in the same 
surface, the two surfaces contained by those lines can never 
meet in any part, no matter how far they are produced.

<note>A geometrical diagram on the right side of the page depicts two parallel triangular planes. A vertical line descends from point 'a' through point 'g' on the upper triangle to point 'd' on the lower triangle. Lines 'gh' and 'gk' are drawn on the upper plane, while 'de' and 'df' are on the lower plane. Points are labeled: a, b, c, g, h, k, d, e, f.</note>

¶ Let there be two lines, **a.b.** and **a.c.**, meeting at an angle at point **a**, which are parallel <note>original: *equidistantes* — literally "equidistant," the standard term for parallel lines in this period.</note> to two lines **d.e.** and **d.f.** that also meet at an angle at point **d**, and let these pairs of lines not be in the same surface <note>term: *superficies* — here meaning a flat, two-dimensional plane.</note>. I say that the planes containing them, into whatever part and however far they are extended, will never meet. For let there be drawn from point **d**, as the 5th proposition of this book teaches, a perpendicular line to the plane of the two lines **a.b.** and **a.c.**, and let this be **d.g.**. From point **g**, let line **g.h.** be drawn parallel to **a.b.**, and **g.k.** parallel to **a.c.**. By the definition, each of the two angles **d.g.h.** and **d.g.k.** will be a right angle. According to the 9th proposition, line **d.f.** will be parallel to line **g.k.**, and line **d.e.** will be parallel to line **g.h.**. Therefore, by the final part of the 29th proposition of the First Book, each of the two angles **e.d.g.** and **f.d.g.** will be a right angle. Consequently, by the 4th proposition of this book, the line **d.g.** will be perpendicular to the plane of the two lines **d.e.** and **d.f.** Since this same line is also, by our hypothesis, perpendicular to the plane of the two lines **a.b.** and **a.c.**, it is clear from the preceding proposition <note>referring to Proposition 14, which states that planes to which the same line is perpendicular are parallel.</note> that what was proposed is proven.

### Proposition 16.

If one plane cuts two parallel planes, their common sections will be parallel.
¶ It is indeed established from the 3rd proposition that when any one plane cuts any two parallel planes, their common sections <note>term: *communes sectiones* — the lines where the planes intersect.</note> will be two straight lines. Since both of these lines are situated in the same intersecting plane, if they were not parallel, they would be supposed to meet at some single point. It would then follow that one and the same point would exist in both of those two common sections. And since one of those common sections is in one of the two planes that were cut, and the other section is in the second plane, it follows that those planes (which were stated to be parallel) would meet at that point. However, this is impossible. Therefore, their common sections will be parallel, which is what was proposed. ¶ From this and the preceding proposition, you can derive a conclusion similar to the 30th proposition of the First Book, namely this: If there are two planes parallel to the same plane, they will also be parallel to each other. For if three planes are positioned such that each of the two outer ones is parallel to the middle one, I say it is necessary that the outer ones are parallel to each other. Let all three planes be cut by two other planes which themselves intersect one another. By this 16th proposition, the common sections of the two outer planes will be parallel to the sections of the middle plane; therefore, by the 30th proposition of the First Book, the sections of the two outer planes will also be parallel to each other. And because these sections meet at the common intersection of the two cutting planes, it is clearly established from the preceding proposition that what we have said is true.

### Proposition 17.

If three or more parallel planes cut two straight lines (whether the lines meet one another or are parallel), it is proven that the segments of those lines are proportional.
¶ Let there be understood any two straight lines passing through three parallel planes, or even more than three. I say that the two segments of those lines intercepted between any two of the planes are proportional to the two segments intercepted between any other two of those parallel planes. For let the two extremities of those two lines be joined by a single line drawn diagonally between them. This diagonal line, together with each of the two lines passing through the planes, will create a plane that cuts the proposed parallel planes. Therefore, if you consider the common sections of these planes—which by the preceding proposition will be parallel—the proposition will be established according to the first part of the 2nd proposition of the Sixth Book <note>The 6th Book of Euclid deals with proportions; Proposition 2 states that a line parallel to one side of a triangle cuts the other sides proportionally.</note>.

### [Proposition 18] If a line stands orthogonally upon a given surface: every surface drawn through that line in any direction will be orthogonally erected upon the same given surface.

¶ Let there be a line **a.b.** erected perpendicularly upon a given surface, and from line **a.b.** let a surface be produced in whatever direction one pleases; I say that this surface is perpendicularly erected upon the proposed surface. For since this surface cuts the given surface, their common section will be a straight line according to the 3rd proposition of this book. Let this section be **b.d.** In this common section, let any point be marked, which is **d**. Let there be drawn from this point, within the surface produced from line **a.b.**, a certain line perpendicular to line **b.d.**, which is **d.c.** By the second part of the 28th proposition of the First Book, line **c.d.** will be parallel <note>original: *equidistans* — literally "equidistant," the standard term for parallel lines in this period.</note> to line **a.b.** Because of this, by the 8th proposition of this book, line **c.d.** is also perpendicular to the proposed surface. Since in this manner any line drawn orthogonally from any point of line **b.d.** to the line **b.d.** itself—within the surface produced from line **a.b.**—is perpendicular to the proposed surface, then by the definition <note>term: *diffinitio* — a formal definition. Euclid refers back to the definitions at the start of Book XI which describe what it means for one plane to be perpendicular to another.</note> of a surface orthogonally erected upon a surface, it is established that what was proposed is true.

<note>A geometrical diagram on the left margin depicts two intersecting triangular planes. The planes intersect along a vertical line e-f. Points a, b, c, d define the vertices of the triangles. Lines are drawn showing the intersection at point e, and auxiliary lines g-h and others are marked within the intersection area.</note>

### Proposition 19.

**If two surfaces intersecting one another are both erected orthogonally upon one surface, their common section will be perpendicular to that same surface.**

¶ Let there be two surfaces **a.b.** and **c.d.** intersecting one another, erected orthogonally upon a given surface; and let their common section be the straight line **e.f.** I say that this line is perpendicular to the given surface. If it were not, let a straight line be produced from point **f** (which is the common boundary <note>original: *terminus*</note> of the sections of the two surfaces and the third surface being cut) that is **f.g.**, situated in surface **a.b.** and perpendicular to the given surface. Likewise, from the same point, let another perpendicular to the same surface be drawn which is situated in surface **c.d.**, and let this be **f.b.** There would then be two lines, **f.g.** and **f.b.**, standing orthogonally from a single point upon the given surface; but this is impossible by the 13th proposition of this book. One should not doubt that such lines can be drawn from point **f** in each of the two surfaces **a.b.** and **c.d.** if **e.f.** were not perpendicular to the given surface. Let line **f.b.** be understood as the common section of surface **a.b.** and the given surface, and line **f.d.** as the section of surface **c.d.** and the given surface. If, therefore, line **e.f.** were perpendicular to both lines **f.b.** and **f.d.**, it would also be perpendicular to the given surface by the 4th proposition of this book. But if it is perpendicular to neither, let **f.g.** be perpendicular to **f.b.** and [another line] perpendicular to **f.d.** Then from point **f**, draw in the given surface a line perpendicular to line **f.b.** which, by the definition of a surface orthogonally erected upon another surface, will contain a right angle with line **f.g.** Therefore, by the 4th proposition of this book, line **f.g.** will be perpendicular to the given surface. In the same way, another line having been drawn from point **f** in the given surface that is perpendicular to line **f.d.**, it follows from the aforementioned definition and the 4th proposition that line **f.b.** is perpendicular to the given surface, which is impossible by the 13th proposition of this book. If it were maintained that line **e.f.** is perpendicular to line **f.b.** but not to line **f.d.**, it follows in a similar manner that two lines, **e.f.** and **f.b.**, are perpendicular to the given surface, which is no less impossible.

**If three plane angles contain a solid angle, any two of those three angles taken together are greater than the remaining one.**
