...the angle is completed at point **a**. I say that any two of those plane angles constituting the solid angle at point **a**, when taken together, are greater than the third. For if these three plane angles were equal to one another, or if only two were equal while the third was less than either of the two equals, it is established by common knowledge <note>original: *communem scientiam* — a reference to the "Common Notions" or axioms that underpin Euclidean logic</note> that what is said is true. But if one of them is greater than either of the remaining two—whether those two are set as equal or unequal—it is still established that this greater angle, when taken together with either of the remaining two, is greater than the third. However, to conclude that those two smaller angles taken together are greater than this third angle (which is set as the largest), proceed as follows: let angle **c.a.d.** be the largest of the three proposed plane angles. From it, I shall therefore cut off angle **c.a.e.** equal to angle **b.a.d.** <note>The OCR text suggests a construction to compare the sum of the smaller angles against the largest face</note> by drawing line **a.e.**, and I will take from this line **a.e.** the segment **a.g.** and from line **a.b.** the segment **a.f.**, which I set to be equal. I will then draw line **b.g.k.** from point **g**, cutting through the surface of the two lines **a.c.** and **a.d.** until it intersects **a.c.** at point **b.** and **a.d.** at point **k.**, and I shall produce lines **f.b.** and **f.k.** Since, therefore, **a.f.** is equal to **a.g.** and **a.k.** is common, then by the 4th proposition of the First Book, **f.k.** is equal to **k.g.** And because by the 20th proposition of the First Book the two lines **b.f.** and **f.k.** are greater than line **b.k.**, it will be by common conception that **b.f.** is greater than **b.g.** Therefore, by the 25th proposition of the First Book, since line **a.f.** is equal to line **a.g.**, angle **f.a.b.** <note>original: *f.a.b.* — likely referring to the angle on the adjacent face</note> is greater than angle **b.a.g.** Thus, by the common notion, it is established that the two angles **b.a.f.** and **f.a.k.** taken together are greater than angle **b.a.k.**, which was to be demonstrated.

# Proposition 21.

### **Every** solid angle is proved to be less than four right angles.

¶ The quantity of a <term>solid angle|An angle formed by three or more planes meeting at a single point (an apex)</term> is determined by the quantity of the plane angles containing the solid itself. And since all the angles of its base are equal to as many right angles as twice the number of its angles, minus four, as was demonstrated in the 32nd of the First Book. # Proposition 22.

**If** there be three plane angles, of which any <note>original: *quinq[ue]* — likely a scribal abbreviation for *quicumque*, meaning "any" or "whichever"</note> two taken together are greater than the third, and if they be contained by lines equal to one another: it is possible to construct or constitute a triangle from the three bases subtending those angles from the ends of the equal lines.
¶ Let there be three plane angles **b.a.c.**, **e.d.f.**, and **g.h.k.** as proposed: namely, such that any two of them are greater than the third; and let the six sides containing them be equal, which are **a.b.**, **a.c.**, **d.e.**, **d.f.**, **g.h.**, and **g.k.**; and let three bases be subtended to them, which are **b.c.**, **e.f.**, and **h.k.** I say, therefore, that a triangle can be constructed from these three bases. For let angle **b.a.l.** be equal to angle **d.e.f.**, and line **a.l.** be equal to line **d.e.**, and let **l.b.** and **l.c.** be drawn. Then, by the 4th proposition of the First Book <note>The "SAS" (Side-Angle-Side) theorem</note>, line **l.b.** will be equal to line **e.f.** Indeed, from the hypothesis it is established that the total angle **a** is greater than angle **g**, for any two of the three angles **b.a.c.**, **d.**, and **g.** were greater than the third; therefore, by the 24th proposition of the First Book, line **l.c.** is greater than line **h.k.** And since, by the 20th proposition of the First Book, the two lines **l.b.** and **b.c.** are greater than line **l.c.**, it follows that the two lines **l.b.** and **b.c.** are much more certainly greater than line **h.k.** Since, therefore, **l.b.** is equal to **e.f.**, the two lines **b.c.** and **e.f.** will be greater than line **h.k.** It is thus established in this manner that any two of the three lines **b.c.**, **e.f.**, and **h.k.** are longer than the third. Therefore, by the 22nd proposition of the First Book, it is established that what is said is true: this only being added, that if the two angles **b.a.c.** and **d.** taken together are equal to two right angles, then the two lines **l.a.** and **a.c.** will form one line by the 14th proposition of the First Book; since it is equal by hypothesis to the two lines **g.h.** and **g.k.**, which by the 20th proposition of the First Book are longer than line **h.k.**, and since by the same [proposition] the two lines **l.b.** and **b.c.** are longer than line **l.c.**, it follows as before that **b.c.** and **e.f.** taken together are longer than **h.k.** But if the two aforesaid angles are greater than two right angles: by the 21st proposition of the First Book, the two lines **a.l.** and **a.c.**, and therefore also the two **g.h.** and **g.k.**, will be shorter than the two which are **l.b.** and **b.c.**; wherefore, as before, **b.c.** and **e.f.** taken together are longer than line **h.k.**

It is necessary, by hypothesis, that each of those sides surrounding the three proposed equal angles be such that it is impossible for them to be smaller, equal to, or larger [than the radius of the circle]. For if a line extending from the center **g** to the circumference of the circle **def** were equal to any side—**ad**, **ae**, **be**, **bf**, **cf**, **cd**—it would follow, by the conditions set forth and granted in Book 1, Proposition 8, that the three proposed angles **a**, **b**, and **c** would be equal to the three angles **dge**, **egf**, and **fgd**. And since these three angles are equal to four right angles <note>In Euclidean geometry, the angles around a single point on a plane always sum to 360 degrees, or "four right angles."</note>, as is easily shown from Book 1, Proposition 13 (by slightly extending one of the lines going from the center to the circumference in a continuous straight line), the three angles **a**, **b**, and **c** would also be equal to four right angles, which contradicts the premises. Furthermore, if it were larger, then by placing the three triangles containing angles **a**, **b**, and **c** over the three triangles dividing the triangle **def** <note>original: *triangulum d.e.f.* — likely referring to the triangular arrangement within the circle</note>, such that each shares a base and the bases are placed upon equal bases, and angles **a**, **b**, and **c** fall toward point **g**, it would follow from Book 1, Proposition 21 that the three angles **a**, **b**, and **c** are greater than the three angles **dge**, **egf**, and **fgd**. Thus, they would be greater than four right angles, which is even further contrary to the premises. It remains, therefore, that each of the six sides surrounding the three proposed angles is greater than the line extending from the center **g** to the circumference **def**, and therefore also greater in its square <note>original: *potentiū* — a technical term referring to the "power" or square of a line's length</note>. Let there be, therefore, a line **gb** which is perpendicularly erect <note>original: *orthononaliter erecta*</note> upon the surface of the angle or circle **def** according to Book 11, Proposition 12. Let the three hypotenuses <note>In this 3D context, "hypotenuses" refers to the slanted edges of the pyramid connecting the elevated point to the base.</note> **bd**, **be**, and **bf** be drawn, which I say contain three plane angles equal to the three proposed angles, constituting a solid angle at point **b**. For since the square of line **ad** is equal to the two squares of the lines **dg** and **gb** by hypothesis, and the square of line **db** is equal to the same by the penultimate proposition of the first book <note>This refers to the Pythagorean Theorem (Book 1, Proposition 47).</note>, it is necessary that line **ad** be equal to line **db**. In the same way, line **ae** is equal to line **eb**. Therefore, by Book 1, Proposition 8, since the bases are also equal, angle **a** will be equal to angle **dbe**. Similarly, angle **b** will be equal to angle **ebf**, and angle **c** will be equal to angle **fbd**. Thus, it is clear that we have achieved what we set out to do.

# Proposition 24.

**IF** a solid is contained by parallel surfaces <note>original: *equidistantibus superficiebus* — literally "equidistant surfaces," the term used for parallel planes</note>, its opposite surfaces are equal to one another and are formed of parallel sides <note>i.e., they are parallelograms</note>. Regardless of what others may say, a solid contained by parallel surfaces must be contained by an even number of surfaces. Just as there cannot be fewer than six, so there can be any even number exceeding six. For it is established that a hexagonal column can be contained by 8 surfaces, which are parallel to each other in opposite pairs; likewise, an octagonal column by 10, a decagonal by 12, and so on in this fashion unto infinity. But of all these solids contained by parallel surfaces, which I declare to be infinite in variety, only that one is called a "parallelepiped" <note>original: *parallelogrammū* — in this period, the term for a 2D parallelogram was sometimes applied to the 3D solid; the text clarifies this is the specific six-sided variety.</note> whose surrounding surfaces are all parallelograms, and this type must necessarily be bounded by exactly six surfaces. It is concerning such a solid, bounded by only six surfaces, that I say this 24th proposition should be understood. Therefore, consider such a solid body **ab**, and imagine its surfaces in your mind as a solid habit; it will be evident to you that each of them cuts four of the others, and its four sides are the common sections of the cutting surface and the four it cuts. Moreover, let those four cut surfaces be parallel in opposite pairs by hypothesis. It follows from the double application of Book 11, Proposition 16, that the four sides of this cutting surface and the four cut surfaces are parallel to each other in pairs. This is therefore established. Furthermore, from Book 1, Proposition 34, it is manifest that all opposite sides of these six surfaces are equal. Therefore, the two sides containing a plane angle in each surface will be equal to the two sides containing a plane angle in the surface opposite to it. The angles contained by those pairs of sides are also equal by Proposition 10 of this book...

### Proposition .25.

If a plane cuts a solid parallelogram <note>Euclid uses "solid parallelogram" to refer to what we now call a *parallelepiped*—a three-dimensional figure where every face is a parallelogram.</note> parallel to two of the opposite surfaces of the solid, the two partial bodies which are joined at that cutting surface as if at a common boundary are proportional to their bases.

<note>A geometric diagram shows a long parallelepiped (a solid with parallel sides) divided into several sections by vertical planes. The vertices and line segments are labeled with letters: p, a, c, f, l along the top edge; g, h in the middle; and q, n, e, d, b, k, m along the bottom edge.</note>

Let the body **a.b.** be a solid parallelogram, and let the surface **c.d.** cut it parallel to its two opposite surfaces, which are **a.c.r.f.b.** And let surface **g.b.** be the base of the solid **a.b.**, which is established by the previous proposition to be a figure of parallel sides. Let the common section of the two surfaces **c.d.** and **g.b.** be the line **h.d.**, which is established by the 3rd proposition of this book to be a straight line, and by the 16th of this book to be parallel to **g.c.** Therefore, the two surfaces **g.d.** and **b.b.** <note>original: *b.b.* — likely a typo in the 1482 edition for *h.b.* or *b.h.*, referring to the subdivided base.</note> are parallelograms, and they are the bases of the two partial bodies into which the surface **c.d.** divides the solid **a.b.** I say, therefore, that the ratio of solid **a.d.** to solid **b.c.** is as the base **g.d.** is to the base **b.b.** 

For let four lines penetrating surface **c.d.** at its angles be extended as far as desired on both sides; these are **a.f.r.e.b.** with the remaining two parallel to them. Let portions be taken from all of them on the side of point **b.** as many as desired, and let each be set equal to line **b.d.**, and on the side of point **c.** let others similarly be taken as many as desired and set equal to line **c.d.**, upon which solid parallelograms are constructed on both sides according to the requirements of their length. Let the solids on the side of point **b.** be **f.k.z.l.m.**, and on the side of point **e.** be the solids **a.n.z.q.** 

By the definition of equal and similar bodies, each of the solids **f.k.z.l.m.** will be equal to solid **c.b.**, and each of **a.n.z.q.** is equal to **a.d.** Therefore, let the argument be made just as in the first proposition of the sixth book <note>Book VI, Proposition 1 is the foundational proof for the proportionality of triangles and parallelograms sharing the same height.</note>. For just as solid **c.m.** is a multiple of solid **b.c.**, so is base **b.m.** a multiple of base **b.b.** And just as solid **q.c.** is a multiple of solid **a.d.**, so is base **q.b.** a multiple of base **g.d.** And if base **b.m.** is equal to base **q.b.**, then solid **c.m.** is equal to solid **q.c.** by the definition of equal and similar bodies; and if the base is smaller, the solid is smaller; and if larger, the solid is larger. This is by the same definition, by cutting a larger base down to the equality of the smaller and describing a solid parallelogram upon it. Therefore, by the definition of proportionality, the ratio of solid **a.d.** to solid **c.b.** is as base **g.d.** to base **b.b.**, which is what was proposed. 

If any surface cuts a <term>seratilis: a prism, literally a "saw-cut" body, referring to a solid with a constant triangular cross-section</term> parallel to its two opposite triangular surfaces, the two partial bodies joined at that cutting surface as a common boundary will be proportional to their bases.

<note>A geometric diagram shows three connected triangular prisms (seratilis) seen from the side. The vertices are labeled with letters: a, g, d on the top; b, b, e in the middle; and c, k, f on the bottom.</note>

For let **a.f.** be a prism whose two triangular surfaces are **a.b.c.** and **d.e.f.** It is established by the definition of a prism that each of the three surfaces **a.b.d.e.**, **b.c.e.f.**, and **a.c.d.f.** is a parallelogram. Let surface **g.b.k.** cut this prism parallel to its two opposite surfaces **a.b.c.** and **d.e.f.** I say that the ratio of prism **a.k.** to prism **g.f.** is as the base **a.k.** to base **g.f.** 

This is proved just as with the solid parallelograms. For lines **a.d.**, **b.e.**, and **c.f.** having been extended in both directions, and prisms having been made between them on the side of point **e.** equal to prism **g.f.**, and others on the side of point **b.** equal to prism **a.k.** in any number, according to the definition of proportionality: if you survey all these things with a vigilant mind, it will not be difficult for you to conclude what we have said.

Upon the point **e.** of the proposed line **e.f.**—which may lie as the proposer wishes, either flat or rising upward—it is ordered [to construct the angle]...

Since **b.k.** and **k.l.** are equal to **m.n.** and **m.p.**, and the angles **b.k.l.** and **m.n.p.** are right angles, then by the 8th proposition of the first book <note>The "Side-Side-Side" (SSS) theorem.</note>, angle **n.e.p.** will be equal to angle **b.a.l.** In a similar manner, you will prove angle **g.e.n.** to be equal to angle **c.a.d.** It is therefore established that we have achieved what we intended; if you, diligent student, persist, you will be able to perform what is requested of you without stumbling, regardless of how many sides the proposed solid angle **a.** may contain.

### Proposition 29.

<note>A geometric diagram in the middle left margin shows two parallelepipeds sharing a base (labeled a, b, c, d), with their top surfaces (labeled e, f) aligned along the same horizontal line.</note>

All solids of parallel surfaces <term>equidistantiū supficieꝝ</term> <note>This refers to parallelepipeds—solids with six faces where opposite faces are parallel.</note> of equal height and established on the same base upon one line are proved to be equal.
It is true that solids of parallel sides of equal height, or established between parallel surfaces upon one and the same base, are equal to each other, just as was demonstrated in the 35th [proposition] of the first [book] concerning surfaces of parallel sides <note>parallelograms</note> established on one base and between parallel lines. But some of such solids are said to be established "upon one line," and those are the ones where two opposite sides of the uppermost surfaces are extended in a straight line as one line; and concerning such, this 29th [proposition] proposes to demonstrate that they are all equal to each other. But there are others which are not said to be established upon one line, and those are the ones where whichever two opposite sides of the uppermost surfaces are taken, when extended in a straight line, they do not form one line; and concerning such, the following [proposition] will propose to demonstrate that they also are all equal to each other. Therefore, let there be two parallelepiped solids of equal height, or established between parallel surfaces **a.b.** and **a.c.**, upon one base which is **a.d.**, whose uppermost surfaces are **e.b.** and **f.c.** And let two opposite sides of these uppermost surfaces, when extended in a straight line, be one line, and these are **c.f.** and **b.c.** <note>The text likely means segments of the same line.</note> I say, therefore, that solids **a.b.** and **a.c.** are equal. This, if you construct its figure according to what is required in action or thought, and proceed just as in the 35th [proposition] of the first [book], doing the same here with prisms <term>serratilibus</term> as you did there with triangles, you will be able to conclude easily. There will occur to you here the same variations in solids which you know occurred there in surfaces.

### Proposition 30.

<note>A complex geometric diagram at the bottom left shows two parallelepipeds sharing a base (a, b, c, d) with staggered upper surfaces (e, f) that do not lie on the same line, intersected by auxiliary construction lines forming a third prism (m, n, p, q).</note>

All solids of parallel surfaces of equal height which were established on the same base, but not upon one line, are proved to be equal.
Now let there be two parallelepiped solids of equal height, or between parallel surfaces, and let them be on one and the same base, but not established upon one line. I say again that they are equal. For let there be two parallelepiped solids **a.b.** and **a.c.** of equal height, or established between parallel surfaces on one base which is **a.d.**, but not upon one line; and let their uppermost surfaces be **e.b.** and **f.c.**, whose opposite sides when extended in a straight line will not be one line. Since these, by hypothesis, are in one surface because the proposed solids are between parallel surfaces, it is necessary that two sides of one of them, extended in a straight line, intersect two of the other extended in a straight line. Therefore, let two opposite sides of surface **e.b.** be extended, which are **e.g.** and **b.h.**, and two opposite sides of surface **f.c.**, which are **k.f.** and **c.l.**, and let them intersect each other at four points **m.n.p.q.** The surface **m.n.p.q.** of parallel sides will be equal to each of the three surfaces: one of which is the common base of the proposed solids, which is **a.d.**, and the remaining two are the uppermost surfaces of the same solids, which are **e.b.** and **f.c.** Thus, lines having been drawn from the four points **m.n.p.q.** to the four angles of the base **a.d.** related to them in a direct relationship—which are **n.a.**, **m.r.**, **p.f.**, **q.d.**—a parallelepiped solid **a.q.** will be completed on the same base with each of the first two, and of equal height, and upon one line with each of them. Therefore, by the preceding [proposition], either of the two proposed solids, which are **a.b.** and **a.c.**, is equal to solid **a.q.** by common notion <note>original: *per conceptionem*; referring to Euclid's first common notion: things which are equal to the same thing are also equal to one another.</note>.

two bases are reciprocal to their heights, those solids are necessarily equal to each other. Whenever there are two equal solids of parallel surfaces <term>solida equidistantiū superficiez</term> <note>These are parallelepipeds: three-dimensional figures with six faces, where each pair of opposite faces is parallel.</note>, their bases and heights must be reciprocal <term>mutekesias</term> <note>original: *mutekesias*; a Latinized Greek term used in medieval geometry to describe "reciprocal proportion," where the ratio of the bases is the inverse of the ratio of the heights.</note>, and vice versa, just as was proposed regarding equiangular parallelograms in the 14th proposition of the sixth book <note>The text cites the 13th, but in the standard Euclidean numbering, the reciprocal proportions of parallelograms are found in Book VI, Proposition 14.</note>. However, in this 34th proposition, this is proposed to be demonstrated for those parallelogrammatic solids in which the lines of height stand orthogonally <note>original: *orthogonaliter*; at right angles (90 degrees).</note> upon their parallelogrammatic bases; but that which follows proposes the same for all others.

Let there be now two equal parallelogrammatic solids, **a.b.** and **c.d.**, whose bases are **a.e.** and **c.f.**, and let the lines of their heights be erected orthogonally upon the bases; let the height of solid **a.b.** be line **e.b.** and of solid **c.d.** be line **f.d.** If, therefore, the two lines **e.b.** and **f.d.**, which determine the heights of those solids, are equal to each other: since the solids themselves are also equal by hypothesis, their bases **a.e.** and **c.f.** will be equal from the converse of the 31st proposition. Therefore, the bases and heights will be reciprocal; and thus the first part of the proposition is established. And conversely, the second part will be established: if the heights and bases are reciprocal, and the heights are set as equal, then the bases will also be equal; and thus by the 31st proposition, the solids will be equal, and so the second part is established.

But if indeed the lines **e.b.** and **f.d.** are not equal, let **f.d.** be greater, and from it let **f.g.** be cut off to equal **e.b.**, and with the three other lines that are the heights of solid **c.d.** cut to the same measure at points **h**, **k**, and **l**, let the parallelogrammatic solid **c.g.** be completed, equal in height to solid **a.b.** It will then be, from the previous proposition, that solid **a.b.** is to solid **c.g.** as base **a.e.** is to base **c.f.** Since, therefore, **c.d.** is equal to **a.b.**, it will be (by the first part of the 7th proposition of the fifth book) that **c.d.** is to **c.g.** as **a.e.** is to **c.f.** However, by the previous proposition, the ratio of solid **c.d.** to solid **c.g.** is as the side **m.f.** to **f.l.** <note>The author is comparing the volumes by comparing their heights or corresponding side lengths when the bases are the same.</note>, which is evident if one of the lateral surfaces of solid **c.d.** (specifically **f.m.**) is understood as the base. But by the 1st proposition of the sixth book, **f.m.** is to **f.l.** as **d.f.** is to **f.g.**, and therefore (by the 7th of the fifth book) as **d.f.** is to **b.e.** Therefore, base **a.e.** is to base **c.f.** as height **d.f.** is to height **b.e.** Thus the first part is established.

The second part, since it is the converse of the first, you shall prove in the opposite manner: for with the same arrangement remaining, let the ratio of base **a.e.** to **c.f.** be as height **d.f.** to **e.b.** I say then that solids **a.b.** and **c.d.** are equal. For it will be, from the 7th of the fifth book, that **d.f.** is to **f.g.** as **a.e.** is to **c.f.** But from the previous proposition, solid **a.b.** is to **c.g.** as base **a.e.** is to **c.f.** Therefore, **a.b.** is to **c.g.** as **d.f.** is to **f.g.** From the 1st of the sixth book, **d.f.** is to **f.g.** as **m.f.** is to **f.l.**, and from the previous proposition, solid **c.d.** is to **c.g.** as **m.f.** is to **f.l.** Thus, **c.d.** is to **c.g.** as **a.b.** is to **c.g.** Therefore, from the 9th of the fifth book, **a.b.** and **c.d.** are equal, which is what was proposed.

<note>A perspective drawing depicts a rectangular parallelepiped, a three-dimensional box-like shape, with its corners labeled 'a', 'b', and 'e' to assist in following the geometric proof provided in the text.</note>

### Proposition 35.

<note>A geometric diagram shows two overlapping parallelepipeds. One stands vertically while the other is inclined or shifted, sharing elements of the same base or height. Points are labeled with letters including 'c', 'h', 'k', 'f', 'g', 'l', and 'm' to illustrate the transformation of oblique solids into right-angled ones for the sake of comparison.</note>

If two solids of parallel boundaries <term>equidistantiū terminoꝝ</term> <note>Another term for parallelepipeds.</note> are equal, their bases will be reciprocal to their heights. If indeed their bases are reciprocal to their heights, any two bodies of parallel surfaces are proven to be equal.

Whereas the previous proposition dealt with parallelogrammatic solids whose lines of height rise orthogonally upon their bases, this 35th proposition proposes it indistinctly for all such solids. It is fitting, however, to demonstrate this from the previous one, just as we demonstrated the 32nd and 33rd. For when any two solids of parallel sides are constructed, if the lines of height stand orthogonally upon their bases, the truth of the statement is established from the previous proposition. If, however, from the four angular points of the uppermost surface in both solids, four lines are dropped perpendicularly to the bases, or from the angular points of the lowest surfaces four lines are erected, between which two parallelogrammatic solids are completed equal in height to the prior solids: then these two solids will be equal to the two prior solids by the 29th and 30th propositions. Since, therefore, these and those have the same bases and the same heights, and since what this 35th proposition proposes is true for the latter [the right-angled solids] by the previous proposition, it will also be true for the former [the oblique solids].

# **PROPOSITION 33** If two solids with parallel surfaces are similar, the ratio of one to the other will be the triplicate ratio of any of its sides to the corresponding side of the other.

<note>original: "proportio triplicata"; the triplicate ratio is what we would call the "cube" of a ratio. For example, if the sides of two boxes are in a ratio of 2:1, their volumes are in a triplicate ratio of 8:1 (2x2x2 to 1x1x1).</note>

Let there be two solids, **a.b.** and **c.d.**, which are parallelogrammatic and similar. I say that the ratio of one to the other is as the ratio of one of its sides to the corresponding side of the other, but in triplicate; just as the ratio of two similar surfaces is as the duplicate ratio <note>The square of the ratio.</note> of their corresponding sides, as was demonstrated in the 18th proposition of the sixth book.

For if the solids **a.b.** and **c.d.** were equal, since they are assumed to be similar, it would follow from the definitions of similar bodies and similar surfaces that all sides of one are equal to their corresponding sides of the other. Therefore, since the triplicate ratio (or any ratio taken any number of times) of two equal quantities results in nothing but a ratio of equality, it is clear that the proposition holds true in this case.

But if they are unequal, let **a.b.** be the larger. Let its length be **b.c.**, its width **e.f.**, its height **f.a.**, its base **c.r.**, and its top surface **a.n.** Of the solid **c.d.**, let the length be **d.g.**, the width **g.b.**, and the height **b.c.** It follows from the definition of similar bodies <note>original: "dione similiū coꝛpoꝛū"; abbreviation for "definitione similium corporum".</note> and the definition of similar surfaces, and from the present hypothesis, that the ratio of **a.f.** to **c.b.**, and **f.e.** to **b.g.**, and **e.b.** to **g.d.** is one and the same ratio.

Therefore, let there be taken from line **a.f.**—which is clearly larger than line **c.b.**—a segment **f.k.** equal to **b.c.** Let the other three lines determining the height of solid **a.b.** be cut to the same equality, and between them let there be completed a parallelogrammatic solid **k.b.**, equal in height to solid **c.d.** Let the two lines of the base be extended, **e.b.** to **l.** and **r.b.** to **m.**, and let **b.l.** be equal to **g.d.** and **b.m.** equal to **b.g.** Complete the surface of parallel sides **m.l.**, which will be equal and similar to **b.d.** Upon this surface, let there be erected a parallelogrammatic solid **p.q.** according to the precise height taken from solid **a.b.** Thus, **p.q.** will be equal and similar to solid **c.d.**

Furthermore, between the lines **r.b.** and **b.l.**, complete the surface of parallel sides **b.t.**, upon which let there be erected a parallelogrammatic solid **x.l.** of the same height as both solids **k.b.** and **p.q.**, filling one of the two gaping angles between them. Since the two solids **a.b.** and **p.q.** are similar (because both are assumed similar to solid **c.d.**, and bodies similar to the same body are similar to each other, as is clear from the definition of similar bodies and the 20th proposition of the sixth book), it is manifest from the 25th proposition <note>Likely referring to a definition of continued proportions applied to solids.</note> taken three times that between the two solids **a.b.** and **p.q.**, there fall two solids **k.b.** and **x.l.** in a continued proportion.

Therefore, once the figure is appropriately established or constructed, and the hypotheses are firmly committed to memory, you may easily conclude the proposition from the first proposition of the sixth book. **Shake off your sluggishness and pay close attention** <note>original: "Excute torporem et diligenter attende"; a characteristic remark by the editor Campanus of Novara, urging the reader to focus on the difficult proof.</note>, and you will know from the 25th proposition of this book that the ratio of solid **a.b.** to solid **k.b.** is as the surface **a.r.** to the surface **k.r.**, and therefore from the first of the sixth book, as the line **a.f.** is to the line **k.f.**

Similarly, the ratio of solid **k.b.** to solid **x.l.** is as the surface **k.r.** to the surface **x.t.**, and thus as the line **f.r.** to the line **r.t.** Furthermore, the ratio of solid **x.l.** to solid **p.q.** is as the surface **r.l.** to the surface **l.m.**, and thus as the line **r.b.** to the line **b.m.**

From the hypothesis, it is clear that the ratio of line **f.r.** to line **r.t.** and line **r.b.** to line **b.m.** is the same as the ratio of line **a.f.** to line **k.f.** Therefore, from the definition of triplicate ratio placed in the introduction to the fifth book, it is established that the ratio of solid **a.b.** to solid **p.q.** (and therefore also to solid **c.d.**) is as the ratio of line **a.f.** to line **k.f.** tripled. Since line **k.f.** was set equal to line **c.b.**, it is clear that what was stated is true.

It should also be known that whatever has been demonstrated through this 33rd proposition <note>The OCR says 36, but the content is the 33rd proposition of Euclid's Book XI.</note> and the three immediately preceding it concerning parallelogrammatic solids, is also true of prisms <term>seratilibus</term> <note>original: "seratilibus"; literally "saw-cut" solids, referring to prisms whose bases are commonly triangles or quadrilaterals.</note> whose bases are generally triangles or quadrangles. This will be clear to the ingenious observer from the 28th, this 33rd, and the seven preceding propositions. For if there be any prisms of equal height upon the same base or upon equal bases, whether triangular or quadrangular, since they are half of the parallelogrammatic solids of their heights (from the 28th), they will be equal (from the 29th) and so forth.

Therefore, solid **a.b.** is equal to solid **a.c.**, which proves the proposition. 

¶ You may also prove the converse of this and the preceding proposition, if you wish, by leading the argument to an impossibility <note>original: "ducendo ad impossibile"; a method of proof known as *reductio ad absurdum*, where one assumes the opposite of what they want to prove and shows it leads to a logical contradiction.</note>. You will then prove this cut-off portion is equal to the lower solid based on this proposition and the one before it; and therefore, it would be equal to the whole solid from which it was cut, according to common knowledge <note>original: "ex coi scia" (ex communi scientia); referring to the "Common Notions" or axioms at the start of Euclid's Elements, specifically that "the whole is greater than the part."</note>.

## Proposition 31

**Solids** of parallel surfaces <note>parallelepipeds</note> constructed on equal bases, if they are of equal height and their lateral edges stand perpendicularly over the bases, will be equal to one another.

¶ And this is also true: that all solid parallelograms on equal bases and situated between parallel surfaces—or having the same height—are equal to one another, just as it was proven regarding surfaces of parallel sides <note>parallelograms</note> on equal bases and between parallel lines in the 36th proposition of the first book. However, of such solids, some have lateral edges that rise perpendicularly <note>original: "orthonogaliter"; at right angles.</note> over their bases, which this 31st proposition proposes to demonstrate are equal. But there are others whose lateral edges are not perpendicularly erected over their bases, which the following proposition proposes to demonstrate are equal. 

Therefore, let there be understood two bases, **a.b.** and **c.d.**, which are equal and have parallel sides, yet are not of the same shape; rather, let **a.b.** be a long tetragon <note>a rectangle</note> and **c.d.** be like a *helmuaym* <note>original: "helmuaym"; a medieval Latin term derived from Arabic meaning a rhombus or rhomboid.</note>. Let there be two solids of parallel sides constructed of equal height, and let the lines erected upon the angles of the proposed bases be perpendicular to them. I say that these two solids are equal to each other. 

Therefore, let two sides of base **a.b.** be extended—specifically those containing angle **b**—as far as **f** and **e**, and let angle **f.b.g.** be made equal to angle **c** of base **c.d.** Let two lines **b.f.** and **b.g.** be taken equal to the two sides of base **c.d.** which contain angle **c**, and let the surface of parallel sides **b.h.** <note>The OCR reads "b.b.", but the diagram and logic suggest the surface "b.h." defined by the points in the margin.</note> be completed, which will be equal and similar to base **c.d.** 

From there, let **b.e.** be drawn parallel to **b.f.**, and **f.k.** parallel to **b.e.** The quadrilateral surface **b.k.** of parallel sides will be equal to **b.h.** according to the 35th proposition of the first book. And since **b.h.** is equal to **c.d.**, by common notion **b.k.** will be equal to **a.b.** 

Let the surface of parallel sides **b.l.** then be completed by extending line **k.f.** until it meets one of the sides containing angle **a** at point **l**. Now, upon the three surfaces of parallel sides, which are **b.h.**, **b.k.**, and **b.l.**, let solids be constructed of the same height as the solid constructed on base **a.b.**, and let the edges of all these solids be erected perpendicularly to the bases. Let the bases and the solids constructed upon them be called by the same names. 

It is clear, then, from the definition of equal and similar solids, that the two solids **b.h.** and **c.d.** are equal and similar. Regarding solids **b.h.** and **b.k.**, it is established from the 29th proposition that they are equal, for they are of equal height and constructed upon one and the same base, and that surface is erected upon line **b.f.** 

Furthermore, according to the 25th proposition <note>of Book XI</note>, the ratio of solid **a.b.** to solid **b.l.** is as the ratio of base **a.b.** to base **b.l.** By the same reasoning, the ratio of solid **b.k.** to solid **b.l.** is as the ratio of base **b.k.** to base **b.l.** Since both bases **a.b.** and **b.k.** have the same ratio to base **b.l.**, then according to the first part of the 7th proposition of the fifth book, both solids **a.b.** and **b.k.** will have the same ratio to solid **b.l.** 

Therefore, according to the first part of the 9th proposition of the fifth book, the two solids **a.b.** and **b.k.** are equal. And because solid **b.k.** is equal to solid **b.h.**, and solid **b.h.** is equal to solid **c.d.**, it follows from common knowledge that solid **a.b.** is equal to solid **c.d.**, which is what was to be proposed.

## Proposition 32

**If** parallelepipeds <term>solida equidistantium superficierum</term> <note>Literally "solids of parallel surfaces." In modern geometry, these are called parallelepipeds—six-sided figures where every pair of opposite faces is parallel.</note> established on equal bases are of equal height, but their angular edges <note>The vertical or slanted lines connecting the base to the top surface.</note> do not stand perpendicularly over the bases: it is necessary that they be equal to one another.

¶ Having constructed two bodies as proposed, namely that they are of parallel boundaries and of equal height and on equal bases, not standing upright over their bases but both inclined upon them. If, however, from the four angles of their top surfaces, perpendicular lines are drawn to their bases—which from Proposition 6 will be individually parallel and also, by hypothesis, individually equal to one another, for they define the height of the proposed solids—and if between them solids of parallel sides are completed, it is established from the previous proposition that these two last-constructed solids are equal to each other. And since the two original solids and the two subsequent ones share the same bases (namely their top surfaces), it is established from Proposition 29 or 30 and this common knowledge <note>original: "communi scientia"; referring to the Axioms or Common Notions of Euclid, specifically that things equal to the same thing are equal to each other.</note>: that whatever things are equal to the same thing are equal to each other, which is what was proposed. From these, you can indirectly demonstrate the converses of this and the previous proposition using the same means if you wish, in the same manner and by leading to the same inconvenience <note>original: "ad idem inconveniens"; a logical contradiction or *reductio ad absurdum*.</note> as in the deduction of the converses of the two preceding ones: for you would suppose two solid parallelograms <note>In the 15th century, the term "solid parallelogram" was often used interchangeably with parallelepiped.</note> to be equal and upon equal bases, and you would prove them to be of equal height; or you would suppose them to be of equal height and equal, and you would prove them to be upon equal bases.

## Proposition 33

**All** parallelepipeds <note>original: "solida equidistantium superficierum"</note> of equal height are proportional to their bases. ¶ Let there be two parallelepipeds of equal height established upon two bases **a.b.** and **c.d.** I say that the proportion <term>proportio</term> <note>The ratio or relationship in size.</note> of those two solids, one to the other, is as the proportion of their bases, which are **a.b.** and **c.d.**, one to the other. It is indeed established from Proposition 24 that each of these two bases has parallel sides: therefore, let two opposite and parallel sides in surface **a.b.** be extended, and between them let a surface of parallel sides be made, which shall be **f.e.**, equal to **c.d.** Then, above the surface **f.e.**, let a solid parallelogram be completed of the same height as that which was established above base **a.b.**, and let that surface which rises above line **b.f.** be their common boundary. Now, let these solids and their bases be called by the same names. Since, therefore, base **f.e.** is equal to base **c.d.**, by Proposition 31 or 32, solid **f.e.** will be equal to solid **c.d.** But because the rising surface above line **b.f.** cuts the total solid **a.e.** parallel to two opposite sides: it follows from Proposition 25 that the proportion of solid **f.e.** to solid **a.b.** is as base **f.e.** is to base **a.b.** And since **c.d.** and **f.e.** are equal both as bases and as solids—the bases by hypothesis, and the solids by Proposition 31 or 32—it follows from Proposition 7 of the Fifth Book, applied twice (once for the bases and once for the solids), that there is one proportion for solids **a.b.** and **c.d.** and for bases **a.b.** and **c.d.**, which is what we wished to demonstrate. Nor is it difficult to demonstrate the converse of this by the same means, just as with the converses of the preceding ones. For you would suppose two solid parallelograms to be proportional to their bases, and you would prove them to be of equal height; and if an opponent claims one is higher, you would cut from it a solid parallelogram of equal height to the lower one, and the cut-off part and the lower one would be proportional to their bases by hypothesis and by this rule. And since the total was also higher (from which you cut the part) and it was proportional to those same bases by hypothesis, it follows from the first part of Proposition 9 of the Fifth Book that the whole (which the opponent says is higher) and the part you cut from it are equal <note>This leads to the contradiction that a part is equal to the whole.</note>.

In a quadrilateral, all angles are equal to four right angles according to Proposition 32 of the First Book <note>original: "ex .32. primi"</note>: thus it is necessary that the two remaining angles of one be equal to the two relative remaining angles of the other. Since these two remaining angles in any given case are also equal to one another, it is necessarily proved that each surface of solid *a.d.* is equiangular <note>Having the same angles.</note> to its relative surface in solid *b.c.* Therefore, from the second part of Proposition 13 of the Sixth Book, the bases of the two proposed solids will be equal. For they are equiangular and have reciprocal sides. If, therefore, the lines of height stand perpendicularly upon the bases, it is clear from Proposition 31 that they are equal. For since these lines are equal and they themselves determine the height of the solids, the solids will be equally high. 

But if the lines of their heights do not stand perpendicularly on their bases, then by dropping perpendiculars from their summits to the bases, these perpendiculars will be equal to one another according to the previous demonstration. For they will be just as they were in the previous parts of the proof in the figure where the two lines *p.q.* and *l.n.* were shown to be necessarily equal. Because, therefore, the height of all solids is defined <note>original: "diffiniť"</note> by the perpendiculars descending from their summits to their bases, the two solids *a.d.* and *c.b.* will be equal according to Proposition 32. 

We can also prove the converse of this, if it is desired, in the opposite manner: as if the parallelepiped <term>palellogramū</term> <note>A medieval Latin shorthand for parallelepipedum, a six-sided solid where each face is a parallelogram.</note> body *a.d.* is equal and equiangular to the parallelepiped body *b.c.*, and body *b.c.* is contained by the mean of the three lines containing body *a.d.*, the three lines containing body *a.b.* will be in continuous proportion. For since the two parallelepiped solids *a.d.* and *c.b.* are equal and of equal height by hypothesis <note>original: "ypothesi"</note>, they will be on equal bases according to the converses of Propositions 31 and 32. And because their bases are equiangular, it follows from the first part of Proposition 13 of the Sixth Book that their sides are reciprocal; thus the proportion of *a.b.* to *b.c.* is as *b.c.* to *c.d.*, wherefore the proposition stands.

## Proposition 39

**If** there are any number of proportional lines, the solids of parallel and similar surfaces <note>specifically similar parallelepipeds</note> created from each will also be proportional. If, however, the solids of parallel and similar surfaces are proportional, the lines by which those solids are contained will also be proportional. A similar thing is proposed in Proposition 21 of the Sixth Book regarding surfaces <note>Referring to the areas of similar plane figures.</note>. 

¶ For let there be four lines, *a, b* and *c, d*, which are proportional, and upon these let four parallelepiped solids be constructed, called by the same names, which are specifically similar. For once two have been constructed at will upon the two lines *a* and *c*, the others are to be established according to the instructions of Proposition 27. I say that these four solids are proportional, and vice versa. For let two more lines, *e* and *f*, be added to the two lines *a* and *b* in continuous proportion <note>A sequence where the ratio between successive terms is constant, e.g., a:b = b:e = e:f.</note>, just as Proposition 10 of the Sixth Book teaches; and from the two lines *c* and *d*, let another two be added, which are *g* and *h*. It is therefore clear from Proposition 36 and from the definition of triplicate proportion <note>The ratio of the cubes of the sides, used to compare the volumes of similar solids.</note> which was placed at the beginning of the Fifth Book, and from this hypothesis—because solids *a* and *b* are specifically similar to each other, and solids *c* and *d* are specifically similar to each other—that the proportion of solid *a* to solid *b* is as the proportion of line *a* to line *f*; likewise, the proportion of solid *c* to solid *d* is as line *c* to line *h*. And because, by Proposition 22 of the Fifth Book, the proportion of line *a* to line *f* is as line *c* to line *h*, it follows from Proposition 11 of the Fifth Book that solid *a* is to solid *b* as solid *c* is to solid *d*. Thus the first part is established. 

The second part is thus: let there be two solids, *a* and *b*, specifically similar to each other, and two others, *c* and *d*, specifically similar to each other. Let all be parallelepipeds and let it be assumed they are proportional. I say that the lines *a, b* and *c, d* upon which they are constructed are proportional. For let it be that, according to Proposition 10 of the Sixth Book, as line *a* is to line *b*, so line *c* is to line *k*. And let there be made, according to Proposition 27 of this book, upon line *k* a solid specifically similar to solid *d*, which shall also be called *k*. And it will be, from the definitions of similar bodies and similar surfaces in Proposition 20 of the Sixth Book, that body *k* is specifically similar to body *c*. Therefore, by the first part of this Proposition 39 already proved, the proportion of solid *a* to solid *b* will be as the proportion of solid *c* to solid *k*. And since the same proportion was that of solid *c* to solid *d*...

**I**f the sides of two opposite faces of a cube are each cut into two equal halves, and from these points of section two surfaces [planes] emerge, cutting through each other across the cube, then their common intersection must necessarily bisect the diameter of the cube, and in turn, be bisected by that same diameter.

¶ Establish a cube, which shall be **a.b.**, regarding which it is clear by definition <note>original: "per dionem," a common abbreviation for "per definitionem"</note> that all the lines containing it are equal and its surfaces are rectangular; for such a body we call a cube. Let its base, therefore, be surface **a.c.d.e.**, and its topmost surface **b.f.g.h.** Let its right surface be **a.e.g.b.** and its left surface **b.f.c.d.** Let the nearer surface be **d.e.h.b.** and the further **a.c.g.f.**, and let its diameter be **a.b.** Therefore, let all the sides of any two opposite faces be divided into equal halves. And let these be the right and left surfaces whose sides are divided. I say, let the four sides of the right face be divided at the four points **o, p, q, r**, and the four of the left face at the four points **k, l, m, n**. Let the opposite points in these surfaces be joined by drawn lines **o-p** and **q-r**, which intersect at point **t**. Likewise, join **k-l** and **m-n**, which intersect at point **s**. <note>The Latin text uses the "long s" (ſ).</note> Let two surfaces be completed, intersecting each other and the cube, by drawing lines **o-k**, **p-l**, **q-m**, and **r-n**. Let the common section of these two surfaces be the line **s.t.** I say, therefore, that line **s.t.** divides the diameter **a.b.** and is divided by that same diameter into equal parts. This is evident because both of them pass through the center of the cube.

Alternatively, what was proposed is demonstrated as follows: let two lines **t.a.** and **t.b.** be extended, and likewise two lines **s.c.** and **s.b.** From Proposition 4 of the First Book, **a.t.** will be equal to **t.b.** and **s.c.** equal to **s.b.** It is also clear from the first part of Proposition 29 of the First Book that angle **p.t.q.** is equal to angle **a.q.t.**, and from Proposition 4 of the First Book, angle **b.t.p.** is equal to angle **t.a.q.** Thus, from Proposition 32 of the First Book, the whole angle **b.t.q.** together with angle **q.t.a.** is equal to two right angles; therefore, by Proposition 14 of the First Book, line **a.b.** will be a single [straight] line. Similarly, line **a.b.** will be a single line. And since from the ninth [proposition], line **a.c.** is parallel <term>equidistans|parallel</term> to line **b.h.** (for each is parallel to line **d.e.**) and since they are equal because they are sides of the cube, it follows from Proposition 33 of the First Book that the two lines **a.b.** and **c.h.** are equal and parallel. Therefore, by common notion <note>original: "per conceptionem" — referring to the "Common Notions" or axioms at the start of Euclid's Elements</note>, their halves, which are **a.t.** and **b.s.**, will be equal. From the seventh [proposition] of this book, it is manifest that line **s.c.** is in the surface of the two lines **a.b.** and **b.c.**, and this same line **a.b.**, which is the diameter of the cube, is also the diameter of the parallelogram surface **a.c.h.b.** Thus, line **s.t.** intersects the diameter **a.b.**; let it intersect at point **u**. I say, then, that line **s.u.** is equal to line **u.t.**, and line **a.u.** is equal to line **u.b.** Consider two triangles **a.t.u.** and **b.s.u.**, whose angles at **t** and **s** are equal to each other; similarly, their angles at **a** and **b** are equal to each other from the first part of Proposition 29 of the First Book, because line **a.t.** is parallel to line **s.b.** and because they are also equal to each other. It follows from Proposition 26 of the First Book that which was proposed [is true]. The same may be concluded in the same way even if solid **a.b.** is not a cube, but a parallelogrammic solid body <term>solidum corpus parallelogramum|a parallelepiped</term>, whether contained by equal lines or unequal lines, and whether erected orthogonally upon its base or even...

<meta>This page continues the exploration of Book XI of Euclid's Elements. While the previous page discussed Propositions 39 and 40 regarding prisms and cubes, this page returns to the foundational properties of prisms (referred to here as "seratilia") and introduces Proposition 37, which concerns the relationship between angles and perpendiculars in three-dimensional space.</meta>

...from the following: for from these it is clear that solid parallelepipeds <note>Parallelepipeds are six-sided solids where every face is a parallelogram.</note> are equal to twice the prisms <note>original: "seratilibus" — literally 'sawn' or 'cut' solids, used by Euclid to refer to prisms</note> themselves. Similarly, if there are two prisms upon common triangular or common quadrangular bases of equal height, they will be proportional to their bases, just as is held concerning solid parallelepipeds in the 33rd [proposition]. For, according to the 28th [proposition], they are half of the solid parallelepipeds of their own height; and there is one proportion for solid parallelepipeds of their height and their bases according to the 33rd. Therefore, since the proportion of solid parallelepipeds is the same as that of prisms—because as the simple is to the simple, so the double is to the double, according to the 15th [proposition] of the fifth [book]—and the proportion of the bases of the solid parallelepipeds is as the proportion of the bases of the prisms. For either the bases of the prisms and the solid parallelepipeds will be the same—and this will indeed be the case when the bases of the prisms are quadrangular, for then the solid parallelepipeds are to be completed from the prisms upon those same bases—or the bases of the prisms will be half the size of the bases of the solid parallelepipeds. This indeed occurs when the bases of the prisms are common triangles; for then the solid parallelepipeds are to be completed from the prisms by adding triangular surfaces to the bases of the prisms, so that the bases of the prisms, with the added triangular surfaces, become surfaces of equal and parallel sides. Consequently, the proportion of the prisms is as the proportion of their bases. 

In the same way, if the prisms are equal and are on common triangular bases or common quadrangular bases, their bases will be in reciprocal proportion <note>A "mutual" or reciprocal proportion means that as the size of the base increases, the height must decrease to maintain the same volume.</note> to their heights. If their bases are reciprocal to their heights, the prisms themselves will be equal, just as was proposed concerning solid parallelepipeds in the 34th and 35th [propositions]. This is easily clear from what was said in the 35th. If, however, the prisms are similar to one another, the proportion of one to the other will be as the triplicate ratio <note>The triplicate ratio is the modern equivalent of cubing the ratio of the sides (e.g., if the sides are 2:1, the volume is 8:1).</note> of the proportion of the side of one to the corresponding side of the other, just as the 36th [proposition] proposes concerning solid parallelepipeds, which will be easily clear to you from that same 36th [proposition]. If, from those similar prisms, completed solid parallelepipeds are formed, you will prove those solids themselves to be similar; which is an easy matter to handle from the definition of similar bodies and similar surfaces, and from the fact that prisms are posited as being similar to one another from the 34th [proposition] of the first [book].

**I**f there are two equal plane angles upon which two inclined lines <note>original: "ypothemisē" — likely a Latinization of a Greek term for lines standing over or inclined toward the plane, here serving as the edges of a solid angle.</note> are raised in the air, containing with the underlying sides of the angles individual angles equal to one another, and if two points are marked on those inclined lines from which two perpendiculars are dropped to the surfaces <note>In this context, "surfaces" refers to the planes containing the original angles.</note> of the proposed angles, and from the points upon which the perpendiculars fall, two straight lines are drawn to those same two plane angles, it is proved that the two angles contained by those two lines and the two inclined lines are equal to one another. 

Let there be two equal plane angles **a** and **d**, contained by lines **a-b** and **a-c**, and **d-e** and **d-f**. Upon them, let two lines be raised as inclined lines, **a-g** and **d-h**. Let angle **g-a-c** be equal to angle **h-d-f** <note>Note: The text reads 'b-d-f', likely a scribe's error for 'h-d-f'.</note> and angle **g-a-b** be equal to angle **h-d-e**. Let two lines **a-m** and **d-n** be drawn. I say, therefore, that angle **g-a-m** is equal to angle **h-d-n**. If line **a-k** is equal to **d-l**, it is well indeed. If not, however, let **a-p** be taken from line **a-g** equal to **d-l**, and from point **p** let a perpendicular be dropped to the surface of angle **a**, which line becomes **p-q**. It is manifest, therefore, that point **q** is on line **a-m**, which is easily established for the diligent observer from the 6th [proposition] of this [book] and the definition of parallel lines, which must necessarily be in one surface. From here, let two perpendiculars be drawn from point **q**, one to line **a-b**, which is **q-r**, and another to line **a-c**, which is **q-s**. Similarly...

## Proposition 38

<note>A diagram showing three horizontal line segments labeled 'a', 'b', 'c', and 'd', illustrating proportionality.</note>

A **solid** contained by three **proportional** lines will be equal to a **solid** which is contained by equal sides of the **mean** line, if both of their angles are mutually equal to one another.

Let this be understood concerning **parallelepipeds** <note>original: "solidis palellogramis" — literally 'parallelogrammic solids'.</note>; for concerning these, of whatever sort they may be, provided they are **equiangular**, it is true that the [solid] contained by three proportional lines is equal to that which is contained by the mean of them, just as was proven concerning rectangular surfaces in the 16th [proposition] of the sixth [book], and is evidently drawn out for non-rectangular surfaces from the second part of the 13th [proposition] of the same. For since the solid angle **b.** is placed equal to the solid angle **a.**, it is necessary that one angle of each surface of solid **a.** be equal to one angle of its relative surface in solid **b.c.**; therefore, by the 34th [proposition] of the first [book], their opposites will be equal. ### Proposition 41.

<note>The page features two sets of geometric diagrams. The top set consists of two three-dimensional figures: one is a prism divided into smaller units with points labeled a, b, c, d, h, k, p, q; the second is a smaller prism structure labeled e, f, g, l, m, n, r, s, t. If there are two prism-like bodies <term>serratilia</term> <note>original: "corpora serratilia"—literally "saw-like bodies." This is the term Euclid's early translators used for prisms, specifically those with triangular bases, because their profile resembles the teeth of a saw.</note>, one of which has a triangular base and the other a parallelogram base, and the parallelogram is double the triangular base, and if these two bodies are of equal height, it is necessary that those two bodies be equal.

Let the parallelogram surface **a.b.c.d.** be double the triangular surface **e.f.g.** and upon these two surfaces let two prisms of equal height be formed. Let the prism which is above the quadrangular base be **a.b.c.d.k.** <note>The OCR text here contains some repeating letters (a.b.b.d.c.k.) likely representing the vertices of the solid.</note>, whose base is the proposed parallelogram **a.b.c.d.** Let its other parallelogram surfaces be **e.a.b.d.k.** and **b.c.k.**, while its two triangular surfaces are **a.b.b.** and **d.c.k.** 

Now let the prism which is over the triangular base **e.f.g.** be **e.f.g.l.m.n.**, of which one of the two triangular surfaces is the aforementioned base; the other is the triangle **l.m.n.** Of its three parallelogram surfaces, the first is **e.f.l.m.**, the second is **e.g.l.n.**, and the third is **f.g.m.n.** 

I say, therefore, that these two proposed prisms are equal to one another. For let two parallelogram solids <note>Parallelepipeds.</note> be completed by adding to each of the two proposed prisms another prism equal to itself. To the first prism on the same base, let the prism **a.p.b.d.q.k.** be joined, whose two triangular surfaces are **a.p.b.** and **d.q.k.**, and its three quadrilaterals: the first is **a.b.d.k.**, which is the common boundary between itself and the one to which it is joined; the second is **a.d.p.q.**, and the third is **p.q.b.k.**

To the second prism, let another prism equal to itself be joined in this manner: let another equal triangle, which is **e.g.r.**, be joined to the first triangle **e.f.g.**, so that the whole surface **e.f.g.r.** is a parallelogram. Upon this triangle let the prism **e.g.l.r.l.n.f.** be formed, which, with the one to which it is joined, completes a parallelogram solid. Of this joined prism, the two triangular surfaces are **e.g.r.** and **l.n.f.**, and the three parallelograms are: first **e.l.r.f.**, second **e.l.g.n.** (which is the common boundary to itself and the one it is joined to), and third **g.r.n.f.**

It is therefore manifest from the definition of equal and similar solids that the two prisms composing the parallelogram solid **a.k.** are equal to each other. Likewise, the two composing the parallelogram solid **e.n.** are equal to each other. But indeed, from Proposition 31 or 32 of this book, the two [completed] solids **a.k.** and **e.n.** are equal to each other. Since, therefore, the proposed prisms are the halves of these solids, it is established by common knowledge <note>Referring to Euclid's "Common Notions," specifically that halves of equals are equal.</note> that they are equal. For whatever things are equal, their halves must necessarily be equal. Thus, that which was proposed is clear.

### Proposition 2.

The ratio of any two circles to one another is as the ratio of the square of its diameter to the square of the diameter of the other. <note>This is a foundational theorem of geometry, proving that a circle's area is proportional to the square of its diameter.</note>

¶ Let there be two circles **a.b.** and **c.d.**, whose diameters are also called **a.b.** and **c.d.** I say, therefore, that the ratio of circle **a.b.** to circle **c.d.** is as the square of diameter **a.b.** to the square of diameter **c.d.** For it is manifest from this common principle—as great as any magnitude is to some second magnitude, so great must any third be to some fourth—that the ratio of the square of diameter **a.b.** to the square of diameter **c.d.** is as circle **a.b.** to some surface which we shall call **e.**, of whatever figure or form it may be placed. However, it is impossible for this [surface **e.**] to be greater or smaller than circle **c.d.** For if it is possible that it is smaller than circle **c.d.**, let it then be smaller by the surface **f.**; thus circle **c.d.** is equal to the two surfaces **e.** and **f.** taken together.

It is established, therefore, from the 1st [proposition] of the tenth [book] <note>This refers to the "Method of Exhaustion." It states that if you continually subtract more than half of a quantity, you will eventually be left with a remainder smaller than any pre-assigned quantity (**f.** in this case).</note> that so many times can there be subtracted from circle **c.d.** and its remainders [a part] greater than half, until some quantity is left smaller than **f.** Therefore, let the square **c.d.g.h.** be inscribed in it, as the 6th [proposition] of the fourth [book] teaches; concerning which it is established that it is greater than half of the circle. For the square which is double to it is the [square] circumscribing the circle, as is clear from the penultimate [proposition] of the first [book] and the 7th of the fourth. If, therefore, the segments of the circle lying upon the sides of the square, taken together, were less than surface **f.**, it suffices. But if not, let the four arcs lying upon the said sides be divided equally, and let the points dividing those arcs be connected to the ends of the sides by straight lines. For example, let arc **c.g.** be divided equally at point **k.** and let lines **k.c.** and **k.g.** be drawn, and so for the others.

And each of the triangles described upon the sides of the square will be greater than half of the segment in which it exists, because every isosceles triangle <term>ysochelis</term> <note>original: "triangul⁹ ysochelis"—a triangle with at least two equal sides.</note> is half of the parallelogram [formed] on its base, by the 41st [proposition] of the first [book]. Let it be, therefore, that the segments lying upon the sides of the inscribed octagon, taken together, are less than surface **f.** If this were not yet the case, one would not cease dividing the arcs whose sides of the last described figure are chords equally, and inscribing an equilateral figure of twice as many sides as the first, always subtracting from the segments of the circle more than half, until by the 1st [proposition] of the tenth [book], the segments lying upon the sides of some such figure inscribed in the circle, taken together, will be less than surface **f.** Let them now be as described; and from what precedes, the octagon **c.d.** will be greater than surface **e.** Therefore, in circle **a.b.**, let a similar octagon be inscribed in the same way, which shall be called **a.b.**; and from the preceding [proposition], let the ratio of octagon **a.b.** to octagon...

**c.d.** as the square of the diameter **a.b.** is to the square of the diameter **c.d.**; therefore, by the 11th [proposition] of the fifth [book], the ratio of circle **a.b.** to surface **e.** is the same. Thus, by permutation, the ratio of polygon **a.b.** to circle **a.b.** is as the ratio of polygon **c.d.** to surface **e.** Since polygon **c.d.** is greater than surface **e.**, polygon **a.b.** would be greater than circle **a.b.** This, however, is impossible <note>The Latin text reads "non est" (is not), but the mathematical logic of the proof by contradiction requires this to be "is impossible," as an inscribed polygon cannot exceed the area of its circle.</note>; therefore, surface **e.** is not less than circle **c.d.** But neither is it greater. Therefore, just as surface **e.** cannot be less than circle **c.d.**, so it cannot be greater; it must therefore necessarily be equal. Wherefore, by the second part of the 2nd [proposition] of the fifth [book], that which was proposed is clear.

### Proposition 3.

<note>A geometric diagram depicts a tetrahedron (a pyramid with a triangular base) labeled with vertices **a**, **b**, **c**, and **d**. The pyramid is subdivided by internal lines connecting the midpoints of its edges. Points **h**, **k**, and **l** are marked on the edges descending from the apex **a**. Points **e**, **f**, and **g** are marked on the edges of the base **bcd**. The diagram illustrates how the large pyramid is composed of two smaller pyramids and two triangular prisms, which Euclid calls "serratilia."</note>

Every pyramid whose base is a triangle can be divided into two equal pyramids similar to each other and to the whole pyramid, and into two *serratilia* <term>serratilia</term> <note>original: "serratilia"—literally "saw-like" solids. In modern geometry, these are triangular prisms. Euclid uses them to approximate the volume of the pyramid.</note> which, both taken together, must necessarily be greater than half of the whole pyramid. Let there be a pyramid **a.b.c.d.** upon the triangular base **b.c.d.**, and let its solid vertex be angle **a.**, from which three edges <note>original: "ypothenuse"—here used generally for the slanted edges of the pyramid.</note> **a.b.**, **a.c.**, and **a.d.** descend to the three angles of the base. Let all the sides of the base be divided equally at three points **e.**, **f.**, and **g.**, and likewise the three slanted edges be divided equally at three points **h.**, **k.**, and **l.** Let two lines **e.f.** and **e.g.** be drawn on the base. Its base is thus divided into three surfaces, of which two are the two triangles **b.e.f.** and **e.g.d.**, which—from the second part of the 2nd [proposition] of the sixth [book] and the definition of similar surfaces—are established to be similar to each other and to the whole base, and equal to each other. From the 8th [proposition] of the first [book], the third [surface] is a four-sided figure; it is a parallelogram, namely **c.f.g.e.**, which is established to be double the triangle **e.g.d.** from the 40th and 41st [propositions] of the first [book]. Then, let two edges **h.e.** and **h.f.** be dropped from point **h.**, and from point **k.** the edge **k.g.**, and let the lines **h.k.**, **k.l.**, and **l.h.** be drawn. Thus, the whole pyramid **a.b.c.d.** is divided into two pyramids, which are **h.b.e.f.** and **a.h.k.l.**, and two *serratilia*, of which one is **c.h.f.g.k.c.** <note>The letter **c** is repeated in the OCR, likely referring to the vertices of the prism.</note> and is upon the quadrangular base **c.f.g.e.**, and the other is **e.g.d.h.k.l.** and is upon the triangular base **e.g.d.** Concerning the two pyramids **h.b.e.f.** and **a.h.k.l.**, that they are equal to each other and similar to themselves and to the whole pyramid **a.b.c.d.** is clear from the definition of equal and similar bodies, and from the 10th and 11th [propositions] of the [eleventh] book, and from the second part of the 2nd [proposition] of the sixth [book]. Concerning the two *serratilia*, that they are equal is clear from the last [proposition] of the 11th book. How, indeed, both *serratilia* taken together are greater than half of the whole pyramid is manifest from this: that each of them is divisible into two pyramids, of which one is triangular and equal to one of those two into which the total pyramid is divided, and the other is quadrangular and is double the other. Wherefore, both *serratilia* taken together are three-quarters of the total divided pyramid. If you desire to know this proportion, consult the sixth [proposition] of this 12th book; but it suffices for you to know for the present purpose that those two *serratilia* taken together exceed [the other two pyramids] by any given quantity.

The corollary indeed is manifest from this: that similarly the bases of the partial pyramids relate to each other just as the pair of prisms of the one relate to the pair of prisms of the other. ...let there be subtracted from it two <term>prisms</term> <note>original: "seratilia"—literally 'saw-cut' solids; the term used in this era for prisms.</note> which, from the preceding proposition, are more than half of the pyramid itself. Likewise, from each of the two remaining partial pyramids, let two prisms be taken away in the aforementioned manner. Let this be done repeatedly until, from pyramid **b**, the opponent is forced by the first [proposition] of the 10th [book] <note>A reference to Euclid's method of exhaustion, which allows one to prove equality by showing that the difference between two quantities can be made smaller than any given value.</note> to admit that what remains is less than solid **d**.

Let us understand that as many prisms have been subtracted from pyramid **a** as we subtracted from pyramid **b**. From the corollary of the preceding proposition, it follows that as base **a** is to base **b**, so are the prisms subtracted from pyramid **a** to the prisms subtracted from pyramid **b**. 

But pyramid **a** was to body **c** [in the same ratio]; thus, the prisms of pyramid **a** are to the prisms of pyramid **b** as pyramid **a** is to body **c**. Alternately <note>original: "permutatim"—a logical step in ratios where the middle terms are swapped.</note>, the prisms of pyramid **a** are to pyramid **a** as the prisms of pyramid **b** are to body **c**. Since the prisms of pyramid **b** are greater than body **c**, the prisms of pyramid **a** would be greater than pyramid **a**. And because this is impossible, body **c** will not be less than pyramid **b**, nor will it be greater. 

For if it were assumed to be greater, since the ratio of base **a** to base **b** is as pyramid **a** is to body **c**, then conversely, base **b** to base **a** would be as body **c** is to pyramid **a**. By the same common knowledge, it would follow that pyramid **b** is to some body **d** [as base **b** to base **a**]. It follows from the 14th [proposition] of the fifth [book] that body **d** would be less than pyramid **a**, because pyramid **b** is assumed to be less than body **c**. From this, it has been demonstrated that an impossibility follows—namely, that the prisms subtracted from a pyramid would be greater than the pyramid from which they are subtracted. Therefore, it remains that body **c** is equal to pyramid **b**, since it can be neither less nor greater; and the ratio of pyramid **a** to pyramid **b** is as base **a** to base **b**. This is what was to be demonstrated.

And since from the 6th [proposition] of this 12th book, the second prism is triple to the proposed pyramid—for it is one of the three pyramids into which the prism is divided—it will also follow by common knowledge that the proposed prism is triple to the proposed pyramid.

¶ All pyramids whose bases are triangular and of equal height are proportional to their bases. The proposed pyramids will also be proportional to their bases.

¶ If there be any two pyramids of equal height, and the base of one is triangular, but the other is quadrilateral or multi-sided: it follows that the pyramids themselves are proportional to their bases.

¶ For example: Let there be understood two pyramids of equal height upon two bases, **a** and **b**. Let base **a** be triangular, and base **b** be pentagonal. Thus, by the 24th [proposition] of the 5th [book], assumed as many times as necessary: it is established that what we have said is true.
