### Proposition 7

IF two pyramids with triangular bases are equal in volume, their bases will be reciprocally proportional to their heights. If, however, the bases and heights are reciprocally proportional, it is necessary that those pyramids be equal to one another.
¶ What the 34th and 35th [propositions] of the 11th book proposed concerning parallelogram solids <note>solidis paralelogramis—these are parallelepipeds, or three-dimensional boxes where opposite faces are parallel.</note>, and what we demonstrated in the 36th of the same regarding <term>prisms</term> <note>original: "seratilibus"—literally 'saw-cut' solids, a term used in the 15th century to describe prisms.</note>, this 7th proposition of the 12th book proposes regarding pyramids having triangular bases. Let two equal pyramids be understood [standing] upon two <term>trigones</term> <note>original: "trigonos"—an older term for triangles.</note> or triangles *a* and *b*, which shall also be called *a* and *b*. I say, therefore, that the proportion of base *a* to base *b* is as the proportion of the height of pyramid *b* to the height of pyramid *a*; and if this is the case, I say the pyramids *a* and *b* are equal. Let two other triangles, *c* and *d*, be applied to the two triangles *a* and *b*, so that both surfaces *ac* and *bd* become parallelograms <note>original: "equidistantium laterum"—literally 'of equidistant sides'.</note>. From these pyramids, let parallelogram solids [parallelepipeds] be completed upon the bases *ac* and *bd*, of equal height to the proposed pyramids, which shall similarly be called *ac* and *bd*. It is therefore manifest from the 6th [proposition] of this 12th book that pyramid *a* is the sixth part of the solid *ac*, and pyramid *b* is the sixth part of solid *bd*. Therefore, from the 35th of the 11th book, the proposition is argued: the first part from the first, and the second part from the second.
¶ Likewise, if any two many-sided pyramids are equal, their bases will be reciprocally proportional to their heights. If indeed their bases are reciprocal to their heights, it is necessary that those pyramids be equal.
¶ If the bases of both are triangular, it has been demonstrated that what we said is true. If only one is [triangular]: let it be *a*, and let the base of the other pyramid be *b*, and let a triangle *c* be taken equal to the polygon *b*. Let a pyramid be made upon *c* of equal height to the pyramid which is upon *b*; let *a*, *b*, and *c* be the names of the pyramids and the bases. Since, therefore, by hypothesis, the two pyramids *a* and *b* are equal, and from the last [proposition] placed before the 6th of this book, the pyramids *b* and *c* are equal, it follows from <term>common knowledge</term> <note>original: "communi scientia"—referring to the Common Notions or Axioms of Euclid, such as 'things equal to the same thing are equal to each other'.</note> that the two pyramids *a* and *c* are equal. Therefore, their bases are reciprocal to their heights from the first part of this 7th [proposition]. Since the bases *b* and *c* are equal, the heights of pyramids *b* and *c* will also be equal. From the first and second parts of the 7th [proposition] of the 5th book, the bases *a* and *b* are reciprocal to the heights of pyramids *a* and *b*. The second part is proved in the reverse manner: for if base *a* is to base *b* as the height of pyramid *b* is to the height of pyramid *a*, it will follow from the 2nd and 1st parts of the 7th [proposition] of the 5th book that base *a* is to base *c* as the height of pyramid *b* is to the height of pyramid *a*. Thus, from the second part of this 7th [proposition], the two pyramids *a* and *c* are equal, wherefore by common knowledge the two pyramids *a* and *b* are also equal. If, however, neither of the proposed pyramids is triangular but both are polygonal—for example, one pentagonal and the other hexagonal, which we shall call *a* and *b*—let a triangle *c* be similarly taken equal to the hexagon *b*, upon which a pyramid is made equal in height to pyramid *b*. Thus, the two pyramids *b* and *c* will be equal. Therefore, the two pyramids *a* and *c* are also equal by the same concept. Wherefore base *a* is to base *c* as the height of pyramid *c* is to the height of pyramid *a*, for this has just been demonstrated. It follows from the 7th [proposition] of the 5th book that base *a* is to base *b* as the height of pyramid *b* is to the height of pyramid *a*. The converse is evident in the reverse manner: for if base *a* is to base *b* as the height of pyramid *b* is to the height of pyramid *a*.

### Proposition 8.

FOR any two similar pyramids whose bases are triangles, the ratio of one to the other is as the <term>triplicate ratio</term> <note>triplicate ratio—this is the ratio of the cubes of the lengths. In modern terms, if the ratio of the sides is $s_1:s_2$, the ratio of the volumes is $s_1^3:s_2^3$.</note> of a side to its corresponding side.
¶ Given two similar pyramids having triangular bases, complete from them two <term>parallelogram solids</term> <note>solidis parallelogramis—parallelepipeds, or box-like solids where opposite faces are parallel.</note> in the manner described in the demonstration of the preceding [proposition]. These two parallelogram solids will be similar because the pyramids are assumed to be similar to each other. For the two solid angles which are common to the pyramids and the parallelogram solids are contained by face angles equal in number and quantity; also, the sides containing those face angles are proportional. Therefore, from the 34th [proposition] of the 11th book, the three faces of the parallelogram solids constituting the common solid angles are equiangular and have proportional sides. They are therefore similar by the definition of similar surfaces; wherefore, from the 24th and 13th of the fifth [book], all six surfaces of these two parallelogram solids are similar to one another. Therefore, by the definition of similar bodies, the solids themselves will be similar. Since the ratio of the solids and the pyramids is the same from the 1st of the fifth [book]—for the solids are six times the pyramids by the 6th [proposition] of this [book]—and since the ratio of the solids is as the triplicate ratio of their corresponding sides from the 36th <note>The text cites the 36th of the 11th book, though in modern editions this property of similar parallelepipeds is usually Proposition 33.</note> of the 11th book; and since the sides of the solids are the same as the sides of the pyramids, it will also follow from the 11th of the fifth [book] that the ratio of the proposed pyramids is as the triplicate ratio of their corresponding sides: which is what was proposed.
¶ Furthermore, if there are any two similar <term>many-sided pyramids</term> <note>original: "piramides laterate"—pyramids with polygonal bases rather than just triangles.</note>, the ratio of one to the other will be as the triplicate ratio of its side to the corresponding side of the other.

<note>In the right margin, three geometric diagrams illustrate the concepts of exhaustion and the construction of solids:
1. At the top, a circle with a center point labeled 'a'. An inscribed square is shown, with lines connecting the center to the vertices. Additional lines from the center bisect the sides of the square to touch the circumference, illustrating how to form an inscribed octagon to approximate the circle's area.

...since body .c. can neither be smaller nor larger than the **round pyramid** .b. <note>In this text, Euclid uses "round pyramid" (*piramis rotunda*) to refer to what we now call a cone.</note>, it will necessarily be equal to it. And so, from the second part of the seventh proposition of the fifth book, the proposition is established. 

Let it not escape our notice, however, that the process of this demonstration is restricted only to those **columns** <note>original: "columnas"—referring to cylinders.</note> and round pyramids whose **axes** <note>The axis is the central line around which the shape is balanced.</note> stand perpendicularly upon their bases: for such were defined at the beginning of the eleventh book. Nonetheless, the property demonstrated here commonly applies to all round columns and similar round pyramids, whether their axes are erected <term>orthogonally</term> <note>At a right angle (90 degrees).</note> upon the bases or are inclined upon them. 

For the sake of clarity, let these be called by different names: those round columns and pyramids whose axes stand orthogonally are called **erect**; the others are called **inclined**. And because in the beginning of Book XI, only those columns or round pyramids were defined which we call "erect"—the former indeed by the motion of a rectangle, the latter by the motion of a right-angled triangle—we therefore deem it appropriate to define round columns and pyramids with definitions that apply commonly and <term>univocally</term> <note>Applying the same name to different things that share the same characteristics.</note> to both erect and inclined round columns and pyramids. 

When, therefore, a point is marked outside the surface of some described circle and is joined to the circumference of that circle by a straight line, if that line—while the marked point remains fixed—is rotated around the described circle until it returns to the place where it began to move: the body contained by the curved surface which this line describes by its motion and by the circle itself around which it is rotated, I call a **round pyramid**. The circle around which this line is rotated I call the **base** of the pyramid. The fixed point marked outside the circle's surface I call the <term>cone</term> <note>original: "conum"—here meaning the apex or vertex of the pyramid.</note> of the pyramid; and the straight line connecting the center of the base with the apex of the pyramid I call the **axis** or **arrow** <note>original: "sagittam"—literally "arrow," used here as a synonym for the height or axis.</note> of the pyramid. When this arrow is perpendicular to the base, I say the pyramid is **erect**; when it is inclined, I call the pyramid **inclined**. 

Likewise, when two equal circles are described in parallel surfaces which one flat surface passing through their centers has cut, and they are joined by a straight line that connects the corresponding sections of the two circumferences: if this line is rotated along the circumferences of those circles, remaining parallel to the position from which it began to move until it returns to its place, the body contained by the curved surface which this line describes by its motion and by the two proposed circles, I call a **round column**. Its axis or arrow is the straight line connecting the centers of the two circles. And when this arrow is perpendicular to the surface of both circles, I say the column is **erect**. When, however, it is inclined upon the base, I say the column is **inclined**. 

And when there are two round pyramids or columns from whose axes two surfaces emerge orthogonally to their bases, and the angles which the axes and the common sections of these surfaces and bases contain are equal to each other, and the proportion of the axis of one to the axis of the other is as the radius of the base of one to the radius of the base of the other: then I say those two pyramids to one another, or those two columns to one another, are **similar**. 

With these definitions established, it must be demonstrated that for any two similar round pyramids or similar round columns, whether they be erect or inclined, the proportion of one to the other is as the <term>triplicate proportion</term> <note>In modern mathematics, this is the ratio of the diameters cubed ($d^3$).</note> of the diameter of the base of one to the diameter of the base of the other—which was demonstrated for the erect ones alone. To this end, however, we first set forth a necessary antecedent.

<note>A geometric diagram is positioned in the upper right margin. It depicts a circle with a central point labeled 'b'. Within this circle, both a square and a regular octagon are inscribed. ...let a **polygonal pyramid** <term>polygonal pyramid</term> <note>original: "laterata piramis"—a pyramid with a base made of straight lines (a polygon) rather than a circle.</note> be subtracted, whose base is the square inscribed in circle .b.: which, as was proved above, will be greater than half of the **round pyramid** <note>A cone.</note>. And from the remainder of it, let pyramids of the same height be subtracted, standing upon the triangles of the segments of circle .b.; and let this be done as many times until the remainder of the round pyramid .b. is less than the solid .d., according to the first [proposition] of the tenth [book] <note>Euclid uses the "method of exhaustion" here, repeatedly dividing the remaining area to prove that the difference between a circle and an inscribed polygon can be made smaller than any given value.</note>.

And from the preceding premise, all the angles which the axis of pyramid .a. contains with the individual lines drawn from the center of circle .a. to the angles of the polygon inscribed in it, will be equal to their relative angles which the axis of pyramid .b. contains with the individual lines drawn from the center of circle .b. to the angles of the polygon inscribed in it.

Argue the rest just as before in the tenth [proposition]. It is established, therefore, concerning all similar round pyramids, that their proportion is as the **triplicate** <note>The "triplicate ratio" is the ratio of the cubes ($x^3:y^3$). Euclid is proving that if you double the diameter of a cone's base, its volume increases eightfold (2 to the power of 3).</note> of the diameters of their bases. And because every **round column** <note>A cylinder.</note> is triple to its pyramid <note>A cylinder has three times the volume of a cone with the same base and height.</note>—for this is sufficiently demonstrated whether the columns and their pyramids are right or inclined—it follows from the 15th [proposition] of the fifth [book] that the proportion of any similar round columns is also as the triplicate of their diameters.

### Proposition 11.

**It is necessary that any two round pyramids [cones] or cylinders of equal height are proportional to their bases.**

Upon two circles .a. and .b., let there be placed, as before, two round pyramids of equal height, which are similarly called .a. and .b., and two round columns of equal height assigned the same letters .a. and .b. I say, therefore, that the proportion of the two pyramids .a. and .b., and of the two columns .a. and .b., is as that of the two circles .a. and .b. 

This will be manifest concerning the columns if it is first demonstrated concerning the pyramids, for every round column is triple to its pyramid. Concerning the pyramids, however, it will be established by indirect demonstration <note>A proof by contradiction (reductio ad absurdum).</note> in this manner. For, from common knowledge, let there be a proportion of the round pyramid .a. to some solid, just as circle .a. is to circle .b. Let that solid be .c. I say that solid .c. cannot be greater nor less than the round pyramid .b. 

First, let it be less by the quantity of solid .d. Therefore, let a square be inscribed in circle .b. and let there be subtracted from the round pyramid .b. a polygonal pyramid whose base is the square inscribed in circle .b., and from the segments of the pyramids, let there be subtracted pyramids...

...standing upon the triangles of the segments of the circle; and let this be done as many times until the remainder from the **round pyramid** <note>original: "piramide rotunda"—in Euclidean geometry, a cone is often referred to as a "round pyramid."</note> **.b.** is less than the solid **.d.**; then the **polygonal pyramid** <term>polygonal pyramid</term> <note>original: "laterata piramis"—a pyramid with a many-sided, straight-lined base rather than a circular one.</note> subtracted—which the partial subtracted pyramids compose—will be greater than the solid **.c.** Let there be inscribed, therefore, in circle **.a.** a polygon similar to that polygon which is the base of the polygonal pyramid **.b.**, and let a polygonal pyramid be completed upon it by drawing lines from the vertex of the polygonal pyramid **.a.** to the angles of the inscribed polygon. And these two polygonal pyramids, **.a.** and **.b.**, will be of equal height. For this is the point proposed concerning round solids: wherefore the proportion of the polygonal pyramid **.a.** to the polygonal pyramid **.b.** is as its base to the base of the other, namely as polygon **.a.** is to polygon **.b.** For this was demonstrated in the sixth [proposition] of this [book]. But indeed, polygon **.a.** is to polygon **.b.** as circle **.a.** is to circle **.b.**, which is manifest from the first and second [propositions] of this [book]: thus the polygonal pyramid **.a.** is to the polygonal pyramid **.b.** as the round pyramid **.a.** is to the solid **.c.** Wherefore, by **permutation** <note>original: "permutatim"—a logical step in Greek proportion theory where if A:B = C:D, then A:C = B:D.</note>, the polygonal pyramid **.a.** is to the round pyramid **.a.** as the polygonal pyramid **.b.** is to solid **.c.** And since the polygonal pyramid **.b.** is greater than solid **.c.**, it follows that the polygonal pyramid **.a.** is greater than the round pyramid **.a.** But this is impossible: for it is a part of it <note>Euclid is using a "reductio ad absurdum" argument here; a part cannot be greater than the whole.</note>. Therefore, solid **.c.** will not be less than the round pyramid **.b.** 

But if an adversary should pose that it is greater, we shall demonstrate that the same impossibility follows again. For by **inverse proportionality** <note>original: "conuersam proportionalitatem"</note>, the proportion of solid **.c.** to the round pyramid **.a.** will be as circle **.b.** is to circle **.a.** Let there also be the same [proportion] of the round pyramid **.b.** to some solid which is **.d.** Since, therefore, solid **.c.** is greater than the round pyramid **.b.** by hypothesis, it will follow from the 14th [proposition] of the fifth [book] that the round pyramid **.a.** is greater than solid **.d.** Thus the proportion of circle **.b.** to circle **.a.** will be as the round pyramid **.b.** to a certain solid less than the round pyramid **.a.** But this was demonstrated before to be impossible. For thus it follows that a part is greater than its whole. Therefore, solid **.c.** is neither less nor greater than the round pyramid **.b.**, but only equal to it. Thus, from the second part of the seventh [proposition] of the fifth [book], conclude the proposition. But so that what follows might be demonstrated more easily and without confusion, a useful antecedent must be set forth first, which is:

¶ If a certain **surface** <note>In this context, a "plane."</note> should cut a **round column** <term>round column</term> <note>original: "rotundam columnam"—a cylinder.</note> parallel to its base: the two partial solids which are terminated at that cutting surface will be proportional to the segments of the **axis** <note>The central line of the cylinder.</note> of the column.

¶ This is similar to what was proposed in the 25th [proposition] of the eleventh book concerning solid parallelepipeds; nor is this only true concerning round columns, but rather simply concerning all columns, whether they be **polygonal** <note>Prisms.</note> or round. He who firmly holds the argumentation of the first [proposition] of the sixth [book] or the 25th of the eleventh will be able to demonstrate this easily: for here, no differently than there, the proposition must be argued from the definition of **discontinuous proportionality** <note>original: "incontinue proportionalitatis"—proportions involving four distinct terms (A:B as C:D).</note> which was placed in the introduction of the fifth book. However, one should observe that whatever surface cuts a column parallel to its base also cuts it parallel to the surface of its opposite base. For whatever surfaces are parallel to one surface are also parallel to each other, as you have learned from what was said in the sixteenth [proposition] of the eleventh book. Wherefore it is manifest that all round columns whose bases are equal are proportional to their heights. The same is also true of polygonal [columns]. The same is also true of round pyramids and even polygonal ones, which will be established concerning pyramids if it is first proved concerning columns. For every column is triple to its pyramid; the round one from the ninth [proposition] of this [book], and the polygonal one from those things demonstrated above in the eighth [proposition].

# XII

<note>A vertical diagram depicts a cylinder with a cone inscribed inside it. The vertex of the cone is marked 'b' at the top circular face, the midpoint of the cylinder’s axis is marked 'e', and the circular base is marked 'a'.</note>

->Proposition 12<-

**I**f two **round pyramids** <note>original: "piramides rotunde"—the term used by Euclid for cones.</note> or **columns** <note>original: "columne"—the term used for cylinders.</note> are equal, their bases and heights will be **reciprocal** <note>original: "mutue"—inversely proportional. If the volumes are the same, the one with the larger base must have a smaller height.</note>. If, however, their bases and heights are reciprocal, it is necessary that those pyramids or columns be equal. ¶ The height of pyramids is determined by lines descending perpendicularly from the **cones** <note>original: "conis"—here meaning the vertices or tips of the cones</note> to the bases; and of columns from their highest surfaces to the bases. Let there be, therefore, two equal round pyramids **.a.b.** and **.c.d.**, and two equal round columns **.a.b.** and **.c.d.** Let the common bases of both the pyramids and the columns be the two circles **.a.** and **.c.**, and let the common heights of both the pyramids and columns be determined by the lines **.a.b.** and **.c.d.** I say that the proportion of circle **.c.** to circle **.a.** is as the height **.a.b.** is to the height **.c.d.**, and vice versa. Now, if this is proven for the columns, it will be certain for the pyramids, since every round column is triple its pyramid. If, therefore, the two heights **.a.b.** and **.c.d.** are equal, the proposition is established from the previous [proposition]. But if they are unequal, let **.a.b.** be the greater, and let **.a.e.** be taken as equal to **.c.d.**, and let column **.a.b.** be cut by a surface at **.e.** parallel to its base **.a.** From the preceding premise, column **.a.b.** will be to column **.a.e.** as height **.a.b.** is to height **.a.e.** Therefore, from the first part of [Proposition] 7 of the Fifth [Book], column **.c.d.** is to column **.a.e.** as height **.a.b.** is to height **.a.e.** Wherefore, by the second part of [Proposition] 7 of the Fifth, as height **.a.b.** is to height **.c.d.** From the premise, however, column **.c.d.** is to column **.a.e.** as circle **.c.** is to circle **.a.** Thus, by [Proposition] 11 of the Fifth, height **.a.b.** is to height **.c.d.** as base **.c.** is to base **.a.** Thus the first part is established. The second part will be established conversely, with the same arrangement remaining. For let it be that as base **.c.** is to base **.a.**, so is height **.a.b.** to height **.c.d.** I say that the two columns **.a.b.** and **.c.d.** are equal. For from the second part of [Proposition] 7 of the Fifth, height **.a.b.** will be to height **.a.e.** as base **.c.** is to base **.a.** And because from the premise, column **.c.d.** is to column **.a.e.** as base **.c.** is to base **.a.**, and from the preceding premise, column **.a.b.** is to column **.a.e.** as height **.a.b.** is to height **.a.e.**, it follows from [Proposition] 11 of the Fifth that as column **.c.d.** is to column **.a.e.**, so is column **.a.b.** to the same **.a.e.** Therefore, from the first part of [Proposition] 9 of the Fifth, the two columns **.a.b.** and **.c.d.** are equal. Wherefore the second part is also established.

->Proposition 13<-

**W**hen two circles drawn from one center are proposed, to describe within the larger circle a **polygonal** <term>polygonal surface</term> <note>original: "multiangulam superficiem"—literally a "many-angled surface," or a polygon.</note> of equal sides that does not touch the smaller circle at all. ¶ Let there be two circles **.a.b.c.d.** and **.e.f.** drawn from one common center, which is **.g.** I say that within the larger one, which is **.a.b.c.d.**, it is possible to describe one equilateral polygon such that none of its sides touches the smaller circle, which is **.e.f.** For these two circles are divided into quadrants by two diameters intersecting each other perpendicularly at their center, which are **.a.c.** and **.b.d.** Let **.e.f.** be the diameter of the smaller, part of the diameter **.a.c.**, which is the diameter of the larger. Thus, from point **.e.**, let a line be drawn on both sides to the circumference of the larger, perpendicular to the diameter **.e.f.**, which meets the circumference of the larger on this side at point **.b.** and on that side at point **.k.** From the corollary of [Proposition] 15 of the Third [Book], the line **.b.k.** will be **tangent** <note>original: "contingens"—touching at a single point.</note> to the smaller circle. After this, divide the quadrant **.a.b.** of the larger circle into equal parts at point **.l.**, according to the teaching of [Proposition] 29 of the Third. Then again, divide arc **.a.l.** into equal parts at point **.m.** Since you may do this many times, you must necessarily eventually arrive at an arc which is smaller than arc **.a.b.**; let this be **.a.m.** This is necessary because when there are two unequal quantities, if from the larger of them more than half is taken, and again from the remainder half is taken, it is possible for this to be done so many times until finally the remainder is smaller than the smaller of the original quantities, as was demonstrated in the first [proposition] of the Tenth [Book]. Therefore, when by so dividing, the arc becomes as small as you like, smaller than **.a.b.**

<note>A geometric diagram shows two concentric circles with center 'g'. A vertical diameter 'af' and horizontal diameter 'dc' intersect at 'g'. A series of points 'k, n, a, m, l, h, b' are marked on the upper half of the outer circle. Chords connect these points to form part of a polygon. A line segment 'eb' is drawn from 'e' (on the inner circle) to 'b' (on the outer circle), tangent to the inner circle at point 'e'.</note>

attaining such a kind as this arc **.a.m.** Let arc **.a.n.** be taken equal to arc **.a.m.**, and let two lines **.a.m.** and **.n.m.** be drawn. Therefore, since arc **.a.k.** is equal to arc **.a.b.** (which is manifest from the second part of the third [proposition] of the third [book], the fourth of the first, and the 28th of the third), and because arc **.a.n.** is equal to arc **.a.m.**, it will be by common knowledge <note>original: "ex cōmuni scientia"—referring to Euclid's Common Notions or Axioms.</note> that arc **.n.k.** is equal to arc **.m.b.** Therefore, the two lines **.m.n.** and **.k.b.** are parallel; thus the line **.m.n.** will not be able to touch circle **.e.f.**, whereby, much more so, the line **.a.m.** cannot touch it. ¶ Since, therefore, it is established that circle **.a.b.c.d.** is divisible into arcs equal to arc **.a.m.**, and therefore by the 28th of the third [book], it likewise follows that within the circle itself equal chords can be continuously fitted to chord **.a.m.**, forming a polygon within the circle. It is manifest that within the larger circle an equilateral polygon, one side of which is line **.a.m.**, can be inscribed; and since line **.a.m.** does not touch the smaller circle (which is evident from the first part of the 13th of the third and the definition of lines equally distant from the center of a circle), the inscribed polygon touches the smaller circle with none of its sides, which is what was proposed. ¶ But why do you doubt that the two lines **.m.n.** and **.k.b.** are parallel when the two arcs **.n.k.** and **.m.b.** are equal? This has been attained with unshakable truth, because in one circle, if two lines do not intersect each other, and if equal arcs are intercepted between those lines on the circumference, the lines will be parallel. Draw indeed from the center **.g.** the line **.g.p.** perpendicular to the line **.m.n.**, which should intersect line **.b.k.** at point **.q.**; then draw the lines **.g.m.**, **.g.n.**, **.g.k.**, **.g.b.**, and under the two arcs **.n.k.** and **.m.b.** extend two chords which are also called **.n.k.** and **.m.b.** By the 28th of the third [book], these chords **.n.k.** and **.m.b.** will be equal because the arcs are equal; and by the second part of the third [proposition] of the same third [book], line **.n.p.** will be equal to line **.m.p.** Since, therefore, each of the two angles which are **.a.d.p.** is a right angle by the definition of a perpendicular, by the fourth of the first [book], angle **.n.p.g.** will be equal to angle **.p.g.m.** Moreover, by the 8th of the first [book], angle **.k.g.n.** is equal to angle **.b.g.m.** Thus, by the common knowledge <note>Common Notion 2: If equals are added to equals, the wholes are equal.</note> that if you add equals to equals, the totals will be equal, angle **.k.g.q.** will be equal to angle **.q.g.b.** Therefore, by the fourth of the first [book], line **.k.q.** will be equal to line **.q.b.**; wherefore, by the first part of the third [proposition] of the third [book], line **.g.q.** will be perpendicular to line **.k.b.** Therefore, from the first part of the 28th of the first [book], the two lines **.n.m.** and **.k.b.** are parallel, and this is what you were complaining of doubting. ¶ It is also possible to demonstrate this another way: for let line **.n.b.** be drawn, and by the last [proposition] of the sixth [book], angle **.b.m.n.** will be equal to angle **.n.b.k.**, because arc **.b.m.** is equal to arc **.n.k.** Therefore, by the 27th of the first [book], line **.m.n.** will be parallel to line **.b.k.** You may also prove the converse in a reciprocal manner if you wish: for if line **.m.n.** is parallel to line **.b.k.**, arc **.n.k.** will be equal to arc **.m.b.**, for by the first part of the 29th of the first [book], the two angles **.b.m.n.** and **.n.b.k.** will be equal; and thus by the last of the sixth [book], the two arcs **.n.k.** and **.m.b.** will also be equal.

<note>A geometric diagram illustrates a circle with a central point 'g'. A vertical diameter contains points 'p' and 'q'. Two horizontal chords, 'n-m' at the top and 'k-b' at the bottom, are shown. Lines extend from the center 'g' to points 'n', 'm', 'k', and 'b' on the circumference, forming triangles that demonstrate the properties of parallel chords and equal arcs.</note>

## Proposition 14.

**G**iven two spheres having one center, to construct within the larger of them a solid of many faces <note>original: "solidum multarum basium"—this refers to a polyhedron, a three-dimensional shape with flat faces.</note> that does not touch the surface of the smaller sphere. Once this is constructed, if in the smaller sphere or in any other sphere a similar body is understood to be constructed, the ratio of the solid of many faces constructed within the larger sphere to the solid of many faces constructed within the smaller or other sphere will be as the triplicate ratio <note>original: "proportio triplicata"—this is the ratio of the cubes of the diameters (Diameter³ : diameter³).</note> of the diameter of the larger sphere to the diameter of the smaller or the other sphere.

<note>A complex geometric diagram illustrating a sphere containing inscribed circular arcs and polygonal bases. ¶ Let two spheres be given, **.a.b.c.d.** and **.e.f.**, having one and the same center, which is **.g.**; and let the larger of them be sphere **.a.b.c.d.** and the smaller be sphere **.e.f.** We wish to construct within the larger of them a body of many bases <note>A polyhedron, or a solid with many flat faces.</note> such that none of its bases touches the surface of the smaller sphere. Since we wish to do this, let us cut both proposed spheres at the same time by a single plane surface passing through their common center. By the definitions of the sphere and the circle, the common sections of this cutting surface and the surfaces of the proposed spheres will be lines containing circles. Let these, therefore, be two circles, **.a.b.c.d.** and **.e.f.**, whose center is the center of the sphere, which was proposed to be **.g.** We shall then divide <note>original: "quadrabimus," literally "to square," but here meaning to divide into four quadrants using perpendicular diameters.</note> these two circles by two diameters intersecting each other orthogonally at the common center, which shall be **.a.c.** and **.d.b.** Next, following the instructions of the previous [proposition], we shall inscribe within the larger circle an equilateral polygon, none of whose sides touches the smaller circle. For the sake of example, let it suffice to have inscribed an equilateral dodecagon <note>A 12-sided polygon.</note> such that in the quadrant of the larger circle itself, which is **.c.d.**, there are three sides of this dodecagon, which are chords **.d.b.**, **.b.k.**, and **.k.e.** Since these are equal, by the first part of the 27th [proposition] of the third [book], their arcs will also be equal. From then on, from the two points **.b.** and **.k.**, which are the endpoints of the middle chord, we shall extend two diameters, which are **.b.m.** and **.k.l.**, and upon the center **.g.** we shall erect line **.g.n.** perpendicular to the surface of circle **.a.b.c.d.**, which we shall extend until it meets the surface of the larger sphere at point **.n.** Then, let me conceive of four surfaces cutting the proposed spheres: each of which cuts them along line **.g.n.**; but the first of them through line **.g.n.** and diameter **.d.b.**; the second through line **.g.n.** and diameter **.b.m.**; the third through line **.g.n.** and diameter **.k.l.**; and the fourth through line **.g.n.** and diameter **.c.a.** By the definitions of the sphere and the circle, the common sections of these surfaces and the surface of the larger sphere will be lines containing circles. And the inscribed portions, such as between point **.n.** and the four points **.d.**, **.b.**, **.k.**, and **.c.**, will be quadrants of these circles, which quadrants are **.d.n.**, **.b.n.**, **.k.n.**, and **.c.n.** This happens because all the angles which line **.g.n.** contains with each of the diameters drawn in the surface of circle **.a.b.c.d.** are right angles, by the definition of a line perpendicular to a surface; and indeed, right angles at the center are subtended by a quarter circumference, which is clearly apparent from the last [proposition] of the sixth [book].

From the definition of equal circles, it is manifest that each of these four circles is equal to circle **.a.b.c.d.** For the diameter of all of them is the diameter of the larger sphere. Therefore, by the 15th [proposition] of the fifth [book], their quadrants are equal. Wherefore, the five arcs which are **.d.n.**, **.b.n.**, **.k.n.**, **.c.n.**, and **.d.c.** are equal. Therefore, in each of the four quadrants of the erected circles, let subtending chords <note>original: "ypothemisales chorde," referring to chords that subtend an arc, forming the sides of the inscribed body.</note> be fitted, each of which is equal to a chord of the laid-out circle <note>The horizontal base circle.</note>, which are the sides of the polygon inscribed in it; and one of these is chord **.d.b.** Let these chords be: in the first [quadrant], **.d.q.**, **.q.r.**, and **.r.n.**; in the second, **.b.s.**, **.s.t.**, **.t.r.**, and **.r.n.**; in the third, **.k.u.**, **.u.x.**, **.x.z.**, and **.x.n.**; and in the fourth, let them be **.c.o.**, **.o.p.**, and **.p.n.** And let lines be drawn connecting the ends of these subtending chords, which are **.q.f.**, **.f.u.**, **.u.o.** and **.r.t.**, **.t.x.**, **.x.p.** You see, therefore, that within a quarter part of the upper hemisphere of the larger sphere, which quarter part is **.d.n.c.**, a body of 9 bases <note>faces</note> has been inscribed, of which the three that meet at point **.n.** are triangular, while the others are quadrangular. The subtending sides of these quadrangular surfaces are equal, but not parallel. However, the lines drawn between any two circles are parallel to each other and to the chords of the laid-out circle, but they are not equal to each other. <header>BOOK XII</header>

<note>A detailed geometric diagram of a sphere containing complex inscribed arcs and a polygonal frame. A central vertical axis (line n-g) is intersected by several horizontal and curved lines. Points are labeled with lowercase letters: n (at the top), r, p, l, m, q, d, y, b, h, k, f, s, g (at the center), and others along the vertical axis (t, u, x, z). Chords connect various points on the sphere's surface to form an inscribed polyhedral solid, illustrating how a multi-faceted shape can be constructed within the sphere's volume.</note>

If you drop perpendiculars from the ends of the elevated arcs <note>original: "corauctoꝝ"; a medieval Latin term often used in Euclid translations to refer to the arcs raised above the base circle in this specific construction</note> to the surface of the circle lying at the base, it is established that these perpendiculars fall upon the diameters of the circles which the elevated arcs join, as you will easily perceive from what was demonstrated in the 13th proposition of the 11th book. For example: let there be two perpendiculars, **.q.y.** and **.s.f.**, dropped from the two ends of the elevated arc **.q.s.**, falling on the diameters **.d.b.** and **.b.m.**; and let the lines **.q.g.** and **.y.s.** be drawn. From the 4th proposition of the 6th book, there will be two similar triangles, **.q.y.d.** and **.s.f.b.** Therefore, the ratio of the two perpendiculars **.q.y.** and **.s.f.** will be the same as the ratio of the two chords **.q.d.** and **.s.b.** Since the chords are equal, the perpendiculars will also be equal. Moreover, they are parallel to one another by the 6th proposition of the 11th book. Therefore, by the 33rd proposition of the 1st book, the elevated arc-line **.q.s.** is equal and parallel to the line **.y.s.** And because, by the second part of the 2nd proposition of the 6th book, the line **.y.s.** is parallel to the chord **.d.b.** and smaller than it, it follows from the 9th proposition of the 11th book that the elevated arc **.q.s.** is also parallel to the chord **.d.b.** and smaller than it by definition. Since, therefore, the chords which are the sides of the polygon inscribed in the base circle are all equal to chord **.d.b.** and do not touch the smaller sphere, it is necessary that no side of these bases of the inscribed body—whether they be four-sided or three-sided—touches that same smaller sphere, as all these sides are equal to or smaller than those chords.

Furthermore, I say simply that none of these bases can touch the smaller sphere at any of its points. It is manifest from the second part of the 2nd proposition of the 11th book that these bases are entirely contained within a single flat surface, because every straight line drawn through any of their points parallel to the elevated arc is necessarily smaller than the chord of the projected circle. If, therefore, the connections of the other quadrants of the larger sphere—both of the upper hemisphere and the lower—are woven together in a similar fashion with quadrilateral and trilateral surfaces, there will be a body of 72 bases <note>A 72-faced polyhedron</note> inscribed in the larger sphere that does not touch the surface of the smaller sphere at all, just as was proposed. I say, moreover, that if a similar body is established in any other sphere, the ratio of one body to the other will be as the triplicate ratio <note>The "triplicate ratio" is the ratio of the cubes; in modern terms, the volume of the spheres is proportional to the cube of their diameters.</note> of the diameter of one sphere to the diameter of the other. For, by the 72nd [part], the bases of both bodies will be the bases of just as many many-sided pyramids whose vertices are all at the centers of the spheres themselves. You will complete these pyramids if you extend lines to the centers of the spheres from each of the angles of the inscribed bodies (which are the ends of the chords and elevated arcs). Therefore, strive to prove from the definition of similar bodies that all the pyramids of one are similar to their corresponding pyramids in the other. Once this is proven, it follows from the 8th proposition of this book that the ratio of each pyramid of one to its relative in the other is as the triplicate ratio of the semi-diameters <note>radii</note> of the spheres themselves. For the semi-diameters of the spheres are the sides of all these pyramids. And since the ratio of semi-diameters and diameters is the same (by the 15th proposition of the 5th book), you will easily conclude the proposition by the 13th proposition of that same book.

### Proposition 15 <note>In modern editions of Euclid's Elements, this is typically Book XII, Proposition 18.</note>

<note>A circular diagram showing an inscribed hexagon within a circle, with a second smaller concentric circle inside. The diagram is labeled with points a, b, g, and h. Point g is the center of the circles, illustrating the relationship between spheres and their diameters.</note>

<note>A decorative woodcut initial 'O' featuring floral patterns and scrolling vines, typical of the Ratdolt 1482 printing style.</note> **O**f any two spheres, the ratio of one to the other is as the triplicate ratio of its diameter to the diameter of the other.

¶ Let there be two spheres, **.a.b.** and **.c.d.**, whose diameters are **.a.b.** and **.c.d.** I say that their ratio to one another is as the triplicate ratio of their diameters. The demonstration of this is that the ratio of sphere **.a.b.** to a sphere smaller than sphere **.c.d.**, or to one larger, cannot be as the triplicate ratio of diameter **.a.b.** to diameter **.c.d.** Let the ratio of sphere **.a.b.** to a sphere **.e.f.** be as the triplicate ratio of diameter **.a.b.** of sphere **.a.b.** to diameter **.c.d.** I shall demonstrate, therefore, that sphere **.e.f.** can be neither smaller nor larger than sphere **.c.d.** For if an opponent claims it is smaller, I will imagine it to be contained within sphere **.c.d.** and centered around the same center, and I shall inscribe in sphere **.a.b.** [a solid...]

...of the same sphere. It is established, therefore, from the second part of the premise and from the 12th and 11th propositions of the 5th book, that the ratio of sphere **a.b.** to sphere **e.f.** is the same as the ratio of the many-sided body <note>original: "corporis multarum basium"; a polyhedron</note> **a.b.** to the many-sided body **c.d.** For each ratio is as the diameter **a.b.** to the diameter **c.d.** tripled <note>original: "triplicata"; in Euclidean geometry, the "triplicate ratio" refers to the ratio of the cubes of the lengths</note>. This follows from the hypothesis on one hand, and from the second part of the premise on the other. Therefore, by permutation, the ratio of sphere **a.b.** to the many-sided body **a.b.** is the same as the ratio of sphere **e.f.** to the many-sided body **c.d.** Since sphere **a.b.** is greater than the many-sided body **a.b.**, sphere **e.f.** must also be greater than the many-sided body **c.d.** But this is impossible, for the body is a part of it. Therefore, sphere **e.f.** is not smaller than sphere **c.d.** 

If an adversary should say that it is greater, we shall refute him in this way: by converting the proportionality, the ratio of sphere **e.f.** to sphere **a.b.** will be as the diameter **c.d.** to the diameter **a.b.** tripled. Let there be a sphere **g.b.** in the same ratio to sphere **c.d.** Then, from the 14th proposition of the 5th book, sphere **g.b.** will be smaller than sphere **a.b.**, because sphere **c.d.** was posited as smaller than sphere **e.f.** Therefore, the ratio of sphere **c.d.** to some sphere smaller than sphere **a.b.** is as the diameter **c.d.** to the diameter **a.b.** tripled. But this is impossible, for from this it follows that a part would be greater than its whole, as was demonstrated before. Thus, sphere **e.f.** is neither greater nor smaller than sphere **c.d.** Therefore, from the 7th proposition of the 5th book, conclude the proposed theorem, which brings an end to the twelfth book.

### The Twelfth Book ends. The Thirteenth Book begins.

### Proposition 1.

<note>A circular diagram is positioned at the top right, showing a large circle with an inscribed hexagon. Inside the hexagon is a smaller circle tangent to its sides. Points on the vertical axis are labeled 'c' (top) and 'd' (bottom) for the outer circle, and 'e' (top) and 'f' (bottom) for the inner circle. This illustrates the relationship between concentric spheres and inscribed polyhedra.</note>

<note>A simple circle appears below the hexagon diagram, labeled with 'e' at the top and 'f' at the bottom.</note>

When a line has been divided according to a ratio having a mean and two extremes <note>This refers to the "extreme and mean ratio," known today as the Golden Ratio. A line is divided such that the whole line is to the greater segment as the greater segment is to the lesser</note>: if a line equal to half of the whole divided line is added in length to the greater segment, it is necessary that the square of the line composed of these two be five times the square of the half of the divided line.

Let line **a.b.** be divided at point **c.** as taught in the 29th proposition of the 6th book. Let its greater segment be line **b.c.**, to which line **b.d.** is joined directly, which is equal to half of the whole **a.b.** I say that the square of line **c.d.** will be five times the square of line **b.d.** 

Let there be a square of line **b.d.**, which is square **d.e.**, and around this square place a gnomon <note>A gnomon is the L-shaped figure remaining when a smaller square is removed from a larger one</note> according to the size of line **b.c.**, with the diameter **f.b.g.** drawn. Let the surrounding gnomon be **e.g.d.** From the 22nd proposition of the 6th book, the resulting composite surface **b.k.** will be as the square of line **c.d.** I say, therefore, that square **b.k.** is five times square **d.e.** 

Let **e.l.** be the square of the surrounding gnomon, around which another gnomon is placed to the size of line **a.c.**, with the diameter **f.b.** extended to **m.** Let this gnomon be **c.m.l.**, and let lines **c.n.** and **p.l.** be drawn parallel to the opposite sides, intersecting each other on the diameter **f.m.** at point **g.** It is manifest from the 22nd proposition of the 6th book that the composite of this second gnomon and the square **c.l.**—let this square be **a.q.**—is the square of line **a.b.** By the 4th proposition of the 2nd book, this must be four times the square **d.e.**, because line **b.d.** is half of line **a.b.** 

Since, from the first part of the 16th proposition of the 6th book, the surface **a.n.** and therefore, by the 43rd proposition of the 1st book, the surface **m.l.** is equal to the square **c.l.**; for **a.n.** (and thus **m.l.**) results from multiplying **b.a.** by **a.c.**, and **c.l.** results from multiplying **c.b.** by itself. And since from the 1st proposition of the 6th book **a.l.** is double **l.d.**, and therefore equal to **l.d.** and **c.c.** <unclear>c.c.</unclear> taken together from the 43rd of the 1st, it will be by this common notion: if you add equals to equals, the wholes will be equal. Square **a.q.** is equal to gnomon **e.g.d.** Therefore, this gnomon is four times the square **d.e.**, just as square **a.q.** was. Thus, the whole square **b.k.**, since it consists of the single and the quadruple, will be—by common notion—[five times the square].

<header>BOOK XIII</header>

...fivefold to the same, which is what was proposed. The same is also evident from the fourth proposition of the second book, because the square of line **a.b.** is four times the square of line **b.d.** And by the second proposition of the same book, the rectangle formed by **a.b.** and **b.c.** and **a.c.** is equal to the square of **a.b.**; for the rectangle formed by **a.b.** and **b.c.** is equal to twice the rectangle formed by **b.d.** and **b.c.**, which is clear from the first proposition of the second book, since **a.b.** is double **b.d.** Moreover, that which is formed by **a.b.** and **a.c.** is, according to the first part of the 16th proposition of the sixth book, equal to the square of **b.c.** Thus, by common knowledge <note>original: "comem sciam" (communem scientiam); a reference to Common Notions or axioms</note>, the rectangle formed by twice **b.d.** and **b.c.** and the square of **b.c.** is equal to the square of **a.b.**, and therefore it is four times the square of **b.d.** Wherefore, when the square of **b.d.** is added, the whole sum—namely, twice the rectangle of **b.d.** and **b.c.** with the square of **b.c.** and the square of **b.d.**—will be fivefold. And since, by the fourth proposition of the second book, this whole is equal to the square of **c.d.**, it is clear that what we have said is true.

### Proposition 2.

<note>To the left of the main text block, there is a faint, almost transparent geometric diagram. It depicts a circle with an inscribed square and several intersecting lines, including diagonals and a horizontal line through the center. Small letters are barely visible at the vertices and intersections.</note>

If to any line divided into two parts, where the square of the whole is five times the square of one of its portions, a line is added until that same portion and the added line together become double the other portion: then that double line will be divided according to the ratio having a mean and two extremes <term>extreme and mean ratio: Now known as the Golden Ratio; a line is divided such that the ratio of the whole line to the larger segment is the same as the ratio of the larger segment to the smaller</term>, and its greater portion will be the middle line. 

This is the converse of the preceding proposition and will be demonstrated in a twofold way, just as that one was, by a reverse path while keeping the same arrangement of parts. For example: let the square **b.k.** be five times the square of **d.e.**, and let line **a.b.** be double the line **b.d.** I say that line **a.b.** is divided at point **c.** according to the ratio having a mean and two extremes, and its greater portion is the middle line, which is **c.b.** 

It is clear from the 4th proposition of the second book that the square **a.q.** is four times the square **d.e.** Thus, the gnomon <term>gnomon: the L-shaped figure remaining after a smaller square is removed from a larger one</term> **g.d.e.** is equal to the square **a.q.** Therefore, the two supplements **l.d.** and **z.c.e.** taken together are as much as the gnomon **c.m.l.**, and those same supplements taken together are, from the first proposition of the sixth book, as much as **a.l.**, and therefore as much as **c.q.** It follows that **c.q.** is equal to the gnomon **c.m.l.** When the surface **l.n.** is taken away from both, the square **c.l.** will be equal to the surface **a.n.** Since the surface **a.n.** is formed from **a.b.** and **a.c.**, and the square **c.l.** is the square of line **c.b.**, then by the second part of the 16th proposition of the sixth book, the ratio of **a.b.** to **b.c.** is as **b.c.** is to **c.a.** Therefore, from the definition of a line divided according to the ratio having a mean and two extremes placed at the beginning of the sixth book, the proposition is concluded. 

In another way: since the square **c.d.** is by hypothesis five times the square **b.d.**, the square **a.b.** is, by the fourth proposition of the second book, four times the same. But the square **c.d.** is, by the same proposition, equal to the square of **c.b.** and the square of **b.d.** and twice the rectangle of **b.d.** and **c.b.** It follows that the rectangle of twice **b.d.** and **c.b.** with the square of **c.b.** is equal to the square of **a.b.** But twice the rectangle of **b.d.** and **c.b.** is as much as the rectangle of **a.b.** and **b.c.**, because **a.b.** is double **b.d.** Therefore, the rectangle of **a.b.** and **b.c.** with the square of **b.c.** is equal to the square of **a.b.** And since, by the second proposition of the second book, the rectangle of **a.b.** and **b.c.** and **a.c.** is equal to the square of **a.b.**, it follows from common knowledge that the square of line **b.c.** is equal to the rectangle of **a.b.** and **a.c.** Thus, by the second part of the 16th proposition of the sixth book and the definition, the proposition is established.

### Proposition 3.

When a line has been divided according to the ratio having a mean and two extremes, if half of the greater portion is joined directly to the lesser portion: the square of the resulting composite line will be five times the square of that half-portion of the greater segment.

Let line **a.b.** be divided at point **c.** according to the ratio having a mean and two extremes, and let its greater portion be line **c.b.**, which is divided into two equal parts at **d.** I say that the square of line **a.d.** is five times the square of line **c.d.** Let the square of **a.b.** be described, which shall be **a.e.**, in which is drawn...

...of the diameter **b.f.** and the lines **g.c.** and **p.b.**; likewise **k.l.** and **m.n.**, which are parallel to the opposite sides and intersect each other upon the diameter at the two points **p.** and **q.**, and away from the diameter in two other places **r.** and **s.** It is therefore evident from the 22nd proposition of the sixth book, or from the corollary of the fourth proposition of the second book, that all the areas existing within the square **a.e.** which the diameter divides in half are squares. Furthermore, it is established from the 43rd proposition of the first book and the first of the sixth that the four areas which are **a.r.**, **m.p.**, **p.b.**, and **s.f.e.** are equal to one another. Indeed, the last two, **p.b.** and **s.f.e.**, are equal to each other by the first proposition of the sixth book. Since, therefore, from the present hypothesis and the definition of a line divided as proposed <note>original: "secundum quod proponitur divise"</note> by the first part of the 16th proposition of the sixth book, the square **c.l.** is equal to the area **a.g.**, and therefore also to the <term>gnomon<note>A gnomon is the L-shaped figure remaining after a smaller parallelogram is removed from the corner of a larger one.</note></term> **r.f.s.**, because the area **a.r.** is equal to the area **p.b.** And since, from the fourth proposition of the second book, the square **c.l.** is four times the square **r.s.**—which is the same as the square of the line **c.d.**—it follows from common knowledge <note>original: "communi scientia"; refers to self-evident axioms or common notions</note> that the square **m.b.** is five times the square **r.s.**; for it consists of the fourfold gnomon and the square **r.s.** taken together. This is what was proposed.

The same may be shown otherwise: since the line **b.c.** is divided into equal parts at point **d.** and the line **a.c.** is added to it, then from the 6th proposition of the second book, the rectangle formed by **a.b.** and **a.c.** together with the square of the intermediate segment **c.d.** will be equal to the square of **a.d.** But because the rectangle formed by **a.b.** and **a.c.** is equal to the square of **c.b.** by the first part of the 16th proposition of the sixth book, and this square is four times the square of **c.d.**, the truth of what is said is clearly seen.

You may also, if you wish, conclude the antecedent from its consequence by a retrograde process in a twofold manner. For, with the same arrangement remaining, let the square **m.b.** be five times the square **r.s.**; the gnomon **r.f.s.** will then be equal to the square **c.l.**, for each is four times the square **r.s.** But since the area **a.g.** is equal to the aforementioned gnomon, it is necessary that the same area be equal to the aforementioned square. Wherefore, by the second part of the 16th proposition of the sixth book and the definition, the line **a.b.** is divided at point **c.** according to the <term>extreme and mean ratio<note>The Golden Ratio, where the whole line is to the larger segment as the larger segment is to the smaller one.</note></term>, and its greater segment is the line **c.d.**

The same is shown another way: since by hypothesis the square of line **a.d.** is five times the square of line **c.d.**, and from the 6th proposition of the second book, that same square is equal to the rectangle formed by **a.b.** and **a.c.** together with the square of **c.d.**, it follows that the rectangle of **a.b.** and **a.c.** with the square of **c.d.** is five times that same square of **c.d.** Therefore, when the square is taken away, the remainder—namely, the rectangle of **a.b.** and **a.c.**—will be four times the square. And since, by the fourth proposition of the second book, the square of line **c.b.** is also four times the same, it is necessary that the rectangle of **a.b.** and **a.c.** be equal to the square of **c.b.** Wherefore, again by the second part of the 16th proposition of the sixth book and the definition, the line **a.b.** is divided according to the extreme and mean ratio at point **c.**, and its greater segment is the line **c.b.**

In the same way also, if from the greater segment of any line divided according to the aforesaid proportion <note>The "extreme and mean ratio" or Golden Ratio.</note>, a length equal to the smaller segment is subtracted: the greater segment itself will be divided according to that same proportion, and its own greater segment will be the line that was subtracted. For example: Let line **a.b.** be divided at point **c.** as proposed, and let the greater segment be **a.c.**, from which **c.d.** is subtracted equal to **c.b.** I say that **a.c.** is divided according to the same proportion at point **d.**, and that its greater segment is the line **d.c.** For since, by definition, **b.a.** is to **a.c.** as **a.c.** is to **c.b.**; and from the seventh proposition of the fifth book, **a.c.** is to **c.b.** as **a.c.** is to **c.d.**; it will be, from the eleventh of the same book, **b.a.** to **a.c.** as **a.c.** to **c.d.** Therefore, by the 19th proposition of the fifth book, it follows that the ratio is as the remainder **c.b.** is to the remainder **d.a.** But from the seventh of the same book, **c.b.** is to **d.a.** as **a.c.** is to **c.d.**, so that **a.c.** is to **c.d.** as **c.d.** is to **d.a.** Therefore, by the definition, what we have stated is established. Thus, neither the addition which the author proposes, nor the subtraction which we propose from the opposite—no matter how far either may be extended—departs from the specific property of the division of the original line.

If any line is divided according to a proportion having a mean and two extremes, the squares produced from both the whole line and the smaller segment, when taken together, are triple the square described from the larger segment.
¶ Let line **a.b.** be divided at point **c.** by the oft-mentioned proportion, and let its greater segment be line **c.b.** I say that the squares of the two lines **a.b.** and **c.a.**, when taken together, are triple the square of line **c.b.** For these two squares taken together are, by the seventh proposition of the second book, equal to the square of **c.b.** plus double the rectangle formed by **a.b.** and **a.c.** Likewise, because the rectangle formed by **a.b.** and **a.c.** is equal to the square of **c.b.** (by the definition and the first part of the 16th proposition of the sixth book), the proposition is made manifest.

When any rational line is divided according to a proportion having a mean and two extremes, it is necessary that both segments be an <term>apotome<note>The original Latin uses "residuum." For let its greater segment be **a.c.**, to which is added the line **a.d.** in a straight line, equal to half of the whole line **a.b.** Therefore, **d.a.** will also be rational, according to the sixth proposition of the tenth book and the definition. Wherefore, by the 68th proposition of the tenth book, line **a.c.** is an apotome, since the two lines **c.d.** and **d.a.** are both rational and commensurable only in power. Furthermore, if a line is so divided as proposed and the greater segment is rational, the smaller segment will be an apotome. For example: let **a.b.** be divided at **c.** as before according to the said proportion, and let the greater segment **a.c.** be rational. Let it be divided into two equal parts at **d.** By the third proposition of this book, the square of **d.b.** will be five times the square of **d.c.** But because **d.c.** is rational (since it is half of **a.c.**), it follows that the two lines **d.b.** and **d.c.** are rational and commensurable only in power; wherefore, as before, line **c.b.** is an apotome. <header>XIII</header>

it is still necessary that each of its segments be a remainder <note>original: *residuum*. In Euclidean geometry, this refers to an "apotome," a specific type of irrational line formed by subtracting a rational line from another rational line that is only commensurable with it in power.</note>. For let **a.b.** be rational in power only <term>rational in power only: lines whose squares are commensurable with a standard unit, even if the lengths themselves are not.</term>, divided as proposed at point **c.**, and let some line rational in length be taken, which is **d.e.**, which is also divided at **f.** according to the aforesaid proportion. It is manifest, therefore, from the second proposition of the 14th book <note>This refers to the "supplementary" book of the Elements often attributed to Hypsicles of Alexandria.</note>—which is strengthened by an unshakable demonstration without the help of any of the things that follow—that the proportion of **a.b.** to **d.e.** is as **a.c.** to **d.f.** and as **c.b.** to **f.e.** Since, therefore, **a.b.** is commensurable with **d.e.** in power, it follows from the first part of the 10th proposition of the tenth book that **a.c.** is commensurable with **d.f.** and **c.b.** with **f.e.** in power. And because each segment of line **d.e.** is a remainder, as is clear from the preceding, it follows from the 95th proposition of the tenth book that each segment of line **a.b.** is also a remainder, but not of the same species, as was demonstrated there. Wherefore it is established that all lines—whether rational in length or in power only—when divided according to the ratio having a mean and two extremes <note>The Golden Ratio.</note>, both segments are remainders. And note that the first part of the present demonstration, by which it is demonstrated that the greater segment of a line divided according to the ratio having a mean and two extremes is a remainder if the whole line is rational, proceeds from sufficient grounds whether the whole line is set as rational in length or in power only. But the second part, by which this is demonstrated concerning the smaller segment—that it too is a remainder if the whole is rational—does not proceed from sufficient grounds unless the whole is rational in length. However, the third part, by which it is proved that the smaller segment is a remainder, proceeds sufficiently whether the greater segment is rational in length or in power only. Therefore, to conclude that the greater segment of a line divided in the aforesaid way is a remainder, it suffices to set the whole divided line as rational in power only; but to conclude this also for the smaller segment by means of the greater, it suffices to set the greater segment as rational in power only. But to conclude this concerning the smaller segment directly, it is necessary to set the whole line as rational in length, or one must use the second proposition of the 14th book, as has been said.

If any pentagon having three equal angles is equilateral, it is proved that the same pentagon is also equiangular.
Let pentagon **a.b.c.d.e.** be equilateral, and let any three of its angles—whether taken consecutively or non-consecutively—be equal to one another. Let angles **a**, **c**, and **d** be those three which are set as equal to one another; I say the whole pentagon is equiangular. Let these angles be subtended by chords **b.e.**, **b.d.**, and **e.c.**, and let the whole pentagon be divided into a triangle and a quadrilateral whose two diagonals are the chords of the two nearest equal angles, cutting each other inside the quadrilateral itself at point **f.** By the fourth proposition of the first book <note>The Side-Angle-Side theorem.</note>, base **b.e.** will be equal to base **b.d.**, and angle **a.e.b.** will be equal to angle **c.d.b.** And since, by the fifth of the first book <note>The property that angles opposite equal sides in an isosceles triangle are equal.</note>, angle **b.e.d.** is equal to angle **b.d.e.** because the two sides **b.e.** and **b.d.** are equal, it will be from common knowledge <note>The "common notions" or axioms of Euclid.</note> that the total angle **e** is equal to the total angle **d**. Similarly, you will prove total angle **b** to be equal to total angle **c**; for by the fourth of the first, base **b.e.** is equal to base **e.c.**, and angle **a.b.e.** is equal to angle **d.c.e.** By the fifth of the same first book, angle **e.b.c.** is equal to angle **e.c.b.**; therefore, from common knowledge, total angle **b** is equal to total angle **c**. If, likewise, three angles **b**, **c**, and **d** taken consecutively are equal, the pentagon will also be equiangular: for from the 4th of the first, base **b.d.** is equal to base **c.e.**, and angle **c.d.b.** to angle **d.c.e.**, and angle **b.d.c.** to angle **e.c.d.** Wherefore, by the sixth of the first, the two lines **c.f.** and **f.d.** will be equal, since the two angles of triangle **f.e.d.** <note>The text likely refers to the triangle formed at the intersection; context suggests the small triangle at the base.</note> which are at the base **c.d.** are equal. Therefore, from this common knowledge, line **f.b.** will be equal to line **f.c.**, for the whole **b.d.** was equal to the whole **c.e.**, and therefore by the fifth of the first, angle **f.b.e.** will be equal to angle **f.e.b.** By the same, however, is angle **a.b.e.**...

...is equal to angle $a.e.b.$ Therefore, by common notion <note>original: *cōem ſciam* (communem scientiam). In Euclid, these are the "Axioms" or "Common Notions," such as "if equals be added to equals, the wholes are equal."</note>, the whole angle $b.$ is equal to the whole angle $e.$ For the three partial angles composing the one are equal to the three partial angles composing the other, each being equal to its relative part. ¶ It is manifest, therefore, that the three angles $e. b. c.$ not taken continuously in the proposed pentagon are equal. ### Proposition .8.

<margin>
<note>A geometric diagram consisting of a circle with an inscribed equilateral triangle labeled a, b, and c. Radial lines connect the center d to vertices b and c. A chord connects point b to point e.</note>
</margin>

The square described on the side of any equilateral triangle is triple the square on the radius <note>original: *dimidij diametri*, literally "half the diameter."</note> of the circle by which the triangle itself is circumscribed. ¶ Let there be an equilateral triangle $a.b.c.$ circumscribed by a circle around center $d,$ just as the fifth [proposition] of the fourth book teaches, and let the diameter $a.d.e$ be drawn in it. I say, therefore, that the square of line $a.b.$ is triple the square of the semi-diameter <term>semi-diameter: the radius of a circle, extending from the center to the circumference.</term> $a.d.$ For let two lines $b.d.$ and $d.c.$ be drawn, and let the chord $b.e.$ be subtended to arc $b.c.$ By the eighth [proposition] of the first [book], angle $b.a.d.$ will be equal to angle $c.a.d.$ wherefore, by the last [proposition] of the sixth [book], arc $b.e.$ is equal to arc $e.c.$ And because from the 27th [proposition] of the third [book], the three arcs $a.b, b.c,$ and $c.a$ are equal to one another because their chords, which are the sides of the triangle <note>original: *trigoni*</note>, are equal by hypothesis, arc $b.e.$ will be a sixth part of the circumference. Therefore, chord $b.e.$ will be the side of an equilateral hexagon inscribed in the same circle. Wherefore, by the corollary to the 15th [proposition] of the fourth [book], line $b.e.$ is equal to the semi-diameter $a.d.$ ¶ It is manifest, moreover, from the first part of the 30th [proposition] of the third [book] that angle $a.b.e.$ is a right angle. Therefore, the square of line $a.e.$ is equal to the squares of the two lines $a.b.$ and $b.e.$ <note>The OCR text reads *b.c.*, but the geometric proof requires line *b.e.*, which represents the side of the hexagon.</note> taken together, by the penultimate [proposition] of the first [book] <note>This refers to Proposition I.47, the Pythagorean Theorem.</note>. But indeed, the square of $a.e.$ is quadruple the square of $b.e.$ by the fourth [proposition] of the second [book], since line $a.e.$ is double $b.e.$ It remains, therefore, that the square of $a.b.$ is triple the square of $b.e.,$ and therefore triple the square of $a.d.,$ which is what was proposed. Let it not be hidden from us that line $b.c.,$ which is the side of the triangle, divides the semi-diameter $d.e.$ into equal parts. Let the point of division be $f.$ It stands, therefore, by the fourth [proposition] of the first [book] that $b.f.$ is equal to $f.c.,$ and therefore by the first part of the third [proposition] of the third [book], all angles at $f.$ are right angles. Wherefore, by the penultimate [proposition] of the first [book], the square of $b.d.$ is equal to the squares of the two lines $d.f.$ and $f.b.$ Truly, the square of $b.e.$ is equal to the squares of the two lines which are $b.f.$ and $f.e.$ And because $b.d.$ is equal to $b.e.,$ it will be from a common notion that the two squares of the two lines $b.f.$ and $f.d.$ taken together are equal to the two squares of the two lines $b.f.$ and $f.e.$ taken together. Having subtracted the square of $b.f.$ from both sides, it will be from a common notion that the remaining square of $f.d.$ is equal to the remaining square of $f.e.$ Wherefore line $f.d.$ is equal to line $f.e.$ by this common notion: those whose squares are equal are themselves equal. From this it is manifest that the perpendicular drawn from the center of a circle to the side of an equilateral triangle inscribed in it is equal to half the line drawn from the center of the same circle to its circumference.

Angle $c.$ will be equal to angle $b.d.c.$ from the 5th proposition of the first book <note>original: "ex .5. pꝛimi" — referring to the 'Pons Asinorum', that the base angles of an isosceles triangle are equal.</note>, because line $c.b.$ is equal to line $b.d.$ from the 15th corollary of the fourth book. Also, angle $d.b.c.$ is equal to angle $c.$ from the 5th of the first; therefore, from the 32nd of the first, angle $a.d.b.$ will be double angle $d.b.c.$ And since the same angle $d.b.c.$ is double angle $e.$, it follows that angle $a.d.b.$ is quadruple angle $e.$ For it is a common notion <note>original: "ex cōi ſcia" (ex communi scientia) — an axiom or self-evident truth in Euclidean geometry.</note> that whatever is double a double is quadruple. And since this same angle $a.d.b.$ is quadruple angle $b.d.c.$ from the last proposition of the sixth book, because arc $a.b.$ is quadruple arc $b.c.$, it is necessary from the common notion that angle $e.$ be equal to angle $b.d.c.$ If, therefore, two triangles are understood, the total triangle $d.e.c.$ and the partial triangle $b.d.c.$, since the total angle $e.$ is equal to the partial angle $b.d.c.$ and angle $c.$ is common to both, it is necessary from the 32nd of the first that they be equiangular. Therefore, by the 4th of the sixth, the proportion of the two sides $e.c.$ and $c.d.$ containing angle $c.$ in the total triangle is as the two sides $d.c.$ and $c.b.$ containing the same angle in the partial triangle. Because by proportion $e.c.$ to $d.c.$ is as $d.c.$ to $c.b.$ from the second part of the 7th of the fifth, and $d.c.$ to $c.b.$ is as $e.b.$ to the same from the first part of the same, it follows from the 11th of the fifth that the proportion of $e.c.$ to $e.b.$ is as $e.b.$ to $b.c.$ Therefore, by the division, conclude the proposed: that line $e.c.$ is divided according to a <term>mean and two extremes ratio: now commonly known as the Golden Ratio, where the ratio of the whole line to the larger segment is the same as the larger segment to the smaller.</term> and its greater portion is the side of the hexagon, which is what we were required to demonstrate. ¶ It also follows to demonstrate the converse, which is easily done by the reverse path; for Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century astronomer.</note> assumes this in the 9th chapter of the first book of the *Almagest* <note>original: "almageſti" — the definitive astronomical manual of the Middle Ages.</note> to demonstrate the quantity of the chords of the arcs of a circle.

<margin>
<note>A geometric diagram of a circle containing construction lines for geometric proofs, including vertical and horizontal diameters and several chords in different quadrants, likely related to the construction of regular polygons like the hexagon or decagon.</note>
</margin>

¶ I say, therefore, that if any line is divided according to a proportion having a mean and two extremes, and its greater portion is the side of a hexagon of some circle, its smaller portion will be the side of a decagon of the same circle. But indeed, if the smaller is the side of a decagon, the greater will be the side of a hexagon. For let the previous arrangement remain, with line $e.c.$ divided at point $b.$ according to the aforesaid proportion, and let its greater portion be $e.b.$ I say that for whatever circle line $e.b.$ is the side of the hexagon, line $b.c.$ is the side of the decagon of the same; and for whatever circle line $b.c.$ is the side of the decagon, line $e.b.$ is the side of the hexagon.

And since angle $a.d.b.$ is quadruple angle $e.$ from the 32nd of the first applied twice, and the 5th of the same applied twice, it follows that the same angle $a.d.b.$ is quadruple angle $b.d.c.$ Therefore, from the last of the sixth, arc $a.b.$ is quadruple arc $b.c.$ Therefore, line $b.c.$ is the side of the decagon inscribed in $a.b.c.$ But if line $b.c.$ were the side of the decagon of circle $a.b.c.$, $e.b.$ would be the side of the hexagon of the same. For let $e.b.$ be the side of the hexagon of circle $f.$, and from the aforesaid, $b.c.$ will be the side of the decagon of the same. Let it be understood, therefore, that equilateral decagons are inscribed in the two circles $a.b.c.$ and $f.$, all of whose sides will be equal to line $b.c.$ And because every equilateral figure inscribed in a circle is equiangular, as proved in the 15th of the fourth book, it follows that both decagons are equiangular. Therefore, they are similar by the definition of similar surfaces. ## ¶ Proposition .10.

<margin>
<note>A geometric diagram displays a circle with a horizontal diameter labeled $a-d-c$, where $d$ is the center. A vertical radius $d-e$ extends to the top.
