**The square of the side of an equilateral pentagon is equal to the square of the side of an equilateral hexagon plus the square of the side of an equilateral decagon, provided they are both inscribed in the same circle.** <note>original: "Omne latus pentagoni equilateri tanto potentius ē latere exagoni equilateri quantū potest latus decagoni..." — The term "power" (potentius/potest) refers to the area of the square built upon that line segment.</note>

Let there be a circle $a.b.c.$ with center $d$ and diameter $a.d.c.$, and let an equilateral pentagon $a.b.e.f.g.$ be inscribed in it. From the center $d$, let a perpendicular be drawn to the side $a.b$, and let it be extended until it meets the circumference at point $b$ <note>The letter 'b' is reused for different points in the diagram; here it refers to a point on the arc.</note>. Let two chords $a.b$ and $b.b$ be drawn; these will be equal to each other according to the second part of the 3rd proposition of the third book and the 4th of the first. Therefore, the two arcs $a.b$ and $b.b$ are also equal to each other according to the 27th of the third book. Thus, each of the two chords $a.b$ and $b.b$ is the side of an equilateral decagon inscribed in the proposed circle.

I say, therefore, that the square of line $a.b.$, which is the side of the pentagon, is equal to the two squares of the two lines $b.d.$ and $a.b.$ taken together, of which the first is equal to the side of the hexagon (from the conclusion of the 15th of the fourth) and the second is the side of the decagon. Let there be drawn from the center $d$ a perpendicular to the line $a.b.$ (the side of the decagon) which is extended to the circumference; let this be $d.k.$, which intersects line $a.b.$ (the side of the pentagon) at point $l$. Let line $b.l.$ be drawn. It is established from the second part of the third book and the 4th of the first and the 27th of the third that the line $d.k.$, being perpendicular to the chord $a.b.$, divides both the chord and the arc into two equal parts. Therefore, arc $a.k.$ is equal to arc $k.b.$; wherefore, by the last proposition of the sixth book, angle $a.d.l.$ is equal to angle $l.d.b.$

Thus, by the 4th of the first, the base $a.l.$ is equal to the base $l.b.$ Then, by the 5th of the first, angle $l.a.b.$ is equal to angle $l.b.a.$ And since also, by the same proposition, angle $b.a.b.$ is equal to angle $b.b.a.$, it follows that angle $l.b.a.$ is equal to angle $b.b.a.$ Therefore, by the 32nd of the first, the two triangles $b.a.b.$ and $a.b.l.$ are **equiangular** <note>meaning they are 'similar' triangles, having the same angles even if they are different sizes</note>: for the angle $b.$ of the larger is equal to the angle $b.$ of the smaller, and angle $a.$ is common to both.

Thus, by the 4th of the sixth, the proportion of $b.a.$ to $a.b.$ is as $a.b.$ to $l.a.$ Wherefore, by the first part of the 16th of the sixth, the product of $b.a.$ and $a.l.$ is equal to the square of line $a.b.$, which is the side of the decagon. Since the semicircle $a.c.e.$ is equal to the semicircle $a.f.e.$ and arc $a.e.$ is equal to arc $a.f.$, the remaining arc $e.c.$ will be equal to the remaining arc $f.c.$ Therefore, arc $e.c.$ is half of arc $e.f.$, and thus equal to arc $a.b.$ and double the arc $b.k.$ And because arc $e.b.$ is double the arc $b.b.$, the whole arc $e.c.b.$ will be double the whole arc $b.b.k.$ according to the 13th of the fifth.

Consequently, by the last of the sixth, angle $c.d.b.$ is double the angle $b.d.l.$ And since angle $c.d.b.$ is also double the angle $b.a.d.$ (by the 32nd and 5th of the first, for the two sides $d.a.$ and $d.b.$ are equal), angle $b.d.l.$ will be equal to angle $b.a.d.$ Thus, by the 32nd of the first, triangle $b.d.l.$ will be equiangular to triangle $b.a.d.$ For angle $d.$ of the smaller is equal to angle $a.$ of the larger, and angle $b.$ is common to both. Therefore, by the 4th of the sixth, the proportion of $a.b.$ to $b.d.$ is as $b.d.$ to $l.b.$ Wherefore...

## ¶ Proposition .11.

<margin>
<note>A geometric diagram showing a circle with a horizontal diameter and multiple intersecting chords and radii, labeled with letters including a, b, c, d, e, f, k, l. This construction relates to the proportions within an inscribed pentagon.</note>
<note>A geometric diagram of a circle with an inscribed pentagon labeled b, a, e, d, c clockwise from the top left. Two chords, ac and be, intersect at a point labeled f in the center of the pentagon.</note>
</margin>

If from two adjacent angles of an equilateral pentagon described within a circle, two straight lines are subtended from the ends of its sides, each will cut the other according to the **extreme and mean ratio** <note>This is the Golden Ratio. In a regular pentagon, the diagonals intersect such that the ratio of the whole diagonal to the larger segment is the same as the ratio of the larger segment to the smaller segment.</note>, and the greater portion of it will be equal to the side of the pentagon itself.

Let there be an equilateral pentagon $a.b.c.d.e.$ inscribed in a circle marked with the same letters, and let two of its adjacent angles, which are $a$ and $b$, be subtended by two straight lines $a.c.$ and $b.e.$, intersecting each other at point $f$. I say, therefore, that each of these is divided at point $f$ according to the **extreme and mean ratio**, and that the greater portion of each is equal to the side of the pentagon. For it is clear from the 27th proposition of the third book that the five arcs of the circle circumscribing the proposed pentagon (of which the sides of the pentagon are chords) are equal to one another. Therefore, from the last proposition of the sixth book, the four angles $a.e.b.$, $a.b.e.$, $b.a.c.$, and $b.c.a.$ are equal to one another. For the arcs $a.b.$, $a.e.$, and $b.c.$ are equal to one another; and since the arc $c.d.e.$ is double the arc $b.e.$, from the last proposition of the sixth book, the angle $c.a.e.$ will also be double the angle $c.a.b.$ But indeed, from the 32nd proposition of the first book, angle $a.f.e.$ is double the angle $f.a.b.$ Therefore, angle $a.f.e.$ is equal to angle $f.a.e.$, wherefore, by the sixth proposition of the first book, line $a.e.$ is equal to line $f.e.$ Furthermore, the two triangles $a.b.e.$ and $a.f.b.$ are equiangular <note>Similar triangles.</note> by what has been said and by the 32nd proposition of the first book: for angle $e$ of the larger triangle is equal to angle $a$ of the smaller, and angle $b$ is common to both. Therefore, by the fourth proposition of the sixth book, the ratio of $e.b.$ to $b.a.$ is as $b.a.$ is to $f.b.$ And since $e.f.$ is equal to $a.b.$ (because it was proven equal to $a.e.$), it follows from the seventh proposition of the fifth book that the ratio of $b.e.$ to $e.f.$ is as $e.f.$ is to $f.b.$ Wherefore, by definition, the line $e.b.$ is divided according to the **extreme and mean ratio**, and its greater portion is equal to the side of the pentagon itself. If this is true of line $e.b.$, it will also be true of line $a.c.$ from the seventh and fifth propositions of the fifth book and the definition; for the whole $b.e.$ is equal to the whole $a.c.$ from the fourth proposition of the first book, and their portions are equal to one another from the sixth proposition of the first book and common knowledge: for the portions $a.f.$ and $b.f.$ are equal from the sixth proposition of the first book. Therefore, the remaining parts $f.e.$ and $f.c.$ will be equal to each other by subtraction <note>original: "ex conceptione" — a reference to Common Notions, specifically "If equals be subtracted from equals, the remainders are equal."</note>; or, if you prefer, you can demonstrate the proposition regarding line $a.c.$ more easily by proceeding with it just as was done before with line $e.b.$

is rational in length: therefore, by the last part of the 7th [proposition] of the tenth [book], the line $m.k.$ is rational in power only <note>original: "rationalis in potentia tantum"; this means the square of the line is a rational area, but the line's length cannot be expressed as a simple fraction.</note>; and because line $b.m.$ is more powerful than line $m.k.$ by the square of a line incommensurable to it in length—as will be proven in what follows—the line $b.k.$ will be a **fourth residual** <note>A "residual" (or apotome) is a specific type of irrational line formed by subtracting one rational line from another. A "fourth residual" is a specific sub-type defined in Book X.</note> by the definition of a fourth residual.

That which we assumed for proof is clear as follows: let the number $r$ be five times the number $f$, and let $t$ and $f$ together be as much as $r$ (as if $r$ were five, $f$ were one, and $t$ were four); and let line $b.m.$ be more powerful than line $m.k.$ by the square of line $x$. Since, therefore, the square of line $b.m.$ is to the square of line $m.k.$ as the number $r$ is to the number $f$, it will be—by converse proportionality—that the square of line $b.m.$ is to the square of line $x$ as the number $r$ is to the number $t$. Therefore, by the last part of the 7th [proposition] of the tenth [book], line $x$ is incommensurable in length to line $b.m.$

There is no doubt, then, that $b.k.$ is a fourth residual. It is truly manifest from the 34th [proposition] of the third [book] that the rectangle formed by $b.k.$ and $k.g.$ is equal to that formed by $a.k.$ and $k.c.$; therefore, it is also equal to the square of $k.c.$, because $a.k.$ is equal to $k.c.$ Thus, when the square of $b.k.$ is added to both, it will be—from the penultimate [proposition] of the first [book] <note>Proposition I.47, the Pythagorean Theorem.</note>—that the rectangle formed by $b.k.$ and itself plus $k.g.$ is equal to the square of $b.c.$

And because, from the first [proposition] of the second [book], the area formed by $b.k.$ with itself and with $k.g.$ is equal to that formed by $b.k.$ and $g.b.$, the line $b.c.$ will be the side of the square <note>original: "latus tetragonicū"</note> of the surface contained by the two lines $g.b.$ and $k.b.$ Since the line $g.b.$ is rational and the line $b.k.$ is a fourth residual—and since a line whose square is equal to an area contained by a rational line and a fourth residual is a **minor** line <note>A "minor line" is an irrational line defined in Book X, Prop 76. Euclid is classifying the specific type of irrationality found in the side of a pentagon.</note>, as is established from the 89th [proposition] of the tenth book—it is necessary that line $b.c.$, which is the side of the equilateral pentagon inscribed in the proposed circle, be a **minor** line, which was to be demonstrated from the beginning.

In this way, therefore, it follows that the side of an equilateral pentagon inscribed in a circle is a minor line if the diameter of the circle in which it is inscribed is rational in length. But even if the diameter of the circle is rational in power only, it is still necessary that the side of the equilateral pentagon inscribed in it be a minor line.

For let line $a$ be rational in power only, upon which a circle is described, and let an equilateral pentagon be inscribed in that circle, one side of which is $b.c.$; let the pentagon and circle be called $a$. I say that line $b.c.$ is a minor line. For let some line $d$ be taken which is rational in length, and let a circle be drawn upon it in which an equilateral pentagon is inscribed, and let one of its sides be line $e.f.$, and let the pentagon and circle be called $d$. It is established, therefore, from this 12th [proposition] that $e.f.$ is a minor line since the diameter $d$ is rational in length.

Since truly the proportion of pentagon $a$ to pentagon $d$ is as the square of line $b.c.$ to the square of line $e.f.—for each is, from the second part of the 15th [proposition] of the sixth [book], as line $b.c.$ to line $e.f.$ doubled—the ratio of pentagon $a$ to pentagon $d$ is as the square of $b.c.$ to the square of line $e.f.$, and [as] the square of diameter $a$ to the square of diameter $d$ (from the first [proposition] of the 12th [book]). By the 11th [proposition] of the fifth [book], the square of line $c.b.$ will be to the square of line $e.f.$ as the square of diameter $a$ to the square of diameter $d$. Since the squares of the two diameters $a$ and $d$ are commensurable <note>original: "cōicantia"; meaning they share a common measure.</note>—because both are rational by hypothesis—the squares of the two lines $b.c.$ and $e.f.$ will also be commensurable by the first part of the 10th [proposition] of the tenth [book]. Therefore, line $b.c.$ is commensurable in power with line $e.f.$ And because line $e.f.$ is a minor line, it follows from the 100th [proposition] of the tenth [book] that $b.c.$ is also a minor line, which is what was proposed. Whether, therefore, the diameter of some circle be rational in length or in power only, it is necessary that the side of the equilateral pentagon inscribed in it be a **minor** line.

In this context, it refers to the ratio between the square of the diameter and the square of the side.</note> in power to the side of the same pyramid.

# BOOK XIII

<note>A geometric diagram showing a horizontal line segment divided into parts b, c, and a. From point c, a perpendicular line rises to point d, which is then connected to points b and a, forming a right-angled triangle d-c-a within a larger triangular projection.</note>

...b, d, and d, a. Afterward, let a circle f, g, b be made upon center e, whose radius <note>original: "semidiameter"</note> is equal to line c, d. In this circle, according to the second [proposition] of the fourth book, let an equilateral triangle f, g, b be inscribed; from the center e, let lines e, f, e, g, and e, b be drawn to its angles. Then, upon center e, let a line e, k be erected according to what the 12th [proposition] of the eleventh book <note>The OCR notes "tenth or eleventh"; in standard editions of Euclid, the construction of a perpendicular to a plane is in Book XI.</note> teaches. Let this line e, k be set equal to line a, c and perpendicular to the surface of circle f, g, b. From point k, let the hypotenuses <note>The slanted edges of the pyramid.</note> k, f, k, g, and k, b be let down. Thus, a pyramid of four triangular and equilateral bases will be completed. I assert that this pyramid is circumscribable by the assigned sphere, and I also assert that the square of the diameter of the proposed sphere is sesquialter <note>original: "sesquialterum"; a ratio of 3:2, or one-and-a-half times.</note> to the square of the side of the constructed pyramid.

It is established from the first part of the corollary to the 8th [proposition] of the sixth book that line c, d is the mean proportional <note>original: "medio loco proportionalis"; a value between two others such that a:b = b:c.</note> between a, c and c, b. Therefore, from the corollary of the 17th [proposition] of the same book, the square of line a, c is to the square of line c, d as line a, c is to c, b. Therefore, when combined, the square of a, c and the square of c, d [together] are to the square of c, d as line a, b is to b, c. Consequently, by the penultimate [proposition] of the first book <note>A reference to the Pythagorean Theorem (I.47).</note>, the square of a, d is to the square of c, d as line a, b is to b, c. Since line a, b is triple to b, c—and a, c was also double to it—the square of a, d will also be triple to the square of d, c. However, from the 8th [proposition] of this book, the square of f, g is triple to the square of e, f. Since, by our hypothesis, d, c is equal to e, f, it follows from common knowledge <note>original: "ex communi scientia"; referring to the Axioms or Common Notions of Euclid.</note> that a, d is equal to f, g.

And because, by the definition of a line perpendicular to a surface, the line e, k forms right angles with each of the lines e, f, e, g, and e, b (each of which is equal to line c, d), and because e, k itself is equal to line a, c, and angle c is a right angle: then by the fourth [proposition] of the first book, each of the three lines k, f, k, g, and k, b is equal to line a, d. It is manifest, therefore, that the constructed pyramid consists of four equilateral triangular bases.

That this pyramid can be circumscribed by the assigned sphere, understand as follows: imagine line e, l is added in a straight line to e, k, and let e, l be equal to line c, b, so that the whole line k, l is equal to a, b (which is the diameter of the assigned sphere). Now imagine this line e, l to be beneath the circle f, g, b and also perpendicular to its surface from the lower side, just as e, k is from the upper side. Each of the three lines e, f, e, g, e, b—and indeed any radius of the circle f, g, b—will be the mean proportional between k, e and e, l, just as d, c is between a, c and c, b; for these are equal to those, each to its relative part.

If, therefore, a semicircle is described upon line k, l and rotated until it returns to the place from which it began to move, then by the definition of equal spheres, the sphere described by the motion of this semicircle will be equal to the assigned sphere. For spheres are equal if their diameters are equal, just as was said of circles at the beginning of the third book. It is necessary for this semicircle to pass through the three points f, g, and b, which are the solid angles of the constructed pyramid. Similarly, I say that if this semicircle described upon line k, l is rotated until it returns to its starting point, it will touch the circle f, g, b at all points of its circumference.

This is proven by this ancient truth: if a straight line stands perpendicularly upon a straight line, and is placed as a mean proportional between the parts of the line upon which it stands or around which it stands, and if a semicircle is described upon that line to which it is perpendicular, the circumference of that semicircle must necessarily pass through the extremity of the line placed perpendicularly as the mean proportional. Since all radii of the circle f, g, b are perpendicular to the line k, l and are mean proportionals between its parts (which are k, e and e, l), it follows that the semicircle described upon k, l, if rotated, will pass through all points of the circumference f, g, b and through all the solid angles of the constructed pyramid. Thus, by the definition of a figure being inscribed within a figure, the constructed pyramid is inscriptible within that sphere which the semicircle drawn upon line k, l describes by its motion. And because this described sphere is equal to the assigned sphere by the definition of equal spheres, it follows from common knowledge that this constructed pyramid is circumscribed by the assigned sphere...

...circumscribable, which is what was proposed. The corollary <note>A "corollary" is a proposition that follows directly from one already proved.</note> is demonstrated thus: Since line **a, b** is triple to line **b, c**, by inverse proportionality **a, b** will be sesquialter <note>original: "sesquialtera"; a ratio of 3:2, or one and a half times.</note> to line **a, c**. Therefore, from the second part of the corollary to the 8th [proposition] of the sixth book and the corollary to the 17th of the same, the square of line **a, b** will also be sesquialter to the square of line **a, d**. Since line **a, d** is equal to the side of the constructed pyramid, and **a, b** is the diameter of the sphere, it is clear that what the corollary states is true. 

Lest anyone should doubt the ancient truth proposed, we wish to confirm it by demonstration in this manner: Let there be, therefore, upon line **a, b**, a perpendicular line **c, d** which is placed as a mean proportional <note>A value $x$ such that $a:x = x:b$.</note> between the parts of line **a, b**, which are **a, c** and **c, b**, so that the ratio of **a, c** to **c, d** is as **c, d** to **c, b**. And upon line **a, b**, let a semicircle **a, c, b** be described. I assert that the circumference of this semicircle will pass through point **d**, which is the extremity of the perpendicular. If it does not, it will either cut line **c, d** or pass above it entirely, encompassing it without touching. 

Let it first cut line **c, d** at point **e**, and let lines **e, b** and **e, a** be drawn. From the first part of the 30th [proposition] of the third book, the total angle **a, e, b** will be a right angle. Therefore, from the first part of the corollary to the 8th [proposition] of the sixth book, the ratio of **a, c** to **c, e** is as **c, e** to **c, b**. But indeed, from the second part of the 8th [proposition] of the fifth book, the ratio of **a, c** to **c, e** is greater than **a, c** to **c, d**, because **c, e** is smaller than **c, d**. Since, therefore, **c, e** is to **c, b** as **a, c** is to **c, e**, and **c, d** is to **c, b** as **a, c** is to **c, d**, it follows by the 12th [proposition] of the fifth book that the ratio of **c, e** to **c, b** is greater than **c, d** to **c, b**. Therefore, by the first part of the 10th [proposition] of the fifth book, **c, e** is greater than **d, c**—namely, a part being greater than its whole, which is impossible. Therefore, the circumference of the semicircle will not cut line **c, d**.

Now, let it pass above, and let **c, d** be extended to the circumference; let the whole line be **c, e**, and let lines **e, b** and **e, a** be drawn. It will follow, as before, that line **c, d** is greater than line **c, e**, which is also impossible. Thus the proposition is established. 

Similarly, we say that if there is any right angle subtended by a base upon which a semicircle is drawn, it is necessary for the circumference to pass through that right angle. The first part of the 30th [proposition] of the third book proposes the converse of this. That what we say is true is established thus: 

¶ Let there be a right angle **a, b, c** subtended by base **a, c**, and upon it let a semicircle be drawn. I say that its circumference will pass through point **b**, where the lines containing the right angle meet. The demonstration of this is that it will pass neither above nor below. If it should pass otherwise: first, let it be below, as **a, e, c**, and from angle **b** let line **b, d** be drawn perpendicular to the base **a, c**, which cuts the circumference of the semicircle at point **e**, and let lines **e, a** and **e, c** be drawn. Angle **a, e, c** will be a right angle by the first part of the 30th [proposition] of the third book. But that angle is greater than angle **a, b, c** by the 21st [proposition] of the first book; this, however, is impossible according to the third postulate, since both are right angles—the latter by hypothesis and the former by the first part of the 30th [proposition] of the third book. Therefore, the circumference of the semicircle will not pass below angle **b**. 

Next, let it pass above, as **a, f, e, c**, and let the perpendicular **d, b** be extended until it meets the circumference of the semicircle **a, f, e** at point **f**, and let lines **f, a** and **f, c** be drawn. By the first part of the 30th [proposition] of the third book, angle **a, f, c** will be a right angle. Since angle **a, b, c** was also a right angle by hypothesis, an impossibility follows by the 21st [proposition] of the first book, just as in the beginning. Therefore, what we stated remains. This is necessary for the knowledge of what follows.

Afterward, let a square be made whose sides are all equal to line **b, d**; let it be **e, f, g, b**, upon whose four angles let there be erected...

...as [proposition] 12 of the eleventh [book] teaches: four lines perpendicular to the surface of the square itself, of which each is also set equal to line **b, d**—let these be **e, k**, **f, l**, **g, m**, and **h, n**. These four perpendiculars will each be parallel to one another according to the sixth [proposition] of the eleventh [book]. And the angles they contain with the sides of the square are right angles, by the definition of a line perpendicular to a surface. Then, let the extremities of these perpendiculars be joined by drawing lines **k, l**, **l, m**, **m, n**, and **n, k**. The complete cube will thus be contained by six square surfaces. For it is established by [proposition] 34 of the first [book] that the four surfaces surrounding it—which are those whose opposite sides are the four perpendiculars—are all squares. As for the base, this was already established. Regarding its top surface, which is **k, l, m, n**, it is also square by [proposition] 34 of the first and [proposition] 10 of the eleventh. Therefore, from the fourth [proposition] of the eleventh, it is manifest that each individual side of this cube stands orthogonally <note>at right angles</note> to its two opposite surfaces. Now, to demonstrate that this cube is circumscribable by a given sphere: in one of its surfaces, let a diagonal be drawn—for example, in its base, let it be **e, g**. And from the other end of this diagonal and line **a, b**, let the diameter of the cube **e, m** be drawn. From the penultimate [proposition] of the first [book] <note>The Pythagorean Theorem, Proposition I.47.</note>, the square of **e, g** is double the square of **f, g**, and therefore also double the square of **g, m**, because **g, m** is equal to **f, g**, as all sides of a cube are equal to one another. And since again, from the penultimate of the first, the square of **e, m** is equal to the squares of the two lines **e, g** and **g, m** (because angle **e, g, m** is a right angle by the definition of a perpendicular line to a surface), the square of **e, m** will be triple the square of **m, g**. This is clear from the double and the single. And since from the second part of the corollary to [proposition] 8 of the sixth [book] and from the corollary to [proposition] 17 of the same, the square of **a, b** is also triple the square of **b, d** (because line **a, b** is triple line **b, c**), and **b, d** is equal to **g, m**, it follows from common knowledge <note>original: "ex coi scia," short for "ex communi scientia," referring to a common mathematical axiom.</note> that **e, m** (the diameter of the cube) is equal to **a, b** (the diameter of the sphere). Thus, if a semicircle is described around line **e, m** and rotated until it returns to its starting point, the described sphere will be equal to the assigned sphere by the definition of equal spheres. But since this semicircle will pass through point **g** (because angle **e, g, m** is a right angle), and by the same reasoning through every other individual right angle of the cube—which is clear from the premise immediately preceding this 14th—it is established that the constructed cube is circumscribed by the assigned sphere, because it is circumscribed by its equal; which is what was to be demonstrated. The demonstration of the corollary was made clear in the process of this demonstration.

### Proposition 15

**To construct a body of eight triangular and equilateral bases** <note>A regular octahedron.</note> circumscribed by a given sphere; and it will be clear that the square of the diameter of that sphere is double the square of the side of the body.

> ¶ Let the diameter of the assigned sphere be **a, b**, which is divided equally at point **c**. Upon this line, let a semicircle **a, d, b** be drawn, and let **c, d** be drawn perpendicular to **a, b**. Join point **d** with **a** and **b**. Describe a square whose sides are each equal to line **b, d**, and let this square be **e, f, g, h**, in which two diagonals **e, g** and **f, h** are drawn, intersecting each other at point **k**. It is established from [proposition] 4 of the first [book] that each of these diagonals is equal to line **a, b** (the diameter of the sphere), since angle **d** is a right angle from the first part of [proposition] 30 of the third, and each of the individual angles **e, f, g, h** is a right angle by the definition of a square. It is established again that these same two diagonals **e, g** and **f, h** divide each other equally at point **k**; this is easily deduced from [proposition] 5 of the first, [proposition] 32, and the sixth of the same. Therefore, let line **k, l** be erected perpendicular to the surface of the square at point **k**, and let it be equal to half the diameter **e, g** or **f, h**. Let the hypotenuses **l, e**, **l, f**, **l, g**, and **l, h** be drawn. From these things that have been set out and the penultimate of the first [book] repeated as often as necessary, each of these hypotenuses will be equal to one another and equal to the sides of the square. You have therefore a pyramid of four equilateral and triangular bases established upon a square.

<note>A geometric diagram showing a square inscribed within a circle. A vertical diameter l-m passes through the center k of the square. Lines extend from the poles l and m to each vertex of the square (e, f, g, h), illustrating an octahedron inscribed within a sphere.</note>

From here, therefore, place a similar pyramid below the square itself in this manner: extend the line **l, k**, piercing through the square as far as **m**, so that **k, m**—which lies below the square—is equal to **l, k** which lies above it. And join point **m** with each of the angles of the square, drawing four other <term>slant edges</term><note>original: "ypothemiſas". These are the lines forming the edges of the lower pyramid.</note> which are **m, e**, **m, f**, **m, g**, and **m, h**. Regarding these, it is also manifest from the preamble of the first book—just as with the others in the upper part—that they are equal to one another and to the sides of the square. We have therefore completed a solid of eight <note>The Latin text '4.baſiū' likely refers to the four additional faces just constructed, completing the eight-faced octahedron.</note> triangular and equilateral bases. 

That this solid is circumscribable by the assigned sphere is understood as follows: it is established that the line **l, m** is equal to the diameter of the assigned sphere, for each of them is equal to the diameter of the square. Therefore, if a semicircle is drawn upon the line **l, m** and rotated until it returns to its original position, the sphere which it describes by its motion will be equal to the assigned sphere, as is gathered from the definition of equal spheres. Indeed, this semicircle will pass through the four angles of the square and, simply put, through all the points of the circumference of the circle circumscribing the square. This is because the semi-diameter of the square (such as line **f, k**) and the portions of line **l, m** (which are **l, k** and **k, m**) are equal to one another. 

Wherefore, from the definition of what it means for one figure to be inscribed in another, the constructed solid is inscribed within the sphere described by the motion of this semicircle; and thus also within the assigned sphere by the common concept, since they are equal to one another by definition. Furthermore, the corollary is clearly established: for there are two lines **d, b** and **d, a** equal from the fourth [proposition] of the first book; and therefore the square of **a, b** is double the square of **b, d** from the preamble of the first book. The side of the constructed solid is equal to line **b, d**; therefore, the corollary is true.

### Proposition 16.

<note>A geometric diagram of a semicircle with diameter a-b and center c. A perpendicular line c-d rises from the center to the arc. A triangle is formed by connecting points a, b, and d. This construction is used to find the side of an icosahedron relative to the diameter of a sphere.</note>

To construct a solid of twenty triangular and equilateral bases <note>An icosahedron.</note> circumscribed by a given sphere having a rational diameter; and it will be clear that the side of the same solid is an irrational line, specifically the one called the <term>minor</term><note>A "minor" line is a specific type of irrational line defined in Book X of Euclid’s Elements, resulting from the subtraction of two specific irrational areas.</note>. 

Let the diameter of the assigned sphere also be **a, b**, which is assumed to be rational either in length or in power only. Let it be divided at point **c** so that **a, c** is four times **c, b**. Let a semicircle **a, d, b** be drawn upon it, and let **c, d** be drawn perpendicular to **a, b**, and let line **d, b** be drawn. Then, according to the length of line **d, b**, let a circle **e, f, g, h, k** be drawn around center **l**, in which an equilateral pentagon is inscribed, marked with the same letters. From the center **l** to the angles of this pentagon, let the lines **l, e**, **l, f**, **l, g**, **l, h**, and **l, k** be drawn. 

Again, in the same circle, let an equilateral decagon be inscribed: let all the arcs whose chords are the sides of the pentagon be divided into two equal parts, and from the middle points to the ends of all the sides of the inscribed pentagon, let straight lines be directed. Likewise, upon each angle of the pentagon, let a perpendicular <note>Latin: "cathecus" or "cathetus".</note> be erected as taught in the twelfth [proposition] of the eleventh [book], each of which should also be equal to line **b, d**. Let the extremities of these five perpendiculars be joined by <term>connecting lines</term><note>Latin: "corauſtis". These are the chords connecting the tops of the perpendiculars.</note>. From the sixth [proposition] of the eleventh [book], these five erected perpendiculars will be parallel to one another. Since they are equal, their five connecting lines joining their extremities will also be equal to the sides of the pentagon, according to the thirty-third [proposition] of the first [book]. 

Therefore, from each summit of each perpendicular, let down two slant edges <note>Latin: "ypothemiſas".</note> to the two surrounding angles of the inscribed decagon. By joining the ends of these ten slant edges descending from the five extremities of the perpendiculars to the five points (which are the middle angles of the inscribed decagon), another pentagon is formed, which will also be equilateral by the twenty-third [proposition] of the third [book]. When you have done this, you will see that you have completed ten triangles whose sides are the ten slant edges, the five connecting lines, and the five sides of the second inscribed pentagon. To conclude that these ten triangles are equilateral: since both the semi-diameter of the described circle and any of the erected perpendiculars are equal to line **b, d**, from the corollary of the fifteenth [proposition] of the fourth [book], any of the perpendiculars is equal to the side of an equilateral hexagon in the circle whose semi-diameter...

Therefore, let **l, m** be divided into equal parts at **q**. Since, therefore, the square of **n, q** is five times the square of **q, m** (from the 3rd proposition of this book), it will also be (from the 15th proposition of the fifth book) that the square of **p, n** is five times the square of **l, m**. Indeed, from the fourth proposition of the second book, the square of **p, m** is four times the square of **q, n**; and the square of **l, m** is four times the square of **q, m** from the same. Four times to four times is as simple to simple, as witnessed by the 15th proposition of the fifth book. But truly, the square of **a, b** is five times the square of **b, d** from the second part of the corollary to the 5th proposition of the sixth book; and from the corollary to the 17th of the same, **a, b** is also five times **b, c** because **a, c** was four times the same. Because, therefore, **l, m** is by hypothesis equal to **b, d**, it will be by common knowledge that **a, b** is equal to **n, p**.

Thus, if a semicircle is described upon the line **n, p**, and it is rotated until it returns to its first place, the sphere described by its motion will be equal to the proposed sphere by the definition of equal spheres. And since the line **l, m** is a mean proportional between **l, n** and **n, m**, and therefore between **l, n** and **p, l**, any semi-diameter of the circle will also be a mean proportional between **l, n** and **l, p**. And since **l, m** is equal to the semi-diameter of the circle, the semicircle described upon **p, n** will pass through all points of the circumference of circle **e, f, g**, and therefore through each of the angles of the solid constructed standing in that circumference. And because, by the same reasoning, the individual connecting lines joining the extremities of the corner altitudes with the extremity of the central altitude are mean proportionals between **p, m** and **m, n** (because each of them is equal to **l, m**), it follows that the same semicircle also passes through the remaining angles of the established icosahedral figure. Therefore, this body is circumscribable by a sphere.

## Proposition 17.

<note>A geometric diagram showing a construction within a rectangular frame labeled with points **a, b, c,** and **d** at the corners. Inside, a series of lines and points (**e, f, g, k, l, m, n, o, p, q, r, s**) illustrate the inscription of a dodecahedron within a sphere, showing the relationship between a cube and the pentagonal faces. **To construct a body of twelve equilateral and equiangular pentagonal bases <note>a dodecahedron</note> circumscribed by a assigned sphere; and it will be clear that the side of the same body is an irrational line, specifically that which is called the <term>remainder</term><note>original: "residuum"; also known in modern geometry as an apotome. It is a line formed by the difference of two rational lines that are only commensurable in power.</note>.**

Let a cube be made according to what the 14th proposition of this book teaches, circumscribable by the assigned sphere. Let two surfaces of this cube be **a, b** and **a, c**. Let us now imagine that **a, b** is the top surface of the cube and **a, c** is one of the sides. Let line **a, d** be common to these two surfaces. Therefore, in surface **a, b**, let two opposite sides be divided into equal parts, namely **d, b** and the side opposite to it; and let the points of division be joined by the line **e, f**. Also, let the side **a, d** and the side opposite to it in surface **a, c** be divided into equal parts at the points of division and joined by a straight line, the middle of which is **g, b** <note>original: "g.b."</note>. Let point **b** be the midpoint of line **a, d**. Similarly, let line **e, f** be divided into equal parts at **k**, and let **b, k** be drawn. Therefore, divide each of the three lines **e, k**, **k, f**, and **g, b** according to <term>extreme and mean ratio</term><note>original: "proportione habente medium et duo extrema"; this is the "Golden Ratio." A line is divided such that the whole is to the larger part as the larger part is to the smaller.</note> at the three points **l, m, q**. Let their larger portions be **l, k**, **k, m**, and **g, q**, which are clearly equal since the whole lines divided were equal—namely, each of them being half of the side of the cube. Then, from the two points **l** and **m**, erect perpendiculars to surface **a, b** (as taught in the 12th proposition of the eleventh book), making each of them equal to line **k, l**; let these be **l, n** and **m, p**. Similarly, from point **q**, erect a perpendicular **q, r** to surface **a, c**, which you should make equal to **g, q**. Draw the lines **a, l**, **a, n**, **a, m**, **a, p**, **d, m**, **d, p**, **d, l**, **d, n**, **a, r**, **a, q**, **d, r**, and **d, q**.

It is therefore manifest from the fifth proposition of this book that the two lines **k, e** and **e, l** are, in power, triple to line **k, l**, and therefore also to line **l, n**, since **k, l** and **l, n** are equal. But truly, **k, e** is equal to **e, a**. Therefore, the two lines **a, e** and **e, l** are in power triple to line **l, n**. Wherefore, from the penultimate proposition of the first book <note>Pythagorean Theorem</note>, **a, l** is in power triple to **l, n**; and therefore, by the same logic, **a, n** is in power quadruple to **l, n**. Since every line is in power quadruple to its half, it follows from <term>common knowledge</term><note>original: "communi scientia"; the common notions or axioms of geometry.</note> that **a, n** is double in length to **l, n**. And because **l, m** is double to **l, k**, and **k, l** and **l, n** are equal, **a, n** will be equal to **l, m**, for their halves are equal. And because from the 33rd proposition of the first book **l, m** is equal to **n, p**, **a, n** will be equal to **n, p**. In the same way, you will prove that the three lines **p, d**, **d, r**, and **r, a** are equal to each other and to the two previously mentioned lines. Thus, from these five lines, we have an equilateral pentagon, which is **a, n, p, d, r**.

But perhaps you will say that it is not a pentagon because it is not, perhaps, all in one plane, which would be necessary for it to be a pentagon. That it is entirely in one plane, hold thus: let there proceed from point **k** a line **k, s** perpendicular to surface **a, b**, which is equal to **l, k**. It will be, because of this, equal to each of the two lines **l, n** and **m, p**. Since it is parallel to each of them (from the sixth proposition of the eleventh book), and therefore with both in the same surface (from the definition of parallel lines), it is necessary that point **s** be on the line **n, p** and that it divides it into equal parts. Let two lines **r, b** and **b, s** be drawn. There are thus two triangles, **k, s, b** and **q, r, b**, established upon one angle, namely **k, b, q**. And the proportion of **k, b** to **q, r** is as **k, s** to **q, b**, for as **g, b** to **q, r**, so **k, b** to **q...**

# BOOK XIII

<note>A detailed geometric diagram is located on the left side of the upper text block. By the 7th proposition of the fifth book, as **r, q** is to **q, b**, so **k, f** is to **q, b**. Similarly, **g, b** is to **q, r** as **q, r** is to **q, b**, because **q, r** is equal to **g, q**. Therefore, by the 30th proposition of the sixth book <note>This proposition describes the "extreme and mean ratio," known today as the Golden Ratio.</note>, the line **r, b, s** is a single [straight] line. For this reason, according to the second proposition of the eleventh book, the entire pentagon we are discussing lies in a single plane. I also state that it is equiangular. Since **e, k** is divided by the <term>extreme and mean ratio</term><note>original: "proportione habente medium duoque extrema"; the division of a line such that the ratio of the whole to the larger part is the same as the ratio of the larger part to the smaller.</note> and **k, m** is equal to its greater part, then by the first four [propositions], the whole line **e, m** is also divided by the extreme and mean ratio, and its greater part is **e, k**. Thus, by the 8th [proposition], the two lines **e, m** and **m, k**—and therefore the two lines **e, m** and **m, p**, since **m, p** is equal to **m, k**—are <term>triple in power</term><note>original: "potentia triplum"; this means the sum of the squares of the two lines is three times the square of the other line.</note> to the line **e, k**, and thus also to the line **a, e**, for **a, e** is equal to **e, k**. Therefore, the three lines **a, e**, **e, m**, and **m, p** are quadruple in power to the line **a, e**. 

It is established by the penultimate proposition of the first book <note>Referring to the Pythagorean Theorem (Book I, Prop 47).</note>, applied twice, that the line **a, p** is equal in power to the three lines **a, e**, **e, m**, and **m, p**. Thus, **a, p** is quadruple in power to the line **a, e**. Truly, since the side of the cube is double the line **a, e**, it is also quadruple in power to it by the 4th proposition of the second book. Therefore, by common knowledge, **a, p** is equal to the side of the cube. Since **a, d** is one of the sides of the cube, **a, p** will be equal to **a, d**, and therefore by the 8th proposition of the first book, angle **a, r, d** is equal to angle **a, n, p**. In the same way, you may prove that angle **d, n, p** is equal to angle **d, r, a**, because you will prove that line **d, n** is quadruple in power to half the side of the cube. Since, from these facts, the pentagon is equilateral and has three equal angles, it will be equiangular by the seventh proposition of the first book. 

If, therefore, by this method and reasoning, we construct an equilateral and equiangular pentagon upon each of the remaining sides of the cube, a solid contained by twelve equilateral and equiangular pentagonal surfaces will be completed; for a cube has twelve sides <note>In this construction, each of the 12 edges of the internal cube serves as the base for the "peak" of one of the 12 pentagonal faces of the dodecahedron.</note>. It remains to demonstrate that this solid can be circumscribed by the given sphere. Let two surfaces be extended from line **f, k** cutting the cube, one of which cuts it along line **b, k** and the other along line **e, f**. By the 40th proposition of the eleventh book, the common section of these two surfaces will cut the diameter of the cube and be cut in turn by that diameter into equal parts. Let the common section of these be the line **k, o** reaching to the diameter of the cube, so that **o** is the center of the cube, and let lines **o, a**, **o, n**, **o, p**, **o, d**, and **o, r** be drawn. It is certain that each of the two lines **o, a** and **o, d** is a semi-diameter <note>Radius.</note> of the cube, and therefore equal to line **d, e**. Furthermore, it is established from the 40th of the eleventh book that the line **o, k** is equal to **e, k**, namely half the side of the cube. And because **k, f** is equal to **k, m**, the line **o, f** will be divided at point **k** by the extreme and mean ratio, and its greater part will be the line **o, k**, which is equal to **e, k**. Thus, by the 8th [proposition] of this book, the two lines **o, f** and **f, k**—and therefore **o, f** and **f, p**, since **f, p** is equal to **k, f**—are triple in power to the line **o, k**, and thus to half the side of the cube. 

Wherefore, by the penultimate proposition of the first book, line **o, p** is triple in power to half the side of the cube. From the conclusion of the 14th proposition of this book, it is established that the semi-diameter of a sphere is triple in power to half the side of the cube which the same sphere circumscribes. Thus, **o, p** is as great as the semi-diameter of the sphere circumscribing the proposed cube. By the same reasoning, all lines drawn from point **o** to the individual angles of all the pentagons described upon the sides of the cube—namely to those angles which belong to the pentagons and are not shared with the surfaces of the cube, such as the three angles **n, p, r** in the established pentagon—are equal. As for those lines coming from point **o** to the angles of the pentagons that are common to both the pentagons and the surfaces of the cube, such as the two angles **a** and **d** in the present pentagon, it is certain that they are equal to the semi-diameter of the sphere circumscribing the cube; for they are the semi-diameters of the cube according to the 40th of the eleventh book. But truly, the semi-diameter of the cube is as the semi-diameter of the sphere circumscribing it, as appears from the reasoning of the 14th proposition. It is therefore evident that all lines drawn from point **o** to the individual angles of the dodecahedron are equal to one another and to the semi-diameter of the sphere. Therefore, a semicircle drawn over the entire diameter of the sphere or cube, if rotated, will pass through all of them.

...its angles; therefore, by definition, it is circumscribable by the assigned sphere. I say further that the side of this figure is an **irrational line**, specifically the one called a **remainder** <note>original: "residuum"; in Euclidean geometry, this refers to an 'apotome,' an irrational line formed by subtracting a rational line from another rational line that is only commensurable with it in square.</note>, provided that the diameter of the circumscribing sphere is rational in length or in power. Since the diameter of the sphere is—from the 14th proposition of this book—triple in power to the side of the cube <note>meaning the square of the diameter is three times the square of the cube's side</note>, the side of the cube will be rational in power if the diameter of the sphere is rational in length or power.

Furthermore, it is established from the 11th proposition that the line **r, p** divides the line **a, d** (which is the side of the cube) according to the **extreme and mean ratio** <term>extreme and mean ratio</term><note>Now commonly known as the Golden Ratio.</note>, and that its greater part is equal to the side of the pentagon. Since this greater part is a "remainder" according to the sixth proposition of this book, it is manifest that the side of the **dodecahedron** figure is a remainder, which is what we intended to demonstrate.

Thus, through the 13th proposition and the four following it, five bodies with equal sides and equal angles have been constructed, each of which is circumscribable by an assigned sphere. These solids are:
*   The first, with four triangular bases, is called the **tetrahedron**.
*   The second, with six square bases, is called the **cube** or **hexahedron**.
*   The third, with eight triangular bases, is called the **octahedron**.
*   The fourth is the **icosahedron** solid, which has twenty triangular bases.
*   The fifth consists of twelve pentagonal bases and is called the **dodecahedron**.

These five are called the **regular solids** because they are equiangular and equilateral, and they can be inscribed within a sphere and within one another.

### It is impossible for there to be more than these five equilateral and equiangular solids.

To constitute any **solid angle** <term>solid angle</term><note>A corner where three or more planes meet, such as the point of a pyramid.</note>, it is necessary for at least three surface angles to meet. A solid angle cannot be formed from only two surface angles. Because three angles of any equilateral and equiangular **hexagon** are equal to four right angles <note>Three 120-degree angles equal 360 degrees, forming a flat plane rather than a corner.</note>, and because three angles of a **heptagon** (or any figure with more sides) are greater than four right angles—as is clearly drawn from the 32nd proposition of the First Book—it is impossible for them to form a solid.

Since every solid angle must be less than four right angles <note>360 degrees</note> according to the 21st proposition of the Eleventh Book, it is impossible for three angles of a hexagon or heptagon—or indeed any equilateral and equiangular figure with more sides—to constitute a solid angle. Therefore, no regular solid figure can be constructed from hexagonal surfaces or those with more sides.

If three angles of an equilateral hexagon already equal or exceed four right angles, then four or more angles will exceed it even more strongly. However, it is manifest that three angles of an equilateral **pentagon** are less than four right angles, while four angles are greater than four right angles. Thus, it is possible to constitute a solid from three angles of a pentagon, but impossible from four or more. Consequently, only one solid is constructed from equilateral pentagons: the one called the **dodecahedron**, in which the angles of the pentagons meet in threes to complete the solid angles.

The same reasoning applies to four-sided equilateral and equiangular figures as to pentagons. Every four-sided figure that is equilateral and equiangular is, by definition, a **square**. All its angles are right angles by the 32nd proposition of the First Book. Therefore, it is possible to constitute a solid angle from three such surface angles <note>3 x 90 = 270 degrees</note>, but from four or more it is impossible <note>4 x 90 = 360 degrees</note>. For this reason, only one solid is built from such four-sided figures: the one we call the **cube**.

Regarding equilateral **triangles**, six of their angles are equal to four right angles <note>6 x 60 = 360 degrees</note>. Therefore, fewer than six will be less than four right angles, and more will be greater. Thus, it is impossible to form a solid angle from six or more such triangles, but it is possible from five, four, or three.
1. When **three** angles of an equilateral triangle form a solid angle, a body of four triangular bases (the tetrahedron) is perfected.
2. When **four** meet, a body of eight...

...bases, which we called the **octahedron**. But truly, if five angles of equilateral triangles meet to form a **solid angle** <term>solid angle</term><note>A solid angle, or vertex, is where three or more faces of a geometric solid meet at a single point.</note>, the resulting body will be an **icosahedron**, having twenty bases of equilateral triangles. ## Proposition 18.

<note>A geometric diagram showing a semicircle on a horizontal diameter. Points on the diameter are labeled from left to right as a, k, D, c, m, b. From point a, a vertical line extends upwards to point g. A line connects g to point D (the center of the diameter), intersecting the arc of the semicircle at point h. A line also connects g to b. Vertical perpendicular lines are drawn from the diameter to the arc: h-k, f-D, e-c, and n-m. Chords are drawn connecting a-e, b-e, a-f, b-f, and b-n. A point p is marked on the arc between n and b.</note>

<margin>s</margin>
**To find the sides of the five aforementioned bodies, which are circumscribable by the same sphere, when only the diameter of that sphere is given.**

Let **a, b** be the diameter of a certain sphere proposed to us, from which we are commanded to derive the sides of the five aforementioned bodies. Let us therefore divide this diameter at point **c**, so that **a, c** is double the length of **c, b**; and also at the midpoint **d**. Upon this diameter, let us draw a semicircle **a, f, b**, and from its circumference let two lines be drawn perpendicular to the line **a, b**, namely **c, e** and **d, f**. Let the points be joined: **c** with **a**, **c** with **b**, **f** with **a**, and **f** with **b**. It is therefore manifest from the 13th demonstration that **a, e** is the side of the figure with four triangular equilateral bases <note>the tetrahedron</note>; and from the 14th demonstration that **e, b** is the side of the **cube**; and from the 15th demonstration that **f, b** is the side of the figure with eight triangular equilateral bases <note>the octahedron</note>.

Next, let a line **a, g** be produced from point **a**, perpendicular to **a, b** and equal to the same **a, b**. Join **g** with **b**, and let **h** be the point where the line **g, d** intersects the circumference of the semicircle. Draw **h, k** perpendicular to **a, b**. Because **g, a** is double **a, d**, it follows from the 4th proposition of the 6th book that **h, k** is double **k, d**. For the two triangles **g, a, d** and **h, k, d** are equiangular by the 32nd proposition of the 1st book, because angle **a** of the larger triangle is equal to angle **k** of the smaller (both being right angles) and angle **d** is common to both. Therefore, by the 4th proposition of the 6th book, **h, k** is **quadruple in power** <term>quadruple in power</term><note>In Euclidean geometry, "quadruple in power" means the square of the first line is four times the area of the square of the second line.</note> to **k, d**. 

Thus, from the penultimate proposition of the 1st book <note>The Pythagorean Theorem</note>, **h, d** is **quintuple in power** to **k, d**. Since **d, b** is equal to **h, d** (both being radii from the center of the semicircle), **d, b** will also be quintuple in power to **k, d**. Truly, since the whole line **a, b** is double the whole **b, d**, just as **a, c** (subtracted from the first, **a, b**) is double **c, b** (subtracted from the second, **b, d**), it follows from the 19th proposition of the 5th book that the remainder **b, c** is double the remainder **c, d**. Therefore, the whole **b, d** is triple **d, c**, and thus the square of **b, d** is nine times the square of **d, c**. Since the square of **b, d** was only five times the square of **k, d**, it follows from the second part of the 15th proposition of the 10th book that the square of **d, c** is less than the square of **k, d**, and therefore **d, c** is less than **k, d**. 

Let **d, m** be made equal to **k, d**, and produce **m, n** up to the circumference so that it is perpendicular to **a, b**, and join **n** with **b**. Since **d, k** and **d, m** are equal, then by the definition of lines equidistant from the center, the two lines **h, k** and **m, n** are equidistant from the center and therefore equal to one another, by the 13th and 3rd propositions of the 3rd book. Thus, **m, n** is equal to **m, k** <note>original: "m, k," though the logic refers to the segment proportions</note>, for **b, k** was equal to it. And because **a, b** is double **b, d**, and **k, m** is double **d, k**, and the square of **b, d** is quintuple the square of **d, k**, it follows from the 15th proposition of the 5th book that the square of **a, b** is likewise quintuple to the square of **k, m**. For the square of a double length relates to the square of another double length just as the square of the simple length relates to the square of the simple length. 

From the 16th demonstration, it is manifest that the diameter of the sphere is quintuple in power to the radius of the circle circumscribing the faces of the icosahedron. Therefore, **k, m** is equal to the radius of that circle. Since the diameter of the sphere **a, b** is quintuple in power both to the radius of the circle of that figure and to **k, m**. Furthermore, from the same demonstration, it is manifest that the diameter of the sphere consists of the radius of the hexagon and twice the side of the decagon of the circle of the icosahedron. Since **k, m** stands as the radius of the hexagon, and **a, k** is equal to **m, b** (being the remainders after equal parts are taken from the whole), then **m, b** stands as the side of the decagon. Because **m, n** is equal to the radius of the hexagon (being equal to **k, m**), it follows from the penultimate proposition of the 1st book and the 10th proposition of this book that **n, b** is the side of the pentagon inscribed in the circle of the icosahedron. And since the 16th demonstration shows that the side of this pentagon is the side of the icosahedron itself, it is established that the line **n, b** is the side of that figure.

# XIII

Therefore, let **e, b**, which is the side of the cube circumscribable by the assigned sphere, be divided at point **p** according to the <term>extreme and mean ratio</term><note>Known today as the Golden Ratio, this is a proportion where the ratio of the whole line to the larger segment is the same as the ratio of the larger segment to the smaller segment.</note>; and let its greater part be **p, b**. It is established from the demonstration of the previous proposition that **p, b** is the side of the figure of twelve bases <note>The dodecahedron.</note>. Thus, the sides of the five aforementioned bodies have been found from the diameter of the sphere proposed to us. For **a, e** is the side of the <term>pyramid of four bases</term><note>The tetrahedron.</note>; **e, b** is the side of the cube; **f, b** is the side of the octahedron; while **n, b** is the side of the icosahedron; and finally, the line **p, b** is the side of the dodecahedron.

Which of these sides are greater than others is determined as follows: it is certain that **a, e** is greater than **f, b**, for the arc **a, e** is greater than the arc **f, b**. Likewise, **f, b** is greater than **e, b**, and **c, b** is greater than **n, b**. But I also say that **n, b** is greater than **p, b**. For since **a, c** is double **c, b**, it follows from the fourth proposition of the second book that the square of **a, c** will be four times the square of **c, b**. Furthermore, it is established from the second part of the corollary to the eighth proposition of the sixth book, and from the corollary of the seventeenth proposition of the same book, that the square of **a, b** is triple the square of **b, e**. But according to the twenty-first proposition of the sixth book, the square of **a, b** is to the square of **b, e** as the square of **b, e** is to the square of **c, b**, because the proportion of **a, b** to **b, e** is as **b, e** to **b, c** from the second part of the corollary of the eighth proposition of the sixth book. Thus, by the eleventh proposition of the fifth book, the square of **b, e** is triple the square of **c, b**. And since the square of **a, c** is four times that same square, as was shown, it follows from the first part of the tenth proposition of the fifth book that the square of **a, c** is less than the square of **b, e**, and therefore the line **a, c** is greater than line **b, e**, and thus **a, m** is much greater than **b, e**. It is truly manifest from the ninth proposition of this book that if line **a, m** is divided according to the extreme and mean ratio, its greater part will be the line **k, m**, which is equal to **m, n**. But when **b, e** is divided according to the same ratio, its greater part is line **p, b**. Since the whole line **a, m** is greater than the whole line **b, e**, then **m, n** (which is equal to the greater part of **a, m**) will be greater than **p, b** (the greater part of **b, e**). This is manifest from the second [proposition] of the fourteenth book, which is established by firm demonstration without the help of any of those that follow. Therefore, by the nineteenth proposition of the first book, it is even more certain that **n, b** is greater than **p, b**. 

Wherefore it is clear that the sides of these five aforementioned bodies exceed one another in almost the same order in which the bodies themselves follow one another. For in the cube and the octahedron alone does this have an exception: the side of the octahedron exceeds the side of the cube, although the cube is listed before the octahedron. They place the cube before the octahedron for this reason: because by the same division of the diameter of the assigned sphere, the side of the pyramid having four triangular bases and the side of the cube were found. Therefore, **a, e**, the side of the pyramid, is greater than the sides of the other bodies; after it is **f, b**, the side of the octahedron, which is greater than the sides of the following bodies. Third in order of magnitude follows **e, b**, the side of the cube. In the fourth place is **n, b**, the side of the icosahedron. Finally, the smallest of all is **p, b**, the side of the <term>duodecedron</term> or dodecahedron.

## Proposition 1.

Every perpendicular drawn from the center of a circle to the side of a <term>pentagon</term><note>A five-sided polygon.</note> inscribed within that circle is proved to be equal to both half the side of the <term>decagon</term><note>A ten-sided polygon.</note> and half the side of the <term>hexagon</term><note>A six-sided polygon.</note> inscribed in the same circle, when those two halves are joined together in a straight line. It is therefore evident that the perpendicular drawn from the center of the circle to the side of the pentagon is equal to the perpendicular drawn from the center to the side of the triangle joined together with half the side of the decagon inscribed within the same circle.

[Symbol] Let line **a, b** be the side of an equilateral pentagon inscribed in a circle whose center is **c**, and let a perpendicular be drawn from center **c** to the line **a, b**. By the second part of the third proposition of the third book, this perpendicular will divide the line into two equal parts and its arc also into two equal parts.

# BOOK XIV

<note>A geometric diagram is situated in the upper-left margin. It consists of a circle with a vertical diameter. The top point of the diameter is labeled 'd', the center 'c', and the bottom 'g'. A horizontal chord 'ab' intersects the diameter at point 'e'. A point 'f' is marked on the radius segment 'cg' below the center. Line segments connect point 'd' to 'b' and point 'f' to 'b'.</note>

From the 4th [proposition] of the first book and the 27th of the third, let this perpendicular line be **c, d**, cutting **a, b** at point **e** and its arc at point **d**. Therefore, as we have said, line **a, e** is equal to line **e, b**, and arc **a, d** is equal to arc **d, b**. Let line **d, b** be drawn, concerning which it is established that it is the side of an equilateral <term>decagon</term><note>A ten-sided polygon.</note> inscribed in the given circle, since it subtends half of a fifth of the whole circumference <note>One-tenth of the circle’s boundary.</note>.

I say, therefore, that line **c, e** is equal to half of line **c, d** and half of line **d, b** joined together in a straight line. Let the diameter **d, c, g** be completed, and let **c, f** be equal to **c, d**, and let **b, f** be drawn. From the 4th of the first book, **b, f** will be equal to **b, d**, and therefore by the 5th of the first book, angle **b, d, f** will be equal to angle **b, f, d**. 

However, it is established from the last [proposition] of the sixth book that angle **g, c, b** is four times angle **b, c, d**, because arc **g, b** is four times arc **b, d**. But indeed, by the 32nd of the first book, angle **g, c, b** is double angle **b, d, c**, for it is the exterior angle to the two [interior] angles **b, d, c** and **d, b, c**, which are equal by the 5th of the first book. Therefore, angle **b, d, c** is double angle **b, c, d**. Wherefore angle **b, f, d** is also double angle **b, c, f**. But angle **b, f, d** is equal to the two interior angles **b, c, f** and **c, b, f** by the 32nd of the first book. Thus the two angles **b, c, f** and **c, b, f** are equal; and therefore by the 6th of the first book, **c, f** is equal to **b, f**. 

And therefore **c, f** is also equal to **b, d**, for **b, d** and **b, f** are equal to each other. Wherefore half of **c, d** with half of **b, d** is as much as half of **c, d** with half of **c, f**. But indeed, half of **c, d** with half of **c, f** is as much as half of **c, f** twice, with half of **f, d**. Now, half of **c, f** twice is as much as **c, f**, and half of **f, d** is as much as **e, f**. Thus **c, e** is as much as half of **c, d** with half of **d, b**, which is what was proposed <note>original: "qd̄ ē ppositū" (quod est propositum), a phrase marking the completion of a proof, equivalent to Q.E.D.</note>. 

The conclusion stands thus: it is manifest from the 8th [proposition] of the thirteenth book that a perpendicular drawn from the center of a circle to the side of an inscribed <term>triangle</term><note>An equilateral triangle.</note> is equal to half of the line drawn from the center to the circumference <note>The radius.</note>; this indeed is demonstrated there and is concluded as a sort of corollary. Since, therefore, from this first [proposition] of this 14th book, it is clear that the perpendicular drawn from the center of a circle to the side of a <term>pentagon</term><note>A five-sided polygon.</note> is equal to half of the line drawn from the center to the circumference and half of the side of the decagon; it follows that the perpendicular drawn from the center of the circle to the side of the pentagon is equal to the perpendicular drawn from the center to the side of the triangle, plus half of the side of the decagon inscribed within the same circle. And this is what is proposed by the conception.

Now, therefore, must be explained what **Aristeus** <note>Aristeus the Elder (c. 370–300 BC), a Greek mathematician who wrote on regular solids.</note> says in the book entitled *Exposition of the Knowledge of the 5 Bodies*, as well as **Apollonius** <note>Apollonius of Perga (c. 240–190 BC), known as the 'Great Geometer' for his work on conic sections.</note> in his second endowment, concerning the proportionality of the figure of 12 bases to the figure of 20 bases: that the ratio of the surfaces of a figure having 12 bases <note>The dodecahedron.</note> to the surfaces of a figure having 20 bases <note>The icosahedron.</note> is the same as the ratio of the volume of the 12-based body to the 20-based body. 

For the line drawn from the center of the pentagonal face of the 12-based figure (the dodecahedron) to its circumference is like the aforementioned line from the center of the triangular face of the 20-based figure (the icosahedron) to its circumference. These are the words of the great Apollonius himself. They are to be understood concerning a figure of 12 and a figure of 20 bases that can both be circumscribed by one and the same sphere. For the ratio of the volume of the dodecahedron to the volume of the icosahedron, when both are circumscribed by the same sphere, is as the ratio of all the surfaces of the dodecahedron taken together to all the surfaces of the icosahedron taken together, just as Apollonius records in the first part of the aforementioned words. 

This is also established by a solid demonstration in the tenth [proposition] of this 14th book. And the circle circumscribing the pentagonal face of the dodecahedron is equal to the circle circumscribing the triangular face of the icosahedron when the dodecahedron and the icosahedron are circumscribed by the same sphere, just as Apollonius himself records in the second part of the aforementioned words. This is also confirmed in the fifth demonstration of this book. Therefore, the preceding matters must be set forth to corroborate the pronouncements of such great men with unshakable truth.

<note>On the right side of the page, there is a geometric diagram consisting of two parallel horizontal lines. The top line is marked with four points, labeled from left to right: 'a', 'c', 'b', and 'g'. The bottom line is marked with four points, labeled from left to right: 'd', 'f', 'e', and 'h'. Whatever happens to one line divided according to the <term>proportion having a mean and two extremes</term><note>original: "proportione habentem medium et duo extrema." This is the classical definition of the Golden Ratio: a line is divided such that the ratio of the whole line to the larger segment is the same as the ratio of the larger segment to the smaller one.</note> is proven to happen to every line divided in the same way, etc.

Let each of the two lines **a, b** and **d, e** be divided according to the proportion having a mean and two extremes; the first at point **c** and the second at point **f**. Let the greater segments be **a, c** for the first and **d, f** for the second. I say, therefore, that the ratio of both [whole lines] to their greater segments is one and the same ratio; likewise, the ratio of both to their smaller segments is one ratio, and also the ratio of the greater segments to the smaller ones is one; and the same applies conversely, alternately, combined, separately, and by conversion. For whatever happens to one of them is nothing other than what happens to the other.

It is established from the definition of a line divided according to the proportion having a mean and two extremes, and from the first part of the 16th [proposition] of the sixth book: that the rectangle formed by **a, b** and **b, c** is equal to the square of **a, c**. In the same way, the rectangle formed by **d, e** and **e, f** is equal to the square of **d, f**. Therefore, the ratio of the rectangle of **a, b** and **b, c** to the square of **a, c** is the same as the ratio of the rectangle of **d, e** and **e, f** to the square of **d, f**, for both are a ratio of equality. Therefore, four times the rectangle of **a, b** and **b, c** to the square of **a, c** is as four times the rectangle of **d, e** and **e, f** to the square of **d, f**, which follows from the 15th [proposition] of the fifth book. By alternating and equal proportionality, it is manifest that, by combining, four times the rectangle of **a, b** and **b, c** plus the square of **a, c** compared to the square of **a, c** is as four times the rectangle of **d, e** and **e, f** plus the square of **d, f** compared to the square of **d, f**.

Now, let a line **b, g** be added to the line **a, b** in a straight line, which is equal to **b, c**; and to **d, e**, let a line **e, h** be added, equal to **e, f**. It is therefore manifest from the 8th [proposition] of the second book that four times the rectangle of **a, b** and **b, g** plus the square of **a, c** is equal to the square of line **a, g**. Similarly, four times the rectangle of **d, e** and **e, h** plus the square of **d, f** is equal to the square of **d, h**.

But indeed, from common knowledge, four times the rectangle of **a, b** and **b, c** is equal to four times the rectangle of **a, b** and **b, g**, because **b, c** and **b, g** are equal. Similarly, four times the rectangle of **d, e** and **e, f** is equal to four times the rectangle of **d, e** and **e, h**, because **e, f** and **e, h** are also equal. Therefore, from the first part of the 7th of the fifth book and the 11th of the same fifth book, the square of **a, g** is to the square of **a, c** as the square of **d, h** is to the square of **d, f**.

Wherefore, from the second part of the 21st [proposition] of the sixth book, the ratio of line **a, g** to line **a, c** is as the ratio of line **d, h** to line **d, f**. And by combining, **a, g** and **a, c** are to **a, c** as **d, h** and **d, f** are to **d, f**. But indeed, **a, g** with **a, c** is the same as double **a, b**, and **d, h** with **d, f** is the same as double **d, e**. Therefore, double **a, b** is to **a, c** as double **d, e** is to **d, f**. And alternately, double **a, b** is to double **d, e** as **a, c** is to **d, f**. But double **a, b** is to double **d, e** as **a, b** is to **d, e** from the 15th of the fifth book. Therefore, **a, b** is to **d, e** as **a, c** is to **d, f**. Thus, [the same holds] alternately, and by reversal, and by conversion, and separately, and combined; which was what had to be shown.

line **a.b.** Since, therefore, each of the two lines **a.b.** and **a.d.** is divided according to the <term>proportion having a mean and two extremes</term><note>The Golden Ratio.</note>, there will be, by the preceding [proposition], one same ratio for both of them to their greater portions. Or otherwise: to the line **a.b.** let there be added **b.d.** equal to **b.c.**; and by the fourth [proposition] of the thirteenth [book], the whole line **a.d.** will be divided according to the proportion having a mean and two extremes, and its greater portion is the line **a.b.** Thus, by the first part of the ninth [proposition] of the thirteenth [book], which we demonstrated immediately following it, in whatever circle line **a.b.** is the side of the hexagon, in that same [circle] line **b.d.**—and therefore line **b.c.**, which is equal to it—is the side of the decagon. 

We can also demonstrate the same thing by another way, if it pleases. For let **e.f.** be equal to **a.b.**, which is also divided at **g** according to the proportion having a mean and two extremes, and let its greater portion be the line **f.g.** It is established, therefore, from the premise that just as **a.b.** is equal to **e.f.**, so **a.c.** is equal to **e.g.** and **c.b.** is equal to **g.f.** And since **b.d.** was added to **a.b.** as the side of the decagon of that circle in which **a.b.** is the side of the hexagon, it will be, as was said before from the ninth [proposition] of the thirteenth [book], that the whole line **a.d.** is divided according to the proportion having a mean and two extremes, and its greater portion will be line **a.b.** Thus, by the premise, **a.b.** is to **b.d.** as **f.g.** is to **g.e.** Therefore, by the first part of the fifteenth [proposition] of the sixth [book], that which is formed by **a.b.** and **g.e.** is equal to that which is formed by **b.d.** and **f.g.** And since **a.b.** is equal to **e.f.**, that which is formed by **e.f.** and **g.e.** is equal to that which is formed by **b.d.** and **f.g.** But that which is formed by **e.f.** and **g.e.** is equal to the square of **f.g.** by the definition of a line divided according to the proportion having a mean and two extremes and from the first part of the sixteenth [proposition] of the sixth [book]. Therefore, that which is formed by **b.d.** and **f.g.** is equal to the square of **f.g.**; thus, from the first [proposition] of the sixth [book], line **b.d.** is equal to **f.g.** And because **f.g.** is equal to **c.b.**, **c.b.** will also be equal to **b.d.** and the side of the decagon, which was to be shown.

The pentagon of the figure with twelve bases <note>Dodecahedron</note> and the triangle of the figure with twenty bases <note>Icosahedron</note>, which the same sphere circumscribes, are circumscribed by one and the same circle.

¶ Let there be a sphere whose diameter is **a.b.** circumscribing two solid figures, namely the dodecahedron, of which one of the twelve pentagons is **c.**, and the icosahedron, of which one of the 20 triangles is **d.** Now, let two circles be circumscribed about the pentagon **c.** and the triangle **d.** upon two centers, **d.** and **c.**; for the former, circle **f.c.** by the 14th [proposition] of the fourth [book], and for the latter, circle **f.d.** by the 5th [proposition] of the same [book].
