## Proposition 6.

The area <note>original: "quadratum"</note> which is thirtyfold the rectangle <note>original: "tetragoni"</note> contained under the perpendicular drawn from the center of the circle circumscribing the pentagon of the twelve-faced figure <note>the dodecahedron</note> to the side of the pentagon, and under the side of that same pentagon, is of necessity proved to be equal to all the surfaces of the twelve-faced body taken together.

¶ Let pentagon **a** be one of the 12 bases of the dodecahedron figure, and let one of its sides be **b.c.**; and let there be circumscribed around it, according to the 14th [proposition] of the fourth [book], a circle about center **a**. Let lines **a.b.**, **a.c.**, and **a.d.** (perpendicular to **b.c.**) be drawn. I say, therefore, that thirty times the rectangle produced from **a.d.** and **b.c.** is equal to all the surfaces of the dodecahedron taken together. For it is established that pentagon **a** is divisible into five triangles equal to triangle **a.b.c.** from the 8th [proposition] of the first [book]. Thus, all 12 pentagons of the dodecahedron—since they are all equal and similar to pentagon **a**—are divisible into 60 triangles, each of which (by the 8th of the first book) is equal to triangle **a.b.c.** The rectangle produced from **a.d.** and **b.c.** is double the triangle **a.b.c.** by the 41st [proposition] of the first [book]; therefore, thirty times the rectangle of **a.d.** and **b.c.** is sixtyfold triangle **a.b.c.**, for as the simple is to the simple, so is the double to the double. Since, therefore, all the surfaces of the dodecahedron taken together are sixtyfold the triangle **a.b.c.**, it follows that thirty times the rectangle produced from **a.d.** and **b.c.** is equal to all the surfaces of the dodecahedron taken together, which is what was proposed.

### Proposition 8.

The ratio of all the surfaces of the body of twelve bases <note>the dodecahedron</note> taken together to all the surfaces of the body of twenty bases <note>the icosahedron</note> taken together, which are both circumscribed by the same sphere, is the same as the ratio of the side of the cube which the same sphere circumscribes to the side of the triangle of that same body of twenty bases.

For example, let the line **a.b.** be divided according to a ratio having a mean and two extremes at point **c.**, and let its greater portion be **a.c.** Let **d.e.** be a line equal to half of **a.b.**, and **d.f.** be half of **a.c.** I say, therefore, that **d.e.** is divided at **f.** according to a ratio having a mean and two extremes, and its greater portion is **d.f.** For it is established from the 15th [proposition] of the fifth book that the ratio of **a.b.** to **a.c.** is the same as the ratio of **d.e.** to **d.f.**, namely double to double is as single to single; wherefore by permutation, **a.b.** is to **d.e.** as **a.c.** is to **d.f.** Therefore, by the 19th [proposition] of the fifth book, **c.b.** is to **f.e.** as **a.b.** is to **d.e.** Thus, **c.b.** is double **f.e.**, just as **a.b.** is double **d.e.** Since, therefore, the whole **a.b.** is double the whole **d.e.**, and the individual parts of **a.b.** correspond to the individual parts of **d.e.** <note>in the same double ratio</note>, wherefore from the 15th of the fifth and the 11th of the same, and by the division of the line...

Therefore, by the 2nd [proposition] of this book, the ratio of **b.** to **a.b.** is as **d.e.** to **g.d.** Wherefore, by the first part of the 15th [proposition] of the sixth [book]: the product of **b.** and **g.d.** is equal to the product of **a.b.** and **d.e.** From the preceding corollary, it is manifest that the ratio of all the surfaces of the dodecahedron (whose side is **a.b.**) taken together to all the surfaces of the icosahedron (whose side is **a.c.**) taken together is as the product of **a.b.** and **d.e.** to the product of **a.c.** and **g.d.** Therefore, from the first part of the 7th [proposition] of the fifth [book] and the 11th of the same, the ratio of the product of **b.** and **g.d.** to the product of **a.c.** and **g.d.** is as the surfaces of the dodecahedron to the surfaces of this icosahedron. But indeed, the ratio of the product of **b.** and **g.d.** to the product of **a.c.** and **g.d.** is, by the 1st [proposition] of the sixth [book], as **b.** to **a.c.** Thus, by the 11th [proposition] of the fifth [book], the ratio of all the surfaces of that dodecahedron to all the surfaces of this icosahedron is as **b.** to **a.c.**, which is what was proposed. We can prove this same thing in another way, if we first grant a necessary antecedent, which is: **¶ If an equilateral pentagon is inscribed in any circle, the rectangle contained by three-quarters <note>original: "dodrante"</note> of the diameter of that circle and by five-sixths <note>original: "dextante"</note> of the line subtending the angle of that pentagon is necessarily equal to the area of the same pentagon.** ¶ Our ancestors divided every whole into 12 equal parts by intellect and reason, and all these parts together they called the **As** <note>original: "assem"</note>. Eleven of these parts they called a **Deunx**; ten, a **Dextans**; nine, a **Dodrans**; eight, a **Bisse**; seven, a **Septunx**, **Septans**, or **Quicunx**; six, a **Semis**; five, a **Quincunx**; four, a **Triens**; three, a **Quadrans**; two, a **Sextans**; and one they called an **Uncia**. These they designated in order with such figures as are very often found in ancient books:

# BOOK 14

<header>XIV</header>

¶ The ounce <note>original: uncia</note>, which we have already said is the twelfth part of the *as* <note>The 'as' was the basic Roman unit for weight or currency, divided into 12 ounces.</note>, is itself divided into 12 further fractions. However, they divided it in another way. For they called half of an ounce a **half-ounce** <note>semivncia</note>. A third part they called a **duella**. A fourth part, a **sicilicus**. A sixth part, a **sexcula**. An eighth part, a **drachma** <note>dragma</note>. A twelfth part, a **semisicilicus** <note>semiſſiclā</note>. An eighteenth part, a **tremis** <note>tremiſſem</note>. A twenty-fourth part, a **scruple** <note>ſcrupulū</note>. A forty-eighth part, an **obolus**. A seventy-second part, a **bissiliqua**. A ninety-sixth part, a **carat** <note>ceratē</note>. The very last, which is the 144th part of the ounce itself, they named a **siliqua**. To these twelve fractions of the ounce, later writers added the **calculus**. A *calculus* is the 192nd part of an ounce; the reason for this addition was so that the naming of these fractions could ascend or extend to the smallest extreme of the harmonies of the *fourth* <note>diateſſeron</note> and *fifth* <note>diapente</note>, which are distinguished by the intervals of tones and semitones. They marked all of these in order with the following figures:

¶ Therefore, the meaning of what is stated is this: that if an equilateral pentagon is inscribed in any circle, the product of three-quarters of the diameter of the circle and five-sixths <note>original: dextans; a Roman term for ten-twelfths or five-sixths</note> of the line subtending one of the angles of the inscribed pentagon is equal to the area of the pentagon. For example: Let there be a circle **a.b.c.** with center **d.**, and let there be inscribed in it (according to the 11th proposition of the Fourth Book) an equilateral pentagon, two sides of which, containing one of its angles, are **a.b.** and **b.c.** Let the line **a.c.** subtend the angle at **b.**, and let the diameter **b.d.e.** be drawn, cutting the line **a.c.** into equal parts at point **g.** Let **d.f.** be half of **d.e.**, and let **g.b.** be double **b.e.** Then **b.f.** will be three-quarters <note>original: dodrans; a Roman term for nine-twelfths</note> of the diameter; for it is three parts out of four of it. And **a.b.** will be the five-sixths <note>original: dextans</note> or sixths of **a.c.**; for it is five-sixths of it. Now let line **a.d.** be drawn: I say that the product of **b.f.** and **a.b.** is equal to the pentagon inscribed in the circle. For since **a.g.** is perpendicular to **b.d.**, it follows from the 41st proposition of the First Book that the product of **b.d.** and **a.g.** is double the triangle **a.b.d.** Therefore, the product of **b.f.** and **a.g.** will be triple that same triangle, and the product of **b.f.** and **b.g.** will be double, and the product of **b.f.** and the whole line **a.b.** will be fivefold. Since the entire pentagon is five times that same triangle, it is established that the product of **b.f.** and **a.b.** is equal to the pentagon, and that was what was to be demonstrated.

¶ Therefore, regarding the proposition from the beginning, let us now demonstrate by another way as we promised. Let there be inscribed in a circle with center **b.** a pentagon of the 12-faced figure <term>dodecahedron</term> and a triangle of the 20-faced figure <term>icosahedron</term> which the same sphere circumscribes. For it is established from the 5th proposition of this book that the pentagon of this dodecahedron and the triangle of that icosahedron are circumscribed by the same circle. Let the pentagon be **a.b.c.d.e.** and the triangle **a.f.g.**, and let line **b.e.** subtend angle **a.** of the pentagon, which from the demonstration of the 17th proposition of the Thirteenth Book will be the side of the cube that the same sphere encloses. Let the diameter **a.b.k.** be drawn, cutting both lines **b.e.** and **f.g.** perpendicularly and into equal parts—the latter at point **l.** and the former at point **m.** I say then that the ratio of all the surfaces of the dodecahedron to all the surfaces of the icosahedron (where the pentagon and triangle are inscribed in the proposed circle) is as line **b.e.** (the side of the cube enclosed by the same sphere) is to line **f.g.** (the side of the triangle of the icosahedron). For it is clear from the corollary of the 8th proposition of the Thirteenth Book that line **b.m.** is half of line **a.b.**, and therefore **a.m.** will be three-quarters <note>original: dodrans</note> of the diameter **a.k.**; for it is three-fourths of it. Let **l.n.** be double **n.e.**, and **b.n.** will be five-sixths <note>original: dextans</note> of **b.e.**; for it is five parts of its sixth part. Thus, by the preceding premise, the product of **a.m.** and **b.n.** will be equal to the pentagon **a.b.c.d.e.** Moreover, the product of **a.m.** and **m.f.** is equal to the triangle **a.f.g.** Therefore, from the 1st proposition of the Sixth Book, the ratio of the pentagon to the triangle is as **b.n.** to **m.f.** Wherefore, twelve times that pentagon to twenty times this triangle are as twelve times the line **b.n.** to twenty times the line **m.f.**, which is manifest from the 15th proposition of the Fifth Book and by equal proportionality. Moreover, twelve times **b.n.** is as ten times **b.e.**, for 12...

Furthermore, the twenty-fold area of *m.f.g.* is as the ten-fold area of *f.g.* Since *f.g.* is double to *m.f.*, therefore two times the ten-fold of that pentagon to the twenty-fold of that triangle is as the ten-fold of *b.e.* to the ten-fold of *f.g.* And because twelve times the area of that pentagon is the total surface of the dodecahedron, and twenty times the area of this triangle is the total surface of the icosahedron, and because (by the 15th proposition of the fifth book) the ratio of the ten-fold of *b.e.* to the ten-fold of *f.g.* is the same as the simple ratio of *b.e.* to *f.g.*, it will follow (by the 11th proposition of the fifth book) that the ratio of all the surfaces of the dodecahedron taken together to all the surfaces of the icosahedron taken together is as *b.e.* to *f.g.* And this is what we were required to demonstrate.

## Proposition 9

<margin>
<note>A circular geometric diagram contains an inscribed pentagon and an equilateral triangle. The center of the circle is labeled 'a'. Pentagon vertices are labeled 'd', 'e', 'b', and 'c'. Additional points 'f' and 'g' are labeled within the circle, and a chord 'e-g' is drawn.</note>
</margin>

If any line is divided according to a ratio having a mean and two extremes <note>This refers to the "Golden Ratio," where the whole line is to the larger segment as the larger segment is to the smaller.</note>, the ratio of the line whose square is equal to the squares of the whole line and its greater segment, to the line whose square is equal to the squares of the whole line and its lesser segment, will be as the ratio of the side of a cube to the side of the triangle of the twenty-based body <note>term: "corpus viginti basium," referring to the icosahedron</note> together with the cube itself contained in the same sphere.

¶ Let the line *a.b.* be divided according to a ratio having a mean and two extremes, and let its greater segment be the line *a.c.* Let a circle *d.b.e.* be described around the center *a.* according to the length of the line *a.b.* In this circle, let an equilateral pentagon be inscribed (from the 11th proposition of the fourth book) whose one side is *d.e.*, and from the second proposition of the same book, an equilateral triangle whose one side is *d.f.* Let the line *e.g.* subtend one of the angles of the pentagon, which is *d.* It is established, therefore, from the 5th proposition of this book, that the sphere circumscribing the dodecahedron whose pentagon side is *d.e.* also circumscribes the icosahedron whose triangle side is *d.f.* From the demonstration of the 17th proposition of the thirteenth book, it is manifest that the same sphere circumscribes the cube whose side is *e.g.* 

Therefore, let line *h.* be taken as the line whose square is equal to the whole line *a.b.* and its greater segment *a.c.* <note>h² = ab² + ac²</note>, and let *k.* be taken as the line whose square is equal to the whole line *a.b.* and its lesser segment *b.c.* <note>k² = ab² + bc²</note>. I say, then, that the ratio of *e.g.* to *d.f.*—that is, the side of the cube to the side of the triangle of the icosahedron contained by the same sphere as the cube—is as *h.* to *k.* 

It is indeed established from the corollary of the 15th proposition of the fourth book that *a.b.* is as the side of a hexagon inscribed in the circle *b.d.e.* Therefore, from the third proposition of this book, *a.c.* is as the side of a decagon <note>a ten-sided polygon</note> of the same circle. Thus, by the 10th proposition of the thirteenth book, the square of *d.e.* is equal to the squares of the whole *a.b.* and its greater segment *a.c.*, wherefore *d.e.* is equal to *h.*, for the square of each of them is as much as the squares of the two lines *a.b.* and *a.c.* taken together. 

Furthermore, it is clear from the 8th proposition of the thirteenth book that the square of *d.f.* is triple the square of *a.b.* But indeed, from the 5th proposition of the same book, it is evident that the square of *k.* is also triple the square of *a.c.* Therefore, from the second part of the 21st proposition of the sixth book, the ratio of *d.f.* to *a.b.* is as *k.* to *a.c.* By permutation, *d.f.* is to *k.* as *a.b.* is to *a.c.* 

And because from the demonstration of the 17th proposition of the thirteenth book it is manifest that if *e.g.* is divided according to a ratio having a mean and two extremes, its greater portion will be as *d.e.*, it will be (by the 2nd proposition of this book) that the ratio of *e.g.* to *d.e.* is as *a.b.* to *a.c.* Wherefore, by the 11th proposition of the fifth book, *e.g.* to *d.e.* will also be as *d.f.* to *k.*, and by permutation, *e.g.* to *d.f.* as *d.e.* to *k.* And since (by the first part of the 7th proposition of the fifth book) *d.e.* is to *k.* as *h.* is to *k.*—because *d.e.* and *h.* are equal—it will be (by the 11th proposition of the fifth book) that *e.g.* is to *d.f.* as *h.* is to *k.*, which is what was proposed. 

Not only, however, is the ratio of the cube's side *e.g.* to the icosahedron's triangle side *d.f.* as *h.* to *k.*, but it is simply as any two lines, one to the other, where one's square equals the whole of any line divided in extreme and mean ratio plus its greater segment, and the other's square equals the whole plus its lesser segment. For the ratio of such individual lines is the same. For example: let the previous hypotheses regarding lines *a.b.*, *h.*, and *k.* remain, and let any other line *l.m.* also be taken, divided according to a ratio having a mean and two extremes at point *n.*, and let the greater portion be *l.n.* Let line *p.* be the line whose square equals the whole *l.m.* and its greater segment *l.n.*, and let line *q.* be the line whose square...

</margin>

upon the whole line *l.m.* and its smaller portion *m.n.* I say, therefore, that the ratio of *p* to *q* is as *b* to *k*. For it is established from the second [proposition] of this [book] that *b* to *a* is as *l.m.* to *l.n.* Therefore, by the first part of the 21st [proposition] of the sixth [book], the ratio of the square of *b* to the square of *a* is as the square of *m.l.* to the square of *n.l.* Wherefore, by composition <note>In Euclidean geometry, "composition" of a ratio refers to adding the consequent to the antecedent (if a:b, then a+b:b).</note>, the square of *b* to the square of *a.c.* is as the square of *p* to the square of *l.n.*, and by permutation, the square of *b* to the square of *p* is as the square of *a.c.* to the square of *l.n.* By the same type of argument, it follows that the ratio of the square of *k* to the square of *q* is as the square of *c.b.* to the square of *m.n.* And because from the second [proposition] of this [book] and from the first part of the 21st [proposition] of the sixth [book], the square of *a.c.* is to the square of *l.n.* as the square of *c.b.* is to the square of *m.n.*, it will follow from the 11th [proposition] of the fifth [book] that the square of *b* to the square of *p* is as the square of *k* to the square of *q*. Wherefore, by the second part of the 21st [proposition] of the sixth [book], *b* is to *p* as *k* is to *q*. And by permutation, *b* is to *k* as *p* is to *q*, which was to be demonstrated. And lest any room for doubt should obscure those things which remain to be demonstrated, we think certain things should yet be set forth first, so that the following matters may remain unshaken by the firm strength of demonstration.

¶ **If any plane surface cuts any sphere, the common boundary** <note>original: "communis differentia"</note> **of the cutting plane surface and the curved surface of the sphere will be a circumference containing a circle.**

<margin>
<note>A geometric diagram depicts a circle representing a cross-section of a sphere. Point 'd' is the center of the sphere, located above the plane of the circle. Point 'c' is the center of the circle in the plane. Lines 'd-a' and 'd-b' are radii of the sphere extending to the circumference of the cross-section. Line 'd-c' is the perpendicular from the sphere's center to the plane. Lines 'c-a' and 'c-b' are radii of the resulting circle.</note>
</margin>

¶ Let there be, therefore, some plane surface cutting a sphere, and let the line *a.b.* be the common section of the cutting surface and the surface of the sphere. I say that the line *a.b.* is the circumference of a circle. For the center of the sphere is either in the cutting plane surface or outside it. If it is within it, let it be placed wherever it happens to be, and let it be *c*. Since, therefore, the whole line *a.b.* is on the surface of the sphere, and since all lines drawn from the center of the sphere to its circumference are equal—as is established from the definition of a sphere—it follows that all lines drawn from point *c* to line *a.b.* are equal. Therefore, by the definition of a circle, the surface which the line *a.b.* contains is a circle, and its center is *c*, namely the same as the center of the sphere. If, however, the center of the sphere is outside the cutting surface, let it be placed anywhere and let it be *d*. From this, according to the teaching of the 11th [proposition] of the eleventh [book], let the line *d.c.* be drawn perpendicular to the cutting surface; and from the same center *d*, let two straight lines be drawn to any points on the line *a.b.*, which shall be *d.a.* and *d.b.*, and let *c* be joined with *a* and with *b*. And the two lines *d.a.* and *d.b.* will be equal because they [extend] from the center of the sphere to its surface. Furthermore, from the definition of a line perpendicular to a surface, it is manifest that the angles *d.c.a.* and *d.c.b.* are right angles. Therefore, by the penultimate [proposition] of the first [book] <note>The Pythagorean Theorem, Proposition I.47</note> and by this common notion—that things which are equal to the same thing are equal to each other—the squares of the two lines *c.d.* and *c.a.* taken together will be equal to the squares of the two lines *d.c.* and *c.b.* taken together. Thus, the square of *d.c.* being removed from both sides, the square of *c.a.* will be equal to the square of *c.b.*, wherefore also line *c.a.* [is equal] to line *c.b.* By the same kind of reasoning, it is necessary that all lines drawn from point *c* to line *a.b.* be equal; therefore, by the definition of a circle, the surface which line *a.b.* contains is a circle, and its center is *c*, which was proposed.

¶ **From this it is manifest that when a surface cuts a sphere through its center, the resulting section on the surface of the sphere is a line containing a circle whose center is the center of the sphere. When, however, the surface cuts the sphere not through its center, the section produced on the surface of the sphere is also a line containing a circle, whose center is that point upon which falls the perpendicular drawn from the center of the sphere to the cutting surface.**

¶ Furthermore, I say that:

¶ **If in any sphere there are equal circles, the perpendiculars drawn from the center of the sphere to the surfaces of those circles will be equal to each other.**

<margin>

¶ Let there be two equal circles, **b** and **c**, marked in a sphere whose center is **a**. Let perpendiculars be drawn from the center of the sphere—namely from point **a**—to their surfaces, following the method taught in the 11th proposition of the eleventh book: specifically **a.b.** to the first circle and **a.c.** to the second. I say that the two lines **a.b.** and **a.c.** are equal. For let straight lines be drawn from points **b** and **c** to the circumferences of those circles as one pleases: in this one **b.d.**, and in that one **c.e.**, and join **a.d.** and **a.e.** And since, by the definition of a line standing perpendicularly upon a surface, each of the two angles **a.b.d.** and **a.c.e.** is a right angle. But indeed, from the second part of the preceding corollary, it is manifest that the two points **b** and **c** are the centers of circles **b** and **c**, and therefore the two lines **b.d.** and **c.e.** are their radii <note>Original: *semidiametri*</note>. Since these circles are defined as equal, it follows from the definition of equal circles that these radii are equal. And because the two lines **a.d.** and **a.e.** are equal—as they are drawn from the center of the sphere to its surface—it will follow from the penultimate proposition of the first book <note>This refers to Proposition I.47, the Pythagorean Theorem, which is the second-to-last in Book I.</note> that the two perpendiculars **a.b.** and **a.c.** are equal, which was to be demonstrated. Now, therefore, let us return to the proposal.

->Proposition 10<-

**T**he ratio of the body <note>In this context, "body" refers to the volume of the solid.</note> of a dodecahedron to the body of an icosahedron, when both are enclosed by one and the same sphere, is as the ratio of all its surfaces taken together to all the surfaces of the other taken together.
¶ This is what we mentioned earlier, following the demonstration of the first proposition of this book, on the authority of Aristaeus and Apollonius <note>Aristaeus the Elder and Apollonius of Perga were Greek mathematicians whose works on "Comparison of the Regular Solids" are synthesized here in Book XIV.</note>; the demonstration of it is evidently drawn from those things which preceded. From the fifth proposition of this book, it is manifest that the circles—of which one circumscribes the pentagonal face of the dodecahedron and the other the triangular face of the icosahedron, both bodies being contained by one sphere—are equal to each other. Therefore, the perpendiculars drawn from the center of the sphere to the surfaces of all the circles circumscribing the pentagons of this dodecahedron and the triangles of that icosahedron, falling into their centers, will be equal to each other, as is manifest from the preceding. For all these circles, according to the fifth proposition of this book, are equal to each other. Now, the pyramids whose bases are the pentagons of the dodecahedron and whose vertices <note>Original: *coni*, literally "cones," but here used for the apex of the pyramids.</note> are at the center of the sphere, and the pyramids whose bases are the triangles of the icosahedron and whose vertices are likewise at the center of the sphere, are of equal height. The height of all these pyramids is measured or determined by the perpendiculars falling from the vertices to the bases. It is necessary for pyramids of equal height to be proportional to their bases, just as was proved in the sixth proposition of the twelfth book. Thus, the ratio of a pyramid whose base is a pentagon of the dodecahedron to a pyramid whose base is a triangle of the icosahedron is as the ratio of that pentagon to that triangle. Therefore, by the 24th proposition of the fifth book, the ratio of twelve times <note>Original: *duodecupli*</note> that pyramid whose base is a pentagon of the dodecahedron to the pyramid whose base is a triangle of the icosahedron is as twelve times that pentagon to that triangle. Now, these 12 pyramids whose bases are the 12 pentagons of the dodecahedron constitute the whole body of the dodecahedron itself. And the 12 pentagons constitute all its surfaces. Thus, the ratio of the body of the dodecahedron to a pyramid whose base is a triangle of the icosahedron is as the ratio of all the surfaces of the dodecahedron to the triangle of the icosahedron. Wherefore, again by the 24th proposition of the fifth book, the ratio of the body of the dodecahedron to twenty times <note>Original: *vigincuplū*</note> that pyramid whose base is a triangle of the icosahedron is as all the surfaces of the dodecahedron to twenty times the triangle of the icosahedron. Since, therefore, twenty times this pyramid is as the whole body of the icosahedron, and twenty times that triangle is as all the surfaces of that icosahedron, the ratio of the body of the dodecahedron to the body of the icosahedron—both being enclosed within one and the same sphere—will be as the ratio of all the surfaces of the dodecahedron taken together to all the surfaces of the icosahedron taken together. This, then, is the fixed and solid opinion of the aforementioned philosophers concerning the ratio of these two bodies, strengthened by demonstration.

To this, the following must also be added: for since the ratio of the side of a cube to the side of the triangle <note>The "side of the triangle" refers to the edge of one of the twenty equilateral triangular faces of the icosahedron.</note> of the icosahedral body, both enclosed by the same sphere, is the same as the ratio of all the surfaces of the dodecahedron taken together to all the surfaces of the icosahedron enclosed in the same sphere, as was demonstrated in the 8th proposition of this book; it follows from the 11th proposition of the fifth book that the ratio of the body of the dodecahedron to the body of the icosahedron, both of which are circumscribed by one sphere, is the same as the ratio of the side of a cube inscribable in that same sphere to the side of the triangle of the icosahedron. Furthermore, since when any line is divided according to the ratio having a mean and two extremes <note>This is the classical definition of the Golden Ratio.</note>, the ratio of the line powerful over <note>In Euclidean geometry, "powerful over" (*potens super*) means the square of the line. The author is discussing the ratio of the squares of the segments.</note> the whole and its greater part to the line powerful over the whole and its lesser part is as the side of a cube inscribed in any sphere to the side of the triangle of the icosahedron circumscribed by the same sphere, as was demonstrated in the 9th proposition of this book; it will also be, from the 11th proposition of the fifth book, that when any line is divided according to the ratio having a mean and two extremes, the ratio of the line powerful over the whole and its greater part to the line powerful over the whole and its lesser part is as the ratio of the body of the dodecahedron to the body of the icosahedron, both of which one and the same sphere circumscribes. From these things, therefore, it is manifest that the ratio of the side of a cube inscribed in any sphere to the side of the triangle of the icosahedron circumscribed by the same sphere—likewise the ratio of all the surfaces of the dodecahedron to all the surfaces of the icosahedron, both circumscribed by the same sphere—and again, the ratio of the line powerful over any line divided according to the ratio having a mean and two extremes and over its greater part to the line powerful over the same and over its lesser part, and also the ratio of the body of the dodecahedron to the body of the icosahedron, both of which one and the same sphere contains, is one and the same ratio. Therefore, the power of a line divided according to the ratio having a mean and two extremes is wonderful: for while many things worthy of admiration by those philosophizing come together in it, this principal or particular quality proceeds from the invariable nature of higher principles, so that it rationally reconciles solids so diverse, both in magnitude and in the number of bases as well as in shape, in a certain **irrational symphony**. Indeed, it has been demonstrated that the ratio of the dodecahedron's body to the icosahedron's body, both of which one sphere encompasses, is as the ratio of the line powerful over any line divided according to the aforementioned ratio and its greater part, to any line powerful over the same and its lesser part. Since, however, we have said nothing regarding the three other regular bodies, let us strive to say something about them.

**In every equilateral triangle, if a perpendicular is drawn from one of its angles to the base, the side of the same triangle will be found to be sesquitertial in power to that perpendicular.** <note>A "sesquitertial" ratio (*sexquitertium*) is 4:3. "In power" means the square of the side is 4/3 the square of the altitude.</note>
¶ For let there be an equilateral triangle **a.b.c.**, and let the line **a.d.** be drawn from angle **a** perpendicular to the base. I say that **a.b.** is sesquitertial in power to **a.d.** From the 5th proposition of the first book, the two angles **b** and **c** are equal; and because the angles at **d** are right angles, the line **b.c.** will be divided into equal parts at point **d** by the 26th proposition of the first book. Therefore, from the fourth proposition of the second book, the square of **b.c.** is four times the square of **b.d.**, and thus also the square of **a.b.** is four times the square of **b.d.** For it is an equilateral triangle; therefore, by the penultimate proposition of the first book <note>The Pythagorean Theorem.</note>, the squares of the two lines **a.d.** and **b.d.** taken together are four times the square of **b.d.** Thus, the square of **a.d.** is three times the square of **b.d.** Therefore, the proposition is established.

In Euclid’s geometry, a line is "rational in power" if the area of the square built upon it is a rational number, even if the length of the line itself is an irrational square root.</note>; however, from the last part of the tenth book, by means of the premise, it will be incommensurable to line $a.b$, and therefore also to line $b.d$, which is as if its half. ->Proposition 13<-

<note>A geometric construction is shown in the left margin. At the top are three horizontal line segments of decreasing length, labeled 'a', 'b', and 'c' from top to bottom. All the surfaces of either of two solids—one being a pyramid of four triangular and equilateral bases <note>A tetrahedron</note> and the other being a body of eight triangular and equilateral bases <note>An octahedron</note>—taken together: if the diameter of the sphere circumscribing them is rational, they compose a medial surface.

For if the diameter of the sphere circumscribing either of the two proposed bodies is rational, whether in length or in power only: it will be from the first corollary of the 13th proposition of the thirteenth book that the side of the pyramid is rational in power, and from the first corollary of the 15th proposition of the same book, the side of the body of eight bases <note>The octahedron</note> is also rational in power. Wherefore, by the premise, the triangles which are the bases of either body will be medial surfaces. And because the triangles of either body are equal to one another: it will be from the 21st proposition of the tenth book that all the surfaces of either of them taken together compose a medial surface, just as was proposed, etc.

->Proposition 14<-

If one and the same sphere circumscribes a tetrahedron and an octahedron, one of the bases of the tetrahedron will be sesquitertial <note>A sesquitertial ratio is 4:3. In modern terms, the area of one face of the tetrahedron is 1.33 times the area of one face of the octahedron when both are in the same sphere.</note> to one of the bases of the octahedron; moreover, it is necessary that all the bases of the octahedron taken together have a sesquialterate <note>A sesquialterate ratio is 3:2 or 1.5:1. This means the total surface area of the octahedron is 1.5 times the total surface area of the tetrahedron.</note> proportion to all the bases of the tetrahedron taken together.

Let there be a sphere whose diameter is $a$, circumscribing a pyramid whose side is $b$, and an octahedron whose side is $c$. I say, therefore, that the equilateral triangle whose side is $b$ is sesquitertial to the equilateral triangle whose side is $c$, and that the surface composed of the eight equilateral triangles of which each side is $c$ is sesquialterate to the surface composed of the four equilateral triangles of which each side is $b$. For it is established from the corollaries of the 13th proposition of the thirteenth book that the square of $a$ is to the square of $b$ as 6 is to 4. Therefore, conversely, the square of $b$ is to the square of $a$ as 4 is to 6. From the corollary of the 15th proposition of the same book, it is manifest that the square of $a$ is to the square of $c$ as 6 is to 3. Thus, through equal proportionality, the square of $b$ is to the square of $c$ as 4 is to 3. But the square of $b$ is to the square of $c$ as the equilateral triangle whose side is $b$ is to the equilateral triangle whose side is $c$ (for in both cases it is as the side $b$ to $c$ in a duplicate ratio <note>A "duplicate ratio" in Euclidean terms is equivalent to squaring the ratio of the sides to find the ratio of the areas.</note>, according to the second part of the 18th proposition of the sixth book). Therefore, the equilateral triangle with side $b$ is to the equilateral triangle with side $c$ as 4 is to 3; wherefore the first part of the proposition is established. From this, the second part is evidently drawn: for by proportional conversion, the equilateral triangle with side $c$ will be to the equilateral triangle with side $b$ as 3 is to 4. Therefore, eight times the equilateral triangle with side $c$ is to four times the equilateral triangle with side $b$ as eight times three is to four times four. This is as 24 is to 16. And since eight times the equilateral triangle with side $c$ is all the bases of the octahedron, and four times the equilateral triangle with side $b$ is all the bases of the pyramid, and since the ratio of 24 to 16 is sesquialterate, it follows that the surface composed of all the bases of the octahedron is to the surface composed of all the bases of the pyramid in a sesquialterate proportion, just as we said.

### Proposition 15

If a pyramid of four triangular and equilateral bases <note>A tetrahedron, the simplest of the five Platonic solids, having four equal faces, each an equilateral triangle.</note> is placed within any sphere, it is necessarily proved that if a straight line is drawn from any of its angles through the center of the sphere to the base, it falls into the center of the circle circumscribing the base and stands perpendicularly upon that same base.

Let there be a pyramid $a.b.c.d$ of triangular and equilateral bases placed within a certain sphere whose center is $f$. And since any of the four angles of this pyramid can be its vertex <note>original: "conus", literally "cone," referring here to the apex or top point of the pyramid.</note> and any of the four triangles its base: let us imagine now its solid angle $a$ to be the vertex and imagine triangle $b.c.d$ to be the base. Let us understand circle $b.c.d$ to be circumscribed around this base. Then, from point $a$, which we have imagined as the vertex of the pyramid, let us draw to the base $b.c.d$ a straight line passing through point $f$, which is the center of the sphere circumscribing the pyramid about which we are discussing; and let this line meet the surface $b.c.d$, which we imagined as the base of the pyramid, at point $e$. I say therefore that point $e$ is the center of circle $b.c.d$ and that line $a.f.e$ is perpendicular to surface $b.c.d$.

For I will produce lines $f.b, f.c, f.d$; and because the four points $a, b, c, d$ are on the surface of the sphere whose center is $f$ (because it was stated that this sphere circumscribes this pyramid), all four lines $f.a, f.b, f.c, f.d$ will be equal to one another, for they are drawn from the center of the sphere to its surface. Therefore, because the two sides $a.f$ and $f.b$ of triangle $a.f.b$ are equal to the two sides $a.f$ and $f.c$ of triangle $a.f.c$, and the base $a.b$ is equal to base $a.c$ (for the pyramid was stated to be equilateral): it will be from the eighth proposition of the first book that angle $a.f.b$ is equal to angle $a.f.c$. And therefore by the 13th of the first book, angle $b.f.e$ will also be equal to angle $c.f.e$. In the same way you will prove angle $d.f.e$ to be equal to angle $c.f.e$; for it is necessary from the eighth of the first that angle $a.f.e$ <note>The text likely intended to compare triangles $a.f.c$ and $a.f.d$ to establish the equality of the angles at the base.</note> be equal to angle $a.f.d$, whereby by the 13th of the first, angle $c.f.e$ will also be equal to angle $d.f.e$. Therefore the three angles $b.f.e, c.f.e, d.f.e$ are equal to one another.

Therefore, lines $e.b, e.c$, and $e.d$ having been drawn, it follows from the fourth proposition of the first book, applied twice, that they are equal to one another. And therefore by the 9th of the third book, point $e$ is the center of circle $b.c.d$. And because the perpendicular drawn from the center of a sphere to the surface of any circle intersecting it falls upon the center of that same circle—as you have learned from those things which were demonstrated before, namely from those which immediately precede the tenth proposition of this book—it is proven that line $a.f.e$ is perpendicular to the surface of the circle $b.c.d$ <note>Original text says "a.b.c", which appears to be a typesetting error for the base "b.c.d".</note>, just as is proposed. If it were otherwise, there would be two centers of the same circle, which nature abhors as an impossibility.

### Proposition 16

A solid of eight triangular and equilateral bases <note>An octahedron, a Platonic solid with eight faces, each an equilateral triangle.</note> that is circumscribed by a sphere is divisible into two pyramids of equal height, whose height is equal to the radius <note>original: "semidiametro".</note> of the sphere; moreover, the base of each is a square which is half the square of the diameter of the sphere.

Let there be a body of eight triangular and equilateral bases whose six angles are $a, b, c, d, e, f$, circumscribed by a sphere whose center is $g$. It is established, therefore, that the six points $a, b, c, d, e, f$ are on the surface of the sphere whose center is $g$. If, therefore, the center $g$ is joined with any of these six points, the lines joining it to them will be equal to one another, since they are from the center of the sphere to the surface. Since, however, from the corollary <note>original: "conel.", an abbreviation for *corollarium*.</note> of the 15th proposition of the thirteenth book, the diameter of the sphere is in power double the side of this body <note>This means the square of the diameter is twice the square of the side of the octahedron.</note>, it will be from the fourth of the second book that the side of this body will be in power double the radius of the sphere. Therefore the square of $e.f$ is double the square of $c.g$, and therefore equal to the two squares of the two lines $c.g$ and $g.f$. And so by the penultimate proposition of the first book <note>The Pythagorean Theorem (Book I, Proposition 47).</note>, angle $c.g.f$ is a right angle. By the same reason [it is proven for] any of the triangles $f.g.d...$

### Proposition 17.

If a sphere circumscribes a pyramid of four triangular and equilateral bases <note>A tetrahedron.</note>, the ratio of the square <note>original: "tetragoni"</note> contained by a line <term>potentialiter</term> <note>A Latin mathematical term meaning "in power," referring to the side of a square whose area is being discussed.</note> in a <term>sesquitertia</term> <note>A ratio of 4:3 (one and one-third).</note> ratio to the <term>dodrans</term> <note>A term meaning three-quarters (3/4).</note> of the side of the pyramid itself, and by a line in a ratio of <term>superquinquepartient-vicesimas-septimas</term> <note>A complex fractional ratio meaning 1 and 5/27 (or 32/27).</note> of that same three-quarters, to the square of the diameter of the sphere, is as the ratio of the body of the pyramid itself to the body of eight triangular and equilateral bases <note>An octahedron.</note>, when both are circumscribed by the same sphere.

Let there be a sphere whose diameter is $a.b$ and center $h$, circumscribing a pyramid of four triangular and equilateral bases $a.c.d$, and let the body of eight triangular and equilateral bases be $e$. Let the line $l.m$ be <term>potentialiter</term> in a <term>sesquitertia</term> ratio to the <term>dodrans</term> (three-quarters) of the line $a.c$ (which is the side of the pyramid), and let line $n.m$ contain the aforementioned three-quarters and five-twenty-sevenths of itself. Let $p$ be the square of the diameter $a.b$. I say, therefore, that the ratio of the pyramid $a.c.d$ to the octahedron $e$ is as the ratio of the surface of $l.m$ by $m.n$ to the square $p$. For let us imagine the solid angle $a$ to be the apex of the pyramid, and the base of the pyramid (of which one side is $d.c$) to cut the diameter of the sphere at point $f$. As is manifest from the reasoning of the 13th proposition of the thirteenth book, $a.f$ will be double $f.b$; and since $a.b$ is also double $h.b$, it follows from Proposition 19 of the fifth book that $b.f$ is double $h.f$. Therefore, $a.f$ is quadruple $f.b$. Let us therefore imagine a surface cutting the pyramid $a.c.d$ through the center of the sphere and parallel to its base. Let line $g.k$ be the common section of this surface and the triangle $a.c.d$. From Proposition 17 of the eleventh book, the ratio of $c.a$ to $a.g$ will be as $f.a$ to $a.b$. Therefore, $c.a$ is to $a.g$ as 4 is to 3; for such is the case from the inverse proportion of $f.a$ to $a.b$. It is also established from the second part of Proposition 29 of the first book, and Propositions 16 and 10 of the eleventh, and the first part of the second proposition of the sixth, and the definition of similar surfaces and similar bodies, that the pyramid $a.g.k$ is similar to the pyramid $a.c.d$. Therefore, from Proposition 8 of the twelfth book, the ratio of pyramid $a.c.d$ to pyramid $a.g.k$ is as the triple ratio <note>The ratio of the cubes.</note> of $c.a$ to $a.g$; that is, as 4 to 3 tripled. It is established from the second proposition of the eighth book that the ratio of 4 to 3 tripled is as 64 to 27. Therefore, the ratio of pyramid $a.c.d$ to pyramid $a.g.k$ is as 64 to 27. Let there be made an equilateral triangle $q.r.f$ from a line equal to $a.g$, which is established to be three-quarters of line $a.c$, and let line $q.t$ be produced perpendicular to $r.f$. From the 11th proposition of this book, line $q.t$ will be <term>potentialiter</term> in a <term>sesquitertia</term> ratio to line $q.r$, and therefore equal to $l.m$. Let there also be added to line $r.f$ the line $f.x$, such that the ratio of $r.x$ to $r.f$ is as 64 to 27, and let it be divided...

Since all lateral pyramids of equal height are proportional to their bases, as demonstrated in the 6th proposition of the twelfth book, the ratio of pyramid $a.g.k$ to each of those parts into which the octahedron $e$ is divided is as its base is to their bases. Therefore, by the 24th proposition of the fifth book, the ratio of pyramid $a.g.k$ to the whole octahedron $e$ is as its base—which is established to be equal to triangle $q.r.f$—is to the bases of both pyramids into which $c$ is divided, taken together. These bases are established to be equal to the square of the diameter of the sphere by the preceding demonstration, namely $p$. Since, therefore, the ratio of pyramid $a.c.d$ to pyramid $a.g.k$ is as the triangle or rectangle $l.n$ to triangle $q.r.f$, namely 64 to 27, and the ratio of pyramid $a.g.k$ to the octahedron $e$ is as triangle $q.r.f$ to square $p$, it follows by equal proportionality that the ratio of pyramid $a.c.d$ to the octahedron $e$ is as the rectangle $l.n$ to the square $p$. And this was that which was to be demonstrated. <note>original: "hoc erat demonstrandum"</note>

¶ From the preceding, it is therefore manifest that the perpendicular line coming from the center of a sphere—which circumscribes a pyramid <note>A regular tetrahedron.</note> of four triangular and equilateral bases—to any base of that pyramid is equal to one-sixth part of the diameter of the sphere.

¶ Since all the triangles surrounding the pyramid are similar and equal, the circles circumscribing them will also be equal. Therefore, the perpendiculars from the center of the sphere to these circles at their centers will also be equal. Moreover, the perpendiculars falling to the circles are the perpendiculars to the bases of the pyramid; thus, the perpendiculars to the bases are equal to one another. Furthermore, the line $b.f$ is perpendicular to the base of the pyramid $a.c.d$. Since it is established from what was said before that $b.f$ is a sixth part of the diameter $a.b$, it remains true as concluded by the corollary. This may be demonstrated another way, provided the following antecedent is first established by firm reason:

¶ In every equilateral triangle, the line descending from one of its angles perpendicularly above the base is triple the length of the perpendicular drawn from the center of the circumscribing circle to any side of the triangle.

¶ For let triangle $a.b.c$ be equilateral, and let $d$ be the center of the circle circumscribing it, from which lines are drawn to each angle; these lines are manifest to be equal, as they are from the center of the circle to the circumference. Let the three points $a, b, c$ be on the circumference of the circle circumscribing the triangle. Let $a.d$ be extended continuously and straight until it meets side $b.c$ at point $e$. It is established from the eighth proposition of the first book that angle $a.d.b$ is equal to angle $a.d.c$, and therefore from the 13th proposition of the first book...

<note>Three geometric diagrams are placed in the left margin:

Angle $b.d.e$ is equal to angle $c.d.e$; wherefore, by the fourth proposition of the first book, line $b.e$ is equal to line $e.c$. And the angles which are at point $e$ <note>The OCR reads 'c', but the geometric context requires point 'e' at the base of the altitude.</note> are right angles; thus $d.e$ is perpendicular to $b.c$, originating from the center of the circle circumscribing the triangle $a.b.c$. Furthermore, $a.e$ is also perpendicular to $b.c$, originating from one of the angles of the aforementioned triangle. I say, therefore, that $a.e$ is triple the length of $e.d$. For it is established that the rectangle formed by $d.e$ and $e.b$ is equal to triangle $b.d.c$; likewise, the rectangle formed by $a.e$ and $e.b$ is equal to triangle $a.b.c$. Since triangle $a.b.c$ is triple the size of triangle $d.b.c$, the rectangle formed by $a.e$ and $e.b$ will be triple the rectangle formed by $d.e$ and $e.b$. Since, according to the first proposition of the sixth book, the ratio of the rectangle of $a.e$ and $e.b$ to the rectangle of $d.e$ and $e.b$ is the same as the ratio of $a.e$ to $e.d$, it follows that $a.e$ is triple $e.d$, just as was proposed.

¶ It is therefore necessary that a perpendicular falling from any angle of an equilateral triangle onto the opposite side must pass through the center of the circle circumscribing that triangle.

¶ Now, let us fulfill what we promised. To this end, let us imagine a pyramid <note>A tetrahedron.</note> with four equilateral triangular bases, one of which is triangle $a.b.c$. This pyramid is inscribed in a sphere whose center is $d$. Let the line $d.e$ be drawn perpendicular to the surface of triangle $a.b.c$, which necessarily falls upon the center of the circle circumscribing said triangle. I say, therefore, that line $d.e$ is one-sixth part of the diameter of the sphere circumscribing the proposed pyramid. For I shall draw the line $d.c$ and the line $c.f$ perpendicular to line $a.b$. From the previous corollary, it is established that $c.f$ passes through point $e$ and, from the preceding premise, is triple the length of $e.f$. It is also established from the fourth proposition of the second book that if the square of the diameter of the sphere (whose center is $d$) is 36, then the square of the semi-diameter $d.c$ is 9. From the corollary of the 13th proposition of the thirteenth book, the square of $b.c$ is 24, and by the 11th proposition of this book, the square of $c.f$ is 18. By the preceding premise, the square of $c.e$ is 8. Because, by the penultimate proposition of the first book <note>The Pythagorean Theorem.</note>, the square of $d.c$ is equal to the squares of the two lines $d.e$ and $e.c$, and the square of $d.c$ is 9 and the square of $c.e$ is 8 (relative to the diameter's square being 36), there remains 1 for the square of $d.e$. Thus, line $e.d$ is 1 unit while the diameter of the sphere is 6 units, which was to be proven. By the same type of demonstration, it will be shown to us that the semi-diameter of a sphere circumscribing a body of eight equilateral triangular bases <note>An octahedron.</note> is triple in power <note><term>In power</term>: A term used to describe the relationship between the squares of lines. If a line is "triple in power" to another, its square is three times the square of the other.</note> to the perpendicular descending from the center of the circumscribing sphere to any of its bases. Indeed, it is established, as was said before, that since all the bases of this body are equal and similar, the circles circumscribing them will be equal; therefore, the perpendiculars falling from the center of the sphere to the centers of those circles will be equal to one another. And since the perpendiculars to the circles of the bases are also perpendicular to the bases themselves, it follows that the perpendiculars from the center of the sphere to each individual base are equal to one another. If, therefore, what we say is proven regarding the perpendicular to one of its bases, the proposition is verified. Let triangle $a.b.c$ be, as before, one of the bases of the octahedron circumscribed by a sphere with center $d$, and let the rest be as before. Since, by the 15th corollary of the thirteenth book, the diameter of the sphere is potentially double <note>The square of the diameter is twice the square of the side.</note> the side of the octahedron, it follows that the side of the octahedron is potentially double the semi-diameter of the sphere. Therefore, when the square of line $b.c$ is 12, the square of line $d.c$ (which is the semi-diameter of the sphere) will be 6. From the 11th proposition of this book, when the square of $b.c$ is 12, the square of $c.f$ is 9. And from the preceding premise, the square of $c.e$ is 4. Thus, since the square of $d.c$ (the semi-diameter) is 6 and the square of $c.e$ is 4, and because by the penultimate proposition of the first book the square of $d.c$ is equal to the squares of the two lines $c.e$ and $e.d$, it follows that the square of $e.d$ is 2, just as the square of $d.c$ is 6. Therefore, what we stated is established.

# XV

<note>A perspective line drawing depicts a cube oriented with one vertical edge in the foreground. The vertices are labeled: 'd' at the top; 'a' and 'c' at the upper corners; 'b' and 'h' near the center; and 'e', 'f', and 'g' at the bottom corners. Straight lines drawn across the faces represent diagonals that define an inscribed tetrahedron—a pyramid with four triangular faces.</note>

Twice the square described by the diameter of a sphere circumscribing a cube is equal to all the surfaces of that same cube taken together. Furthermore, it is proven by necessity that the perpendicular line drawn from the center of the sphere to any of the surfaces of the cube is equal to half of the side of the same cube.

It is manifest from the corollary to the 14th proposition of the thirteenth book that the diameter of a sphere enclosing a cube is triple in power <note>original: "tripla est in potentia"; this geometric term means that the square of the diameter is three times the square of the cube's side</note> to the side of the cube. Therefore, since the square of the diameter of the sphere is triple the square of the side of the cube, twice the square of the sphere's diameter is equal to six times the square of the side of the cube. Now, all the surfaces of a cube are six squares produced by the side of the cube multiplied by itself. Thus, twice the square of the diameter of the sphere is equal to all the surfaces of the cube. The first part of the proposition is therefore established. The second part you may easily prove from the 18th, 19th, and 40th propositions of the eleventh book.

From these things, it necessarily follows that the solidity <note>meaning the volume</note> of the cube is produced from half the side of the cube multiplied by two-thirds <note>original: "bisse"</note> of the square produced from the diameter of the sphere encompassing the cube.

**Here ends the fourteenth book. Here begins the fifteenth book.**

### Proposition 1.

**Within a given cube, to describe a body having four triangular bases of equal sides.** <note>This "body" is a regular tetrahedron.</note>

Let there be a cube whose base is the square *a.b.c.d*, and its topmost surface the square *e.f.g.h*. It is convenient to construct it by this method: let a perpendicular be raised from each angle of a square base (described according to any line from the 45th proposition of the first book) according to the measure of the side of that square, following the 12th proposition of the eleventh book. By the 6th proposition of the eleventh book, these perpendiculars are established as being parallel to one another. Let each pair of these be joined at the top by a line parallel to the side of the base square. Thus, it is established that a cube is composed; for its four lateral surfaces are squares according to the 33rd and 34th propositions of the first book and the definition of a square. Concerning the top surface, it is also manifest that it is a square from the 10th (or rather the 24th) proposition of the eleventh book and by the common notion that things equal to the same thing are equal to each other, and by the definition of a square.

If, therefore, one wishes to inscribe in this cube a body of four equilateral triangular bases: in the base and in the top surface, let two diagonals be drawn, of which one connects the two bottom ends of two perpendiculars, and the other connects the top ends of the other two. You will understand these to be *a.c* and *b.f*. Then, from the two points *b* and *f* which terminate the diameter of the top surface, let down two pairs of diagonals "hypotenuse-wise" <note>original: "ypothemisaliter"; meaning to draw them as diagonals across the side faces</note> which divide the lateral surfaces. You will imagine these to be from *b*, namely *b.a* and *b.c*; and from *f*, namely *f.a* and *f.c*. I have declined to draw these diagonals in this flat figure lest a multitude of lines confuse the understanding. If, therefore, you complete this figure as is proper, either in fact or in the mind, you will see that from the six diagonal lines dividing the six surfaces of the cube, a pyramid of four triangular bases <note>a tetrahedron</note> is perfected. By definition, it is established that this is inscribed in the given cube. It is also clear that the bases of this pyramid are equilateral because, by the 4th proposition of the first book, all six of these diagonals are equal to one another.

# BOOK XV

<note>A geometric diagram illustrates a tetrahedron—a pyramid with four triangular faces—labeled with vertices 'a', 'b', and 'c' at the base and 'e' at the apex. A central point 'd' is positioned in the middle of the base triangle, which is enclosed by a circle. Internal lines and points 'f', 'g', 'h', 'k', 'l', and 'm' represent the midpoints of the pyramid's edges. When connected, these points define an octahedron (a solid with eight triangular faces) perfectly inscribed within the larger pyramid.</note>

->**Within a given solid having four triangular and equilateral bases, to distinguish a solid of eight triangular bases of equal sides.**<-

If one desires to inscribe an octahedron <note>original: "octoedron"</note> within a pyramid of four triangular and equilateral bases, it is first necessary to construct the pyramid itself, which is composed by a certain method in this manner. Let an equilateral triangle <note>original: "trigonus equilaterus"</note> be established according to the length of any line, which shall be 'a.b.c.', around which a circle is circumscribed about center 'd'. Let 'd.e.' rise perpendicular to the surface of the triangle according to the 12th proposition of the eleventh book. Let this line be double in power <note>original: "dupla esse in potencia"; a geometric term meaning the square of the line 'd.e.' is twice the square of the circle's radius</note> to the radius of the circle circumscribing triangle 'a.b.c.'. From point 'e', let three hypotenuses <note>original: "ypothemise"; here referring to the slanted edges of the pyramid</note> fall upon the three points 'a', 'b', and 'c'. Thus the pyramid of four triangular and equilateral bases is completed.

Now, draw the lines 'd.a.', 'd.b.', and 'd.c.'. Since the angles which line 'e.d.' makes with each of the lines 'd.a.', 'd.b.', and 'd.c.' are right angles by the definition of a perpendicular to a surface, and since the square of line 'e.d.' is by hypothesis double the square of the radius of circle 'a.b.c.', it follows from the second-to-last proposition of the first book <note>The Pythagorean Theorem, Book I, Prop. 47</note> that the square of each of the three hypotenuse lines 'e.a.', 'e.b.', and 'e.c.' is triple the square of the radius of circle 'a.b.c.'. Furthermore, from the 8th proposition of the thirteenth book, the square of each of the three sides of triangle 'a.b.c.' is also triple the square of the radius of the same circle. Therefore, all sides of the established pyramid are equal to one another, which is why it is of equilateral bases.

Since we then wish to include an octahedron within it, we shall divide each of its six edges into two equal halves. We will connect the midpoint of each edge with the midpoints of all the remaining edges with which it shares a surface angle. For example, I will divide the sides of the base at points 'f', 'g', and 'h', and the hypotenuses falling from 'e' at points 'k', 'l', and 'm'. I will connect point 'f' with points 'g', 'h', 'k', and 'l'; and point 'm' with those same 'g', 'h', 'k', and 'l'; and 'g' with 'h' and 'l'; and 'k' with 'h' and 'l'. Behold! The solid of eight triangular faces is now completed, contained by these twelve lines joining the midpoints of the edges of the constructed pyramid. It is manifest from the 4th proposition of the first book—repeated as often as necessary—that these eight faces are equilateral. The solid itself is inscribed within the established pyramid according to the <gloss>definition</gloss> <note>abbreviated in original as "dione"</note>, just as we were ordered to perform.

### Proposition 3.

**To construct a figure of eight equal triangular faces within an assigned cube; we intend to inscribe an octahedron in a cube.**

How a cube should be composed was sufficiently stated in the first proposition of this book. Therefore, once the cube is constructed, let a pyramid of four triangular and equal sides be designated within it according to the first proposition. Within that pyramid, let an octahedron be distinguished according to the preceding proposition. Once this is done, what we desired will be accomplished simultaneously. For it is established by the reasoning of the first proposition that all sides of the inscribed pyramid are the diagonals of the faces of the cube. By the reasoning of the preceding proposition, it is clear that all the vertices of the octahedron distinguished in this pyramid are on the edges of the pyramid itself. Therefore, it is manifest that all the angular points of this octahedron are on the faces of the assigned cube. Thus, according to the <gloss>definition</gloss> <note>abbreviated in original as "dione"</note>, we have the proposition.

Alternatively, the same can be done by finding the centers of all the faces of the cube, just as in the 9th proposition of the fourth book. From the center of the top surface, drop four hypotenuses to the centers of the four lateral surfaces; and from the center of the bottom surface, raise four other hypotenuses to the centers of those same lateral surfaces. Also, connect the centers of the four lateral surfaces with four straight lines; namely, in such a way that the centers of those faces which intersect each other are connected...

For instance, join the center of the front face with the center of the right and with the center of the left; likewise, join the center of the final face <note>likely the back face</note> with these same centers—that is, with the center of the right and the center of the left. You thus have a solid of eight triangular bases <note>an octahedron</note> formed by these twelve lines which connect the centers of the cube's surfaces. Therefore, those twelve lines connecting the centers of the cube's surfaces, and the angles contained by these lines meeting in pairs at the midpoints of the cube's edges, are subtended <note>stretched underneath or opposite an angle</note>; they will be equal to one another according to the fourth proposition of the first book, or even, if you prefer, according to the penultimate proposition of the first book <note>referring to the Pythagorean Theorem, 1.47</note>. Therefore, a solid of eight triangular and equilateral bases has been designated within the proposed cube, which is what was to be done, etc.

->**Proposition 4**<-

# To figure a cube within a given solid of eight triangular and equilateral bases.

Do not doubt that you shall construct the solid of eight triangular and equilateral bases <note>the octahedron</note> by a certain doctrine in this manner: with any straight line erected orthogonally <note>at a right angle</note> upward upon some plane, divide it into equal parts, and from its midpoint draw out two perpendicular lines which together form a single line. These two lines intersecting each other—namely, the first which is erected orthogonally upon the placed plane, and the other which intersects it orthogonally at its midpoint—are situated in the same surface according to the first part of the second proposition of the eleventh book. Therefore, upon the surface in which they are situated, at their common point of intersection, erect a perpendicular as the 12th proposition of the eleventh book teaches. Make this line penetrate that same surface on both sides, and set all six segments of these three lines to be equal from the point where they intersect. For in this way, each will divide the others equally and orthogonally. Thus, since there are three lines, any two of them will contain the venerable sign of the health-giving cross <note>original: "salutifere crucis venerandū signū"; a religious metaphor for the three-dimensional XYZ coordinate axes meeting at right angles</note> at right angles. From the highest point of the line erected upon the plane, let down four hypotenuses <note>term: <term>ypothemisa</term> — a Latinized Greek term for the slanted edges or "hypotenuses" of the solid's faces</note> to the extremities of the two lines intersecting it. Then, from the lowest point of that same erected line, raise four other hypotenuses to the same extremities of the two intersecting lines. Finally, connect the extremities of these hypotenuses with four straight lines forming a square. For these twelve lines—namely, the four hypotenuses descending from the highest point of the erected perpendicular, the four raised upward from its lowest point, and the remaining four lines connecting the extremities of these hypotenuses—will be equal to one another, as proven by the penultimate proposition of the first book, without repeating the point of joining many times. Wherefore it is established that the solid bounded by these is contained by eight triangular and equilateral bases. If it then pleases you to inscribe a cube within this solid, labor to find the centers of the eight triangles surrounding it according to the fifth proposition of the fourth book. Once found, connect them with twelve lines by this law: that the center of each of these triangles be joined by a straight line to the center of each of the three triangles bordering its sides. It is not suitable to depict a figure of this thing in a plane <note>The author notes the difficulty of drawing a 3D cube-within-an-octahedron on 2D paper</note>; therefore, it remains for you to conceive in your mind what is said, and, if you please, complete it in actual practice and work.

For you will see that the centers of these triangles, positioned in an orderly fashion, are connected by twelve lines to contain a cube. It remains for you to demonstrate that it is enclosed by equilateral and rectangular surfaces. For it will not be a cube unless all its surfaces are squares. Therefore, from any angle of the triangular surfaces of the <term>octahedron<note>original: "octocedri"; a solid with eight triangular faces.</note></term>, draw a perpendicular to the side opposite that angle. It is established from the 11th proposition of the fourteenth book that these perpendiculars are equal to one another and divide the sides on which they stand perpendicularly into equal parts. Thus, it is clear that these perpendiculars meet in pairs at the same point on the side they stand upon. It is also clear from those things demonstrated in the 17th proposition of the fourteenth book that they pass through the centers of the triangles. Therefore, they pass through the extremities of the sides of the enclosed body, and those portions intercepted between the centers of the triangles and their sides are shown to be equal from the same demonstrations. It is also evident from the 8th proposition of the first book that the angles contained by these perpendiculars meeting in pairs are equal. And because these perpendiculars and their portions intercepted between the centers and the sides surround the same angles, the angles contained in pairs by the lines falling perpendicularly from the centers of the triangles to the sides will also be equal to one another. Since the sides of that body we are discussing <note>the inscribed cube</note> subtend these angles, it follows from the frequently used fourth proposition of the first book that the enclosed body is equilateral and also rectangular. For if you draw diagonals in each surface, you will prove from the fourth of the first that all these diagonals are equal to one another by means of the angles contained by the two perpendiculars passing through the extremities of those diagonals, provided you have first proved these angles to be equal to one another from the 8th of the first. Since, therefore, the diameters <note>here meaning diagonals</note> of the square bases of this body are equal to one another, it is necessary from the frequently repeated 8th of the first that the sides of these same bases are equal, and that the square bases themselves are equiangular. Moreover, from the 32nd of the first, all the angles of each are equal to four right angles. It follows that they are rectangular; thus, by the definition of a square, they are squares. Therefore, it is manifest that the inscribed body is a cube, just as we intended.

->Proposition 5<-

# To inscribe a <term>pyramid<note>Specifically a tetrahedron; a solid with four triangular faces.</note></term> of four triangular and equilateral bases within an assigned body of eight triangular and equilateral bases <note>an octahedron</note>.

Within the assigned body of eight bases, inscribe a cube according to the instructions given previously, and within the inscribed cube, inscribe a pyramid as the first proposition teaches. Since the angles of this pyramid are also the angles of the cube, as is manifest from the demonstration of the first proposition, and all angles of the cube are on the surfaces of the assigned octahedron according to the previous proposition, all the angles of this pyramid will also be on the surfaces of the body of eight bases when we are commanded to inscribe it. Therefore, by definition, it is manifest that we have done what was sought.

XV

in the previously mentioned centers of all the triangles bounding the entire <term>icosahedron<note>original: "ycocedron"; a regular solid with 20 triangular faces.</note></term>, connect them with 30 straight lines in such a way that you join the center of each one with the centers of all those surrounding it with which it shares a side. When you have done this, you will see that from those 30 lines, twelve pentagons are formed, positioned opposite the 12 <term>solid angles<note>That is, the vertices of the icosahedron.</note></term> of the given icosahedron. You will prove these pentagons to be equilateral just as you did in the previous proposition regarding the bases of the cube. For it is necessary that the centers of any two triangles sharing the same side are separated by the same distance. It remains for you to reason out that they are also equiangular. 

It is evident from the reasoning in the 16th proposition of <term>the thirteenth book<note>Euclid's Book XIII focuses on the construction of the five regular "Platonic" solids.</note></term> that the given body of twenty bases can be circumscribed by the same sphere whose diameter is like the diameter of this body—namely, the lines which connect two of its opposite angles. If, therefore, this diameter is cut through the middle, the point of section will be the center of the sphere circumscribing it. Thus, let perpendiculars be drawn from that center to the surfaces of all the pentagons (following the 11th proposition of the eleventh book), and from the point where they meet each pentagon, draw straight lines to each of its angles. Then, connect the center of the sphere with each of the angles of those pentagons. 

Proceed then to prove they are equiangular in this way: Since all the circles circumscribing the triangles of the icosahedron are equal, all the perpendiculars coming from the center of the sphere to them and falling into their centers will be equal. Therefore, all the lines coming from the center of the sphere to the angles of any pentagon are equal. For the angles of the pentagons are the centers of the circles circumscribing the triangles of the icosahedron. Therefore, by hypothesis and from <term>the penultimate proposition of the first book<note>original: "ex penultima primi"; referring to the Pythagorean Theorem (Book I, Proposition 47).</note></term>, using the same type of argument by which we reasoned above in the 14th proposition, and because when a plane surface cuts a sphere not through its center, the resulting circumference contains a circle, it is necessary that the five lines coming from the meeting point of the perpendicular (drawn from the center of the sphere to the surfaces of all the pentagons) to the five angles of each pentagon are equal to one another. Therefore, a circle can be circumscribed around all these twelve pentagons. Since they are equilateral, you may conclude they are also equiangular, which was what was to be shown.

### Proposition 7.

-> Within a given body of twelve equilateral and <-
-> equiangular pentagonal bases, to construct a body of twenty <-
-> equilateral triangular bases: <-

Seek how one ought to compose a body of twelve equilateral and equiangular pentagonal bases from the 17th proposition of the thirteenth book. But learn here how a body of twenty triangular and equilateral bases is suited to be inscribed within it. This is done by finding the centers of its pentagons, as in the 14th proposition of the fourth book, and connecting them to one another with 30 lines by this rule: the center of each pentagon is joined to the center of every pentagon sharing a side with it, such that the center of each pentagon is connected to the centers of the five pentagons bounding or surrounding it. 

When you have done this, twenty triangles will present themselves, formed by these 30 lines connecting the centers of the pentagons. And these twenty triangles will be opposite the twenty solid angles of the <term>dodecahedron<note>original: "duodecedri"; a regular solid with 12 pentagonal faces.</note></term> itself, enclosing a body of twenty triangular bases which we shall demonstrate to be equilateral. The 12 solid angles of this body of 20 bases will be located at the centers of the 12 pentagons bounding the given dodecahedron. Prove that these 20 triangles are equilateral thus: draw perpendiculars from the centers of the pentagons to the sides, and all these perpendiculars will be equal. Therefore, you will prove them two by two from...
