BOOK XV

by the <term>eighth [proposition] of the first [book]<note>Euclid’s Elements, Book I, Proposition 8: The "Side-Side-Side" (SSS) congruence theorem for triangles.</note></term> they contain equal angles; and because the lines connecting the centers of the pentagons subtend <note>subtend: to be opposite to an angle in a geometric figure</note> those angles contained by pairs of perpendiculars: since all the perpendiculars are equal, it follows from the <term>fourth [proposition] of the first [book]<note>Book I, Proposition 4: The "Side-Angle-Side" (SAS) congruence theorem.</note></term> that all the lines connecting the centers of the pentagons are equal, which is what was proposed. 

To understand that the pairs of perpendiculars contain equal angles and are all equal to one another, collect the reasoning as follows: From the fifth and 26th [propositions] of the first [book], it is established that each of these perpendiculars divides the sides of the pentagons upon which they fall into two equal parts. They are equal to each other when lines are drawn from the centers of the pentagons to each of their angles. Therefore, pairs of perpendiculars falling upon the same side will meet at the same point of that side, because each divides that side—which is common to the two pentagons from whose centers they originate—into equal parts. 

Therefore, extend these pairs of perpendiculars through the centers of the pentagons to the angles opposite the common side where they meet. Subtend two lines to those same angles; from the demonstration of the 17th [proposition] of the <term>thirteenth [book]<note>Book XIII, Proposition 17: Describes the construction of a dodecahedron and its relationship to a circumscribing sphere and an internal cube.</note></term>, it is manifest that these lines are like the side of a <term>cube<note>original: "cubi"</note></term> circumscribable by the same sphere as the proposed <term>dodecahedron<note>original: "duodecedro"</note></term>. For this reason, it is clear that they are equal, because all sides of a cube are equal. It is also clear from the ninth [proposition] of the eleventh [book] that they are parallel, because both are parallel to the common side where the pairs of perpendiculars meet. 

Furthermore, it is established that these same lines are divided into equal parts by these perpendiculars. Thus, by the 33rd [proposition] of the first [book], all lines connecting the points where the pairs of perpendiculars meet upon these lines (which we said would be like the sides of a cube) are equal to one another. For they are all like the side of a cube. Therefore, by the eighth [proposition] of the first [book], the angles contained by the pairs of perpendiculars are equal. Wherefore, by the fourth [proposition] of the same book, the lines connecting the centers of the pentagons are also equal to each other. Thus, a body of twenty triangular bases and equal sides <note>An icosahedron.</note> has been inscribed in the proposed dodecahedron, just as we were commanded.

### Proposition 8.

<note>A decorative woodcut initial 'S' featuring a floral and leaf pattern.</note> **G**iven a proposed solid of twelve pentagonal and equilateral bases, to distinguish a cube within it.

<note>A decorative woodcut initial 'C' with scrollwork and foliage.</note> **S**ince a dodecahedron is constructed upon the edges of a cube, as is evident from the 17th [proposition] of the thirteenth [book], once the dodecahedron is built, it is fitting for a cube to be inscribed within it. For since there are twelve pentagons, if you subtend one <term>chord<note>A straight line segment whose endpoints both lie on a circular arc or, in this case, the face of a polygon.</note></term> to one angle of each pentagon—just as you see the figure of the cube requires—you will complete the six equilateral and right-angled surfaces of a cube from those twelve chords, encompassing the body. 

That these surfaces are equilateral is established by the fourth [proposition] of the first [book]. That they are right-angled is shown by the same type of argument by which we demonstrated in the sixth [proposition] of this book that the bases of a dodecahedron inscribed in a given <term>icosahedron<note>original: "ycocedro"</note></term> are equiangular. Indeed, it is clear from the 17th [proposition] of the thirteenth [book] that the proposed dodecahedron can be inscribed in a sphere. From the center of that sphere, draw perpendiculars to all the quadrilateral surfaces (as the 11th [proposition] of the eleventh [book] teaches), and from the point of intersection, direct straight lines to the individual angles of those quadrilateral surfaces. 

Then, join those same angles of the quadrilateral surfaces with the center of the sphere. These lines connecting the center of the sphere with the angles of the quadrilateral surfaces will be the radii of the sphere. Because the squares of the perpendiculars are taken away from the squares of these radii, there remain (by the penultimate [proposition] of the first [book] <note>Pythagoras' Theorem, Book I, Prop 47.</note>) the squares of the lines connecting the point of intersection of the perpendiculars with the angles of the quadrilateral surfaces. Therefore, it is necessary that circles can be circumscribed around all these quadrilateral surfaces.

and therefore it is necessary that they be equiangular since they are equilateral. And because, from the 32nd <term>proposition</term> of the first [book] <note>Book I, Proposition 32: The sum of the interior angles of a triangle is two right angles, and for any polygon, it is possible to determine the total sum of angles.</note>, the angles of each of them taken together are equal to four right angles, it follows that they are rectangular <note>original: "rectangulas"</note>; thus nothing is lacking in the inscribed body regarding the definition of a cube.

### Proposition 9

<note>A decorative woodcut initial D features floral motifs and foliage within a square border.</note>

**G**iven a dodecahedron <note>original: "duodecedro"</note>, finally, to include an octahedron <note>original: "octocedron"</note> within it.
¶ Having constructed the dodecahedron as in the 17th [proposition of the thirteenth book] and according to the sixteen sides of its surfaces—namely those which join the <term>perpendiculars</term> <note>original: "cathecos"</note> erected over the six lines cutting the opposite sides of the surfaces of the cube into equal parts as if they were <unclear>exhausted</unclear>—divide them into equal parts: and these, joined two by two to each other, continue through three lines which will cut each other through the middle point of the cube's diameter into equal parts, according to the 38th <note>OCR 48; likely referring to Book XI, Proposition 38 regarding the intersection of diagonals</note> [proposition] of the eleventh [book]. It will also be that two of them divide each other at right angles. If, therefore, you join the extremities of these three lines with 12 straight lines, there will be produced for you a body of eight triangular and equilateral bases <note>an octahedron</note>, according to the fourth [proposition] of the first [book], or if preferred, from the penultimate [proposition] of the first [book]: which is what was required to be shown.

### Proposition 10

<note>A decorative woodcut initial I features floral patterns and scrolling vines within a square border.</note>

**W**ithin an assigned dodecahedron, it still remains to distinguish a pyramid <note>pyramid: referring here to a regular tetrahedron</note> of four triangular and equilateral bases.
¶ Inscribe a cube in the assigned dodecahedron according to the eighth [proposition] of this [book], and in that cube, a pyramid according to the first [proposition]. Since, therefore, the angles of the pyramid are in the angles of the cube, as is clear from the reasoning of the first [proposition], and the angles of the cube are in the angles of the dodecahedron from the reasoning of the eighth [proposition]: the angles of the pyramid will also be in the angles of the dodecahedron. Thus, what we wished for is established.

### Proposition 11

<note>A decorative woodcut initial P with ornate foliage and a background of fine lines within a square border.</note>

**W**ith an icosahedron <note>original: "ycocedro"</note> proposed, to fashion a cube within it.
¶ A dodecahedron is inscribed in an icosahedron according to the sixth [proposition], and a cube in the dodecahedron according to the eighth; it is established, moreover, from the demonstration of the sixth that all the angles of the dodecahedron fall upon the center of the bases of the icosahedron, and the angles of the cube are in the angles of the dodecahedron: thus the angles of the cube are in the centers of the bases of the icosahedron. We have, therefore, what was proposed.

### Proposition 12

<note>A decorative woodcut initial I, similar in style to the previous ones, featuring a stylized floral design.</note>

**T**o a given icosahedron, it is required to inscribe a pyramid of four triangular and equilateral bases.
¶ If you inscribe a cube in the given icosahedron from the preceding [proposition], and you include a pyramid in that cube from the first [proposition], there will be no need to hesitate in satisfying the requirement of the icosahedron. It is necessary to know, however, that since there are five <term>regular bodies</term> <note>the Platonic solids: tetrahedron (pyramid), cube, octahedron, dodecahedron, and icosahedron</note> whose mutual inscription within one another is determined in this 15th book, if each one of them were inscribable in any other, 20 such inscriptions would occur. For as each of the five could contain the other four, four times five inscriptions, which is 20, would necessarily result. But in truth, only the octahedron is suitable to be inscribed in the pyramid. For there are no bases or angles or sides in a pyramid upon which the angles of a cube, or an icosahedron, or even a dodecahedron, could touch the extremities of that pyramid.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the inter-relationships between the five Platonic solids, specifically focusing on which bodies can be contained within others, and concludes the volume with Proposition 13 and the printer's colophon.</meta>

<margin>2</margin>
¶ The cube is also fit for the reception of the pyramid <note>In this context, Euclid refers to the tetrahedron as a "pyramid."</note> and the octahedron, just as the octahedron is fit for the reception of the pyramid and the cube alone, because of how they fit within one another. You shall place the 12 angles of the icosahedron, or the 20 angles of the dodecahedron, so that each falls upon the individual parts of the others. The icosahedron, however, although it can encompass the others with a suitable surrounding, cannot itself be the receptacle of the icosahedron alone. For the six angles of the octahedron regard each other in pairs by diametrical opposition, and the lines connecting them divide each other equally and orthogonally <note>original: "orthogonaliter," meaning at right angles.</note>. Therefore, they return those three-fold right angles of that glorious sign at the sight of which demons are terrified <note>The "glorious sign" likely refers to the Pythagorean pentagram or the geometric arrangement of axes within a sphere, which held mystical significance in the Middle Ages.</note>. Thus, neither the bases, nor the angles, nor the sides of the icosahedron can receive these under its own orientation, for you will not find in it six bases, six angles, or six sides containing themselves in this diametrical and orthogonal opposition. The dodecahedron, however, has denied a home to none of the others in its embrace; indeed, it exists as the receiver of all. For this reason, the ancient disciples of Plato <note>Referring to the Timaeus, where Plato associates the five solids with the elements.</note> appropriately assigned or have assigned the figure of the dodecahedron to the heavens, just as they assigned the form of the pyramid to fire, because it flies upward in a pyramidal shape. And they assigned the octahedron to the air. Indeed, just as air follows fire in the lightness of its motion, so the octahedron matches the form of the pyramid in its readiness for movement. They dictated the figure of twenty bases <note>The icosahedron.</note> for water; for since it, by the plurality of its bases, is more circular than the others within a sphere, it seemed to agree more with the motion of a fluid thing than a climbing one. Some indeed gave the figure of the cube to the earth; for what in a larger figure requires more violence for motion than a <term>tessera</term> <note>original: "theffera" (tessera), a square block or die.</note>? And among the elements, what is found more fixed and constant than the earth? If, therefore, out of the 20 inscriptions, you reject the 3 which the pyramid does not sustain, and the pairs from which the nature of the cube and octahedron are alien, and again the one which the figure of the icosahedron rejects, there will remain only 12 inscriptions: one for the pyramid, two for the cube and octahedron, three for the icosahedron, and four for the dodecahedron—about all of which I believe I have sufficiently argued elsewhere.

### Proposition 13

<note>A decorative woodcut initial F featuring white vine-work and floral patterns on a dark background within a square border.</note>

**H**aving constructed any of the five regular bodies, to inscribe a sphere within it.
¶ From the thirteenth book, it is therefore manifest that each of these five bodies can be inscribed in a sphere. Now, conversely, it will be established that a sphere can be inscribed in each of them. For from the center of the circumscribing sphere, let perpendiculars go out to all the bases of any one of them, which must necessarily fall within the circles circumscribing those bases. And since all the circles circumscribing them are equal, these perpendiculars will also be equal. Therefore, if you describe a circle around the center of the circumscribing sphere according to the quantity of one of those [perpendiculars], and lead its semicircle around until it returns to the place from which it began to move, because it must necessarily pass through the extremities of all the perpendiculars, you will prove from the 15th <term>corollary</term> <note>Referring to Book III of the Elements.</note> of the third [book] that the sphere described by the motion of this semicircle touches all the bases of the assigned body at the meeting points of the perpendiculars. For the sphere cannot touch more of the bases of the body than the rotated semicircle touched while it was moving. Therefore, it is clear that we have inscribed a sphere within the assigned body, just as was proposed.

¶ The work of the Elements of Euclid of Megara <note>Medieval tradition incorrectly identified Euclid the mathematician with Euclid of Megara, the philosopher.</note> on the art of geometry, in which also the commentaries of the most discerning Campanus <note>Campanus of Novara, whose 13th-century translation and commentary were used for this first printed edition.</note> conclude. Erhard Ratdolt of Augsburg, most skillful printer, printed [this] in Venice. In the year of salvation 1482, on the eighth day before the Calends of June [May 25th].

This is the first printed edition of Euclid’s *Elements*. The Latin translation was made about 1120 by Adelard (Aethelard) of Bath, an early English scholastic philosopher. It was based on the Arabic version of the work. However, it is probable that Adelard, who lived for a time in the Norman kingdom of Sicily and knew Greek, used also the Greek original. His translation was revised about 1260 by Campanus of Novara, a chaplain to Pope Urban IV, who, following the Greek text more closely, rendered the “demonstrations” clearer and more complete.

The first translation made directly from the Greek text was by Bartolomeo Zamberti, and was published in 1505 at Venice. Zamberti had the worst opinion of Campanus’s style and scientific observations; the first he described as “barbarous” and the latter he called “scarecrows, nightmares, and phantasies.” His own translation, in its turn, was severely criticised by the defenders of Campanus. The Greek original of the *Elements* was first printed in 1533.

The Library has several of the sixteenth-century editions of the work, among them the one published by Henri Étienne in 1516 in Paris, containing both Campanus’s and Zamberti’s versions. But of the greatest interest to us is the first English edition in the translation of Sir Henry Billingsley, printed in 1570 by John Daye. This monumental work of 464 leaves, with its hundreds of illustrations, is one of the finest products of the early English press.

The 1482 Venice edition of the *Elements* was the first important printed mathematical book. As the German printer pointed out in his dedicatory letter to the Doge, “although books by ancient and modern authors were published at Venice every day, little or nothing mathematical had appeared.” But the volume is remarkable also from a typographical <note>the art and technique of arranging type</note> point of view. The letters are well-cut and the printing is neat. Beautiful initials decorate almost every page and, placed on the wide margins, hundreds of diagrams illustrate the text. There has been a considerable controversy among bibliographers <note>scholars who study books as physical objects</note> about these diagrams. Ratdolt refers to them in his dedicatory letter: “After much labor I had discovered,” he wrote, “a method by which geometrical figures may be as easily reproduced as letters printed.” According to some, this means that Ratdolt cut his figures in soft metal instead of wood; that he used “clichés” <note>metal printing plates</note> and not woodcuts. The use of metal would also account for the perfection of his initials and border ornaments, in which he attained a delicacy of line unknown to any previous printer.

Ratdolt was born about 1443 at Augsburg, where he lived till 1474. His whereabouts during the next two years are unknown. He may have worked at Nuremberg with Regiomontanus <note>Johannes Müller von Königsberg, a famous Renaissance mathematician and astronomer</note>, who had a private press there, thus acquiring a taste for the publishing of mathematical books by the side of the great mathematician and astronomer. In 1476 he established himself at Venice, where some fifty German printers were already at work. For two years he was in partnership with two of his countrymen, Bernhard Maler and Peter Löslein, then continued alone till 1486. After these ten years at Venice he returned to his native city. Enjoying a high reputation as a craftsman and a prosperous business man, he worked steadily till his death in 1528.

There is no need of commenting here on Euclid or the *Elements*. Euclid lived in Alexandria, during the reign of the first Ptolemy. In the early editions of his work he is often called “of Megara” <note>original: "Megarensis"</note>, confusing him with another Euclid, a disciple of Socrates, who was born at Megara in Greece. Even to-day little is known about the life of the great Alexandrian mathematician. The *Elements*, on the other hand, is known to every schoolboy. The geometry, both plane and solid, that is taught in the secondary schools is nothing else but Euclid's work as he wrote it. The arrangement of the axioms, postulates, theorems, problems, and propositions in the modern text-books on geometry largely follows the work of the old Alexandrian.

It is difficult to determine now to what extent Euclid was a discoverer and to what extent a compiler. Geometrical knowledge in Egypt and in Greece was considerable before his time. Possibly, his main share in the work was the logical arrangement of the material and the clearer development of the proofs. But even if he was merely an editor, he deserves his fame. He succeeded in making geometry — within limits, of course — an attractive science.

Bought in April, 1916.
